FOREVER FREE AND OPEN
A CITIZEN'S CONDEMNATION OF CANADA

Raised by a citizen of the United States under the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence, and laid before the President and the Congress in exercise of the right "to petition the Government for a redress of grievances"

AGAINST Canada, heir to every treaty the Crown signed for British North America and to every breach of them. Our own Treaties in Force files Jay, Ghent, Rush–Bagot and the Convention of 1818 under one name: CANADA.

This condemnation falls on the Canadian state. Not on the Canadian people.

I. YOUR OWN SIGNATURE

The Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909. You will be judged by it. Article I: navigation of the boundary waters "shall forever continue free and open for the purposes of commerce" to both countries "equally," under laws "applying equally and without discrimination."
Rush–Bagot, 1817: the Lakes all but disarmed, by both of us, on faith.
Ghent, 1814: peace. The Convention of 1818: the 49th parallel.
Our rule, from 1823: "The American continents … are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers." To the colonies already standing, Monroe gave his word: "With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power we have not interfered and shall not interfere." That word was for colonies.

II. THE COUNTS

1. THE ROAD SOUTH, 1777
Your soil was the Crown's road into New York. "Burgoyne's plan called for him to lead a large force south from Canada and drive for Albany," while St. Leger was sent down the Mohawk "light in artillery and British troops and heavy in Indians and Loyalists."

2. THE POSTS, 1783–96
The peace of 1783 bound the Crown to leave our northern forts. It kept them. Jay's treaty won "a surrender of the northwestern posts (already agreed to in 1783)" and "ultimately granted Britain additional rights." We paid twice for the same forts.

3. THE RAISIN AND THE FORT, 1813
Of some 400 Americans caught in the rout at Frenchtown, about 220 were killed and 147 captured. "When the British departed, they left the Americans who were too wounded to walk in the homes of Frenchtown inhabitants," under "a small British detachment." The next morning warriors returned, "killing and scalping many of the remaining Americans." Our official estimates: "a dozen named individuals killed and up to 60 more who were probably killed in this manner." The Crown counted "about six." That December at Fort Niagara, "British soldiers bayoneted Americans as they were surrendering."

4. THE CAROLINE, 1837
"Canadian troops seized the Caroline in a New York port, killing one crewman in the process," and set her adrift toward the Falls. When one of them bragged of it in New York, London said he "had acted as a member [of] the British forces" and that it "would take responsibility for his actions." An American killed on American soil, and the Crown owned it.

5. THE BASE, 1864
While the Union bled, your soil was the rebels' base. The Crown's own Foreign Secretary, summing up our protest, wrote of "various acts of aggression from Canada, namely, the seizure and destruction of the Philo Parsons and Island Queen on the lakes, and the attack upon the town of St. Albans, in Vermont, by a party of twenty-five men, issuing from the British territory." Our Secretary of State wrote that the Crown's neutrality had failed, in its colonies above all, and would keep failing "so long as asylum is allowed there to active agents of the enemies of the United States," free to use British borders "as a base for felonious depredations against the citizens of the United States." Your judge freed the raiders anyway, on "whatever technical grounds may have been found for delivering from custody the St. Albans raiders." We had already given notice on the Lakes.

6. THE FISHERMEN, 1886
The Gloucester schooner David J. Adams was "still held in custody at Digby, Nova Scotia." The Ella M. Doughty, the City Point and the George W. Cushing were seized or detained too. "All of the vessels so seized or detained were vessels licensed for fishing under the laws of the United States," and "no other cases of such seizure or detention have occurred than those in the ports of the Dominion of Canada."

7. THE BOOZE, 1923
Our Secretary of State wrote of "the large amounts of intoxicating liquor that are smuggled into the United States from Canada." Your government's answer: "the export of liquor is not prohibited from Canada," and "there exists no provision in the customs laws or regulations which would warrant the refusal of clearance papers" to ships bound where it was banned. You cleared the cargoes anyway.

8. THE SMOKE, 1925–38
A smelter at Trail poisoned Washington State's valley. You paid "three hundred and fifty thousand dollars, United States currency," then "seventy-eight thousand dollars ($78,000)" more.

9. THE WARHEADS, 1963
Partners in NORAD, holding our launchers, yet "Canada has thus far not accepted any arrangements for warheads for BOMARCs and F–101B's which appear practical to us." Your Prime Minister, our State Department recorded, "beclouded the whole issue of nuclear weapons for Canadian forces with misleading references to Nassau."

10. THE ENERGY PROGRAM, 1980
The National Energy Program came down on American capital. Our envoy opened with "shock and disappointment." Your Finance Minister's answer: foreign ownership "could not be allowed to continue indefinitely."

11. THE SCREEN, 1984
You made American investors promise to buy Canadian. A GATT panel, on our complaint: "inconsistent with Article III:4."

12. THE MAGAZINES, 1997
You taxed split-run magazines out of your market. The WTO struck it on our complaint.

13. THE MILK, 1999–2003
You subsidized your milk exports past your promises, and lost. You rebuilt the scheme; the Appellate Body found government still controls "virtually every aspect of domestic milk supply and management." You lost again.

14. CLASS 7, 2016–17
Your farmers and processors built a milk class "to decrease imports of U.S. milk protein products into Canada." Under USMCA your government had to kill it.

15. THE QUOTAS, 2021–26
You sold us dairy access, then handed the quotas to your own processors. We won the panel. Over quota, American cheese pays "245 percent" and butter "298 percent."

16. THE LAW AGAINST BARGAINING, 2025
The first law of your new Parliament: "the Minister must not make any commitment on behalf of the Government of Canada, by international trade treaty or agreement," that would open your dairy, poultry or egg quotas or cut the tariff over them. You outlawed bargaining with us over dairy, poultry and eggs.

17. THE TAX, 2024–25
A 3 percent digital services tax, "retroactive to January 1, 2022." Halted the day before collection.

18. THE STREAMERS AND THE NEWS, 2023–25
You take "5 percent of their Canadian revenues" from American streamers, under rules that "may effectively exclude Canadian streaming services from the new obligations." Your regulator decides "who is a journalist."

19. THE COUNTER-TARIFFS, 2025
"25 per cent tariffs on $155 billion worth of imported goods" (C$): "orange juice, peanut butter, wine, spirits, beer, coffee," then our cars. Ontario surcharged the power it sends New York, Michigan and Minnesota, lifted it the next day, and put in writing that it "retains the ability to reinstate a surcharge at any time."

20. THE SHELVES, 2025–26
By the end of 2025, every provincial liquor board but Alberta's and Saskatchewan's had "ceased distributing U.S. alcohol beverages." In a year, your imports of American alcohol "decreased by about 81%, or $582 million."

21. THE BIDS, 2025
Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia moved "to exclude U.S. businesses from tenders," "from price penalties on bids from U.S. businesses to complete prohibitions." Then Buy Canadian.

22. THE CARS, 2025–26
"Canada imposes certain tariffs and quotas on cars imported to Canada from the U.S., but not on imports from other countries." In a year, your imports of our vehicles fell "approximately 22%, or $5.6 billion."

23. THE WALK-AWAY, 2026
"Canada walked away from a near-final trade deal with the United States this past summer," and from 8 September laid counter-tariffs "of 15, 25 and 50 per cent" on "$27.6 billion in imports from the U.S." (C$), by your own count.

24. THE OTHER DOOR, 2026
You opened your market to "up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles," at "6.1%." Bourbon came off your shelves; Beijing's cars came in.

25. THE PIRATES, 2025–26
Still on our Watch List: "Levels of online piracy remain very high in Canada." Your drug-price board "excludes the United States" from its basket.

III. CONVICTED ALREADY

Trail: you paid in 1935, and again in 1938. GATT: against you, 1984. The WTO: against you in 1997, 1999 and 2003. A USMCA panel: against you, 2021–22. The President, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930: on 20 July 2026, against "Canada's discriminatory treatment of American products"; on 8 September, again, because Canada had "maintained and in fact increased its discrimination against U.S. commerce with respect to U.S. alcoholic beverages."

IV. CONDEMNATION

A road south for an invading army. Forts held after a peace that gave them up. The wounded left behind, the surrendering bayoneted. A boat seized in our port. Raiders sheltered while the Union bled. Fishermen seized. Booze cleared for our shores. Smoke over Washington State. Warheads stalled. Capital driven out. Milk subsidized past your promises. Quotas rigged. A law against bargaining. A tax backdated. Bourbon pulled, Beijing's cars let in. Free and open, forever, you signed.

You were never our friend. You were a neighbor with a hand out and a door half shut. You took our defense, our market and our patience, and called it partnership every time.

From 1777 to 2026, by your own signature and the findings of the forums that ruled against you, the Canadian state stands condemned.

There is no reprieve.

V. THE TERMS I WOULD SET

I hold no office and set no terms. But had I the power, these would be the terms, set today, without reprieve.

UPON CANADA
I. Return the land: the 5,012 square miles of the Maine country Britain took in 1842; the whole of Vancouver Island, let go in 1846; the line of 1818; and every site we held or built and handed back, Redcliff, the Newfoundland bases and the Canadian stretch of the Alaska Highway among them. Yield it all by the consent of the people who live there, for governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed."
II. Cede the Arctic, forever: your Arctic economic zone; some 1.2 million square kilometers of continental shelf you laid before the United Nations' Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf on 23 May 2019; and the waters between your Arctic islands, the Northwest Passage among them, which you call internal and we call an international strait. Withdraw the submission, renounce every claim present and future, and never contest what the United States claims.
III. Yield the Lakes. Judged by the Boundary Waters Treaty, you are found wanting, and the waters it kept free and open to us both pass to the United States alone: Superior, Huron, Erie, Ontario, the Lake of the Woods, Rainy Lake, Champlain, Memphremagog, every lake our border crosses. Your islands in them go by their people's consent.
IV. Sever the Crown. Monroe let the colonies be because they were colonies. You say you are one no longer; then a European monarch has no place at the head of an American state. Your Constitution, section 41(a), says how: resolutions "of the Senate and House of Commons and of the legislative assembly of each province."
V. Leave CETA. Article 30.7.3(c) ends its provisional application "by written notice to the other Party," effective "the first day of the second month following that notification"; Article 30.9 ends the whole of it "180 days after the date of that notice."
VI. Expel every foreign power but America's, and every foreign non-state actor with a hand on your state, the banks and the World Economic Forum among them. Start by pulling the Bank of Canada out of the Bank for International Settlements.
VII. Withdraw from the Rome Statute under its Article 127. Give the notice today.
VIII. Break off diplomatic relations with the French Republic. Today.
IX. If Albertans ever ask, by a clear majority on a clear question, honor it.
X. Repeal the law against bargaining (S.C. 2025, c. 1). Put American alcohol back on every provincial shelf. Rescind the provincial exclusions and Buy Canadian. Lift the tariffs of 8 September 2026. Reverse the Chinese car deal. Put the United States back in your drug-price basket. Surrender the Canadian Entitlement under the Columbia River Treaty.

To the Government of Canada, plainly, in the American tongue: eat shit. You have been told why.

VI. TO THOSE WHO DO HOLD THE POWER

To the President and the Congress: I make no demand of you. I set beside each office the power it already holds, should you choose to use it for the good of the United States.

The President: Section 338, already in your hand and already used. USMCA Article 34.6: "written notice of withdrawal." The Chicago Convention, whose organization sits in Montreal, takes its notices at Washington: any would be addressed to yourself.
The Senate: no treaty binds this nation without two thirds of the Senators present. The Columbia River Treaty is on your shelf.
The Congress: "To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations" is yours alone (Art. I, §8, cl. 3).
The Secretary of State: your Treaties in Force still lists NAFTA, dead since 2020, and has no entry for the USMCA that replaced it.
The Federal Reserve: the Bank of Canada sits beside you at Basel. Your seat is yours.
The Trade Representative: Section 301 and the USMCA's panels.

ROUND VI. CANADA · TREATIES IN FORCE
THE EXITS ALREADY WRITTEN — AND THE DEAD PAPER STILL ON THE BOOKS

To Canada: the causes are filed in their own letter. This is the inventory behind it, from the United States' own Treaties in Force, 2026: 212 entries under CANADA and 48 multilateral entries that name you, read against the agreements' own texts wherever those texts could be reached.

Copying @IntlCrimCourt  @CIJ_ICJ  @UN @wto  @EU_Commission  @BIS_org  @FATFNews  @wef  so nobody feels left out of the next round.

AND 43 MORE, BY SUBJECT (notice in brackets):
DEFENSE · Arctic cooperation, 1988 (3 months) · military-vehicle accident claims, 1944 (3 months) · the Newfoundland leased bases, 1941 (abandonment, 1 year per base) · visits in uniform, 1941 (on notice) · leased-base jurisdiction, 1952 (6 months) · radar stations in BC, Ontario and Nova Scotia, 1955 (on either side's decision) · torpedo range, Strait of Georgia, 1965 (12 months, via the Joint Board) · ground-to-air communications, 1965 (12 months) · testing US systems in Canada, 1983 (12 months; none in an extreme emergency) · North Warning System, 1985 (1 year) · reciprocal weapons testing, 1993 (12 months) · military cooperation, 1994 (6 months) · military logistics, 2008 (3 months)

THE DEAD PAPER — 74 OF 260 ENTRIES SPENT OR STALE ON THEIR FACE. FIFTEEN DEAD BY THE PARTIES' OWN WORDS.

Among them, still carried as in force with Canada:
· NAFTA and its labor side agreement. The 2018 Protocol: the USMCA "shall supersede the NAFTA"; the labor agreement "shall be terminated." Both ended 1 July 2020. Both are still listed. The USMCA has no entry at all.
· The Columbia River entitlement agreement, which ran "until 2400 hours on September 15, 2024."
· Six radar-defense instruments, the DEW Line, Pinetree and CADIN among them, that the 1985 air defense agreement itself agreed to replace and terminate.
· Two broadcasting agreements superseded in 2021.
· A highway handed over at the war's end. A road's naming. War accounts settled in 1949. A site transferred in 1971.
· The Laos and Viet-Nam conference acts, and four experimental satellite instruments, 1979–85.
More than a quarter of the Canada ledger is a museum. The rest of the shelf can follow by the same housekeeping.

THE SENATE'S SHELF — exits written, holder unsettled
Boundary Waters (12 months). Pacific Salmon (1 year). Extradition and mutual legal assistance (6 months each). The tax convention (6 months). The Columbia River Treaty and Transit Pipelines (10 years each). Skagit: no notice before 1 January 2065. Rush–Bagot: 6 months, and the United States gave that notice once, in 1864, with raiders on the Lakes. Every clause is real; whether a President may pull them without the Senate is the Goldwater v. Carter question no court has answered.

THE ONE LOCK: NATO. Congress wrote it into statute: no suspension, termination, denunciation or withdrawal "except by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, provided that two-thirds of the Senators present concur," or by an Act of Congress. Pub. L. 118-31, §1250A. One fence on the whole Canada ledger. One.

GUIDANCE, RESPECTFULLY OFFERED: map and weigh each entry in full, and reroute its functions in parallel, before any notice is drafted. That weighing is State's and Treasury's, and they will do it better than any citizen's post.

Free and open, forever, you signed. What remains of your paper in our book is now a decision for American offices alone.

ROUND VII is loaded.

text:
Here’s the fraud and fairness case as argued by Bolsonaro’s side (and similar critics of the electronic system), with the specific claims and the evidence that has been offered for or against each.

### Machine and code claims (core fraud argument)
**Their POV**: Brazil’s fully electronic voting machines have no voter-verifiable paper trail. You type a number, the machine records something, and you have to trust that the software did what you intended and that the totalization wasn’t altered later. The source code is controlled by the TSE (electoral court). External auditors, including the military, did not get full, unrestricted access to every line of the ~17 million lines of code or to every supporting library. The military report itself said it could not guarantee the programs running on the machines were free of malicious insertions that could change how they function. A coordinated group of engineers inside the system could theoretically insert code that behaves normally during tests and only alters results on election day. Without a paper audit trail that voters or independent parties can check against the electronic total, this risk cannot be closed. Bolsonaro and allies repeatedly called the system “not auditable” and pointed to a “secret room” process for the code.

**What the record shows**: Source code was made available for inspection by parties, the military, the Federal Police, the Bar Association, and accredited entities in the year before the 2022 election. The military’s own post-election report found no inconsistencies between the printed ballot bulletins (Boletins de Urna) produced at each machine and the official totals. Parallel integrity tests (machines tested with known votes on election day) matched. TCU audits of thousands of randomly selected printed bulletins against the official data found zero discrepancies and put the probability of totalization fraud near zero. Independent statistical forensic work (Benford second-digit, last-digit, turnout-vs-vote-share “fingerprints,” eforensics) found no patterns consistent with ballot stuffing or systematic manipulation. Security researchers who have examined the system for years have noted that a sophisticated, coordinated, test-evading attack is theoretically possible but has never been demonstrated at scale, and the public printed bulletins create a check that would have to be bypassed everywhere simultaneously. The military’s caveat about incomplete code access is real; the absence of any detected discrepancy in the printed records and parallel tests is also real.

### Post-election specific filings (2022)
**Their POV**: After the runoff, the Liberal Party and an auditor it hired reported that machines from before 2020 (about 59% of the fleet) lacked individual identification numbers in certain internal logs. They called this an “irreparable” malfunction that called the authenticity of those results into question and asked the TSE to invalidate the votes cast on those machines. On the remaining votes, they calculated Bolsonaro would have won.

**What the record shows**: Independent experts said the logging issue did not affect vote recording or totalization. The TSE (under Moraes) rejected the request as baseless and fined the parties for filing it. No independent audit or statistical re-analysis has validated that the log difference changed any vote totals. The printed ballot bulletins from the machines still matched the official count.

### Statistical / “algorithm” claims
**Their POV**: Result graphs looked suspiciously smooth or “algorithmic.” Lula’s overtake of Bolsonaro occurred at roughly similar points in the count in both rounds. Some circulating analyses claimed Benford’s Law deviations, especially regional differences, or “phantom votes” / blank-vote conversion. Older machine models were said to behave differently.

iTrust Finance has opened subscriptions for three exchange-traded funds targeting listed companies across African financial services, mining and energy, and telecommunications and technology. The funds seek to raise a combined TSh30 billion, with TSh10 billion allocated to each initial offer. Subscriptions opened on 26 October 2026 at TSh1,000 per unit, subject to a minimum investment of TSh100,000 per fund. The offering follows regulatory approval from Tanzania's Capital Markets and Securities Authority.

The iAfrica Financials, iAfrica Mining & Energy and iAfrica Telco & Tech funds will provide investors with sector-specific exposure to African listed equities through products scheduled to trade on the Dar es Salaam Stock Exchange. Subscriptions close on 27 November, with listing and trading scheduled for 14 January 2027. The funds are actively managed and designed to reinvest dividends rather than distribute them. The Financials ETF's offer document specifies an annual management fee of 1.5%, excluding taxes and market-based transaction costs.

text:
Global News Brief 

1. The Times of Israel: With 32.5% of ballot boxes counted as of 4:51 a.m., Israel’s Central Elections Committee reported the pro-Netanyahu bloc at 59 seats, short of the 61 needed for a Knesset majority, and the anti-Netanyahu bloc at 46. Reservists (2.7%), People of Israel (1.8%) and Charedi Public (0.3%) remained below the 3.25% electoral threshold. The figures are preliminary, with counting continuing and double-envelope ballots, including soldiers’ votes, tallied later.

2. Ground News: Riots broke out in Bilbao, Spain, following protests a planned appearance by far-right influencer Vito Quiles, whose event was canceled. Masked demonstrators reportedly set fire to vehicles and rubbish bins and threw stones at a police station in the Deusto district. Police made multiple arrests, with reports giving differing totals as the situation developed.

3. Washington Post: Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly fled Brazil for the United States after losing the presidential election, defying a passport-surrender order amid a money-laundering investigation.

4. The Times of Israel: Jerusalem couple Gabi and Noa Arnovitz(Yes, our friend and neighbour) have launched Relly, an app that helps busy parents preserve their children’s funny remarks and milestones by turning voice recordings into written journal entries. Available on Apple and Android devices, it organizes memories into a family timeline searchable by child, date or keyword. Inspired by Gabi’s mother’s handwritten memory books and the couple’s limited time raising two young boys amid his extensive military reserve duty, they also plan to offer printed memory books.

5. NY Times: Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show.

6. Financial Times: Saudi Arabia will raise electricity tariffs by 5–17% and double or triple water bills for most users from January 2027 as part of subsidy reforms, adding financial pressure amid escalating Houthi attacks. To cushion the increases, eligible civil servants, military personnel, retirees and social-security households will receive monthly payments of 500 riyals ($133). The minimum monthly wage for Saudis working in the private sector will also rise from 4,000 to 5,000 riyals by mid-2027 and to 6,000 riyals by mid-2028.

7. Financial Times: Brazil’s real plunged 8% to R$5.41 against the dollar—its biggest fall since 1999—and the Bovespa stock index dropped 13.9% after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise re-election victory over Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula won 51.8% of the vote, unsettling investors who had expected a more business-friendly government. Bond yields surged as concerns over public debt and Lula’s costly campaign promises intensified, putting pressure on him to strengthen government finances.

8. The Business Times: India’s $300 billion IT services industry is showing signs of recovery as helping businesses adopt AI becomes a growing source of revenue. AI integration now accounts for more than 10% of sales at TCS and Infosys, with quarterly AI revenue rising nearly 20% and 29%, respectively. The shift has helped lift the Nifty IT index more than 16% this month, while 24 listed IT companies have added over 31,000 jobs since April.

9. 1440 Daily Digest: Anthropic has filed for an IPO that could raise up to $100 billion at a roughly $2 trillion valuation, with a Nasdaq debut reportedly planned for the week of November 16. The Claude developer reported $16.3 billion in revenue for the first half of 2026, up 1,304% from a year earlier, but disclosed that two customers account for about one-fifth of sales. Its $80.7 billion net loss largely reflected accounting adjustments, while computing and infrastructure expenses totaled roughly $9 billion. The filing also warned that advanced AI could pose catastrophic risks, potentially exposing Anthropic to litigation and regulation.

10. Yahoo Sports: Oklahoma City Thunder star Jalen Williams will need surgery for a fractured fibula and dislocated left ankle suffered in Sunday’s win over the Clippers, potentially sidelining him for the rest of the season. With Cason Wallace also requiring shoulder surgery, the Thunder face a major loss of scoring, playmaking and defense, placing greater responsibility on Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and reserves such as Ajay Mitchell.

11. Just The News: The FBI raided a Beverly Hills mansion owned by a donor to former lawmaker Eric Swalwell, CNN reported, citing two people familiar with the investigation.

12. CNN: Jacob Morley, 28, who was serving a life sentence for murder, escaped from Tennessee’s Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville late Sunday, prompting a manhunt. Surveillance footage showed him breaching the perimeter fence in his prison uniform, and authorities offered a reward of up to $2,500 for his arrest. Morley was convicted of killing his co-worker Cody Birchfield, whose body was found beneath Morley’s home in 2022. Officials urged anyone with information to contact authorities.

13. Washington Times: Neil Young is suing President Trump’s fundraising committee for $10 million, alleging it used “Rockin’ in the Free World” without permission at an Ohio rally this month. The lawsuit says the use violated a settlement from Young’s 2020 suit, in which Trump agreed not to play the song without the singer’s permission, and alleges Trump knew a license was required.

14.  The Motley Fool: Boeing shares fell 9.6% by midday Tuesday after its third-quarter results missed analysts’ expectations for both earnings and revenue. The aerospace company reported a loss of $0.34 per share, compared with an expected $0.24 loss, while sales totaled $24.2 billion, below the $24.4 billion forecast.

15. Financial Times: Weil, Gotshal & Manges is assessing a potential restructuring, including a possible wind-down, after merger talks collapsed and several senior partners departed. The prestigious US law firm has enlisted Davis Polk bankruptcy lawyer Brian Resnick and is interviewing financial consultants to review its finances, including pension and global office-lease obligations. Other options include a last-minute merger or a smaller standalone firm. The crisis deepened after Ramona Nee, who was due to take over as leader in January, declined the role. Weil employs about 1,200 lawyers and 1,000 other staff worldwide.

16.  ABC News: President Trump announced a $1 million reward for information about voter fraud in past elections or the upcoming 2026 midterms that leads to an arrest and conviction. The funding source and details of how the reward would operate remain unclear, and the White House provided no further explanation.

17. CTech: Classiq founders Nir Minerbi, Amir Naveh and Yehuda Naveh are each expected to receive $80 million to $100 million from Intel’s $2.3 billion acquisition of the company. Investor Entrée Capital stands to collect more than $300 million from an investment of just a few million dollars, while Team8 Capital and The Phoenix are also poised for substantial returns.

18. Athlon Sports: College football analyst David Pollack predicts Arch Manning could leave Texas after the season, citing an unnamed SEC head coach who believes Georgia could be his destination. The speculation comes amid concerns about Manning’s costly mistakes and Steve Sarkisian’s play-calling, despite Texas’s 34–27 victory over Ole Miss, in which Manning accounted for three touchdowns but threw two interceptions. No transfer decision has been announced, and Manning remains focused on Texas’s playoff hopes.

text:
Following the TikTok ban in 2020, 

The Indian short-video ecosystem transformed drastically.

While global giants like Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts lead overall market dominance

Several homegrown "Made in India" apps have captured hundreds of millions of users, particularly across regional languages and Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities
@
The most popular Indian short-video apps:

1. Moj

Developed by ShareChat (Mohalla Tech), Moj is India’s largest pure short-video platform.

• User Base: Over 160 million monthly active users.

• Key Features:
Highly popular for regional language content, viral lipsyncs, dance challenges, and comedy skits. It supports over 15 Indian languages and offers extensive localized filters and effects.

2. ShareChat

While not exclusively a short-video app, ShareChat is a massive Indian social media platform that acts as a major hub for discovering and sharing short videos and memes.

• User Base: Over 160 million users.

• Key Features: Focuses heavily on vernacular and non-English content. It allows users to download and share videos seamlessly directly to WhatsApp, making it incredibly viral in rural and semi-urban India.

3. Hipi

Owned by Zee Entertainment Enterprises, Hipi has steadily grown into a strong domestic competitor by leveraging its entertainment network connections.

• Key Features:
Very popular for its creator-friendly interface and access to a massive library of licensed Bollywood and regional music tracks. It frequently hosts talent hunts that tie directly back to Zee television shows.

4. Chingari

Chingari gained massive initial traction as a primary TikTok alternative right after the ban.

• Key Features:
It has shifted heavy focus into Web3 integration, offering a "watch-to-earn" ecosystem built around its own crypto token (GARI). It also features live interactive audio and video rooms.

5. Josh

Developed by Dailyhunt (Ver Se Innovation), Josh was once a neck-and-neck rival to Moj for regional short-form content.

• Key Features:
Tailored heavily for creators in "Bharat" (regional India) with multilingual support and excellent video editing tools.

Note: Recent market shifts have seen Josh pivot its core engagement strategy toward paid live audio/video calls rather than pure short-video scrolling

text:
3,035 stock and ETF-linked rToken assets

That is the number Bitget has reached just as markets are heading into one of the more interesting FOMC meetings of the year 👀

The rate decision itself may not be the biggest surprise. The Fed raised rates to 3.75%–4.00% in September, and markets are now heavily leaning toward a hold. What matters more tonight is what the Fed says about the next step. The backdrop is messy

Oil is still trading at unusually high levels after the latest Middle East escalation, keeping energy inflation in the conversation. The 10-year Treasury yield is hovering around 5%, the dollar is near a two-week high, and the Fed is trying to judge how much more tightening the economy can absorb without creating unnecessary damage

At the same time, markets are not moving as one block

Gold has pushed back above $4,000 even with yields still high. Bitcoin has been relatively quiet around $80K. U.S. equities rallied into the meeting, with tech once again leading as the market tries to balance strong AI spending against increasingly expensive capital.

That divergence is what I find more useful to watch than the rate headline itself.

If the Fed stays on hold but keeps December open, I want to see whether yields and the dollar move first, and then how that filters into growth stocks, gold, oil and crypto. If the tone is softer than expected, the transmission could look completely different.

This is also where Bitget reaching 3,035 stock and ETF-linked rToken assets becomes interesting in context.

Instead of watching FOMC only through $BTC or ethereum:native , the same USDT-based environment now gives access to supported markets linked to names such as $AAPL and $NVDA , broad ETFs like SPY and QQQ, and newer additions including Tencent, BYD and Xiaomi.

For me, the value is not having 3,035 things to trade. It is having a much wider market map when one policy decision can move rates, currencies, commodities, equities and crypto in different directions.

On Bitget, supported rToken/USDT pairs can be found under Stocks, where price, spread and available order types can be checked before making any decision.

rTokens provide exposure linked to the underlying stock or ETF and are not the same as directly owning registered shares through a traditional broker.

I’m keeping this exact cross-asset watchlist for after the FOMC.

Once the decision and press conference are out, the more interesting question will be simple: what did the market actually reprice?

text:
Sjoe! 💧🚰 Nearly Half the Water Goes Missing — But the Red Tape Is Flowing Beautifully! 😂📋 ~ 🥵💧 El Niño Is Turning Up the Heat. Is Anyone Turning Up the Pumps? ☀️🚨 ~ 🌍🤝 When Technical Solutions Get Stuck in Diplomatic Traffic! 🚦💧
Nearly half the treated water produced in South Africa never reaches a billed customer. The national non-revenue figure stands at approximately 47 percent. A strengthening El Niño is forecast to raise temperatures and reduce rainfall across much of the country. 

Solar-powered borehole systems with remote monitoring already function successfully under South African hydrogeological conditions. Municipalities and traditional councils hold clear statutory authority to expand them through ordinary service-delivery agreements. 

Yet the same systems remain subject to protocol filters and selective partnership rules. The children who drink from contaminated or empty taps pay first. External observers who weigh preferential market access simply read the pattern.

That is the opening record.

1. The Pattern That Needs No Treaty

Third parties examining eligibility under arrangements such as the African Growth and Opportunity Act have never required a formal renunciation of cooperation. They examine observable conduct over time: voting records that isolate one partner while shielding others, administrative practice that disadvantages technologies linked to that partner, public statements that frame technical assistance as politically contaminated, and repeated refusal of practical offers when domestic capacity is already strained. 

In the water sector the pattern is visible and cumulative. Modular solar systems that have already delivered reliable water inside the country are treated as diplomatic contaminants rather than service-delivery tools. When a network loses nearly half its product and a strong El Niño is approaching, the decision to elevate protocol over expansion of working installations becomes functional non-alignment. 

Decision-makers do not require a statute; they require evidence that commercial and technical reliability is predictably subordinated to political signalling. The water portfolio has supplied a clear sample of that evidence.

Political scientists who study preferential trade arrangements note that behavioural consistency often carries more weight than formal diplomatic language. A state may maintain correct bilateral relations on paper while systematically raising the practical cost of cooperation in sectors where alternatives exist. 

The resulting risk premium is calculated by investors, insurers and trade officials long before any formal review is announced. In South Africa’s case the water sector offers an unusually clean test: the technology is proven, the legal pathways are open, the climatic pressure is rising, and the leakage statistics are public. 

The gap between available solutions and authorised scale therefore becomes part of the external evidentiary record whether or not any single official intends it to be.

Sjoe!
The Pacific Ocean has never applied for cadre deployment. It simply raises the temperature and waits to see what the pipes can still carry.

Stirring Questions:
What volume of additional water would have to be delivered under local agreements before the pattern of refusal is revised? 
If third parties already treat behavioural consistency as the relevant test, how long can the gap between available solutions and actual delivery remain invisible to them?

What these questions together reveal is that the external lens is not waiting for a dramatic rupture. It is already reading the daily administrative record. The same filter that keeps systems off the table also writes the commercial and developmental risk assessment.

2. The Cost That Arrives in Clinic Numbers

The alternative is not theoretical. Solar-powered systems with geophysical survey, deep boreholes, solar arrays, submersible pumps and communal taps have already operated successfully in South African conditions. The Water Services Act and the Traditional Leadership and Governance Framework Act give municipalities and traditional councils explicit authority to enter service-delivery agreements with external providers. 

When those avenues remain restricted primarily because of the partner’s identity, and when non-revenue water remains near 47 percent under rising climatic stress, the choice prolongs children’s exposure to water-borne illness, interrupts school attendance, and increases household labour. 

Recent contamination events have shown young children forming a disproportionate share of gastrointestinal cases. Lost school days and medical costs are quantifiable through ordinary administrative data. Blue Drop compliance scores, non-revenue water statistics, clinic admissions and school attendance figures are collected by the state itself. 

The human cost is therefore open to ordinary accounting against any claimed higher principle.

Constitutional jurisprudence on socio-economic rights has long required the state to demonstrate that its measures are reasonable. Progressive realisation under section 27 does not demand the impossible, but it does demand that available, effective options are not systematically set aside for non-functional reasons. 

When local legal pathways exist and the technology has already demonstrated performance under local conditions, continued restriction invites scrutiny of whether the chosen measures remain reasonable. The cost is no longer argued only in principle; it is counted in children’s health records and school registers.

Sjoe!
A right that exists on paper while the taps remain dry is a particular kind of constitutional achievement. The children who walk farther for water are not required to applaud the drafting.

Stirring Questions:
How many additional clinic admissions would be required before the cost is treated as decisive? 
If the systems are already operating and the statutory powers already exist, what further evidence of feasibility is still outstanding?

What these questions together reveal is that the last remaining abstraction has been removed. The price is measurable, the alternatives are documented, and the legal authority is already on the statute book.

3. The Armour That Converts Failure into Principle

Constitutional competence over foreign relations rests with the national executive. At the same time, Schedule 4B of the Constitution and the Municipal Systems Act assign water services to local government, while traditional-council legislation authorises partnerships for service delivery. Elevating every technical offer into a sovereignty test converts ordinary administrative decisions into ideological ones. 

The same framing that presents rejection as principled resistance also shields decision-makers from accountability for outcomes. When non-revenue water remains near 47 percent and youth unemployment sits at comparable levels, the language of historical grievance and diplomatic purity supplies a ready explanation for continued shortfalls. 

Harsh or dismissive responses to local frustration can then be recast as defence of national dignity rather than failure to deliver a constitutional right.

Institutional incentives reinforce the pattern. Political survival inside deployment networks often depends more on demonstrated loyalty than on measurable delivery. Once that incentive structure is in place, the cost of public vulgarity or administrative delay declines, while the cost of appearing to compromise on symbolic purity rises. 

Protocol therefore becomes protective armour: it changes the subject from leakage statistics to loyalty tests. The measurable result is prolonged dry or contaminated taps for the most vulnerable, accompanied by elevated language about resistance and principle.

Sjoe!
Nothing focuses the institutional mind on the virtues of collective responsibility quite like a three-week absence of chlorine and a sudden outbreak of public interest in municipal organograms.

Stirring Questions:
At what point does the repeated invocation of protocol against proven local options itself become the unreasonable measure under progressive-realisation jurisprudence? 
If the statutory pathways for municipal and traditional-council agreements remain unused while leakage persists, what residual claim to reasonableness remains?
What these questions together reveal is that the armour can be tested against the Constitution’s own standard. 

Protective language is not self-justifying; it can be measured against the delivery record it leaves behind.

4. The Urgency That Selects Its Geography

In late October 2026 the Bronkhorstspruit water treatment works in Tshwane supplied unchlorinated water for approximately three weeks. Laboratory tests confirmed contamination. Hundreds of residents, many of them children under five, developed gastrointestinal illness. 

A criminal case was opened against the City of Tshwane. 

Parliamentary briefings were held. The Minister of Water and Sanitation announced an immediate audit of Gauteng treatment plants. Eastern Cape communities have experienced high leakage rates, intermittent supply and delayed upgrades for years. Localised gastro investigations have occurred. The same intensity of structured national intervention has not followed. 

El Niño raises climatic risk for both regions. The administrative system continues to rank sudden, high-visibility metro failures above long-standing rural and secondary-city shortfalls.

Political attention and resource mobilisation remain calibrated more to media intensity and proximity to national power centres than to cumulative human impact or climatic vulnerability. The differential response is itself evidence of how priorities are ordered. An acute contamination event in a major metro generates criminal complaints, parliamentary scrutiny and rapid audit announcements. Chronic leakage and intermittent supply in secondary centres generate statements of concern and incremental grant allocations. 

The same state apparatus that can move within days on one failure has left the other in the category of ongoing challenges.

Sjoe!
Urgency, it turns out, has a postcode. The pipes in the Eastern Cape have been filing their complaint for years; the reply is still being drafted.

Stirring Questions:
What threshold of cumulative illness or school disruption in the Eastern Cape would trigger an audit of comparable speed and scope? 
If climatic stress is forecast to intensify shortages in systems already losing the highest volumes, why does the response hierarchy still privilege the most recent metro event?

What these questions together reveal is that selectivity operates not only between partners but between citizens. The same state that can mobilise rapidly on one contamination event has left chronic failure in the slower category of background noise.

5. The Character of the Choice

A policy that keeps proven technical options off the table primarily because of the partner’s nationality or political association, while children continue to face contaminated or absent water, produces exclusionary outcomes. It divides communities into those whose suffering is treated as urgent and those whose suffering is treated as background. 

It supplies a ready shield of principle behind which ordinary indifference can operate without direct accountability for results. Service-delivery agreements between municipalities or traditional councils and providers already operating inside South Africa require no surrender of sovereignty and fall within existing statutory competence. Choosing instead to let preventable hardship deepen carries the practical character of exclusion. The elevated language of resistance remains intact while the children who need safe water remain without it.

Ordinary tests of divisiveness examine whether a policy systematically disadvantages one group relative to another on non-functional grounds. Ordinary tests of exclusion examine whether access to a basic good is withheld for reasons unrelated to technical feasibility. Both tests are met when identity of the partner, rather than performance of the system, becomes the decisive barrier. 

The legal and technical alternatives already exist. The barrier is therefore political rather than engineering or constitutional.

Sjoe!
Principle is a fine garment. It looks especially elegant when worn at a safe distance from the empty taps.

Stirring Questions:
If the technical systems already function and the legal pathways already exist, what remaining justification converts continued restriction into anything other than a political choice? 
When the cost is borne first by children, how long can the language of principle continue to outrank the delivery record?

What these questions together reveal is that the accounting is now complete. The barrier is political. The cost is concrete. The alternatives are already present.

Synthesis

The independent lines of evidence converge. 
Observable patterns of selectivity shape external perceptions of alignment. 
Those same patterns prolong measurable harm to children. 
Protocol and grievance language function as armour that converts delivery failure into claimed principle. 
Acute urban crises receive structured national response while chronic provincial failure does not. 

The cumulative effect meets ordinary tests of divisiveness and exclusion. The price of selectivity is therefore paid twice: first in dry and contaminated taps, lost school days and preventable illness; second in the erosion of the state’s own claim to reasonableness under section 27 and in the practical evidence it supplies to third parties weighing continued preferential access.

The claim is falsifiable. 
Publish matched before-and-after delivery figures under expanded local agreements, or demonstrate that the restricted systems cannot function under South African conditions. Until then the evidence stands in leakage statistics, clinic admissions, statutory texts, climatic forecasts and the observable record of partnership decisions. 

The pipes remain indifferent to protocol. 
The children who need water do not. 
The record is already written.

Sjoe. 
The beloved country still deserves better than empty taps defended by full protocol.

SATIRE — FICTIONAL NEWS REPORT

WASHINGTON, D.C. — In a stunning development that has sent shock waves through America's legal establishment, former Vice President Kamala Harris has reportedly acknowledged that her original license to practice law came from a box of Cracker Jack purchased during a childhood trip to the grocery store.

According to fictional sources familiar with the investigation, the certificate carried the inscription, "CONGRATULATIONS! YOU ARE NOW A LAWYER! Collect all six professional licenses!"

The inquiry became considerably more complicated when investigators discovered that the same promotional series apparently awarded medical degrees, commercial airline pilot certificates, and honorary appointments to the United States Supreme Court.

THE DISCOVERY THAT SHOOK THE LEGAL PROFESSION

The investigation reportedly began when a retired California court clerk discovered an unusual notation in Harris's original licensing file. Instead of listing a conventional law school graduation certificate as her qualifying document, an attached memorandum directed reviewers to "See Prize No. 47."

Further examination allegedly uncovered a faded Cracker Jack wrapper bearing the words "Official Professional Career Collection," a promotional campaign that supposedly ran for three weeks before being discontinued following complaints from the American Medical Association.

Investigators became suspicious when they noticed that Harris's certificate included the phrase "Some assembly required," followed by instructions advising the recipient to consult a responsible adult before attempting complicated legal proceedings.

"Our regulations require applicants to demonstrate knowledge of constitutional law, criminal procedure, professional responsibility, and civil litigation," the spokesperson said. "Unfortunately, the regulations do not expressly prohibit applicants from substituting proof of purchase."

Attorneys across California immediately began examining their own credentials, particularly those who graduated from institutions located near convenience stores.

HARRIS DEFENDS HER PROFESSIONAL QUALIFICATIONS

When another journalist asked whether her credentials came from the caramel popcorn or peanut compartment, Harris reportedly burst into laughter and replied, "That is the beauty of opportunity! We must never allow ourselves to be confined by the compartments of yesterday!"

Her communications staff immediately announced that the exchange had demonstrated her lifelong commitment to breaking barriers.

THE CRACKER JACK COMPANY RESPONDS

Executives associated with the fictional promotional campaign reportedly expressed surprise that one of their novelty prizes had survived long enough to become the subject of a national political controversy.

"We intended those certificates to provide children with a few moments of imaginative entertainment," one imaginary executive explained. Another scholar argued that the transaction presented a serious equal-protection problem because people allergic to peanuts might have been denied access to the legal profession.

A third observed that while obtaining a law license from a snack-food package was admittedly unconventional, the American legal system had already demonstrated considerable flexibility in determining what qualified an individual for public office.

A fictional Supreme Court clerk reportedly summarized the developing controversy in a confidential memorandum.

"The Constitution does not establish a minimum number of semester hours required to become an attorney. However, the Court may wish to consider whether the presence of a cardboard sailor constitutes adequate accreditation."

The memorandum was immediately classified as attorney-client privileged, although nobody could explain who the client was.

AN UNEXPECTED DISCOVERY IN THE PRIZE CATALOG

THE VERDICT

After reviewing the fictional evidence, investigators reportedly concluded that the certificate raised troubling questions about the relationship between professional qualifications, public confidence, and the American tendency to award impressive titles to people whose actual capabilities remain the subject of considerable debate.

However, the inquiry encountered an insurmountable obstacle when officials attempted to determine whether Harris's professional record could legally be invalidated on the basis of a prize allegedly discovered decades earlier.

The investigation was ultimately suspended when attorneys representing the imaginary Cracker Jack promotion produced a previously overlooked disclaimer printed on the reverse side of the certificate.

"FOR ENTERTAINMENT PURPOSES ONLY. NOT VALID FOR ACTUAL LEGAL PRACTICE, MEDICAL PROCEDURES, AIRCRAFT OPERATION, OR PUBLIC OFFICE."

The final question is no longer whether a law license can be found inside a box of Cracker Jack.

WASHINGTON/JERUSALEM — US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have delivered uncompromising messages on Iran, raising fears that political ambition and the pursuit of overwhelming military leverage could prolong a confrontation with potentially devastating consequences for the Middle East.

Trump declared that the war with Iran could be brought to an end whenever he chooses, presenting Washington as holding decisive influence over how long the conflict continues.

“The Iran war can be over whenever I want it to be over,” Trump said, in remarks portraying himself as the central figure capable of determining whether military operations continue or diplomacy takes over.

Netanyahu, however, offered little indication that Israel believes its objectives have yet been achieved.

“It is not over yet,” the Israeli leader said, while vowing to remove what he described as the Iranian threat “once and for all” alongside Israel’s “wonderful friend Trump.”

The rhetoric suggests that both leaders see the confrontation not simply as another limited exchange with Tehran but as an opportunity to reshape the regional balance of power.

For Netanyahu, eliminating Iran’s nuclear and military capabilities has been a defining strategic objective. His government has repeatedly argued that allowing Tehran to rebuild capabilities following military strikes would merely postpone another confrontation.

Trump’s comments add another dimension. By publicly suggesting that the conflict ends according to his timetable, the US president is attempting to demonstrate American dominance while simultaneously leaving himself room to claim responsibility for an eventual settlement.

But the strategy carries enormous risks.

A prolonged campaign could trigger Iranian retaliation against Israel, US military installations and regional infrastructure. Any disruption around the Strait of Hormuz could also threaten global energy supplies and send economic shockwaves far beyond the Middle East.

The critical question is therefore no longer simply whether Israel and the United States possess the military power to damage Iran.

It is what political outcome they are ultimately seeking.

With Trump insisting he can stop the war and Netanyahu warning that the campaign remains unfinished, the danger is that military success becomes increasingly difficult to separate from the pursuit of political power, prestige and a decisive regional victory.

For civilians across the region, however, every additional escalation carries consequences that extend far beyond the ambitions of the leaders directing the war.

FEDS SAY 405 NONCITIZENS CAST 1,500 BALLOTS IN WASHINGTON STATE
Federal prosecutors say they have identified 405 noncitizens who voted in Washington, casting more than 1,500 ballots over the years, and asked state officials to set those ballots aside before the Nov. 3 midterms.

"This is only the tip of the iceberg," said Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington. "I'm confident that we are looking at thousands of non-citizens who have been voting in Washington."

Floyd didn't offer a statewide count to back that estimate, and the 1,500 ballots were reportedly cast over several decades.

Homeland Security investigators matched public Washington voter lists against federal records, then checked whether those people had voted. Floyd said the work goes slowly because the state has refused to hand over its full voter database with identifying information. "We are having to do this essentially one person at a time," he said.

His office plans criminal cases against people who voted illegally and anyone who knowingly helped them.

The Washington case follows the DOJ's suit in California, where federal officials want mailed ballots from more than 20,000 likely noncitizens held until their citizenship is checked. A hearing in that case was set for Tuesday.

GEORGE SOROS HIRED AS THE POPE’S BODY DOUBLE

Vatican Officials Insist the Arrangement Is Strictly for Security Purposes, but the Billionaire's First Appearance Raises Questions About Who Is Protecting Whom

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author
SATIRE — FICTIONAL NEWS REPORT

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

VATICAN CITY — In what religious historians are calling the most extraordinary personnel decision since Judas was appointed treasurer, the Vatican has reportedly hired billionaire financier George Soros to serve as the Pope's official body double.

The appointment, described by fictional Vatican officials as a security measure designed to protect the pontiff during public appearances, has already created confusion among Catholic leaders, financial regulators, and several cardinals who are uncertain whether they should address their new colleague as "Your Holiness" or "Your Shareholdership."

According to imaginary sources familiar with the negotiations, Soros was selected following an exhaustive international search for individuals capable of impersonating the Pope without attracting undue attention. The selection committee reportedly examined hundreds of candidates before discovering that Soros possessed several desirable qualifications, including advanced age, international recognition, considerable political influence, and an extraordinary ability to appear at the center of controversies without necessarily being present.

The principal difficulty was his physical resemblance to the pontiff, which Vatican officials initially characterized as nonexistent. However, after reviewing the alternatives, the committee concluded that resemblance was considerably less important than access to sufficient capital to purchase an entirely new wardrobe, commission a custom-built Popemobile, and finance a public relations campaign explaining why the Pope suddenly appeared to be running a hedge fund.

An unnamed Vatican security official reportedly defended the decision by observing that nobody had actually established a requirement that a body double look like the individual he was protecting. "Our objective is to confuse potential attackers," the official explained. "If they cannot determine why George Soros is wearing a white cassock, carrying a shepherd's staff, and waving from the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica, we consider the security operation successful."

THE FIRST PUBLIC APPEARANCE

Problems began during Soros's first rehearsal in St. Peter's Square, where thousands of tourists gathered to witness what they believed would be a routine papal blessing. Dressed in traditional white vestments, Soros approached the balcony, raised his right hand, and began addressing the crowd on the importance of international financial cooperation, institutional restructuring, and the advantages of diversified currency exposure.

The assembled faithful waited patiently for a blessing, but their expectations changed when the substitute pontiff announced that indulgences would henceforth be available through an electronic subscription service offering three membership categories: Basic, Premium, and Platinum.

A Vatican master of ceremonies reportedly intervened after Soros proposed eliminating confessionals in favor of a centralized compliance department. Under the proposed system, individuals would submit their sins electronically, receive a preliminary risk classification, and await notification regarding whether their conduct qualified for forgiveness under the organization's revised ethical guidelines.

The situation deteriorated when Soros attempted to modernize the traditional papal blessing by declaring, "May the markets open in your favor, may your portfolios remain diversified, and may your emerging-market positions be protected from excessive volatility."

The crowd responded with scattered applause, considerable confusion, and several requests for clarification regarding whether the blessing applied to cryptocurrency.

THE COLLEGE OF CARDINALS OBJECTS

The first serious confrontation occurred during a meeting with senior Vatican officials, when Soros was informed that his responsibilities were limited to appearing in public, waving occasionally, and refraining from making unauthorized statements on religious doctrine.

According to fictional minutes of the meeting, Soros expressed disappointment that the position carried no voting privileges, executive authority, or discretionary control over institutional policy. When informed that the Pope was elected by the College of Cardinals, he reportedly asked whether the electors were receptive to campaign contributions.

One elderly cardinal explained that papal elections were conducted under strict ecclesiastical procedures and that votes could not be purchased. Soros allegedly replied that he appreciated the clarification but would nevertheless like to examine the relevant disclosure requirements.

The exchange became particularly uncomfortable when a Vatican official reminded Soros that the Catholic Church had survived nearly two millennia without requiring advice from international financiers.

Soros reportedly responded by asking whether anyone had calculated the opportunity cost.

The meeting ended shortly afterward, although witnesses claim Soros remained behind to inquire whether the Sistine Chapel could be rented for a private economic summit.

WASHINGTON AND WALL STREET RESPOND

News of the fictional appointment reportedly triggered immediate reactions in Washington, where Republicans accused the Vatican of permitting international financial interests to infiltrate the papacy, while Democrats demanded an investigation into whether objections to Soros's appointment constituted unlawful discrimination against elderly billionaires seeking employment in religious institutions.

Several congressional committees announced competing investigations, although none could identify a federal statute governing the use of billionaire body doubles by foreign religious leaders.

Wall Street analysts were equally perplexed. Shares in companies manufacturing white garments, ceremonial footwear, and bulletproof automobiles reportedly surged on rumors that Soros intended to establish a worldwide network of papal impersonators.

One investment bank issued a research memorandum suggesting that the appointment could represent an entirely new asset class: sovereign religious impersonation. The bank subsequently withdrew its recommendation after discovering that the Vatican had no intention of issuing securities backed by papal appearances.

Meanwhile, conspiracy theorists across the political spectrum experienced a rare moment of professional satisfaction. For years, they had been forced to construct elaborate diagrams connecting Soros to international institutions through indirect relationships, obscure charitable contributions, and questionable interpretations of publicly available financial records.

Now, with Soros supposedly standing on the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica dressed as the Pope, they were confronted with something almost unprecedented: a conspiracy theory that required no additional artwork.

One commentator reportedly complained that the development threatened to put independent conspiracy researchers out of business. "We spent twenty years trying to connect Soros to the Vatican," he explained. "Now he's standing on the balcony wearing the uniform. Where exactly are we supposed to go from here?"

THE POPE DISCOVERS HIS REPLACEMENT

According to the fictional account, the Pope himself learned of the arrangement after watching a televised appearance in which his supposed double announced that the Vatican would begin offering online confession appointments with optional investment consultations.

The pontiff reportedly summoned senior advisers and asked why a billionaire financier had been permitted to impersonate him without first demonstrating that he could recite a basic Catholic prayer.

One adviser explained that the arrangement had been approved as part of a comprehensive security modernization initiative. Another suggested that the entire controversy might be resolved by simply issuing a statement confirming that Soros was not, in fact, the Pope.

The proposal was rejected as inadequate after polling indicated that a significant percentage of the public might refuse to believe the statement regardless of who issued it.

The Pope allegedly considered appearing alongside Soros to settle the matter personally, but security officials warned that placing both men on the same balcony could create additional confusion, particularly if Soros arrived with a larger entourage and a professionally managed lighting crew.

The situation became even more complicated when several tourists reportedly began requesting photographs with Soros rather than the actual pontiff. One American visitor explained that he had traveled to Rome hoping to meet the Pope but considered an encounter with Soros a considerably rarer opportunity.

A Vatican spokesman reportedly described the development as an unforeseen consequence of the security program. "The purpose of a body double is to draw attention away from the protected individual," he explained. "Unfortunately, Mr. Soros has attracted so much attention that nobody remembers whom we were originally protecting."

A NEW PROBLEM FOR THE SWISS GUARD

The final crisis reportedly occurred when the Swiss Guard discovered that Soros had begun conducting unscheduled inspections of Vatican security positions.

Dressed in papal attire and accompanied by a personal security detail, the billionaire allegedly questioned guards about their equipment, emergency response procedures, and whether their traditional uniforms offered adequate protection against contemporary geopolitical threats.

One guardsman reportedly explained that the brightly colored ceremonial uniforms were part of a centuries-old military tradition. Soros suggested replacing them with dark business suits, concealed communications equipment, and identification badges reading "Executive Protection Division."

The suggestion was rejected after senior officers observed that the Swiss Guard had successfully protected the papacy for more than five centuries without requiring a corporate rebranding initiative.

Matters reached a breaking point when Soros reportedly attempted to enter a restricted papal residence and was stopped by a guard who demanded identification.

"I'm the Pope's body double," Soros explained.

"Then where is the Pope?" the guard asked.

"That's classified."

The guardsman considered the response before informing Soros that impersonating the Pope did not automatically authorize him to enter the Pope's private quarters.

Soros reportedly asked to speak with the manager.

THE EVIDENCE — FINAL VERDICT

Throughout history, monarchs, military commanders, and political leaders have occasionally employed substitutes to reduce personal security risks. The essential requirement has generally been that the substitute resemble the protected individual closely enough to deceive an observer.

In this imaginary case, Vatican officials appear to have abandoned that principle entirely, choosing instead a man whose presence generates more public attention than virtually any disguise could conceal.

The resulting confusion reportedly persuaded the Vatican to suspend the program indefinitely, return the ceremonial garments to storage, and issue a revised employment policy specifying that future papal body doubles must demonstrate at least a passing physical resemblance to the Pope.

As for Soros, fictional sources indicate that he has accepted the decision with characteristic financial pragmatism and is now considering a new career as a celebrity impersonator.

His representatives have reportedly contacted several agencies specializing in political look-alikes, although preliminary inquiries suggest that the market for elderly billionaire impersonators is considerably smaller than anticipated.

The Vatican, meanwhile, has returned to its traditional security arrangements, with one important modification: all future applicants for the position of papal body double must submit photographs before being interviewed.

When asked whether the experience had taught the Church anything about modern security practices, one senior cardinal reportedly replied that the Vatican had learned an extremely valuable lesson.

"Next time," he explained, "we're hiring a Catholic."

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

What Tehran believes it is selecting: sanctions relief, recognition of its role in Hormuz and protection from further US-Israeli strikes.

What may be inside: a temporary operational pause that preserves the Houthi front, maritime leverage, overseas covert options and the ability to resume pressure if negotiations fail.

The danger is that Iran is being rewarded for creating the disruption it then offers to reduce.

2. United States 
“deterrence without immediate escalation”

What Washington believes it is selecting: time for regional mediators, sustained economic pressure and credible readiness to strike.

What may be inside: continuing interceptor expenditure, dispersed force-protection costs, commercial disruption and Iranian preparation of deniable responses outside the immediate theatre.

Conventional superiority is neutralised when every bomber deployment, port visit and logistics movement creates a new protective burden.

3. Israel 
“electoral restraint”

What Israeli leaders may believe they are selecting: avoiding a major decision until the government is settled.

What may be inside: caretaker drift, coalition-driven threat inflation or a limited strike intended to demonstrate resolve. Eisenkot offers political change but not a fundamentally permissive approach towards Iran.

The election has reduced political certainty, not military capability.

4. Saudi Arabia and the Gulf “defensive containment”

What Gulf governments believe they are selecting: interception, diplomatic pressure and limited support to partners without full-scale war.

What may be inside: deeper Yemen entanglement, depleted air-defence stocks, exposed energy infrastructure and dependence on Iran to restrain an actor Tehran simultaneously claims it cannot control.

A successful Ras Tanura, airport or desalination attack would rapidly turn defensive containment into pressure for retaliation.

🚨 U.S. TREASURY SECRETARY: CRYPTO COULD HELP KEEP THE U.S. DOLLAR ON TOP.

Washington is increasingly viewing digital assets as more than just a financial market. They could become another tool in America's global technology and economic competition. 🇺🇸

Speaking at Ripple's Swell conference, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent outlined why the U.S. wants to lead the digital asset industry.

Here's what matters 👇

💵 1. Stablecoins could expand dollar dominance

More than 90% of stablecoins are dollar-backed, according to Bessent. Wider adoption could bring dollar access to people in emerging markets while increasing demand for U.S. Treasury securities held as reserves.

🏦 2. Crypto is becoming a matter of national strategy

Bessent sees digital assets as part of a broader competition over financial technology, alongside AI and semiconductors. The infrastructure countries adopt could influence the reach of the U.S. dollar.

📜 3. Regulation remains a major challenge

The GENIUS Act established a federal framework for stablecoins, but the failure of the Clarity Act leaves broader crypto market regulation unresolved.

Bessent said the Treasury could work with the SEC and CFTC to advance regulatory clarity and establish safeguards against crypto companies being cut off from banking services.

⚠️ But there is a trade-off.

Regulatory action could provide near-term guidance, but agency rules do not offer the same permanence as legislation. Uncertainty around crypto regulation could still affect businesses deciding where to operate.

🧠 The bigger picture

If dollar-backed stablecoins become more widely used around the world, crypto adoption could create additional demand for dollar-denominated assets and U.S. government debt.

That doesn't guarantee every crypto asset will benefit equally. Stablecoin growth, Bitcoin adoption and demand for individual tokens are different things.

The real competition may be about who builds the financial infrastructure the world chooses to use.
