🏷️ Sjoe! When the Stamp Is Not the Law: Who Authorised the Secrecy? ⚖️ ~ 🛟 Sjoe! Praising the Lifeboat While the Ship Sinks 🚢 ~ 🔎 The Evidence Scorecard: Test the Stamp, Test the Slogan, Test the Results 📊
On 21 October 2026 the Madlanga Commission heard a sentence that should have been routine. Advocate Ben Winks submitted that the Minimum Information Security Standards are “a document of the Executive” and “not a law,” that the Protection of State Information Bill “has never been assented to by the President” and “is not law,” and that therefore “there is no law on the statute books that provides for decisions to classify or declassify” (Madlanga Commission, 2026). 

Officials, he argued, must still explain why particular information needs protection rather than rest on the stamp. 

Evidence leader Matthew Chaskalson replied that the commission is not a high court and cannot set classifications aside. Both statements can be true at once. The stamp was left without a statute beneath it.

That hearing day states the entire argument. A label—whether “Top Secret,” “non-aligned,” or “virtuous”—does not decide the character of the practice it names. Character is the content, the pattern and the measurable effect. 

Constitutional limits on rights must be authorised by law of general application; a policy document, however long-standing, does not itself supply that authorisation. The same ordinary demand travels from classification to foreign-policy slogans.

Sjoe!
A stamp without a statute is rather like a parking ticket written on the back of a grocery list: it may look official, yet the magistrate still wants to see the by-law.

Questions Stirring: 
What residual legal authority, if any, still supports a classification decision once MISS is conceded to be policy and the Bill is not law? 
How does that residual authority, if it exists, change the weight a commission or court must give the stamp itself?

Why these questions together matter: they force the structural fact into the open. If no clear statute authorises the stamp, every secrecy claim must still be justified by the character of the information. That is the same test later applied to every other label.

1. The Pattern Behind the Policy

Cabinet approved MISS on 4 December 1996. It has remained policy. The Protection of State Information Bill, introduced in 2010, passed both Houses in 2013, was returned by President Zuma, travelled forward again, and was returned by President Ramaphosa in 2020 on constitutional grounds. 

Parliamentary legal services later agreed with many of those reservations. 

As of late 2026 the Bill has not been assented to (Parliament of the Republic of South Africa, 2010–2026). Classification therefore continues under executive practice rather than an Act of general application. That non-statutory character is the structural fact, not a technical footnote. 

Every secrecy claim must still be justified by the substance of the information.

The same structural observation applies to non-alignment. It is a policy orientation set out in white papers and party documents, not a statutory constraint. It can shift without a new Act. That flexibility is why third parties may test it against observable conduct. 

AGOA Section 104 already supplies one such test: the President must determine that a country is making continual progress toward a market-based economy that protects property rights and eliminates barriers to United States trade and investment, and that it “does not engage in activities that undermine United States national security or foreign policy interests” (African Growth and Opportunity Act, 19 U.S.C. § 3703). 

The statute leaves “undermine” to be read from the pattern.

The pattern is public and independently checkable. United Nations General Assembly voting records on specific resolutions are tabulated. Defence ministries publish dates, participants and stated purposes of joint naval and air exercises. Government Gazettes and court judgments record the application of ownership and procurement rules—including Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment equity requirements—to firms from different countries. 

Ministerial statements can be placed beside the outcomes of related domestic litigation. None of these items requires a new treaty. They require only a scorecard and the willingness to fill it from primary sources. 

Economic consequences follow directly: differential ownership rules raise the cost of entry for some investors relative to others; voting and exercise patterns signal to capital markets and to AGOA reviewers alike.

Sjoe!
Non-alignment without a statute is rather like a weather vane that insists it points north while the wind keeps blowing from the east. The vane can still be painted any colour you like.

Questions Stirring: 
Which three public indicators, scored over a rolling five-year window, would a reasonable AGOA reviewer treat as sufficient to establish functional alignment or non-alignment? 
If non-alignment is policy rather than statute, what institutional mechanism currently constrains a sudden shift, and where is that constraint recorded?

Why these questions together matter: they turn an abstract slogan into a falsifiable score. Independent lines of evidence—votes, exercises, investment rules, litigation outcomes—either converge on the label or they do not. 

Convergence is persuasive; divergence is the character of the practice.

2. Substance, Not Slogan

Place the same scorecard beside a domestic crisis and the test does not change. Official data from the Department of Water and Sanitation and successive No Drop reports place national non-revenue water at approximately 47.3 percent (Department of Water and Sanitation, 2024–2026; ministerial parliamentary replies).

The figure covers physical leaks, illegal connections and billing failures. El Niño cycles can reduce surface-water availability and raise temperatures, amplifying existing losses. These are documented facts of infrastructure, governance and climate. They are not, by themselves, a crime against humanity.

Article 7 of the Rome Statute requires that the listed acts form part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against any civilian population, committed with knowledge of the attack. An “attack” is a course of conduct involving the multiple commission of those acts pursuant to or in furtherance of a State or organisational policy. 

Extermination includes the intentional infliction of conditions of life calculated to bring about the destruction of part of a population. Other inhumane acts require the intentional causation of great suffering (Rome Statute, 1998, Art. 7). A 47.3 percent loss rate, even when worsened by drought and accompanied by selective refusal of particular offers of assistance, does not supply the directed-attack, knowledge or specific-intent elements. 

The virtue label attached to the refusal does not fill the gap. International comparisons are instructive: high non-revenue water appears in many middle-income systems under fiscal and capacity stress; none of those cases has been treated as meeting Article 7 without proof of the additional elements. 

The character of the conduct is still measured by the same standard applied to the classification stamp and the non-alignment slogan.

The scorecard therefore remains open. 
Columns for UN votes, joint exercises, differential application of ownership rules, statements versus court outcomes, and the AGOA statutory criteria can be filled from public sources. 
A separate column for domestic infrastructure outcomes—non-revenue water, repair rates, acceptance or refusal of feasible technical assistance—can sit beside them. 

The sum is not a moral verdict. It is a pattern. Patterns are what remain when every stamp, slogan and virtue claim is set aside. Incentives matter: officials who can rest on a label face lower immediate costs than officials who must continually justify the substance. 

The cumulative record shows the cost of that incentive.

Sjoe!
Calling a 47 percent leak “virtue” because certain helpers were turned away is rather like praising the captain for the colour of the lifeboats while the hull is open to the sea.

Questions Stirring: 
If a dashboard already contains the public indicators required by AGOA Section 104, what additional weight, if any, should sustained high non-revenue water under known climate stress receive when the same government selectively declines assistance? 
What primary documents—Gazettes, voting databases, defence releases, Auditor-General reports—would be necessary and sufficient to populate that dashboard without secondary narrative?

Why these questions together matter: they keep the legal line visible. Crisis, leakage and selective refusal are relevant facts; they do not automatically become a directed attack. Independent lines of evidence must still converge on every element of Article 7 before the threshold is crossed. Until they do, the character remains that of governance and infrastructure failure, not international crime.

Set the stamp down. Set the slogan down. Set the virtue claim down. What remains is the pattern the public record already contains: a classification regime resting on 1996 Cabinet policy because the Bill was never assented to; a non-alignment orientation that can be scored against votes, exercises, ownership rules and litigation outcomes; an AGOA statute that already asks whether activities undermine United States national security or foreign policy interests; and a Rome Statute threshold that a 47.3 percent non-revenue-water figure does not by itself cross. 

The cumulative evidence converges on one testable claim. Official labels do not determine character. Character is the independently verifiable pattern of content, effect, knowledge and organisation. 

The claim is falsifiable: produce a statute that fully authorises classification without further justification, or a multi-year pattern that matches the non-alignment label in both directions, or evidence that meets every element of Article 7, and the scorecard changes. 

Until then the scorecard stands.

Sjoe!
At the end of the day the stamp, the slogan and the virtue claim can all be filed in the same drawer. The drawer is labelled “pending substance.” It has been pending since 1996.

The 2026 Alaska Senate election is a stark illustration of the structural failures inherent in the state's current political system. We are watching a race that is not merely a contest between two individuals, but a symptom of how the administrative state and entrenched elites manipulate outcomes to neutralize genuine conservative opposition.
The central issue in this race is the ranked-choice voting system. This mechanism is designed to reward establishment figures and suppress the authentic, populist energy that characterizes the historic American people. It forces candidates to appeal to a broad, fractured consensus rather than speaking clearly to the convictions of a coherent nation. When you look at how the primary functioned, the system effectively allowed the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, and the Democrat, Mary Peltola, to advance while maneuvering through a field that dilutes the clear-cut choice voters deserve.
Regarding the candidates:
Dan S. Sullivan (R): As the incumbent, Sullivan represents the status quo of the GOP establishment. His tenure has been marked by the typical "go-along-to-get-along" mentality that characterizes the D.C. uniparty. He is an operative of the same managerial class that treats national interests as negotiable and the border as an afterthought. He has failed to offer the robust, nationalist defense of our heritage and sovereignty that the current moment demands.
Mary Peltola (D): Peltola’s candidacy relies on cultivating a crossover coalition, masking the reality that the Democrat party, as a whole, is actively dismantling the foundations of Western Christian civilization. Whether she frames herself as a "moderate" or not, she aligns with a party infrastructure that pushes anti-family, anti-border, and anti-nationalist policies. Her success would be a clear signal that the constituency in Alaska is being misled by a narrative of "moderate" representation that ultimately serves the interests of the leftist cultural revolution.
The polling reflects a highly competitive race, with analysts showing a tight margin. The fact that an incumbent Republican is struggling to secure his seat against a Democrat in a state that, by all rights, should be securely in the hands of patriots, tells you everything you need to know about the lack of inspiring, nationalist leadership within the Republican party.
The race is a microcosm of the broader struggle for the American soul. It is not just about a Senate seat; it is about whether voters will continue to be seduced by institutional maneuvering or if they will eventually reject the regime’s choices entirely. Until candidates emerge who unapologetically prioritize the historic American people, border security, and the preservation of Christian order—rather than just playing the game—we will continue to see these hollow, manipulated contests that fail to resolve the core crises facing our nation.

text:
The Journal of Mad Writing (Halloween Monster “Roleplay” 6) Part 27

I stared down at the journal, turning another brittle page between my bony fingers, though I was beginning to wonder whether there was anything left in the book worth understanding.

Calling it a journal felt generous. It was more like a collection of madness bound together with cracked leather and rusted clasps, its pages crowded with strange diagrams, frantic scribbles, half-finished prayers, and drawings that seemed to grow more disturbing the longer I looked at them. Some pages were covered in circles within circles, connected by lines that wandered like veins across the parchment, while others contained sketches of things that had too many limbs, too many eyes, or, in one particularly unpleasant instance, no head at all, despite having what appeared to be three faces growing out of its chest.

There were repeated phrases, written in different hands, or perhaps the same hand at different stages of its deterioration.

*Restore the broken.* *Complete the incomplete.* *Nothing unfinished may remain.*

That last one had been underlined so many times the nib had nearly torn through the page. I turned another leaf. And there I was. Or, at least, something that was supposed to be me.

The illustration depicted a skeletal figure standing beneath a blackened sky, surrounded by symbols I couldn't begin to decipher. There were notes scrawled in the margins, measurements, arrows, little annotations about my bones, my shadow, and the strange ember burning in my ribcage. Whoever had drawn this had apparently spent a great deal of time imagining what I might become. But it was the name that caught my attention. A line of text identified the figure, followed by a space where a name should have been, an empty stretch of yellowed parchment surrounded by dark, ugly scratches. The ink around it had bled into the fibers, yet the space itself was strangely clean, as though the name had been erased before the ink could even dry.

I ran a finger over it. Nothing. No hidden letters. No impression beneath the parchment. Just an absence that felt more deliberate than any writing in the book. I had seen that kind of absence before, hadn't I? The blank spaces in the ledger. The names that vanished. The things the Girl claimed to remember, and the things the Spirit insisted never existed. I leaned closer to the page. There was a little note beside the illustration.

*The subject was foretold.* Foretold by the Father. My ribs tightened around the ember.

"Oh," I muttered. "That's... not good."

The Father hadn't merely taken an interest in me after I arrived at St. Brigid's. He hadn't simply watched me stumble through his prison, break its rules, raise an army, and accidentally turn myself into something capable of impaling an iron nightmare. Someone had been writing about me. Someone had anticipated me. And judging by the state of the journal, that someone hadn't taken the news particularly well.

I turned the page.

The writing grew larger, more frantic. The letters slanted violently across the parchment, with whole sentences squeezed into margins and crossed out so aggressively that the paper had begun to peel. Brother Mozgus. His name appeared repeatedly, sometimes accompanied by prayers, sometimes by curses. It seemed that before the Father had become the towering thing of ash and feathers that haunted the Ossuary, before his purpose had curdled into something cruel and incomprehensible, Brother Mozgus had become obsessed with the same impossible ambition: to cure the broken.

Not merely me.

Everyone.

He wanted every inmate in the Ossuary restored, every incomplete soul mended, every wandering identity returned to its rightful owner. At first, the writings suggested that his intentions might have been noble. He recorded treatments, experiments, lessons, and elaborate repentance exercises intended to prepare the prisoners for their eventual restoration. Then the entries changed. The treatments became punishments. The lessons became interrogations. The repentance exercises became ordeals that dragged on long after the prisoners had begged for mercy. I found a crude drawing of a row of inmates kneeling beneath a great crucifix, their heads bowed while a tall figure stood over them with a rod in his hand. Someone had scratched out the faces of every prisoner. In the margin, a sentence had been written so many times that I could barely distinguish the words.

*They must learn to accept what they are.*

I thought of the screaming I had heard through the walls. The sounds of iron against stone. The prisoners returning from Calva's chambers with their bodies trembling and their eyes looking toward something no one else could see.

Well. That sounded familiar. One entry caught my eye in particular.

**Rosarah Sterling.**

A young student, full of potential, according to the accompanying notes. She had apparently been brought into the Ossuary to learn, to be corrected, to be made into whatever the authorities believed she ought to become.

Then she went bad.

That was the phrase used in the journal. *Went bad.* As though she were a piece of fruit left in a cellar. The writing described her refusal to participate in the repentance training, her resistance to the lessons, and her eventual passing. A few lines mentioned her unusual abilities, though whoever had recorded them had either been unwilling or unable to explain what they were.

There was no comforting conclusion. No explanation of what happened to her, or whether she had ever been given a choice. Just a small, hurried note at the bottom of the page.

*The student failed to accept correction.*

I closed the journal halfway.

"Wonderful," I whispered. "A school where the detention can kill you."

A cold draft swept through the chamber. The ember in my chest dimmed. I looked back down. The next illustration had been drawn in a much steadier hand. And this one was rather impressive.

It showed me standing above a landscape of jagged mountains, with a dark cloud coiling around my skeletal body like a living mantle. A crimson radiance poured from my ribcage, tracing the delicate architecture of my bones in burning lines, and the shadows around me rose into great spiraling ribbons that stretched toward the heavens.

My feet were nowhere near the ground. I was flying. Or perhaps soaring was the more appropriate word, because the figure in the illustration seemed to drift through the midnight sky itself, wrapped in a storm of black vapor and starlight, with wisps of darkness trailing behind it like the torn edges of a funeral shroud.

A long cape billowed from its shoulders, although it appeared to be woven from shadow rather than cloth, its ragged edges dissolving into flocks of tiny black shapes that resembled bats, crows, or perhaps pieces of the night torn loose by the wind.

In one hand, the skeletal figure held a scepter crowned with a grinning skull, its hollow eye sockets burning with twin red flames. A crooked silver crown floated above its skull, surrounded by a ring of spectral candles, each one flickering with a different colored fire. Its fingers were long and elegant, tipped with blackened claws, and delicate chains hung from its wrists, carrying tiny bells that seemed to ring even in the stillness of the illustration. The darkness gathered around its spine like wings, enormous and ragged, spreading outward into a pair of shadowy pinions that swallowed the stars behind it. Its skull had been adorned with intricate markings, spiraling runes carved into the bone, while its empty eye sockets glowed with the same scarlet light that ran through its ribs. A storm swirled around its head, and below it, a procession of lesser skeletons marched across the mountains, carrying lanterns made from skulls.

It was magnificent. Terrifying, certainly, but magnificent. I tilted my head.

"Wow. That guy got quite the imagination."

I examined the little notes surrounding the drawing.

*The Sovereign of the Last Night.* *The Crowned Remnant.* *The King Beneath the Bells.*

I paused.

"Three titles? Really? Couldn't settle on one?"

There was another sentence beneath them, written in smaller letters.

*He shall rule over all things forgotten, and nothing lost shall remain beyond his reach.*

The ember stirred again. For a moment, I thought I heard a whisper from somewhere deep inside my ribcage.

*He does not know what he is looking at.*

I shut the book.

"Not now."

The whisper subsided. I was about to call for Blake when I noticed something moving along the wall. A small face had appeared between two blocks of ancient stone. A pale forehead. Two eyes. A little nose. The Girl. She watched me from the crack, her expression unreadable, her chin resting on a hand that seemed to emerge from the wall itself. I stared back.

"Do you ever knock?"

"No."

"Of course not."

She glanced at the journal.

"You found it."

"That's generally what happens when you send someone to retrieve something."

"You read it."

"I did. Some of it, anyway. I'm not sure I want to know what the rest says."

Her eyes moved to the illustration I had left open. For the briefest moment, her expression changed. Not fear, exactly. Recognition. Then it vanished.

"You knew him before he went mad, didn't you?" I asked.

The Girl looked toward the corridor behind me.

"Yes."

"Brother Mozgus?"

"He was like a father to me."

She spoke quietly, with none of her usual teasing.

"Long ago."

I studied her face.

"Are you the girl in this journal? Rosarah Sterling?"

Her eyes narrowed.

"Where did you find that name?"

"In the book.”

“I know, I found some things in the gem. You know, the one I had you retrieve. The former Warden's little souvenir."

She frowned and  said nothing.

"That was you, wasn't it? You were his student."

"Yes."

I waited for her to elaborate. She didn't.

"Do I need to speak your name to learn about you?" I asked. "Is that how this works? I say the right words, and suddenly I know your life story? A gift of the spirit?"

Her fingers curled against the stone.

"I already told you. You don't get to know what happened."

"Then perhaps you could tell me why you sent me after the things you did."

"No."

"Why you needed the collar."

"No."

"Why you keep appearing in places where you have no business being."

"Because I can."

"You're a remarkably helpful person."

She gave me a thin smile.

"I hate her."

"Who?"

"The Warden."

That got my attention.

"Sister Calva?"

"She was my teacher. She saw what I could do."

The Girl's voice grew sharper.

"She saw the power I had, and she was afraid."

"What power?"

She hesitated. For someone who could crawl through walls, steal fragments of her own soul, and apparently hijack my body whenever she felt like it, she seemed surprisingly reluctant to discuss her abilities.

"I could see things other people couldn't," she said at last. "Things that weren't there yet. Things that had already happened. Sometimes I could see them in people, sometimes in places."

"Prophecy?"

"Not exactly."

"That's helpful."

"I could pull names from the ether. Names people had lost, names they had never spoken, names that belonged to things that shouldn't have names at all."

I glanced at the journal.

"That sounds rather useful."

"It was."

"And the other ability?"

Her eyes drifted toward the ceiling.

"I could sense how people felt about me, even from far away. Their affection. Their hatred. Their fear."

"That sounds miserable."

"It was."

For once, she didn't sound like she was trying to win an argument.

"I tried to learn from the Sister," she continued. "I did everything she asked. I listened to her lessons. I followed her rules. I wanted her to teach me how to understand what I was seeing."

"And she refused?"

"She was frightened. She locked me away."

The Girl's fingers disappeared into the wall, one by one.

"She said it was for my own good."

I thought of Calva's familiar explanation for everything.

Safety.

Protection.

Repentance.

Funny how many terrible things could be justified with a comforting word.

"That does sound like her," I said.

The Girl watched me.

"Do you believe me?"

"I believe you were hurt. I'm less certain about everything else."

"Good."

"Good?"

"You're learning."

I leaned against the table, the journal resting between us.

"I feel like there's more going on than you're letting on."

"There is."

"Care to elaborate?"

"No."

"You're exhausting."

"You don't get to know what happened. You don't get to say my name. I won't let you."

"Then how am I supposed to trust you?"

She looked directly into my empty eye sockets.

"You can't."

That answer was so immediate that I had nothing to say.

"You can only use me to your advantage," she continued. "That's what people do here. The Warden uses you. The Father uses you. Even the thing inside you uses you."

The ember flared. I didn't like that she had mentioned it.

"Careful," I said.

"Am I wrong?"

I didn't answer. The Girl smiled faintly.

"Even now, you could get into trouble for talking to me. You know that, don't you?"

"Yes. I'm beginning to notice a pattern."

"I know what I must do on Halloween."

There it was again. Halloween. The word seemed to hang between us, heavier than it ought to have been.

"To get free?" I asked. "Or to get revenge?"

Her expression hardened.

"To make things right."

"That's a rather loaded answer."

"That's all you're going to get from me."

"You're not going to tell me what you want?"

"No."

"Not even a hint?"

She tilted her head.

"You've had enough hints."

Then the stones around her face began to shift.

"Wait," I said. "What exactly do you mean by make things right?"

She was already sinking into the wall.

"Ask the Father."

"That's the last person I want to ask!"

Her smile lingered for another moment. Then she disappeared. The wall was whole again. I stood there, staring at the place where her face had been, while the journal lay open beneath my hand. There were many things I didn't understand about the Ossuary. The Father. The Girl. The bells. My name. But I was beginning to suspect that all these mysteries were connected, and that every answer I found only brought me closer to something that had been waiting for me for a very long time.

"Well," I muttered, "that's reassuring."

"Talking to the walls again?"

I turned. Blake was standing in the doorway, his waxen face twisted into a familiar expression of weary amusement.

"Technically, the wall was talking to me."

"Ah. Much better."

He glanced at the journal.

"Find anything useful?"

"Depends on your definition of useful. I learned that the previous Warden was a lunatic, the current Warden is probably a lunatic, and I'm apparently destined to become some sort of skeletal night king."

Blake stared at me.

"You're what?"

I turned the journal around and showed him the illustration. He leaned closer. For several seconds, he said nothing. Then he pointed at the floating crown.

"Do you get to keep the hat?"

"I don't know."

"Shame. You'd look ridiculous without it."

"Thank you, Blake."

"Anytime, kid."

He reached for the flintlock resting on the table, carefully checking the weapon before tucking it against himself.

"Come on. Let's get out of this slice of hell."

He headed into the corridor, then paused and looked back at me.

"You coming?"

I took one last look at the journal. The illustration of the crowned skeleton seemed darker than before. The red ink across its ribcage had begun to shine faintly, as though a little ember had been trapped beneath the parchment. I closed the cover.

"Yeah. I'm coming."

I followed Blake out, though I couldn't shake the feeling that something in the room had noticed us leaving. And that it was disappointed.

***

The corridor outside was cold enough to make my bones ache. Which was impressive, considering I didn't have any flesh left to complain about it. Blake walked ahead, his footsteps producing a soft, sticky sound against the stone. The flintlock rested in his hands, and every so often he glanced over his shoulder to make sure I was following.

The prison was unusually quiet.

Normally, there would be shouting from the cells, the distant clatter of chains, the muttering of prisoners arguing with themselves or with things that weren't there. Now there was only the occasional creak of ancient timber and the whisper of air moving through cracks in the masonry.

Somewhere far away, a bell chimed. Blake stopped. I stopped with him. We listened. Nothing followed.

"Was that one of the bells?" I asked.

"Probably."

"That didn't sound particularly convincing."

"I'm a wax man, kid. Not a bell expert."

We continued. As we approached the main corridor, I noticed that several of the candles had gone out. The ones that remained burned with thin, colorless flames. A pair of inmates stood outside their cells, staring toward the ceiling. One of them began whispering a prayer. The other was counting on his fingers. I remembered Calva's warning.

*Don't count the bells.*

I hurried past them. At the end of the corridor, a familiar click-clack approached. Sister Calva emerged from the shadows. Her dark habit swept over the floor, and her rusty billhook tapped against the stone with every measured step. She looked at Blake, then at me, then at the flintlock. Her expression did not improve.

"Did you get it?"

Blake lifted the gun slightly.

"Right here."

"I was asking him."

"Oh."

I straightened.

"Yes, we got it."

Calva's gaze moved to my skull.

"You talked to her."

I hesitated. Blake slowly turned his head toward me. There was a long silence.

"Yes," I admitted. "But…"

"What did she tell you?"

"Not much."

"That's not an answer."

"She said you were her teacher."

Calva's face remained still.

"And?"

"She said you were afraid of her."

For the first time, I saw something shift behind Calva's https://t.co/KYOFPQAZMt was gone almost immediately.

"What else?"

"She said she knew what she had to do on Halloween."

Calva's grip tightened around the handle of her billhook.

"What did she say she intended to do?"

"Make things right."

The Warden stared at me. Then she gave a short, humorless laugh.

"Of course she did."

"Do you know what that means?"

"I know what she believes it means."

"Which is?"

"Not your concern."

"Funny. Everyone keeps telling me that."

Calva stepped closer.

"Listen carefully, skeleton man. Whatever she tells you, whatever she promises, you must remember that she is not a child who has merely lost her way."

Her voice lowered.

"She is something that has learned to wear the shape of one."

I glanced at the wall behind her.

"She told me you tormented her."

Calva's expression hardened.

"She was a bad student."

"That's what the journal said about her, too."

"She hurt the others. She showed no remorse for what she was, or what she might become. She was brought here to learn."

"Learn what?"

"Control. Restraint. Repentance."

"Sounds like a lovely curriculum."

Her eyes narrowed.

"You weren't there."

"No. I wasn't."

"She was ill," Calva continued, her voice becoming colder. "The doctors could not help her. Her condition worsened, and her abilities became increasingly difficult to contain. She saw things that should never have been seen. She spoke names that should never have been spoken."

"Then why keep her here?"

"Because there was nowhere else to take her."

For a moment, the corridor seemed to grow colder. Calva looked away.

"She was my responsibility."

That sounded almost like regret. Almost. Then she thrust out her hand.

"Give me the flintlock."

Blake offered it to her. Calva took the weapon with both hands, examining its dark metal barrel, the worn wooden stock, and the strange markings carved into the lock. Her thumb traced a symbol near the trigger. The expression on her face changed. Not fear. Recognition.

"Where did you find this?"

"With the other things," I said. "Why?"

She didn't answer immediately. Instead, she tilted the flintlock toward the candlelight. The markings seemed to shimmer. A faint clicking sound came from somewhere inside the weapon. I stepped backward.

"Is it supposed to do that?"

"No."

"Wonderful."

Calva's fingers tightened around the stock.

"This is a relic."

"Of course it is."

"An old one."

She turned it over.

"The Iron Warden fears it. The thing you encountered below is not simply a creature of iron. It is a remnant of an older authority, bound to mechanisms and laws that no longer serve their original purpose."

"That sounds like a very elaborate way of saying it's a giant metal nightmare."

"It is also a way of saying that it can be stopped."

She examined the weapon again.

"If we use this against it, we may be able to keep it away from the upper prison."

"May?"

"Don't become greedy, skeleton. Certainty is a luxury we cannot afford."

She slipped the flintlock beneath her cloak. Then she looked at me, and for the briefest moment, her expression softened.

"Ah, listen to me talking your ear off."

I glanced at my skull.

"I'd offer you the other one, but…"

"Go rest."

"Yes, Sister."

"You've earned it."

She began to turn away, then paused.

"One more thing."

I waited.

"Toll is back."

I remembered the frantic prisoner, his wild eyes, his endless counting.

"Back from where?"

"Repentance."

Calva adjusted her cloak.

"He is feeling much better. You should speak to him."

Something about the way she said it made the ember in my chest grow cold.

"Much better," I repeated.

"Yes."

Then she walked away.

Click-clack.

Click-clack.

Click-clack.

Her footsteps faded into the depths of the Ossuary. Blake and I stood in silence. Finally, he glanced at me.

"Well."

"Well."

"Want to see the patient?"

I looked toward the corridor where Calva had disappeared.

"Not particularly."

"Me neither."

We went anyway.

Toll's cell was several corridors away, tucked into a narrow passage where the walls were stained with damp and the ceiling hung low enough to make me feel as though the prison were leaning over to listen. The door stood slightly ajar. Blake pushed it open.

"Toll?"

The cell was dim. A narrow cot stood against one wall, its blankets neatly folded. A tin cup sat on a little table, beside a plate of untouched food. Toll sat on the edge of the cot. His hands rested on his knees. His clothes were clean. His face was not. Fresh scars crossed his forehead and cheeks, and his wrists were wrapped in stained bandages. There were marks around his throat, too, angry red lines disappearing beneath his collar. His eyes, once wild and restless, were now fixed on some invisible point across the room. He looked almost peaceful. That was the worst part.

The bells rang.

A deep, resonant toll rolled through the walls, followed by another, then another, each note vibrating through the stone and into my bones. Toll did not flinch. He didn't even blink. Blake stepped inside.

"Hey, Toll."

No response.

"Heard the Warden did a number on you."

Blake shifted uneasily.

"How are you holding up?"

Toll stared forward. The bells continued. I watched his hands. They didn't move.

"Can you hear us?" I asked.

Toll's lips parted. For several seconds, nothing came out. Then he spoke.

"The bells..."

His voice was so quiet I almost missed it. Blake crouched beside him.

"What about them?"

"They were wrong."

The bells rang again. Toll didn't react.

"They were always wrong," he whispered. "But I thought... I thought I could understand them. I thought if I counted them, if I listened long enough, I could find the pattern."

His fingers twitched.

"I was wrong."

Blake looked at me. I said nothing. Toll swallowed.

"They weren't ringing for the hours. Not for the prayers. Not for the dead."

His face remained blank, but his voice began to tremble.

"They rang when something changed."

The room seemed to tighten around us.

"When history was rewritten," he continued. "When something was altered. When a name was taken away, or something that never existed was made real."

I thought of the journal. The blank space where my name should have been. The missing inmates. The prison that had somehow always existed, even though it had been built upon the remains of a catastrophe. Toll's head tilted a fraction.

"The bells were telling me."

"Telling you what?" Blake asked.

"When the world changed."

The bells rang again. A low note shuddered through the floor. Toll's mouth opened slightly. For the first time, his expression changed. Not into fear. Into recognition.

“The Warden took most of my hearing… it takes everything I got to…” he freezes. “Your name," he whispered.

I felt the ember flare.

"What?"

"The bells..."

He looked at me. His eyes were wet.

"They started calling your name."

My fingers curled.

"I told no one my name.."

Blake looks at me. "I know."

"Then how could they call it?"

Toll shook his head slowly.

Published January 5, 2003 - 6:20 p.m.
A year has passed since President Kim Dae-jung and North Korean leader Kim Jong-il held the first-ever summit meeting between North and South Korea.

South Korean corporations wholeheartedly welcomed the historic talks, thinking it could give them the inside track to the North's human and natural resources, as well as its market.

At the end of last year, the two Koreas reached a series of agreements on double tax prevention, investment guarantees, dispute resolution mechanisms and payment clearance. The agreements are awaiting ratification by the National Assembly.

The Unification Church completed an auto repair factory near Pyongyang last September, and Taechang has opened a mineral water factory near Mount Kumgang.

The Fall of Babylon (Revelation 18)
Revelation 17 showed us the fall of Rome. Revelation 17:16 showed the great prostitute made desolate and naked. She is stripped of her power and authority and is burned up with fire. God is the one who purposed this fall to occur. Revelation 18 describes the impact and meaning of the fall of Rome.

Fallen Is Babylon (18:1-3)
Another angel comes down from heaven, carrying great authority and full of glory. He calls out the message of judgment. Babylon is fallen because of its great immoralities. Once again the angel speaks with prophetic certainty. Though Rome has not fallen yet at the time of the writing of Revelation, the angel declares its fall in the past tense to show how surely Rome and her empire will fall. Rome has become a dwelling place of wickedness and evil. Not only has Rome been the heart of wickedness, but the nations “have drunk the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality.” The nations are not innocent. They also have been participants in the immorality of Rome. The merchants of the earth has prospered through the immorality of Rome. History reveals the luxurious living that took place in Rome over the centuries because of its extensive trade routes. Trade extended well past the border of Rome’s empire, which was millions of square miles. Trade routes also existed to India and China. Archaeology has found many pottery sherds from the far east. The merchants were made rich by buying, selling, and trading goods with Rome.

Call To God’s People (18:4-8)
Another voice calls out from heaven for God’s people to come out from her. This is a prophetic reference from Jeremiah and Isaiah’s ministries.

Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy, proclaim it, send it out to the end of the earth; say, “The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!” (Isaiah 48:20 ESV)Depart, depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing; go out from the midst of her; purify yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the LORD. (Isaiah 52:11 ESV)“Flee from the midst of Babylon; let every one save his life! Be not cut off in her punishment, for this is the time of the LORD’s vengeance, the repayment he is rendering her. Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD’s hand, making all the earth drunken; the nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations went mad. (Jeremiah 51:6–7 ESV)

The call of the voice from heaven is for the people of God to remove themselves from the ways and immoralities of Rome. Do not participate in the sinfulness of that world. Otherwise, you will share in the plagues that are coming upon Rome and her empire. The judgment of the seven bowls showed seven plagues being poured out on the beast and its throne. God gives an important warning. If you act like the world, you will be judged with the world. Come out from the world and separate yourselves from the Roman ways and sins. They have heaped up their sins as high as the heavens and God has remembered those sins. God is going to pay her back. God is going to pay her double for her deeds. This is just because its sins were so severe that it not only affect them, but also carried the whole world into sinfulness with its idolatry and paganism. God calls for a double portion to be mixed for her in the cup. Recall that we saw this cup as the cup of God’s anger poured full strength (Revelation 14:10). The voice from heaven says that we need to make it a double. Double up the portion in the cup of God’s anger.

Verses 7-8 continue to explain why God’s wrath is so violent against Rome and her empire. Rome glorified itself and lived in luxury. No one gave glory to God for their prosperity. They elevated themselves and glorified themselves. Further, they think they will never fall. They think that these times will never change. They think this prosperity will never end because they think they did it all. They rule and think that rule will never end. God says in verse 8 that this is the reason that they will be struck down suddenly. Rather than life and prosperity, the empire will crumble into death, mourning, and famine. Revelation is not predicting that Rome fell in one day, just as the scriptures are not predicting other nations falling in one day (cf. Isaiah 47:9). It is a symbol of the suddenness of the loss of power and authority. It would seem that the empire would never end and suddenly the empire will be in trouble. It will lose its power and be destroyed. This is the imagery of the fire. Revelation is not predicting Rome literally burning (cf. Isaiah 47:14). The fire is a symbol of judgment. Its time of glory and rule is over. The empire has fallen. Rome has lost her power.

Before we leave verses 4-8 we must see this paragraph contains very important messages for our country. The parallels are very strong. We are full of prosperity and wealth just like Rome. Most live in wasteful, luxurious living just like Rome. Our country shows the same arrogance in thinking that it is the world power that will never fall. Certainly the sins of our nation are heaped as high as heaven. The more this nation turns people away from the true God to worship false gods and religions, the closer we come to meeting the same judgment that Rome met for its sins.

text:
You have shifted the standard of evidence in successive replies.

You began by asserting that the 2018 elections were stolen from PML-N as the culmination of a campaign that started with a “fake” 2014 dharna, and that PTI therefore has no moral ground to raise the issue of stolen elections. When asked why Khawaja Asif contacted Bajwa on election night while trailing, you replied that he was “always pro-establishment.” When shown his own anti-establishment speech in the National Assembly, the position shifted again to the claim that all politicians lie and that Imran does too. Earlier the conditional “if Imran gets another chance he will collude” was restated as a certainty (“it is a matter of when”).

These successive adjustments do not engage the contemporaneous record. After the 2013 elections, FAFEN data show PML-N candidates filed more petitions before election tribunals (approximately 64–66) than PTI candidates (approximately 51–58). PTI’s public demand at the time was limited to the reopening of four specific National Assembly constituencies; the tribunals examining those seats identified irregularities including missing stamps and invalid votes. The 2014 sit-in lasted 126 days and was a real protest, not a fabrication. In 2018 Imran publicly offered to open any constituency in which PML-N alleged rigging; PTI candidates subsequently filed more election petitions (76) than PML-N candidates (43). PTI also secured roughly four million more votes than PML-N while PML-N retained strength in central Punjab. EU observers recorded pre-poll measures that disadvantaged PML-N rather than a clean transfer of the result.

If the 2018 election had already been stolen from PML-N, there was no operational reason for Asif to contact the Chief of Army Staff on election night while trailing, nor for results to be issued on unsigned white paper (a sequence Asif has himself described). Speculation about future conduct does not cancel the documented Form-45/47 discrepancies of 2024, nor does it erase the petition numbers and tribunal findings from 2013 and 2018.

"Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them! Woe to the inhabitants of the earth and the sea! For the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, because he knows that he has a short time." 

- Revelation Chapter 12:12

The Serpent: "You will surely not die. For God knows that in the day you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."

- Genesis 3:4-5

Socialism: "We promise you this. We promise you that.  Vote for us, you guinea pigs."

The deception is ancient. Only the packaging has changed. 

The strategy is as old as Eden: exploit human desire, prey upon discontent, promise a better existence, and make people believe that what they crave can be obtained without consequence. Dress the promise in the language of compassion, equality, and security, and the deception becomes more seductive.

But promises are not proof, benevolent rhetoric is not a guarantee of benevolent outcomes, and good intentions do not abolish the consequences of bad ideas. When political power exploits people's hopes to secure their obedience, the price may ultimately be paid in personal liberty, individual responsibility, and human dignity.

The serpent offered the fruit. The politician offers the promise. Both know the power of telling people what they long to hear.

And the most dangerous deception is not the one that appears evil, but the one that disguises itself as salvation.

The question is not merely what is promised, but what is concealed, what is surrendered, and who ultimately pays the price.

Brazil’s left is using the courts against Flávio Bolsonaro while ignoring the rule changes that helped Lula. On Tuesday Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino ordered the Federal Police to investigate possible foreign financing of Flávio’s campaign, including contacts with the Rockbridge Network co-founded by JD Vance. The claims came from another candidate who offered no public evidence that money actually reached the campaign. Rockbridge denies any involvement.

This sits on top of everything else already happening. Flávio is contesting the two-hour voting extension ordered by Justice Cristiano Zanin after polls had closed in many places. Brazil’s own TSE president said there was no rule authorizing that extension. The TSE is Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, the body that runs national elections.

Minutes after the race was called, a PSOL deputy called for Flávio’s arrest and passport seizure so he couldn’t leave the country. PSOL is the Socialism and Liberty Party, a left-wing party further left than Lula’s PT. PT is the Workers’ Party, Lula’s longtime party. Now another inquiry opens into unproven foreign contacts.

This is what the left does with lawfare. They try to overwhelm you with it so they win on sheer numbers, not on sensibility or statute. They don’t want to give people enough time to push back and expose the previous abuse of power.

They just keep abusing power and prosecute anyone who dares to call them out. Lula and his coalition are tyrants. It’s as simple as that. They’ve weaponized their judicial system and Supreme Court to act as a weapon against opposition. Everyone can see it.

Brazilian law bars foreign campaign assistance, so looking into reported discussions is within the rules. The pattern is what matters. The same institutions that treated an unauthorized extension for voting during the election as ordinary administration treat any conservative challenge as a threat that needs immediate investigation.

Democrats and leftists abroad praised Lula’s win anyway. They stay quiet about the court moves against the man who won’t concede. This is how the left operates once it holds institutional power. Change the rules mid-count, label the opponent a criminal, and open new inquiries while the challenge is still pending. Sunday in Brazil was the latest example. Tuesday’s order is more of the same.

text:
QUAS PRIMAS: ENCYCLICAL OF POPE PIUS XI ON THE FEAST OF CHRIST THE KING TO OUR VENERABLE BRETHREN THE PATRIARCHS, PRIMATES, ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND OTHER ORDINARIES IN PEACE AND COMMUNION WITH THE APOSTOLIC SEE.
.
Venerable Brethren, Greeting and the Apostolic Benediction.
In the first Encyclical Letter which We addressed at the beginning of Our Pontificate to the Bishops of the universal Church, We referred to the chief causes of the difficulties under which mankind was laboring. And We remember saying that these manifold evils in the world were due to the fact that the majority of men had thrust Jesus Christ and his holy law out of their lives; that these had no place either in private affairs or in politics: and we said further, that as long as individuals and states refused to submit to the rule of our Savior, there would be no really hopeful prospect of a lasting peace among nations. Men must look for the peace of Christ in the Kingdom of Christ; and that We promised to do as far as lay in Our power. In the Kingdom of Christ, that is, it seemed to Us that peace could not be more effectually restored nor fixed upon a firmer basis than through the restoration of the Empire of Our Lord. We were led in the meantime to indulge the hope of a brighter future at the sight of a more widespread and keener interest evinced in Christ and his Church, the one Source of Salvation, a sign that men who had formerly spurned the rule of our Redeemer and had exiled themselves from his kingdom were preparing, and even hastening, to return to the duty of obedience.
2. The many notable and memorable events which have occurred during this Holy Year have given great honor and glory to Our Lord and King, the Founder of the Church.
3. At the Missionary Exhibition men have been deeply impressed in seeing the increasing zeal of the Church for the spread of the kingdom of her Spouse to the most far distant regions of the earth. They have seen how many countries have been won to the Catholic name through the unremitting labor and self-sacrifice of missionaries, and the vastness of the regions which have yet to be subjected to the sweet and saving yoke of our King. All those who in the course of the Holy Year have thronged to this city under the leadership of their Bishops or priests had but one aim - namely, to expiate their sins - and at the tombs of the Apostles and in Our Presence to promise loyalty to the rule of Christ.
4. A still further light of glory was shed upon his kingdom, when after due proof of their heroic virtue, We raised to the honors of the altar six confessors and virgins. It was a great joy, a great consolation, that filled Our heart when in the majestic basilica of St. Peter Our decree was acclaimed by an immense multitude with the hymn of thanksgiving, Tu Rex gloriae Christe. We saw men and nations cut off from God, stirring up strife and discord and hurrying along the road to ruin and death, while the Church of God carries on her work of providing food for the spiritual life of men, nurturing and fostering generation after generation of men and women dedicated to Christ, faithful and subject to him in his earthly kingdom, called by him to eternal bliss in the kingdom of heaven.
5. Moreover, since this jubilee Year marks the sixteenth centenary of the Council of Nicaea, We commanded that event to be celebrated, and We have done so in the Vatican basilica. There is a special reason for this in that the Nicene Synod defined and proposed for Catholic belief the dogma of the Consubstantiality of the Onlybegotten with the Father, and added to the Creed the words "of whose kingdom there shall be no end," thereby affirming the kingly dignity of Christ.
6. Since this Holy Year therefore has provided more than one opportunity to enhance the glory of the kingdom of Christ, we deem it in keeping with our Apostolic office to accede to the desire of many of the Cardinals, Bishops, and faithful, made known to Us both individually and collectively, by closing this Holy Year with the insertion into the Sacred Liturgy of a special feast of the Kingship of Our Lord Jesus Christ. This matter is so dear to Our heart, Venerable Brethren, that I would wish to address to you a few words concerning it. It will be for you later to explain in a manner suited to the understanding of the faithful what We are about to say concerning the Kingship of Christ, so that the annual feast which We shall decree may be attended with much fruit and produce beneficial results in the future.
7. It has long been a common custom to give to Christ the metaphorical title of "King," because of the high degree of perfection whereby he excels all creatures. So he is said to reign "in the hearts of men," both by reason of the keenness of his intellect and the extent of his knowledge, and also because he is very truth, and it is from him that truth must be obediently received by all mankind. He reigns, too, in the wills of men, for in him the human will was perfectly and entirely obedient to the Holy Will of God, and further by his grace and inspiration he so subjects our free-will as to incite us to the most noble endeavors. He is King of hearts, too, by reason of his "charity which exceedeth all knowledge." And his mercy and kindness[1] which draw all men to him, for never has it been known, nor will it ever be, that man be loved so much and so universally as Jesus Christ. But if we ponder this matter more deeply, we cannot but see that the title and the power of King belongs to Christ as man in the strict and proper sense too. For it is only as man that he may be said to have received from the Father "power and glory and a kingdom,"[2] since the Word of God, as consubstantial with the Father, has all things in common with him, and therefore has necessarily supreme and absolute dominion over all things created.
8. Do we not read throughout the Scriptures that Christ is the King? He it is that shall come out of Jacob to rule,[3] who has been set by the Father as king over Sion, his holy mount, and shall have the Gentiles for his inheritance, and the utmost parts of the earth for his possession.[4] In the nuptial hymn, where the future King of Israel is hailed as a most rich and powerful monarch, we read: "Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of thy kingdom is a scepter of righteousness."[5] There are many similar passages, but there is one in which Christ is even more clearly indicated. Here it is foretold that his kingdom will have no limits, and will be enriched with justice and peace: "in his days shall justice spring up, and abundance of peace...And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth."[6]
9. The testimony of the Prophets is even more abundant. That of Isaias is well known: "For a child is born to us and a son is given to us, and the government is upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God the mighty, the Father of the world to come, the Prince of Peace. His empire shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace. He shall sit upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom; to establish it and strengthen it with judgment and with justice, from henceforth and for ever."[7] With Isaias the other Prophets are in agreement. So Jeremias foretells the "just seed" that shall rest from the house of David - the Son of David that shall reign as king, "and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth."[8] So, too, Daniel, who announces the kingdom that the God of heaven shall found, "that shall never be destroyed, and shall stand for ever."[9] And again he says: "I beheld, therefore, in the vision of the night, and, lo! one like the son of man came with the clouds of heaven. And he came even to the Ancient of days: and they presented him before him. And he gave him power and glory and a kingdom: and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed."[10] The prophecy of Zachary concerning the merciful King "riding upon an ass and upon a colt the foal of an ass" entering Jerusalem as "the just and savior," amid the acclamations of the multitude,[11] was recognized as fulfilled by the holy evangelists themselves.
10. This same doctrine of the Kingship of Christ which we have found in the Old Testament is even more clearly taught and confirmed in the New. The Archangel, announcing to the Virgin that she should bear a Son, says that "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father, and he shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end."[12]
11. Moreover, Christ himself speaks of his own kingly authority: in his last discourse, speaking of the rewards and punishments that will be the eternal lot of the just and the damned; in his reply to the Roman magistrate, who asked him publicly whether he were a king or not; after his resurrection, when giving to his Apostles the mission of teaching and baptizing all nations, he took the opportunity to call himself king,[13] confirming the title publicly,[14] and solemnly proclaimed that all power was given him in heaven and on earth.[15] These words can only be taken to indicate the greatness of his power, the infinite extent of his kingdom. What wonder, then, that he whom St. John calls the "prince of the kings of the earth"[16] appears in the Apostle's vision of the future as he who "hath on his garment and on his thigh written 'King of kings and Lord of lords!'."[17] It is Christ whom the Father "hath appointed heir of all things";[18] "for he must reign until at the end of the world he hath put all his enemies under the feet of God and the Father."[19]
12. It was surely right, then, in view of the common teaching of the sacred books, that the Catholic Church, which is the kingdom of Christ on earth, destined to be spread among all men and all nations, should with every token of veneration salute her Author and Founder in her annual liturgy as King and Lord, and as King of Kings. And, in fact, she used these titles, giving expression with wonderful variety of language to one and the same concept, both in ancient psalmody and in the Sacramentaries. She uses them daily now in the prayers publicly offered to God, and in offering the Immaculate Victim. The perfect harmony of the Eastern liturgies with our own in this continual praise of Christ the King shows once more the truth of the axiom: Legem credendi lex statuit supplicandi. The rule of faith is indicated by the law of our worship.
13. The foundation of this power and dignity of Our Lord is rightly indicated by Cyril of Alexandria. "Christ," he says, "has dominion over all creatures, a dominion not seized by violence nor usurped, but his by essence and by nature."[20] His kingship is founded upon the ineffable hypostatic union. From this it follows not only that Christ is to be adored by angels and men, but that to him as man angels and men are subject, and must recognize his empire; by reason of the hypostatic union Christ has power over all creatures. But a thought that must give us even greater joy and consolation is this that Christ is our King by acquired, as well as by natural right, for he is our Redeemer. Would that they who forget what they have cost their Savior might recall the words: "You were not redeemed with corruptible things, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb unspotted and undefiled."[21] We are no longer our own property, for Christ has purchased us "with a great price";[22] our very bodies are the "members of Christ."[23]
14. Let Us explain briefly the nature and meaning of this lordship of Christ. It consists, We need scarcely say, in a threefold power which is essential to lordship. This is sufficiently clear from the scriptural testimony already adduced concerning the universal dominion of our Redeemer, and moreover it is a dogma of faith that Jesus Christ was given to man, not only as our Redeemer, but also as a law-giver, to whom obedience is due.[24] Not only do the gospels tell us that he made laws, but they present him to us in the act of making them. Those who keep them show their love for their Divine Master, and he promises that they shall remain in his love.[25] He claimed judicial power as received from his Father, when the Jews accused him of breaking the Sabbath by the miraculous cure of a sick man. "For neither doth the Father judge any man; but hath given all judgment to the Son."[26] In this power is included the right of rewarding and punishing all men living, for this right is inseparable from that of judging. Executive power, too, belongs to Christ, for all must obey his commands; none may escape them, nor the sanctions he has imposed.
15. This kingdom is spiritual and is concerned with spiritual things. That this is so the above quotations from Scripture amply prove, and Christ by his own action confirms it. On many occasions, when the Jews and even the Apostles wrongly supposed that the Messiah would restore the liberties and the kingdom of Israel, he repelled and denied such a suggestion. When the populace thronged around him in admiration and would have acclaimed him King, he shrank from the honor and sought safety in flight. Before the Roman magistrate he declared that his kingdom was not of this world. The gospels present this kingdom as one which men prepare to enter by penance, and cannot actually enter except by faith and by baptism, which, though an external rite, signifies and produces an interior regeneration. This kingdom is opposed to none other than to that of Satan and to the power of darkness. It demands of its subjects a spirit of detachment from riches and earthly things, and a spirit of gentleness. They must hunger and thirst after justice, and more than this, they must deny themselves and carry the cross.
16. Christ as our Redeemer purchased the Church at the price of his own blood; as priest he offered himself, and continues to offer himself as a victim for our sins. Is it not evident, then, that his kingly dignity partakes in a manner of both these offices?
17. It would be a grave error, on the other hand, to say that Christ has no authority whatever in civil affairs, since, by virtue of the absolute empire over all creatures committed to him by the Father, all things are in his power. Nevertheless, during his life on earth he refrained from the exercise of such authority, and although he himself disdained to possess or to care for earthly goods, he did not, nor does he today, interfere with those who possess them. Non eripit mortalia qui regna dat caelestia.[27]
18. Thus the empire of our Redeemer embraces all men. To use the words of Our immortal predecessor, Pope Leo XIII: "His empire includes not only Catholic nations, not only baptized persons who, though of right belonging to the Church, have been led astray by error, or have been cut off from her by schism, but also all those who are outside the Christian faith; so that truly the whole of mankind is subject to the power of Jesus Christ."[28] Nor is there any difference in this matter between the individual and the family or the State; for all men, whether collectively or individually, are under the dominion of Christ. In him is the salvation of the individual, in him is the salvation of society. "Neither is there salvation in any other, for there is no other name under heaven given to men whereby we must be saved."[29] He is the author of happiness and true prosperity for every man and for every nation. "For a nation is happy when its citizens are happy. What else is a nation but a number of men living in concord?"[30] If, therefore, the rulers of nations wish to preserve their authority, to promote and increase the prosperity of their countries, they will not neglect the public duty of reverence and obedience to the rule of Christ. What We said at the beginning of Our Pontificate concerning the decline of public authority, and the lack of respect for the same, is equally true at the present day. "With God and Jesus Christ," we said, "excluded from political life, with authority derived not from God but from man, the very basis of that authority has been taken away, because the chief reason of the distinction between ruler and subject has been eliminated. The result is that human society is tottering to its fall, because it has no longer a secure and solid foundation."[31]
19. When once men recognize, both in private and in public life, that Christ is King, society will at last receive the great blessings of real liberty, well-ordered discipline, peace and harmony. Our Lord's regal office invests the human authority of princes and rulers with a religious significance; it ennobles the citizen's duty of obedience. It is for this reason that St. Paul, while bidding wives revere Christ in their husbands, and slaves respect Christ in their masters, warns them to give obedience to them not as men, but as the vicegerents of Christ; for it is not meet that men redeemed by Christ should serve their fellow-men. "You are bought with a price; be not made the bond-slaves of men."[32] If princes and magistrates duly elected are filled with the persuasion that they rule, not by their own right, but by the mandate and in the place of the Divine King, they will exercise their authority piously and wisely, and they will make laws and administer them, having in view the common good and also the human dignity of their subjects. The result will be a stable peace and tranquillity, for there will be no longer any cause of discontent. Men will see in their king or in their rulers men like themselves, perhaps unworthy or open to criticism, but they will not on that account refuse obedience if they see reflected in them the authority of Christ God and Man. Peace and harmony, too, will result; for with the spread and the universal extent of the kingdom of Christ men will become more and more conscious of the link that binds them together, and thus many conflicts will be either prevented entirely or at least their bitterness will be diminished.
20. If the kingdom of Christ, then, receives, as it should, all nations under its way, there seems no reason why we should despair of seeing that peace which the King of Peace came to bring on earth - he who came to reconcile all things, who came not to be ministered unto but to minister, who, though Lord of all, gave himself to us as a model of humility, and with his principal law united the precept of charity; who said also: "My yoke is sweet and my burden light." Oh, what happiness would be Ours if all men, individuals, families, and nations, would but let themselves be governed by Christ! "Then at length," to use the words addressed by our predecessor, Pope Leo XIII, twenty-five years ago to the bishops of the Universal Church, "then at length will many evils be cured; then will the law regain its former authority; peace with all its blessings be restored. Men will sheathe their swords and lay down their arms when all freely acknowledge and obey the authority of Christ, and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father."[33]
21. That these blessings may be abundant and lasting in Christian society, it is necessary that the kingship of our Savior should be as widely as possible recognized and understood, and to the end nothing would serve better than the institution of a special feast in honor of the Kingship of Christ. For people are instructed in the truths of faith, and brought to appreciate the inner joys of religion far more effectually by the annual celebration of our sacred mysteries than by any official pronouncement of the teaching of the Church. Such pronouncements usually reach only a few and the more learned among the faithful; feasts reach them all; the former speak but once, the latter speak every year - in fact, forever. The church's teaching affects the mind primarily; her feasts affect both mind and heart, and have a salutary effect upon the whole of man's nature. Man is composed of body and soul, and he needs these external festivities so that the sacred rites, in all their beauty and variety, may stimulate him to drink more deeply of the fountain of God's teaching, that he may make it a part of himself, and use it with profit for his spiritual life.
22. History, in fact, tells us that in the course of ages these festivals have been instituted one after another according as the needs or the advantage of the people of Christ seemed to demand: as when they needed strength to face a common danger, when they were attacked by insidious heresies, when they needed to be urged to the pious consideration of some mystery of faith or of some divine blessing. Thus in the earliest days of the Christian era, when the people of Christ were suffering cruel persecution, the cult of the martyrs was begun in order, says St. Augustine, "that the feasts of the martyrs might incite men to martyrdom."[34] The liturgical honors paid to confessors, virgins and widows produced wonderful results in an increased zest for virtue, necessary even in times of peace. But more fruitful still were the feasts instituted in honor of the Blessed Virgin. As a result of these men grew not only in their devotion to the Mother of God as an ever-present advocate, but also in their love of her as a mother bequeathed to them by their Redeemer. Not least among the blessings which have resulted from the public and legitimate honor paid to the Blessed Virgin and the saints is the perfect and perpetual immunity of the Church from error and heresy. We may well admire in this the admirable wisdom of the Providence of God, who, ever bringing good out of evil, has from time to time suffered the faith and piety of men to grow weak, and allowed Catholic truth to be attacked by false doctrines, but always with the result that truth has afterwards shone out with greater splendor, and that men's faith, aroused from its lethargy, has shown itself more vigorous than before.
23. The festivals that have been introduced into the liturgy in more recent years have had a similar origin, and have been attended with similar results. When reverence and devotion to the Blessed Sacrament had grown cold, the feast of Corpus Christi was instituted, so that by means of solemn processions and prayer of eight days' duration, men might be brought once more to render public homage to Christ. So, too, the feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus was instituted at a time when men were oppressed by the sad and gloomy severity of Jansenism, which had made their hearts grow cold, and shut them out from the love of God and the hope of salvation.

text:
SPARTACUS

C.111-71 BCE

While little is known conclusively about the life of Spartacus, historical records agree that he was a famous former gladiator who led the most successful slave rebellion in arcient Roman history. Formerly from Thrace, a region northwest of Macedonia, Spartacus was enslaved by the Romans and was then trained as a gladiator in Capua. Along with 70 others, he escaped from a gladiatorial training camp and spent two years trying to avoid recapture while raiding towns for supplies. Spartacus proved himself a master military tactician, leading two successful victories over the Romans.

Leaders who changed history - James Bennet

One of my favourites (besides Christ) is Guru Nanak. 

The practice of langar, or "free kitchen", first popular with 12th and 13th-century sufis (Islamic mystics), was adopted by Nanak. All visitors to a gurdwara (place of worship) are offered a free meal regardless of their caste, religion, gender, or ethnicity.

In his youth, Nanak rebelled against the religious dogma that dominated Indian society, where Hinduism classified people according to their profession, placing them in one of numerous castes and sub-castes. People could not marry across castes, or eat certain foods prepared for them by someone of a lower caste. The only way to achieve a higher social status was to live a virtuous life and be rewarded after death by reincarnation into a different caste. Those outside the caste structure, at the very bottom of society, were known as "untouchables".

Nanak's family were of a high caste, but at the age of 11 he refused the traditional janeu (sacred thread) which boys were expected to wear to indicate their caste. Aged 12, he married, then aged 16 followed his father into accountancy and had a family. However, he gradually withdrew from everyday life, becoming more interested in pursuing spiritual ideals. According to Sikh tradition, Nanak would go to the river before sunrise to bathe, meditate, and sing hymns. On one occasion in 1499, he left his clothes by the side of a stream and disappeared. He returned after three days proclaiming to have seen a vision of God and wanting to spread his message.

Nanak declared that God existed outside of the confines of religious dogma, and refused to follow Hinduism or Islam.

Instead, he wanted to teach the world about a new democratic, spiritual existence in which there was a universal God above all religions, where men and women were equal, and adopted an ethic of honest work and a selfless devotion to helping those in need.

From 1500 to 1524, Nanak spent his years writing, teaching, and spreading Sikhi (his doctrine meaning disciple). He covered an estimated 17,000 miles (28,000 km) on five different tours, known as Udasis, that took him across India and as far afield as Sri Lanka, Tibet, Myanmar (Burma), Turkey, and the Arab countries. His teaching attracted many converts including Muslims and Hindus - among the most devoted was his Muslim travelling companion Bhai Mardana.

Philosophy and final days:
Nanak shunned ritual and superstitious practices, which he saw as meaningless, believing that people are responsible for their own actions and can only earn forgiveness by direct meditation with God. Outspoken on equality for women, he contradicted long-held Hindu traditions that forbade women from certain aspects of worship, such as entering a temple. He also formalised the three duties every Sikh must cary out in their daily life: Naam Japna (neditate on God's name), Kirat Karn earn an honest living), and Vand Chhakna (share one's earnings).

Towards the end of his life, Nanak lived in Kartarpur, a village in central Punjab. It is likely that Nanak had reached Guru status (an inspired religious teacher) by this time, and taught and granted blessings to disciples who gathered around him. He died in 1539, aged 70.
