text:
By @RDiavolos 
The Choices We Made - A Malfoid AU Fanfics
(Writer’s note: This takes place when the group arrived at Shell Cottage in the deathly hallows.)

A loud crack shattered the peace of the coastline. Six figures appeared a few feet above the sand, hung there for a fraction of a second, and fell in an undignified tangle of limbs. Ron landed face-first with a muffled grunt, Hermione collapsed beside him, and Griphook rolled down a shallow slope without once letting go of the Sword of Gryffindor. Harry struck the ground on his stomach, dragging Draceana down alongside him. For several seconds, none of them moved. Only the surf continued its steady advance and retreat.
Ron was the first to raise his head. He spat out a mouthful of sand, glanced wildly from the empty shore to the cottage beyond the dunes, and pushed himself to his feet. "We're alive!" he shouted, his relief turning into a breathless laugh. "We're alive, Hermione!"
He dropped beside her and helped her sit up, careful of the injuries she had suffered at the manor. Hermione was pale and shaking, but she managed a faint smile. "Yes, Ron. I noticed."
Ron looked over his shoulder. "Harry! You all right, mate?"
Harry groaned and pushed himself up on his elbows, his glasses crooked and sand in his hair. "Yeah. I think so." Draceana sat up beside him, blinking at the unfamiliar stretch of shore. Beyond the grassy dunes stood a small cottage, its windows catching the afternoon light. The manor was gone. Her father, her aunt, the drawing room—they were all impossibly far away. Where in Merlin's name has he taken me? She stared at Harry, who was brushing sand off his sleeves as though landing on a beach with a Malfoy was perfectly ordinary.
"Looks like we've arrived at Shell Cottage," Harry said.
Ron, still supporting Hermione, grinned. "Yeah, and in one piece. More or less."
"Harry! Ron! Hermione!"
Voices came from the direction of the cottage. Bill Weasley and Fleur Delacour were hurrying over the dunes with Luna, Dean, and Ollivander. Luna was the first to reach them, smiling with her usual serenity. "You're safe. That's wonderful."
Fleur immediately went to Hermione, who looked close to collapsing, while Bill clapped a hand on Ron's shoulder. "We were beginning to worry," Bill said. "What happened in there?"
"Long story," Ron answered, glancing at Hermione. "Very long story."
Luna, meanwhile, tilted her head at Harry and Draceana. "Oh. You're still holding hands."
Everyone looked. Harry's fingers were still wrapped around Draceana's hand. Somewhere during the journey his grip had shifted from the wrist he had seized in the drawing room, and neither had thought to release the other. Harry looked down and flushed. Draceana followed his gaze; colour rushed to her cheeks. "How long are you planning to hold my hand, Potter?!" she demanded, smacking his fingers away and folding her arms.
Harry recoiled. "Sorry!"
She looked determinedly toward the sea. "Honestly. Have you no sense of personal space?" The complaint lacked most of its usual bite, which only made Ron stare harder.
"Malfoy?" Dean had stopped several paces away. His expression shifted from surprise to anger as he took in her dishevelled hair and the sleeve covering her left forearm. "Draceana Malfoy? Why is she here?"
Draceana lifted her chin. "Well spotted, Thomas. Your eyes seem to work as well as your mouth. And its not like I want to be here, that glasses had the gal to pull me here.” she pointed at harry.
Dean turned to Harry. "She's a Death Eater! Harry, why did you bring her here?"
Hermione stirred beside Fleur. "Dean, it's not—"
"Her family had us locked up!" Dean snapped, looking between them. "What were you thinking?"
Harry opened his mouth. "Because..."
He didn't finish. A cold feeling had worked its way along his spine. Bill and Fleur were here, and so were Luna, Dean, and Ollivander. Ron held Hermione upright. Griphook was sitting some distance away with the sword across his knees. Everyone had made it. Yet he hadn't heard the voice that should have greeted him before any of the others. Harry turned slowly, searching the sand. "Dobby?"
Near the edge of the dunes lay a small, motionless figure. Harry began running before he was certain of what he had seen. "Dobby!" He stumbled to his knees beside the house-elf and carefully turned him over. Dobby's eyes were half-open, his breathing thin and uneven. For an instant Harry thought the journey had exhausted him. Then he saw the dark stain spreading across the elf's clothes, and the silver handle protruding from his chest. Bellatrix's knife. The flash of it in the drawing room returned with sickening clarity, as did the precious seconds he had spent reaching back for Draceana. "DOBBY! HELP! SOMEBODY HELP!"
Bill and Fleur ran to him. Fleur knelt at once and drew her wand. "Move your arm a little, Harry. Let me see."
Harry shifted just enough for her to examine the wound, but would not put Dobby down. Fleur murmured a healing charm. A pale glow passed across the blood-soaked fabric without stemming the bleeding. Bill leaned in and tried a second spell, his expression growing grave. "Come on,"
he muttered, attempting it again. Harry looked from one to the other. "Do something! Please!"
"We are trying," Bill answered. Fleur's eyes met her husband's, and Harry saw what neither wished to say.
"No. There has to be something else." Harry looked over his shoulder at Hermione, who was struggling to remain standing with Ron's help. "Hermione, you know spells—"
"Harry," she whispered, tears gathering in her eyes. She could barely speak, let alone raise her wand. Luna knelt quietly on the other side of Dobby, her face unusually solemn. Ron reached Harry's shoulder, then stopped, helpless before the sight of the knife.
"Harry... Potter..."
Dobby's voice was scarcely louder than the breeze. Harry bent over him immediately. "I'm here. I'm right here, Dobby."
A faint smile touched the house-elf's face. "Harry Potter... is safe."
Harry swallowed against the tightness in his throat. "Yes. Yes, we're safe. You did it. You saved us all." Dobby's little hand moved against Harry's sleeve, and Harry enclosed it gently in his own. "We'll get you inside," he said, though his voice had begun to shake. "Bill and Fleur will help. You can rest. You don't have to do anything else."
Dobby was still looking at him. He seemed to be trying to say one last thing. Harry leaned closer until he could feel the elf's faint breath on his cheek. "Harry... Potter..." Dobby whispered. The smile remained for a moment after his voice faded. Then his eyes went still, and the small hand in Harry's fingers no longer moved.
Harry waited for the next breath. When it didn't come, he leaned forward and called the elf's name. He tried once more, quieter this time, as though Dobby might wake if he didn't startle him. Bill slowly lowered his wand, while Fleur pressed a trembling hand over her mouth. Harry understood at last, but his arms tightened around the small body anyway, unwilling to let go. He bowed his head over Dobby, and a broken sob escaped his lips, silencing everyone around him. Ron stood nearby with one hand resting on Hermione's shoulder, his gaze lowered toward the sand. Dean turned away, unable to watch, while Luna remained kneeling beside Harry, gently resting a hand on his back.
Several paces behind them, Draceana stood alone, clutching her left arm so tightly that her fingers began to ache. She recognized those enormous ears, that little face, and the familiar voice that had once echoed through the halls of Malfoy Manor whenever someone called for him. Dobby. The same house-elf who had served her family for as long as she could remember. He had cleaned her room, prepared her clothes, and attended to her every whim, always with that nervous, apologetic manner she had grown so accustomed to. She had known him almost her entire life, yet until today, she had scarcely given him a second thought since her father lost him all those years ago. And now, after returning to the manor of his own free will to rescue the very people her family considered enemies, he lay lifeless in Harry Potter's arms, murdered by her own aunt.
Draceana bit her lower lip until she tasted blood. Across the sand, Harry was weeping over a house-elf her family had once regarded as little more than property. She had never seen anyone mourn a servant like that, much less the boy who had spent years enduring her insults. For a moment, she wanted to approach him, to say something, anything that might offer even the smallest comfort. But what could she possibly say? Dobby had died saving them, and she had been one of the people he had come back for. Her gaze fell to the sand beneath her feet, and the courage to move deserted her.
I... I'd only ruin everything again… She remained where she was, trembling silently as the sea breeze lifted the loose strands of her platinum-blonde hair.

***
By sunset, a small grave stood above the beach. Harry sat directly before it, his knees clutched to his chest and his arms wrapped around them. The rough inscription on the stone read: Here lies Dobby, the greatest house-elf. His fingers were reddened and scratched, and dirt remained beneath his nails. He had insisted on digging without magic, working until his hands ached. Ron and Dean had eventually helped with the earth; Luna had suggested they each say a few words. Harry had scarcely spoken through any of it. Now the farewell was over, and the grave lay quiet in the last light of day.
Draceana had watched the burial from a distance, standing apart from the others as they gathered around Dobby's grave to pay their respects. She watched Harry lower the last handful of earth onto the small mound, his fingers trembling as he brushed the remaining dirt from his palms. Even after the others had finished saying their farewells, he remained seated before the marker, staring at the inscription as though he had nowhere else to go. Draceana couldn't bring herself to look away. She had known Dobby for most of her childhood, yet it was Harry Potter, of all people, who had given him a proper burial. The thought left her with an uncomfortable feeling she couldn't quite explain.
Eventually, Bill suggested that everyone return to the cottage. Hermione was still recovering from Bellatrix's torture, and Ollivander and the others were exhausted from their imprisonment. Most began making their way back, but Dean stopped when he noticed Draceana standing a short distance away. His expression hardened. "Hang on. What about her?" he demanded, gesturing toward the blonde girl. "She's one of them! You can't seriously expect us to let a Death Eater stay here, can you?"
"Not now, Dean," Ron replied, glancing toward Harry, who hadn't so much as turned his head at the commotion. "We've got enough to deal with."
"Enough to deal with?" Dean repeated incredulously. "Ron, her family had us locked up! You saw what they did to Hermione. How are we supposed to trust her?"
Hermione stirred against Ron's shoulder, looking pale and barely able to remain on her feet. "Dean, please..." she murmured, struggling to keep her voice steady. "She helped me. I don't know why, but she did." Her gaze briefly moved toward Draceana before returning to Dean. "And Ron's right. This really isn't the time."
Dean looked as though he wanted to argue further, but Luna gently took his arm before he could speak. "Harry needs some quiet," she said, her usually dreamy voice carrying an unusual firmness. "And we're all terribly tired. Perhaps we could leave this discussion for another time." Dean glanced toward Harry, then back at Draceana. Whatever he had been about to say, he swallowed it with obvious reluctance. With a frustrated sigh, he turned and followed the others toward the cottage.
Draceana remained where she was, watching them disappear over the dunes. She supposed she could follow them, although Thomas would undoubtedly object to sharing a roof with her. And he wasn't entirely wrong to do so, was he? Her family had imprisoned them. Her aunt had tortured Granger. She herself bore the Dark Mark on her arm. Why should any of them welcome her? Perhaps it would be better if she simply left. She could walk along the shore until she found a road, then a village, and eventually some way of returning to Malfoy Manor. Her parents were still there, after all. Whatever awaited her at home, at least she would no longer be imposing herself upon people who had every reason to despise her.
What am I even doing here? Her gaze wandered toward the distant lights of Shell Cottage, where the others had already begun gathering inside. Then she looked back toward the grave. Harry hadn't moved. He remained seated before the little stone marker, his shoulders slumped and his head lowered, apparently oblivious to the conversation that had taken place behind him. Draceana watched him for a long moment, her fingers curling nervously against the fabric of her sleeves. There were so many things she wanted to say to him, so many questions she had carried since that terrible morning in the Hogwarts bathroom. Yet seeing him like this, grieving over someone her family had once treated as property, made every word seem terribly inadequate.
Against her better judgment, she took a hesitant step toward him, then another. But after only a few paces, she stopped. Her eyes remained fixed on the familiar figure sitting alone before the grave. She could approach him. She could sit beside him, perhaps offer some small comfort, just as she had once done after Cedric Diggory's death. But that had been years ago, before the Dark Mark, before Dumbledore's death, before the bathroom and everything that had happened between them. She no longer knew whether Harry would welcome her presence, or whether she even had the right to offer it.
So Draceana remained standing where she was, caught between the desire to approach him and the fear that she would only make things worse, while Harry continued staring silently at Dobby's grave.
***
The next few days at Shell Cottage were uncomfortable, to say the least. For a place that had become a refuge for so many people, there was remarkably little peace to be found within its walls. Everyone had survived Malfoy Manor, but survival had left its marks upon them, and the relief of having escaped was gradually giving way to exhaustion, grief, and the unpleasant realization that the war was still far from over.
Bill and Fleur did everything they could to make their unexpected guests comfortable. Despite the sudden arrival of so many people, neither complained about the additional work. Fleur prepared meals, changed bedsheets, and made certain that everyone had clean clothes, while Bill attended to whatever else was needed, occasionally checking the protective enchantments surrounding the cottage. They were gracious hosts, offering warm smiles and reassuring words whenever they could, although even they could not entirely conceal their concern for the weary collection of fugitives now occupying their home.
Luna spent much of her time looking after Mr. Ollivander, who remained frail after his long imprisonment. She brought him tea, helped him settle into a comfortable chair, and listened patiently whenever the elderly wandmaker felt inclined to speak. She also made an effort to keep Dean company, particularly whenever his thoughts returned to the blonde girl who had somehow become one of their fellow guests. Dean had made no secret of his displeasure at Draceana's presence. More than once, he questioned why they were allowing a Death Eater to remain under the same roof, and although Luna gently reminded him that they were all safe for the moment, his resentment was not so easily dismissed.
Hermione, meanwhile, spent most of her time resting. Bellatrix's Cruciatus Curse had left her terribly weak, and even sitting upright for too long could exhaust her. Ron rarely left her side, bringing her meals, helping her move about, and insisting that she rest whenever she attempted to do something herself. Naturally, Hermione protested that she was perfectly capable of looking after herself, only for Ron to remind her that she had nearly collapsed trying to walk across the room that morning. Bill found the whole situation rather amusing, occasionally teasing his younger brother about his newfound attentiveness. Ron would turn bright red and tell him to mind his own business, while Hermione pretended not to notice the small smile tugging at her lips.
For all their difficulties, there was at least a certain warmth among them. They had endured terrible things together, and although nobody was particularly cheerful, they could still find comfort in familiar faces, shared conversations, and the occasional bit of laughter. Even Dean, despite his foul mood, had Luna to talk to. Everyone had someone to turn to, someone who understood what they had been through or was willing to listen when the memories became too much.
Everyone, it seemed, except Harry Potter and Draceana Malfoy.
Harry had become unusually quiet since Dobby's death. He still answered when spoken to and occasionally joined the others for meals, but his responses were brief, and his attention often seemed to be elsewhere. Ron and Hermione noticed, of course, but neither knew quite what to say. They had seen Harry grieve before, and they understood how deeply Dobby's death had affected him. Ron occasionally tried drawing him into a conversation, while Hermione would offer a few gentle words of concern whenever she felt strong enough. Harry always assured them that he was all right, though the tired expression behind his glasses suggested otherwise.
Every evening, shortly before sunset, Harry would leave the cottage and make his way toward the little grave overlooking the sea. Sometimes he remained there until the last traces of daylight disappeared, sitting quietly before the stone marker he had carved with his own hands. When he eventually returned, he rarely joined the others in conversation. Instead, he would settle into a chair near the corner of the sitting room, draw his knees toward his chest, and stare at the floor for what seemed like hours. Nobody pressed him for an explanation. They were worried, certainly, but each of them was struggling with wounds of their own, and there was only so much comfort they could offer when they barely possessed enough strength to look after themselves.
Draceana often watched him from across the room.
She had never seen Potter quite like this. Even after Cedric Diggory's death, when she had found him sitting alone and crying, there had still been something familiar about him. He had eventually recovered enough to argue with her, to become irritated by her remarks, and to behave like the infuriating Gryffindor she had known for years. Now, however, he seemed almost determined to withdraw from everyone around him. Whenever their eyes happened to meet, Harry would look away, and Draceana, caught between indignation and uncertainty, would pretend she hadn't been watching him in the first place.
Not that her own circumstances were particularly pleasant.
She had been given a place to sleep, clean clothes, and more food than she could reasonably complain about. Fleur treated her with the same courtesy she extended to the other guests, while Bill remained polite whenever they crossed paths. Yet beyond those ordinary gestures of hospitality, nobody seemed particularly eager to speak with her.
Under ordinary circumstances, Draceana would have returned his hostility with a particularly cutting remark. She had never been one to tolerate being looked down upon, least of all by someone she considered beneath her. But every time a familiar insult rose to her lips, she remembered where she was, whose family had imprisoned these people, and the ugly black mark concealed beneath her sleeve. So she held her tongue. Instead, she settled for glaring whenever she caught someone looking at her, which did little to make her appear more approachable.
It was a miserable arrangement.
At meals, she usually sat at the far end of the table, answering Fleur's occasional questions with stiff politeness before returning her attention to her plate. When the others gathered in the sitting room, she would find somewhere out of the way and occupy herself with whatever book happened to be available. Sometimes their conversations would drift toward Hogwarts, the Weasleys, or people they had known before the war, and Draceana would listen without contributing. She recognized many of the names, of course, and on more than one occasion she nearly interrupted to correct something she considered particularly foolish. Yet she always stopped herself.
After all, what right did she have to join their conversations?
She was not their friend. She was not a member of the Order of the Phoenix. She was a Malfoy, a marked Death Eater, and the daughter of the man whose home had become a prison for several of the people now sharing this cottage. Even Granger, who had spoken in her defense after the funeral, had admitted that she didn't understand why Draceana had helped her. Nobody knew what to make of her presence, and Draceana was beginning to suspect that she didn't know either.
There was, however, one person who could have explained everything.
Potter.
The same stubborn, reckless idiot who had seized her hand at Malfoy Manor and refused to leave without her. He had dragged her away from her family, brought her to an unfamiliar place filled with people who despised everything her surname represented, and then proceeded to behave as though she scarcely existed.
At first, Draceana tried to be patient. Potter was grieving, after all. Even she could understand that much. Dobby had died saving them, and Harry had been the one holding him when he took his final breath. She had watched him dig the grave, seen him sitting before it long after everyone else had gone, and understood that approaching him with demands for an explanation would accomplish very little.
So she waited.
Perhaps tomorrow, when he was feeling better, he would finally speak to her. Perhaps he would explain why he had insisted on bringing her here, what he expected her to do, or how long he intended for her to remain. She wasn't asking for much. A few words would have sufficed. Even one of his usual irritating remarks would have been preferable to this dreadful silence.
But tomorrow came, and Potter said nothing.
Then another day passed.
And another.
By the fourth day, Draceana's patience had begun wearing dangerously thin. She could tolerate Thomas's suspicious looks, Weasley's indifference, and even the awkward silences that seemed to follow her whenever she entered a room. What she could not tolerate was being kept in the dark about her own future, particularly when the person responsible for bringing her here refused to acknowledge her.
Worse still, her parents remained at Malfoy Manor

text:
Rewind the last three seconds of that clip.

Whatever slides into the frame at the end has nine brains, three hearts and blue blood. It can taste with its skin, change color faster than you can blink, and squeeze through a hole the size of a coin.

It is also not the smartest thing in that video by accident. It is the smartest thing in that video by design. A different design than yours. Built from scratch, on a separate branch of evolution, 500+ million years after we stopped sharing an ancestor.

Read this slowly. By the end you will watch that clip differently.

────────────

1. NINE BRAINS. NOT A METAPHOR.

An octopus has roughly 500 million neurons. That is the same ballpark as a dog.

Here is the part that breaks your mental model: about two thirds of those neurons are not in its head. They sit in its arms.

One central brain. Eight smaller clusters of nervous tissue, one per arm. Each cluster can sense, decide and act on its own.

So when people say "an octopus has nine brains," scientists wince a little, because the real picture is stranger. It is not nine equal brains. It is one boss with very little micromanagement skills and eight employees who barely wait for orders.

The boss says: "Go check that crevice."

The arm says: "On it." Then it explores, tastes, feels, grabs, rejects, tries again. The boss finds out about the result later. Sometimes it seems the boss finds out about everything last.

That is not a bug. That is the whole architecture. And it works absurdly well.

────────────

2. THE ARM THAT KEEPS WORKING AFTER IT'S GONE

In lab experiments, a severed octopus arm keeps reacting. Touch it, it recoils. Offer it food, it grabs and passes it along toward where the mouth would be.

Read that again. No central brain connected. Still doing a coherent job.

Now imagine your hand holding a conversation with a stranger while you are busy somewhere else, then handing you a business card you never asked for.

That is the daily working life of an octopus.

And it gets better. Each arm carries hundreds of suckers, around 2,000 across the whole animal, and every single sucker is both a hand and a tongue. They carry chemical sensors. An octopus does not just touch a rock. It tastes the rock.

Picture walking through your home, and every step is also a bite.

It reaches into a dark crack it cannot see, and it knows what is inside before its eyes ever get a vote.

────────────

3. THREE HEARTS, BLUE BLOOD, AND A WEIRD LAZINESS

Two hearts push blood through the gills. A third pushes it to the rest of the body.

The blood is not red. It is blue, because it carries oxygen with a copper-based molecule called hemocyanin instead of the iron-based hemoglobin in your veins. Copper-blood is better in cold, low-oxygen water, which is exactly where a lot of octopuses live.

Here is the twist nobody expects: when an octopus swims, the main heart stops beating.

Swimming is expensive for it. The body heart literally pauses. So, if it has a choice, an octopus crawls. It prefers to walk along the bottom, arm over arm, saving the heart for emergencies.

The most capable hunter in the reef, built to treat swimming as a last resort.

There is a lesson about energy management in there somewhere. Most humans have not learned it.

────────────

4. A COLORBLIND ANIMAL THAT WINS EVERY CAMOUFLAGE CONTEST

This is the paradox that scientists still argue about.

Most octopuses appear to have only one type of light receptor in their eyes. By the standard definition, they are colorblind.

And yet they can match the color of a coral, a rock, a patch of algae, a sandy slope, sometimes with a precision that makes trained divers look straight at the animal and see nothing.

How do you match a color you cannot see?

Part of the answer is the skin. Octopus skin contains light-sensitive proteins, the same family used in eyes. In other words, the skin itself may be reading the light. There is also a wild hypothesis that the strange U-shaped pupil lets the animal extract color information by using blurred wavelengths in a way no camera engineer would design on purpose.

The hardware is even more ridiculous: thousands of tiny pigment sacs called chromatophores, each one wired directly to muscles, each one under direct neural control. The animal does not "paint" itself. It rewrites its own skin like a screen.

Not just color. Texture too. Smooth to bumpy, flat to spiky, in a fraction of a second, with muscle-driven bumps called papillae.

A shape-shifting, color-changing, texture-editing animal that may not technically see color.

If you think you understand it by now, you do not.

────────────

5. NO BONES. ONE RULE.

An octopus has no skeleton. No spine, no ribs, no shell. Almost the entire animal is soft muscle.

It does have exactly one hard part: the beak, made of a tough, chitin-based material, shaped like a parrot's, hidden in the center where the arms meet.

And that creates the rule that governs everything it does:

If the beak fits, the octopus fits.

That is why a 40-pound giant can pour itself through an opening you would struggle to push your fist into. It is why aquarium keepers lock lids, then lock the locks, then add weights, and still wake up to an empty tank.

The beak is also not just a mouth. Octopuses use it, along with a tongue-like ribbon of tiny teeth called a radula and a tiny drill-like organ, to bore through the shells of clams and snails. Some inject a paralyzing saliva afterward. A drilled hole, a dose of chemistry, dinner.

Soft body. Hard rule. Tiny, precise, lethal tool.

Hold that thought. Tools are where this story gets uncomfortable.

────────────

6. THE ANIMAL THAT CARRIES A HOUSE

In 2009, researchers filmed veined octopuses in Indonesia doing something that no one expected from an animal with no spine.

They picked up discarded coconut shell halves from the seafloor, stacked them, then carried them across open ground, running on the tips of their arms in a clumsy shuffle that scientists half-jokingly called stilt walking.

Then they assembled the shells into a hiding place, a portable bunker, when danger showed up.

Why this matters: carrying an object you do not need right now, to use it later, in a different place, is a very different level of thinking than grabbing a stick to reach a snack. It requires planning. It requires seeing a piece of garbage as a future solution.

Most animals do not do this. Some primates do. Some crows do.

And a cousin of the clam does too.

Stay with me. That was the warm-up.

────────────

7. THE ESCAPE ARTISTS

In 2016, an octopus named Inky disappeared from his tank at a national aquarium in New Zealand.

The staff found a trail of evidence: a gap left at the top of the enclosure, wet marks across the floor, and a narrow drainpipe, about 50 meters long, that led straight into the ocean.

Inky reportedly made the whole trip, squeezed through a pipe, and was gone.

He was not the first.

In a German aquarium decades earlier, an octopus nicknamed Otto reportedly kept shorting out the electricity by squirting a jet of water at a bright lamp above his tank. The staff, baffled by repeated blackouts, eventually caught him in the act.

In laboratories, octopuses have unscrewed jars from the inside. They have learned to open childproof bottles. Keepers have reported them sneaking out of tanks at night, crossing the floor, raiding a neighboring tank for crabs, then returning home before the morning shift.

Think about the sequence. Know where the food is. Plan the route. Avoid detection. Eat. Return. Close the lid.

That is not instinct. That is a heist.

────────────

8. IT KNOWS WHO YOU ARE

Here is an experiment that should make you slightly nervous.

Researchers had two people in identical uniforms approach giant Pacific octopuses in their tanks. One person always fed the animal. The other always poked it with a bristly stick.

After a few days, the uniforms stopped mattering. The octopuses behaved differently toward each person, even though they looked the same. Calm and curious toward the friendly one. Defensive, with color flashes and jets of water, toward the unfriendly one.

It could tell two humans apart. Without a face like ours. Without ever seeing a face like ours in the wild, because there are no humans in the deep ocean to practice on.

Individual octopuses also seem to have personalities. Some are shy. Some are bold. Some are, as keepers have described them, social show-offs. Some are sulky and grumpy for weeks.

You are not looking at a biological machine. You are looking at a character.

────────────

9. THE FISH THAT WORK FOR AN OCTOPUS (AND THE PUNCH)

In the Red Sea, researchers have documented octopuses hunting in teams with fish such as groupers and wrasses.

The fish sweep the reef. The octopus pokes into the cracks. Whoever flushes out prey, the other cuts off the exit. Different species, different bodies, one operation.

Then the part that went viral in science circles: sometimes the octopus punches a fish.

Not randomly. Cameras showed arms striking fish partners that seemed to be slacking off or getting in the way, and sometimes the strike looked like a clear shove aimed at keeping the group in line. Scientists are careful to say it may be a way to push fish out of the way for the octopus's own advantage. Still, it looks a lot like management.

An animal with no social learning from parents, no group, no culture, apparently running a mixed-species task force and enforcing discipline.

And remember: it lives, on average, one or two years.

We will come back to that. It is the saddest part.

────────────

10. OCTLANTIS

Off the coast of eastern Australia, divers found something nobody had a word for yet.

A patch of seafloor where dozens of gloomy octopuses lived side by side, in dens carved out of sand and rock, surrounded by mounds of discarded shells, the leftovers of countless meals. Piles of trash that one animal after another kept adding to. The scientists nicknamed the site Octlantis.

Octopuses are supposed to be loners. Solitary, territorial, the textbook example of a mind that does not need other minds.

And here they were, packed close, interacting, signaling with color, chasing each other away, occasionally mating, and, in a detail that made the internet lose its mind, occasionally throwing shells and silt at one another.

Yes. Throwing. Researchers later analyzed hours of footage and found that some throws were aimed at specific neighbors, and that the animals seemed to pick their target.

A city, a garbage dump, and a lot of drama.

All built by an animal that grows up without ever meeting its parents.

────────────

11. THEY SLEEP. AND SOMETHING HAPPENS WHILE THEY DO.

In 2021, a team filmed sleeping octopuses and noticed a pattern.

Most of the time, the animal sleeps quietly: pale skin, pupils narrowed to slits, barely moving. This is the calm phase.

But every so often, for about a minute, the whole animal comes alive. Skin flashes through rapid patterns of color and texture. Eyes twitch. Arms curl. Then it all goes dark again, and the cycle repeats.

It looks almost exactly like REM sleep in mammals, the stage when we dream.

Nobody can prove an octopus dreams. But look at what is happening: an animal whose skin is directly linked to its brain is running a light show while unconscious, and the patterns resemble the ones it uses when it is awake and hunting or hiding.

Some researchers think it may be replaying memories. Others think it is rehearsing. We still do not know.

The honest scientific position is: we just watched a mind on a different branch of the tree of life run the same nightly routine as ours, and we have no idea what it sees.

────────────

12. THE GENOME THAT LOOKS LIKE IT WAS WRITTEN BY SOMEONE ELSE

In 2015, scientists published the first octopus genome. It had about 33,000 protein-coding genes, noticeably more than a human's roughly 20,000.

It also had huge expansions in two gene families linked to brain function and communication between neurons. Families that, in vertebrates, matter a lot for how the nervous system wires itself.

Then came the finding that made geneticists stop mid-sentence. Octopuses and their relatives edit their own RNA on a scale no one thought was possible. Instead of treating the DNA instruction as final, the animal rewrites the message before building the protein, thousands upon thousands of times, especially in the nervous system.

Why would an animal do this? One idea: it lets the body adjust its neurons on the fly, tuning them to temperature or conditions in the moment, without waiting for evolution to change the DNA.

The price may be steep. The more heavily the animal edits, the less room evolution has to change the underlying code. Some scientists suspect that is part of why octopus genomes change slowly.

In other words: this animal traded the slow lane of evolution for a fast lane of improvisation.

You are not looking at a weird fish. You are looking at an alternative approach to building a mind.

────────────

13. THE LAST THING THE MOTHER DOES

Here is the part where the story turns.

An octopus mother lays her eggs, sometimes tens of thousands of them, and then stays. She guards them. She cleans them. She blows fresh water over them to keep them oxygenated. She does not leave to hunt. She stops eating.

And slowly, over weeks or months, she dies.

In 2014, a deep-sea robot filmed a mother octopus brooding her eggs on a rock wall about 1,400 meters (nearly a mile) below the surface in Monterey Canyon. Researchers kept coming back. She was still there. She stayed for four and a half years, the longest known brooding period of any animal.

By the end, her skin was pale and loose, her eyes cloudy. She finally disappeared. The eggs had hatched.

Biologists found the trigger. A small structure near the eye, called the optic gland, appears to act as a self-destruct switch. In a classic 1970s experiment, researchers removed it from mothers after egg-laying. The females resumed eating, grew larger, and lived much longer than normal.

Think about what that means. The biology of the animal is designed so that the moment its single great task is done, a switch flips and it begins to dismantle itself.

A mind that can unscrew jars, plan escapes, recognize faces and dream, and a body programmed to die right on schedule.

────────────

14. THE PART THAT SHOULD KEEP YOU UP AT NIGHT

Humans and octopuses last shared an ancestor roughly 550 to 600 million years ago. That ancestor was probably a tiny, flat, wormlike creature with a very simple nervous system.

After that, the two lineages walked away from each other.

One of them eventually built vertebrates, mammals, primates, and us. The other built mollusks, then snails and clams, and then, through a series of events we are still reconstructing, a soft, boneless, eight-armed thing that solves puzzles.

That means complex intelligence did not evolve once on Earth.

It evolved at least twice, independently, in bodies with nothing in common.

Different hardware. Different wiring. Different blood. Different eyes. Different relationship to the idea of a "head."

And still the same outputs: curiosity, play, memory, deception, personality, sleep that looks like dreaming.

If you wanted to know whether minds are rare, this is the answer, and it is not comforting for anyone who thought we were special: the universe seems to produce them when the conditions are right, and it is not picky about what they are made of.

If a mind can be built from a worm's descendant in a cold, dark ocean, what else is possible?

Hold that question. Now go back and watch that clip again.

────────────

15. THE DEFENSE SYSTEM THAT READS LIKE A SPY MANUAL

Let's talk about what an octopus does when things go wrong, because the toolbox is ridiculous.

Step one: disappear. Match the background, freeze, and let the predator swim past.

Step two: if spotted, flash. Sudden, high-contrast patterns that startle the attacker for a split second, the same trick as a magician's misdirection.

Step three: ink. The cloud is not just a smokescreen. It contains compounds that can irritate and dull the senses of a predator that hunts by smell, and the blob itself can be shaped into a decoy, a dark, vaguely octopus-sized shape that hangs in the water while the real animal jets away in another direction, usually in a new color.

Step four: jet propulsion. Suck in water, blast it out through a funnel. Instant escape, direction controlled by pointing the funnel.

Step five: lose an arm. Some species can drop a limb, which keeps wriggling and distracts the attacker. The arm grows back later.

Step six, for the truly committed: impersonate something worse.

The mimic octopus of Indonesia is the champion here. In the open, it has been observed flattening itself to look like a poisonous flatfish, then tucking six arms into a hole and spreading two out to look like a banded sea snake, then dangling its arms to resemble a spiny lionfish. Different threats, different costumes, picked from a menu.

And then there is the one that doesn't need a costume. The blue-ringed octopus is the size of a golf ball, and carries a neurotoxin, produced with help from bacteria living in its tissues, strong enough to paralyze an adult human. There is no antidote. When it is calm, it looks like a beige pebble. When it is angry, it lights up with electric blue rings, nature's version of a warning label in a language everyone understands.

Disappear, distract, deceive, deter. Four D's. All improvised in under a second.

────────────

16. THE EXPERIMENT THAT SHOULDN'T HAVE WORKED

In 2018, a team of researchers did something that sounds like a bar bet.

They gave octopuses a dose of MDMA.

Why? Because the human brain uses a chemical messenger called serotonin to regulate mood and social behavior, and MDMA acts on the molecule that handles it. Researchers noticed that the octopus version of that molecule contains the same key binding site as ours, preserved across more than half a billion years of separate evolution.

If the site is the same, will the effect be the same?

Octopuses are famously antisocial. Normally, they hide from each other. But after the drug, the animals spent more time in the chamber with another octopus, moved closer, and touched the neighbor in a way scientists described as unusually relaxed and curious.

What the study does and does not prove is debated. But the take-away is breathtaking: some of the chemical machinery behind social feeling is ancient. It was there before the split. It was there in the last worm. It is older than bones, older than eyes in their modern form, older than the idea of a face.

Your capacity to feel warmth toward another being may be older than your species, your class, your phylum, and most of the animal kingdom.

────────────

17. THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART

Here is where the story stops being only amazing and starts asking something of you.

If an animal can plan, recognize individuals, solve puzzles, show personality, sleep in a way that looks like dreaming, and possibly feel pain in ways similar to ours, what do we owe it?

In 2021, a major review commissioned by the UK government looked at the evidence and concluded that cephalopods, including octopuses, should be treated as sentient beings. The country wrote that into law the following year.

Meanwhile, companies in some parts of the world have been racing to build the first large-scale octopus farms. The pitch is straightforward: wild populations are under pressure, demand is high, and the animal is valuable.

The problem is equally straightforward. Octopuses are solitary, intelligent, escape-prone, and prone to stress. Crowding them into tanks, feeding them other animals, and killing them at a fixed size is something many scientists say is hard to justify on welfare grounds. Some US states have since moved to ban octopus farming before it starts.

I am not telling you what to think about eating octopus. I am telling you that the question is no longer silly, and that the animal in the question is, by every serious measure, closer to a mind than to a mussel.

The old line between "food" and "someone" just moved a few meters in the water.

────────────

18. WHY THIS STORY HITS HARDER THAN IT SHOULD

Because every octopus is, in a way, an argument.

An argument that intelligence is not a ladder with humans at the top. It is a bush with many branches, some of which grew in directions we would never have designed.

An argument that a body can be a brain. That "thinking" does not have to happen in one place. That a creature with no bones can out-think creatures with skulls.

An argument that you can have no parents, no school, no culture, a life measured in months, and still solve a problem that would stump a toddler.

An argument that curiosity is not a luxury item that only big mammals can afford. It is the default setting of any nervous system with enough room to wonder.

And the most uncomfortable one: an argument that the universe is probably full of minds that do not look like ours, and that we are very bad at recognizing them when they are inches away.

We spend billions scanning the sky for alien intelligence.

Meanwhile, one is hiding under a rock in the shallows, watching us through a rectangular pupil, deciding whether we are worth the trouble.

────────────

19. THE MATH THAT MAKES IT WORSE

Most octopuses live one to five years. Many species, closer to one or two.

Hatchlings drift away as tiny plankton. Nobody teaches them to hunt, to hide, to read a reef. There is no mother to copy, no elder to ask, no school, no inherited tradition passed down in the water.

Every single octopus is a first-generation genius.

It learns the whole world from zero, alone, in the time it takes a human toddler to learn to tie a shoe. And then the clock runs out, and everything it figured out leaves with it.

Imagine what this animal could do with a lifespan of eighty years and a library.

Now imagine that it already does this much without one.

────────────

20. IF YOU REMEMBER ONLY THREE THINGS

One. The octopus is not a smart animal that happens to live in the sea. It is a different kind of intelligence that happens to share the planet with us.

Two. Most of what it does is not trained, taught or inherited. It is invented on the spot, by an animal that has never met an elder of its own kind.

Three. The reason this matters is not the animal. It is the mirror. Every fact above is a small crack in the idea that we are the default setting for a mind.

Share it if it hit. Argue with it if it didn't.

────────────

21. NOW DO THIS

Scroll back up. Watch that clip again. Don't skim it.

This time, watch what the arms are doing. Watch the way the animal keeps itself exactly as exposed as it needs to be, and not one centimeter more. Watch for the moment where it stops being scenery and becomes a decision.

Once you know what you are looking at, you cannot unsee it.

Every film of an octopus is a recording of a thought. And most of us have been watching them like they are screensavers.

If this changed how you see that clip, send it to the one person who still says "it's just an animal."

If you want more posts that take a few seconds of footage and turn them into a very long night of staring at the ceiling, follow. I post when the ocean does something that should not be possible.

And leave a reply with the strangest animal fact you know. I read every one.

Somewhere down there, something with nine brains just read it too.

P.S. The clip is twelve seconds long. The lineage of the animal in it is hundreds of millions of years old. Give it one more watch and notice how quickly you stop saying "it" and start wondering what it wants.

Then tell me you're not curious about what it does next. Bookmark this post so you can find it before the next one tricks you, too.

text:
True story:

At nine years old, John O'Leary was given less than a 1% chance of surviving the night.

In 1987, after a horrific accident with gasoline in his family's garage, John suffered third-degree burns covering nearly 100% of his body. Wrapped in bandages, blind from the swelling, and unable to speak because his lungs were scorched, John lay in total darkness in a St. Louis burn unit. The doctors were certain it was his final night.

Then, a miracle walked into his room.

Jack Buck, the legendary Hall of Fame broadcaster for the St. Louis Cardinals, had heard about the little boy's accident. Though he had never met the O'Leary family, Buck drove to the hospital, scrubbed in, and stood beside John's bed. He leaned down and said, "Kid, wake up. You are going to live. You are going to survive."

Buck left the room weeping, overcome by the sheer trauma the boy was enduring. A nurse gently told him the heartbreaking truth: there was no hope, and the boy wouldn't make it. Jack Buck had done his good deed. He could have walked away.

But the next day, Buck came back. And he kept coming back.

He promised John that if he survived, he would have "John O'Leary Day" at the ballpark. Buck offered tough love and practical redemption alongside his promises. Knowing John had lost his fingers to amputation and needed to rebuild his motor skills, Buck sent him a baseball signed by legendary shortstop Ozzie Smith.

He included a note: "If you want another one, write a thank you note."

Through excruciating pain, John learned to hold a pen again. He wrote the note. Jack sent another ball. John wrote again. By the end, Jack Buck had sent John 60 signed baseballs, forcing the young boy to literally write his way back to life.

Years later, John asked Jack's son, Joe Buck, why this famous man had spent so much time on an ordinary boy. The answer was simple: Jack Buck grew up poor during the Depression, served in the military, and understood that true greatness is found in how you serve the broken people in front of you, rather than in a broadcast booth. He never told the media what he was doing. He just showed up.

Today, John O'Leary is more than a survivor. He is a husband, a father, and a man who has inspired millions to realize that their deepest scars can become their greatest strength.

We do not have to wait for the world to change. Like Jack Buck, we just have to show up for the people right in front of us.

🔴US voters turning against data centers raises risks for Asian suppliers

🔹A nationwide backlash against AI data centers is shaping the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, creating political friction that could slow projects and ripple out to Asian suppliers of chips, servers, and related equipment.

🔹In deep-red Jackson County, Ohio, farmer Kasey Hoover Hall rejected a lucrative offer for family land and helped organize local opposition that put a large data-center campus on hold. Registered Republicans like Hall are now considering voting Democratic to punish politicians seen as too friendly to the industry. Similar resistance has emerged across the country: a YouGov poll found more than 60% of Americans (including 52% of Republicans) would oppose a data center near them. Roughly 60% of projects under construction sit in states Donald Trump won in 2024.

🔹Critics frame the facilities as “billionaires’ toys” that raise electricity prices, consume water and land, and arrive with little local input. At least 45 of 89 large new projects were blocked or delayed in the second quarter of 2026; about 40 local ballot measures aim to restrict them. In Ohio’s Senate race, Republican Jon Husted’s support for data centers has become a liability against Democrat Sherrod Brown. Even some Republican governors have shifted toward moratoriums.

🔹The slowdown threatens Asian firms that have thrived on U.S. AI infrastructure demand—Taiwanese server and component makers, South Korean chipmakers, and Chinese equipment suppliers. Industry executives acknowledge the “era of frictionless siting” is ending and stress the need for better community engagement, while arguing semiconductor fabs face less opposition because they create more lasting jobs. Grassroots resistance is expected to continue after Election Day.

text:
$CHEF Q3 2026 earnings: Chefs' Warehouse raises its outlook, while warehouse costs edge up

The Chefs' Warehouse, a supplier of specialty ingredients and meat to upscale restaurants, grew volume and widened profit margins simultaneously. Sales from businesses owned a year ago rose 10%, while gross margin expanded in both food divisions and lifted cash profit 26%. Chief executive Christopher Pappas said Middle East sales returned to last year's levels, and the company raised its full-year targets across the board.

• Sales from businesses owned a year ago: +𝟏𝟎.𝟑% (total net sales: $1.14B (+11.2%))
• Gross margin: 𝟐𝟓.𝟎% (+0.84 percentage points from a year ago)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟎.𝟔𝟔 (+32% from a year ago)
• Full-year Adjusted EBITDA outlook: 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 $𝟗𝐌 (middle of the range: $319M (+24%))

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because case volume held above 6% even after the distributor finished lapping last year's Texas program exits, proving that demand is not an accounting quirk. In addition, the Middle East rebound removed the main drag on international sales. One caution: warehouse and pay costs grew slightly faster than revenue, and by our math the raised full-year outlook still implies fourth-quarter sales growth slows to 7%.

The question now is whether the implied fourth-quarter slowdown is just management's usual caution or a sign that cooling food inflation and higher warehouse costs will cap profit gains. If the plan is simply conservative, holiday restaurant traffic and protein margins will push full-year results above the top of the range as they did last year. Fourth-quarter gross margin and overhead ratios will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐑𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐀𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐁𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐅𝐨𝐨𝐝 𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬
The Chefs' Warehouse distributes specialty ingredients and center-of-the-plate proteins (meat and seafood) to upscale restaurants. For a third straight quarter, profit margins expanded in both divisions at the same time. Total gross margin rose 0.84 percentage points from a year ago to 25.0%, which lifted operating margin by 0.6 percentage points to 4.4%.

• Center-of-the-plate gross margin: up 1.37 percentage points from a year ago
• Specialty gross margin: up 0.63 percentage points from a year ago
• Adjusted EBITDA (operating cash profit before interest, taxes, depreciation and stock pay): up 26% to $82.2 million, or 7.2% of sales

This simultaneous gain matters because protein and specialty margins often moved in opposite directions during 2025. The distributor credited the higher gross profit dollars to "increased sales volumes, price inflation and acquisitions". That pricing power kept profit growing more than twice as fast as sales, keeping its 2030 target of a 7.5% to 8.0% cash profit margin on track.

What to watch: fourth-quarter gross margin, where the updated full-year plan implies 24.6% at the middle of the range. A reading near 25.0% would show that protein pricing gains are holding through the holiday quarter.

🟢🟢 𝐕𝐨𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐝 𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐄𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝
Skeptics argued that first-half volume growth looked good only because the food group was comparing against 2025 quarters when it shut down low-margin Texas poultry and produce programs. Management finished lapping those exits in the second quarter, so the third quarter offered the first clean test of demand. Chief executive Christopher Pappas pointed to "solid year-over-year growth in unique item placements and unique customers".

• Unique item placements (different products sold per customer): up 7.2% from a year ago, matching the second quarter
• Specialty cases sold from businesses owned a year ago: up 6.1%, against 6.0% in the second quarter
• Center-of-the-plate pounds sold from businesses owned a year ago: up 6.6%, against 8.8% in the second quarter
• Unique customers: up 4.4%, accelerating from 3.6% in the second quarter

Holding case growth above 6% while customer additions sped up proves that restaurant demand is genuine rather than a comparison quirk. Because placement growth leads case volume, the 7.2% placement pace supports steady volume into year-end.

What to watch: unique item placement growth in the fourth quarter. A reading above 6% would confirm that chefs are still ordering more items per delivery.

concern eased — 𝐌𝐢𝐝𝐝𝐥𝐞 𝐄𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐑𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐋𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫'𝐬 𝐋𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥
Regional conflict cut the distributor's Middle East revenue to about 75% of prior-year levels in the first quarter and 94% in May and June. That shortfall reduced total company growth by nearly one percentage point in the second quarter and was the main risk management cited for its cautious full-year outlook.

"Revenue trends in recent weeks have been approximately 100% of prior-year, as food-away-from-home activity is supported by local residents and ex-patriots returning from the summer off-season", Pappas said. A second straight quarter of recovery, combined with the raised full-year outlook, turns the region from a growth drag back into a neutral comparison, even though the company still does not disclose Middle East profit.

What to watch: international revenue in the third-quarter filing's geographic note. A figure near last year's $93 million would verify that the rebound held across the whole period.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐖𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐚𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡
The long-term margin case rests on filling new distribution centers in Texas, New England, Las Vegas and the Midwest so overhead grows more slowly than revenue. In the second quarter, selling, general and administrative expenses (warehouse, delivery and office overhead) fell by 0.7 percentage points of sales. In the third quarter, that cost ratio moved the other way, rising 0.2 percentage points from a year ago to 20.6% of sales.

• Selling, general and administrative expenses: up 12.1% to $233.4 million, faster than the 11.2% sales rise
• Stock compensation (employee pay in shares, excluded from adjusted EBITDA): up 89% from a year ago to $9.3 million
• Fourth-quarter interest expense implied by the full-year table: $17.2 million at the middle of the range, against $9.0 million in the third quarter

The company blamed the overhead rise on "higher costs associated with compensation and benefits, facilities and distribution to support sales growth, fuel costs, as well as higher depreciation expense driven by facility and fleet investments". Management also raised its full-year stock pay estimate by $2 million and its interest forecast by $5.5 million, likely tied to redeeming its 2028 convertible debt (bonds that can turn into shares).

What to watch: selling, general and administrative expenses as a share of sales in the fourth quarter. Another year-over-year rise would show that new warehouse and pay costs are eating into gross margin gains.

🔴 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐏𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐚 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧
Pappas said that "Momentum continued into October, and as we head into the busy holiday season". Even after lifting its full-year sales target by $35 million at the middle of the range, the distributor's outlook points to a sharp fourth-quarter slowdown by our math.

Subtracting the first nine months from the new full-year target leaves fourth-quarter sales growth of 7.0% at the middle of the range, down from 11.2% in the third quarter. The same math leaves fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA up 10.4%, less than half the third quarter's 26.3% pace. Lapping last year's Italco acquisition trims about 0.7 percentage points of growth, so most of the gap is management caution that has repeated for three quarters.

What to watch: fourth-quarter revenue against the $1.20 billion to $1.25 billion range implied by the full-year plan. Finishing near the bottom would mean holiday dining actually slowed.

🔴 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐏𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬
Sales from businesses owned a year ago rose 10.3% in the third quarter, while volume rose 6.1% in specialty cases and 6.6% in protein pounds. By our math, higher food prices supplied nearly 4 percentage points of that underlying sales growth, similar to the second quarter's 4.9% inflation boost.

Because the distributor charges a percentage markup on many items, rising food costs lift both revenue and gross profit dollars per box. If beef and specialty food prices flatten or fall, revenue growth would drop toward the 6% volume rate and gross margin gains would narrow. Detailed sales tables by food line, such as produce and dairy, are not in the release and await the quarterly filing.

What to watch: the gap between underlying sales growth and volume growth in the fourth quarter. A narrower gap paired with a gross margin below 24.5% would show that easing inflation is hurting unit profits.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝟑𝟗 𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐤𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔): $𝟏𝟏𝟓.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Free cash flow (operating cash minus equipment spending) jumped more than fivefold from $22.0 million in the first nine months of 2025, by our math. In the third quarter alone, the food distributor generated $36.0 million of free cash flow because inventory grew only 5.0% from a year ago while higher profits flowed into cash.

𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓𝟔𝟒.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Carrying net debt (total balance-sheet debt minus cash) fell 15.6% from $668.3 million a year ago, by our math. The US company paid down $30 million on its asset-based credit line during the first nine months and lifted cash to $164.7 million, which cut third-quarter interest expense to $9.0 million from $10.5 million.

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑𝟗𝟖.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Accounts receivable (money owed by restaurant customers for delivered food) rose 14.8% from $347.5 million a year ago, outpacing the 11.2% rise in third-quarter sales. The increase reflects strong September sales momentum as restaurants stocked up after the slower summer months, absorbing $15.7 million of operating cash over the first nine months.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬: $𝟒.𝟓𝟔–𝟒.𝟔𝟏 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $4.50–4.60 billion
Raised. Management lifted the middle of the full-year sales range by $35 million, calling for 10.5% growth for the year. By our math, that leaves fourth-quarter sales growth of 7.0% at the middle of the range, down from 11.2% in the third quarter. It is the second raise this year (+$0M in Q1, +$150M in Q2, +$35M in Q3).

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭: $𝟏.𝟏𝟑𝟎–𝟏.𝟏𝟒𝟎 𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $1.102–1.125 billion
Raised. The distributor moved the middle of the range up by $21.5 million, or 13.0% full-year growth. By our math, the outlook implies fourth-quarter gross profit growth of 8.6% and a 24.6% gross margin, down from 25.0% in the third quarter but 0.4 percentage points above last year's fourth quarter. The raise follows moves of +$0M in Q1 and +$49M in Q2.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $𝟑𝟏𝟕–𝟑𝟐𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠅 raised from $305–315 million
Raised. Finance chief Jim Leddy's updated table lifts the middle of the cash profit range by $9 million to 23.5% full-year growth, following moves of +$0M in Q1 and +$29M in Q2. By our math, that leaves fourth-quarter growth of 10.4% at a 7.25% margin. Inside the reconciliation table, full-year net income rose to $108.5–110.0 million, while interest expense was raised $5.5 million to $45.5–46.5 million.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐐𝟒 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐣𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐭𝐨 $𝟏𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧?
Nine-month interest expense was $28.8 million, and Q3 was $9.0 million, yet the full-year outlook table raises interest by $5.5 million to $45.5–46.5 million. Does the implied $17.2 million fourth-quarter charge include one-time costs from redeeming the 2028 convertible notes announced in August?

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰 𝐐𝟑 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬?
Selling, general and administrative expenses grew 12.1% and rose to 20.6% of sales, reversing the second quarter's 0.7-point efficiency gain. How much of that increase came from new facility openings and stock compensation versus ongoing wage and fuel inflation?

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝟏.𝟑𝟕-𝐩𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐢𝐧 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐣𝐮𝐦𝐩?
Center-of-the-plate gross margin expanded by 1.37 percentage points while pounds sold rose 6.6%. How much of that margin expansion came from passing through higher beef prices versus selling more custom-cut steaks, and why does the Q4 plan imply total gross margin slips to 24.6%?

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐨 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐞, 𝐝𝐚𝐢𝐫𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝?
The earnings release does not include the product-category revenue table or the digital ordering share that management previously highlighted. Did produce keep growing near the second quarter's 34% pace, and did dairy and egg revenue stop falling?

text:
She was 15.

She got in a cab. 

Police say she ended up stripped, stabbed, and trapped in his basement.

Thankfully, she was able to fight her way out.

Oct. 22, Baltimore.

A 15 year old girl needed a ride to pickup carryout. A man in a white Hyundai offered her a ride.

It was an unlicensed cab, and she would pay via Cash App.

During the ride, the driver went the wrong way.

When she called him out about it, he put her in a headlock.

He dragged her into his basement apartment.

He ripped off her clothes.

He stabbed her. About 5 times.

One wound collapsed her lung. 

She clawed at him.

She found a fire extinguisher, and bashed him with it, and ran.

Naked, barefoot, and bleeding.

She banged on doors until someone let her call 911.

She's expected to survive.

Abubakarr Barrie, 23, was found through the Cash App number.

He still had her phone in his possession.

He was arrested on Oct. 24.

9 counts, including attempted 1st degree murder and kidnapping.

No bond, thank goodness.

He has prior arrests, but no convictions. 

Preliminary hearing is set for Nov. 25.

Lock him up forever.

🇺🇸 https://t.co/LjthxyenWa — WHAT IF AMERICA'S NEXT GREAT DIGITAL PLATFORM WAS BUILT AROUND ONE SIMPLE PROMISE: GET THE RIGHT ANSWER?

Imagine moving to a new state.

You need to register your vehicle.

Understand local taxes.

Find healthcare coverage.

Apply for a business license.

Compare insurance options.

Research schools.

Understand employment regulations.

And navigate government services.

You open your browser.

Search.

Click.

Read.

Compare.

Search again.

One website contradicts another.

A government page sends you somewhere else.

An article is outdated.

An AI chatbot gives you a confident answer without a reliable source.

text:
1/ Scalping did not begin with Native Americans. 

Scalping as a war trophy existed among some Native nations before Europeans arrived. The Crow Creek site in South Dakota, dated around 1325, held the remains of roughly 486 people, more than 90 percent of whom showed cut marks consistent with scalping. 

A handful of smaller sites in Nebraska, Arizona and Illinois add a few dozen more individuals across several centuries. Explorers such as Jacques Cartier in 1535 and members of the de Soto expedition in 1540 recorded the practice among tribes they encountered. That evidence is real, though limited in scale.
What the invaders added was a state system. 

In 1616 an epidemic swept the New England coast, killing up to 90 percent of people in some villages. Survivors described finding skulls and bones still lying above ground where families could not bury each other. 

The English arrived in 1620 into that emptiness and called it providence. The suffering that followed was deliberate. Land was seized, agreements were broken or redrawn, and food stores were destroyed. In 1622 the Virginia Company ordered colonists to burn Native cornfields as a war tactic. Plymouth did the same during the Pequot War. Burn the fields, starve the people, take what remains.

In 1637, colonial militia and their Native allies surrounded the Pequot fort at Mystic, Connecticut, and set it on fire. Hundreds of men, women and children burned to death inside. That was the opening act of the Pequot War, and it happened years before any scalp bounty existed. Scalping by Native nations in that period was retaliation and survival accounting in a war they did not start. Every society fought its own wars. 

England spent centuries fighting Scotland, Wales and Ireland. France and Spain tore each other apart for generations. Tribal warfare in North America was no different in kind.

What had no parallel in Europe was a government putting a price on a human scalp and paying it from the public treasury. In 1641 the Dutch governor Willem Kieft of New Amsterdam offered the first colonial bounty for Indian scalps. Massachusetts followed in 1644. By 1689, during King William’s War, Massachusetts paid eight pounds from the public treasury for each Indian scalp, plus whatever plunder the soldiers kept. In 1696 the rate was fifty pounds for a man fourteen or older and twenty five for a woman or child. By 1702 it was ten pounds for anyone aged ten or older, twenty for a fighting age man, and a hundred pounds by the 1720s. 

New Hampshire authorised a hundred pounds per male scalp in 1724. 

Children under ten were not paid for as scalps. They were sold into slavery, and the hunters kept the proceeds.
Hannah Dustin, who killed ten Abenaki captives including six children in their sleep in 1697, was paid fifty pounds by the Massachusetts General Assembly and became a colonial heroine. A bronze statue of her holding scalps still stands in Haverhill. 

Research by the Upstander Project found at least sixty nine government scalp edicts across the Dawnland between 1675 and 1760, and at least fifty more elsewhere until 1885. More than nine thousand pounds was paid from colonial treasuries, millions in today’s money, plus hundreds of thousands of acres of land. Towns such as Westbrook in Maine and Shirley in Massachusetts were founded on that land by the men who collected. In 1755 Lieutenant Governor Spencer Phips of Massachusetts issued an edict calling for the Penobscot to be pursued, captivated, killed and destroyed.

During King Philip’s War in 1675 Native raiders killed around 800 English, some of them scalped, though exact scalp counts were not recorded because bounties were not yet widespread. One later compilation of atrocities on both sides from 1511 to 1890 counted 9,156 killed by Native Americans and 7,193 by people of European descent, covering every form of killing rather than scalping alone.

text:
Dan Tapiero on Getting Rich in Crypto, Knowing When to Sell, and Building Wealth That Lasts

In this episode of When Shift Happens, I sit down with @DTAPCAP, founder of @50TFunds, to discuss what it really takes to build and preserve wealth in crypto. Drawing on 35 years of investing experience, including working alongside legendary investors Stanley Druckenmiller, Julian Robertson, and Steve Cohen, Dan shares why patience is often more valuable than intelligence, how he avoided investing in FTX, and why he believes the biggest opportunities in blockchain are still ahead.

Wealth Is What You Keep, Not What You Spend

Dan begins with a lesson he frequently shares with his children: "You are wealthy because you have money, not because you spend it." Having spent decades around some of the world's wealthiest investors, he has observed a difference between genuine financial security and outward displays of success. In Greenwich, Connecticut, where he previously lived, families with generations of accumulated wealth often occupied modest homes, while newly wealthy residents purchased enormous properties and expensive luxuries.

For Dan, wealth is less about demonstrating purchasing power and more about retaining the freedom that money creates. Spending is not inherently wrong, but without limits, even substantial fortunes can be lost. He also challenges the assumption that becoming rich solves every problem. Wealth brings comfort and independence, but can introduce new responsibilities, unwanted attention, and complications.

Learning to Take Risks Before Everyone Agrees

Dan's career illustrates another essential principle: meaningful opportunities rarely come with widespread approval. Before establishing 50T Holdings, he co-founded a physical gold investment business, GBI. For years, people questioned why he was pursuing gold when it attracted relatively little interest, but the business prospects later improved dramatically as gold prices rose.

His early conviction in Bitcoin and blockchain attracted similar skepticism. "You have to be comfortable living a little bit in the gray with uncertainty," he explains. Investors must develop the confidence to act on well-researched opportunities before the broader market recognizes their potential. By the time everyone agrees an investment is attractive, much of its potential upside is gone.

Why Dan Passed on FTX

Perhaps the clearest illustration of Dan's investment discipline is his decision to avoid FTX. During the crypto boom, investors urged him to back the exchange, but he remained unconvinced, particularly by its valuation. His firm generally targets investments valued at approximately five to ten times revenue, but FTX was valued at roughly 50 times revenue, far outside his preferred range. Instead, he invested in Deribit, a cryptocurrency options exchange, at approximately six to seven times net profit. Deribit subsequently became a major success for his fund when Coinbase acquired it.

Dans explains that investors often become enthusiastic when prices are high but retreat when opportunities become cheaper. In fact, he struggled to raise his fourth fund during the 2023–2024 bear-market period, despite his extensive track record. That fund then became his most successful, generating more than 250% in gross gains.

Patience Gets You Into Wealth. Selling Helps You Keep It.

Dan describes crypto as "the easiest place in the world to make money" but one of the hardest places to hold on to it. Much of this difficulty comes from investor psychology. For instance, investors who experience enormous gains often become emotionally attached to their ‘wins’ and struggle to sell, while those who endure prolonged losses may sell immediately when prices recover just to escape the discomfort.

Dan believes both reactions demonstrate why patience and emotional detachment must be learned. He also emphasizes the importance of establishing an exit strategy before purchasing an asset. Even when there are fundamental reasons to keep holding, taking some profits can protect the gains already achieved.

For younger investors especially, he cautions against optimizing for immediate riches. Although taking risks early in life can create opportunities, recovering from significant financial losses can take years. His preferred approach is to think in five- or ten-year periods, allocate capital deliberately, and recognize that surviving market downturns is essential to long-term compounding.

The Next Opportunity

Dan remains deeply optimistic about blockchain's long-term potential. He compares the internet's digitization of information with blockchain's emerging ability to digitize money, ownership, and value. Stablecoins, tokenized government securities, and decentralized trading platforms represent early examples, but Dan believes the larger opportunity lies in tokenizing illiquid assets, particularly real estate and farmland.

His interest stems partly from an agricultural investment business he established years earlier. Despite farmland representing an enormous asset class, ordinary investors had limited opportunities to access large, professionally managed portfolios. Tokenization could eventually change that. Dan imagines a future where property records, financial assets, and legal documentation can be managed through interconnected blockchain systems, simplifying transactions that currently require numerous intermediaries.

What Does a Rich Life Actually Look Like?

Toward the end of the conversation, Dan offers a more personal definition of success. For him, a rich life means independence, time with family, intellectual curiosity, travel, and the freedom to pursue interests that matter. Despite his success, he continues attending conferences, meeting entrepreneurs, and exploring unfamiliar ideas rather than settling into a comfortable routine.

After decades navigating financial markets, Dan's perspective ultimately returns to a simple distinction. Wealth is not defined by the biggest trade, the fastest return, or the lifestyle it can display. It comes from making thoughtful decisions, remaining patient when others lose conviction, and working towards your personal definition of enough.

Let Cmd(R, x): religion R commands x as a standing duty.
