text:
Trump’s CDC Resurrects 'Buried' Data on Armed Self-Defense | Tim O'Brien, PJ Media

Gun control advocates have a bad habit of attempting to rewrite history. Few of their revisionist efforts, however, have been as brazen as their campaign to strong-arm the Biden administration into scrubbing the website of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention of accurate but inconvenient data on defensive gun uses. Now, as the Trump administration restores the agency’s longstanding acknowledgement of basic defensive gun use data, gun control advocates have audaciously declared it a “politically motivated” move to “inflate” defensive gun use numbers.

It’s hilariously bad faith framing, even for them.

For years, the CDC’s website included a small but objective and accurate section providing information on defensive gun use data and related research. It linked to a 2013 report commissioned by the CDC itself, and in a single sentence informed the public that the report “indicates a range 60,000 to 2.5 million defensive gun uses each year.” The CDC only removed this information from the website in 2022 at the behest of gun control advocates, who spent a year in private closed-door meetings with the agency, browbeating it with demands to erase the defensive gun use data for purely and blatantly political reasons. One prominent gun control activist went so far as to attack the data as something that “needs to be killed, buried, dug up, killed again and buried again.”

Their anger is somewhat ironic, given that the CDC’s original online characterization was arguably far more favorable to gun control advocates’ claims than the actual language of the 2013 report. Compared to the one-sentence website summary, for example, the report offered a more robust and positive assessment of the available research, including evidence that defensive gun use effectively decreases the risk of victim injuries. The website also neglected to include the report’s assessment that “defensive use of guns by crime victims is a common occurrence.”

The 2013 report, moreover, strongly downplayed the lower end of the defensive gun use estimate range, asserting that “almost all national survey estimates” actually fall within a range of 500,000 to 2.5 million incidents. It noted that only a few outlier scholars reached “radically lower estimates” of 60,000 to 120,000 times a year, based on a survey that didn’t even specifically ask about defensive gun use. More recent and comprehensive studies have only bolstered the evidence for annual defensive gun use numbers well into the 1-to-2.5 million range.

To celebrate the CDC’s “resurrection” of its buried defensive gun use data, here are some of the defensive gun use stories you probably missed last month (and that gun control advocates love to pretend rarely happen):

- Sept. 1, Lehigh Acres, Fla. — A man with an extensive criminal history shoved another person to the ground during an argument that started when the victim ordered the man to leave his property. The man then stood over the victim and threatened him with a pickaxe, prompting the victim to shoot the man in self-defense. Police later arrested the pickaxe-wielding assailant for aggravated battery with a deadly weapon.

- Sept. 7, Birmingham, Ala. — Two intruders broke into a home and refused to leave even after the homeowner confronted them, leading to a physical altercation. The homeowner eventually armed himself and fired one round at the intruders in self-defense, grazing one and sending both fleeing. Police quickly apprehended the suspects, who each face charges for second-degree burglary and harassment. The suspect who allegedly drove the getaway vehicle faces an additional DUI charge.

- Sept. 10, Kerrville, Texas — Police believe that a homeowner who shot and critically wounded a man did so in self-defense after the man came to his house and threatened him with a knife over an alleged debt.

- Sept. 15, Orland Park, Ill. — Security camera footage captured the moment a concealed carry permit holder successfully turned the tables on a masked man who tried to rob him at gunpoint as he filled his tank at a gas station. The permit holder quickly drew a gun from his waistband and fired multiple shots at the would-be robber, who dropped his weapon and fled after sustaining a gunshot wound to the cheek. The 20-year-old suspect was later arrested and charged with attempted armed robbery, possession of a stolen weapon, and other weapons-related felonies.

- Sept. 16, North Olmstead, Ohio — Local officials announced that they dismissed a murder charge initially filed against an 18-year-old who fatally shot his older brother, after finding that the evidence—including 911 recordings and witness statements—supported the young man’s claim that he acted to protect his mother, sister, and cousin when his brother attacked them.

- Sept. 19, Anton Chico, N.M. — After an 18-year-old woman left her ex-boyfriend at a gas station during an argument, the ex-boyfriend stole a truck and chased the woman to a residence nearly 40 miles away. He ultimately drove away from the residence with the 18-year-old’s car, leaving her to wait for her mom to pick her up. As she and her mom drove home, they encountered the ex-boyfriend, who’d been waiting for them. He shot at their car and caused them to crash, then shot at the mother’s boyfriend when he showed up to help. The mother’s boyfriend, however, returned fire until he could “subdue” the gunman, whose criminal charges now include aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and car theft.

- Sept. 21, Bowman, Ga. — When the owner of a vacant house confronted a burglar whom he discovered on the property, the burglar decided to assault the owner rather than flee. The owner shot the combative burglar, who, in turn, reconsidered his stance on running away. The now-wounded suspect fled but didn’t make it far before police apprehended him.

- Sept. 24, Ft. Lauderdale, Fla. — Police say that two armed men broke into an Airbnb rental home and tried to rob the renter. The renter was also armed and exchanged gunfire with the intruders, critically injuring one and sending both fleeing. Police eventually arrested the two suspects for attempted murder and home invasion with a firearm.

- Sept. 26, San Francisco, Calif. — A masked burglar—with a large husky in tow—broke into an elderly Vietnam vet’s home by drilling out the lock on his front door. The noise awakened the vet, who retrieved a handgun and shot the intruder after a brief altercation that left the vet with minor injuries. The wounded intruder fled, leaving his uninjured canine companion behind. Police found him about three miles away and arrested him.

- Sept. 28, Indianapolis, Ind. — A woman shot and wounded a man who allegedly hit her with his car during an incident of domestic violence. Police arrested the man for domestic battery with a deadly weapon and, in consultation with local prosecutors, declined to pursue charges against the woman.

- Sept. 29, Charlottesville, Va. — Two would-be burglars climbed their way onto a second-story balcony to force their way into an apartment, but were met by an armed resident who exchanged gunfire with them until they fled. Police quickly apprehended one suspect, who’d been shot in the chest, and are still searching for the other.

These armed victims are something far more than data points to be manipulated, buried, or strategically recast for political gain. Their stories prove to the world just what the right to keep and bear arms is worth in the situations where it’s needed the most.

Gun control advocates spent decades insisting that defensive gun uses are too rare to matter. When the data proved them wrong, they didn’t change their argument or their tune—they just lobbied the government to change its website. Now that Trump’s CDC has dug the numbers back up, these same gun control advocates can’t seem to remember who buried them in the first place. And every month, we’ll keep sharing fresh stories to bring to life the data that just won’t stay dead.

https://t.co/Bz9fFDjWMm

📅 October 28, 2026 · Past 12 Hours

🔴 DISASTER
• SPAIN HIGH-SPEED TRAIN CRASH: Two high-speed trains — a Renfe AVE and a private Iryo service — collided south of Madrid near Urda in Toledo province early Wednesday, killing at least 30 people with the toll still rising (Spanish media report 40+). About 500 passengers were aboard; the Madrid–Seville line is suspended while rescue teams work the scene.
• CYCLONE ARNAB SLAMS INDIA'S ANDHRA PRADESH: The storm made landfall near Kakinada with gusts around 140 km/h, forcing roughly 85,000 people to evacuate. Authorities report at least 3 deaths and 31 homes damaged, with coastal train services cancelled.

🗳️ ISRAEL POLITICS
• NO CLEAR WINNER IN ISRAEL'S VOTE: With about 77% counted, Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc leads on 54 seats versus 47 for challenger Gadi Eisenkot's bloc, with Arab parties at 19 — short of the 61 needed for a majority. Netanyahu claimed a "decisive majority among the Zionist and Jewish public," but coalition bargaining could take weeks.

🌍 DIPLOMACY
• SECRET UKRAINE MEDIATION: Fox News reports First Lady Melania Trump secretly brokered a historic Russia–Ukraine ceasefire deal as an undisclosed intermediary — an exclusive claim not yet confirmed by Kyiv or Moscow. If confirmed, it would be the most senior informal U.S. channel in the war to date.

💻 TECH & AI
• MICROSOFT OFFERS BUYOUTS TO 60,000: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees — more than a quarter of its global workforce — to contain costs and help fund its AI investment push. The offer covers staff in the US, Canada, India and the UK at level 70 and below.
• ANTHROPIC FILES ITS IPO: The Claude maker filed its S-1 on Monday, planning to list on Nasdaq as "ANT" with $16.3B in first-half 2026 revenue and a headline $80.7B net loss (mostly non-cash accounting charges). It posted its first profitable operating quarter — $974M — and is expected to target a valuation above $2 trillion.

⛽ ENERGY & CLIMATE
• HORMUZ OIL SPILL CLOSES UAE BEACHES: Oil from a tanker struck near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the UAE coastline, prompting closures including all beaches in Ras Al Khaimah plus sites in Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah. Officials warn of environmental and health risks as cleanup continues.
• TANZANIA'S FIRST GAS FIND IN A DECADE: Tanzania has announced its first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years, which the energy minister called a "major milestone" for the East African nation.

---⚠️ Sources: Reuters, AP, BBC, CNN, Al Jazeera, CNBC, Fox News

Following the TikTok ban in 2020, 

The Indian short-video ecosystem transformed drastically.

While global giants like Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts lead overall market dominance
@
Several homegrown Swadeshi>
@
"Made in India" apps have captured hundreds of millions of users, particularly across regional languages and Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities
@
The most popular Indian short-video apps:

1. Moj

Developed by ShareChat (Mohalla Tech), Moj is India’s largest pure short-video platform.

• User Base: Over 160 million monthly active users.

• Key Features:
Highly popular for regional language content, viral lipsyncs, dance challenges, and comedy skits. It supports over 15 Indian languages and offers extensive localized filters and effects.

2. ShareChat

While not exclusively a short-video app, ShareChat is a massive Indian social media platform that acts as a major hub for discovering and sharing short videos and memes.

• User Base: Over 160 million users.

• Key Features: Focuses heavily on vernacular and non-English content. It allows users to download and share videos seamlessly directly to WhatsApp, making it incredibly viral in rural and semi-urban India.

3. Hipi

Owned by Zee Entertainment Enterprises, Hipi has steadily grown into a strong domestic competitor by leveraging its entertainment network connections.

• Key Features:
Very popular for its creator-friendly interface and access to a massive library of licensed Bollywood and regional music tracks. It frequently hosts talent hunts that tie directly back to Zee television shows.

4. Chingari

Chingari gained massive initial traction as a primary TikTok alternative right after the ban.

• Key Features:
It has shifted heavy focus into Web3 integration, offering a "watch-to-earn" ecosystem built around its own crypto token (GARI). It also features live interactive audio and video rooms.

5. Josh

Developed by Dailyhunt (Ver Se Innovation), Josh was once a neck-and-neck rival to Moj for regional short-form content.

• Key Features:
Tailored heavily for creators in "Bharat" (regional India) with multilingual support and excellent video editing tools.

Note: Recent market shifts have seen Josh pivot its core engagement strategy toward paid live audio/video calls rather than pure short-video scrolling.

text:
Microsoft just offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees today. Here's what you need to know.

The program is called the Voluntary Exit Offer. It was announced Monday in a memo to employees. The memo says the offer is new for the company and that Microsoft will learn from it.

It is open to employees in participating teams in the US, Canada, India and the UK. Reports say eligibility covers staff at level 70 and below, including senior leaders. There is no age or tenure requirement. Data center teams are among those excluded.

The terms resemble Microsoft's standard severance offer. Eligible staff get severance-style benefits based on where they live, plus career-planning resources. One report puts US terms at a minimum of 60 days of base pay, capped at up to 39 weeks.

The goal is to control headcount without layoffs. Microsoft is trimming labor costs and redirecting spending toward AI, while protecting its AI infrastructure investments. Commentators say headcount and revenue growth are diverging at big tech companies. Others say this is how AI job cuts happen, through voluntary exits and slower hiring instead of mass layoffs.

Key numbers:
- About 60,000 employees eligible
- Roughly a quarter of the workforce, 25% to 27% depending on the count
- 223,000 employees globally as of June
- Four countries covered: US, Canada, India, UK
- MSFT stock at $529.84, up 1.02%

Microsoft has not said how many people will accept the offer.

SpAItial launches Echo-3 for 3D modeling

SpAItial has just released Echo-3, an app that turns your iPhone into a powerful tool for capturing real-world spaces in stunningly accurate 3D models.
What Is Echo-3?

Echo-3 is not just another 3D scanner or camera rig; it’s an innovative application that leverages AI to create photorealistic Gaussian Splat models of any space you capture with your phone. The app allows users to walk around a room, capturing everything from walls and furniture to intricate details, and then uses advanced algorithms to reconstruct the scene in 1D.
How Does It Work?

The process is surprisingly simple:

1. Capture: Open the SpAItial app on your iPhone and start walking slowly around the space you want to capture.
2. Generate: The app’s AI analyzes the captured data and generates a photorealistic Gaussian Splat model, ensuring that even partially hidden areas are filled in with plausible geometry.
3. Explore and Share: Once the 3D model is ready, you can explore it interactively, take measurements, and share links to view the model in any web browser.
Why Should You Care?

Echo-3 democratizes access to sophisticated 3D modeling technology by making it available on mobile devices. No more expensive hardware or specialized equipment—just your phone and a free app. This makes it accessible for home renovators, architects, real estate professionals, and anyone interested in exploring the potential of 3D models.
What’s New?

The standout feature of Echo-3 is its ability to handle partial captures and missing data effectively. The AI can accurately recreate unseen areas based on context and existing data, ensuring that even if you miss a corner or two while walking around, the app will still provide a complete and accurate 3D model.
What Is Stored?

When you use Echo-3, your captured data is processed by SpAItial’s servers to generate the 3D models. The resulting models are stored on their cloud infrastructure, allowing you to access them from anywhere with an internet connection. You can also download and save these models locally if needed.
What Is Excluded?

Echo-3 does not store personal data beyond what is necessary for generating and accessing your 3D models. It doesn’t collect or retain any information about individuals unless explicitly provided by the user, such as names or contact details when sharing links to models.
User Controls

Users have control over their captured data through various settings within the app:
• Privacy Settings: You can choose whether to share your models publicly or keep them private.
• Data Management: You can delete any 3D model from both SpAItial’s servers and your local device at any time.
Availability

Echo-3 is currently available as a free download for iPhone users. The app requires an active internet connection to process the captured data and generate models, but once generated, you can view them offline.
Technical Details

The Echo-3 application uses advanced AI algorithms to create Gaussian Splat models, which are highly detailed representations of real-world spaces. These models are not just visually accurate; they also capture physical properties like lighting and texture, making them incredibly useful for a variety of applications. The app’s on-screen guides help users ensure that all critical areas are captured during the initial walk-through.
Practical Use Cases
• Home Renovation: Homeowners can use Echo-3 to visualize changes before committing to renovations.
• Real Estate Marketing: Real estate agents can create immersive 3D tours of properties, enhancing online listings and attracting more potential buyers.
• Architectural Design: Architects can quickly capture existing spaces for reference in design projects.
Limitations

While Echo-3 offers impressive capabilities in generating detailed 3D models from mobile captures, it does not prove that AI has reached a point where it can replace traditional surveying methods entirely. There are still limitations to the technology and scenarios where high-precision measurements or specialized equipment remain necessary. For instance, complex industrial settings with intricate machinery might require more precise tools than what Echo-3 currently offers.
What This Does Not Prove

Echo-3 is a powerful tool for quickly capturing and visualizing spaces in 3D without needing expensive hardware. However, it does not prove that AI has reached a point where it can replace traditional surveying methods entirely. text:
If your picture of fishing ends when the boat docks, a lot of women disappear.

Women repair gear, sort and process the catch, sell fish and keep the accounts. Women also fish, from boats and from shore. Yet official records can focus on onboard employment, leaving much of the work that keeps a fishing business going outside the frame.

A 2024 FAO study of Mediterranean and Black Sea fisheries estimated that women held 38% of jobs in the post-harvest stage. It also warned that the available figures probably undercounted women’s work, especially in small-scale fisheries. Describing someone as a family helper can make a working person vanish surprisingly efficiently.

One revealing detail concerns a professional card. In its discussion of Tunisia, the study describes a fishing professional card that provides access to social protection and credit. Obtaining it requires following a training schedule.

That sounds straightforward until you ask who can attend.

If a course clashes with selling the catch, requires a journey someone cannot afford, or assumes another person will look after the children, the invitation offers much less than it appears to. Attendance starts measuring who can rearrange their life around the course.

Information has a similar problem. A Tunisian interviewee described how men working onboard vessels had more contact with fisheries officials through data collection. Women doing shore-based fishing, marketing or processing could struggle to reach those same officials for training or administrative support.

There is a nasty loop here. Work that gets counted creates contact with institutions. That contact brings information and opportunities. Work outside the count leaves its workers having to find another way in.

The study’s interviews involved 24 people across five countries. Their experiences cannot stand for every coastal community, but they show how much can go wrong between announcing an opportunity and making it usable.

A training programme can be open to everyone on paper and still mostly reach people who already have transport, spare time and contact with officials. The women who cannot attend may then appear in the next report as a group that needs more encouragement.

Changing that takes practical work: different schedules, affordable travel, direct contact with women’s organizations. It also means letting those women help decide what the programme is for. They may have priorities that never made it onto the course outline.

Our guide to the study:

text:
Kilchattan Bay, on the southern end of the Isle of Bute, is a small Scottish coastal village with a quiet charm. Victorian villas line the waterfront, overlooking a broad sandy bay, while the steep hillside behind gives shelter from the prevailing westerly winds.

It’s a place for an unhurried wander along the shore, watching the water and exploring the old pier. For those wanting to stretch their legs, the West Island Way starts here, following the rugged coastline towards the southern tip of Bute. Nearby, the ruins of St Blane’s Church offer a glimpse into the island’s long history.

Peaceful, scenic and full of character, Kilchattan Bay is somewhere to slow down and enjoy the simple pleasure of being beside the sea.

#kilchattanbay #isleofbute

text:
Inside Anthropic's Initial Registration Statement ($ANT): Five Share Classes, Two Single-Share Governance Classes, $16.3B in Half-Year Revenue, and the Multi-Chip Compute Commitments

Anthropic, PBC has filed its initial registration statement and applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT; the price range has not yet been set. A Delaware public benefit corporation, the company states its specific purpose as "the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity," and describes its own design as "a novel capital and corporate governance structure."

1. Five common classes, two of them a single share each
• Class A carries one vote per share and is the class offered to the public. Class N is non-voting; its holders are "primarily strategic business partners," it generally converts to Class A on transfer to an unaffiliated third party, and Amazon Web Services receives Class N shares when its convertible notes convert. Class E is issued to employees other than the co-founders, votes only on certain limited matters, and has no economic rights.
• Class T: one share, no economic rights, held by the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which the filing describes as an independent body of five financially disinterested voting trustees. The share generally elects and removes the Class T directors, who constitute a majority of the board. The company says the Trust is designed to supply "the incentives and insights" for balancing stockholder returns, those affected by its conduct, and its stated purpose.
• Class F: one share, no economic rights, to be issued immediately before the offering closes to an LLC whose sole initial members are the seven co-founders. It carries 50.1% of total voting power on matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of all non-Class T directors, and the filing states that this voting power is not subject to dilution from new Class A issuance. If a majority of the continuing founders cannot agree, the share generally votes in proportion to the Class A vote. The company states it believes the co-founders are "distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission."
• Under a stockholders' agreement, the Trust and the Founder LLC can together elect all members of the board, and the company will be a controlled company under Nasdaq rules. The filing states that Class A holders generally will not be able to affect the outcome of any stockholder vote or director election, regardless of how they vote.

2. Public benefit share issuance
• The company contributed 846,840,960 Class N shares, representing 5% of fully diluted shares as of 30 June 2026 (assuming full conversion of the Amazon notes), to its wholly owned Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. The shares are legally outstanding but are not treated as outstanding for accounting purposes.
• The board has also approved a framework under which it may, at its discretion, issue the fund up to an additional 2% of then-outstanding shares (including options, restricted stock units, other convertible securities, and the fund's own holdings) each time the share price rises 50% above the prior milestone, beginning at the IPO price.

3. From operating loss to net loss, and the cash flow
• Revenue: $41 million (2023), $386 million (2024), $4,585 million (2025); $16,286 million in the six months ended 30 June 2026, against $1,163 million in the same period of 2025.
• First-half 2026 operating expenses included $8,945 million for compute and infrastructure (H1 2025: $2,334 million) and $3,152 million for personnel, which includes $2.2 billion of stock-based compensation. 2025 included a $1,500 million Bartz settlement.
• Operating loss narrowed from $2,135 million to $693 million half-year over half-year. The six-month net loss of $80,748 million mainly reflects a $72,388 million change in the fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities and SAFEs, which the filing attributes primarily to an increase in its enterprise valuation, and $8,757 million of other expense tied to fair-value recognition under its note purchase agreements, partly offset by $1,111 million of interest income.
• Net cash from operating activities was an inflow of $3,929 million in the first half of 2026, against an outflow of $1,513 million in the first half of 2025; purchases of property and equipment were $482 million. Preferred stock issuance brought in $110,432 million net in the half, and cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments stood at $131,651 million at 30 June 2026.

4. Compute and infrastructure commitments across four chip families
• The company states that it trains and serves Claude natively across four major chip families (AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs) using a proprietary orchestration layer that enables it "to optimize workloads for price and performance," and that it has operated in "a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute." The prospectus describes what it calls its most significant existing arrangements, and notes it is party to others not described. The amounts below are of different kinds (spending minimums, "up to" ceilings, and estimates), and several are excluded from the filing's contractual obligations table.
• Usage-independent spending commitments: at least approximately $114.5 billion with Google (April 2026 to July 2033) and at least $110.0 billion with Amazon (May 2026 to April 2036), each "regardless of actual usage," with a true-up payment if actual spend falls short, and each non-cancelable except on the provider's uncured material breach. At least $44.9 billion with Microsoft (November 2026 to May 2033), also regardless of actual usage, non-cancelable except on Microsoft's uncured material breach or, per tranche, for undelivered tranches.
• Additional TPU capacity: a commitment to procure additional TPU compute from TPU providers, including Google, for delivery between 2028 and 2031. Payments depend on the capacity made available, its deployment, pricing mechanics and certain deployment conditions; the company estimates them at approximately $125.0 billion to $150.0 billion, not included in the contractual obligations table.
• Broadcom equipment leases: five-year master equipment leases providing TPU-based compute capacity, accounted for as finance leases, with aggregate rent of approximately $161.2 billion excluding interest. Rent is payable quarterly, typically from when equipment is "ready for service." The leases are non-cancelable by either party except in the case of a default, are guaranteed by Anthropic, PBC and secured by the leased equipment, and the company may, in certain circumstances, finance a certain amount of quarterly rent under the 2026 lease through convertible promissory notes.
• NVIDIA GPU capacity: agreements with https://t.co/nxqmZZ9DkM LLC (formerly https://t.co/NfAY48sPBZ LLC), a wholly owned subsidiary of Space Exploration Technologies Corp., for up to $120.5 billion over terms extending into 2029, approximately $3.1 billion per month once all capacity is delivered (expected December 2026). Following initial non-cancelable periods ending in January 2027 and March 2027, either party may cancel each agreement on 90 days' advance written notice. Agreements with Nscale for up to approximately $44.6 billion over terms extending into 2033, and with Lambda for approximately $41.3 billion over terms extending into 2034, with fees accruing only as capacity is delivered and accepted. Nscale's are cancelable in limited circumstances, including missed delivery or service-availability requirements; for Lambda's August 2026 agreement (approximately $34.9 billion of the total), either party may terminate if Lambda does not timely secure the facility lease.
• AMD: a hardware supply agreement for an initial tranche of Helios rack-scale capacity in calendar 2027, subject to conditions on deployment proposals. It specifies no fixed dollar commitment; if the initial capacity is procured in full, the company expects expenditures to exceed $20.0 billion over the term, not included in the contractual obligations table, with potential additional capacity of up to approximately the initial commitment. The company cannot cancel except on AMD's uncured material breach.

The multiple is the debate; the structure is the fact.

text:
$REPL Q2 2027 earnings: Replimune launches its melanoma drug, and trial cuts shrink losses

Replimune, a cancer biotechnology firm, shifted from drug development to commercial sales while cutting its operating loss. The company recorded no revenue before the quarter ended in September, then delivered its newly approved skin cancer therapy Tudriqev to the first patients on October 6. Chief executive Sushil Patel said more than 15 hospitals have already prescribed the treatment, while winding down older clinical trials cut quarterly operating expenses by 33% to $56 million.

• Operating loss: $𝟓𝟔.𝟑𝐌 (-33% from a year ago)
• Cash and short-term investments: $𝟑𝟎𝟕.𝟖𝐌 (up from $195.3M last quarter)
• Prescribing hospitals: >𝟏𝟓 (since October 6 launch)
• Cash funding outlook: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (greater than 12 months)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🟢 Bullish

The story got better because the launch started on schedule with broad insurer support and a rebuilt $308 million cash cushion. Inclusion in national cancer guidelines and an unrestricted label helped the sales team reach over 70% of its 200 target hospitals quickly. One caution: the August stock sale and September loan draw increased the share count by 14% from a year ago and pushed debt interest costs higher.

The question now is how quickly hospital interest turns into collected revenue. Either routine skin injections drive fast repeat orders, or the need to coordinate radiologists for deep-organ injections slows patient volumes. Next quarter's first reported product sales will provide the answer.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐓𝐮𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐪𝐞𝐯 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐌𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐨𝐦𝐚 𝐏𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐁𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞
Replimune, a biotechnology firm that develops virus-based cancer therapies, started commercial sales of its first approved medicine right after the quarter closed. Its lead treatment is Tudriqev (previously called RP1), a modified virus injected into tumours alongside the immunotherapy drug nivolumab for adults with advanced skin melanoma. “The response from physicians has been enthusiastic and both oncologists and interventional radiologists are eager to bring TUDRIQEV into their practices,” chief executive Sushil Patel said.

Doctors gave the first patient doses on October 6, and clinics began ordering the drug “for next day delivery immediately upon availability”. The launch is moving fast because the approved label covers patients “with no requirement for prior BRAF treatment, and can be injected into superficial, deep and visceral lesions, including lung and liver”.

• Prescribing clinics: more than 15 institutions in the first three weeks
• Priority hospitals contacted: over 70% of the initial 200 targets (more than 140 accounts by our math)
• Treatment guidelines: listed as a Category 2A recommendation by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN, an alliance of cancer centres)
• Supply on hand: “more than a year of inventory on hand, produced at its in-house manufacturing facility”

What to watch: the first reported product revenue in the third-quarter results. Because the drug shipped on October 6, next quarter will offer the first dollar reading on how quickly those 15 clinics turn prescriptions into paid sales.

🟢 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐖𝐢𝐧𝐝-𝐃𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐛𝐲 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝
While the drug maker prepared for its first commercial launch, it cut its operating loss by a third from a year ago. Total operating costs fell 33.2% to $56.3 million, down from $84.3 million in the prior year. Research and development (R&D, the cost of running clinical trials and lab work) drove most of the savings, dropping 40.6% to $34.4 million.

Replimune spent less because it wound down three older clinical trials—IGNYTE, ARTACUS and CERPASS—and reduced staff costs. Selling, general and administrative expenses (SG&A, the cost of sales teams and corporate overhead) also fell 17.0% from a year ago to $21.9 million. Both expense lines included $10.6 million of non-cash stock compensation by our math.

What to watch: research and development spending over the second half of the year. Continuing declines would confirm that the cost savings from finished trials more than offset the cost of enrolling the Phase 3 IGNYTE-3 and Phase 2/3 REVEAL studies.

🟢 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐃𝐫𝐚𝐰 𝐑𝐞𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐁𝐮𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫
A new cancer drug launch requires a large cash cushion before insurer payments arrive. The Massachusetts biotech ended September with $307.8 million in cash, up 57.6% from $195.3 million three months earlier. It raised $141.0 million net by selling stock and pre-funded warrants in August, and it drew another $15.0 million from its long-term loan in September.

By our math, cash burn before financing dropped to $43.5 million in the second quarter, down from $73.6 million in the first quarter. Lower clinical trial spending slowed the cash drain just as the new financing arrived, giving the business more breathing room for the Tudriqev rollout.

What to watch: quarterly cash burn before financing in the third quarter. A number near or below $45 million would show that early commercial receipts and lower research costs are keeping the cash drain in check.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐎𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐃𝐫𝐚𝐰𝐬 𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬
Funding the company through stock sales and venture loans carries a clear cost for existing owners. The weighted average share count rose 14.4% from a year ago to 105.2 million shares, and it climbed 8.6% from the first quarter alone after the August stock and warrant offering.

At the same time, borrowing more money is lifting interest bills while falling cash balances over the past year reduced interest income. Interest expense on debt jumped 69.6% from a year ago to $2.5 million after the September loan draw, while investment income fell by half to $1.9 million.

What to watch: additional drawdowns on the debt facility and the diluted share count as pre-funded warrants convert. Further loan draws would push quarterly interest costs higher before Tudriqev sales cover operating expenses.

🔴🔴 𝐋𝐚𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐡 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 𝐓𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤 𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬
Patel highlighted rapid hospital interest in Tudriqev, yet the company gave no sales forecast for the year and faces rising commercial bills. While selling and administrative costs fell from a year ago, they rose 15.5% from last quarter to $21.9 million as the sales force geared up for the October launch.

In addition, the drug requires an injection directly into deep tumours such as the lung and liver, which requires interventional radiologists and complex hospital workflows. Finally, the US regulator granted accelerated approval based on tumour shrinkage rates, so keeping the drug on the market depends on “verification of clinical benefit in a confirmatory trial(s)”—specifically the ongoing IGNYTE-3 survival study.

What to watch: selling, general and administrative costs alongside initial product sales next quarter. If commercial overhead grows faster than early prescription revenue, cash burn will climb again despite the research cuts.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 (𝟐𝟕𝐐𝟐): $𝟐𝟕𝟖.𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇄ reversing
Working capital—short-term assets minus short-term bills—rebounded 71.5% from $162.4 million last quarter after shrinking for four straight periods. The August stock sale and September debt draw drove the increase, leaving a larger short-term buffer to fund commercial inventory and receivables.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 (𝟐𝟕𝐐𝟐): -$𝟎.𝟓𝟒  ⇘ decelerating
The net loss per share narrowed 40.0% from -$0.90 a year ago and shrank from -$0.72 in the first quarter. Lower clinical trial expenses cut the total net loss by 31.3% to $57.1 million, while a higher share count spread the loss across more shares.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐰𝐚𝐲: 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝟏𝟐 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Greater than 12 months
Unchanged. Replimune said its $307.8 million in cash will “enable us to fund operations for greater than twelve months” from the filing date, covering the Tudriqev rollout and ongoing trials. By our math, at the second quarter's $43.5 million cash burn rate, the balance equals roughly seven quarters of funding before counting any product revenue.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐓𝐮𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐪𝐞𝐯?
Management noted multiple insurer policies and over 15 prescribing hospitals, but it did not disclose wholesale pricing or expected gross-to-net discounts. Investors need unit pricing to calculate how many patients the company must treat to cover its $56 million quarterly operating expense.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐩𝐫𝐞-𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭?
The August offering included both common stock and pre-funded warrants, raising $141 million net. Because pre-funded warrants sit outside the basic share count until exercised, knowing the exact warrant count will clarify total future dilution.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐞𝐩-𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐝𝐨𝐩𝐭𝐞𝐝?
The approved label allows injections into deep organs like the lung and liver, which requires interventional radiologists alongside oncologists. Sharing the split between surface skin injections and deep organ procedures would show whether hospital scheduling slows adoption.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐞𝐧𝐫𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐈𝐆𝐍𝐘𝐓𝐄-𝟑 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐄𝐕𝐄𝐀𝐋?
Both the 400-patient IGNYTE-3 confirmatory study and the 280-patient REVEAL uveal melanoma study are actively enrolling, yet the release gave no patient counts or completion dates. Since full approval depends on IGNYTE-3, enrollment progress is critical.

Russia’s 🇷🇺 False Mediation: Arms to Ethiopia 🇪🇹 Undermine Peace Offer to Eritrea 🇪🇷 

Moscow’s Dialogue Proposal Coincides with Advanced Weapons Transfers to Addis Ababa

Russia’s recent offer to mediate between Eritrea and Ethiopia appears increasingly hollow as Moscow simultaneously finalizes major arms deliveries that strengthen the Ethiopian military amid Addis Ababa’s open demands for access to Eritrea’s sovereign coastline.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Alimov stated that Moscow is ready to host contacts between the two sides, including on the sidelines of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on 28–29 October 2026, if both parties agree. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki are both expected to attend.¹ Yet the timing undercuts the gesture: on the summit’s opening day, Abiy announced Ethiopia’s receipt of the first 12 Sukhoi Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, with four S-400 air-defence batteries to follow—delivered a year ahead of schedule.²
Ethiopia’s Aggressive Posture and Russian Enablement
These deliveries form part of a broader pattern. Ethiopia has also received Russian Orion-E drones and Yak-130 trainers, while Moscow has signed agreements to help the landlocked country rebuild a navy.³ ⁴ Ethiopian leaders have repeatedly framed “sovereign access to the sea” as irreversible, language Eritrea regards as a direct challenge to its territorial integrity and a potential prelude to aggression. Eritrea has already severed diplomatic ties after Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and expelled Eritrean diplomats.
Rather than pressing Ethiopia to respect Eritrean sovereignty, cease hostilities, and end reported support for Eritrean opposition groups, Russia is arming the side making expansionist claims. Historical precedent reinforces the concern. From 1977 to the early 1990s, the Soviet Union supplied Ethiopia with billions of dollars in weaponry that sustained campaigns against Eritrean independence forces.⁵ In the late 1990s, under Boris Yeltsin, Russia provided Ethiopia with superior Su-27 fighters while selling Eritrea the less capable MiG-29; Russian sources reportedly informed Ethiopian counterparts of Eritrea’s purchases, tipping the air balance.⁶
Eritrea’s Consistent Support for Russia Goes Unreciprocated
Eritrea has long demonstrated goodwill toward Russia. It was one of only five UN member states to vote against the 2022 General Assembly resolution condemning Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, opposing unilateral sanctions and calling for diplomacy.⁷ Asmara has also refrained from offering Russia a naval base, preserving strategic balance. Yet these positions have not translated into Russian pressure on Ethiopia to halt its Red Sea ambitions or proxy activities.
Double Standards in the Sudan War
Russia’s regional role further highlights inconsistency. While Wagner-linked elements previously backed Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces (RSF), official Russian channels have engaged the Sudanese Armed Forces. Meanwhile, investigations by Reuters and the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab have documented Ethiopian territory and military facilities being used to train and support RSF fighters operating against Sudanese government forces.⁸ Ethiopia, now receiving advanced Russian systems, stands accused of facilitating this proxy dimension.
Eritrea has publicly noted these contradictions. A mediation offer unaccompanied by demands that Ethiopia respect Eritrean sovereignty, stop arming opposition elements, and end regional destabilization risks appearing as cover for continued military support to Addis Ababa rather than genuine peace facilitation. Russia describes both countries as partners and calls for restraint; actions on the arms front speak louder.

Footnotes
¹ Alimov statements to Izvestia, reported by TASS and others, 16–17 October 2026. ² Abiy Ahmed announcement, 28 October 2026; Fana Media Corporation. ³ Aviation Expo 2026 displays; DefenceWeb and related reporting.

text:
I met Jide through a mutual friend at a get-together where a small group of my old schoolmates had organized. It wasn't the typical alumni reunion, but the atmosphere that evening was warm, incredibly amazing, and genuinely welcoming. 

It was Richard's housewarming. He's always been that bright, respectful, and ambitious kind of guy. We got really close after college, attending the same coaching center while preparing for IJMB with my best friend, Lara. 

Six years passed since we left college, but our bond remains just as strong as it was before uni and the strides of life.

Richard had always been the one who remembered everybody's birthday, checked up on people without expecting anything in return, and somehow managed to bring people together even when life had scattered us in different directions. 

So when he invited us to celebrate his new apartment in Lekki, I didn't hesitate. 

Lara and I arrived a little after seven in the evening. The apartment was beautiful, the music was soft, and the smell of grilled chicken, peppered gizzard, and freshly prepared jollof rice filled the air. 

Everybody seemed to have a story to tell. 

There was Tobi, who had recently returned from the UK and wouldn't stop talking about the weather. There was Sandra, who had just gotten engaged and kept flashing her ring at anybody who cared to look. And there was Femi, who had somehow managed to turn a simple conversation about rent into a twenty-minute lecture about the country's spiral economy. 

I was laughing at one of his jokes when Richard suddenly appeared beside me with a tall, dark-skinned man dressed in a black shirt and cream trousers. 

"There's somebody I want you to meet," Richard said, smiling mischievously. 

I looked at him suspiciously. 

"Richard, if this is another one of your friends you're trying to set me up with, please, I'm not interested." 

The stranger laughed. 

"Wow. You haven't even met me, and I've already been rejected?" 

I turned to him. 

"And you haven't even introduced yourself, and you're already complaining." 

He leaned forward. 

"Fair enough. My name is Jide." 

"Okay, Jide." 

"Just okay?" 

"What else do you want me to say?" 

He smiled. 

"At least tell me your name so I can remember the woman who destroyed my confidence in less than thirty seconds." 

I laughed it off cause I'm just that blunt type.

"You're dramatic." 

"And you're avoiding the question." 

I told him my name, and he repeated it slowly, as if he wanted to commit it to memory. 

Richard shook his head. 

"Please, both of you should behave yourselves. Jide, this is my friend. She's a very stubborn woman, so don't let her innocent face deceive you." 

I rolled my eyes. 

"And Richard is a very annoying man, so don't let his good manners deceive you." 

Everybody laughed, and just like that, Jide found himself standing beside me for the next twenty minutes. 

He wasn't the loudest man in the room. He didn't spend the evening bragging about his car, his job, or the amount of money in his account. He listened when people spoke, asked thoughtful questions, and laughed without trying to dominate every conversation. 

When I mentioned that I work in the digital marketing industry, he didn't immediately ask how much I earning or whether my company was hiring. 

Instead, he asked what I enjoyed most about my work. 

I remember thinking that it was refreshing to meet a man who seemed genuinely interested in the person standing in front of him. 

At some point, he offered to get me a drink. 

"Anything without alcohol," I said. 

"Noted." 

He returned with a bottle of water and a glass of juice. 

I smiled. 

"Thank you." 

"You're welcome." 

It was such a small thing, but I noticed it. 

Maybe that was where my problem started. 

I began noticing every little thing he did. 

The way he pulled out a chair when I wanted to sit. The way he looked at me whenever I spoke, as though there was nobody else in the room. 

Before the evening ended, we had exchanged numbers. 

And when I got home that night, I found a message waiting for me. 

Jide: I hope you got home safely. 

Me: Yes, I did. Thank you. 

Jide: Good. I enjoyed talking to you tonight. 

Me: Same here. 

Jide: Can I see you again? 

I stared at the message for a while before replying. 

Me: Let's see how it goes. 

Jide: I'll take that as a challenge. 

I laughed and dropped my phone on the bed. 

I had no idea that, months later, I would look at that very conversation and wish I had never replied. 

Because if I had known what I know now, I would have walked away from Jide the moment he introduced himself. 

But life doesn't give you spoilers. 

Sometimes, it gives you exactly what you prayed for, only for you to discover that your prayer came wrapped in a lesson you never asked to learn. 

And Jide? 

Jide was about to become the most expensive lesson of my life.

To be continued........

"The proposal presented by Qatar sets a seven-day timeline addressing both Tehran's and Washington's concerns, laying ​out daily confidence-building steps that each side must take, the official briefed on the negotiations said. The timeline could begin early ⁠next week and several countries would act as guarantors of the deal, the official added.

Shortly afterwards, a senior Iranian official involved in the talks said Qatar had presented ​only "unacceptable ideas and not an offer", and that Tehran's policy on showing no flexibility over the nuclear issue remained unchanged.
Washington wants Iran's decades-long nuclear programme to be part of ​negotiations to end the war from the outset, while Iran says its conditions — which include an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports — must be met first. Iran rejects Western concerns that its nuclear programme is military in nature.

ATTACK ON SAUDI OIL REFINERY
In late September, Iran presented another seven-day proposal under which Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi ​said the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important energy shipping channels, could be reopened if certain conditions were met. US President Donald Trump rejected it, prompting ​further Qatari mediation.
The draft discussed in Tehran on Sunday was different from that proposal, the official briefed on the negotiations said, though the details of the latest plan were not immediately clear. ‌The official ⁠had previously told Reuters that the Qatari mediators had coordinated with Washington before going to Tehran.

Earlier mediation efforts to end the war that the US and Israel launched on February 28 helped produce an interim peace agreement in June, but it quickly unravelled.

In recent weeks, Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi forces have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia — a key US ally and the world's largest crude exporter — opening a new front in the eight-month-old war.

Oil prices rose more than 1% to more than $115 per barrel on Wednesday ​after a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia's ​largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, stoking concerns over ⁠supply risks.

Fighting with the Houthis intensified last month as the militant group advanced against Saudi-backed forces towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another important shipping lane on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula from Hormuz.

CONCERNS ABOUT RISK OF NEW STRIKES
The official briefed on ​the negotiations said there were concerns ahead of Sunday's meeting in Tehran that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, fighting for ​another term in a general election, ⁠could resume attacks on the Islamic Republic this week.

On Friday, US President Donald Trump repeated threats to strike Iran again, while Iranian security officials told Reuters Tehran had drawn up detailed plans to attack Gulf undersea cables if the US and Israel resumed attacks.

On Monday, top officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan also met Iranian officials in Tehran as part of ⁠de-escalation efforts. ​Qatar said on Tuesday that Iran needs to stop threats against Arab Gulf states and open the ​Strait of Hormuz to show good intentions for mediation efforts to succeed.

Gulf states came under sustained bombardment earlier in the war.

The war also reignited fighting between Israel and the Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah. It has ​eroded Trump's approval ratings ahead of the US midterm elections that decide control of Congress."

WHY DID NATO EXPAND TOWARDS RUSSIA? 
"No one contends that NATO is being expanded for the benefit of military contractors."   - New York Times, 1998

"American arms manufacturers, who stand to gain billions of dollars in sales of weapons, communication systems and other military equipment if the Senate approves NATO expansion, have made enormous investments in lobbyists and campaign contributions to promote their cause in Washington.
The end of the cold war has shrunk the arms industry and forced it to diversify.
But expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization -- first to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, then possibly to more than a dozen other countries -- would offer arms makers a new and hugely lucrative market.

Under NATO rules, new members are required to upgrade their militaries and make them compatible with those of the Western military alliance, which oversees the most sophisticated -- and expensive -- weapons and communication systems in the world."

🇺🇸🇸🇦🇾🇪 TRUMP WANTS CHEAPER FUEL BEFORE THE ELECTIONS. THE HOUTHIS HAVE OTHER PLANS. 🇮🇷

Donald Trump is facing an increasingly uncomfortable situation in the Middle East, just days before Americans vote in the November 3 midterm elections.

Saudi Arabia has been asking Washington for direct military assistance against Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis. Trump has repeatedly declined to authorize American strikes, even as the group has intensified attacks against Saudi territory and threatened infrastructure critical to global energy supplies.

According to Reuters, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman personally sought Trump's help. Washington offered intelligence and targeting assistance instead of direct military intervention.

The White House has been concerned that another American military operation could provoke wider retaliation, threaten shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and place additional pressure on already volatile oil markets.

But the fighting has continued.

Saudi forces have struck Houthi-controlled facilities in Yemen, while the Houthis have launched missiles and drones toward Saudi airports and energy infrastructure. An earlier attack on Saudi Aramco's complex in Dhahran caused a fire, and the group has since claimed further attacks against the kingdom's oil network.

On October 26, the Houthis claimed to have targeted Saudi oil pumping stations, although Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed those strikes.

Trump has accused the Houthis of deliberately trying to drive up oil prices before the American elections. He has also warned that he will remember their actions after November 3.

The political problem is obvious. Rising energy prices are particularly unwelcome for an administration already facing public frustration over fuel costs.

But there is no simple military solution. American strikes could weaken Houthi capabilities while simultaneously risking retaliation against oil infrastructure and international shipping, potentially worsening the very price pressures Washington wants to contain.

Trump has chosen to avoid direct intervention for now. That has not stopped the escalation, and the consequences are reaching well beyond Yemen.

With the elections approaching, the White House is confronting a crisis in which neither military escalation nor restraint offers a guaranteed way to stabilize energy markets.

Trump’s Negotiating Style: Bully First, Back Down Later

After two years in the White House, the world is getting to know President Trump’s playbook: intimidate first, pile on the pressure, and keep threatening until the other side gives in—or he is forced to retreat. This is not the behaviour of a statesman than a hard-nosed businessman. He has used similar tactics throughout his real estate career, sometimes successfully, sometimes not.

The Iran war is his latest test. After a five-month pause, he is assembling a formidable naval force near the Strait of Hormuz to pressure Tehran into accepting his terms. Yet even overwhelming military power may not force Iran to surrender. Trump wants Tehran to stare into the mouth of hell and become frightened enough to yield. 

But there is a greater-than-even chance that Iran will get scarred. The approaching midterm elections may further constrain his options.

Greenland offers another example. Trump pressured Denmark and Europe to surrender control of the strategically important island. When they resisted and prepared to stand firm, he settled for far less: expanded American military access and opportunities to explore mineral resources—arrangements Denmark had been prepared to discuss anyway, with royalties attached.

Is his threat to withdraw from NATO genuine? He has backed his rhetoric with plans to withdraw some American forces from Europe. Yet European countries are increasingly preparing to defend themselves, particularly after Washington threatened to reduce its support for Ukraine. Europe is already shouldering more responsibility, demonstrating that American pressure can produce consequences Trump may not intend.

Canada has proved an even tougher opponent. Trump pushed intimidation to the extreme, even raising the prospect of Canada becoming America’s 51st state. A Canadians province overwhelmingly rejected that idea, giving him a political black eye. His pressure over trade has also failed to force Ottawa into submission. 

Canada walked away from negotiations, surprising Washington. Now, with neither side able to ignore its largest trading relationship, back-channel discussions have resumed. Trump has begun suggesting that a deal is near. If negotiations succeed, it may represent a climbdown from his earlier demands.

India has followed a similar course. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has resisted pressure to accept a trade agreement on unfavourable terms. Trump now repeatedly suggests that a deal is close. Again, the language of confrontation may be giving way to the realities of negotiation.

China is a different challenge. Its dominance in rare-earth processing gives Beijing leverage that American threats cannot easily overcome.

Trump needs to recognise that intimidation is not a substitute for diplomacy. Countries have their own interests, pride and red lines. His negotiating style may win concessions occasionally, but it can also alienate allies, strengthen resistance and leave America worse off.

If Republicans suffer substantial losses in the midterm elections, voters may deliver the clearest warning yet: bullying the world has limits, and eventually the bully pays a price.

text:
🇶🇦🇮🇹|The Fire at Ras Laffan Reaches Terminals in Italy and Kitchens in South Asia

October 27, 2026, Rome. Italian energy company Edison received a notification from QatarEnergy: three more shipments of liquefied natural gas (LNG) could not be delivered. The destination was an LNG terminal on the Adriatic Sea. This marks the 17th shipment canceled since April 2026, totaling 2.2 billion cubic meters of natural gas. The period of "force majeure" has been extended through the end of December 2026.

Edison is not the only victim. Customers in Pakistan and Bangladesh received the same notification that the force majeure would persist until the end of the year. Supplies for India’s Petronet LNG scheduled for November have also been canceled.

In legal terms, "force majeure" refers to events that are "unforeseeable, unavoidable, and insurmountable." It sounds like an act of God but the fire at Ras Laffan was no such thing.

💥 Ras Laffan: 17% of Capacity Lost, with a 3-to-5-Year Repair Timeline

March 2026. Iranian missiles struck Qatar’s Ras Laffan Industrial City the world’s largest hub for LNG production and export. QatarEnergy confirmed that LNG production trains 4 and 6 were damaged, representing a combined capacity of 12.8 million tonnes per year, 17% of Qatar’s total LNG export capacity.

A senior official at QatarEnergy told Reuters that repairs would take three to five years, with an estimated loss in annual revenue of $20 billion.

This is not merely a "supply chain disruption." It is the physical consequence of a sovereign state’s energy infrastructure coming under attack, an attack that occurred within a specific context: the war between the United States, Israel, and Iran.

The Iranian strike was not random. Iran identified Ras Laffan and the Mesaieed Industrial City as facilities linked to the "war machine." Qatar hosts one of the largest U.S. military bases in the Middle East, Al Udeid Air Base, which serves as a forward headquarters for CENTCOM. U.S. forces launch combat missions against Iran from this location, and KC-135 tanker aircraft take off from there to refuel planes engaged in the bombing of Iran.  Iran’s strike on Ras Laffan in March 2026 was a direct response to the ongoing war. Qatar, by hosting U.S. military infrastructure and serving as a logistical node for the conflict, has had to bear the consequences.

The legal invocation of "force majeure" masks a simpler reality: the costs of war are spilling over from the battlefield into the energy markets is a path of transmission dictated by Iran.

🎯 South Asia: 99% Dependency and an Unspoken "Fiscal Crisis"

Edison is a European buyer. Europe possesses alternative supply sources, strategic reserves, and the fiscal capacity to absorb shocks in spot market prices.

South Asia has none of these.

In 2025, Qatar accounted for 99% of Pakistan’s LNG imports and over 70% of Bangladesh’s. When the "force majeure" notices from QatarEnergy reached Islamabad and Dhaka, these nations were left with no buffer.

Pakistan was forced to pay over $1 billion to secure LNG supplies on the spot market ahead of the winter season. In Bangladesh, natural gas demand dropped by more than 3 million tonnes due to the surge in spot prices. India and Pakistan each saw a reduction of approximately 1.5 million tonnes; India’s total natural gas demand fell by 1.5 million tonnes that year.

"Force majeure" protects the seller shielding QatarEnergy from liability for breach of contract but it offers no protection to the populations on the buying end. From household kitchens in Pakistan to power plants in Bangladesh and fertilizer factories in India, the burden is felt through the shock of spot prices and the stark reality of cancelled contractual supplies.

While the case of Edison’s 17 shipments represents a contractual dispute, the disappearance of 3 million tonnes of demand in South Asia reflects a grim reality: millions of people can no longer afford the energy they need.

📜 Qatar’s Dual Role

Qatar is no mere bystander in this war.

It is a major non-NATO ally of the United States. The Al Udeid Air Base serves as the forward headquarters for U.S. Central Command. During the 2026 conflict, Qatar permitted the U.S. military to launch combat operations against Iran from its territory.  It is also a stakeholder in Israel’s natural gas interests. Qatar is integrated into the Eastern Mediterranean’s natural gas architecture through both investments and contractual agreements.

When a country provides a base for a war, and its energy export facilities are subsequently struck by the opposing side, this is no "accident." It is an extension of the logic of war. Iran’s strike on Ras Laffan in March 2026 was not an attack on the Qatari people; it was a strike against nodes on Qatari soil that serve the war effort against Iran.

The term "force majeure" is merely a device used to translate this political-military reality into the language of a commercial notice.

⚔️ Who Pays, Who Decides

Those paying the price: Consumers in Pakistan, facing soaring LNG prices ahead of winter; factories in Bangladesh, forced to cut production due to gas shortages; urban gas users in India, compelled to reduce consumption in the face of spot-market prices; and Italy’s Edison, scrambling to source replacement cargoes on the spot market.

Those making the decisions: Washington initiated the war; Tel Aviv is a participant; Qatar provided the base; Iran chose the time and place for its response; and QatarEnergy issued the "force majeure" notice.

Every link in this chain is the result of a deliberate choice none of it stems from the kind of "unforeseeable and unavoidable" natural force implied by the term "force majeure." The fires at Ras Laffan are the product of political decisions, while the cold stoves in South Asian kitchens are the final, downstream consequence of those same political choices.

🔻 The Mirror

QatarEnergy says: "Force majeure."

The ruins at Ras Laffan say: Iranian missiles struck production trains 4 and 6.

Washington says: "We are maintaining regional stability."

Pakistan’s LNG bill says: Over $1 billion just to get through the winter.

Edison says: "Cargo number 17 has been cancelled."

Demand data from Bangladesh says: 3 million tons have vanished.

This is not a "supply chain crisis."  This is a war initiated by Washington and Tel Aviv, a war whose costs are being passed on to the energy markets, at a time and in a manner of Iran’s own choosing. The term "force majeure" serves as little more than a convenient fig leaf to cover this reality.

When a nation chooses to provide a base for war, the subsequent targeting of its energy infrastructure is not a matter of "force majeure," it is a matter of simple arithmetic. If Iranian missiles fly toward Ras Laffan, it is not because of the people of Qatar; it is because Qatari territory hosts the command nodes for the war against Iran.

Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

text:
Why did NATO expand Eastward despite Baker's assurances to Gorbachev that it never would if Germany reunited?

"No one contends that NATO is being expanded for the benefit of military contractors."   - New York Times, 1998
"American arms manufacturers, who stand to gain billions of dollars in sales of weapons, communication systems and other military equipment if the Senate approves NATO expansion, have made enormous investments in lobbyists and campaign contributions to promote their cause in Washington.
The end of the cold war has shrunk the arms industry and forced it to diversify.
But expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization -- first to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, then possibly to more than a dozen other countries -- would offer arms makers a new and hugely lucrative market.
America's six biggest military contractors have spent $51 million on lobbying in the last two years, according to an analysis prepared for The New York Times by the Campaign Study Group, a research company in Springfield, Va.
If lobbying costs were included from all companies that perform military-related activities, like computer and technology firms, they would dwarf the lobbying effort of any other industry.

''Like any other American manufacturer, they are looking for markets abroad,'' said Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan, a New York Democrat who opposes the proposed NATO expansion. ''Most every other customer they can think of, we have forbidden them to sell anything to.''
Under NATO rules, new members are required to upgrade their militaries and make them compatible with those of the Western military alliance, which oversees the most sophisticated -- and expensive -- weapons and communication systems in the world. The companies that win the contracts to provide that ''inter-operability'' to the aging Soviet-made systems in Eastern Europe will benefit enormously from NATO's eastward expansion.
Thus the sums spent on lobbying and for campaign contributions are relatively small compared with the potential benefits in the new markets provided by a larger NATO, particularly from the sale of big-ticket items like fighter aircraft.

The top individual giver to the Democratic Party last year was Bernard L. Schwartz, chairman of Loral Space and Communications, which is partly owned by Lockheed."

Afghan national Afsar Safi, who arrived in the UK by small boat in 2021, has had his sentence increased from two years and six months to four years for kidnapping and sexually assaulting a seven year old girl after the Court of Appeal ruled his original sentence unduly lenient.

On September 6, 2025, Safi approached the seven-year-old girl at his asylum hotel in Acton, west London, and offered her an apple before inviting her to his room.

She refused five times before Safi grabbed her by the arm and forced her into his room, where he kissed her on the cheek. Speaking through a Pashto interpreter, he later admitted kissing the child, claiming he acted out of love for children and that people did this back home.

The girl managed to escape and alert hotel security. In court, she described being too frightened to tell Safi to stop. Her victim impact statement revealed the lasting psychological effects of the assault, including nightmares that caused her to wake up crying. She also continues to feel unsafe around men when alone.

Safi denied both charges but was subsequently convicted of kidnapping and sexual assault of a child at Isleworth Crown Court on April 27, 2026. His defence referred to his difficult childhood, claiming he had been taken from his family at the age of 10 and forced to work for the Taliban. His barrister said Safi had received just three years of education and spoke limited English. His asylum claim, which reportedly referenced links to the Taliban from childhood, was refused.

On June 12, 2026, Safi was initially sentenced to two years and six months in prison. Reports stated he could potentially be released on licence after serving as little as six months. The Solicitor General challenged the sentence as unduly lenient and insufficient to reflect the seriousness of the offences.

On October 23, 2026, the Court of Appeal increased Safi’s sentence to four years. Lord Justice Jeremy Baker said it was difficult to escape the conclusion that Safi had selected the girl because of her age and inability to resist, ruling that the original sentence failed to reflect the seriousness of his offending. Safi was also placed on the sex offenders register for seven years.

Despite Safi arriving in the UK by small boat in 2021 and being convicted of kidnapping and sexually assaulting a seven year old child, there was no mention in court or police statements of deportation proceedings or any recommendation that he be removed from the UK after completing his sentence.

And NOW MAJOR!

Here are the greatest piano masterpieces written in E-flat, D-flat, C, G, and D major:

☀️ E-Flat Major (Heroic and Majestic)
E-flat major is traditionally associated with nobility, courage, and a grand, open-hearted brilliance.

Ludwig van Beethoven – Piano Concerto No. 5 in E-Flat Major, Op. 73 "Emperor": The ultimate heroic concerto, opening with an unprecedented, triumphant piano cadenza that sweeps across the entire keyboard.

Frédéric Chopin – Nocturne in E-Flat Major, Op. 9, No. 2: Arguably the most famous piano piece ever written, featuring a beautiful, operatic melody that floats effortlessly over a rolling bass.

Franz Joseph Haydn – Piano Sonata No. 52 in E-Flat Major, Hob. XVI:52: Haydn’s final and greatest sonata, written in London. It utilizes full, rich chordal textures inspired by the wider dynamic range of early English grand pianos.

🌌 D-Flat Major (Dreamy and Serene)
With five flats, D-flat major is warm, deeply resonant, and velvety. Nineteenth-century composers used it to capture late-night intimacy and ethereal beauty.

Claude Debussy – Clair de Lune: A masterpiece of Impressionism that perfectly mimics the shimmering, cool glow of moonlight filtering through trees.

Frédéric Chopin – Raindrop Prelude, Op. 28, No. 15: Famous for its repeating, hypnotic A-flat/G-sharp note that sounds exactly like raindrops pattering on a roof before a dark storm rolls in.

Franz Liszt – Consolation No. 3 in D-Flat Major: A deeply peaceful piece heavily inspired by Chopin's nocturnes. It features a floating, song-like melody that offers pure emotional solace. 

🏛️ C Major (Pure and Radiant)
With no sharps or flats, C major represents innocence, clarity, structural purity, and a celebratory, untarnished joy.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart – Piano Sonata No. 16 in C Major, K. 545 "Sonata Semplice": The quintessential Classical sonata, instantly recognizable for its perfectly balanced, scales-and-arpeggios elegance.

Robert Schumann – Fantaisie in C Major, Op. 17: A massive, passionate monument of Romantic music, written as a desperate musical love letter to his future wife, Clara, while they were forced apart.

Franz Schubert – Wanderer Fantasy in C Major, D. 760: A spectacular, thunderous work so technically demanding that Schubert himself once threw his hands up in frustration and said, "Let the devil play it!"

🌿 G Major (Pastoral and Bright)
G major has a light, rustic, and gentle quality. It often evokes nature, folk dances, and crisp morning light.

Johann Sebastian Bach – Goldberg Variations, BWV 988: A monumental set of 30 variations that begins and ends with a breathtakingly tender, quiet Aria.

Ludwig van Beethoven – Piano Concerto No. 4 in G Major, Op. 58: Revolutionary for its time because the solo piano quietly introduces the main theme all by itself, breaking the tradition of starting with a loud orchestral introduction.

Maurice Ravel – Piano Concerto in G Major: Infused with brilliant 1920s jazz idioms and Basque folk music, featuring a sparkling, energetic first movement and a sublime, slow second movement.

👑 D Major (Triumphant and Joyful)
Historically associated with trumpets, victory, and celebration, D major sounds incredibly bright, open, and vibrant on the piano.

Johann Sebastian Bach – Toccata in D Major, BWV 912: A free-flowing, improvisational youth work that explodes with theatrical energy, rapid-fire runs, and infectious joy.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart – Sonata for Two Pianos in D Major, K. 448: A dazzling duet full of rapid, conversational dialogue between two pianists (famous for being the core piece used in studies regarding the "Mozart Effect").

Joseph Haydn – Piano Sonata No. 50 in D Major, Hob. XVI:37: A brisk, witty, and highly popular sonata that zips along with continuous, playful energy.

text:
Detroit, 1937. A young entertainer's wife had their first baby, and the hospital would not let them leave until he paid $75.

He had $7. He put it in a church poor box and asked a saint for ten times as much by the next day.

The next day he was offered radio work, for $75.

His name then was Amos Jacobs. He was the son of Lebanese immigrants and had grown up in a big family in Toledo, Ohio. He had done some radio and nightclub work, and he was struggling.

The saint was Jude, one of the Twelve.

That is the story as his second daughter, Terre, tells it. She says she heard him tell it a million times.

A few years later he went to Chicago. He took a new name there, Danny Thomas, so his relatives wouldn't know he was back in nightclubs.

He was a hit at the 5100 Club, and the owners asked him to stay on as a part-owner. Unsure, he went into St Clement's church and prayed to Jude again: "Show me my way in life, and I will build you a shrine."

In the church he found a leaflet. Jude's national shrine, it said, was right there in Chicago. He told the saint he had brought him to his home town.

The shrine was a parish on the city's far southeast side, where many families lived off the steel mills. In 1929 its priest had begun novenas there to a saint few Catholics then knew. On the last night of one, 28 October 1929, more than 1,000 people stood outside the church.

That was the day the stock market fell nearly 13 percent.

Jude goes by three names. Luke calls him Judas. Matthew and Mark name a Thaddaeus instead, and tradition takes them to be one man. The Gospels give him one question, at the Last Supper, and John takes care to say this Judas was not Iscariot.

The shrine says he was widely honoured in the Middle Ages, then slipped into obscurity, perhaps because people confused him with Judas Iscariot. Catholics call him the patron saint of impossible causes. No one is sure how the title began.

Catholics and Orthodox ask the saints to pray for them. Most Protestants honour Jude as one of the Twelve without praying to him.

Soon an agent from William Morris saw Danny Thomas's act. He went on to nightclubs across the country, then films, and from 1953 his own television show, Make Room for Daddy.

He kept the promise. The shrine he built was a hospital for children with catastrophic diseases, open to every race and religion. St. Jude Children's Research Hospital opened in Memphis on 4 February 1962.

Families are never billed there for treatment, travel, housing or food.
