text:
She gave her name as Margo. Five minutes later the woman who had hired her off a Bronx street corner was calling her Margie, and by the end of the day she was calling her Mary. Marvel Cooke scrubbed that apartment's linoleum on her hands and knees and was paid three dollars and forty cents by the clock on that woman's wall, twenty cents short of her own carfare home.

On those same corners in 1935, fifteen cents bought an hour of a woman's life.

The hour was the part they stole.

They called it the Bronx slave market, and it was not one corner. The two where the bidding ran heaviest sat at 167th Street and Jerome Avenue and at Simpson and Westchester Avenues, and Marvel Cooke, looking back on it fifteen years later, put the number across the whole borough at twenty or thirty.

Black women stood on those corners and waited for white housewives to buy them by the hour.

Baker and Cooke put the going rates on paper. Fifteen cents an hour, twenty, twenty-five, and thirty if a woman was lucky.

They came as early as eight in the morning. Some were still standing there at one in the afternoon with nothing.

Rain or shine, cold or hot. Old women and young women, some worn down and some carefully dressed, and every last one of them holding a paper bag.

The bag held her work clothes. It was how you could tell, from across a street, what a woman was standing there for.

Most of them rode down from Harlem on the train. The ones who did not have the nickel for the fare walked it.

At Jerome Avenue there were benches around a green square, and Ella Baker and Marvel Cooke called that the more humane of the two markets for exactly that reason. The women there had somewhere to sit.

At Simpson Avenue there was nothing. The women leaned against store fronts and lamp posts, or they went up and down the block hunting for a discarded box to drag over and rest on.

That is the whole difference between the two corners, and it is worth holding onto. One had benches and the other had garbage.

Before 1929 most of these women had been working. Some had held steady places in the big houses in the rich Eighties, or out in Westchester and on Long Island, at wages that covered a life.

Then the crash came. The woman who had employed them either started doing her own floors or fired the Black worker to hire a white one who had just been let out of something better.

The employment agencies took a fee whether or not they placed you, and they placed white women first. Relief was thin and slow and came with a caseworker attached to it.

So the corner. Not because it promised anything, Baker and Cooke wrote, but because a woman in that position had run out of doors.

The crash also produced a brand new class of employer. The lower middle class housewife who had never in her life been able to afford help could suddenly have a woman on her knees scrubbing linoleum for a quarter.

The buyer walked the line looking the women over. Cooke wrote that she all but undressed them with her eyes, measuring how much work each one looked able to stand.

Then she asked the price and beat it down as far as the woman would let her. The figure they landed on was always below what the agencies asked and below what the women had agreed among themselves.

What got bought was heavy. Floors scrubbed on the knees, tubs of blankets and furniture covers, mattresses beaten, walls washed down, a week of laundry crammed into a day.

The job every one of them dreaded was windows. In a Bronx apartment house that meant sitting out on the ledge with the top sash pulled down across your lap and the street underneath you.

One woman was badly hurt falling from a sixth floor window. Another woman fell and died.

The Domestic Workers Union eventually wrote a contract that simply banned the task outright.

In September 1935 a woman named Millie Jones sat down to lunch with two strangers on Simpson Avenue and told them what a week of it actually came to.

She had worked in the neighborhood for five dollars a week and carfare. The apartment had six rooms and fifteen windows, and every single week she washed all fifteen of them.

If her employer found one speck on one pane, Millie Jones did the window again.

Mondays she washed. Tuesdays she finished whatever ironing Monday had not swallowed, and with a husband and two grown sons in that house it came to twenty-one shirts a week, ten sheets, and at least two blankets.

Every floor in the place got washed and waxed on her hands and knees, every week. Two or three times a week she stripped the covers off all the furniture and beat the mattresses.

One of the sons put his hands on her. She said fighting him off left her about as tired as the work did.

She lasted five weeks. Then she asked for one Sunday off, because her boyfriend was coming up from Washington on an excursion train, and she was told that if she did not come in on Sunday she need not come in again.

She did not go back. That is how she ended up on a corner in the Bronx.

The day before she met the two strangers she had not had a cent in her pocket and took the first thing offered. She went to work at eleven in the morning and finished at five, washing windows, scrubbing floors, and cleaning the baby's soiled laundry.

She said she had been surprised to be fed at all, because plenty of them gave you nothing.

At the end of it she was handed thirty-five cents. Her employer explained that a quarter had been taken out for the lunch.

Six hours. Millie Jones did the arithmetic out loud at the table, and the number she came to was ten cents an hour.

That was the ordinary shape of the theft, and it hardly ever touched the price agreed on the sidewalk.

The clock got turned back an hour while the woman was in another room. Work got criticized at the end of the day so the full amount would not have to be handed over.

More got piled on than had been bargained for. Some days a woman worked the whole day through and was sent home with nothing at all.

The rate was public and the hours were private, and every person in that market understood which of the two was worth stealing.

The two strangers who bought Millie Jones that lunch had come off the train at Simpson and Westchester on the morning of 14 September 1935, carrying beat-up bags and dressed to look like they had nothing.

Ella Baker was a Harlem organizer who had spent the early thirties building Black consumer cooperatives. Marvel Cooke was a newspaperwoman who had come up through The Crisis as W. E. B. Du Bois's assistant.

They took a position outside the flower shop on the corner and waited to be bought.

The shop window behind them had gardenias in it, and roses, and the first chrysanthemums of the season. All of it priced, all of it reasonable.

It took almost no time at all. A woman came up, looked the two of them over, asked what they worked for, and walked off the instant they asked what she paid.

She was bargaining with a stronger woman by the lamp post within the minute, and she led her away down a side street two blocks off.

The other women on the corner did not trust the newcomers. Then it began to rain and a dozen of them crowded into the five and ten doorway together, and after that the talking came easier.

A West Indian woman who had spent the morning patrolling the block, all but daring somebody not to hire her, hushed the group so the store manager would not push them all back out into the wet.

They finished the conversation in whispers under the awning.

A man in plain clothes had been trailing the two reporters for a while by then, waiting for a chance to run them in for soliciting. When they split up he lost them, and when they stood together he grinned and winked.

An elderly couple came looking for somebody to send up to their daughter's place on Jerome Avenue. The husband said twenty-five cents an hour and the wife scowled and said twenty, and they explained that the carfare would be paid once she got there.

Five or six women turned them down flat.

And on an upturned soap box sat a woman who had already lined up work for the next day and could afford to be choosy.

She had watched the old couple strike out and was pleased about it. When a fresh group came down the elevated steps and started underselling the corner, she said those were the ones who made it bad for everybody, and that the corner had run them off once already the week before.

Then she said somebody ought to organize them or something.

She said it sitting on a box she had pulled off the street because there was nowhere else to sit, and she said it as though it were somebody else's job.

It was not somebody else's job. It was already happening on that block.

By that autumn the Simpson Avenue corner had a rough union of its own, with no charter, no dues and no name.

Women who took less than thirty cents an hour got run off. For the holiday that year the regulars held together and refused to go out for less than thirty-five.

That is a wage floor, set on a sidewalk, by women who had no legal right to one. Congress had written domestic workers out of the Social Security Act that August and out of the labor relations act that July.

When the federal wage and hour law arrived in 1938, they were left out of that as well.

Dora Jones and Rosa Rayside were building the Domestic Workers Union, Local 149, through those same years. By 1937 it ran somewhere between three hundred and fifty and a thousand members and it opened a free hiring hall on White Plains Road.

Jones could never crack the street corners. The women out there told her they did better on the sidewalk than at any agency, and she was blunt about how hard they were to reach.

The union organized in the only way that was available to it, which was one woman at a time, on foot, outside churches and subway entrances, in the hours after a full day of somebody else's floors.

In the autumn of 1949 it ran a course in Negro history. A union down to a hundred and twenty-five paid-up members had decided that the way to reach exhausted women was to teach them their own history, and it brought in new members.

Nina Evans, who was running Local 149 by then, said the aim was for Black workers to walk erect, in dignity and pride, alongside their white allies.

Thirteen years before that course, Louise Thompson Patterson had published an essay that used these corners as its evidence and put a phrase into print that nobody had used before. She wrote that Black women were exploited three times over, as workers, as women, and as Black people.

In 1937 the Amsterdam News reprinted a version of the Baker and Cooke report for Harlem readers.

In 1938 a Federal Writers' Project worker named Vivian Morris put on old clothes and went to the corners herself. On 6 December that year she sat down with a woman named Minnie Marshall, and two of Morris's manuscripts are still held at the Library of Congress, one of them titled simply Price War in the Bronx Slave Market.

In 1939 a Columbia graduate student named Lois Taylor did the same thing and stayed with it for months. Her fieldwork became her master's thesis in 1940.

In 1937, two years before Taylor started, a photographer named Robert McNeill walked up to those corners with a camera.

He was nineteen. He had left a pre-med course at Howard University the year before, enrolled at the New York Institute of Photography, and gone out to shoot the Bronx market as part of a series on Black domestic workers.

He was shooting it for Fortune magazine, and Fortune turned the pictures down.

They ran instead in Flash, a magazine for Black readers, as a thirteen photograph feature.

One of those photographs is in the Smithsonian American Art Museum. It shows women standing on the corner at 170th Street waiting for somebody to buy an hour of their time, and the title comes off the movie poster on the wall behind them, which is advertising a picture to people with an afternoon to spare.

The negatives are at the Library of Congress, catalogued as the Bronx slave market, 1937 to 1938. Two Black women waiting for day labor, and a third woman, probably white, standing there talking terms with them.

Their faces are in that frame. Not one of them has a name attached.

In 1937, the same year McNeill was shooting, a domestic worker named Pansy Kennedy sued her employer for ten dollars and sixty cents in unpaid wages, and she won.

The magistrate who heard it, F. Anthony Burke, used the occasion to announce from the bench that domestic workers were living it up on relief money and had no real interest in working. Several papers ran with it in July 1938, and Marvel Cooke answered it in the Amsterdam News nine days later.

In the autumn of 1939 a worker named Bessie Brown was hospitalized after her employers, a wealthy white couple in Mount Vernon, attacked her when she refused to leave their house without her wages.

She sued them for assault, with help from the International Labor Defense, and she lost. The not guilty verdict was read out to a packed courthouse, and afterward she said she was glad she had done it, because it had put the conditions in front of people who would otherwise never have heard of them.

By December 1939 the state was finally paying attention. Frieda Miller, New York's industrial commissioner, set up a Committee on Street Corner Markets and put Dora Jones on it.

The committee reported in June 1940 and recommended two free employment agencies for the Bronx.

Then nothing happened for eight months.

On 26 February 1941, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia ran his own investigation.

He did not announce it. He sent the police, with the Welfare Department helping, out to the corners.

They collected the women. Accounts of how many differ, with about a hundred in one telling and sixty-four in the Herald Tribune's.

Some of the women understood there was work in it. Others were told there was a day's pay and a meal in it if they would act as witnesses.

They were taken to relief centers and questioned for hours.

A great deal of that questioning was about whether they were collecting home relief.

A market existed in which Black women were bought by the hour and robbed of their time, and the city's answer was to send police to gather up the women and interrogate them about their finances.

Every person collected that morning was somebody looking for work.

The American Civil Liberties Union condemned it, and so did the National Negro Congress.

Dora Jones called it an act of terror.

La Guardia said the women had come voluntarily and that the surprise had been necessary to get truthful answers.

Weeks later the finding came out. The city had determined that no exploitation was taking place on the Bronx slave market, because the women it questioned were being paid thirty-five cents an hour and not ten.

The city had reduced the entire question to the hourly rate. It had thirty-five cents in one column, and years of documented testimony about turned-back clocks, unpaid hours and work piled past the bargain in no column at all.

The report's recommendation was the same two employment agencies the committee had already asked for a year earlier.

One true thing did come out of those interrogations, and it demolished a lie. Almost none of the women picked up that morning were on home relief.

The magistrate's speech from the bench had been wrong, and it was the mayor's own police work that proved it. Nobody went back and told the papers that had printed it.

The Simpson Day Worker Center opened at 1029 Simpson Street on 1 May 1941. Free, indoors, out of the weather, a few steps from the corner where Baker and Cooke had stood six years before.

The Militant ran a headline on it that has never been improved. The Bronx slave market, it said, had merely been moved indoors.

That was accurate. The bidding went on in there, warmer and drier, and what passed between an employer and a worker was not closely watched.

By that September the committee reported six thousand placements in five months and called it a success.

What actually emptied the corners was not the city. It was the war, which pulled labor into the factories and paid for it properly.

Then the war ended, the factory work went, and the women came back.

Marvel Cooke went back too, alone, in the last days of 1949.

She stood in front of the Woolworth's on 170th Street between Jerome and Walton Avenues with her own paper bag, and the women gathered around her the way they had fifteen years earlier.

Backs pressed to the store glass, bags held in front of them. Staring out into the street.

The rate was seventy-five cents an hour now, and set against what milk and bread and meat had done in that decade it came to almost no gain at all.

The first job she took, she quit. A woman hired her outside the Woolworth's at eighty cents an hour and walked her up Townsend Avenue to a dark three room apartment on the ground floor.

She was put on a bedroom window with six panes to each half, and she washed it sitting on the ledge, counting them off one at a time as she went.

Twenty minutes, and the glass came up clean.

Then she did the living room and the venetian blinds, and while she worked the old woman slipped back into the bedroom with a rag.

She came out and said the corners had not been done and two panes had been missed.

Cooke had counted. She had been warned on the corner that morning that this is exactly the move, that they invent a fault at the end so they can shave the pay.

She dropped the rag in the bucket, climbed down off the ledge, told the woman she had washed every pane and that the woman knew it, and walked out leaving the dirty water standing in the middle of the living room floor.

Forty minutes. She was offered payment for the time and turned it down and was back on the corner before eleven.

The second job was the one that broke her.

It was the wet, muggy day after the two day Christmas holiday, and nobody was hiring. She waited with six other women for one hour, then two, and four of them gave up and went home.

A young couple came and looked the line over and picked the woman standing next to her, who was younger and looked fitter, and she went off trailing behind them.

Then a small elderly woman with a bird-like face asked whether she wanted a few hours.

Seventy-five cents an hour, for an amount of work nobody specified.

On the walk to the apartment on Morris Avenue, the woman told her she had been hiring girls off the street for twenty years and had never once been disappointed, because she always picked nice ones.

Then she said Cooke looked like somebody who belonged in an office.

Then she asked her name.

Cooke gave the name Margo, close enough to her own that she would answer to it.

Five minutes later the woman was calling her Margie.

By the end of the day she was calling her Mary.

The apartment was two rooms and a bath with the kitchen at one end of the living room. The woman watched her change into her work clothes, taking stock of her build.

She rinsed clothes and hung them to dry. She dusted down the walls of the whole apartment with a makeshift mop.

She ironed a man's shirt, four full length ruffled curtains and a tablecloth. She took the stove apart and cleaned it through.

She scrubbed the refrigerator, a cabinet, the sink, the tub and the shelves above the sink. She rubbed oil into every piece of furniture in the place.

The old woman sat in a chair the entire time and watched every movement. Once or twice she got up to flick imaginary dust off something Cooke had already finished, and then sat back down.

Last came the floors, which were linoleum, and which were to be done on hands and knees.

Cooke stood up and said she could not do it. She said the method had gone out with the Civil War, that there were easier ways, and that if it had to be done that way there should at least be a knee pad.

The old woman did not raise her voice. She said gently that all her girls did the floors this way, that this was how she liked them done, and that if Mary would just finish this one she would call it a day.

Cooke finished the floor.

Then she changed into her street clothes and the woman counted three dollars and forty cents into her hand, which was exactly what the clock in that apartment said she was owed, and which did not include her carfare.

Twenty cents.

She was too tired to ask for it.

The law had nothing to say about that twenty cents, or about the clock, or about the floor. In 1950, fifteen years after the first exposé, a domestic worker was covered by workmen's compensation only if she put in forty-eight hours a week for one employer, and by unemployment insurance only if she was one of four or more household workers in a single home for fifteen days in the year.

Which is to say she was covered by nothing, because almost nobody worked like that.

The state had free employment offices by then, in Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens. They were sited where the demand for household labor was, which meant they were sited where few Black people lived.

There was no household office in Harlem, where most of the applicants came from.

So the women stayed on the corner. And the ones on relief stayed on the corner on purpose, because an employment record would cost them part of a check that was about to be cut again in January.

Here is what it costs to carry this properly, and it costs nothing.

Go and look at Robert McNeill's photographs. The Library of Congress has digitized them with no known restrictions on publication, one of them belongs to the Smithsonian American Art Museum, and Fortune magazine would not print a single one of them.

Then find Minnie Marshall's interview, taken on a December day in 1938 and free to read, because she is one of the very few women out of all those corners whose name anybody wrote down.

And when this story comes across your feed with a line about how the mayor stepped in and put a stop to it, add the rest of it. The mayor sent police to collect the women, questioned them about their relief checks, and announced that nothing was wrong.

New York City put up an official marker in 2015 for the colonial slave market that stood at Wall and Pearl Streets from 1711 to 1762. It was the first the city had ever raised for that market, and it arrived more than two hundred and fifty years late.

Then search the marker databases for 167th and Jerome, and search them again for Simpson and Westchester, and see what comes back.

The women who stood there had already worked out the truth of the place long before any of it was written down, and one of them handed it to a stranger on a wet sidewalk in the winter of 1950.

"Don't let them turn the clock back on you."

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXKqi
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

In Some Guys Talking Episode 25 premiering Friday, hosts Brian Holler and Aaron Washington sit down with Ernest Toney, Founder and Principal of BIPOCann, to discuss cannabis social equity, entrepreneurship, mentorship, and the challenges facing small businesses in the regulated cannabis industry.

Ernest shares his journey from growing up in rural Virginia to witnessing Colorado's legalization firsthand, working at MJBiz, and founding BIPOCann in 2020.

https://t.co/qn08NN9Vtt

The conversation explores why receiving a cannabis license doesn't guarantee business success, how mentorship and access to professional networks can help entrepreneurs overcome barriers, and why building a sustainable cannabis business requires patience, community, and a long-term strategy.

📌 Episode Highlights:

✅ Meet Ernest Toney
Ernest founded BIPOCann in 2020 to address gaps in minority representation and cannabis business ownership. His organization now focuses on business development, technical assistance, education, and mentorship for social equity licensees and underserved entrepreneurs.

✅ From Rural Virginia to Colorado's Cannabis Industry
Ernest discusses growing up around cannabis stigma and unequal enforcement, moving to Denver before Colorado legalized adult-use cannabis, and eventually entering the industry through MJBiz's marketing and partnerships team.

✅ Why a Cannabis License Isn't Enough
Getting licensed is only the beginning. Ernest explains how funding challenges, municipal delays, real estate complications, compliance requirements, and limited business experience can prevent entrepreneurs from opening or sustaining their businesses.

✅ How BIPOCann Supports Cannabis Entrepreneurs
BIPOCann connects business owners with experienced professionals who can help with accounting, legal requirements, operations, marketing, and business development.

✅ Colorado's Cannabis Business Accelerator
Ernest discusses BIPOCann's partnership with Colorado's Cannabis Business Office, including 15-week mentorship programs, educational workshops, and individualized business advisory services. The organization has supported more than 65 unique Colorado cannabis licensees through its programming.

✅ Mentorship, Networking & Community
Beyond technical assistance, BIPOCann helps entrepreneurs build relationships with other operators, service providers, and industry mentors. Ernest explains how these connections create opportunities for collaboration and business growth.

✅ The Future of BIPOCann
Ernest discusses opportunities to expand mentorship programs beyond Colorado, work with additional state agencies, and offer broader consulting and fractional advisory services.

🗣️ Quote from the Video:

"Small bites, long plan, expand the timeline." – Ernest Toney

Spain's transport minister says human error caused this morning's deadly collision between two high speed trains near Madrid.  At least 64 people were killed. A computer communications failure had turned a signal red, which the first train stopped at, but someone erroneously ordered the train to go through the red signal. It did, and later plowed into the first train. This man was a passenger on the first train.: “Suddenly the train hit us from behind. We saw the train appear on the left and everyone was overturned and some people were thrown out. ”
It's Spain's second deadly train collision this year. A crash in January killed 46 people.

The Kansas City Chiefs have signed Justin Tucker to their practice squad. Tucker, one of the most accurate kickers in NFL history, was released by the Ravens after 16 massage therapists in the Baltimore area accused him of sexual misconduct.

text:
Does the United States Really Need a Public Digital Dollar?

As China advances the digital yuan and Europe develops the digital euro, a fundamental question emerges: Why is the United States relying on private stablecoins rather than issuing a public digital dollar?

The answer may lie in competing visions of monetary power.

China views digital currency as an extension of state-led financial infrastructure. Europe sees the digital euro as a means of preserving monetary sovereignty and reducing dependence on private payment networks. The United States, under the current administration, has taken a different path: rejecting a U.S. CBDC while supporting regulated, dollar-backed stablecoins.

This is not necessarily a rejection of digital money. It is a choice about who should build and control its distribution.

Private stablecoins allow the dollar to reach users beyond traditional banking infrastructure, operate across blockchain networks, and become embedded in global payments and digital asset markets. Meanwhile, reserve requirements can channel a portion of the resulting demand toward short-term U.S. Treasuries.

In effect, the United States can expand the dollar's digital footprint without requiring the Federal Reserve to operate a retail digital currency infrastructure itself.

But this model creates a strategic trade-off.

The wider the dollar economy expands through private issuers, the more its distribution depends on corporate decisions, redemption mechanisms, blockchain infrastructure, and regulatory frameworks. Dollar dominance and direct government control over the networks distributing dollars are not the same thing.

A public digital dollar could offer an alternative settlement instrument backed directly by the central bank, although it would introduce difficult questions around privacy, financial stability, and the future role of commercial banks.

For now, Washington appears to favor private-sector innovation over direct public issuance.

This is where USD1 and other dollar stablecoins become strategically relevant. Their significance should not be measured solely by market capitalization, but by whether they become durable infrastructure for institutional settlement, cross-border payments, and recurring economic activity.

One distinction, however, remains essential:

USD1 adoption does not automatically translate into economic value for WLFI holders.

Dollar expansion, stablecoin growth, and tokenholder value accrual are three separate propositions. Each requires independent evidence.

The real question is not simply whether America needs a public digital dollar.

It is whether privately operated digital dollars can preserve and extend American monetary influence at global scale—and how much of that influence the United States is willing to delegate to private institutions.

DO NOT TRANSFER THESE PRISONERS TO RWANDA. THEY WILL BE KILLED!
While the world focuses elsewhere, Rwanda is quietly lobbying for Senegal to extradite 8 UN Rwandan prisoners who are serving sentences imposed by the UN’s International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) and its Residual Mechanism for their roles in the 1994 Rwanda Genocide. 

Rwanda’s attempt to secure these prisoners through a bilateral deal with Senegal is illegal.

Their custody is governed by agreements between Senegal and the United Nations. Senegal is the host state; it does not “own” the sentences. The residual UN mechanism retains oversight. Any transfer therefore requires proper UN involvement and must comply with international law—including the absolute prohibition on non-refoulement.

Rwanda is lobbying for transfer of these prisoners under new bilateral instruments signed in Kigali on 7 October 2026 (extradition and transfer-of-convicts agreements) and Kigali is quietly building the legal framework with Dakar. The detainees themselves, in a 23 October letter to Senegal’s Justice Minister, have already raised the alarm, citing risks of mistreatment and the UN’s longstanding refusal to place them in Rwanda for security reasons. Amnesty International Senegal has publicly echoed those concerns.

Rwanda’s record disqualifies it from receiving these prisoners:
🆘Prisoners deaths while in Rwanda custody: 
- Gospel singer and government critic Kizito Mihigo was killed in a Kigali police cell in February 2020. Authorities claimed suicide by hanging; Human Rights Watch and others documented prior threats, called for an independent investigation involving UN experts, and received none. 
- Rapper Jay Polly (Joshua Tuyishime) died in Nyarugenge/Mageragere prison in September 2021 and Rwanda blamed it on him for consuming a methanol concoction. 
- Academic, singer, and YouTube commentator Aimable Karasira died on 6–7 May 2026—the very day he was set to be released after serving a five-year while his crime was him fighting for his freedom of speech. He had previously reported torture, sleep deprivation, and beatings in Nyarugenge prison by the government police.
🆘Torture and ill-treatment: Human Rights Watch has documented systematic torture in Rwandan prisons and unofficial facilities, including the “Yordani” method—forcing detainees into tanks of dirty water and beating them. The U.S. State Department has repeatedly described prison conditions as harsh to life-threatening, with arbitrary detention, political prisoners, and failures to investigate suspicious deaths.
🆘Transnational repression: HRW’s reporting details a pattern of killings, kidnappings, enforced disappearances, beatings, and intimidation of Rwandans abroad. A recent case involves a Rwandan dissident found beheaded in Uganda. The playbook includes misuse of Interpol, renditions, and pressure on families inside Rwanda.
🆘The Rusesabagina case: Paul Rusesabagina was lured onto a private jet in Dubai in 2020 and flown to Kigali. Rwandan officials admitted the government paid for the flight. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention later found he had been illegally kidnapped, tortured, and subjected to an unfair trial.
🆘Political imprisonment: Opposition leader and political prisoner Victoire Ingabire, previously imprisoned for nearly eight years in a case the African Court found violated her rights, was rearrested in June 2025 without a warrant. The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention has ruled her current detention arbitrary.
🆘Fueling war and destabilization in the DRC: UN experts have documented Rwanda’s command and control over the militias destabilizing Congo DRC. Rwanda has thousands of RDF troops in eastern DRC and has not ceased to fuel this conflict by which millions of congolese are refugees in their own country, thousands have died as a result and destabilizing the Great Lakes Region has continued even after the December 2025 Washington Accords. 
🆘Rwanda army under sanctions: In March 2026, the U.S. sanctioned the entire Rwanda Defence Force and senior commanders for supporting M23; further sanctions hit related mineral-smuggling networks. The result has been mass displacement, civilian killings, and sexual violence.
🆘Leaders under sanctions: Beyond the RDF itself, senior Rwandan military figures have been sanctioned by the United States for their role in the DRC conflict.

A government that carries out or tolerates these practices, whose senior military figures are under U.S. sanctions, and that has a documented history of transnational repression and suspicious deaths in custody cannot be trusted with the physical safety of UN-sentenced prisoners. Guarantees offered by Kigali have little value given the pattern of non-compliance with international human-rights obligations.

UW–Stevens Point Graduate Student Hayden Walkush Honored with Boone and Crockett Club Fellow Outstanding Achievement Award

MISSOULA, Mont. – The Boone and Crockett Club announced today that Hayden Walkush, a master's student in wildlife at the University of Wisconsin-Stevens Point (UWSP), has been recognized with the Boone and Crockett Fellow Outstanding Achievement Award. The award recognizes a graduate student whose research advances the Club's mission and informs natural resource management and policy decisions in North America. The award highlights and strengthens the connection between students and the Boone and Crockett Club that supports them.

"The Boone and Crockett Club promotes a system of governance in North America where natural resource policy decisions are informed by strong, credible science and our University Programs support these future wildlife scientists. Hayden's research exemplifies this mission and we are proud to present this award to him for his research on black bears in Wisconsin," commented Dr. Steven Leath, the Boone and Crockett Club's executive vice president for administration and co-chair of the University Programs subcommittee.

The Boone and Crockett Wildlife Conservation Program supports graduate students in wildlife conservation and related fields through its University Program Fellows Program. The Club's University Programs offer educational and professional development opportunities that prepare future scientists, decision-makers, and leaders to address the enormous challenges facing wildlife conservation. As part of achieving this broad-based goal, the Club has invested considerable resources in its University Programs to generate credible science on important natural resource issues and train future conservation leaders.

Hayden has been a Boone and Crockett fellow since his undergraduate days at UWSP. His master's research on Wisconsin's black bears is part of a decades-long project at UWSP's Wisconsin Center for Wildlife. Working under advisor Dr. Cady Sartini, he studies how bears move through and respond to a patchwork landscape of working forests, elk restoration areas, and intensive bear hunting activity. His work is part of a long-standing $1 million research project that Boone and Crockett Club members helped revive and fund. His study area includes the Great Divide District of the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest.

"I am absolutely honored to have been selected. It is difficult to put into words how much my time as a Boone and Crockett Fellow has meant to me, both professionally and personally," said Walkush. "As I approach the end of my program, I have been reflecting on the many people who have shaped my journey and encouraged me to find my voice as a conservationist, being a Boone and Crockett Fellow has been a key part of that. A simple "thank you" hardly feels sufficient, but please know I will honor your support by carrying what I have learned into the next stage of my career."

"It is not often that you meet your most capable graduate student during their first few weeks on campus as an undergraduate freshman, but he knocked on my door, introduced himself and asked about how he could get involved with wildlife work," noted Walkush's advisor, Dr. Cady Sartini. "He is bright, capable, and radiates with a love for wildlife. He is resourceful, driven, and a gifted leader. He is exactly what the Boone and Crockett Club would expect out of a leader in the wildlife field, in no small part because the Club has given him the tools and opportunity to put himself there."

More About the Boone and Crockett Club: Founded by Theodore Roosevelt in 1887, the Boone and Crockett Club promotes guardianship and visionary management of big game and associated wildlife in North America. The Club maintains the highest standards of fair-chase sportsmanship and supports science-based resource management through research, education, and policy advocacy.

text:
In 1878, after the long winter killed most of the men in Eau Claire County, Wisconsin, seven Ojibwe and German widows ran the spring maple sugaring together. The lumber companies had taken the husbands; ice on the Chippewa River took the rest. But the sugar maples didn’t care. Every March, the women — Anna, Nodin, Greta, Mindimooyenh, Liesel, Ziibi, and Hilda — tapped 400 trees with hand drills, hung buckets made from hollow logs, and boiled sap day and night in cast-iron kettles. 

They slept in shifts, sang hymns in two languages, and kept each other’s children alive on syrup and snowbread. Lumber barons offered to buy their grove for pennies. Nodin told them: “You sell trees. We keep family. Not the same.” They made 200 gallons that year and paid off every farm. The grove still stands.

text:
This Budget offered the Chancellor the opportunity to reset its relationship with the countryside. Today, however, he showed little interest in seizing that chance. 
 
Extending small business rates relief could help rural businesses, but coupled with hikes in employment costs it remains to be seen whether hardworking rural business owners will see any real benefit. Additionally, while temporarily extending the red diesel duty cut and suspending tariffs on kerosene heating oil and fertiliser are welcome moves, it will come as little solace to farmers still facing enormous threats to their livelihoods. 
 
Before becoming Prime Minister, Andy Burnham pledged to revisit the hated Family Farm Tax. He has failed to do so. This tax continues to tarnish the government’s rural record. It is preventing farmers from making important decisions about their livelihoods, hampering the government’s own mission of creating good growth in every postcode. Working with the custodians of our countryside, we will continue to vocally oppose this tax and call for its abolition. 
 
Additionally, farmers have been encouraged for years to diversify their businesses by creating holiday lets, among other measures; but anyone who has done so is now being punished by yet another increase to the property income tax paid on such lets, further threatening the viability of their business. 
 
At a time when the government should be increasing support for farmers and in the wake of last month’s Sustainable Farming Incentive fiasco, it has slashed DEFRA's funding for 2027-28 by £100m. 
 
This Budget does little to give “breathing space” or fresh hope for the countryside. If this government is serious about growth in every postcode, including in the countryside, it must urgently address the plethora of problems facing rural businesses. Scrapping the Family Farm Tax is the only way to turn a new leaf.

indifferent to the miles I've climbed,
indifferent to the man I've become.

They call it strength.
They call it the gift of another day.
But what is a gift
that cannot be refused?
And what is freedom
to a man condemned to carry
what he never chose to lift?

Anchor: “sounds familiar. donald trump has also spent a huge amount of time lately fixating, exactly like ali said, on minnesota’s somali immigrant community, leveling racist accusations at them, calling them all corrupt. he’s especially targeted minnesota congresswoman ilhan omar, whose washington residence was raided by the department of homeland security and their investigators earlier this month. and of course minnesota has literally been ground zero for the brutal and the lawless immigration raids and all of those armed and masked federal agents that carried out the indescribable on donald trump’s orders. during that offensive, agents shot and killed two americans on the streets of minneapolis, alex pretti and renee nicole good. in a press conference today, the parents of alex pretti said that in the nine months since their son was shot, no one, no one in the federal government has reached out to them. instead the justice department seems to be stonewalling the investigation.”

Alex Pretti’s parents: “minnesotans said no to this injustice. americans said no to this injustice and today we are here begging for the department of justice to do what is right, to hold the men who murdered our son accountable for what they did.”

Anchor: “alex pretti’s younger sister michaela is also speaking out. she posted on instagram last week writing this.”

Michaela: “to everyone around the country that sent our family letters after alex was murdered, a majority of them said, please let us know how we can honor alex or we will do everything to fight for alex. and to that i say, please, please go out and vote. vote for alex, vote for a step closer to justice for my family, vote for all of the victims of ice, vote for your community and your neighbors. alex stood up for his community. so now it is time. we stand up and we fight back.”

Anchor: “peggy flanagan has served as the lieutenant governor of minnesota since 2019. she’s the democratic candidate for senator this year and she joins me now. it’s good to see you. thanks for being here.”

Peggy Flanagan: “thanks so much for having me.”

Anchor: “you just heard alex pretti’s parents on the investigation into his death as well as what his sister had to say. what’s your reaction to all that?”

Peggy Flanagan: “i mean, these parents are incredibly brave and my heart just breaks for them. and i just join michael and susan and michaela in demanding that this evidence be released and shared with state investigators. the fact that they just continue to stonewall this investigation, you see, i mean you can tell in their voices and their demeanor just how heartbreaking all of this is. no parent should have to stand up there and ask for the federal government to simply do their job. they’re just asking for accountability, for justice for their son who was killed and we all saw it happen right with our own eyes. what we have been through is incredibly traumatic here and to see how his family is carrying this and being incredibly brave in this moment and calling out for justice for their son. i’m just, i’m with them and i know that there are so many people in this state who stand with alex pretti and his family.”

Anchor: “i have to ask you more about it because we all watched the ice raids in minnesota together. we all saw regular people who came out to protest and protect their neighbors and offer mutual aid sometimes in super sub-zero temperatures. after all of that, i think there are some people who wonder how is this race, how is your race so close?”

Peggy Flanagan: “i mean, i just say this. i think that minnesotans understand there is just a very clear choice in this race. you know, donald trump, who you mentioned earlier, endorsed my opponent. he has in fact endorsed michelle tafoya multiple times in the last two weeks and that’s because she’s completely aligned with him on so many issues. but when it comes to operation metro surge, she literally used footage of operation metro surge and ice in her campaign rollout video days after renee good was killed. and in fact, she went on a podcast the day renee was killed and said that renee good was responsible for her own death. she has now tried to change her tune a bit. but i think we know that donald trump doesn’t give out his endorsements, you know, willy-nilly. you have to earn it and michelle tafoya has earned it with, you know, flying colors from, you know, her support for the tariffs, the trade war. she platformed january 6 insurrectionists on her podcast and called them really good people and her brothers. she said ice should be called nice and that they’ve treated children really, really well. we all know what happened to liam conejo ramos, right? the 6,200 children who’ve been detained by ice. that is the choice in this race and i think minnesotans deserve someone who will be beholden to them and not do the bidding of donald trump.”

Anchor: “it is deranged. i mean, it was deranged on the ground. it’s deranged to hear someone who could have possibly seen that like i did with my own eyes and think it was anything other than deliberate cruelty on the streets of minneapolis and, you know, throughout the twin cities. there’s the other huge issue here, which is trump is obviously laying the groundwork to challenge your election, elections across the country if you win. there’s also been so much speculation about the other ways that he could interfere with the vote on the ground there. the justice department just notified two minnesota counties to be prepared for federal election observers. what are you doing? how are you prepared for this possible incursion or election interference? at the same time, you’ve got to motivate all of your supporters to go get out to the polls.”

Peggy Flanagan: “so i’d say a couple things. number one, minnesota has one of the best election systems in the entire country. our secretary of state, steve simon, is incredible. the governor’s office, the attorney general’s office, as well as the secretary of state’s office are, you know, working together to make sure, right, that people can vote. i would also just say this, that we’ve got a lot of folks who are on the ground who will also be observers, making sure that so many of the folks who are mobilized around operation metro surge and standing up for their neighbors also are motivating people to get out to vote, to also make sure that people can vote safely and free from interference. but what i would also say is that we have seen tremendous early vote numbers here in minnesota. that i think is really encouraging and if folks are feeling a little nervous about the election, i would just encourage them to vote early. and that’s something that’s available to people up until election day. and, you know, that is the, really, the movement that we are seeing. so many folks who are turning out to vote early, and i feel confident that we will have low drama in these what will happen in alaska as well. that’s outrageous. and, you know, it is clearly a distraction. they know that their policies are not popular. a $5,000 hamburger is similar to, you know, what text:
Wall Street’s Double Test Today: The Fed + Google/Microsoft Earnings — Time for AI to Show the Money

October 28, 2026

1/ Today isn’t just about whether tech stocks rise or fall after earnings. The real question is whether massive AI investments can generate sustainable cash returns. The answer could determine the winners and losers over the next 6–12 months.

2/ The spending is enormous. Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon, which reports Thursday, could collectively spend up to $600 billion on capital expenditures this year.

Meta offers a warning: despite strong results, its increased spending plans overshadowed earnings, sending shares lower the following day. Investors are losing patience with spending that lacks visible returns.

3/ The Federal Reserve is the second major test. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has generally avoided detailed forward guidance, while some officials have signaled that further rate hikes may be necessary to contain inflation.

Higher rates create a double burden for AI infrastructure: more expensive financing and higher required investment returns. Debt-funded expansion is particularly vulnerable.

4/ Oil is adding pressure. Brent crude is trading around $115 per barrel amid Middle East tensions.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Washington has warned Gulf countries to prepare for possible limited military operations after the midterm elections.

Persistent geopolitical risks could keep inflation elevated and complicate the Fed’s policy decisions.

5/ The good news comes from the supply chain.

SK Hynix reported a 632% year-over-year surge in third-quarter operating profit and record revenue, with plans for substantial shareholder returns.

The message is clear: AI hardware demand is real, and chipmakers are already capturing significant profits.

6/ Five stocks to watch over the next 6–12 months:

GOOGL: Trading at roughly 15.8 times earnings, with revenue growth near 20%, Alphabet may offer attractive risk/reward. The key is whether Google Cloud growth can justify rising capital expenditures.

MSFT: Strong execution remains its advantage, but expectations are high. Azure and Copilot need to beat forecasts, not merely meet them.

NVDA / AMD: Their outlook depends heavily on hyperscaler spending guidance. As long as Google and Microsoft maintain AI investment plans, the compute-demand thesis remains intact.

AVGO: A reported $63 billion financing arrangement involving Anthropic helped lift shares about 4% Tuesday. Custom AI chips are increasingly supported by long-term customer commitments.

7/ The Bottom Line

AI hardware suppliers such as SK Hynix and Broadcom are already generating substantial profits. Platform giants such as Google and Microsoft must now prove that their massive investments can deliver attractive returns.

If revenue growth keeps pace with spending, the broader AI ecosystem could continue benefiting.

But if capital expenditures accelerate while returns remain uncertain, Meta’s market reaction could spread to other technology giants.

In a higher-rate environment, valuation corrections can happen much faster.

The next phase of the AI boom won’t be judged by how much companies spend.

It will be judged by how much they earn on that spending.

For market commentary only. Not investment advice.

THE GREAT COSMIC LIQUIDATION OF PLANET EARTH

Or how we became millionaires without being able to afford even a stick of gum

I. CONGRATULATIONS, FRIENDS! WE’VE ALREADY WON. (so they say)

Friends—and all other confused species who pay taxes—
I have excellent news for you. Excellent. Wonderful. Incredible.
It turns out that last night, while you were snoring and drooling on your pillow, an ultra-secret commando unit of military super-intelligence—the kind of guys who can’t find their own keys but can somehow hack the universe—launched:

OPERATION BLACKOUT.

The objective?
Nothing small. Just the Deep State, the Cabal, the global financial system, the international operating system of darkness, your ex who owes you money, and probably the guy who charges you for parking, too.
BAM! A massive strike. No mercy.
Like my appetite at an all-you-can-eat buffet.

The result? TOTAL VICTORY! We now have control over the universal *logarithm* of the entire existing system.

Yes, you heard that right. The *logarithm*. Not an *algorithm*. The *LOGARITHM*. Because when you want to sound smart but have no clue about math, you just add an extra syllable.

II. THE MIRACULOUS PAYOUT: YOU ARE A MILLIONAIRE
(in theory)

But don’t worry, friends. Don’t worry at all.
Because all the confiscated money—EVERY BIT OF IT—is going to be distributed among each and every inhabitant of this planet.

Applause! Confetti! Joy!
We’re going to divvy up the drug money. The proceeds from countless fraudulent operations. The money from the banks, the politicians, the reptilians, the Illuminati, and even that cousin of yours who’s always peddling something. Every child in Africa, every grandparent in Farmingdale, every influencer crying on TikTok.

ALL OF THEM MILLIONAIRES!

It’s communism—but on steroids and with Wi-Fi. It’s like Robin Hood, but with drones and a YouTube podcast.

Picture the scene: 8 billion people checking their bank accounts at the exact same time.

The system collapses. The ATM explodes. Your bank sends you a message:

"Congratulations! You have 47 trillion dollars."

We’re rich! We’re free! We’re...!

III. THE FINE PRINT OF THE APOCALYPSE

But there’s a catch.
There’s always a catch. Just like in marriage. Just like in those "terms and conditions" that nobody ever reads.

In this miraculous offer, it turns out that:

You can’t sell it.
You can’t redeem it.
You can’t spend it.

Wait—what?

Hold on, let me get this "financial genius" straight. You’re telling me I’ve been given all the money in the world, but I can’t actually use it?

It’s like being gifted a Ferrari—but with no engine, no wheels, and no doors. And it’s locked inside a display case. In another country. And, oh, you’re dead.

IT’S PERFECT! We’ve reinvented poverty—only now with bigger numbers!

It’s the same thing, folks. We were handed the biggest coupon in the universe, and when we went to redeem it, they told us: "Oh, no—that was just a metaphor." V. A SARCASTIC CONCLUSION TO HELP YOU SLEEP SOUNDLY

So, rest easy. Sleep soundly.

Superintelligence already controls everything. There are no more "bad guys." There is no more financial system. There is no more darkness.

All that’s left is us, sitting atop a mountain of imaginary gold—unable to even buy a loaf of bread—explaining to our children that, while we are trillionaires, today we’ll be eating plain white rice once again.

But hey, we’re free! Free from the terrible burden of being able to spend money!
Welcome to the future, friends. A place where we all own everything... and yet, we have nothing.

text:
Mornings in the countryside during the 1990s always offered an atmosphere of profound tranquility and comfort. Sunlight would slowly emerge from behind the hills, casting a golden glow over the vast, verdant rice paddies. Dew still clung to the tips of the rice stalks, glistening like pearls caught in the morning light.

The air felt remarkably cool and clean. A gentle morning breeze stirred the rice plants, causing them to sway softly—resembling soothing, green waves. In the distance, the clear, flowing water of the irrigation channels blended harmoniously with the melodious chirping of birds in the trees; their songs served as a natural anthem, welcoming the arrival of a new day.

Amidst this beauty, farmers began their daily tasks. Wearing conical hats and carrying hoes, they walked along the narrow paths between the paddies, greeting one another with warm smiles. Some planted rice seedlings, cleared away weeds, managed the irrigation, or inspected the crops—which were beginning to turn yellow, signaling that the harvest season was drawing near. They carried out their hard work with great patience, accompanied by a gentle breeze and the calming sounds of the natural world.

Occasionally, sparrows could be seen flitting low over the rice fields, while colorful butterflies alighted on wildflowers along the edges of the paddies. The bright blue sky, adorned with wispy white clouds, created a peaceful scene that was a true delight to behold.

The atmosphere of the rice fields in the 1990s taught us that happiness does not always stem from luxury. Peace can be found in fresh air, a pristine natural environment, sincere hard work, and the sense of togetherness among villagers who live with mutual respect for one another. That is a beautiful memory that, to this day, remains etched in the hearts of many—a simple morning, yet one filled with a sense of calm, warmth, and a beauty that is hard to replace.

text:
If AI Agents Trade Crypto 24/7, Who Actually Makes the Money?

I've been watching the rise of AI crypto trading agents, and one thought keeps bothering me.

Imagine a million AI agents trading Bitcoin.

They never sleep.

They monitor every price movement, read thousands of signals, react to breaking news, and execute orders faster than any human sitting in front of a screen.

Some will buy.

Some will sell.

Some will copy other agents.

Some will try to predict what those agents are about to do.

And every one of them will believe its strategy has a reason to make money.

But there's a business in the middle of all this activity that doesn't need to predict the next Bitcoin candle.

The exchange.

That distinction is becoming increasingly interesting to me.

Because I think AI could make cryptocurrency markets much more active without making the average AI trader more profitable.

In fact, the two outcomes could happen at the same time.

More automation.

More trades.

More sophisticated strategies.

And more money lost to the cost of trading.

Here's why.

A few months ago, the idea of giving an AI assistant direct access to a trading account still sounded experimental.

Now exchanges are building infrastructure specifically for it.

In August 2026, Binance introduced Agent OS, allowing authorized AI systems to access market information and execute trades through defined permissions.

Other platforms have been developing similar integrations.

This doesn't prove AI agents can beat the market.

It proves something different.

The infrastructure for letting AI agents trade real money is arriving.

And I think that difference matters enormously.

Connecting an AI model to an exchange is an engineering problem.

Making that connection consistently profitable is a financial research problem.

The first can be solved with APIs, permissions, and reliable software.

The second requires an actual trading advantage.

Those are not remotely the same achievement.

I learned that distinction the expensive-looking way, fortunately without putting real money at risk.

In one of my crypto research experiments, I collected approximately 65 hours of BTC and ETH order-book data.

The study included roughly 234,700 snapshots for each market.

I wanted to understand whether short-term order-flow information could help predict future price movements.

Some of the preliminary relationships were real enough to measure.

But they were small.

At one checkpoint, a stronger combined signal showed only about 0.4 basis points of average gross movement over a 60-second horizon.

That's roughly four thousandths of one percent.

Now compare that with the costs a trader may face when entering and exiting a position.

Exchange fees.

Bid-ask spread.

Slippage.

Market impact.

The signal might exist statistically, yet still be far too small to trade profitably.

That is exactly the kind of result I find useful.

Not because it makes a great screenshot.

Because it forces me to separate predicting a price movement from capturing that movement as profit.

The experiment was exploratory and covered a limited historical window. It was not a certified trading strategy or live track record.

But it taught me something I keep coming back to.

A trading signal can be real. The trade can still lose money.

And AI doesn't repeal that arithmetic.

Consider a hypothetical trading agent.

It makes 100 round trips in a day.

Each trade uses $1,000 of notional exposure.

Suppose it pays 0.10% on entry and 0.10% on exit.

That's $2 in fees per completed round trip.

Across 100 round trips, that's $200 in trading fees.

Before slippage.

Before adverse selection.

Before any additional execution costs.

The agent has to earn more than $200 in gross trading profit just to break even.

These are illustrative assumptions, not a claim about the fees every exchange or trader pays. Actual rates depend on the venue, product, order type and trading tier.

But the calculation exposes something important.

The agent starts every trade with a hurdle.

The exchange may receive a fee whenever a qualifying order executes.

The agent only earns a net profit if its advantage exceeds the cost of execution.

The exchange has a fee model. The trader needs an edge.

That's a very different business proposition.

Now imagine that the AI agent becomes more active.

It finds twice as many signals.

It doubles its trading frequency.

Its dashboard shows twice as much activity.

But what if the new trades are lower quality?

What if the predictive advantage hasn't improved?

Then the agent may simply pay more in fees while taking more risk.

A beautifully automated machine for generating transaction costs.

I suspect this will be one of the biggest traps in AI-assisted trading.

People will confuse activity with intelligence.

They'll see an agent monitoring 500 tokens, scanning social media, reading on-chain flows and executing around the clock.

It will look impressive.

But none of those capabilities proves that the system can identify mispriced assets.

It may only prove that the system is very good at reacting.

And in financial markets, being able to react doesn't guarantee that the reaction is profitable.

There's another problem.

What happens when the other side of the trade is also an AI?

Suppose one agent identifies a momentum signal and buys.

Another sees the same movement and buys a fraction of a second later.

A third is trained to recognize that buying pressure.

A fourth provides liquidity, but adjusts its quotes when it detects informed or aggressive flow.

A fifth looks for signs that the momentum is about to reverse.

Now the market contains several automated systems reacting to one another.

This isn't necessarily a new phenomenon. Algorithmic traders have competed for years.

What's changing is how accessible those capabilities may become.

AI could make it easier for many more people to build strategies and deploy automated execution.

That sounds democratizing.

But it creates a difficult possibility.

If everyone can deploy the same kind of intelligent trading system, the profitable opportunity may disappear faster.

A strategy may look attractive when only a few traders pursue it.

Then more capital arrives.

Entries become more expensive.

Exits become more crowded.

The price adjusts before the slower agents can respond.

And the original opportunity gets competed away.

The agents may become smarter.

The market may become harder to beat.

Both things can be true.

There's also a less obvious question.

If millions of agents compete for small price movements, who benefits from all those orders?

Exchanges are one candidate.

But they're not the only ones.

Market makers may earn spreads or rebates for supplying liquidity, although they also face inventory risk, adverse selection and trading losses.

Execution infrastructure providers may earn fees for routing or processing orders.

Data businesses may sell information to agents trying to identify opportunities.

Security providers may sell tools that prevent compromised agents from misusing trading permissions.

Monitoring services may help traders detect failures before they become catastrophic.

And on decentralized venues, transaction ordering and MEV can affect who captures value from certain transactions.

Not all these businesses will be profitable.

Competition can compress fees and margins.

Some exchanges may spend heavily on incentives, infrastructure and customer acquisition.

Some market makers will lose money.

And rising volume does not automatically translate into rising shareholder returns.

But I think the overall structure is worth studying.

The trader has to be right often enough, or earn enough when right, to overcome costs and losses.

The infrastructure business may have a different source of revenue.

That's why I'm increasingly interested in the economics surrounding automated trading, not just the trading models themselves.

Something else worries me.

AI could make a bad trading strategy look much more convincing.

Imagine an agent that can automatically generate a thousand strategies.

It can backtest them.

Rank them.

Optimize their parameters.

And produce professional reports in minutes.

One of those strategies will probably look spectacular.

Maybe several will.

But if the agent repeatedly searches historical data until it finds a winning combination, it may simply be selecting the luckiest result.

The danger isn't necessarily that the model lies.

It may be following instructions perfectly.

The problem is that a strategy discovered through repeated optimization can look like genuine skill even when it has little predictive power outside the sample.

I've encountered versions of this problem in my own quantitative research.

Promising results weakened or disappeared when I introduced additional tests, realistic costs, and independent data.

I don't treat that as a failure of research.

I treat it as the purpose of research.

The job isn't to find a backtest that wins. It's to discover whether the strategy survives outside the conditions that made it look good.

AI makes it easier to generate candidates.

It doesn't remove the need for independent validation.

And it certainly doesn't guarantee profitable execution.

Now add real money.

A trading agent can misunderstand market data.

It can respond to misleading information.

It can overtrade.

It can miscalculate its exposure.

It can repeatedly execute a flawed strategy because nobody notices the mistake.

A human trader can make those errors too.

But an autonomous agent may repeat them at machine speed.

That changes the risk.

I think financial authority has to be treated separately from analytical capability.

An agent that can analyze markets is not necessarily an agent that should be allowed to trade without limits.

And an agent allowed to trade should not automatically have permission to withdraw or transfer funds.

A sensible architecture would impose deterministic controls outside the model itself.

Maximum position size.

Maximum daily loss.

Limits on order frequency.

Explicit permissions.

Independent reconciliation.

And a reliable way to stop execution when the system behaves unexpectedly.

The important part is that those controls continue working even if the AI makes a bad decision.

I wouldn't trust a system merely because it promises to manage risk.

I'd want to know whether its risk controls can actually stop it.

This leads to a bigger investment question.

Suppose autonomous AI trading becomes a major source of crypto market activity over the next decade.

Who captures the most durable economic value?

My first instinct is to look at the businesses that benefit from the growth of automated financial activity without needing to predict market direction.

Exchanges.

Reliable execution infrastructure.

Risk management.

Data verification.

Custody and permissions.

But I wouldn't buy any of them merely because agent adoption is increasing.

I'd still want to understand their margins, competitive position, costs, and valuation.

A business can benefit from a technological revolution while its investors earn disappointing returns.

And there may be a more surprising outcome.

As AI trading becomes more common, execution fees and spreads could eventually face stronger competition.

More sophisticated traders could route orders toward cheaper venues.

Better execution algorithms could reduce unnecessary turnover.

Internal matching or other mechanisms could lower settlement costs in certain markets.

In other words, AI could initially increase trading activity while eventually putting pressure on the economics of the companies facilitating it.

That is why I don't think the answer is as simple as "just buy the exchanges."

I want to know who retains pricing power after the market becomes more efficient.

Still, there's one prediction I'm willing to make.

The first large wave of AI trading agents will probably create far more trading activity than verified, persistent trading alpha.

Not because AI is incapable of finding useful signals.

But because generating orders is much easier than generating risk-adjusted profits after costs.

An agent can trade 24 hours a day.

It cannot force the market to offer a profitable opportunity 24 hours a day.

Sometimes the best trade is no trade.

I suspect that will remain true no matter how capable the models become.

For my own research, I want to keep separating three things:

A signal that predicts something.

A strategy that looks profitable in a historical simulation.

And a trading system that actually earns money after realistic costs under prospective conditions.

Those are three different levels of evidence.

I don't want to call the first one the third.

And I don't want to give an AI trading agent real capital simply because its backtest is attractive.

The future of autonomous crypto trading could be enormous.

But enormous trading volume and enormous investor profits are not the same thing.

If millions of agents begin trading against one another, some will discover genuine advantages.

Many won't.

The exchanges and infrastructure providers will compete to serve them.

And the market itself will adapt.

What fascinates me most is that the AI revolution may make financial markets more automated without making them any easier to beat.

My current view is simple:

AI may make trading almost effortless.

It won't make profitable trading effortless.

And the people who earn the most from the first wave of autonomous trading may not be the people operating the trading agents.

They may be the people selling the tools, liquidity and infrastructure those agents use.

I'd be interested in the strongest argument against that thesis, especially from developers running real-money agents with independently verifiable, cost-adjusted results.

Because if an AI can consistently beat the market after every cost, I want to study the evidence.

Not the marketing.

— Teraliq Quant

Independent research commentary, October 2026. The fee example is hypothetical. My order-book findings are exploratory historical research, not live trading results or verified alpha. No investment recommendation or promise of returns.

text:
Since Jan. 5, 2025, drivers entering Manhattan at or below 60th Street have paid a congestion toll, $9 at peak hours for a car with E-ZPass. 

Between 2022 and 2025, five New York legislators filed seven bills to exempt Rockland County drivers from that toll, refund it or repeal it. None has left committee, whether its sponsor sat in the majority or the minority. 

The record behind those bills holds several surprises.

One of the exemption's sponsors voted for the bill that created the toll. 

Congestion pricing was one part of New York's 2019 revenue budget bill, which the Senate passed 39 to 23 on March 31, 2019; 

Sen. James Skoufis, an Orange County Democrat, voted yes. 

He later joined a teachers union lawsuit to stop the toll and, in March 2024, filed S8702 to exempt Rockland and Orange residents. He has not refiled it since tolling began.

In August 2022, Assemblyman Ken Zebrowski, a Rockland Democrat, and then-Sen. Elijah Reichlin-Melnick announced they would introduce an exemption; the Senate bill that followed lists no Assembly version. 

In 2024, Zebrowski chaired the Assembly Committee on Corporations, Authorities and Commissions, which received Assemblymember Chris Eachus's version, A9300, that February; the bill never got a vote.

That April, Zebrowski's committee voted down a Republican bill to exempt some city workers, nurses, first responders and patients from the toll. Zebrowski said he did not support congestion pricing but did not see "a legislative piecemeal way" as the best route to exemptions. He resigned from the Assembly in July 2024 to join a lobbying firm.

The only vote any of the seven bills received was forced by a minority senator. Sen. Jack Martins, a Long Island Republican, invoked a Senate rule that lets the sponsor of any bill demand a committee vote. 

On May 13, 2025, his repeal bill drew six of the seven votes it needed, counting two "aye wr" votes; two of the six were Long Island Democrats. All seven no votes came from Democrats, including Pete Harckham, whose district includes Rockland's town of Stony Point.

The Senate sponsors of the Rockland bills never used that rule themselves. Skoufis's exemption was eligible in the spring of 2024, and Sen. Bill Weber's rebate bill, S1952, was eligible in 2025 and 2026; both records show only referrals to committee.¹⁵ Weber, a Rockland Republican, is a co-sponsor of the Martins repeal bill.

Timing: Reichlin-Melnick filed his exemption on Oct. 17, 2022, more than four months after the Senate finished its session and 22 days before the election he lost; it went to the Rules Committee and never moved. 

On June 6, 2024, the day after Gov. Kathy Hochul paused the toll, Weber offered a repeal amendment on a Skoufis bill; after the presiding officer ruled it not germane, the appeal failed on a show of hands that recorded 20 votes and no names.

Public claims did not always match the record. 

After Hochul's pause, a newsletter from Eachus's Assembly office announced that he "leads the way to the indefinite pause" and listed A9300, a bill that never received a committee vote; the pause was the governor's order. 

Four years and seven bills later, Rockland drivers pay the same $9 they paid on the first day.

text:
⛰️ Mountain West — The Ultimate Underdog Test
Low prestige, high potential
Top contenders: Charlotte (9-5), Miami Ohio (9-4), North Dakota State (12-1), Mississippi State (10-4), BYU (10-3).

Charlotte's nine-win season with only half a prestige star is a powerful example of what the league is trying to achieve. NDSU, Mississippi State, and BYU add a different level of competition, creating a diverse group of potential contenders.

However, Air Force (4-8), Army (3-9), Navy (3-9), and ECU (2-10) show that competitive balance is not yet evenly distributed across the entire conference.

Competitive outlook: A surprisingly deep top five, but the lower tier needs development.

Building outlook: This conference offers perhaps the clearest opportunity for a rebuilding user to make a dramatic rise. Closing the gap between Charlotte and the bottom four would make the entire conference more competitive.

🌲 Pac-12 — The Emerging Power Struggle
Multiple contenders, uneven depth

Top contenders: App State (13-3), Rice (10-3), Georgia State (11-3), Duke (9-5).

App State has established itself as a major contender, but Georgia State's 11-3 record with just one prestige star is arguably the conference's most important development story. Rice and Duke add additional championship-level competition.

Oregon's 8-5 record despite three prestige stars demonstrates that brand strength does not automatically produce dominance.

Competitive outlook: A dangerous upper tier, but several teams finished at or below .500, creating a gap between contenders and rebuilding programs.

Building outlook: The key question is whether teams such as UNLV, Nevada, Sac State, and Texas State can improve enough to challenge the upper tier over time.

Year 4 is about sustainability

The 2 STAR LEAGUE has reached a stage where its greatest accomplishment is no longer a single upset or championship. It is the possibility of creating a sustainable ecosystem where different programs can rise, compete, fall back, rebuild, and rise again. 

The American tests whether a conference can develop a new leader.

The Big 12 tests whether an elite champion can be challenged.

The Mountain West tests whether low-prestige programs can close the gap.

The Pac-12 tests whether its strongest programs can create a deeper competitive field.

The ACC promotion tests whether success can translate beyond the original system.
