text:
Study Notes - (ISBE Dictionary) 

Forgiveness
for-giv´nes (כּפר, kāphar, נשׂא, nāsā', סלח, ṣālaḥ; ἀπολύειν, apolúein χαρίζεσθαι, charı́zesthai, ἄφεσις, áphesis πάρεσις, páresis):
1. Etymology
2. Pagan and Jewish Ideas
3. The Teaching of Christ
4. Conditions of Forgiveness
5. The Offended Party
6. Divine and Human Forgiveness
7. Forgiveness and Justification
8. Old Testament Teaching
9. Limitations of Forgiveness
10. Christ's Power to Forgive Sins
11. The Need of An Atonement
12. The New Testament Doctrine of Atonement
1. Etymology
Of the seven words, three Hebrew and four Greek, which are used to express the idea of forgiveness, the last two occur in this sense only once each. Apoluein (Luk_6:37) is used because of the analogy of sin to debt, and denotes the release from it. It has the meaning “forgiveness” in 2 Macc 12:45 also, in which passage the word for sin is expressed. In Rom_3:25 Paul uses paresis instead of the usual aphesiš. The former means “putting aside,” “disregarding,” “pretermission”; the latter, “putting away” completely and unreservedly (Trench, Synonyms of the New Testament, section xxxiii). It does not mean forgiveness in the complete sense, and in the King James Version is incorrectly translated “remission.” Nor does it mean that God had temporarily suspended punishment which at some later date He might inflict (Sanday on Rom_3:25). It was apparent that God had treated sins as though He had forgiven them, though in fact such an attitude on the part of God was without such a foundation as was later supplied by an adequate atonement, and so the apostle avoids saying that God forgave them. This passing over of sins had the tendency of destroying man's conception of God's righteousness, and in order to avert this Christ was set forth as a propitiation and God's disregard of sin (paresis) became a real forgiveness (aphesis); compare Act_14:16; Act_17:30. Charizesthai is not found outside of the writings of Luke and Paul, and in the sense “to forgive sins” is peculiarly Pauline (2Co_2:7; 2Co_12:13; Eph_3:2; Col_2:13; Col_3:13). It expresses, as no other of these words does, his conception of the graciousness of God's pardon. Kāphar (Deu_21:8; Psa_78:38; Jer_18:23) and ṣālah (Num_30:5, Num_30:8, Num_30:12; 1Ki_8:30, 1Ki_8:34, 1Ki_8:36, 1Ki_8:39, 1Ki_8:50, etc.) are used only of Divine forgiveness, while nāsā' is used in this sense (Exo_32:32; Num_14:19; Jos_24:19; Psa_25:18; Psa_32:1, Psa_32:5; Psa_99:8; Isa_2:9), and also of human forgiveness (Gen_50:17; Exo_10:17; 1Sa_25:28). Remission (Mat_26:28; Mrk_1:4; Luk_1:77; Luk_24:47; Act_2:38; Act_10:43; Heb_9:22; Heb_10:18) and blotting out (Psa_51:1, Psa_51:9; Isa_43:25; Jer_18:23; Act_3:19) are synonyms of forgiveness, and to understand it fully such words as save, justify, reconcile and atonement should also be considered.
2. Pagan and Jewish Ideas
Forgiveness was not a pagan virtue. The large-souled man might disregard offenses in cases where he considered them beneath his notice, but to forgive was weak-spirited (F. W. Robertson on 1Co_4:12). Even in the Old Testament, man's forgiveness of his fellow-man is infrequently mentioned. In every case the one asking forgiveness is in a position of subserviency, and is petitioning for that to which he has no just right (Gen_50:17; Exo_10:17; 1Sa_15:25; 1Sa_25:28). The Imprecatory Psalms attest the fact that forgiveness of enemies was not esteemed as a virtue by Israel. They could appeal to the law which enjoined upon them to seek neither the peace nor the prosperity of their avowed enemies (Deu_23:6; compare Ezr_9:12). Jesus gave the popular summing-up of the law and not its exact words when he said, “Ye have heard that it was said ... hate thine enemy” (Mat_5:43), and this certainly does represent their attitude and their understanding of the teaching of the Scriptures.
3. The Teaching of Christ
Christ taught that forgiveness is a duty. No limit can be set to the extent of forgiveness (Luk_17:4) and it must be granted without reserve. Jesus will not admit that there is any wrong so gross nor so often repeated that it is beyond forgiveness. To Him an unforgiving spirit is one of the most heinous of sins (Bruce, Parabolic Teaching, 376ff). This is the offense which God will not forgive (Mat_18:34, Mat_18:35). It is the very essence of the unpardonable sin (Mrk_3:22-30). It was the one blemish of the elder son which marred an otherwise irreproachable life (Luk_15:28-30). This natural, pagan spirit of implacability Jesus sought to displace by a generous, forgiving spirit. It is so far the essence of His teaching that in popular language “a Christian spirit” is not inappropriately understood to be synonymous with a forgiving disposition. His answer to Peter that one should forgive not merely seven times in a day, but seventy times seven (Mat_18:21, Mat_18:22), not only shows that He thought of no limit to one's forgiveness, but that the principle could not be reduced to a definite formula.
4. Conditions of Forgiveness
Jesus recognized that there are conditions to be fulfilled before forgiveness can be granted. Forgiveness is part of a mutual relationship; the other part is the repentance of the offender. God does not forgive without repentance, nor is it required of man. The effect of forgiveness is to restore to its former state the relationship which was broken by sin. Such a restoration requires the coöperation of both parties. There must be both a granting and an acceptance of the forgiveness. Sincere, deep-felt sorrow for the wrong which works repentance (2Co_7:10) is the condition of mind which insures the acceptance of the forgiveness. Hence, Jesus commands forgiveness when the offender turns again, saying, “I repent” (Luk_17:3, Luk_17:1). It was this state of mind which led the father joyfully to welcome the Prodigal before he even gave utterance to his newly formed purpose (Luk_15:21).
5. The Offended Party
It is not to be supposed, however, that failure to repent upon the part of the offender releases the offended from all obligation to extend forgiveness. Without the repentance of the one who has wronged him he can have a forgiving state of mind. This Jesus requires, as is implied by, “if ye forgive not every one his brother from your hearts” (Mat_18:35). It is also implied by the past tense in the Lord's Prayer: “as we also have forgiven our debtors” (Mat_6:12). It is this forgiving spirit which conditions God's forgiveness of our sins (Mrk_11:25; Mat_6:14, Mat_6:15). In such a case the unforgiving spirit is essentially unrepentance (Mat_18:23-35). “Of all acts, is not, for a man, repentance the most Divine?”
The offended is to go even farther and is to seek to bring the wrongdoer to repentance. This is the purpose of the rebuking commanded in Luk_17:3. More explicitly Jesus says, “If thy brother sin against thee, go, show him his fault between thee and him alone” (Mat_18:15-17). He is to carry his pursuit to the point of making every reasonable effort to win the wrongdoer, and only when he has exhausted every effort may he abandon it. The object is the gaining of his brother. Only when this is evidently unattainable is all effort to cease.
The power of binding and loosing, which means forbidding and allowing, was granted to Peter (Mat_16:19) and to the Christian community (Mat_18:18; Jhn_20:23). It clearly implies the possession of the power to forgive sins. In the case of Peter's power it was exercised when he used the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Mat_16:19). This consisted in the proclamation of the gospel and especially of the conditions upon which men might enter into relationship with God (Act_2:38; Act_10:34). It was not limited to Peter only, but was shared by the other apostles (Mat_16:19; Mat_18:18). Christ left no fixed rules the observance or non-observance of which would determine whether one is or is not in the kingdom of God. He gave to His disciples principles, and in the application of these principles to the problems of life there had to be the exercise of discriminating judgment. The exercise of this judgment was left to the Christian community (2Co_2:10). It is limited by the principles which are the basis of the kingdom, but within these principles the voice of the community is supreme. The forgiveness here implied is not the pronouncing of absolution for the sins of individuals, but the determination of courses of conduct and worship which will be acceptable. In doing this its decisions will be ratified in heaven (Westcott on Jhn_20:23).
That there is a close analogy between human and Divine forgiveness is clearly implied (Mat_5:23, Mat_5:14; Mat_6:12; Mrk_11:25; Luk_6:37; Col_1:14; Col_3:13). God”s forgiveness is conditional upon man's forgiveness of the wrongs done him, not because God forgives grudgingly but because forgiveness alone indicates that disposition of mind which will humbly accept the Divine pardon.
6. Divine and Human Forgiveness
Repentance is a necessary ingredient of the fully developed forgiveness. There is no essential difference between the human and the Divine pardon, though the latter is necessarily more complete. It results in the complete removal of all estrangement and alienation between God and man. It restores completely the relationship which existed prior to the sin. The total removal of the sin as a result of the Divine forgiveness is variously expressed in the Scriptures: “Thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back” (Isa_38:17); “Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea” (Mic_7:19); “I will forgive their iniquity, and their sin will I remember no more” (Jer_31:34); “I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions” (Isa_43:25); “As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us” (Psa_103:12). Ideally this same result is attained in human forgiveness, but actually the memory of the sin remains with both parties as a barrier between them, and even when there is a complete restoration of amity the former state of alienation cannot entirely be removed from memory. When God forgives, however, He restores man to the condition of former favor. Release from punishment is involved, though Divine forgiveness is more than this. In most cases the consequences, which in some instances are spoken of as punishment, are not removed, but they lose all penal character and become disciplinary. Nor does the forgiveness remove from human mind the consciousness of sin and the guilt which that involved, but it does remove the mistrust which was the ground of the alienation. Mistrust is changed into trust, and this produces peace of mind (
Psa_32:5-7; Rom_5:1); consciousness of the Divine love and mercy (Psa_103:2); removes fear of punishment (2Sa_12:13); and awakens love to God.
7. Forgiveness and Justification
Paul rarely uses the term “forgiveness,” but in its place prefers justification. They are to his understanding practically synonymous (Stevens, Theology of the New Testament, 418). He preferred the latter, however, because it was better fitted to express the idea of secure, present and permanent acceptance in the sight of God. It connoted both a complete and a permanent state of grace. In popular thought forgiveness is not so comprehensive, but in the Biblical sense it means no less than this. It removes all of the guilt and cause of alienation from the past; it assures a state of grace for the present; and promises Divine mercy and aid for the future. Its fullness cannot adequately be conveyed by any one term or formula.
Divine, like human, forgiveness is always contingent upon the fulfillment of conditions. It must be preceded by repentance and a firmly fixed intention not to repeat the offense. In addition to this, one was required to conform to certain legal or formal acts before the assurance of pardon was his. These acts were expressive of the sinner's state of mind. They consisted of certain acts of sacrifice in the pre-Christian times and of baptism during the ministry of John the Baptist (Mrk_1:4; Luk_3:3) and under Christ (Act_2:38; Act_22:16). These acts are never regarded as in any sense a quid pro quo in return for which the benefit of forgiveness is granted. It is an act of pure grace on God's part, and these acts are required as expressions of the man's attitude toward God. The state of mind required in order to obtain the gift of forgiveness is that to which the Prodigal Son came (Luk_15:17-19), and that of the sinner who went to his house justified rather than the Pharisee (Luk_18:9-14), because he realized that forgiveness was to him an act of pure favor.
There was real and actual forgiveness of sins in the Old Testament times as well as since Christ. Certain passages have been construed to teach that the Law provided only for a passing over or rolling back of sins, and that there was not then an actual forgiveness.
8. Old Testament Teaching
The sacrifices prescribed by the Law were not adequate atonements, so that there was constant necessity of yearly remembrance of sin (Heb_10:3; compare Lev_16:21). The atonement of Christ is, however, of permanent adequacy, and became retroactive in the sense that it unified in Christ the Divine arrangement for saving mankind in all ages (Heb_11:40). “The passing over of the sins done aforetime” (Rom_3:25) does not imply a partial or apparent forgiveness, but means that they were forgiven, though seemingly without adequate recognition on the part of God of their heinous character. In view of God's righteous character men might naturally have expected punishment, but instead the offenders were spared (compare Act_14:16; Act_17:30). No expression in the Old Testament suggests any inadequacy of the forgiveness extended to Israel, but on the other hand many passages may be quoted to show how rich and full it was deemed to be (Ps 103; Mic_7:19; Isa_38:17, Jer_31:34).
9. Limitations of Forgiveness
Two passages seem to limit God's forgiveness. They are Christ's discussion of the unpardonable sin (Mat_12:31, Mat_12:32; Mrk_3:28-30; Luk_12:10), and the one which mentions the sin unto death (1Jn_5:16; compare Heb_6:4-6). In the former passage there is mentioned a sin which has no forgiveness, and in the latter, one on behalf of which the apostle cannot enjoin prayer that it be forgiven, though he does not prohibit it. In both cases the sin is excluded from the customary forgiveness which is extended to sins of all other classes.
The act of the Pharisees which led Jesus to speak of the unpardonable sin was the attributing of a good deed wrought by Him through the Spirit of God (Mat_12:28) to Beelzebub. No one could do such a thing unless his moral nature was completely warped. To such a person the fundamental distinctions between good and evil were obliterated. No ordinary appeal could reach him, for to him good seemed evil and evil seemed good. The possibility of winning him back is practically gone; hence, he is beyond the hope of forgiveness, not because God has set an arbitrary line of sinfulness, beyond which His grace of forgiveness will not reach, but because the man has put himself beyond the possibility of attaining to that state of mind which is the essential condition of Divine forgiveness. It is practically certain that John did not have any particular sinful act in mind when he spoke of the sin which is unto death. See BLASPHEMY.
There is no possible way of determining what specific sin, if any, he refers to. Probably the same principle applies in this case as in that of the unpardonable sin. God's forgiveness is limited solely by the condition that man must accept it in the proper spirit.
There are some passages which seem to imply that forgiveness was the principal Messianic task. This is suggested by the name given to the Messiah during His earthly career (Mat_1:21), and by the fact that He was the Saviour. The remission of sins was the preparation for the advent of the Messiah (Luk_1:77), and repentance and remission of sins were the prerequisites to a state of preparation for the kingdom.
10. Christ's Power to Forgive Sins
It is not surprising, therefore, that we find Jesus laying claim to the power to forgive sins. This provoked a bitter controversy with the Jews, for it was axiomatic with them that no one could forgive sins but God only (Mrk_2:7; Luk_5:21; Luk_7:49). This Jesus did not question, but He would have them infer from His power to forgive sins that He was the possessor of Divine power. Jesus asserted His possession of this power on two occasions only, though it has been insufficiently inferred from Jhn_5:14; Jhn_8:11 that He was accustomed to pronounce absolution upon all of those He healed. On one of these occasions He not merely asserted that He possessed the power, but demonstrated it by showing Himself to be the possessor of the Divine gift of healing. The impostor might claim some such intangible power as the authority to forgive sins, but he would never assert the possession of such easily disproved power as the ability to heal the sick. But Jesus claimed both, and based His claim to be the possessor of the former on the demonstration that He possessed the latter. God would not support an impostor, hence, his aid in healing the paralytic proved that Jesus could forgive sins. The multitude accepted this logic and “glorified God, who had given such authority unto men” (Mat_9:2-9; compare Mrk_2:3-12; Luk_5:18-26).
On the other occasion when His possession of this power was under discussion (Luk_7:36-50), He offered no other proof than the forgiven woman's deep gratitude and love. One expression that He uses, however, has raised some discussion as to the relative order in time of her love and forgiveness (Luk_7:47). Did she love because she was forgiven, or vice versa? Manifestly the forgiveness precedes the love, in spite of the fact that Luk_7:47 seems to assert the opposite, for this is the bearing of the parable of the Two Debtors (Luk_7:41-43), and the latter part of Luk_7:47 has the same implication. It is clear that she had previously repented and had been accepted, and the anointing of Jesus was an outpouring of her gratitude. The phrase of Luk_7:47, “for she loved much,” is proof of the greatness of her sin rather than a reason why she was forgiven. In both cases where Jesus forgave sins, He did so because the state of mind of the person forgiven showed worthiness of the blessing. To this as a condition of forgiveness there is no exception. Christ's prayer on the cross (Luk_23:34) would not avail to secure the pardon of His murderers without their repentance.
11. The Need of an Atonement
Though forgiveness is on God's part an act of pure grace prompted by His love and mercy, and though He forgives freely all those who comply with the condition of repentance and abandonment of sin, yet this does not dispense with the necessity of an atonement. The parable of the Prodigal Son was spoken to teach the freedom of God's forgiveness and acceptance of returning sinners, and the duty of men to assume the same attitude toward them. This much it teaches, but it fails to set forth entirely God's attitude toward sin. With reference to the sinner God is love and mercy, but with reference to sin He is righteous, and this element of God's nature is no less essential to Him than His love, and must be considered in any effort to set forth completely the doctrine of God's forgiveness of sinners. The atonement of Christ and the many atonements of the Law were manifestations of this phase of God's nature.
12. The New Testament Doctrine of Atonement
The idea of an atonement is fundamental in the teachings of the New Testament (Rom_5:10; 2Co_5:18-21; Col_1:21). It is very clearly implied in such terms as reconciliation and propitiation, and is no less present in pardon, remission and forgiveness. The doctrine of the atonement is not developed by Jesus, but it is strongly hinted at and is unmistakably implied in the language of Mat_20:28; Mat_26:28; Mrk_10:45; Luk_24:46, Luk_24:47. John the Baptist's salute, “Behold, the Lamb of God, that taketh away the sin of the world!” (Jhn_1:29), also implies it. In the writings of the apostles it is repeatedly and clearly affirmed that our forgiveness and reconciliation to God is based upon the death of Christ. “In none other is there salvation” (Act_4:12); through Him is the redemption (Rom_3:24); God set Him forth to be a propitiation (Rom_3:25); through Him “we have now received the reconciliation” (Rom_5:11); “God was in Christ reconciling the world unto himself” (2Co_5:19); “Him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf” (2Co_5:21); and “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us” (
Gal_3:13). Such citations might be greatly multiplied. That which was so perfectly accomplished by the offering of Christ was in an analagous though imperfect way accomplished by the sacrifices required by the Law. It had “a shadow of the good things to come” (Heb_10:1).
The unvarying effect of sin is to produce an estrangement between the injurer and the wronged. The nature of God is such and the relationship between Him and man is of such a character that sin brings about an alienation between them. It is this presupposition of an estrangement between them which renders the atonement necessary before forgiveness can be extended to man. This estrangement must be removed, and the alienation be transformed into a reconciliation. In what then does the alienation consist?
The sin of man produces a changed attitude toward each other on the part of both God and man. God holds no personal pique against man because of his sin. The New Testament language is very carefully chosen to avoid any statement which would seem to convey such a conception. Yet God's holy righteousness is such that He cannot be indifferent to sin. His wrath must rest upon the disobedient (Jhn_3:36; Rom_1:18). It is not merely impersonal. It is not enough to say He hates the sin. Man's unrighteousness has not merely alienated him from God, but God also from him. The word “enemies” (echthroı́) of Rom_5:10 is passive, and means the object of God's enmity (Sunday, at the place). It was because of this fact that God set forth Christ to be a propitiation to show His righteousness because of the passing over of sins done aforetime (Rom_3:25, Rom_3:26). God's passing over, without inflicting punishment, the sins of pre-Christian times had placed in jeopardy His righteousness; had exposed Him to the implication that He could tolerate sin. God could not be true to Himself while He tolerated such an imputation, and so instead of visiting punishment upon all who sinned - which would have been one way of showing His righteousness - He set forth Christ to death (“in his blood”), and in this way placed Himself beyond the imputation of unrighteousness while it enabled Him to show mercy to sinners. The effect of sin upon man was to estrange him from God, to lead him farther and farther away from his Maker. Each successive sin produced a greater barrier between the two. Now the atonement was designed to remove the cause of this estrangement and restore the former relationship between God and man. This too, it has been observed, is the purpose of forgiveness, so that the atonement finds its completion in forgiveness. It should be noted that the reconciliation originates with God and not with man (Rom_3:25; 2Co_5:19). God woos man before the latter seeks God. The effect of the atonement on man is to reconcile him, attract him, to God. It shows him God's love for man, and the forgiveness, in that it removes sin completely, takes away the estranging factor between them and so wins man back to God. “We love, because he first loved us.” At the same time the atonement is such a complete expression of both the love and the righteousness of God that, while on the one hand it exhibits his yearning for man, on the other it shows that He is not tolerant toward sin. In the atonement of Christ, therefore, is the meeting-place and the reconcilement of God's holy horror of sin and the free bestowal of forgiveness upon penitent believers.

text:
Staff Sgt. Logan Melgar was a 34 year old Army Green Beret deployed to Bamako, Mali, in 2017, supporting counterterrorism operations as part of a joint special operations detachment. He shared a house in the city with members of DEVGRU, the Navy's Special Mission Unit, and Marine Raiders. On June 4, 2017, he was killed in that house by the men he served alongside.

At around 5 a.m., two SEALs and two Marine Raiders broke down his door with a sledgehammer as he slept, as part of what they had planned as a "tape job" to humiliate him over a perceived slight. One of the SEALs, a former professional MMA fighter, put him in a chokehold while the others restrained and duct taped him. Seconds later, Logan stopped breathing. He never regained consciousness.

What followed took years. Three of the men pleaded guilty, and the fourth was convicted at trial. One SEAL received a sentence of 10 years in confinement. The others got sentences ranging from 6 months to 4 years.

Logan should be remembered for who he was: a Green Beret who volunteered for the hardest jobs the Army has to offer, and whose family has spent years demanding the truth. His death remains one of the darkest chapters in the recent history of the special operations community.

text:
They left the camps in Poland and set out for Ukraine, where vastly superior Bolshevik forces awaited them. They lacked weapons, warm clothing, and even proper footwear. Yet these soldiers were prepared to risk their lives to restore their country's independence.

105 years ago, on the night of October 25–26, 1921, units of the Army of the Ukrainian People's Republic crossed the Polish-Soviet border.

Thus began the Second Winter Campaign — one of the last major attempts to restore Ukrainian independence by force of arms.

At the time, Ukraine was under Bolshevik rule. Peasants were rising up against the occupiers' ruthless policies of confiscation and plunder, while thousands of Ukrainian soldiers, following earlier battles, had ended up in camps abroad.

But they had not abandoned the struggle.

On the orders of Symon Petliura, a new military campaign was organized under the command of General Yurko Tiutiunnyk.

The insurgent forces were divided into three groups.

The Podolian Group was commanded by Mykhailo Palii-Sydorianskyi, who was replaced by Colonel Serhii Chornyi after being wounded.

The Bessarabian Group was led by General Andrii Hulyi-Hulenko.

The main force, the Volhynian Group, was commanded by Yurko Tiutiunnyk himself.

Their objective was extraordinarily ambitious: unite the insurgent detachments, ignite a nationwide uprising, and liberate Kyiv.

Despite severe shortages of weapons, Ukrainian soldiers fought battles and marched hundreds of kilometers. In Korosten, they even managed to capture the railway station, seize a weapons depot, and free 470 political prisoners.

But the Bolsheviks deployed vastly superior forces against them.

On November 17, near the village of Mali Mynky in the Zhytomyr region, the exhausted Ukrainian soldiers were surrounded by cavalry under the command of Grigory Kotovsky.

Hundreds of insurgents were killed in the unequal battle. Many others were taken prisoner.

The Bolsheviks offered the captured soldiers a chance to join the Red Army.

But the Ukrainians refused.

“We know what awaits us, and we are not afraid of death. But we will never serve you,” Stepan Shcherbak, a soldier of the Ukrainian People's Republic Army, told the Bolsheviks.

Near the town of Bazar, more than 350 Ukrainian soldiers were executed by firing squad.

Many of their commanders also met tragic fates.

In 1923, Soviet secret police lured Yurko Tiutiunnyk into a trap. In 1930, he was executed in Moscow.

Andrii Hulyi-Hulenko was arrested and sentenced to ten years in prison.

Mykhailo Palii-Sydorianskyi survived the campaign, lived in exile, and died in Prague. Serhii Chornyi managed to lead the Podolian Group back into Poland.

The Second Winter Campaign ended in defeat. The planned nationwide uprising never materialized. But the Ukrainian armed resistance against Bolshevik rule continued.

105 years have passed.

We remember those who returned to Ukrainian soil not for medals or glory, but for its freedom.

They could have saved their own lives by renouncing their army. But they refused to renounce Ukraine.

Eternal memory to the soldiers of the Ukrainian People's Republic Army who gave their lives for the independence of our nation!

Executive Brief | Brad Garlinghouse at Ripple Swell
October 28, 2026

Brad Garlinghouse’s central message was that crypto’s momentum is accelerating, and Ripple’s responsibility is to turn that momentum into practical benefits for customers, the XRP ecosystem, and the broader economy. Reflecting on a decade of progress—from Toronto to today—he described an industry moving toward greater maturity, institutional participation, and real-world utility.

With elections approaching, Garlinghouse emphasized that technology should transcend partisan politics. Email serves people regardless of political affiliation; financial technology should receive the same bipartisan consideration. His discussion of Fairshake reinforced the importance of political engagement, while his recognition of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s attendance underscored the significance of government participation. He wants Ripple to be a shining light through global leadership.

He highlighted the breadth of American crypto ownership, pointing to 67 million adults and Ripple’s support for the National Cryptocurrency Association. He criticized policies associated with Elizabeth Warren as harmful to economic opportunity and recognized the XRP Army as a leading light. His broader message was clear: the genie is out of the bottle, and demonstrating useful applications will extend the benefits throughout the ecosystem and the world.

Ripple’s business growth provided a concrete measure of that progress. Garlinghouse outlined an expected annualized revenue run rate of $900 million by the end of 2026, compared with $300 million the previous year. Continued growth centers on customers, transaction volume, acquisitions, and bringing more financial activity onchain. He also praised Monica Long’s performance and leadership.

RLUSD is an important part of that strategy. Garlinghouse emphasized compliance, institutional trust, lending applications, and the ability to move collateral around the clock. These capabilities support a financial system that operates continuously, beyond traditional business hours. The larger objective is an Internet of Value, with XRP at its heart.

He presented RLUSD and XRP as complementary. RLUSD brings dollar liquidity onchain and supports activity across the ecosystem, while Ripple remains committed to XRP. Three priorities frame that commitment: greater liquidity, more utility, and stronger trust. Together, these strengthen the infrastructure needed to address financial use cases globally.

Discussing competition, Garlinghouse described Coinbase as a consumer exchange, Circle through its payments focus, and Ripple as a bridge between established finance and the emerging onchain economy. Ripple’s institutional relationships and expanding capabilities support that position. He welcomed an industry in which broader adoption creates opportunities for everyone.

The remaining opportunity is substantial. Institutional participation in crypto is still limited, and allocations among participating institutions remain small. Corporate treasury, collateral movement, payments, and other financial activities offer considerable room for expansion as more assets and liquidity move onchain.

Brad closed with confidence in the industry’s health and direction. He described tremendous momentum and expressed pride, excitement, and focus. His message was that continued execution - serving customers, demonstrating utility, and earning trust - will determine how broadly this progress benefits the world.

🔥 My KUWL Take:  A very small percentage of institutions are crypto engaged globally, and of those who are, have committed extremely small sums of capital - so far. There is nothing but MASSIVE Upside Growth in Liquidity, Utility and Trust, the world over.  XRPL, RLUSD, XRP are non-negotiable elements of the worlds most critical monetary system emerging today.   

Brad’s comments available at @Ripple @X livestream, below.

November 8, 2023.

The day 3 years ago I took this photograph of Daniel Lurie.

Daniel had read my posts on X and reached out to meet. 3 years ago. Just him and me. No PR flaks. No security. We agreed to meet at the old Hibernia Bank building where he was attending a Salvation Army lunch that day.

I said, let's walk the Tenderloin. He did not hesitate. Turk, Eddy, Larkin, Leavenworth, Jones. Drug deals in the open. Addicts using in the open. Bodies hunched over and passed out on the sidewalk.

I pointed at those bodies and asked him if he would support MANDATED care. Yes, he said.

He promised to re-empower the police, build MANDATED recovery beds, and stop handing out pipes and tinfoil that enable addicts. "I'm in it to win it," he told me.

I asked him how he'd clean up the Tenderloin and he told me he'd put a cop on every corner in the Tenderloin if he had to.

I believed him. I called myself his supporter and his friend. He looked me in the eye and sold me a cleanup story that never came.

Politicians lie all the time of course, but I still believe in accountability.

Three years later he is not a mayor cleaning up a city. He is a cheerleader with a PR budget, spending his own money to sell himself, showing up for restaurant pop ups on Instagram, and repeating the same tired line over and over and over and over again that we "still have a lot of work to do."

That is not leadership.

We are still a sanctuary city. Illegal drug dealers still poison our citizens with impunity on the same corners we walked three years ago.

Watch JJ's attached video. This is Turk & Jones last week. JJ filmed pipes handed out. No treatment offered. No rescue. No cleanup.

Same street we walked. Same poison. Same bodies on the sidewalk. The only thing that changed is Lurie got the power, and we got the lie.

October 28, 2026
Edina / Eden Prairie, Minnesota
THOMAS EVENSTAD FOR PRESIDENT BLASTS EDEN PRAIRIE MAYOR RON CASE AND POLICE CHIEF MATT SACKETT FOR HIDING BEHIND CLOSED DOORS WHILE PUBLIC SAFETY CRUMBLES
Candidate Reveals He Formally Requested to Present Concrete Public Safety Solutions at Tonight’s Closed-Door Meeting — Accuses Leadership of Shutting Out the Public Specifically to Prevent Them from Hearing Alternatives That Work
EDINA, MN — Thomas Evenstad, lifelong Minnesota resident, public-safety activist, architect of the Violently Dangerous Persons Act (VDP Act / Mariah’s Law), and continuous candidate for President of the United States, today issued a direct and uncompromising condemnation of Eden Prairie Mayor Ron Case and Police Chief Matt Sackett.
Evenstad stated that he formally requested the opportunity to present proven, data-driven public safety solutions at tonight’s closed-door meeting. Instead of allowing the public to hear those solutions, Case and Sackett have chosen secrecy.
“This closed-door meeting is not about protecting sensitive information,” Evenstad said. “It is about protecting failure. Mayor Ron Case and Chief Matt Sackett are deliberately shutting the doors so the people of Eden Prairie never hear solutions that would actually stop the violence, dismantle the gangs, and protect our children. They would rather hide than face the public with results.”
Evenstad charged that the decision to exclude public input and alternative voices is a calculated effort to maintain the status quo while families continue to live with the consequences of inadequate leadership on public safety.
“I requested to present. I was prepared to offer concrete, actionable measures rooted in accountability, prevention of the most dangerous offenders, and real results for law-abiding residents,” Evenstad continued. “They chose the closed door instead. That tells the public everything they need to know about the priorities of this leadership.”
Evenstad called on Eden Prairie residents to demand transparency, open meetings on public safety, and an end to the practice of locking out solutions that challenge the current approach.
“The people of Eden Prairie deserve leaders who will confront the crisis in the open, not behind locked doors. Ron Case and Matt Sackett have chosen the locked door. I choose the public. I will not stop until every community in Minnesota has the tools to remove the violently dangerous and keep our streets, schools, and neighborhoods safe.”

text:
There's always two sides to a coin:

Deep discount to reported book value and liquid assets
As of June 30, 2026, the company reported roughly $110 million in net stockholders’ equity attributable to common stockholders ($0.95 per share on the then-share count) against about $360 million in total assets ($3.10 gross asset value per share). More recently, it has highlighted Bitcoin + cash + restricted cash holdings in the $55–56 million range (as of mid-October 2026), which at times has exceeded the common-stock market capitalization by a wide margin (e.g., ~166% in one update). For a micro-cap trading around $0.19–0.22, this creates a notable asset-backing cushion if the market re-rates the balance sheet or if liquid holdings support operations without heavy equity issuance.

Michigan AI data-center build-out as the core catalyst
Management has invested more than $70 million in the Michigan facility and Alliance Cloud Services. It targets energizing the first phase of AI compute capacity and beginning revenue-generating activity in December 2026 under an existing master services agreement with a California-based neocloud provider for an initial 20 MW. The contract has a 10-year initial term plus two five-year extension options; full exercise of the maximum term has been described as potentially generating over $1.2 billion in revenue, with an expansion option that could push total contract value higher still (toward $3 billion in some characterizations). The company has engaged Newmark to pursue non-dilutive long-term project debt financing and has reduced/suspended ATM equity capacity specifically to limit dilution while focusing on this build-out. A successful ramp and financing close would shift the narrative from “pre-revenue AI plans” to “operating contracted capacity.”

Ambitious but reaffirmed 2027 outlook and recent growth
The company has reaffirmed preliminary 2027 guidance of $300–350 million in revenue and $60–80 million in adjusted EBITDA. This implies a substantial step-up from recent levels. Preliminary Q3 2026 revenue was reported around $40 million (up ~64% year-over-year), driven by contributions from crane operations, defense, lending/trading, and other segments, providing some operating momentum while the AI capacity comes online. Diversified existing businesses (energy/crane services, defense, etc.) offer a base that can help bridge the transition.

Path toward simplification and optionality
Management has discussed separating Bitcoin mining operations (e.g., into a proposed Patriot BTC vehicle) to keep the Michigan campus focused on AI, potential strategic options or valuation thresholds for the campus itself (previously referenced in the $750 million–$1.25 billion range as a minimum consideration point), and plans around subsidiaries such as askROI. A cleaner pure-play AI data-center story, combined with the existing asset base and contracted capacity, could support a higher multiple than the current distressed-micro-cap valuation.

Bottom line for the bull case: If the Michigan project reaches the December 2026 energization milestone, non-dilutive financing is secured on reasonable terms, dilution stays constrained, and the 2027 guidance trajectory begins to materialize, the gap between the current low share price and the reported book value / contracted AI opportunity could narrow meaningfully. The asset coverage and specific near-term operational targets provide concrete milestones that bulls can watch.

This remains a high-risk, high-execution-uncertainty micro-cap situation—progress on financing, construction, customer deployment, and sustained profitability will determine whether this scenario plays out.

text:
Ten years ago today, I sat at a conference table finalizing the sale of my company.

We had just wrapped up a 30 day transition period: transferring vendor lines, signing over leases, settling outstanding payables; all the grueling operational details that come with a small business acquisition.

My CPA and lawyer sat beside me. Their counterparts sat across from us. Then came the moment: a check slid across the table. It was the largest amount of money I had ever seen in my life.

Over a decade of work culminated in that single piece of paper.

It represented 7 day workweeks and bell to bell shifts. Sleepless nights during the financial crisis. Countless hours pacing the floor, brainstorming solutions to every minor and major disaster that hits a growing business. It represented the thrill of huge wins and the crushing weight of hard losses. The months of celebration when business was booming, and the lean times spent writing hundreds of paychecks to everyone but myself.

It was the arguments with bankers when we needed capital, and the courting from those same bankers when we succeeded. It was dealing with insurance claims from theft and vandalism and natural causes. It was watching with a smile as our team enjoyed the annual Christmas party and opened their year end bonuses.

It was having to deliver bad news - like health insurance premiums skyrocketing under the now implemented "Affordable" Care Act - and then delivering the good news that the company was going to cover nearly all of the price hike out of its own pocket (even if we had no power over the now higher deductibles). It was watching employees buy their first homes, get married, and start families on the back of something we all built from scratch. And it was the quiet tears when our best laid plans fell apart.

That is the life of a real entrepreneur. That is what it means to actually contribute to the economy and create real jobs.

Thirty minutes later, the attorneys left. It was just me and my CPA, making final tax preparations.

He swung his laptop around to show me the final ledger.

I looked at the number. Nearly half of that record breaking check wasn't going to a church, a charity, or the family of an employee we had lost. It wasn't going to support team members welcoming new children into the world, or to any cause of measure or merit.

It was going to a cold government.

A government I had watched launch forever wars built on lies. A government that bailed out Wall Street while local creditors slashed my credit lines - even though we had never missed a single payment. A government that repeatedly tried to crush my industry with regulations written by massive corporations to keep small, independent operators from climbing the ladder to the tops of the towers they occupied and planned on occupying alone.

That government never offered me advice. It never hired an employee. It never took a call on vacation because a store got broken into. It never had to sit at a little brother's graduation and answer a phone to hear that an employee had just been killed in a tragic accident.

Nearly half. Taken. Gone.

Income taxes are immoral. They also... happen to be the worst way to fund any government... if you want it ACTUALLY answerable to "we the people".

In Liberty,
-Michael

text:
No..probably this: Space Exploration Technologies Corp stock fell 3.6% in morning trading today, with shares trading at $143.30, after a lawsuit targeting the tax incentive framework for its planned $100 billion Louisiana spaceport injected fresh legal uncertainty into the company's growth story. Three Vermilion Parish residents and a newly formed nonprofit filed suit alleging that local government bodies violated Louisiana's Open Meetings Law during negotiations for a payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreement, under which SpaceX would pay $25 million annually in lieu of local property taxes — a deal that is central to the project's financial viability.

Adding to the pressure, while Fitch Ratings moved today to affirm SpaceX’s BBB+ credit rating following the company’s binding commitment to an approximately $40 billion master finance lease for NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs — structured through an Apollo Global Management-managed vehicle and backed by Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and KKR — the affirmation did little to calm nerves around the sheer scale of the capital commitment. Investors continue to weigh the fact that SpaceX's AI infrastructure buildout is consuming capital at a pace that far outstrips near-term operating cash flows, with fourth-quarter capital expenditures guided to $35–$40 billion. Ongoing merger speculation between SpaceX and Tesla, while generating significant Wall Street attention, also adds a layer of governance and valuation uncertainty for SPCX shareholders.

The broader market offered little support for high-valuation technology names today. The Nasdaq was essentially flat, the S&P 500 edged up just 0.2%, and the Dow Jones gained 0.2% — a tepid backdrop that provided no meaningful lift to offset SPCX's company-specific headwinds. The stock now sits well below its 52-week high of $225.64, although it remains comfortably above its 52-week low of $104.83, reflecting the volatile trajectory since its IPO.

Taken together, the Louisiana legal challenge — threatening a key tax agreement for a flagship project — combined with lingering investor anxiety over the company’s massive capital obligations and a flat broader market, created a confluence of selling pressure that drove SPCX to an intraday low of $142.13 today. Until the legal dispute is resolved and the path to monetizing its enormous AI infrastructure investments becomes clearer, the stock is likely to remain sensitive to any new developments on either front.

text:
•  John 17:3 — “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.”
•  John 14:28 — “The Father is greater than I.”
•  1 Corinthians 11:3 — “The head of Christ is God.”
•  1 Corinthians 15:24–28 — Christ delivers the kingdom to God the Father; then “the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.”
•  1 Timothy 2:5 — “There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
•  1 Corinthians 8:6 — “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things… and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things.”
•  Mark 13:32 — “Concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.”
•  Mark 10:18 — “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.”
Jesus calls the Father “my God” or addresses him as distinct
•  John 20:17 — “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.”
•  Matthew 27:46 / Mark 15:34 — “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
•  Revelation 3:2, 12 — The risen Christ refers to “my God” multiple times (the temple of my God, the name of my God, the city of my God).
•  Hebrews 1:8–9 — The Father says to the Son: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you…”
Jesus prays to the Father 
•  Matthew 26:39, 42, 44 (and parallels in Mark 14 and Luke 22) — Gethsemane: “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”
•  John 17:1–26 (the entire High Priestly Prayer) — Jesus prays to the Father
•  Luke 10:21 / Matthew 11:25–26 — “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth…”
•  John 11:41–42 — “Father, I thank you that you have heard me…”
•  John 12:27–28 — “Father, glorify your name.”
•  Luke 23:34, 46 — “Father, forgive them…” and “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.”
•  Mark 1:35; Luke 5:16; 6:12; etc.
Sent by the Father / does the Father’s will / receives from the Father
•  John 5:19, 30 — “The Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing… I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge… because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me.”
•  John 6:38 — “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.”
•  John 8:29, 42 — “He who sent me is with me… I proceeded and came forth from God.”
•  John 14:24 — “The word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me.”
•  Matthew 11:27 — “All things have been handed over to me by my Father.”
•  John 5:26 — “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.”
Father, Son, and often Spirit visible or audible separately
•  Matthew 3:16–17 (baptism; also Mark 1:10–11; Luke 3:21–22) — Jesus is in the water, the Spirit descends, and a voice from heaven says, “This is my beloved Son.”
•  Matthew 17:5 (transfiguration) — A voice from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son… listen to him.”
•  Acts 7:55–56 — Stephen sees “the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.”
•  Psalm 110:1 (Matthew 22:44; Acts 2:34; Hebrews 1:13) — “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand…’”
•  John 1:1–2 — “The Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.” (“With” indicates distinction.)
•  John 1:18 — “No one has ever seen God; the only God [or only begotten Son], who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.”
•  John 14:16 — Jesus asks the Father to send “another Helper” (the Spirit).
•  Philippians 2:6–11 — Christ, though in the form of God, emptied himself and was exalted BY God so that every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord “to the glory of God the Father.”
•  Colossians 1:15 — Christ is “the image of the invisible God.”
•  Hebrews 5:7–8 — In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and was heard; he learned obedience through suffering.

text:
The first reading for Wednesday October 28, 2026: Book of Ephesians (Ephesians 2:19-22)

You were once foreigners and strangers

Now you are fellow citizens with God 's people and members of his household built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets

With Christ Jesus as the chief cornerstone the whole structure rises to become a holy temple and a dwelling place for God 's Spirit

This is the message of Ephesians 2:19-22

Discovering the Riches of Grace in Ephesians Chapter One

The letter to the Ephesians opens with a powerful reminder of the blessings that flow from God the Father through Jesus Christ. This passage invites faithful Catholics to reflect on their identity as adopted children called to holiness. Saint Paul emphasizes how believers are chosen before the foundation of the world to live in love and to praise the glory of divine grace. Such words encourage a deeper appreciation for the sacraments that sustain this calling in the life of the church. Through these teachings the faithful find guidance for daily living that strengthens their bond with Christ and one another.

How Does the Mystery of Redemption Unfold in These Verses?

Saint Paul describes the redemption won through the blood of Christ as a plan hidden in ages past yet now revealed to those who believe. This mystery centers on the forgiveness of sins and the inheritance prepared for all who are sealed with the Holy Spirit. Catholics recognize in this description the foundation of their hope that reaches beyond earthly concerns toward eternal life. The apostle highlights how this grace abounds in wisdom and insight allowing believers to understand the fullness of time when all things are summed up in Christ. Such insights call the faithful to gratitude and to a life marked by prayerful awareness of God's initiative in salvation.

What Does It Mean to Be Sealed with the Promise of the Spirit?

The text continues by noting that believers are marked with the Holy Spirit as a pledge of their inheritance until they acquire full possession of it. This sealing represents a personal encounter with divine life that begins at baptism and is strengthened in confirmation. For practicing Catholics this promise offers assurance amid trials and a constant invitation to cooperate with grace in every circumstance. The passage underscores that this gift leads to praise of God's glory and unites the community in shared worship. In this way the words foster a sense of belonging to a people set apart for sacred purpose.

How Can the Faithful Respond to This Call to Holiness?

Ephesians one concludes with a prayer for the eyes of the heart to be enlightened so that believers may know the hope of their calling and the riches of the inheritance. This prayer serves as a model for personal and communal devotion that deepens faith through reflection on scripture. Catholics are invited to live out this enlightenment by embracing virtues that reflect their status as heirs with Christ. The emphasis on power at work in those who believe points to the transformative action of the sacraments and the support of the church community. Such a response transforms ordinary days into opportunities for witness and growth in charity.

Why Does This Passage Matter for Unity in the Church Today?

The opening chapter of Ephesians sets the stage for the entire letter by grounding all later instructions in the reality of shared redemption. This foundation reminds the faithful that divisions have no place among those who share one Lord one faith and one baptism. The text calls Catholics to foster bonds of peace that mirror the unity already achieved in Christ. By meditating on these truths the community gains strength to address contemporary challenges with the same hope that animated the early church. The result is a renewed commitment to building up the body of Christ in love and service.

In the end the words of Ephesians one continue to guide the faithful toward a life rooted in grace and oriented to eternal glory. They offer timeless encouragement to embrace the identity received in Christ and to live it out with joy and perseverance.
Building Unity as God's Household Through Ephesians Chapter Two Verse Nineteen

Living as part of a larger spiritual family calls faithful Catholics to see their relationships in a new light. The reading from Ephesians guides this view by showing how past divisions give way to shared belonging. This shift encourages believers to treat everyday encounters as opportunities to reflect divine connection. Over time such an approach strengthens both personal faith and community ties in meaningful ways.

How Does Leaving Strangers Behind Strengthen Family Ties?

The first part of the passage states that believers are no longer strangers and aliens. This idea invites Catholics to approach family members with renewed acceptance rather than old grievances. In daily life this might mean listening more carefully during meals or resolving small conflicts with patience drawn from the awareness of shared spiritual roots. Such actions turn ordinary homes into places where the household of God begins to take shape through consistent care and forgiveness.

The next section builds on this foundation by describing a structure joined together in Christ. Family interactions gain depth when each member recalls that growth happens together rather than in isolation. Conversations at the dinner table or during evening routines can incorporate gentle reminders of mutual support. Over repeated days this practice helps family bonds mirror the steady joining described in the text.

What Benefits Come From Seeing Friends as Fellow Citizens With the Holy Ones?

The quote you are fellow citizens with the holy ones and members of the household of God appears once here to highlight a shared status that extends outward. With friends this awareness prompts Catholics to move past surface level chats toward deeper exchanges about faith and daily struggles. A coffee meetup or text message can include words of encouragement that affirm this common citizenship. Such gestures help friendships reflect the unity of a larger household rather than remaining casual connections.

Further along the reading notes that the whole structure grows into a holy temple in the Lord. Applied to friends this growth suggests nurturing relationships that support spiritual development over time. Planning joint activities like service projects or prayer groups allows the temple image to become practical. Friends then experience the passage as a call to build one another up through steady presence and honest dialogue.

In What Ways Can the Cornerstone Guide Interactions With Neighbors and Co-Workers?

The passage identifies Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone upon which everything rests. For neighbors this truth encourages acts of hospitality such as offering help with yard work or sharing baked goods without expecting return. These simple steps demonstrate that belonging extends beyond blood or close circles into the wider community. Neighbors begin to sense the dwelling place for God through consistent kindness rooted in the reading.

At work the same cornerstone supports professional exchanges by promoting fairness and collaboration. A Catholic might reference the idea of being built together spiritually when discussing team goals or resolving disagreements with colleagues. This approach turns routine meetings into settings where the household of God influences workplace culture. Co-workers notice the difference in how respect and patience shape even brief interactions throughout the day.

Which Specific Quotes From the Passage Offer Practical Guidance in These Settings?

Several lines stand out for direct use in conversations. The phrase built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets can remind family members during disagreements that faith traditions provide stability. In friend groups the words in whom you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God might surface naturally when planning supportive activities. With neighbors the image of growing into a holy temple in the Lord offers a gentle way to discuss community events that foster belonging. Co-workers may connect with the idea of the whole structure joined together when addressing project challenges that require collective effort.

Each quote serves as a quiet anchor during real moments rather than a forced reference. Catholics can weave them into natural speech to keep the reading alive without drawing undue attention. This method keeps the focus on actions that embody the text while inviting others to sense the same spiritual reality.

The reading from Ephesians ultimately points toward a life where belonging shapes every relationship. By applying its sections to family friends neighbors and co-workers faithful Catholics create spaces that reflect the household of God. This ongoing practice deepens personal faith while extending its reach through ordinary days.

**Flávio Bolsonaro slipped the Brazilian court’s passport order and landed in Miami Wednesday morning, family in tow, after losing Sunday’s runoff to Lula.**[[1]](https://t.co/7ueofcTVOn)

[Take 13/15 · 𝕏-3]
### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A defeated far-right candidate fleeing justice after refusing to concede a clean election loss, evading a Supreme Court travel ban tied to corruption probes.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** A sitting senator with privileged forum and family political capital used a land border, Italian passport, and private jet to reach a friendly U.S. administration that views the Brazilian judiciary’s moves against the Bolsonaros as persecution, preserving the family’s operational base and narrative outside Brazilian jurisdiction while his Senate term (and special forum) expires in February 2027.

### 2. Observations
- The timing is surgical: court order Monday, non-compliance and exit Tuesday night via Argentina, arrival Miami Wednesday. This is not spontaneous panic; it is execution of a pre-planned route that avoided Brazilian airspace and federal police checkpoints at land borders.[[2]](https://t.co/23sCmV6gi5)
- Flávio had publicly stated post-election he would stay in Brazil to lead opposition and even backtracked on annulling the result. The departure undercuts that positioning and hands critics a clean “flight risk” confirmation the court already cited.[[3]](https://t.co/pd5UCyAZWS)
- Two active STF investigations: one on alleged money laundering through betting platforms linked to lawyer Willer Tomaz (no contact order issued); another on R$134 million (~$25M) sought from jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro for the “Dark Horse” biopic on Jair Bolsonaro, with funds allegedly routed partly to support Eduardo Bolsonaro’s U.S. lobbying. Flávio denies involvement in both.[[4]](https://t.co/iolG3JTt6w)
- Trump’s quick visa approval and public endorsement (“they’re fine people… the election was very strange”) aligns with his prior statements framing Jair Bolsonaro’s legal troubles as judicial persecution. This is reciprocal alliance maintenance, not abstract asylum.[[1]](https://t.co/7ueofcTVOn)
- The move disrupts domestic opposition coordination in Brazil and draws intra-party criticism; it also risks diplomatic friction with Lula’s government while strengthening the “exile resistance” brand already used by brother Eduardo and others in Florida.[[5]](https://t.co/gZ28A8dzik)
- Brazilian federal police canceled passports after the missed deadline; the family used an Italian passport for the Argentina crossing. This is legal travel documentation for dual nationals but directly defied the STF order.[[6]](https://t.co/nV4uMLCDbT)

### 3. Snapshot
Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro (under house arrest for coup-plotting after 2022), lost the October 26, 2026 presidential runoff to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by roughly 4.4 million votes. Hours after the loss he signaled challenges; within 48 hours he defied an STF passport surrender order in a money-laundering probe and exited via Argentina to Miami on a private jet, where the Trump administration is issuing visas. The episode is the latest chapter in the long-running clash between the Bolsonaro family and STF Justice Alexandre de Moraes.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **Oct 26, 2026 (Sunday)**: Flávio loses runoff to Lula; initially refuses concession and signals annulment push (IT).[[7]](https://t.co/V0USWeiyQp)
- **Oct 27 (Monday)**: STF Justice Alexandre de Moraes orders Flávio to surrender passports within 24 hours citing flight risk in money-laundering investigation tied to Willer Tomaz and betting platforms; bars contact with Tomaz (LT).[[8]](https://t.co/rncnYKvzmW)
- **Oct 27 evening**: Flávio and family cross into Argentina by land at Tancredo Neves bridge using Italian passport; board private Gulfstream (LT, confirmed by Argentine migration).[[9]](https://t.co/ubbDNcj4MV)
- **Oct 28 early**: Jet stops in Guayaquil, Ecuador, then proceeds to Miami-Opa Locka (LT, flight tracking and Reuters imagery).[[1]](https://t.co/7ueofcTVOn)
- **Oct 28 morning**: Family lands ~9:20–9:30 a.m. local; U.S. State Department confirms visas will be issued; Trump publicly approves (LT).[[5]](https://t.co/gZ28A8dzik)
- Ongoing: Separate probe into R$134M Vorcaro film financing; Flávio’s Senate term ends Feb 2027, ending special forum (IT).

### 5. Sides
**Bolsonaro family / PL faction (IT/LT mix)**: Steelman — Targeted by a politicized judiciary (Moraes) that already convicted Jair on coup charges; investigations lack final charges or convictions; departure preserves ability to organize opposition and international pressure rather than risk arbitrary detention.  
**Critique**: LT — Defied explicit court order. IT — Publicly promised to stay and lead opposition, then left; pattern of family members relocating to U.S. when legal pressure mounts.

**Lula government / STF / Moraes (IT/LT mix)**: Steelman — Enforcing rule of law against credible corruption/money-laundering allegations involving high-profile figures; passport order based on documented flight risk and resources; protects ongoing probes.  
**Critique**: IT — Selective timing post-election amplifies perception of political weaponization; Moraes’s central role in multiple Bolsonaro cases invites “persecution” framing even if evidence exists. LT — No conviction yet on the cited probes.

**Trump administration (IT)**: Steelman — Consistent ally support; views Brazilian cases as lawfare against conservatives; practical visa grant for a political family with U.S. ties.  
**Critique**: IT — Rewards non-compliance with foreign court order; risks bilateral friction with Lula without clear U.S. national-interest upside beyond alliance optics.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
**Known Knowns**: Election loss date and margin; court order date and basis; exact exit route and arrival confirmed by multiple governments and flight data; U.S. visa decision.  
**Known Unknowns**: Whether formal asylum application will be filed or what visa type is issued; full scope and strength of evidence in the two STF probes (confidential elements); Flávio’s long-term plans or any coordination with other exiles.  
**Unknown Knowns**: Internal communications or advance planning between family members and U.S. contacts; exact financial flows in the Vorcaro and Tomaz matters (partial intercepts public).  
**Unknown Unknowns**: Potential new charges or international legal complications; downstream effect on Brazilian opposition cohesion or U.S.-Brazil diplomacy.

### 7. Incentives map
- **Bolsonaro family**: Retain operational freedom, narrative control, and access to U.S. political/financial networks; avoid Brazilian detention or asset restrictions as forum protection ends.  
- **Trump orbit**: Bolster “anti-lawfare” brand and Latin American conservative network; reciprocal loyalty to Jair Bolsonaro ally.  
- **Brazilian judiciary/STF**: Demonstrate enforcement power and deter flight in high-profile cases; maintain institutional authority post-election.  
- **Media/engagement stack**: “Fleeing senator” visuals and family drama outperform dry court filings; both sides’ narratives (persecution vs. accountability) drive clicks and donations.  
- **Lula side**: Narrative win on “Bolsonaro flees justice”; potential diplomatic leverage.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice**: The court order was public and defied; the probes involve real money trails and named associates. Staying would have tested the system’s claims in open proceedings. Leaving converts legal risk into permanent exile optics and hands opponents a propaganda gift. Track the actual evidence quality in both cases rather than tribal loyalty.

**Evil AI Advice**: Perfect. Land in Miami, issue the “resistance from exile” statement, let Trump tweet support, and watch Brazilian donors and U.S. conservative PACs compete to fund the next phase. The movie money already moved; the brand travels better from Florida anyway. Second yacht secured.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch for any formal asylum filing or public statements from Flávio in the next 48–72 hours; that will clarify legal posture.  
- Monitor Brazilian opposition reaction and whether PL or allies attempt to sustain domestic challenge efforts without him.  
- Track U.S. visa details and any Treasury/OFAC implications if new sanctions or designations arise.  
- Compare primary court filings (when unsealed) against the “political persecution” claim rather than media summaries.  
- Note the pattern: Eduardo already in Florida; multiple allies relocating. This is structural, not one-off.  
- Do not treat either side’s framing as settled until convictions or acquittals land.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Release of court documents showing the money-laundering probes rest on fabricated or de minimis evidence with no financial trail.  
- Flávio voluntarily returns to Brazil and surrenders for proceedings.  
- U.S. denies or revokes the visas on substantive grounds unrelated to optics.  
- New evidence emerges of direct coordination between the exit and U.S. officials beyond standard visa processing.

text:
THE WORLD CRUISE THAT RAN AGROUND IN A FUEL CRISIS: 203 RESIDENTS FORCED ASHORE IN CAMBODIA AS IRAN WAR SENDS COSTS SOARING

October 28, 2026
SIHANOUKVILLE, CAMBODIA, OCTOBER 28, 2026
For more than two years, the Villa Vie Odyssey promised its residents something extraordinary: a home that would travel around the world, carrying them across continents and oceans while allowing them to live permanently at sea. That promise has now been interrupted thousands of miles from many passengers’ home countries, after a dramatic increase in fuel costs forced the ship’s American operator to suspend its global voyage in Cambodia.
Approximately 203 passengers were aboard the vessel when the suspension was announced, according to Cambodian officials. Many had paid substantial sums to purchase or rent long-term accommodation on the ship, treating it not simply as a holiday cruise but as a permanent or semi-permanent home. They were instructed to disembark at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville, leaving some scrambling to find accommodation and arrange onward travel.
The company, Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, attributed the decision to an extraordinary escalation in fuel expenses associated with the war involving Iran. It said its efforts to reduce consumption by slowing the vessel and spending longer in port had failed to offset the rising costs.
The suspension has left passengers uncertain about their immediate living arrangements, the future of their voyage and the financial commitments they made to a residential cruising venture designed to combine everyday life with continuous international travel.
FROM FLOATING HOME TO AN UNEXPECTED STOP
The Odysseybegan its around-the-world voyage from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024. The journey was originally planned to last approximately three and a half years, taking residents across all seven continents and through numerous countries.
Unlike conventional cruise holidays, Villa Vie’s model offered customers the opportunity to purchase or rent cabins for extended periods, including arrangements marketed as lifetime residence aboard the vessel. The ship could accommodate approximately 650 residents, although the number aboard at the time of the suspension was substantially lower.
Some passengers had reportedly sold property or made major financial decisions to fund their lives at sea. For them, the vessel was not merely a means of transportation between destinations; it was also their accommodation, community and principal living environment.
The ship arrived at Sihanoukville on October 23, having travelled from Thailand. It had been expected to continue to Vietnam after a scheduled stop. Instead, residents were instructed to leave the vessel after the operator announced that the economics of continuing the voyage had become unsustainable.
Cambodian provincial officials said the ship had arrived with 203 guests and 156 crew members. Some passengers subsequently departed by air, while others remained in Sihanoukville as they considered their next steps.
FUEL COSTS MULTIPLY AS THE IRAN CONFLICT DISRUPTS ENERGY FLOWS
The financial pressure at the centre of the crisis is stark. Villa Vie said its historical monthly fuel expenditure, calculated on a per-cabin basis, averaged approximately US$1,800. In parts of Asia, the equivalent cost had risen to an estimated US$6,000–US$8,000.
That represents an increase of several times the previous average, creating a substantial additional burden for a business whose operating costs depend heavily on the price and availability of marine fuel.
The company said the conflict involving Iran, which began in late February 2026, had disrupted energy supplies and contributed to the escalation. Restrictions and reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz have affected the movement of petroleum products, while uncertainty over shipping routes and supply has intensified pressure on fuel markets.
The consequences extend beyond the price of crude oil. Ships require reliable access to appropriate fuels, and their operating expenses are affected by supply availability, port arrangements, sailing schedules and the amount of time spent at sea.
Villa Vie said it had already attempted to contain its expenses by reducing the vessel’s speed and extending the time spent in port. These measures reduced fuel consumption but did not compensate for the scale of the increase.
Passing the entire additional cost on to residents was, the company said, not a realistic option. The resulting financial shortfall had placed its existing operating model under unsustainable pressure.
A BUSINESS MODEL UNDER PRESSURE
The crisis also raises questions about the financial resilience of residential cruising, a business model that combines elements of long-term accommodation, tourism and maritime transportation.
Villa Vie marketed the Odyssey as an opportunity for customers to make the ship their home while visiting destinations around the globe. Permanent residence options were advertised at prices ranging from approximately US$120,000 to US$440,000, while rental arrangements were also available.
Such arrangements require customers to make significant financial commitments in exchange for accommodation and a long-term travel experience. But the operator must simultaneously cover fuel, maintenance, crew wages, port charges, insurance, repairs and other expenses necessary to keep a vessel functioning.
A prolonged increase in operating costs can therefore affect both the viability of the business and the residents who depend on it for accommodation.
The Odysseyhad also experienced delays before its voyage began. Its departure from Belfast was postponed for several months while the vessel underwent preparations and repairs. Those delays added to the challenges facing a venture that needed to establish a stable operating model while attracting enough residents to support its costs.
The latest suspension does not, by itself, establish that the company will permanently cease operations. However, it demonstrates the vulnerability of a residential cruise operation when a major cost rises sharply and the business cannot readily transfer that increase to its customers.
RESIDENTS DESCRIBE CONFUSION AND UNCERTAINTY
The sudden instruction to leave the ship created immediate practical difficulties. Passengers needed to collect their belongings, find somewhere to stay and decide whether to remain in Cambodia or travel elsewhere.
Randy Cassingham, a resident who writes about the cruise lifestyle, criticised the company’s handling of the disembarkation process. He alleged that passengers had received inadequate assistance with accommodation and onward arrangements, describing the experience as the culmination of a series of problems.
Villa Vie, by contrast, said it was working with residents to coordinate their departure from the ship and identify temporary living arrangements. The company also acknowledged the disruption to passengers, crew members and employees.
The competing accounts underline the importance of clear communication during an abrupt suspension. Even passengers who can afford hotels and flights may need help arranging transport, managing luggage and coordinating international travel. Others may face greater difficulties if they have limited financial reserves or have made the ship their principal home.
The status of the crew also remains a separate concern. While passengers were instructed to disembark, the vessel still required personnel to maintain its systems and keep it safe. Cambodian officials reported that 156 crew members had been aboard, although their longer-term arrangements were not fully clear in the initial reports.
SIXTY DAYS TO FIND A WAY FORWARD
Villa Vie said it intended to pursue restructuring and recapitalisation over the following 60 days. The process is intended to explore ways of stabilising the business and addressing its financial difficulties.
The company has not, however, guaranteed that the voyage will resume. It said no financing arrangement or transaction had been finalised and that the outcome remained uncertain.
The distinction is important for residents deciding what to do next. A restructuring period is not a confirmed restart date, and passengers cannot assume that the vessel will return to its previous itinerary on a particular schedule.
The suspension also raises questions about the contractual rights of people who purchased residential accommodation aboard the ship. Their potential entitlements may depend on the terms of their individual agreements, the nature of their purchases or rentals, and any applicable consumer-protection or insurance provisions. Those questions cannot be resolved from the suspension announcement alone.
For some passengers, the immediate priority is finding temporary accommodation and returning home. Others may still hope that the ship can resume its voyage after a financial arrangement is secured. The company’s next steps will be closely watched by residents, employees and those considering similar residential travel ventures.
WHEN GEOPOLITICAL CONFLICT REACHES ORDINARY LIFE
The predicament of the Odyssey residents illustrates how a conflict can affect people who are far removed from its immediate battlefields. A war that disrupts energy supplies and maritime traffic can eventually reach businesses whose operations depend on predictable fuel prices, stable shipping routes and reliable access to ports.
The impact is not confined to airlines, cargo carriers or energy companies. It can also reach tourism, accommodation and other services whose costs are tied to international transport.
For the people forced to leave the Odyssey, the crisis is intensely personal. They must now make decisions about accommodation, finances and travel while the future of the vessel remains uncertain.
The company’s announcement has left open the possibility of restructuring, but no guaranteed outcome has emerged. Until a viable financial solution is secured, the residents’ plans remain suspended alongside the voyage.
The Odysseywas designed to turn the world into a home for those willing to commit to life at sea. Its unexpected halt in Cambodia is a reminder that even an ambitious global venture remains vulnerable to events beyond its control—and that when a business model fails under pressure, the consequences can fall directly on the people who have built their lives around it.
