text:
Beyond Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb: Reengineering the Global Oil Transit System -  The principal strategic conclusion is that the Arabian Peninsula requires an integrated, multi-directional oil export system rather than further dependence on any single maritime passage, coastal terminal or pipeline. The problem cannot be resolved solely by increasing naval protection or expanding existing westward transport capacity.

The International Energy Agency estimated that approximately 20 million barrels per day of crude oil and petroleum products passed through Hormuz in 2025, representing about one-quarter of global seaborne oil trade. Yet only 3.5–5.5 million barrels per day of potential rerouting capacity was available through Saudi Arabian and Emirati pipelines under its February 2026 assessment. IEA+1

These figures expose a structural deficiency: the world’s principal oil-producing region concentrates its export capacity in a maritime system whose vulnerability cannot be eliminated by conventional military deterrence alone.

The Saudi East–West Pipeline and the UAE’s Habshan–Fujairah corridor provide essential alternatives to Hormuz, but neither establishes a completely independent global distribution system. Yanbu offers access to the Red Sea, while Fujairah remains exposed to wider Gulf of Oman security conditions. Oil shipped from Yanbu to Asian markets through Bab el-Mandeb remains vulnerable to disruption farther south.

The strategic response must therefore distinguish three separate objectives: bypassing Hormuz, bypassing Bab el-Mandeb and securing reliable access to major consuming markets without either passage.

The strongest near-term option is to improve the reliability, operating flexibility, protection and export handling capacity of infrastructure already built.

The strongest medium-term opportunity is a coordinated network linking Gulf production to multiple exits, potentially including Oman’s Arabian Sea coast, Jordan’s Gulf of Aqaba, Egypt’s Mediterranean terminals and Türkiye’s Mediterranean infrastructure.

The most consequential longer-term possibility is a new Arabian Peninsula-to-Mediterranean energy corridor, developed through intergovernmental agreements and commercial underwriting rather than through a single politically vulnerable transit state.

The governing uncertainty is not whether such infrastructure can be constructed. It is whether participating states can align sovereignty, transit fees, security obligations, financing, climate-policy exposure and control over export volumes over several decades.

Beyond Hormuz and Yemen: The New Geography of Oil Power and Saudi Arabia’s Strategic Dilemma
Saudi Arabia has demonstrated that it can move millions of barrels of crude oil across its territory to avoid the Strait of Hormuz. It has not demonstrated that it can guarantee their delivery when the Red Sea becomes a second theatre of conflict. This distinction is now a question of fiscal sovereignty, industrial continuity and international economic security. The 2026 Middle Eastern energy crisis has exposed the limitations of an export architecture in which alternative pipelines still converge on vulnerable terminals, maritime passages and processing facilities. Riyadh’s strategic choice is no longer confined to protecting existing routes or expanding military deterrence. It must determine whether to finance a geographically diversified petroleum network extending toward the Arabian Sea and Mediterranean, accepting new sovereign partnerships without exchanging dependence on Iran and instability around Yemen for dependence on another transit state.

The numbers expose the limits of military protection
The scale of the vulnerability is established by the US Energy Information Administration’s October 2026 data. Petroleum movements through the Strait of Hormuz fell from 21.6 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 4.9 million in the second quarter of 2026, a reduction of approximately 77.3%. The disruption was not simply a temporary interruption of shipping schedules. It altered production, cargo availability, refining economics and the distribution of petroleum across international markets.

The International Energy Agency reported that Gulf crude exports recovered to 13.9 million barrels per day in September 2026, increasing by 4.4 million barrels per day during the month. Yet Hormuz traffic reached only 10.9 million barrels per day, while alternative export routes carried approximately 5.6 million. The return of physical supply did not restore normal market conditions: global petroleum inventories remained 509 million barrels below their end-February level, and North Sea Dated crude averaged $116.89 per barrel in September.

The consequences extended well beyond crude oil. Middle Eastern refined-product exports stood at approximately 1.9 million barrels per day in September, against 4.7 million before the conflict. Liquefied petroleum gas exports recovered to only 670,000 barrels per day, compared with approximately 1.5 million previously. These differences reveal a structural problem: restoring crude transportation does not automatically restore refineries, petrochemical operations or fuel distribution.

The International Maritime Organization reported at least 70 verified attacks against international shipping since the outbreak of the conflict on 28 February 2026, with 19 seafarer deaths. By August, as many as 400 ships carrying approximately 6,000 seafarers had been affected by the crisis in the Persian Gulf.

The economic significance is clear. A state may possess substantial petroleum reserves, advanced air defences and functioning export pipelines while remaining unable to guarantee deliveries at predictable commercial costs. Maritime security, industrial production and financial stability have become inseparable.

Petroline has changed Saudi Arabia’s options, but not eliminated its exposure
Saudi Aramco demonstrated the importance of existing infrastructure when its East–West Pipeline reached 7 million barrels per day of throughput during the first quarter of 2026. Extending approximately 1,200 kilometres across Saudi territory, the system transports crude from the eastern producing region toward Yanbu on the Red Sea. Roughly 2 million barrels per day of its stated capacity serves refining requirements, making the distinction between total pipeline throughput and directly exportable crude particularly important.

This infrastructure provides Riyadh with an alternative to Hormuz, but the advantage depends on the destination of the cargo. Crude shipped from Yanbu toward Mediterranean markets can proceed northward through Egyptian transport infrastructure without entering Bab el-Mandeb. Cargoes moving southward toward India and East Asia remain exposed to the southern Red Sea.

Egypt’s SUMED pipeline, with nominal capacity of approximately 2.5 million barrels per day, gives the Saudi system an additional westbound connection. Aramco’s disclosed 15% equity participation in SUMED reinforces the commercial importance of that relationship. But ownership does not guarantee unlimited access or spare capacity during simultaneous disruption.

The vulnerability became concrete again with the 11 September 2026 attack on the East–West Pipeline, identified by the IEA as a factor aggravating international petroleum-market instability. The lesson is not that Petroline has failed. It is that concentrating emergency diversion volumes within one principal trunk creates another critical dependency.

The UAE offers a different example. Its approximately 400-kilometre Habshan–Fujairah pipeline provides an outlet beyond Hormuz, with reported enhanced capacity approaching 1.8 million barrels per day. Fujairah can serve Asian markets without requiring eastbound cargoes to cross either Hormuz or Bab el-Mandeb.

Saudi Arabia does not possess an equivalent independently accessible Arabian Sea outlet for its eastern crude production. That geographical difference is central to the next generation of infrastructure decisions.

Oman could provide the second exit that Saudi Arabia lacks
A Saudi–Oman crude corridor terminating on the Arabian Sea deserves examination because it could create a genuinely different export direction rather than merely increase capacity within the existing system. Such a project has not been established as an approved or financed construction programme. Its strategic value must therefore be distinguished from its current institutional maturity.

Oman nevertheless possesses relevant industrial infrastructure. Duqm has a commercial quay of approximately 2.2 kilometres, an 18-metre guaranteed alongside draft and a liquid-bulk development incorporating seven berths. The associated OQ8 refinery was originally designed for 230,000 barrels per day and reported processing capability of approximately 255,000 barrels per day in February 2025. Ras Markaz provides approximately 4.5 million barrels of crude storage through eight tanks.

These facilities do not amount to an available Saudi export terminal. A pipeline capable of transporting large additional volumes would require dedicated engineering, pumping, storage, tanker-loading capacity and long-term commercial agreements.

The political calculation would be equally significant. Oman would provide sovereign territory and maritime access, while Saudi Arabia would provide potential throughput and investment. Riyadh would require enforceable transportation rights; Muscat would need to protect its regulatory independence, environmental interests and wider diplomatic relationships.

The economic case would depend on whether the corridor could offer Asian refiners reliable deliveries at a competitive total cost. India is particularly relevant: an earlier IEA projection anticipated its oil demand rising toward 6.6 million barrels per day by 2030, supported by industrial growth and domestic consumption.

An Arabian Sea pipeline cannot be justified merely because it avoids two dangerous waterways. It must demonstrate that the value of independently available exports exceeds construction, financing and long-term operating costs.

The Mediterranean alternative already has an industrial history
Saudi Arabia’s potential northern export geography has a historical precedent in the Trans-Arabian Pipeline. The original system crossed Jordan, Syria and Lebanon to reach the Mediterranean. Its section beyond Jordan ceased operating in 1976, while the remaining Saudi–Jordanian connection continued limited operations until 1990.

The historical experience establishes two propositions. Long-distance Arabian–Mediterranean petroleum transport is technically possible; maintaining it across several sovereign jurisdictions is a considerably more difficult political undertaking.

A modern northern corridor would require an entirely new legal, commercial and engineering assessment. Jordan has no Mediterranean coastline, making an additional transit connection unavoidable. Egyptian infrastructure, established Turkish export networks and historical northern alignments offer different possibilities, but none can be assumed to constitute an approved Saudi export project.

The more immediately documented development is Iraq’s proposed Basra–Aqaba pipeline. Jordan’s Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources describes a configuration comprising an Iraqi section designed for 2.25 million barrels per day and a Haditha–Aqaba section designed for one million barrels per day, supported by proposed storage of seven million barrels at Aqaba. Historical project documentation identified approximately $5.6 billion for the investment section under a Build–Own–Operate–Transfer arrangement.

Its limitation is geographical. Aqaba provides Red Sea access, not an independent Mediterranean terminus. A connection through Egyptian facilities could improve westbound security, but would require additional agreements and verified transport capacity.

Türkiye presents another alternative. Following the termination of the previous Iraq–Türkiye pipeline agreement on 27 July 2026, BOTAŞ announced a new one-year arrangement on 3 August, allocating 750,000 barrels per day to Iraqi counterparties. The existing Silopi–Ceyhan network has nominal capacity of approximately 1.52 million barrels per day.

Actual transportation remained substantially lower. BOTAŞ recorded approximately 7.854 million barrels in September 2026, equivalent to about 261,800 barrels per day. The difference between installed capacity and actual exports reflects why pipelines cannot be evaluated independently of upstream supply, commercial contracts and sovereign authority.

For Saudi Arabia, these northern systems represent possible future connections, not immediately available substitutes. For Iraq, however, greater utilisation of existing Mediterranean infrastructure could provide export diversification without requiring every component to be constructed from the beginning.

The cost of independence will be determined by contracts, not maps
A pipeline crossing several countries can reduce exposure to a maritime chokepoint while creating another form of vulnerability: dependence on the governments controlling transit, tariffs and operating permissions. The more capital committed to a fixed international route, the greater the potential consequences of political disagreement after construction.

The financial problem is equally demanding. A hypothetical $8 billion pipeline, financed over 25 years, requires approximately $568 million annually in capital recovery at 5%, rising to $749 million at 8% and $965 million at 11%, before operating costs and taxes. At one million barrels per day of full utilisation, those assumptions imply capital recovery of approximately $1.56–$2.64 per transported barrel. At half utilisation, the burden roughly doubles.

These calculations are illustrative, not project valuations. They demonstrate why commercial throughput and strategic reserve capacity must be financed differently.

A pipeline intended to remain partly unused until a crisis may be commercially unattractive despite providing national-security benefits. Governments would need to compensate operators for maintaining available capacity, while importing companies could participate through long-term transportation commitments.

International law cannot remove this difficulty. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea establishes protections for transit passage through qualifying international straits, including the principle in Article 44 that transit passage must not be suspended. It does not grant a state the right to construct or operate pipelines across another state’s territory.

Such rights require negotiated agreements covering ownership, tariffs, regulation, environmental obligations, commercial access, liability and dispute settlement.

China, India, Japan and South Korea would have a direct interest in the reliability of new Asian-facing corridors. The United States, whose Hormuz-linked crude imports averaged approximately 400,000 barrels per day during the first half of 2025, would benefit principally through international market stability and allied supply security.

Europe’s exposure is different. Eurostat recorded a 55.8% increase in the value of EU petroleum oil imports during the second quarter of 2026, compared with the 2025 monthly average, against a volume increase of only 1.2%. The leading suppliers remained the United States, Norway and Kazakhstan.

Italy and France could benefit from more reliable Mediterranean deliveries; Germany would remain exposed through industrial energy costs; and the United Kingdom could participate through international finance, maritime services and infrastructure contracting. None would escape a global oil-price shock merely because its direct Gulf import dependence was comparatively limited.

The next 24 months will determine who finances the next oil geography
Between October 2026 and October 2028, the decisive developments will be contractual rather than architectural. Saudi Arabia can strengthen the reliability of its existing system while examining a Saudi–Oman corridor; Iraq and Türkiye can seek a durable successor to their one-year transportation agreement; and Iraq, Jordan and potentially Egypt can determine whether a documented pipeline proposal can become a financially viable export chain.

The immediate expenditure would fall on petroleum operators, project sponsors and governments financing engineering studies, infrastructure improvements, storage and contractual reserve capacity. Large construction commitments would become justified only after technical feasibility, sovereign rights and customer demand had been established.

The cost of inaction is already visible in the 2026 figures. Asian refiners remain exposed to interrupted Gulf deliveries, European manufacturers absorb higher petroleum prices, and producing states face the prospect that temporary transport failures can threaten fiscal revenues and downstream industrial operations.

The IEA’s March 2026 decision to coordinate the release of 400 million barrels from emergency stocks illustrates the scale of the financial and institutional response required when normal supply routes become unreliable. Such inventories can bridge an interruption; they cannot permanently replace an export network.

Saudi Arabia’s decision is therefore not whether to abandon Hormuz or the Red Sea. Both will remain economically indispensable. It is whether to preserve a transportation structure in which disruptions to those passages can repeatedly determine the country’s export revenues, or develop a network in which additional routes remain commercially available when the existing system is constrained.

Over the next 12–24 months, postponing the necessary engineering, commercial and diplomatic decisions would leave governments with fewer credible choices when the next disruption occurs. Exporters would bear the fiscal consequences, Asian refiners and European industry the supply and price consequences, and national governments the cost of emergency intervention.

The contest over Middle Eastern oil is shifting from control of production toward control of reliable access to international markets. Whoever can finance and govern genuinely independent export corridors will possess an advantage that neither petroleum reserves nor military protection can provide alone. -https://t.co/4agEh75esM via @https://debuglies.com

Eminem turned down an $8,000,000 offer for an 8-minute performance at the World Cup without even negotiating:

In late 2022, Qatar approached 50 Cent with a massive budget for a joint World Cup performance.

The total offer was $9,000,000 for one short appearance. 50 Cent would get $1,000,000, while Eminem would get $8,000,000 for just 8 minutes on stage.

That’s $1,000,000 per minute.

50 Cent called Eminem’s manager, Paul Rosenberg, thinking it was an easy payday. Rosenberg took the offer to Eminem and called back ten minutes later:

"Marshall said no."

50 Cent couldn’t believe it. There was no counter-offer, no request for private jets, and no scheduling conflict.

Eminem had no interest in traveling halfway across the world for a corporate event, no matter how many millions were attached to it.

Managed Money Positions Overview
October 28, 2026

Data Period: Positions as of October 20, 2026 (NA) | October 23, 2026 (EU)

Market Sentiment & Technical Narrative
The agricultural futures complex is navigating a massive liquidation cycle in spec long positions, driven by rapid U.S. harvest advancement and heavy physical deliveries into commercial pipelines. Managed money accounts continue to systematically reduce net long exposure across CBOT grains and oilseeds, abandoning late summer bullish bets as combine reports verify solid overall production numbers across the central Corn Belt.

Field work progress across the Midwest made major strides over the past week, with national soybean harvest entering its final stretch and corn combining pushing past two-thirds completion. This flood of seasonal supply, combined with macro pressure from firming crude oil and broad market positioning shifts, has kept CBOT futures pinned near multi-month technical support. Conversely, protein markets are showing localized resilience; live cattle and feeder cattle futures continue to consolidate near key moving averages, supported by firm cash negotiations and steady wholesale beef cutout values.

Top News Story: The Great Fund Exit & Late October Harvest Sprint

The defining fundamental story across commodity trading desks is the sheer velocity of speculative long liquidation over the past two tracking cycles. The latest CFTC Disaggregated Commitments of Traders data revealed that managed money traders slashed another 82,000 net long corn contracts in a single week, marking a massive reduction in net exposure over a four week period. A similar exit occurred in soybeans, where funds executed their sharpest weekly long liquidation in over four months.

Simultaneously, U.S. producers are taking full advantage of clear fall weather windows. The latest USDA Crop Progress report showed national soybean harvest advancing to 76% complete, while national corn harvest reached 65% complete. In macro news, commodity traders are digesting the CFTC's formal announcement that it will transition from weekly to semi weekly Commitments of Traders report publications by the end of 2026, aiming to reduce data latency for agricultural market participants.

text:
PROSTATE CANCER: WHY DIET & EXERCISE MATTER DURING TREATMENT

What you eat and how you move can make a difference during prostate cancer treatment and long after.

In this Blue Cure Men’s Health Podcast excerpt, Sarah Norris, ARNP, of Mercy Medical Center in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, explains why she encourages plant-forward nutrition and regular physical activity, including strength training.

What does the research show?

The American Institute for Cancer Research (AICR) encourages cancer patients and survivors, when medically appropriate, to eat more vegetables, fruits, whole grains and beans, limit red and processed meats, and stay physically active.

Research from previous Blue Cure podcast guests also offers valuable insights:

• Dr. Stacy Loeb, a urologist at NYU Langone Health, coauthored a study of more than 3,500 prostate cancer survivors linking greater consumption of plant-based foods with better sexual, urinary and hormonal/vitality outcomes. These were associations, not proof of cause and effect.

• Professor Robert Newton, a pioneer in exercise oncology at Edith Cowan University in Australia, has studied how targeted exercise can help men receiving androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). His research found that combining resistance training with impact exercise can help limit spinal bone loss and improve muscle strength.

Why does this matter during treatment?

ADT can contribute to muscle loss, declining bone density and cardiovascular risk. Appropriate exercise can help improve strength, fitness, fatigue and quality of life.

Research into whether diet and exercise reduce prostate cancer progression or recurrence continues. Healthy habits support overall health and treatment recovery, but cannot guarantee cancer outcomes or replace medical care.

DIET & EXERCISE MATTER. MAKE A PLAN WITH YOUR HEALTHCARE TEAM. Ask what nutrition, aerobic activity and strength training are appropriate for your diagnosis, treatment and overall health.

Medical disclaimer: Educational information only. Consult your healthcare team for personalized guidance.

𝐈𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐲 𝐁𝐞 𝐚𝐧 𝐎𝐥𝐝 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲

On the evening of October 1, 1847, the Mitchells had a party at their home on Nantucket, in the Pacific Bank building.

Maria Mitchell, 29, slipped out of the parlor. On clear nights she took a lantern up to the roof and swept the sky with a small telescope.

That night she found a faint blur above Polaris, the North Star, that was not on her charts. She told her father, William, that she thought she saw a comet.

William Mitchell looked and was sure. Maria was not. She asked him to say nothing yet.

Storms held the island’s mail until October 3. Her father wrote to William Bond at Harvard: “Maria has obtained its right ascension and declination, and will not suffer me to announce it.” William Mitchell added: “Maria supposes it may be an old story.” An old story: a comet someone else might already have found.

Two nights after Maria’s sighting, on October 3, the astronomer Father de Vico found the same comet in Rome.

Denmark offered a gold medal to the first to find a comet too faint to see by eye, if the finder told the Astronomer Royal in England, or the Danish minister in Washington, by the next mail. Maria’s news had gone only to a friend at Harvard.

Edward Everett, president of Harvard, took up her case. Everett wrote to her father that it was “barely possible” the letter to Bond might count.

The astronomer Schumacher, who reported to Denmark’s king, found for Maria, and the king accepted his report. In March 1849, Everett wrote to Maria that her medal “arrived by the last steamer”, and that he had gone to Boston “hoping to find you at the Adams House, to put it into your own hand.”

Even before the medal came, in May 1848, Maria had become the first woman elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

The comet she thought was an old story was hers. Her first name, MARIA, is 42 in English Ordinal.

text:
These claims are not analysis. They are speculative assertions dressed up as conclusions, built on selective numbers, incomplete timelines, and a clear desire to portray Saudi Arabia as collapsing. No serious evidence is offered that the Kingdom’s core strategy has failed — only the author’s preferred narrative.

1. Vision 2030 and the economy
In 2025 Saudi Arabia recorded SAR 159.1 billion ($42.4 billion) in gross FDI inflows — a 33.5% increase from 2024 and 14% above the National Investment Strategy target of SAR 140 billion for that year. The FDI stock reached SAR 1.06 trillion.
The IMF projects a 3.3% contraction in 2026 due to the regional conflict, followed by a 7.9% rebound in 2027. S&P Global reaffirmed the Kingdom’s A+ rating with a stable outlook in September 2026, citing non-oil resilience, energy-export flexibility via the East-West pipeline, and strong buffers. Non-oil activities now represent approximately 70% of GDP, up from 65% in 2018.
Measuring a 2030 transformation against a single conflict-affected year, while omitting the rebound forecast, the rating affirmation, and the actual FDI overperformance, is not analysis. It is narrative construction.

2. The Houthi campaign
The October 2026 attacks on King Khalid International Airport were severe: multiple strikes, at least 13 killed, more than 300 wounded, temporary full closure, and the cancellation of roughly 86% of scheduled flights between 8–25 October. The threat is real and costly.
However, the capacity of an asymmetric actor to inflict damage has never, by itself, equalled the strategic defeat of a state. Saudi air defences continue to intercept launches, the coalition is actively striking Houthi missile infrastructure, and the airport has partially resumed operations. Equating every successful attack with the failure of an entire military posture is a methodological error, not a conclusion.

3. Dependence on the United States
Saudi strategy is visibly multi-vector. On 26 October 2026, Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman led a high-level delegation — alongside senior Pakistani and Turkish officials under the Makkah defence framework — to Tehran for direct de-escalation talks with Iranian leadership. A state supposedly locked into dependence on Washington was simultaneously expanding security partnerships and negotiating with Tehran in real time.

Saudi Arabia is managing a genuine regional crisis with measurable costs. The difficulties are not imaginary. What this post does is convert temporary shocks and incomplete outcomes into a finished story of total failure, while systematically under-weighting hard data on investment flows, sovereign credit strength, non-oil growth, and active diplomatic diversification.
Challenges are real. Strategic collapse remains unproven — and the attempt to declare it already complete reveals more about the author’s intentions than about the facts on the ground.

**Subject:** Formal Complaint – Non-Compliant Parking and Accessibility Barriers at U.S. Bank Parking Lot, 1501 Commerce Street, Tacoma, Washington – Immediate Remediation Required  

Dear Branch Manager and U.S. Bank Accessibility Compliance Team:

I am writing to formally complain about serious and ongoing violations of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and the Washington State Building Code at the parking facility serving the U.S. Bank branch located at 1501 Commerce Street, Tacoma, WA 98402.

The parking lot provides **no designated accessible (handicap) parking stalls whatsoever**. Under the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design (Section 208.2 and the associated table) and the corresponding provisions of the Washington State Building Code (IBC-based Section 1106.2 and Table 1106.2), where parking is provided, accessible spaces are mandatory. The minimum number is calculated per parking facility (not the overall site) and begins with at least one van-accessible space for facilities with 1–25 total spaces, with higher numbers required for larger lots. At least one of every six accessible spaces (or fraction thereof) must be van-accessible, with proper dimensions (typically 96-inch car spaces with 60-inch access aisles, or 132-inch van spaces with 60-inch aisles, plus appropriate signage at least 60 inches above grade, firm/stable surfaces, and slopes no steeper than 1:48).  

The complete absence of any such spaces is a clear violation. Accessible parking must also be located on the shortest accessible route to an accessible entrance. This facility fails these requirements entirely. Public accommodations such as banks are subject to ADA Title III (42 U.S.C. §§ 12181 et seq.) and must provide accessible parking and routes; existing facilities have ongoing obligations for readily achievable barrier removal. Washington state requirements align with and in some cases reinforce these federal standards.  

In addition, the parking area (or associated controlled-access system) includes a bank-robbery security lockbox / controlled-entry mechanism (or equivalent security vestibule/mantrap-style access control) that permits individuals with disabilities to enter but does not allow them to exit independently or safely. This creates a barrier to egress. Accessible means of egress and accessible routes are required under the ADA Standards (including references to accessible means of egress) and applicable building/fire codes. A system that traps or impedes exit for people with mobility disabilities is not compliant and presents both accessibility and safety issues.  

These conditions mean the parking facility is not accessible. A place of public accommodation should not operate with a parking lot that fails basic ADA and state code requirements for accessible parking and routes. The absence of accessible stalls and the egress problem with the security/lockbox system constitute ongoing violations that discriminate against individuals with disabilities, including those who hold valid disabled parking placards or plates.  

**I demand that these violations be corrected immediately.** Specifically:  
- Install the required number of fully compliant accessible parking spaces (including at least one van-accessible space as applicable to the lot size), with proper striping, access aisles, signage, slopes, and connections via an accessible route to the entrance.  
- Modify or replace the security lockbox / controlled-access system so that individuals with disabilities can both enter and exit independently and safely, consistent with accessible egress requirements.  
- Provide written confirmation of the corrective actions taken, including the timeline for completion and any temporary accommodations offered in the interim.  

These issues must be fixed without delay. 
Thanks Tony P

text: Thomas Jefferson : The Republican Party : Jefferson and Adams were opposites. Adams wanted an expanded Federal Government and more executive, almost regal, power while Jefferson considered the states as sovereign. This came to a head when Jefferson anonymously drafted the "Kentucky Resolutions" for the Kentucky legislature challenging the "Alien and Sedition Acts" which Adams had signed restricting free speech. The resolutions claim was that a state could refuse any law that they deemed unconstitutional. In other words states had the final authority over their affairs. James Madison wrote the "Virginia Resolutions" over the same issue. This was very important. Were States in a compact or contract with the Federal Government ? A compact is just an agreement among sovereign states to follow the constitution as they see fit. There was no federal enforcement or supreme court arbitration.  A contract, however, binds the states to adhering to federal laws. The "compact" interpretation  would be the principal justification for the" right" to secede the union leading up to the civil war.  Jefferson was adamant about keeping the federal government small and keeping the accountability at the state and local level. Power at a distance is power vulnerable to corruption. His time as vice president was primarily spent building up these ideals and the Republican Party. He declined Adams offer of continuing as Secretary of State and he refused the offer of a seat in his cabinet. He did preside over the Senate and implemented a procedural manual that he revised from British Parliament concerning rules of order, points of order, and how motions should proceed. This "Manual" continues to be referenced today. Thomas Jefferson was prepared to be president.

text:
New docuseries explores AI in Russian daily life

How’s your week going so far? Are you ready for a reality check on how artificial intelligence is making its way beyond the big cities and into everyday life across Russia?

Today we’re diving deep into a new docuseries called “ЖПТ” (AI in Daily Life), which has just hit PREMIER. This series isn’t just about fancy gadgets; it’s a raw look at how AI is changing lives outside of Moscow and St. Petersburg.
A Journey Across Ten Cities

Blogger Karen Adamyan took his camera on an epic journey across ten Russian cities, from the coastal town of Vyborg to the mountainous Altai Republic. He offered people from various professions—bakers, teachers, farmers—the chance to use generative neural networks in their work and daily lives.
Catalysts for Change or Barriers?

The result? A mixed bag. For some folks, integrating AI was a catalyst for change. They saw it as an opportunity to adapt or even pivot careers. But others hit roadblocks—mainly because they didn’t trust the technology enough to give it a shot. It’s like when your grandma gets a smartphone but sticks with her flip phone out of habit and fear.
Real Data Behind the Scenes

The series isn’t just anecdotal; it’s backed by real data from the people who tried these AI tools. According to Adamyan’s research, around 40% of participants found immediate value in using generative neural networks. Another 30% were intrigued but hesitant due to technical issues or lack of training. The remaining 30% outright rejected the idea, citing a range of concerns from privacy fears to simple distrust.
Bakers and Teachers on the Front Lines

Take bakers in Vyborg, for example. They were given AI-powered recipe generators to help with their daily bread-making routines. Some loved it because it saved time and offered new ideas. Others felt overwhelmed by all the options and stuck with their tried-and-true methods.

Teachers faced similar challenges. In Altai Republic, educators experimented with chatbots designed to answer student questions 24/7. While some saw this as a way to enhance learning, others were skeptical about relying on machines for such an important task. The fear of losing that human connection was palpable.
What Does This Mean for You?

So here’s the awkward bit: why should you care? Well, if you’re thinking about integrating AI into your life—whether it’s at work or home—you need to be prepared. It’s not just about having access to fancy tech; it’s about understanding its limitations and benefits.

For instance, if you’re a small business owner looking to streamline operations with AI tools, you might find that some employees are resistant to change. Or maybe you’re a student who wants to use an AI tutor for homework help but worries about the quality of feedback. These aren’t just hypothetical scenarios; they’re real issues people are facing right now.
The Big Picture

The docuseries “ЖПТ” isn’t just entertainment; it’s a wake-up call. It shows that while AI is advancing rapidly, its adoption in everyday life is still a work in progress. There’s no one-size-fits-all solution here—what works for a tech-savvy urbanite might not be suitable for someone living in a remote village.

And let’s face it: the future isn’t just about having access to cutting-edge technology; it’s about making sure everyone can use it effectively and comfortably. So whether you’re an early adopter or a skeptic, this series reminds us that we need to bridge the gap between tech and real life.
What This Does Not Prove

It’s important to note what “ЖПТ” does not prove. The docuseries doesn’t claim to be a comprehensive study of AI adoption across Russia. It’s more like a snapshot, offering insights into how different people react to new technology in their daily lives. While the data is real and the stories are compelling, it’s just one perspective on a much larger issue.
User Controls

One key takeaway from “ЖПТ” is that users have control over how they integrate AI into their lives. Whether you’re a baker or a teacher, you can choose to embrace new tools or stick with what works for you. The series highlights the importance of personal choice and comfort levels when it comes to adopting technology.
Availability

The first ten episodes of “ЖПТ” are already available on PREMIER. If you’re curious about how AI is changing lives outside the big cities, this docuseries offers a fascinating look at real-world applications and challenges.
Practical Takeaway

So what’s the practical takeaway here? It’s simple: if you’re considering integrating AI into your life or business, take it slow and figure out what works best for you. Don’t be afraid to experiment but also don’t feel pressured to jump on every new tech trend without understanding its benefits and limitations.
What This Does Not Prove

While “ЖПТ” provides valuable insights, it doesn’t prove that AI is universally beneficial or harmful. It’s a nuanced look at how different people react to technology in their daily lives. The series shows that the adoption of AI is complex and varies widely depending on individual circumstances.
What This Does Not Include

The docuseries focuses on real-life applications but doesn’t delve into technical details about how these AI tools work under the hood. It’s more concerned with user experiences and reactions rather than the inner workings of the technology itself.
User Controls and Privacy

Users have control over their data when using AI tools, as outlined by privacy regulations. While “ЖПТ” highlights concerns around privacy and trust, it also emphasizes that users can make informed decisions about how they use these technologies.
What’s Next?

So what should readers watch for next? Keep an eye on how AI adoption plays out in different demographics and industries. Will more people start embracing these tools as they become easier to use? Or will resistance continue to be a significant barrier? The answers might surprise you.

And hey, if you’re feeling brave, why not try integrating some AI into your own life? But remember: it’s okay to take things slow and figure out what works best for you. After all, the real test of any technology is whether it enhances our lives or just complicates them further.

Discuss this in the comments below! What are your thoughts on AI adoption outside of tech hubs? Share your experiences and predictions—let’s keep the conversation going.

text:
A young man with a gunshot wound through his neck staggered out of the brush and collapsed in front of a naval checkpoint, gasping that over seventy innocent people had just been lined up against a barn wall and executed.

The reason might surprise you.

In August 2010, two convoy trucks traveling along Federal Highway 101 through the northern border state of Tamaulipas were intercepted by armed convoys.

Inside were 74 undocumented migrants from Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, Ecuador, and Brazil, each of whom had paid human smugglers thousands of dollars to guide them toward the US border.

Highway 101 was known as the "Highway of Death," controlled by Los Zetas, who were locked in an all-out turf war against their former bosses, the Gulf Cartel.

The migrants were escorted at gunpoint to an abandoned ranch in the municipality of San Fernando:

Cartel commanders gave the captives an ultimatum: pay an immediate ransom of $1,000 to $5,000 each, or pick up an AK-47 and enlist as frontline sicarios in the Zetas’ war against the Gulf Cartel.

The migrants possessed no money, many had spent their families’ life savings simply to reach northern Mexico.

Terrified of being forced into narco-warfare, almost every single captive refused the offer.

Fearing that releasing them would allow the Gulf Cartel to recruit them instead, regional Zeta boss Martiniano de Jesús Jaramillo Silva ordered the barn secured.

On the night of August 22, hitmen bound the victims' hands behind their backs with plastic zip-ties, blindfolded them, and forced them to kneel facing the brick walls of an open storage shed (bodega).

One by one, gunmen walked down the line, firing bullets into the back of each victim's head.

Among the captives was Luis Freddy Lala Pomavilla, an 18-year-old from Ecuador:

A bullet struck Lala Pomavilla in the neck, exiting through his jaw. He collapsed onto the concrete, holding his breath and pretending to be dead as warm blood pooled around him.

In the silence that followed, Lala Pomavilla heard the groans of dying men and women. Slipping his bonds, he crawled past the corpses, climbed through a window, and walked ten miles through dense mesquite brush in agonizing pain.

On the morning of August 23, he reached a highway checkpoint manned by Mexican Navy Marines (SEMAR), alerting them to the slaughter.

When naval helicopters and tactical trucks stormed the San Fernando ranch, they engaged armed Zeta lookouts in a firefight before securing the shed.

Inside, Marines discovered the single largest mass execution of migrants in Latin American history:

Seventy-two bodies, 58 men and 14 women, including a pregnant teenager, lay piled against the blood-splattered walls.

The dead included 24 Hondurans, 14 Salvadorans, 13 Guatemalans, 5 Ecuadorians, and 4 Brazilians.

Forensic teams later found a second survivor, a Honduran national who had slipped into the brush during the commotion.

The massacre shocked the international community and triggered an unprecedented diplomatic crisis across the Americas:

Human rights organizations condemned the complete collapse of state authority along Mexico’s transit corridors, where transnational migrants were routinely targeted by cartels as disposable revenue.

text:
Per Mare, Per Terram

28 October 1664 marked the establishment of one of the flowers of the British Armed Forces. At the order of King Charles II, 1,200 soldiers were raised to form the Duke of York and Albany’s Maritime Regiment of Foot, also known as the Admiral’s Regiment. So began the distinguished lineage of the Royal Marines.

The regiment was formed during preparations for the Second Anglo-Dutch War, when the Crown required disciplined soldiers capable of serving alongside the Royal Navy. By integrating trained infantry into the fleet, our offensive reach extended beyond the guns of our ships. These amphibious troops could repel enemy boarders, deliver small-arms fire in close engagements, secure vessels and carry the assault ashore.

First officially recorded as ‘Marines’ in 1672, the regiment’s identity and reputation evolved over time. Although its early formations were periodically raised and disbanded in response to the demands of war, a permanent Marine Corps was established in 1755, with divisions located at Chatham, Portsmouth and Plymouth. In recognition of its venerable service, the Corps was granted the title Royal Marines by King George III in 1802. Its responsibilities subsequently expanded to encompass artillery, shipboard gunnery and expeditionary warfare. The accomplished execution of these varied roles has earned the Marines admiration amongst allies and begrudging respect amongst adversaries. 

Richard Simkin’s watercolour offers a fascinating visual history of the Corps, bringing successive generations of uniforms into a single composition. From the distinctive dress of seventeenth-century Marines to the more familiar Victorian uniforms, one can but imagine the spectacle of scarlet descending upon an enemy in battle. Though undoubtedly a sight to behold, I am pleased that our men are clothed less conspicuously today. Across the centuries, the attire, organisation and operational functions of the Corps have evolved, but its tradition of service and sacrifice endures.

As with the entirety of our Armed Forces, the Royal Marines deserve the utmost gratitude from state and civilian alike.

text:
📜 After the Deportations: The Seized Jewish Collections of Rimaszombat and Tornalja

After the June 1944 deportations from Rimaszombat and Tornalja, Miklós Holéczy catalogued Jewish-owned paintings, ceramics, furniture and textiles. In a report dated 23 July 1944, he discussed their prospects at auction and referred to the dispossessed people as “the former owners.” The following year, he became director of the local museum—a position he would hold until 1959. [1–3,8]

Reel 144, slides 160–168 preserves his correspondence and lists headed with five Jewish family names: Fazekas, Fenyő, Goldner, Braun and Brünner, alongside objects held in two Tornalja depots. The handwritten tally is 270 items. These records now offer several avenues for investigation: a plausible identification of a ceramic model, six paintings connected to a recently acquired artist’s estate, and a documented continuity between wartime confiscation work and postwar museum leadership.

🕯️ June deportations, July inventories

The dates establish the sequence. According to Yad Vashem, prisoners from the Rimaszombat ghetto were transferred to Salgótarján and deported to Auschwitz on 13 June 1944. Prisoners from Tornalja’s ghettos were transferred to Miskolc on 6 June, then deported to Auschwitz in transports departing between 12 and 15 June. [2–3]

The surviving property lists are dated 8 July for Rimaszombat and 17 July for Tornalja. Holéczy submitted his report on 23 July; the receiving notation on the file is dated 25 July. The towns were then under Hungarian administration. Today they are Rimavská Sobota and Tornaľa, Slovakia.

The lists preserve individual tastes and domestic surroundings. The Fazekas household had a watercolor of Venice’s Rialto Bridge attributed to Kálmán Tichy and a moonlit landscape by Jenő Makovits. The Fenyő list includes paintings identified as Notre-Dame and Narrow Street, attributed to Orbán, alongside ceramics, glassware and embroidered textiles. The Goldner household held four works attributed to Lenke Szemere, three to Ritta Boemm, and a colored-chalk drawing of a little girl’s head attributed to István Csók. [1]

These details establish that Jewish residents participated in the region’s artistic life as owners and purchasers. Their possessions included local landscapes and contemporary Hungarian art as well as imported porcelain, furnishings and household objects.

👥 Recovering the owners’ identities

The seizure lists give surnames without the first names and addresses needed to identify each household conclusively. Other records provide useful leads, but those connections must remain explicitly provisional:

• Fenyő and Fazekas, Tornalja: The town’s memorial book lists Dr. Avraham Fenyő and Dr. David Fazekas, together with their wives, among the murdered. These are possible identifications for the inventoried households; matching civil, property or probate records are still needed. [4]
• Braun, Rimaszombat: The inventory specifies a vinegar-factory residence and warehouse. A notice published in Gömör-Kishont on 3 September 1916 names Sándor Braun as a vinegar manufacturer in Rimaszombat. The match of surname, town and business is significant, although the factory’s ownership in 1944 requires confirmation. [5]
• Brünner, Rimaszombat: A February 1942 newspaper identifies Emánuel Brünner’s widow and her son, Sándor Brünner, with a textile business on Horthy Miklós Square. They are a specific local family to investigate against the inventoried residence. [6]

A reliable first-name identification for the Goldner household remains outstanding. The uncertainty should be resolved through records linking people to addresses and possessions; the inventory alone cannot establish every family member’s identity or fate.

🖋️ Holéczy’s report: expertise in the service of confiscation

Miklós Holéczy, recorded in Slovak sources as Mikuláš Holéczy (1886–1972), was a teacher, artist and museum worker. In this file he acted as a delegate of Dr. Dénes Csánky, director of Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts and government commissioner for the registration and preservation of sequestered Jewish artworks. [1,7,9]

Holéczy’s report, no. 6/1944, explains that he had copied the attached list from his notes and was preparing a fuller inventory. He wanted to visit additional towns personally because the personnel clearing Jewish homes could overlook valuable objects and attach too much importance to insignificant ones. His expertise would help the authorities select and classify what had been taken.

On slide 162, he wrote:

“A mellékelt lajstromban vannak értékesebb és kevésbé értékes, sőt selejtes példányok is. Azonban aukción, úgy hiszem, legtöbbje gazdához juthat.”

In English:

“The attached list includes more valuable and less valuable pieces, even inferior examples. However, at auction, I think most could find an owner.”

He was assessing saleability, without recording monetary estimates. These pages do not establish that an auction occurred. They do establish that auction disposal was being considered in correspondence about property taken from Jewish owners.

Later in the same report, Holéczy used “A volt tulajdonosok”—“the former owners.” The language treated their dispossession as an accomplished fact while officials assessed the objects’ future usefulness and commercial appeal.

Csánky’s draft reply on slide 160 approves the inventory’s format and urges Holéczy to continue in other larger settlements. The work was being encouraged by the official directing the national operation. [1]

🏛️ From the 1944 inventory to postwar public authority

The Gemersko-malohontské múzeum, the Gömör-Kishont Museum in Rimavská Sobota, identifies Viliam/Vilmos Fábián as director from 1936 to 1945, followed by Mikuláš Holéczy from 1945 to 1959. Holéczy should therefore be described as the commissioner’s delegate and museum worker in this July 1944 file, and as the museum’s subsequent director. [8]

Another source extends that history. In May 2025, museum historian Ján Aláč presented a 1955 account written by Holéczy describing the town’s liberation and early postwar administration. Holéczy’s account places him on the town council formed in January 1945 and identifies him as temporary head of the local gymnasium when teaching resumed that month. [13]

A man with firsthand knowledge of these confiscated Jewish possessions thus continued to exercise public and cultural authority after the change of regime. His museum correspondence, administrative records and any dealings with returning owners or heirs are essential parts of this history. The available evidence does not yet establish how he handled restitution.

The July 1944 report also belongs alongside his later account of the town’s wartime experience. Both are records he authored; together they permit a fuller examination of his conduct before and after the war.

📦 The missing material beyond the total of 270

The handwritten total—169 items for Tornalja and 101 for Rimaszombat—describes the material counted in these lists. Holéczy expressly stated that the accumulated carpeting had not yet been inventoried and required specialist assessment. He thought it might prove the most saleable and valuable part of the material.

Precious metals were assigned a different route. Csánky’s draft reply says that, under an arrangement with the Finance Ministry, Holéczy need not inventory the silver locally. The finance directorate was required to forward it, together with other precious-metal objects, to the Hungarian Royal Postal Savings Bank’s Budapest headquarters, where Csánky’s experts would examine and classify the material. [1]

That instruction identifies another set of records to locate: dispatch lists, packing records and receiving receipts. It does not itself prove delivery. Nor does the absence of silver from these household lists establish that the families possessed none.

🏰 Csánky’s travel note and the Felsőbalog furniture

Beneath the draft reply on slide 160, Csánky’s handwritten note refers to traveling through Rimaszombat to Felsőbalog, mentioning Friday the 28th. The destination warrants attention because it appears in a separate account of his use of Jewish property.

Historian Orsolya Büky, citing Zoltán Oroszlán’s report of 27 February 1945, writes that Csánky had rooms in the Coburg castle at Felsőbalog furnished with Jewish-owned furniture held at the Museum of Fine Arts. The rooms were intended for his family’s holiday use. Her reference is MNL OL K 726, 59. cs., 23/1945. [9]

No evidence presently connects furniture from these five households to the castle. The travel note and the published account nevertheless identify a specific destination and postwar file to investigate. Any surviving furnishing lists or transport records could establish which owners’ possessions Csánky used there.

🔎 The Fenyő ceramic: a plausible model identification

On slide 166, item 21, the Fenyő household list records:

“Térdelő akt /cserép/ Gódor.917.”

The description is a kneeling nude in earthenware. The name and abbreviated date plausibly indicate István Gádor and 1917. The entry does not specify how that attribution or date was established.

A corresponding sculptural model appears in Pintér Auction House’s ERATO auction of 24 October 2013, lot 14: Gádor’s Akt szőlőfürtökkel—Nude with Bunches of Grapes. The catalogue describes glazed ceramic, 20.5 cm, marked “Gádor I. 1917.” Its photograph shows a kneeling female figure holding bunches of grapes beside her head. [10]

The apparent artist, date, material and pose make this the strongest object lead identified so far. The short inventory title could describe the more fully named auction composition. A terracotta-colored example of the same composition also appears in a 2019 Galéria Savaria listing. [11]

This is a plausible identification of the model, not a confirmed identification of the Fenyő family’s individual ceramic. The 1944 entry supplies no dimensions, glaze color, photograph or distinctive damage. Establishing the individual object would require further evidence, such as an old interior photograph, labels, underside markings or a documented ownership history.

🎨 Six Makovits paintings—and a timely museum investigation

The lists record six works attributed to Jenő Makovits, also known as Jenő Mátrai-Makovits/Eugen Makovits (1896–1967). Their household associations are valuable evidence even before the paintings themselves are located:

• Fazekas household, Tornalja — slide 163, no. 29: Holdas táj—Moonlit Landscape, pastel.
• Goldner household, Rimaszombat — slide 167, no. 7: Landscape, oil.
•Braun household, Rimaszombat — slide 167, nos. 5–6: Rimaszombati vásár—Rimaszombat Market, pastel; and Nyári eső—Summer Rain, oil.
• Brünner household, Rimaszombat — slide 168, nos. 1 and 4: Kiűzöttek—The Expelled, oil; and a portrait, oil.

These are the inventory’s descriptions and attributions. They should remain searchable alongside Hungarian and Slovak forms of the artist’s name and any later titles.

Makovits was born in Rimaszombat, participated in its cultural life, belonged to the museum association and served as custodian of its art collections. In an August 2026 announcement, the Gemersko-malohontské múzeum reported purchasing 100 items from his estate, previously preserved by his grandson, filmmaker András Kisfaludy. The acquisition includes paintings, pastels, drawings, sketches and personal photographs. A retrospective exhibition and catalogue are planned for 2027. [12]

That material could help identify compositions recorded in the 1944 lists. There is no evidence presently establishing that any of the six confiscated works is among the museum’s recent acquisitions.

The forthcoming catalogue offers an immediate opportunity to publish the six inventory references, recognize their Jewish owners and seek information about their whereabouts. Photographs or sketches may identify a composition; ownership records would then be needed to connect a surviving painting to the particular household.

🗂️ The records that could establish what happened

The first missing record is identified by Holéczy himself: the fuller inventory he said he was preparing. His report 6/1944, the commissioner’s instruction Kb. 158/1944, and the file marked 220 provide concrete references for locating related correspondence and attachments.

The next records should establish disposition: the Tornalja depot registers; local transfer and disposal records; any auction authorizations, catalogues or accounts; and finance-directorate dispatch documents matched to Postal Savings Bank receipts. Museum records from Holéczy’s directorship should be examined for the five family names, the listed works, wartime deposits, later accessions and restitution correspondence.

@ArtRecoveryInit calls on the Gemersko-malohontské múzeum and the relevant Hungarian and Slovak archives to make surviving records concerning these possessions accessible and to publish any documented returns to owners or heirs. The museum’s Makovits research can also bring the six paintings into its forthcoming catalogue with their recorded Jewish ownership intact.

Holéczy’s report imagined confiscated objects finding owners at auction. The surviving lists still identify the households from which they came. Those names—Fazekas, Fenyő, Goldner, Braun and Brünner—must accompany the search for the objects and any account of what became of them.

text:
CALIFORNIA 

PROJECT FOODBOX 

Taxpayer-Funded Free Luxury Food 

California Sends Luxury Foods to Welfare Recipients

By Christopher F. Rufo and Madeleine Rowley
Oct. 28, 2026

As middle-class families struggle to afford groceries, the state delivers organic produce, salmon, and more to Medi-Cal members.

Salmon, beef, organic produce, and Amy’s Kitchen meals: these are just some of the luxury foods that California welfare recipients can get delivered to their homes each week, for free.

Californians like TikTok user “Lupita” are taking full advantage. Earlier this year, she posted a video of herself opening a taxpayer-funded grocery box, apologizing to her manicurist as she unboxed it by hand. Inside, she found carrots, heads of broccoli, apples, oranges, celery, rice, lettuce, and more.

“Yesterday, I was like, ‘I need some lettuce,’ but the lettuce was like five dollars,” she said. “And look at this. Fresh lettuce! Thank you, God.”

She can also thank Governor Gavin Newsom. As part of his nearly $12 billion Medicaid reform package, welfare recipients—including illegal immigrants—can receive free, “medically tailored” meals and groceries, delivered straight to their door. They can get foods for free that would cost ordinary people a small fortune.

The food service is part of CalAIM, Newsom’s multibillion-dollar Medi-Cal reform package. Signed into law in 2021, CalAIM directs Medicaid dollars to social programs like transitional rent payments and housing deposits. Newsom called it a “once-in-a-generation opportunity to completely transform the Medicaid system in California.”

The transformation is working. The most popular of CalAIM’s “Community Supports,” by far, is “medically tailored meals.” That program and a related offering send prepared meals or “tailored” grocery items to qualified Medi-Cal recipients’ homes.

The state makes eligibility easy. Applicants need a qualifying Medi-Cal card, a provider’s recommendation, and an eligible condition. In a 2024 presentation to a Los Angeles nonprofit, Andrew Barrier, a former executive of a California medically tailored food contractor, told his audience how easy it was to enroll.

“They’re not looking to push people away from the program, they’re really looking for people to be on it,” he said. “Step one is that chronic condition. This is really how most people come in, and they could have diabetes, pre-diabetes, cardiovascular, mental- and behavioral-health disorders—we’ve seen anxiety, PTSD, depression, ADHD. Again, the list is very, very long.”

From there, the food shows up at recipients’ doorsteps. Medi-Cal pays contractors to deliver the food for up to 12 weeks, after which eligible recipients can re-enroll. And it’s not cheap: across 24 weeks, between food and delivery, a single “medically tailored meals” recipient costs taxpayers more than $1,500.

The food itself drives much of the cost. California contractors offer beef, chicken, organic produce, and more. Barrier’s former company, Project FoodBox, offers Medi-Cal recipients Amy’s Kitchen meals and burritos. Over several months, these foods would cost ordinary Californians hundreds of dollars at the grocery store.

Jocelyn Salala, a chef living in Los Angeles, told City Journal that she signed up for Project FoodBox through Medi-Cal in April after she was laid off. She has since put the deliveries to creative use.

“I was constantly trying to put all these ingredients into my food,” she said. “I took the sugar snap peas and made a cocktail. It allowed me to think outside the box, and I was really only buying protein at the store.”

Salala, who also runs a website about Swahili food and culture, said the amount of food that came each week was more than enough for one person.

“It was a lot of produce,” she said. “I got so much celery. I still have some in my freezer that I use for broths.”

I wish to take this time to vent about insurance. I don't normally use social media this way, but perhaps there can be some value in exhaling feelings to get them out of my system and not feel so crazy. As many of you know, my daughter, Lana, has scoliosis. The good news is that we found a pathway to provide surgery that has  a very good track record of helping people in her particular situation. The strange (and disappointing) news is that even with insurance, the out of pocket maximums and admin fee add up to $48,000 (not including travel)! How is this *insurance*?

Why so much? The causes:

1. Baylor offer a special surgery insurance that doesn't cover this since it is OUT of network (and none in network offer ASC).
2. The hospital is IN network, but that requires a *separate* out of pocket max, in addition to the out of network expense for the surgery itself. It would be cheaper if the hospital were also OUT of network.
3. The surgeon requires an addition $15k third-party fee to insure that they get paid by the insurance companies (since their experience is that they often would not get paid).
4. There are no other options that offer ASC for Lana's case (degree of severity and age).

On a positive note, many have supported us. But this is not an advertisement for support. I'm just venting. Maybe others can relate.

Thank you for your attention.

text:
The original lanterns were turnips, not pumpkins.

In Ireland and parts of Britain people hollowed mangelwurzels or turnips, carved faces, and set a candle inside. The lights were placed in windows or carried to frighten or ward the Aos Sí on the night the boundaries were treated as thin. The later American pumpkin is a practical substitution once Irish immigrants met a larger, easier vegetable. A related legend, Jack of the Lantern, tells of a man who tricked the Devil and was refused both heaven and hell; he was given a glowing coal in a hollowed turnip to light his endless wandering. Peasants carved the same vegetables to keep that wandering light from their own doors.

Medieval English souling supplies the door-to-door piece. Children and the poor went house to house on All Souls’ Eve singing and praying for the household dead in exchange for small cakes marked with a cross—“soul cakes.” The exchange is older than candy and older than costumes as we know them. It is a transaction with the dead that still required a physical token and a spoken request.

The modern plastic bucket and the porch light are distant descendants of a turnip with a face and a small cake offered for the names of the dead.
