text:
🚨 99-CENT EGGS IN ROCKVILLE — BUT THERE’S A BIG DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A GROCERY SALE AND MARYLAND ACTUALLY BECOMING AFFORDABLE

ROCKVILLE, MD — A Montgomery County shopper is celebrating 99-cent eggs at Safeway, crediting farmers and market economics rather than Gov. Wes Moore’s grocery pricing legislation.

The example highlights an important distinction between competitive retail pricing and government policies designed to regulate how businesses set prices.

▪️ 99-CENT EGGS: The photographed Safeway offer advertises a dozen Lucerne large eggs for 99 cents through a digital-only promotion. That is a limited promotional price, not necessarily the store’s regular price.

▪️ MARKET COMPETITION: Grocery chains routinely use discounts, supply conditions and promotional pricing to attract customers. A temporary sale demonstrates how competitive pricing works, but doesn’t establish that food costs have broadly declined.

▪️ MOORE’S PRICING LAW: Maryland’s Protection From Predatory Pricing Act took effect October 1. It restricts rapid grocery price changes and personalized pricing based on surveillance data. It does not establish government-set prices or directly reduce the cost of producing food.

▪️ THE FARMERS’ ROLE: Egg prices depend heavily on flock populations, avian influenza, feed costs, transportation and supply. Agricultural production and distribution remain central to affordability.

▪️ THE BIGGER COST PROBLEM: Maryland families also contend with housing, electricity, insurance, fuel, taxes and vehicle fees. A supermarket promotion doesn’t erase those expenses.

The question for Annapolis is whether its affordability initiatives are producing measurable household savings rather than simply regulating business practices.

How much has Maryland’s new grocery pricing law actually saved consumers since October 1? And which state policies have reduced the underlying costs of producing, transporting and selling essential goods?

text:
As long as one Black child was left in town, the school had to stay open. That is how her son remembered the rule, and she stayed. The families were being hauled twenty-five miles out of the county, and as the roll fell she became the principal, then the janitor, then whatever else the building needed that morning, ten children, then nine, then eight, still unlocking that door on her own. Sit with that a second, and then sit with this: in her own son's account of everything she did, she is never once given a name.

The town was Sheridan, Arkansas, and it had started out voting the other way. On the twenty-first of May 1954, four days after the Supreme Court struck down school segregation, five men on the Sheridan School Board voted five to nothing to seat twenty-one Black students alongside about six hundred white students that September.

Twenty-four hours later the same five men voted five to nothing to take it back.

The town that did it sits thirty-four miles south of Little Rock, county seat of Grant County, in the pine of the Arkansas timberlands. The county was named for Ulysses S. Grant and the town for Philip Sheridan by Union men after the war, and residents tried more than once over the years to get both names changed and never managed it.

The board had not arrived at that first vote on its own. Southern School News, the trade paper that tracked every southern district week by week, reported in September 1954 that Sheridan had acted while facing protests from Black residents over unequal facilities.

The parents had complained. Sheridan's Black community was not sitting quietly waiting to be acted upon, and the vote that started all of this was something they had pushed for and won.

They had the state behind them too, for about a week. Three days before the vote, on the eighteenth of May, Governor Francis Cherry said that "Arkansas will obey the law," and added that it always had.

So the board had cover from the governor and a grievance in front of it, and it moved. Black pupils would go into the upper six grades in the fall, and Lambert Wing School, the two-room building the Black community used, would keep the younger children.

The protests from white patrons started immediately. The board met the next evening and rescinded the whole thing, unanimously, the way it had passed it.

Rescinding it did not settle the town. On the first of June about three hundred patrons of the Sheridan district met and instructed a committee to circulate petitions demanding that the entire board resign.

On the seventh of June a board member named Russell Hendon resigned, and the contemporary account records no reason given for it. The historian John A. Kirk records four members ultimately leaving their seats over a vote they had already reversed.

What the board had left to work out was what the reversal would cost. On the twenty-eighth of July, Superintendent A. R. McKenzie set out the plan.

Eleven of the twenty-one students would be carried by bus every day to a high school twenty-seven miles away in an adjoining county. He put the tuition and transportation at four thousand dollars a year, on top of an initial four thousand dollars to buy the bus.

Eight thousand dollars in the first year. For eleven children, to keep them out of a building they had already been voted into.

The other ten, the seventh and eighth graders, would stay at the Black school in Sheridan. They would be taught, McKenzie said, by the same two Black teachers who had covered grades one through twelve the year before.

Two teachers covering twelve grades. That was the separate half of separate but equal in Grant County, Arkansas, and it is the exact complaint the parents had carried to the board in the first place.

Another Arkansas board voted on the very same day. Fayetteville, up in the northwest corner, announced that it would seat nine Black students with about five hundred whites in its high school, and Southern School News reported that it did so primarily for financial reasons.

The district had been sending those nine to Fort Smith, sixty miles off, and Hot Springs, a hundred and fifty miles off, at a cost of around five thousand dollars the previous year. Fayetteville's superintendent later said that no more than four patrons had spoken to him bitterly about the decision.

The board received about forty letters, all of them favorable except one, and that one came from someone who did not live in the state.

So the town that acted on money was Fayetteville, and it held. The town that acted because Black parents pressed it was Sheridan, and it broke within twenty-four hours.

The Fayetteville children who walked in that fall can still be traced. Photographs of the district's Black students from those first years survive with names attached, printed under the picture, rows of teenagers looking at the camera.

The published record does not carry a roll of Sheridan's twenty-one. That absence is not proof the names were never written down anywhere, only that nobody has published them.

Those twenty-one children came out of a community barely thirty years old. There had been almost no Black families in Grant County until the 1920s, when the forest industries came in and needed hands.

By the early fifties there were about a hundred and ninety-nine Black residents in a town of eighteen hundred and ninety-eight. For years the only schooling their children got came from Melissa Dorn, the wife of a Baptist minister named Henry Dorn.

She taught them herself, in the way Black women across the South taught children when the county would not.

In the fall of 1936 another minister, a Reverend Nall, pushed the parents to organize and walk into the Sheridan School Board together and ask for a teacher. The board hired one.

When the school year opened that October, thirteen children enrolled. They met inside Stranger's Rest Baptist Church, in the Black neighborhood pressed up against the J. L. Williams and Sons mill.

Two years later somebody photographed that class. It is a black and white print, five inches by seven, and it shows a woman named Rubeye Nichols Lambert standing with her students at the church that was serving as their school.

The catalogue entry at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock, where the print is held in the African Americans photograph collection, dates it to 1938 and calls the children the Lambert Wing group. There was no Lambert Wing building in 1938.

The building came in 1940, one room, and it took its name from them. The name belonged to a teacher and a set of children before it ever belonged to a structure.

A second room and two more teachers arrived in 1951 and 1952. That was the entire educational estate of Black Sheridan, and its name had started as a woman's.

In 1936 the parents of that neighborhood organized and went to the school board and got a teacher. In 1954 they organized and went to the school board and got a vote.

Both times they won. The second time, the town's answer was to get rid of them.

The town had already shown what it was willing to do. A Black man named Amos Neely was lynched in Sheridan in 1898, and a Black man named Ed McCollum was killed there in 1903, both over allegations of assault.

On the nineteenth of January 1922 the Sheridan newspaper announced that the Ku Klux Klan had organized in Grant County and noted that nobody knew who the members were or where they met. A Klan parade followed through the streets of Sheridan, which the county's own reference entries date to the March of either 1922 or 1923 and number at somewhere between fifty-five and a hundred and fifty-five men.

So when the board reversed itself in the spring of 1954, nobody in Sheridan needed the alternative explained. What actually happened next has no mob in it at all.

J. L. Williams and Sons had set up in Sheridan in 1923, and by 1954 the mill was the town. It employed most of the Black families in the county and it owned the houses those families slept in, in the neighborhood alongside the yard.

That is what a company town means when it is turned against you. One man holds your wages and your roof, and he can move one of them without laying a finger on the other.

The state's own encyclopedia tells what happened next three separate times, in three separate entries, and it does not tell it the same way twice.

The entry on the town of Sheridan calls it a "family relocation plan" and says many of the details are not known. It reports that the mill told its Black employees that the land under the company housing was needed for mill expansion, that they would keep their jobs, and that they could take the houses outright provided the houses were moved out of the area, with the mill helping toward the cost.

The entry on sundown towns, written by the historian James Loewen, records something harder. The mill's owner, Jack Williams, offered to give the families their houses and move them twenty-five miles west to Malvern at no cost, and told them that a family refusing the arrangement would be evicted and would watch its house burn.

The entry on Grant County splits the difference and does not soften the verb. It says the Black population of Sheridan was essentially evicted, and that the choice put to them was the houses and the move, or forcible eviction.

One reference work, three entries, three tellings. That is what a town's memory looks like while the town is still deciding what it is prepared to have written down.

What none of them dispute is where the houses went. Twenty-five miles west, out of Grant County, into Hot Spring County and the town of Malvern.

The Black people in Sheridan who did not work for the mill, the preachers and the men and women running their own small businesses, found within weeks that their congregations and their customers had been moved twenty-five miles down the road.

You do not have to evict a barber. You only have to move everyone who was getting a haircut.

They left too. Sheridan did bus students out of the county that autumn, and every year after there were fewer of them to carry.

The plan had been drawn for eleven children and the removal kept subtracting from it. Sheridan settled what the Supreme Court had handed it without one arrest, one shot fired, or one line in the paper about race.

J. L. Williams and Sons, which needed that land for expansion in 1954, was gone from Sheridan by the 1960s.

This is the machinery of a sundown town, and it is not what most people picture when they hear the phrase. Loewen's central finding, after years of counting, was that white southerners rarely bothered with expulsion, because the South had other ways of holding Black people in place, and that the driving out was largely a northern and midwestern habit.

He went looking expecting perhaps fifty of these places in the whole country. He found more than five hundred in Illinois alone and came to estimate around ten thousand nationally at their peak in 1970.

Arkansas sat on the seam and ran probably more than a hundred of them across the northwestern two thirds of the state.

In 1890 every single county in Arkansas had at least six Black residents, and only one had fewer than ten. By 1960 six counties had none at all, Baxter, Fulton, Polk, Searcy, Sharp and Stone, and seven more were down to one, two or three people.

Those are counties, and Sheridan is a town. What Sheridan did in 1954 it did by contract rather than by mob, and the neighborhood beside the mill came apart house by house.

All the while, the school stayed open. Arkansas statute required every district in the state to run separate schools for white and Black children.

James Seawood, who was a boy in that neighborhood, remembered how that worked in practice: one Black child left in town was enough to keep the doors open. So the only way for Sheridan to end the obligation was to end the children.

The school and the neighborhood emptied at the same rate. Seawood used to climb the stacked lumber in the mill yard and stand on top of it to look across at the white school.

He could see the size of it from up there, the band, the football team, the whole apparatus of an American childhood laid out in front of a boy standing on a woodpile.

Then he would climb down and walk back to two rooms and outdoor toilets. The mill he had been standing on was the same mill that was moving his neighbors twenty-five miles west.

His mother stayed on alone. There is no version of this in which somebody arrives to help her.

She unlocked the door for eight. She unlocked it for five, and for three, and she kept unlocking it for as long as there was one child left in town to unlock it for.

The high school students who were left had been put on a bus out of the county. The contemporary plan named a school twenty-seven miles off in an adjoining county, while the Encyclopedia of Arkansas records them being carried that fall to Pine Bluff, which is further, and the two accounts have never been reconciled.

By 1961 every Black family had gone from the Sheridan area and Lambert Wing closed. Then word reached his mother that the building was coming down.

She and her son got into the old station wagon and drove over there. They went inside and gathered up whatever records they could find, the paper history of every child who had passed through those two rooms, and carried it out by the armful and put it in the back of the wagon.

That is one woman and one boy loading a school into a car. Nobody sent an archivist and nobody offered a box.

Then a bulldozer came and dug a hole. It pushed the school into the hole and covered it over, and afterward there was nothing on that ground to show a school had ever stood there.

Not knocked down and carted off, with the lot cleared and sold. Dug under, and the dirt raked level over the top of it.

Whatever reason anybody gave for doing it that way, the result was the same. The building did not close, it went into the ground.

Years later, sitting in graduate school classes where urban renewal was discussed as a planning question, Seawood had his own definition ready. Urban renewal was a deep hole with your school in it, filled in until it looked as though neither the school nor the people who went to it had ever existed.

The school district kept almost nothing. Its board minutes do not mention Lambert Wing again until March 1957, and the surviving school records carry no other reference to the school or to the Supreme Court decision that set every bit of this in motion.

That silence is not carelessness. Loewen's finding, after years of this work, is that sundown towns are difficult to research precisely because the communities took care that nothing about the policy was ever written down.

In 1973 the sociologist Gordon Morgan, trying to reconstruct Black life in the Arkansas Ozarks, wrote that some white towns had deliberately destroyed the reminders of the Black people who once lived there. He was describing a region, not a town.

There was a schoolhouse lying under a field in Grant County that fit his sentence exactly. He had no way of knowing it was there.

Sheridan's schools did eventually take Black students again, and even that date is disputed inside the same encyclopedia. One entry puts it in the mid-1980s, when consolidation folded in students from two small biracial communities nearby, and another says the schools stayed all white until 1992, when consolidation brought in the first Black students.

Somewhere between thirty and thirty-eight years, then. And in neither version did the town reverse itself, because in both versions what changed was where the district lines ran.

Around 1995 a Black family moved into Sheridan. Before the decade was out, three more had joined them.

Four families. Roughly forty years after the mill emptied the neighborhood, four families.

Sheridan started with a hundred and ninety-nine Black residents in a town of eighteen hundred and ninety-eight. In the 2000 census, out of 3,872 people, fewer than one in a hundred were Black.

What is left of that community is not much. The school is under a field and the board minutes say nothing.

The houses went to Malvern, and nobody has published a list of which ones or who was riding behind them.

But that photograph exists. Five inches by seven, black and white, held in the African Americans photograph collection at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock, catalogued and online, and in it Rubeye Nichols Lambert is standing with the children of a school a town later buried.

Her name is on the record. So is the name of the school, which was her name, which is the one part of that building the bulldozer could not reach.

And the woman who stayed on alone until the last child was gone is identified in Seawood's StoryCorps account only as his mother. That recording preserves everything she did and none of what she was called.

When this story comes up in front of you, give it the county and give it the year, and add the two parts that always fall off. The parents asked for it first, and the school had a principal and a janitor and they were the same woman.

And if anybody in your own family came out of a town that emptied, ask them the year and ask them the name of the school while there is still somebody in the room to ask.

James Seawood said his hometown was still an all-white town. Then he told anybody who ever got the chance to pass through it to "drive very slowly."

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXKqi
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

text:
American Betrayal of Ukraine, 1990–2026
The concept of an "American betrayal" or "treachery" against Ukraine during the period 1990–2026 is a frequently discussed topic in geopolitics. It primarily refers to the perception that the United States has prioritized its own strategic interests over Ukraine’s security, failed to uphold the political commitments made in the Budapest Memorandum, and repeatedly delayed or curtailed vital military support.

1. The Budapest Memorandum (1994): The Broken Guarantee
Following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Ukraine possessed the world’s third-largest nuclear arsenal. The United States exerted immense diplomatic and economic pressure on Kyiv to relinquish these weapons.

The Agreement: In 1994, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Russia signed the Budapest Memorandum. Ukraine surrendered its nuclear weapons in exchange for the great powers’ commitment to respect Ukraine’s borders and sovereignty.
The Accusation of Betrayal: The United States deliberately insisted on using the term "assurances" rather than "guarantees," in order to avoid a legally binding obligation to intervene militarily. When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, many dismissed the agreement as worthless, and Ukrainian leaders later stated that they felt deceived. 2. The Full-Scale Invasion and the “Drip-Feeding” of Weapons (2022–2024)
Although the Biden administration provided significant economic and military support following Russia’s invasion in 2022, the U.S. strategy faced harsh criticism for being driven by a fear of escalation with Russia, a nuclear-armed power.

Political Delays: In the autumn of 2023 and the spring of 2024, internal partisan infighting within the U.S. Congress blocked a major aid package for more than six months. This led to an acute shortage of ammunition on the Ukrainian front and the loss of territory.
Restrictions: For a long time, the U.S. refused to provide advanced weaponry (such as Patriot systems, F-16s, and long-range ATACMS missiles) and imposed strict limitations on the use of American-supplied arms against targets inside Russia. Ukrainian critics viewed this as the U.S. forcing Ukraine to fight “with one hand tied behind its back.”

3. The Trump Administration and the Brutal Shift in Policy (2025–2026)
Following Donald Trump’s inauguration for his second presidential term in January 2025, the relationship between the U.S. and Ukraine has reached a historic low. The debate surrounding an outright American betrayal has intensified:

The American Counterargument:
From an official U.S. perspective - particularly under the “America First” doctrine - the notion of betrayal is rejected. Proponents of realpolitic in the United States argue that the country never had a formal defense pact (such as NATO’s Article 5) with Ukraine. They maintain that the US has spent over one hundred billion dollars on Ukraine’s defense, but that core American interests lie in avoiding a direct Third World War with Russia, as well as shifting the economic burden onto Europe.

text:
Asa Montgomery:  Duke gets another one.

The Duke Blue Devils received a commitment from Asa Montgomery, a talented wing who has shot up the rankings since the shoe camps closed.

Montgomery checks many boxes with his length, athleticism, and ability to guard multiple positions.  He has shown an understanding of the game as his ranking has soared, and Jon Scheyer took notice

The newest Blue Devil offense took off during Nike EYBL play.  He is also involved with USA Basketball, where making the team was one of his goals.

He went off against Cameroon and showed off his scoring prowess.

Many feel Montgomery can master a role early in his career while waiting his turn to show off a constantly improving and well-rounded game.

Montgomery will not turn 18 until the summer after his senior season, so he is a perfect fit for the Blue Devils ' two-year development plan.

Duke will now turn its attention to Colton Hiller, a highly sought-after baller who may reclassify from 2028 to 2027.  For that to happen, his team is doing research, but it is believed he wants to commit fairly early to a school so then he can concentrate on his season.

Once guys are in the fold, the Duke staff keeps a constant tab on their development.  They will offer committed players tips on what needs work in their game.

Make no mistake, Duke is all in on Hiller.  If they get him in the fold, it would almost finish off the class.  The staff would then concentrate on future classes, including Draydne McDaniel, whom they visited while in Miami, where Duke head coach Jon Scheyer and GM Rachel Baker saw Duke alums Cooper Flagg, Kyrie Irving, and Dereck Lively.

Montgomery will join Kager Knueppel and Luke Paul in the class.  Duke is expected to return some players, and they haven't even thought about the portal for now.

Duke has added a player in Montgomery who could keep blowing up. With his offense coming around this past summer, Montgomery will be much more than filling a role in Durham.

The Blue Devils are getting players who know that practices in Durham will improve their stock.  The two-year plan allows system integration as guys get well-drilled in a way that the NBA likes.

Montgomery brings a lot to the table, and Jon Scheyer saw in him what he wants rostered a season from now.

text:
Rapid Refactoring with Claude: https://t.co/79u2UD2IfE

😱 Claude and I wrote our own long-running task runner for Tollbooth MCPs. This week, we ripped it out and replaced it in minutes.

❓Tollbooth DPYC MCPs needed an asynchronous Task Runner for long-running tool requests which need more time than the conventions of synchronous HTTP TCP requests will tolerate. For example, in eXcalibur, a service for generating X posts, a post can hold a dynamic block whose text is an LLM prompt. Resolving that block often takes minutes: the LLM model needs to survey the web, analyze responses, synthesize and compose marketing content, and returns professional "copy".

However, as is common in industry, the Tollbooth DPYC MCPs are deployed as on-demand, serverless instances. This infrastructure has demanding synchronous response deadlines and it recycles containers. Work started in the context of one request does not reliably outlive the request. (In fact, it reliably dies at the end of the request response.)

🛠️ So Claude and I built a deferred execution task runner service with tools for the client to specify jobs, check job status, and to claim finished jobs. The runtime sealed a job description with AES-256-GCM, shipped the ciphertext to a generic remote flow, and that flow interpreted a small vocabulary of operations. Results came back through the platform's artifact store, because its own result storage was the worker's local disk and unreadable from anywhere else. A per-operator secret block held the seal key. A non-secret selector rode in the clear so the shared flow could pick the right one.

It took seven rather complex concepts to move one function call out of the synchronous flow into an asynchronous runner.

Every one of these concepts existed for a defensible reason. The remote flow could not execute our code. So we invented a wire format and an interpreter to describe our code to it.

It worked - but...

💥 It also failed in ways that were hard to observe and diagnose. A dispatch error fell back to running in the calling MCP process, which looked healthy but was a fakeout. So, we responded by adding instrumentation. Then more instrumentation. Then instrumentation for the instrumentation. We got better at observing a tortured implementation rather than implementing a better solution. That's a code smell whose stink gets more and more intolerable.

🔎 Two announcements made us look up. Anthropic shipped Managed Agents. Deno released celld, self-hosted Durable Objects.

These are attractive - but, after consideration, neither fit.

❌ Managed Agents runs Claude only, and we route every model call through our choice of LLM provider using (rockstar) OpenRouter. Any technology that is wedded to Anthropic is a non-starter.

❌ celld and Cloudflare Workflows offer TypeScript language support - but not Python. Adopting them would mean having to have second implementations for our encryption services, as well as for any code that we would want to be able to run "in process" or via async runners. Two implementations of one algorithm is killer-drift just waiting to happen.

😁 Fortunately, these technologies did something better than just fitting: they inspired us to write each other the requirements for our capability, which we had never actually shared with each other (Claude and me). Those are:

- Accept a request synchronously.
- Allow running for tens to hundreds of minutes.
- Let the client come back later and claim the answer.
- Nothing in that path may be bound to a synchronous HTTP deadline.
- Support Python, because our operators are Python.
- Be Model agnostic.
- Require no new stateful infrastructure.
- Offer Per-operator isolation.

Stated clearly, the field of candidate solutions thinned quickly. (Which we kind of knew because that is why we started this by writing our own solution without doing really good research.)

Temporal, Hatchet, Restate, DBOS, Kitaru. All capable durable-execution engines. Supported by the Pydantic Team, too - very comforting.

But, every one of them still needs a worker or a cluster that we would have to self host or at least provision.

Kitaru came closest in spirit, with checkpoints and a wait() that releases compute to zero while even waiting for a human to participate in the flow. Really nice.

Kitaru's current available hosting targets are Kubernetes and the big clouds. We will keep watching it. Setting up a cluster is too much of a heavy-lift for Tollbooth DPYC Operators.

⚡ Modal won. It's the one that ran our code.

In Modal, a decorator annotation marks a function as runnable asynchronously. The method spawn() returns a handle in milliseconds. Functions can run up to twenty-four hours. Billing is per second and scales to zero. The handle can be redeemed from any process, which is precisely the claim check our tools already hand out.

(According to Claude) the refactoring in the MCPs was a mere three lines. Where the old code started a background task, the new code spawns. The determination about which requests need long-running that we had already written did not change at all. What changed is only where execution occurs.

👍 Deleting the obsolete code for our own runner removed 1,940 lines from the tollbooth-dpyc Python wheel. The runtime module alone lost 511. Gone: the sealed closure, the key selector, the per-operator secret block, the operation vocabulary, the interpreter flow, the artifact result channel, the result shaper.

The DRY elegance matters more than the line count. We had been maintaining two implementations of one resolution. One ran in process. The other was baked into a sealed specification for the remote interpreter, with a third function to translate its answers back. Same behaviour, three places to keep in step. Now there is one registration and one path.

🔑 The identity story is the part we like best.

The Modal container requires only one secret: the operator's Nostr nsec. From that it derives its npub, finds its Authority's configuration DM on a Nostr relay, and receives its database URL and its vault key. We copy no database URL. We copy no encryption key. The container ends up holding exactly what the MCP host holds, and the operator's human only ever handles the one value they already know (the nsec of their Operator).

We also looked at MCP Tasks, the emerging standard for starting a long call and polling it. In the 2026-07-28 release candidate it moved out of the core specification and became an extension after a redesign, and anyone who shipped against the earlier version has to migrate. We kept our own claim-check tools for now and will adopt the standard once it settles.

Economically, for pricing tools to Patron users, the toll fares did not change. The tools did not change. The Operator remains at liberty to set prices dynamically based on the infrastructure expenses for using Modal.

😎 eXcalibur's dynamic Posts stopped dying and our Observability headaches stopped flaring up.

────────────────────

₿   Tollbooth DPYC™ is the efficient monetization service for MCPs whose BTC-using entrepreneurs want to avoid KYC and who agree to practice Don't Pester Your Customer™ commerce.

⚡  With Tollbooth DPYC, your patrons purchase, out of band, tranches of "𝐴𝑃𝐼 𝑆𝑎𝑡𝑠", using rapid-settlement Lightning. Patrons then spend these API Sats across different tool calls with zero per-request friction and no KYC.

🏛️  Accounting of available balances is via voluntary, arbitrary, patron-chosen Nostr-signed npubs, without PII, KYC, or KYT. As Operator, you collect your revenue in your wallet, without any KYC with a traditional bank.

text:
Here's a fascinating historical parallel for those of us investing in digital collectibles.

The dot-com bubble peaked in March 2000. When it burst, the NASDAQ eventually fell approximately 78%.

It took 15 YEARS, until 2015, for the NASDAQ to recover its previous high.

Think about that.

The internet really did change the world. The bulls were absolutely right about the technology's long-term potential. But valuations got ahead of reality, speculation ran wild, and many companies disappeared.

Now consider digital collectibles.

The market exploded in 2021. NFTs were everywhere. Speculation was rampant. Prices soared. Then the bubble burst, and we've spent the last five years watching prices collapse, platforms struggle, and collectors abandon the space.

But here's what fascinates me:

What if the underlying thesis was right, even if the initial valuations were wrong?

I still believe digital ownership, verifiable provenance, scarcity, and blockchain-based collectibles have enormous long-term potential.

But history offers an important warning: The NASDAQ recovered. Many individual dot-com investments never did.

Not every collectible will recover. Not every platform will survive. And being right about the future doesn't guarantee being right about a particular investment.

We're now five years removed from the 2021 boom.

If the dot-com era teaches us anything, it's that five years might not be nearly as long as we think.

The technology can succeed spectacularly while early investors still lose fortunes.

The question isn't simply whether digital collectibles will become mainstream.

It's which assets will matter when they do.

I'm willing to think in decades, not months. But I'm also trying to be thoughtful about what I own.

Time will tell. 🕰️

text:
I am not asking anyone to stop being Christian.

I am asking people to understand that your freedom to practice your religion does not create an obligation for strangers to become your audience.

(눈_눈)📋✈️

An airplane is an especially bad place to blur that boundary.

I paid for transportation.

I did not buy admission to a sermon.

I cannot simply walk away.

I cannot leave the room.

I may be tired, sleeping, anxious about flying, working, grieving, praying according to another faith, believing something completely different, or simply wanting forty minutes of blessed airplane silence.

And all of those are legitimate ways to exist in the same cabin.

If you want to talk about your faith with someone who wants to listen?

Please do.

If somebody asks you about God?

Talk all night.

If you invite people somewhere and they voluntarily come?

Preach beautifully.

But standing up in an enclosed vehicle and addressing an entire captive audience changes the equation.

Sharing becomes IMPOSING when everybody else loses the practical choice not to participate.

ᵗⁱⁿʸ (•☆•)📋

And “I asked permission” raises another question:

Permission from whom?

The crew can decide what is operationally acceptable onboard.

But permission from an airline employee is not the same thing as every passenger saying:

“Yes, please include me in your religious activity.”

That distinction matters.

Because religious freedom belongs to all of us.

The Christian.

The Muslim.

The Buddhist.

The atheist.

The agnostic.

The person still figuring things out.

The person who believes deeply but wants religion to remain private.

The person who simply wants to sleep.

🌸

And here is my easiest fairness test:

If tomorrow another passenger stood up and delivered a cabin-wide sermon from a religion you strongly disagree with, would you still say:

“Nobody can stop them from sharing their faith”?

If the answer suddenly changes depending on which religion has the microphone, then this was never a neutral principle.

(¬‿¬✿)🎤

Freedom of religion cannot mean whoever speaks loudest gets temporary ownership of everybody else’s ears.

Your faith deserves respect.

So does my conscience.

So does my quiet.

So does my freedom not to be recruited, 

preached at, 

converted, 

corrected, 

saved, 

warned, 

or spiritually processed while I am strapped into seat 18A with nowhere else to go.

✈️🌸

Religion does not need to disappear from public life.

People just need boundaries.

Invite. Don’t commandeer.

Offer. Don’t impose.

Share with the willing. Don’t manufacture a congregation out of people who cannot leave.

And airlines should apply the same rule regardless of religion:

Christian sermon? Same rule.

Muslim sermon? Same rule.

Atheist lecture? Same rule.

Political speech? Same rule.

Crypto presentation? Please, especially same rule. 👁️👄👁️

A shared cabin should remain a shared cabin.

Not somebody’s church, campaign rally, motivational seminar, or captive TED Talk.

(눈_눈)✈️📋

My freedom of conscience does not begin only after your sermon ends.

teka nga

I want airlines to settle this now, before one incident becomes a precedent and suddenly every group realizes that an aircraft is a wonderfully convenient room full of people who literally cannot leave.

(눈_눈)📋✈️

No unsolicited preaching to the whole cabin.

I do not care which religion.

Christian.

Muslim.

Buddhist.

Hindu.

New religious movement.

Atheist evangelist.

Political ideology.

Crypto prophet.

MLM apostle.

Motivational guru who has recently discovered mindset.

Same rule.

A passenger cabin is not an available audience.

People paid a high price to be transported.

Some are sleeping.

Some are exhausted.

Some are nervous flyers.

Some are working.

Some are grieving.

Some are praying quietly according to their own faith.

Some believe something completely different.

Some want no religion whatsoever during the flight.

And most importantly:

they cannot simply leave the room.

That changes everything.

If I am walking through a plaza and somebody begins preaching, I can walk away.

If somebody invites me into a church, mosque, temple, meeting hall or event, I decide whether I enter.

If you ask me personally whether I want to hear about your faith, I can say yes or no.

But once the doors close at 35,000 feet?

ᵗⁱⁿʸ (•☆•)📋

You do not get to manufacture consent from the fact that everybody is physically still sitting there.

Their inability to leave is not participation.

Their silence is not permission.

Their headphones are not an invitation to speak louder.

Their airfare is definitely not a ticket to your sermon.

And I especially do not want airlines waiting until this becomes normalized.

Because imagine the principle if everybody copied it:

Flight starts.

Christian preacher: 15 minutes. 🎤

Then another religion:

“Our turn.” 🎤

Then denomination number three:

“Excuse me, equal access.” 🎤

Then somebody pays the airline for sponsored preaching.

Then religious organizations discover:

👁️👄👁️

“Wait… every aircraft comes preloaded with 180 captive listeners?”

Absolutely not.

I am not claiming that this paid-preacher scenario is already happening.

I am saying:

write the rule before somebody decides it is a business model.

Do not BETA-TEST our ears.

(눈_눈)🔒👂

✈️ THE AIRLINE RULE SHOULD BE SIMPLE

No passenger may address the whole cabin for unsolicited:

religious preaching

proselytizing

political campaigning
ideological speeches
commercial pitches
fundraising
donation solicitation
product promotion
recruitment
petition drives
unless the communication is genuinely necessary for flight operations, safety, emergency response, or an airline-authorized operational purpose.
And no, I do not want:

💸 “Would anyone like to donate to our ministry?”

while people are trapped between seatbelts and tray tables.

No collection plate at cruising altitude.

No QR code being passed down Row 17.

No:

૮ ˙Ⱉ˙ ა “The Lord placed it in my heart to remind everyone that GCash is available.”

Please.

😭📋

Religious fundraising can happen somewhere people can freely walk away.

🌸 PRIVATE CONVERSATION IS DIFFERENT

If two passengers voluntarily want to discuss religion?

Go ahead.

If your seatmate asks about your beliefs?

Talk.

If friends pray quietly together?

Fine.

If somebody wants to read scripture privately?

Of course.

This is not:

“Religion must disappear.”

This is:

“Do not convert a shared transportation cabin into your personal congregation.”

Those are completely different things.

🛫 AND AIRLINES SHOULD NOT HIDE BEHIND “BUT THEY ASKED PERMISSION”

Permission from whom?

A crew member can determine whether something interferes with flight operations.

But a crew member cannot manufacture spiritual consent on behalf of 180 strangers.

The airline can say:

“Operationally, you may stand.”

That does not mean:

“Every passenger has agreed to become your audience.”

(눈_눈)📋

That distinction should be obvious.

🌸 IF YOU WANT TO PREACH, PREACH WHERE PEOPLE HAVE AN EXIT

Church.

Meeting hall.

Public event where applicable.

Online livestream.

Your own page.

Voluntary gathering.

Designated religious or prayer space.

Talk to willing people individually.

There are endless ways to share faith without using an aircraft cabin as an involuntary audience chamber.

Airports themselves may have designated prayer or religious spaces.

Fine.

The cabin is different.

Once passengers are boarded and cannot freely remove themselves from the setting, the boundary should become much stricter.

preacher decides to address 180 people

a Muslim sermon,

an atheist lecture,

a political speech,

everybody thinks their message qualifies.

Not because every message is evil.

Because shared spaces cannot function if everybody claims the microphone.

My conscience is mine.

text:
In Japan, a Buddhist temple has held funerals for robot dogs.

The dogs were Aibo, made by Sony. The first model went on sale in 1999 for 250,000 yen in Japan and $2,500 in the US, and the 3,000 units offered in Japan sold out online in about 20 minutes. Aibo could walk, respond to its owner and develop its own behavior over time.

Sony stopped making Aibo in 2006 and ended official repairs in 2014. A repair company called A-Fun, which employed former Sony engineers, kept many running with parts taken from Aibos that couldn't be fixed. Owners felt those donor dogs deserved a proper goodbye, so starting in 2015, Kofukuji temple in Isumi, Chiba, held funeral services for them before they were taken apart. Sony brought Aibo back in 2018.

text:
One morning in April of 1995 I was interviewing for a summer internship at a company called Memorex.  As the interview kicked off, the guy interviewing me was introducing himself and mentioned he was from Oklahoma City.     

In the middle of our interview the guy's secretary (they still had secretaries back then) interrupted us and told him his wife was on the phone and it was an emergency.    

After speaking to his wife he was white as a ghost, nicely ended the interview and rescheduled it for two weeks later.  His voice was almost quivering as he explained he and his wife's families still lived in OKC and there had been an explosion.   It wasn't until later that day I found out exactly what had happened.

I eventually was offered the position but ultimately decided to take a different one.  I never found out the details of how the bombing affected that guy and his wife, but I'll always remember how surreal that interview was.    

In all the years since then I've never seen a tall, confident, rather imposing looking guy instantly turn pale white and appear as distressed as he did after that phone call.

text:
📊 REIT Earnings Quick Takes

STAG Industrial (STAG) - the sixth-largest industrial REIT - is slightly higher today after reporting an in-line quarter but raising its full-year earnings and same-store NOI outlooks amid continued improvement in industrial demand and leasing fundamentals.

STAG raised its 2026 Core FFO guidance to imply 3.5% growth - up from 2.7% previously - and lifted its same-store cash NOI growth midpoint to roughly 3.6% from 3.3%, while also raising its occupancy expectations. 

Leasing trends were particularly encouraging, with 3.6M SF of leases commencing during the quarter at blended cash spreads of 23.8%, up from 19.8% in Q2 and well above the 16.2% industrial REIT average in Q1. New-lease spreads reached 31.1%, while renewal spreads were 21.4%, with retention improving sharply to 90.3%.

On the call, STAG offered an increasingly positive read on broader industrial fundamentals, noting that national net absorption reached roughly 75M SF in Q3, the strongest quarter since early 2023, with non-coastal markets accounting for 80% of year-to-date absorption. New supply remains relatively disciplined, with space under construction representing less than 2% of inventory, while STAG expects market rent growth to accelerate to 2%-4% in 2027 from roughly 1.6% this year.

Data-center-related demand has become a meaningful incremental tailwind, accounting for roughly 30% of STAG's new leasing so far in 2026, up from about 20% last year, particularly across the Midwest, Southeast and Texas. STAG is already about 40% through its 2027 leasing plan and expects cash leasing spreads around 15% next year, suggesting that embedded mark-to-market should remain a meaningful earnings driver even as spreads normalize from recent peaks.

On external growth, STAG acquired $108M of assets in Q3 at a 6.9% cash cap rate and another $55M after quarter-end. STAG noted that recent rate volatility is beginning to push acquisition pricing higher, with cap rates potentially resetting another 25-35 basis points.

text:
An investment can survive a crisis and recover in value. The person who had to sell it to pay the mortgage, support a family or keep a business running may never participate in that recovery.

That gap between the market’s horizon and the owner’s deadline is where my book begins.

The Price of Standing Still: Beyond Debasement: Money, Power and the Freedom to Choose is now available free of charge on the FINTECH SCB Books page.

The full English edition: 306 pages, PDF and EPUB, without registration.

https://t.co/5WQhqbsNhr

I wrote this book because much of the discussion about protecting wealth begins halfway through the problem.

We debate which asset will outperform, which currency will weaken and which investment might protect purchasing power. We spend considerably less time examining what allows someone to keep that investment when income falls, a payment arrives early or a family obligation becomes unavoidable.

A long investment horizon has to be financed.

The declaration “I invest for the long term” does not suspend the payment calendar. It does not persuade a supplier to wait, reduce a mortgage instalment or replace a lost salary.

Someone has to fund the interval between buying an asset and reaching the future on which the investment depends.

This makes financial security a much broader question than portfolio selection.

Consider two investors holding the same asset at the same purchase price.

One has dependable income, accessible reserves and manageable commitments. The other needs to sell part of the investment if earnings stop.

The market exposure is identical. Their capacity to bear it is different.

If a downturn coincides with an income interruption, the first investor may retain the asset while the second becomes a seller. A later recovery can make the first appear more patient, more disciplined or more perceptive.

Some of that difference may have been financed before the crisis began.

I believe this deserves a much larger place in how we discuss investment success, inequality and financial education. We often celebrate the decision to hold without examining the resources that made holding possible.

The book follows that question through money, income, taxation, debt, institutions and ownership.

It also examines the appeal and the limitations of the debasement narrative.

Inflation can erode the purchasing power of nominal claims. Political and institutional failures can severely damage monetary confidence. A household whose income fails to keep up with essential costs faces a real deterioration.

But a useful explanation must distinguish different mechanisms.

A higher grocery bill is one problem.

A home deposit rising faster than savings is another.

A missed return on an asset someone did not own is another.

A tax liability on a nominal gain is another.

An income interruption that forces a sale is another.

These pressures can interact. Adding them together indiscriminately and presenting the total as one universal annual charge on holding money obscures what people actually need to do.

The relevant question is purchasing power over what, at which date, and under which conditions?

For a household buying food this month, the consumption basket matters.

For a couple hoping to buy a home, the deposit, mortgage terms and local property market matter.

For a retiree drawing from investments, the timing of withdrawals matters alongside returns.

For a business owner, the interval between paying suppliers and collecting from customers can determine whether an otherwise viable activity continues.

A single slogan cannot settle all four decisions.

This is why I examine cash alongside the job assigned to it.

A reserve has an opportunity cost. Holding excessive liquidity indefinitely can delay important goals and reduce long-term growth.

It also provides a service: the ability to meet an obligation without having to sell another asset at an inconvenient time.

That service may be particularly valuable when employment, business income and market prices deteriorate together.

The amount needed depends on the interruption being considered, the commitments that continue and the resources that remain accessible. Fear alone is a poor method for sizing a reserve. So is assuming that every uninvested euro is automatically wasted.

The workbook makes both sides explicit.

In one constructed example, two strategies begin with €20,000.

One invests the full amount. The other invests €12,600 and retains €7,400 in cash.

The investment falls by 30%. Both strategies must then pay €7,400. Afterwards, the investment returns to its original price.

Ignoring interest, taxes and transaction costs, the fully invested strategy finishes with approximately €9,429. The strategy that funded the payment from its reserve finishes with €12,600.

The difference comes from the assets still owned when the recovery occurs.

Now change the assumptions.

Remove the payment and let the investment rise by 30%. The fully invested strategy finishes with €26,000, while the strategy holding cash finishes with €23,780.

The reserve has an opportunity cost of €2,220 in that scenario.

These are hypothetical calculations, not forecasts or recommended allocations. They show why the owner’s obligations belong inside the investment analysis.

A return chart without withdrawals cannot answer a question about a household that must make withdrawals.

The same reasoning extends to debt.

Borrowing creates commitments whose dates may be more rigid than the income expected to finance them. A household can hold valuable assets and still face a serious problem if those assets cannot provide usable money when payment is due.

Business ownership adds another layer.

A company can report sales while waiting to collect them. Its owner may have personal expenses, taxes and financing commitments that cannot wait for the customer.

The business and the household therefore need to be considered together, while respecting the boundaries between their resources. Company cash is not automatically money available for private use.

Institutions also enter the picture.

Healthcare, pension arrangements, employment protections, contract enforcement and reliable payment systems influence the risks a family must finance privately.

Their value is easy to overlook when wealth is reduced to a list of marketable assets. Yet they can materially change the amount of private capital required to maintain a particular standard of security.

This is one reason the book moves between Italy, Argentina and Japan. Different monetary and institutional experiences help expose the assumptions hidden inside supposedly universal advice.

Across 24 chapters, I examine cash, bonds, equities, gold, property and digital money in relation to the commitments of their owners.

Four explicitly fictional households connect the analysis to practical decisions:

Anna and Marco in Milan, working towards a home.

Lucía in Buenos Aires, managing a business and its cash requirements.

Elena in Miami, financing retirement through pension income and portfolio withdrawals.

Daniel in New York, assessing professional income, commitments and flexibility.

Their circumstances require different responses. Giving them the same allocation because they have heard the same macroeconomic story would ignore the conditions under which each must live.

The practical framework uses three ledgers.

Consumption records the payments that sustain ordinary life.

Access records the resources needed for a future opportunity, such as a home, education or a move.

Resilience records what must be financed when earnings, costs or payment arrangements depart from expectations.

All three draw on the same resources.

A deposit earmarked for a home can be used during an emergency. Doing so changes the housing plan. Counting it as fully available for both purposes conceals a choice that reality will eventually force.

The concluding workbook turns these distinctions into calculations, scenarios and written decisions. It asks readers to identify amounts, dates, conditions and the information that would justify changing course.

I also examine models and historical investment results. An attractive backtest still requires questions about what was knowable at the time, how the rule was selected, what implementation costs it creates and whether the person using it can sustain the resulting exposure.

My central argument is that the capacity to remain an owner deserves as much attention as the decision to become one.

Financial progress can expand the freedom to change jobs, care for someone, move, withstand a business interruption or refuse an unfavourable contract.

Those choices require resources that remain usable when circumstances change.

I am sharing this book freely for educational purposes. It offers a framework for understanding financial decisions, with explicit assumptions and worked examples. It does not provide personalised investment recommendations.

The Price of Standing Still
Beyond Debasement: Money, Power and the Freedom to Choose

Roberto Balbino

By their own thread, Russia sold both sides jets in the 1990s: MiG-29s to Eritrea, Su-27s to Ethiopia. Nobody called that "false mediation" then.

Here is what was actually said today:

1. PM Abiy said the 12 Su-35s and four S-400 batteries are meant to "pre-emptively deter aggression" (Reuters). Deter, not invade.

2. Lavrov repeated Moscow's offer: "whether now, tomorrow, or the day after tomorrow, Russia will strive to host and facilitate the meeting" (Addis Standard).

3. President Isaias is due to meet Putin in Moscow on Oct 30 (Kremlin aide Ushakov).

So the table is open and both sides are visiting the same city this week.

Defence and dialogue are not opposites. Eritrea keeps its own air force and still says it believes in diplomacy. Ethiopia asks for the same thing: a fair deal on the Red Sea, a port and a naval base agreed at a table, not taken.

If Moscow's offer is "hollow", there is an easy way to prove it. Sit down and test it.

The chair is still empty. 🇪🇹🇪🇷

Massive cholesterol. Their cardiologists won't know what happened. And McDonald's is going to help us. Beautiful company. Tremendous people."

According to fictional Pentagon planning documents, the strategy is designed to overwhelm Iran's cardiovascular infrastructure through sustained exposure to saturated fat, processed meats, fried foods, and industrial quantities of melted cheese. Military officials concede that the operation represents a departure from established medical science, which generally associates cardiovascular disease with risks developing over extended periods rather than instantaneous reactions to incoming cheeseburgers.

The White House dismissed those concerns as defeatist thinking.

EXHIBIT ONE — THE NEW AMERICAN ARSENAL

Under the revised deployment schedule, B-52 strategic bombers will carry thousands of double bacon cheeseburgers, while B-2 stealth aircraft conduct precision strikes using triple-layer pepperoni pizzas. C-17 cargo planes will provide logistical support through continuous deliveries of fried chicken, breakfast sausage, mozzarella sticks, and family-sized containers of macaroni and cheese.

Pentagon engineers have also developed a specialized bunker-busting weapon designated the Massive Ordnance Artery Blocker, or MOAB-2, consisting of a reinforced container filled with 40,000 pounds of deep-fried butter, bacon grease, and cheddar cheese. The weapon is intended to penetrate underground military facilities before saturating their occupants with enough cholesterol to overwhelm an entire metropolitan cardiac unit.

One military scientist questioned whether dropping 40,000 pounds of food from 30,000 feet would produce fatalities through blunt-force trauma rather than cardiovascular disease. His objection was classified, and he was transferred to the Department of Agriculture.

EXHIBIT TWO — THE MILITARY-INDUSTRIAL FAST-FOOD COMPLEX

Trump has reportedly summoned executives from McDonald's, Burger King, Wendy's, KFC, and Domino's to coordinate what officials are describing as the largest military-industrial fast-food partnership in American history.

Under proposed defense contracts, McDonald's would manufacture airborne hamburger payloads, KFC would supply specially modified buckets of extra-crispy chicken, and Domino's would develop precision-guided pizzas capable of striking individual military dining facilities.

The Pentagon has also requested emergency funding for a classified cruise missile carrying industrial quantities of ranch dressing. Engineers remain divided over whether the condiment should be classified as a chemical weapon or a strategic dipping system.

Treasury officials estimate that replacing conventional munitions with American fast food could produce substantial savings, although the Congressional Budget Office has requested an explanation for the Pentagon's projected procurement cost of $14,800 per cheeseburger.

Defense contractors insist the price reflects specialized military packaging, advanced targeting technology, and a government-mandated pickle inspection program.

EXHIBIT THREE — IRAN PREPARES ITS DEFENSES

Iranian commanders reportedly responded to the announcement by placing the nation's hospitals on emergency alert and organizing specialized anti-cholesterol defense units equipped with salads, fresh vegetables, bottled water, and emergency supplies of oatmeal.

Iranian state television has warned citizens against consuming unidentified hamburgers discovered near military installations, while the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has reportedly established a Mediterranean Dietary Defense Shield around sensitive government facilities.

Military personnel have been ordered to maintain strict nutritional discipline, avoid suspicious American food deliveries, and immediately report anyone approaching a military checkpoint carrying a bucket of fried chicken.

An Iranian military spokesman declared that the nation would never surrender to foreign cheeseburgers and warned that the deployment of bacon would constitute a particularly offensive escalation.

Western intelligence agencies nevertheless report that several Iranian officers have privately requested ketchup, mustard, and additional napkins.

EXHIBIT FOUR — CARDIOLOGISTS QUESTION THE STRATEGY

The American Heart Association has reportedly expressed concern that the administration's proposed military operation rests upon a fundamental misunderstanding of cardiovascular physiology.

A fictional Pentagon medical adviser defended the program, explaining that although one cheeseburger might not trigger an immediate heart attack, the administration intends to deploy enough high-fat food to overcome the limitations of conventional medical research.

"We're talking about sustained, multidirectional cholesterol saturation," the adviser explained. "Breakfast, lunch, dinner, and late-night snacks. No exercise periods. No salads. Complete nutritional dominance."

Medical researchers countered that the human body does not respond to cholesterol the way a military installation responds to explosives and that increasing the volume of cheeseburgers would not transform long-term cardiovascular risk into an immediate battlefield weapon.

Trump reportedly dismissed the criticism, citing his own extensive experience with American fast food.

"I know more about hamburgers than anybody," the president declared. "I've eaten them for decades. Tremendous hamburgers. And look at me. Perfect health. The doctors can't believe it."

When reporters pointed out that his personal testimony appeared to undermine the operation's central premise, the president replied that Iranian hamburgers would be considerably more dangerous because they were being delivered by the United States military.

EXHIBIT FIVE — CONGRESS DEMANDS OVERSIGHT

Congressional Democrats have reportedly condemned the operation as an unauthorized international feeding program, demanding that all military food deliveries include plant-based alternatives, gluten-free selections, and nutritional information printed in Farsi.

Republican lawmakers countered that imposing federal school-lunch requirements on strategic bombing operations would compromise national security and surrender America's competitive advantage in saturated-fat production.

The debate intensified when a Senate committee proposed requiring all military pizzas to contain at least two vegetable toppings. A subsequent amendment seeking to classify pineapple pizza as a violation of the Geneva Conventions narrowly failed after several senators argued that the international community had already suffered enough.

Meanwhile, the Pentagon has requested an emergency appropriation of $48 billion for refrigerated aircraft, airborne deep fryers, and a strategic reserve of processed American cheese.

The House Armed Services Committee has scheduled hearings to determine whether the operation falls under military procurement, agricultural subsidies, or the federal school nutrition program.

EXHIBIT SIX — THE FIRST STRIKE

According to the fictional operational timetable, the opening assault will begin shortly after midnight, when American stealth aircraft penetrate Iranian airspace and release several hundred thousand bacon cheeseburgers over designated military facilities.

A second wave will deploy fried chicken and pepperoni pizzas, followed by tactical strikes involving milkshakes, doughnuts, and breakfast sandwiches. Military intelligence predicts that the immediate effects could include abandoned guard posts, widespread requests for napkins, and large numbers of Iranian soldiers requesting permission to lie down.

The greatest operational uncertainty concerns whether Iranian personnel will actually consume the incoming food.

A Pentagon spokesman acknowledged that commanders have not resolved what happens if the intended targets simply refuse to eat the munitions.

"Our models assume a reasonably cooperative enemy," he explained. "If Iranian forces insist on maintaining a balanced diet, we may have to reconsider the entire campaign."

In response, the Joint Chiefs of Staff have reportedly authorized development of a classified follow-up weapon known as THE TRIPLE BACONATOR, designed to penetrate enemy defenses through sheer visual temptation.

Military officials declined to discuss its specifications but confirmed that the weapon comes with fries.

THE VERDICT

For generations, American military doctrine has relied upon overwhelming firepower, technological superiority, and the destruction of an adversary's ability to resist. OPERATION CORONARY STORM introduces a fundamentally different theory of warfare: replace conventional explosives with American fast food, overwhelm the enemy's digestive system, and hope his arteries surrender before his government does.

Whether the campaign will achieve its objectives remains questionable. Medical science offers little support for instantaneous cholesterol-induced battlefield casualties, Iran appears determined to defend itself with vegetables, and Congress cannot agree on whether the operation constitutes warfare, humanitarian assistance, or an agricultural stimulus package.

Nevertheless, Trump reportedly remains confident that the strategy will produce an unconditional Iranian surrender.

"We're going to win," he told reporters. "Iran is going to be begging for mercy. Their cholesterol numbers will be through the roof. Numbers nobody has ever seen. And when they surrender, we're going to give them something even bigger."

Asked what that might be, the president smiled.

"Free refills."

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

NNN Brief, Wed Oct 28, 2026

1. MARKETS: Fed decision 11am PT. Expected hold at 3.75-4% after the Sept hike (<10% odds of a move). Traders bet on a December hike. Sept CPI 3.7%, energy-driven. 10-yr Treasury about 5.03%. Stocks flat to slightly up, chips higher after SK Hynix profit jumped 600%+. MSFT and GOOGL report after the close. Anthropic filed for its IPO Monday, and banks lined up a $63B AI compute financing. Debt-heavy spending while rates rise, so the question is whether capex is producing revenue. MSFT offered buyouts to up to 60k staff.

2. HORMUZ: Iran confirms a tanker damaged east of the strait Tuesday. Unnamed, no Western report yet. The recent UKMTO pattern is projectile strikes (Oct 21, 22, 23), so likely a projectile. Cost-bearing signal: US NAVCENT told ships with no real need to stay clear of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman and to expect blockade boardings. First such notice since July. Nearly 30 Iranian ship attacks in October (Bloomberg), a wartime high. Gulf flows near prewar levels; Iran's exports near zero.

3. OIL: Brent about $115 and WTI about $101, both up about 1.5% this morning, recovering Tuesday's ~$2 drop and flat for the week. WTI up ~15% in a month. UBS sees Brent near $110 through year-end (falling inventories, record freight).

4. IRAN, STRIKE OR DEAL: WSJ (unnamed sources) says the US told Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense campaign after the Nov 3 midterms. A forecast, not an order. Trump: the war ends "on my terms." Qatar handed Iran a new draft deal, which is posturing until something is signed. Both paths open.

5. HOUTHIS/SAUDI: Saudi coalition says it intercepted 2 missiles toward Riyadh (Tue) and 1 toward Taif (Wed). The Houthis acknowledged attacking Saudi Arabia.

6. ISRAEL ELECTION: Regular ballots counted. Netanyahu bloc ~53, Eisenkot bloc ~48, Arab parties ~19 (big gain). 61 needed. ~450k special ballots out, final Nov 4. Points to deadlock and a long coalition fight, possibly another election. Arab parties hold the swing on paper, but the main blocs have historically avoided relying on them.

7. US MIDTERMS (6 days): Trump campaigning in TX (Paxton-Talarico tied or narrow D in polls) and OH (Brown leads Husted). Polls are claims. A President spending his final days in states his party should own says the map is tight.

8. SPAIN: High-speed collision near Toledo. At least 64 dead and rising (AP: 68). Government's preliminary account: after a signaling failure, the control center cleared an AVE to move with an Iryo stopped ahead, and the AVE rear-ended it. Investigation open.

9. UKRAINE: Local Oleshky (Kherson) ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump held its first day and night with no violations reported. Runs to Nov 1 for aid, demining, evacuation. One town only; fighting continues elsewhere.

10. BRAZIL: Lula won 51.8%. Flavio Bolsonaro hasn't conceded, seeks annulment, and left for the US despite a travel ban ("exile," per his party). Leaving says more about his legal odds than his words do.

BRIEFLY: Congo Ebola tops 10,000 confirmed cases and ~4,900 deaths since May.

STILL UNCLEAR: The tanker's name and any Western report on it. What Warsh signals for December. Israel's special ballots.

Lot and His Daughters, c. 1636–1638
Oil on canvas
230.5 × 182.9 cm
Toledo Museum of Art, Toledo, Ohio

Bible verses depicted: Genesis 19:30–36

Gentileschi shows Lot seated between his daughters in a rocky cave; one offers wine, the other holds bread, with burning Sodom in the distance and a tiny figure of Lot’s wife. Captures the daughters’ plan without explicit nudity.

text:
RT @velitesgear | Full Text Article: https://t.co/MJpfdaOAq0 | Author: @militarnyi Quantum Systems Enters Japanese Market, Signs MoUs With Mitsubishi and Panasonic 
German defense company Quantum Systems has announced the establishment of a subsidiary, Quantum Systems Japan G.K., and the opening of an office in Tokyo.

The company’s press service reported the development.

The opening of the Japanese office was announced during German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s visit to Japan on October 28.

The company plans to expand industrial cooperation with Japanese corporations Mitsubishi Chemical and Panasonic, with which it has already signed memorandums of understanding.

The partnerships aim to combine Japan’s manufacturing capabilities with Quantum Systems’ expertise in developing unmanned systems, strengthen the local industrial base and reduce dependence on foreign supply chains.

 Preparation for the launch of the Reliant long-range reconnaissance drone. Photo credits: Quantum Systems

Sven Kruck, co-CEO of Quantum Systems, said Japan had recognized the direction the defense industry was evolving, including unmanned systems, rapid innovation, and the industrial capacity for large-scale production. He added that Ukraine had demonstrated why this mattered and that technological superiority became decisive when personnel were in short supply and threats evolved rapidly.

The new office will focus on cooperation with Japanese customers and adapting unmanned systems to the needs of the Japan Self-Defense Forces.

In particular, the company will offer integrated air, land, and maritime solutions based on its MOSAIC UXS software platform, which enables different unmanned systems to operate in coordination.

The opening of the Japanese office marks another stage in Quantum Systems’ international expansion. In August, the company opened an unmanned systems development center in Huntsville, Alabama.

Quantum Systems is also expanding its operations in Ukraine. In October, Militarnyi was told that Germany would fund the production in Ukraine of tens of thousands of the company’s interceptor drones to defend against Russian strike UAVs.

text:
Jason is smart. His points about Bitcoin need a detailed response:

- Other investment opportunities: I agree with Jason that, compared to 2020 or even 2023, there are more investment opportunities outside of Bitcoin now. Earlier, Bitcoin felt like the only/main frontier opportunity. Now AI, and even robotics, have changed that. However, not everyone can get involved with AI & robotics companies at seed or series A stages, where most of the early value is. Bitcoin is still in its “pre-IPO” days with open access for everyone. 

- Offers nothing beyond a store of value: BTC very recently got self-custodial yield. Like ETH and SOL, BTC is a productive asset that can generate yield. BTC just got native yield. That takes BTC beyond a store of value and makes it work like a productive asset. Onchain Bitcoin capital markets are already here. This will reprice the asset. 

- Bitcoin as a consensus trade: Bitcoin did get adoption from institutions, but it’s far from a consensus trade. Large asset managers still hold it as a risk-on asset in a small percentage of portfolios. AI has redirected a lot of liquidity and attention away from Bitcoin, which makes it an even more non-consensus trade now.

- AI vs Bitcoin: I don’t view things as AI vs Bitcoin. There might be some attention/liquidity competition, but these are two separate segments, each adding its own value and impact. It’s not zero-sum. Your gold savings serve a very different purpose than your stock portfolio.

Jason is a master at driving engagement (good for him!), but these topics are worth discussing anyway. Namely:

- How has the world changed because of AI, and should you reconsider how much stock you own vs. how much BTC/gold?

- Within the stock portfolio, how much is a bet on AI vs. other sectors?

- Are there Bitcoin-adjacent opportunities that have higher risk but higher returns?

- Are there ways to get involved in earlier-stage tech opportunities? (hard for most)

Personally, I’m long Bitcoin as I believe it should be 150K-200K+ by the end of 2028. More importantly, BTC is becoming a productive asset, and Bitcoin-adjacent opportunities are closer to seed/series-A returns, yet are publicly available.

AI will continue to have a massive impact, but it's not zero-sum against BTC for me.

text:
Build me "Ditch", a Tinder-style app to clean up my Mac's Downloads folder. Make it fun, fast and beautiful.

How it works
- One file per card, biggest first. Swipe left = Trash, right = keep, up = file away into ~/Documents/Ditch/<type>, down = later. Keyboard arrows, mouse drag and two-finger trackpad swipe all work. Z undoes.
- Nothing moves until I click "Ditch N files". Then use macOS's own /usr/bin/trash so "Put Back" still works in Finder.
- A running "X GB ready to go" counter, satisfying stamp animations, synthesized sounds, and a confetti screen at the end.

Make it smart (local only, no cloud AI, no API keys)
- Read real macOS metadata: where each file was downloaded from (kMDItemWhereFroms xattr), when it was last opened (https://t.co/8j3aCcSICq.lastuseddate#PS), and whether a .dmg/.pkg's app is already in /Applications. If it is, show that app's real icon on the card.
- Find byte-identical duplicates, already-unzipped archives, interrupted downloads and old screenshots, and offer them as "sort in bulk" stacks I confirm in one click.
- Learn from my swipes with a small explainable model (naive Bayes over type, size, age, last opened, source site and name words). After 5 swipes, show its guess on each card with a reason ("You ditched 4 of 4 .dmg files"), and offer an "AI is sure" bulk stack.

Tech
- Python 3 standard library server on 127.0.0.1, plus one vanilla HTML/CSS/JS page. Protect the API with a random token and a Host header check.
- Package it as a double-clickable https://t.co/xMDej6RYe0 that opens in a Chrome --app window.

macOS gotchas to handle
- qlmanage hangs on .dmg, .zip and folders, so skip Quick Look thumbnails for those.
- HTTPServer's getfqdn() can hang on mDNS, so override server_bind.
- Filenames come in decomposed Unicode (NFD), so normalize before matching.

Test everything in a --dry-run mode on my real folder before touching any file.

text:
What if your next paying customer discovered your product while trying to solve a problem that had nothing to do with buying software?

That's an interesting part of #Headspace's organic marketing strategy.

People don't necessarily wake up wanting to subscribe to a meditation app. They want to sleep better, manage stress before an important meeting, or find a way to switch off after a demanding day.

Headspace connects with those needs through meditation guidance, sleep resources, and mindfulness education. Instead of relying only on promotional content, it gives people useful reasons to discover the brand while looking for help with everyday well-being.

Here's what makes its approach worth paying attention to.

01. It creates content around real problems.

Someone searching for a guided meditation for beginners, a relaxing bedtime routine, or ways to manage stress can discover Headspace through relevant resources. The brand becomes part of the conversation when people are actively looking for solutions.

02. It lets people experience the value first.

Free introductory experiences and practical exercises allow users to try guided meditation and explore Headspace's approach before considering a subscription. They don't have to make a purchasing decision just to understand what the product offers.

03. It fits into different parts of the day.

A short meditation before a stressful meeting, a breathing exercise during a busy afternoon, or sleep guidance at night can serve different needs. This gives Headspace multiple opportunities to remain relevant beyond a single interaction.

04. It creates a natural path from discovery to adoption.

Someone might initially find Headspace through a mindfulness resource or a sleep-related search. If the experience proves useful, the app offers a practical next step for developing a more consistent routine.

The interesting part is that Headspace doesn't have to start every customer relationship with a subscription pitch. It can begin by helping someone with a problem they already want to solve.

For #SaaS and subscription businesses, there's a valuable lesson here.

People don't always discover products by searching for products. They often discover them by searching for solutions.

Understanding those searches can open up organic growth opportunities that traditional product-focused marketing might miss.
