text:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has two Gen Z kids—and his AI warning for the entire generation is: ‘You can’t run away from it, and you can’t wish it away’ | Preston Fore, Fortune

AI’s impact on young people isn’t just a concern for Amazon CEO Andy Jassy as he leads the $2.6 trillion tech giant. With two Gen Z children—ages 25 and 22—who are navigating the same AI revolution reshaping education and the workplace, it’s personal, too.

Jassy’s advice to young people, including his own children, isn’t to shy away from AI. But the 58-year-old also cautioned against letting the technology replace the critical thinking and judgment that have long been essential to success.

“The advice I would give somebody young and I gave my kids was you can’t run away from it and you can’t wish it away,” Jassy said on The a16z Show last week. “It’s going to be incredibly impactful in your life in every experience that you try and use in your work, and it will allow you to invent in ways that just weren’t possible for us before.”

Jassy, who took over as Amazon CEO from Jeff Bezos in 2021, earned a salary of $365,000 last year and has led the company to become No. 1 on the Fortune 500 list.

And he said that embracing AI isn’t just for aspiring tech workers. Jassy encouraged young people from all backgrounds to learn how to use the technology and experiment with what it can do.

“You need to learn about it, educate yourself, use it a lot. Try doing things outside your comfort zone,” Jassy added. “Neither of my kids was a developer, but they’ve used AI to build applications. Use it as a focal point of how you operate day to day and how you use tools at work.”

AI can eliminate grunt work—but Jassy warns that it’s easy to spot using it for writing

Jassy, an alumnus of Harvard Business School, offered business school as an example of how AI can eliminate tedious preliminary work.

“Oftentimes there were a bunch of people who just didn’t do the work—they just didn’t do the reading or the research or the note-taking, and all that kind of goes away with AI,” Jassy said. “AI is going to be able to get everybody to that advanced starting spot much more quickly.”

While AI can help people get to speed faster, Jassy also warned against leaning too heavily on the technology. AI-generated writing, in particular, can be easy to spot as “not quite right,” he said, because the pieces don’t quite fit together.

“I still think you’re going to need human judgment and ingenuity and invention and experimentation and thinking about how all the pieces come together to end up building amazing experiences and businesses,” Jassy said.

“I think you want to use the tools, and they’re going to be huge aids, but I still think critical reasoning and thinking is going to be very important in everything we do.”

Amazon declined Fortune’s request for comment.

Critical thinking is a top skill business leaders are looking for

Jassy isn’t alone in encouraging young people to find a happy medium between embracing the technology—but not letting it replace their ability to think independently.

Billionaire Shark Tank star and KIND bar founder Daniel Lubetzky said that critical thinking will be increasingly sought out across workplaces.

“Being a critical thinker is in high demand, and they’re going to become greater demand. AI is real, but it doesn’t have the creativity that humans have,” Lubetzky told Fortune last year. “If, as young people, you lean into your curiosity, in your critical thinking and in your creativity, you will win.”

To do so, he said Gen Z should focus on studying history and philosophy—and question any and all assumptions.

“Always ask why, and then go one level below double click, triple click, to the sources. Why? Why? Why? Why?” he said. “If you do that, you’re going to develop a mind that’s going to be able to beat anybody else and be more valuable in the workplace.”

Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman has also emphasized the importance of developing skills that will help young workers adapt as AI changes the nature of their jobs.

“You’re going to want to be creative,” Garman said to CNBC last year. “You’re going to want to be [good at] critical thinking. And you’re going to want to be flexible.”

text:
These Ancient Faces Have Watched Over the Desert for More Than 1,000 Years… But What Were They Trying to Tell Us?

Hidden among the towering sandstone cliffs of Utah, USA, are mysterious carvings left behind by Native American people centuries ago. Some show human-like figures with unusual shapes and horned headdresses, while others depict bighorn sheep and other animals that once roamed these rugged lands. Known as petroglyphs, these images were carefully carved into the rock by people of the ancient Fremont culture, who lived across parts of the American Southwest between roughly 300 and 1300 CE.

What makes these carvings so fascinating is that they have survived for centuries, exposed to the harsh desert sun, wind, and changing seasons. They offer rare clues about how these ancient communities lived, hunted, and understood the world around them. Some figures look almost otherworldly, leaving modern visitors wondering whether they represent important people, spiritual beliefs, or stories passed down through generations. Yet their exact meanings remain uncertain, and many of their secrets may never be fully understood.

Imagine standing in a silent desert canyon, surrounded by enormous stone walls, and suddenly noticing a human figure carved into the rock more than a thousand years ago. The person who created it is long gone, but their artwork remains. These are more than ancient markings—they are messages from a world we are still trying to understand.

📍 Location: Utah, American Southwest

Source: National Park Service — Fremont Culture and ancient petroglyphs: "Capitol Reef National Park

text:
🗞️28 October 2026 | Daily Edition
38 developments stood out across crypto today, spanning market structure, ETF flows, stablecoin liquidity, DeFi, institutional adoption, tokenization, payments, protocol development, security, regulation, corporate activity and macro conditions.

1⃣ Bitcoin recovered above $81K ahead of the Federal Reserve decision

Bitcoin recovered toward approximately $81.3K, while Ethereum moved toward $2,360, Solana toward $103 and XRP around $1.33.

The move represents an improvement from repeated tests below $80K earlier in the week, although Bitcoin has still not convincingly reclaimed the $82K-$82.5K region.

🖊️ Market significance: Bitcoin has moved away from immediate breakdown risk, but the market still lacks the price confirmation required to establish a stronger recovery structure.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The setup has improved, but confirmation remains incomplete. Reclaiming $82K-$82.5K and holding it would matter considerably more than simply recovering above $81K.

2⃣ Zcash continued outperforming major cryptoassets

Zcash gained roughly 8%, returning above approximately $1,300 as the network marked its tenth anniversary.

ETF demand, the upcoming NU7 upgrade and debate around the network's development-funding structure remain important background factors.

🖊️ Market significance: ZEC continues to show unusual relative strength while many larger cryptoassets remain subdued.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The relative strength is notable, particularly alongside continued ETF inflows, but I would avoid assigning the price move to a single catalyst. Persistence matters more than one strong session.

3⃣ The Federal Reserve became the immediate macro catalyst

Markets overwhelmingly expect the Fed to leave rates unchanged.

However, the U.S. dollar remains firm, the 10-year Treasury yield is above 5% and investors are focused on whether policymakers signal another rate increase in December.

🖊️ Market significance: Even without an October hike, financial conditions remain restrictive for crypto and other liquidity-sensitive assets.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The decision itself may matter less than the guidance. A pause removes an immediate threat, but it does not create an easing cycle.

4⃣ U.S. crypto ETFs recorded a second consecutive positive session

The broader U.S. spot-crypto ETF complex recorded approximately $94.8M of net inflows on October 27.

The improvement was again concentrated primarily in Bitcoin.

🖊️ Market significance: Institutional flows are beginning to stabilize after the sharp deterioration seen late last week.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Two positive sessions are meaningful progress, but the recovery is still narrow. I would become more constructive if demand broadened beyond Bitcoin.

5⃣ Bitcoin ETFs attracted another $176M

Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $176M of net inflows, led by BlackRock and Fidelity.

Bitcoin products have now produced two consecutive positive sessions.

🖊️ Market significance: Regulated capital is once again beginning to confirm Bitcoin's price stabilization.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is the strongest improvement in the short-term market structure. The next test is persistence rather than another isolated positive day.

6⃣ Ethereum ETF outflows continued

Ethereum ETFs recorded approximately $60M of net outflows, marking another negative session.

The broader multi-week flow trend remains substantially negative.

🖊️ Market significance: Ethereum continues to lag Bitcoin significantly in institutional demand.

🗨️ My viewpoint: ETH still lacks the capital confirmation necessary to strengthen the current market thesis. Persistent withdrawals remain one of its clearest weaknesses.

7⃣ Solana ETF flows also remained negative

Solana products recorded approximately $19M of net withdrawals, extending the recent negative sequence.

🖊️ Market significance: Solana's improving infrastructure continues to contrast with weak regulated-capital demand.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The technology story remains constructive, but capital confirmation has not followed. That divergence continues to matter.

8⃣ Zcash continued receiving ETF inflows

Zcash investment products recorded another approximately $3.5M of inflows, bringing recent weekly inflows toward roughly $46M.

🖊️ Market significance: ZEC remains one of the strongest alternative-asset ETF-flow outliers.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is becoming more interesting because the sequence is persisting. I would still want to see several more weeks before calling it a structural institutional trend.

9⃣ Stablecoin capitalization remained below $300B

Total stablecoin capitalization remained around $299B, continuing its recent contraction.

🖊️ Market significance: The crypto system's dollar-equivalent liquidity base remains weak despite improving Bitcoin ETF flows.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is still the largest counter-signal to the recovery thesis. Bitcoin can attract institutional capital while the broader crypto liquidity environment remains unhealthy.

🔟 DeFi TVL remained depressed around $88B-$89B

Aggregate DeFi TVL remained substantially below recent levels.

Ethereum experienced significant weekly contraction, while major protocols such as Lido and Aave contributed to the decline.

🖊️ Market significance: There is still little evidence of broad capital returning to decentralized finance.

🗨️ My viewpoint: DeFi has stabilized slightly, but stabilization is not expansion. A stronger market requires actual capital growth rather than merely slower withdrawals.

1⃣1⃣ Onchain trading activity continued contracting

Seven-day decentralized spot volume remained around $42B-$43B, while decentralized perpetual activity was also substantially lower.

🖊️ Market significance: The market lacks the participation growth normally associated with a durable recovery.

🗨️ My viewpoint: I would become considerably more comfortable if spot activity began expanding alongside ETF flows. For now, participation remains too weak.

1⃣2⃣ An Avalanche-linked RWA vault lost approximately $1M

A Tranche Vault associated with Fence Finance and Valinor Digital was exploited for approximately $1.01M USDC.

The attacker used flash liquidity and settlement logic before moving funds from Avalanche to Solana.

🖊️ Market significance: Tokenized real-world-asset infrastructure inherits the same smart-contract and settlement risks as the broader DeFi system.

🗨️ My viewpoint: RWA branding does not remove DeFi risk. If tokenized finance depends on programmable contracts, those contracts remain part of the financial attack surface.

1⃣3⃣ Predict .fun lost approximately $398K from user wallets

Twenty-nine wallets were affected across two separate incidents.

The affected transfers were signed using users' own keys, while the prediction-market contracts themselves were not compromised.

🖊️ Market significance: The incident highlights the difference between protocol security and compromised signing infrastructure.

🗨️ My viewpoint: A secure contract does not protect users if the systems surrounding their keys are compromised. Key management remains one of crypto's most important vulnerabilities.

1⃣4⃣ Zilliqa's CEO stepped down while its bridge remained suspended

Zilliqa's CEO resigned while the network continues dealing with security issues affecting X-Bridge and several token contracts.

Native ZIL and the Zilliqa EVM were reportedly unaffected.

🖊️ Market significance: Leadership transition and unresolved bridge risk occurring simultaneously increase operational uncertainty.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The key issue is not the resignation itself. The market needs clarity around affected assets, losses and the timeline for restoring bridge functionality.

1⃣5⃣ Bithumb suffered another internal-security breach

An attacker accessed an employee mobile work environment and obtained personal information.

Bithumb says the system was isolated from its trading infrastructure and customer cryptoassets were not accessible through the breach.

🖊️ Market significance: Internal employee systems remain an important attack vector even when trading and custody infrastructure is segregated.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Security segmentation appears to have limited the financial impact, but employee infrastructure remains part of the broader exchange security perimeter.

1⃣6⃣ Coinbase disclosed a third-party customer-data exposure

A third-party analytics provider exposed contact information belonging to a small subset of Coinbase customers.

Coinbase itself was not breached and customer assets were reportedly unaffected.

🖊️ Market significance: Vendor and analytics infrastructure can create security risks even when the exchange's own systems remain secure.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Third-party risk is increasingly financial-system risk. Security assessment must extend beyond the company itself to every service with access to customer information.

1⃣7⃣ Google moved into institutional crypto-custody security

Google is testing a multi-party computation system designed to distribute signing authority rather than storing a complete private key in one place.

Commercial availability is expected in 2027.

🖊️ Market significance: One of the world's largest technology companies is developing security infrastructure specifically relevant to institutional digital-asset custody.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is structurally important because institutional adoption ultimately depends on custody architecture capable of surviving increasingly sophisticated attacks.

1⃣8⃣ DTCC launched live tokenization infrastructure

DTCC launched a service that can create tokenized representations of securities held at DTC.

Major global financial institutions are participating in the initiative.

🖊️ Market significance: Tokenization is moving directly into the infrastructure underlying the conventional U.S. securities market.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is one of the most important tokenization developments because it involves existing market infrastructure rather than building a parallel financial system from scratch.

1⃣9⃣ Securitize added Stellar to its tokenization infrastructure

Asset managers using Securitize will be able to issue and manage tokenized financial products on Stellar.

🖊️ Market significance: Stellar continues expanding its position as infrastructure for institutional tokenized assets.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Distribution platforms such as Securitize matter because they can bring multiple issuers onto a network rather than relying on individual one-off integrations.

2⃣0⃣ Resistance to tokenized U.S. equities expanded to 33 companies

More large U.S. companies objected to tokenized representations of their shares being offered through the proposed OKX-ICE venue.

More than half of the original planned issuer universe has now objected.

🖊️ Market significance: Issuer consent has become a major obstacle for tokenized equities.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This remains one of the strongest reality checks for the tokenization narrative. Technical feasibility does not automatically create institutional acceptance.

2⃣1⃣ Nearly 90% of large businesses surveyed are testing tokenized money

A survey of large companies found 88% were already deploying or testing tokenized forms of money.

Stablecoins ranked highest, followed by tokenized deposits and tokenized money-market funds.

🖊️ Market significance: Tokenized money is moving beyond financial institutions into corporate treasury and operational use.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The adoption question is shifting from whether companies will experiment to which form of tokenized money becomes most useful operationally.

2⃣2⃣ Brazil's largest bank entered the regulated crypto-brokerage framework

Itaú Unibanco formally registered its existing crypto trading and custody business under Brazil's new regulatory regime.

🖊️ Market significance: Crypto brokerage is increasingly becoming part of ordinary banking services.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The most important adoption often looks boring. A major bank integrating regulated crypto services into existing financial infrastructure is more meaningful than another speculative product launch.

2⃣3⃣ Brazilian companies used stablecoins as an emergency currency hedge

Corporate accounts dominated activity on a major Brazilian crypto platform during election-related market stress.

Stablecoin and Bitcoin volumes surged while conventional markets were closed.

🖊️ Market significance: Stablecoins are functioning as real-time currency and treasury tools rather than merely crypto trading instruments.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is one of the clearest real-world use cases for always-on digital money: companies can hedge currency exposure when conventional financial markets are unavailable.

2⃣4⃣ Moody's assigned investment-grade ratings to RLUSD

Ripple's RLUSD received investment-grade long- and short-term ratings.

The assessment considered reserve quality, liquidity, coverage and redemption arrangements.

🖊️ Market significance: A major ratings agency is evaluating stablecoins using frameworks familiar to traditional institutional investors.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This helps stablecoins move from crypto-native trust toward institutional credit analysis. That matters for treasury and corporate adoption.

2⃣5⃣ Coinbase expanded RLUSD distribution

RLUSD became available across Coinbase's retail, exchange and institutional platforms, with support across multiple blockchains.

🖊️ Market significance: Distribution is becoming a major competitive advantage in the stablecoin market.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Regulation and reserves establish trust, but distribution determines whether a stablecoin actually becomes useful at scale.

2⃣6⃣ Ripple said its product business is approaching a $900M annualized revenue run rate

Ripple reported substantial growth across payments, custody, stablecoins, prime brokerage and treasury services.

RLUSD has also continued expanding.

🖊️ Market significance: Ripple is increasingly becoming a diversified financial-infrastructure company rather than a business dependent on one blockchain product.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The important question is whether revenue growth increasingly comes from recurring financial infrastructure rather than market-cycle-dependent activity.

2⃣7⃣ Ripple and BNY explored tokenized trade finance

The companies are exploring infrastructure that could finance approved corporate invoices and settle payments using RLUSD on XRP Ledger.

🖊️ Market significance: Tokenization is moving into working capital and trade finance, areas with enormous existing financial volumes.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is more interesting than tokenizing another security because trade finance is a real operational problem where faster settlement and programmable liquidity can create measurable economic value.

2⃣8⃣ Robinhood expanded RLUSD integration

RLUSD is being incorporated across Robinhood's chain, Bitstamp and potentially broader consumer and institutional settlement systems.

🖊️ Market significance: Stablecoins are becoming embedded within large distribution platforms rather than existing as standalone crypto products.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The strongest stablecoin networks will likely be built through distribution partnerships, not simply through issuance.

2⃣9⃣ Robinhood's results showed crypto revenue broadening beyond trading

Robinhood reported significant revenue from crypto, its blockchain network and prediction markets.

Robinhood Chain itself generated meaningful activity during its first quarter on mainnet.

🖊️ Market significance: Crypto business models are diversifying away from dependence on spot-trading commissions.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is healthier for the sector. Infrastructure, prediction markets and settlement businesses can provide more durable economics than relying exclusively on trading volumes.

3⃣0⃣ SoFi highlighted the difference between crypto activity and profitability

SoFi reported substantial gross crypto transaction revenue, but after associated costs, net transaction revenue was much smaller.

🖊️ Market significance: High crypto transaction volume does not automatically translate into attractive business economics.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is an important reminder that adoption should be judged by economics, not gross activity alone. Revenue quality matters.

3⃣1⃣ Regulated U.S. crypto perpetual markets continued expanding

Crypto .com and OG .com launched regulated perpetual futures for eligible U.S. traders with leverage up to 5x.

🖊️ Market significance: Products historically concentrated on offshore crypto exchanges are moving into regulated U.S. market infrastructure.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This could gradually shift derivatives activity from offshore venues toward regulated domestic markets, changing liquidity and counterparty structures.

3⃣2⃣ The CFTC sued Utah over prediction-market jurisdiction

The regulator is seeking to prevent Utah from applying state gambling laws to federally regulated prediction markets.

🖊️ Market significance: The case could determine how much authority individual states retain over federally regulated event-contract markets.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is potentially industry-defining. Prediction markets become far harder to scale nationally if every state can independently restrict federally regulated contracts.

3⃣3⃣ Galaxy Digital returned strongly to profitability

Galaxy reported approximately $323M of quarterly net income, reversing the previous quarter's loss.

Trading activity, lending and other businesses improved, while the company announced another share repurchase.

🖊️ Market significance: Institutional crypto businesses can generate substantial profitability even during weaker underlying token markets when operations are diversified.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This supports the broader shift toward crypto companies being judged as financial businesses rather than simply proxies for token prices.

3⃣4⃣ Datavault AI exposed counterparty risk in corporate Bitcoin treasury accounting

Datavault disclosed that it has been unable to access Bitcoin credited to it through a counterparty since June.

The company expects to restate accounts and reduce previously reported assets substantially.

🖊️ Market significance: A corporate treasury can report Bitcoin exposure without necessarily controlling the underlying asset directly.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is an important warning for corporate Bitcoin analysis. Treasury quality depends on custody, legal ownership and withdrawal rights, not merely the BTC number reported on a balance sheet.

3⃣5⃣ Institutional benchmark data is moving onchain

CF Benchmarks introduced infrastructure allowing blockchain applications to verify benchmark pricing across crypto and traditional financial assets.

🖊️ Market significance: Tokenized markets require reliable institutional-grade reference data if they are to support large-scale financial products.

🗨️ My viewpoint: Data infrastructure is one of the quieter but essential layers of tokenization. Markets cannot scale without trusted pricing and benchmarks.

3⃣6⃣ XRP Ledger developers proposed wallets requiring zero XRP balances

A proposal would allow companies to sponsor account reserve requirements and potentially transaction fees for users.

🖊️ Market significance: Removing the requirement for users to first acquire XRP could reduce friction for stablecoin payments and automated agents.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is a practical usability improvement. Mainstream users should not need to understand or acquire a network's native token simply to use a stablecoin application.

3⃣7⃣ Bitcoin mining infrastructure continued converging with AI compute

Luxor raised new capital to expand from Bitcoin-mining infrastructure into AI hardware, compute markets and related services.

🖊️ Market significance: Mining companies are increasingly applying their energy, infrastructure and compute expertise to AI and high-performance computing.

🗨️ My viewpoint: The overlap between mining and AI is increasingly becoming an infrastructure story rather than merely miners searching for another revenue source.

3⃣8⃣ The U.S. Treasury framed crypto as part of preserving dollar dominance

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued that digital-asset infrastructure could strengthen the international role of the dollar.

🖊️ Market significance: Stablecoins and blockchain infrastructure are increasingly being discussed as tools of monetary and geopolitical strategy.

🗨️ My viewpoint: This is an important shift in framing. Crypto policy is moving beyond market regulation toward questions of payment infrastructure, financial competitiveness and dollar influence.

🗨️ My Overall Viewpoint:
The market has improved at the margin but the recovery remains unconfirmed. Bitcoin is back above $81K and BTC ETFs have recorded two consecutive positive sessions, but Ethereum and Solana ETF demand remains weak, stablecoin supply is below $300B, DeFi TVL remains depressed and onchain activity is still contracting.

Structurally, adoption continues accelerating through DTCC tokenization, regulated stablecoins, bank and corporate adoption, institutional custody, payments, trade finance and regulated derivatives. Security and issuer resistance remain the counterweights, showing that integration is progressing but not without operational and governance risks.

My view is that the market is moving from stabilization back toward a recovery attempt. Confirmation requires Bitcoin to hold above $82K-$82.5K, ETF demand to broaden beyond BTC, stablecoin supply to stabilize and DeFi and spot activity to begin expanding.

text:
I find myself telling myself to slow down these days. I spent my entire life sprinting.

Like many people with a chip on their shoulder, I got a complex as a kid that drives me today.

When I was 4 years old, my mom handed me the kitchen phone with one of those very long swirly cords. She said, "Mrs Helm's wants to talk to you.” She spent the next few minutes asking if I would stay and help my teacher “teach” the new kids. Unbeknownst to me, the adults had decided to have me repeat 4k.

This was pretty cool I guess because I was the oldest in my classes and one of the first to get a car in 9th grade. But frankly I started begging my parents to let me skip a grade almost every year. My friends and girlfriends were always older.

On the last few days in 10th grade, my dad asked if I still wanted to skip a grade. The answer was of course. He told me to prepare a presentation on why I should be able to skip. I presented it to him and his best friend over lunch with potato chips at Jason’s Deli.

The pitch worked. I spent that summer taking a few English courses as I was already a head a few years in math. I skipped 11th grade and changed to a public school because none of the private schools would let me skip.

After graduating high school in 3 years, I decided to do the same in college. After a two years of a normal course load, I took 17 hours one summer, got 27 credits that fall with a bunch of night courses and testing out of two courses, and slid into home plate with 14 credits to graduate a year early. I was one course short of not one but two different majors.

Entering law school as the youngest person was a cool turn of events for me. I could barely drink, legally at least, having just turned 21 years old. I did the math and realized I could only shave off a semester, which meant I would not graduate with a big group. I could add an MBA or LLM with an additional year but frankly I didn’t see the point. I had started day dreaming about businesses I could start.

I guess I cruised just a bit in law school. I was the only one there planning not to be an attorney. I lied on my application letter under the advice of others. I was afraid to just say I wanted to be an investment banker like my dad, and I thought a law degree would give me an edge. I threw three years of great parties for that law school.

Graduating in 2010 unfortunately meant the job market for bankers was in the dumps. I ended up in Little Rock, Arkansas which was even smaller than my hometown in Memphis. I had dreamed about moving to NYC after law school. It didn’t happen. I got the IB job in LR and got back on the grind.

Five years in and I was bored. I was putting in equity hours for paychecks and bonuses. My dad and brother both had built and sold multiple businesses by then. They were entrepreneurs.

I got the startup bug living and breathing growth as part of the Synapse team. Twenty outbound a day every day except for Sunday. 996 would have been a light week. I was the first to move out of the house but we had 40 employees working in the house by then, and I needed a life.

I had a side hustle friends and family crypto investment club in 2016/17. Closed it down December 2017 because it felt too risky which in retrospect was genius. Continued the grind as I joined my first crypto startup in 2018. I still had side hustles - lots of working with founders on go-to-market.

Finally, I started my own company in 2020 and hustled until I sold it in 2023. Soft landing but team got jobs and investors thanked me for returning cash. I spent a minute working for the company that acquired mine, helping them grow all their subsidiaries and helping acquire a new one too.

Starting Relayzero’s M&A business last year, I told myself I’d say “no” more. Work only with the best founders with the best likely outcome. This was tough at first. I saw tons of opportunities to help good people with everything from acquire-hires to negotiating with buyers already at the door steps with multi-million dollar offers. None felt right.

Maybe slow down is not the best way to describe it. Zoom out is probably better. Pick waves to ride, not trends to follow. Play long term games.

Saying “no” gave me space to say "yes" when the time was right. Today, we have received offers in the hundreds of millions of dollars for clients. The things that make your name.

I already have a name though. I d​id the work.

text:
From the Georgia Supreme Court record of the Leo M. Frank case, Slides 0712 and 0713 on https://t.co/3RvkpgRoLI are pages 372 and 373 of the brief of evidence. They open the state's exhibits, and the first long one is State's Exhibit B: the statement Leo Max Frank gave N. A. Lanford, Chief of Detectives, on Monday morning, April 28, 1913. The record notes that it was never signed.

Mary Anne Phagan, 13, had been found dead in the basement of the National Pencil Company early Sunday morning, April 27, 1913. Frank was the superintendent. This was his account to the police the next day, almost four months before he made his statement to the jury.

He told Lanford that Saturday was a holiday and the factory was shut down. The office boy and the stenographer left about noon. Then, he said, "this little girl, Mary Phagan came in, but at the time I didn't know that was her name. She came in between 12:05 and 12:10, maybe 12:07, to get her pay envelope, her salary. I paid her and she went out of the office."

Look at what that admits. By his own account Frank was alone in the office when Mary came for her pay, and he was the last person known to have seen her alive. He said it was impossible to see which way she went, and "I didn't pay any particular attention."

And look at what it denies. Mary worked in his factory and collected her weekly pay at his office, and on Saturday he paid her himself. Yet two days later his first statement already insisted she was a stranger whose name he did not know. He held to that claim at the trial. Girls who worked with Mary testified they heard him call her "Mary," as this morning's post on Slide 1264 shows, and he answered only that they were mistaken. Why would an innocent man work so hard to put distance between himself and that child?

The rest of the statement is his timeline. Arthur White and Harry Denham were working on the fourth floor, and Mrs. White left about 1 o'clock. Frank said he locked the doors at 1:10 and went home to dinner, came back just before three, and let the two men out. He had told Newt Lee, the night watchman, to come early because "I may go to the ball game," but he said it was too cold and he came back to the factory instead. Newt arrived at 20 minutes to four.

Slide 0713 carries it to the evening. Frank said he left about six. Outside he met James Milton Gantt, "a man I had fired about two weeks previous," who wanted to go up for a pair of shoes, and Frank told Newt to go with him. At home, Frank said, he tried to telephone Newt and could not get an answer, then reached him at 7 o'clock and asked if Gantt had gotten his shoes and "is everything all right." The statement closes with a detail he offered on his own: "I took a bath Saturday night at my home. I changed my clothes." He added that "this is the suit of clothes I was wearing Saturday."

The jury heard all of this. The Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the conviction on February 17, 1914.

Forever 13 and Never forgotten.

#MaryPhagan #LeoFrank

Appendix: Full slide transcript

Slide 0712

STATE'S EXHIBIT A.
State's diagram of the pencil factory.

STATE'S EXHIBIT B.
Frank's statement made before N. A. Lanford, Chief of Detectives on Monday morning, April 28, 1913, this statement being unsigned.

"I am General Superintendent and Director of the National Pencil Company. In Atlanta I have held that position since Aug. 10, 1908. My place of business is at 37 to 41 So. Forsyth St. We have about 107 employees in that plant, male and female. I guess there are a few more girls than boys. Saturday, April 26th, was a holiday with our Company and the factory was shut down. There were several people who come in during the morning. The office boy and the stenographer were in the office with me until noon. They left about 12 or a little after. We have a day watchman there. He left shortly before 12 o'clock. After the office boy and the stenographer left, this little girl, Mary Phagan came in, but at the time I didn't know that was her name. She came in between 12:05 and 12:10, maybe 12:07, to get her pay envelope, her salary. I paid her and she went out of the office. I was in the inner office at my desk, the furtherest office to the left from the main office. It was impossible to see the direction she went in when she left. My impression was that she just walked away, I didn't pay any particular attention. I didn't keep the door locked downstairs that morning because the mail was coming in. I locked it at 1:10 when I went to dinner. Arthur White and Harry Denham were also in the building. They were working on the machinery, doing repair work, working on the top floor of the building, which is the 4th floor, towards the rear or about the middle of the building, but a little more to the rear. They were tightening up the belts, they are not machinists, one is a foreman in one department and the other is an assistant in another, and Denham was assisting White, and Mrs. White, the wife of Arthur White, was also in the building. She left about 1 o'clock, I went up there and told them I was going to dinner and they had to get out, and they said they had not finished and I said how long will it take, and they said until some time in the afternoon, and then I said "Mrs. White you will have to go, for I am going to lock these boys in here." Anyone from the inside can open the outside door, but not the inside door, which I locked. You can go in the basement from the front through the trap door. No sir, they could get up the steps if I was out. I locked the outer door and the inner door. I got back at three o'clock, and maybe two or three minutes before, and I went to the office and took off my coat and then went upstairs to tell those boys I was back, and I couldn't find them at first, they were back in the dipping room, in the rear, and I said "are you ready" and they said "we are just ready" and I said "all right" ring out when you go down to let me know when you go out, and they rang out, and Arthur White come in the office and said "Mr. Frank loan me $2.00" and I said "what's the matter, we just paid off" and he said "my wife robbed me", and I give him $2.00 and he walked away, and the two of them walked out. I locked the outer door behind them. When I am in there is no need of locking the inner door. There was only one person I was looking for to come in, and that was the nightwatchman. He got there at 20 minutes to four. I had previously arranged for him to get there. On Friday night I told him, after he got his money. I give him the keys and I said "you had better come around early tomorrow because I may go to the ball game" and he come early, because of that fact; I told him to come early and he come 20 minutes to 4. I figured I could leave about 1 o'clock and would not come back, but it was so cold I didn't want to risk catching cold and I come back to the factory as I usually do. He come in and I said "Newt you are early" and he said "yes sir" and he had a bag of bananas with him and he offered me a banana; I didn't see them but he offered me one and I guess he had them. We have told him once he gets in that building ... I was going to be there. He come back about 4 minutes to six; the reason I know that, I was putting the clock slips in and the clock

Slide 0713

was right in front of me. I said, "I will be ready in a minutes" and he went downstairs and I come to the office and put on my coat and hat and followed him and went out. When I went out, talking to Newt Lee was J. M. Gantt, a man I had fired about two weeks previous. Newt told me he wanted to go up to get a pair of shoes he left while he was working there, and Gantt said to me, "Newt don't want me to go up" and he said "you can go with me Mr. Frank" and I said "that's all right, go with him Newt" and I went on home, and I got home about 6:25. Nothing else happened; that's all I know. I don't know what time Gantt came down after he went up. I saw him go in and I locked the door after him, but I didn't try them. I telephoned Newt. I tried to telephone him when I got home, he punches the clock at half hour intervals, and the clock and the phone is in the office, and I didn't get an answer and at 7 o'clock I called him and asked him if Gantt got his shoe and he said yes, he got them, and I said is everything all right and he said yes, and the next thing I knew they called me at 7:30 the next morning. I don't know that our watchman has been in the habit of letting people in the factory at any time. I have never heard of it. I never had any trouble with the watchman about it. As to whether any of our employees go there at night, Gantt did when he was working there, he had a key and sometimes he would have some work left over. I never have seen him go out until I go out, I go out and come back, but he has come back before I left, but that is part of his duty. I took a bath Saturday night at my home. I changed my clothes. The clothes that I changed are at home, and this is the suit of clothes I was wearing Saturday. After I left the shop I went to Jacob's Pharmacy and bought a box of candy for my wife and got home about 6:25.

References

Wikipedia Is Occupied Territory: How Frankite Editors Control the Leo Frank Narrative

The Prosecution's Evidence Is Being Pushed Out of the Story and the Article is Locked

By D. Davis

I believe Wikipedia's article on Leo Frank has been captured by a group of deeply committed pro-Frank activist editors who are determined to protect the established narrative and orthodoxy of his supposed innocence. I call these editors Frankites because their treatment of the case appears to be driven by their commitment to rehabilitating Leo Frank rather than giving readers a complete account of the evidence presented at his trial. One does not need to be Jewish to be a Frankite, a Frankitism is a school of thought often referred to as the Cult of Leo Frank. These Frankites are multigenerational advocates who make it their mission to convince the publish he was innocent, even though his guilt was proven beyond reasonable doubt at trial. The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed that the testimony, exhibits and forensic evidence were more than sufficient for a guilty verdict.

In my opinion, the article has become a form of hasbara-style reputation management and public relations diplomacy for groups like the ADL. It presents a carefully controlled interpretation of the case, giving enormous attention to arguments supporting Frank's innocence while minimizing the prosecution's evidence. 

I cannot perfectly establish that this reflects an organized operation without examining the editors' conduct and communications, but the article itself raises serious questions about selective sourcing and editorial gatekeeping. You can follow the Leo Frank editors to see that they are heavily involved in other areas of Jewish reputational management. They work as a coordinated team of activists. Wikipedia is ideologically occupied, even one of the co-founders has admitted this publicly. And it is now well documented. But humanity is fighting back, in some areas of Wikipedia the occupation has been losing some control.  The Leo Frank article on Wikipedia is under full control of the hasbaras and Frankites. 

Wikipedia's 25-Foot Gray Separation Barrier

What concerns me most is how difficult it has become to introduce the evidence against Frank. The original 1913 Atlanta press reports and Brief of Evidence contains extensive testimony from prosecution witnesses, including Jim Conley, Monteen Stover, Newt Lee, Robert Barrett, and numerous factory employees. Their testimony helped persuade twelve jurors to convict Frank of murdering thirteen-year-old Mary Phagan.

Yet anyone reading Wikipedia could easily come away with the impression that the prosecution had almost no credible case against him. That is a serious problem for an encyclopedia that is supposed to explain history neutrally rather than defend one interpretation of it. The Leo Frank legal defense team's version of the case is the one predominant on Wikipedia. 

Jim Conley's Testimony Deserves a Full Examination

Take Jim Conley, for example. He testified in detail that he helped Leo Frank move Mary Phagan's body after the murder. He also admitted writing the two notes discovered near her body in the factory basement. His account became a central part of the prosecution's case. He described in great detail, that Leo Frank admitted wanting to be with the girl Mary Phagan (have sexual intercourse with her) and that she refused him. Leo Frank admitted striking her and that she fell and hit her head on something. Later Mary Phagan's blood soaked hair was found tangled on a bench lathe in the machine department on the second floor of the factory. 

Conley gave conflicting statements during the investigation, and Frank's lawyers subjected him to lengthy cross-examination. Those contradictions deserve examination. But readers should also be told what Conley actually said, how he explained his actions, what details could be checked against other evidence, and why the jury ultimately accepted enough of his testimony to convict Frank.

Instead, the modern narrative often treats Conley as the murderer and Frank as his poor innocent victim. That theory should be subjected to the same demanding examination as the prosecution's account.

Then there are the other witnesses. Monteen Stover testified that Frank was absent from his office during a critical period around noon. Robert Barrett described hair and suspected bloodstains found on the second floor. Newt Lee described what he regarded as unusual behavior by Frank. Female factory employees testified about alleged improper conduct by Frank toward women and girls at the factory. More than 10 girls testified to Leo Frank's lasciviousness. At the Coroner's inquest they described how Leo Frank tried to make them engage in sexual activities. There names are Nellie Pettis and Nellie Wood, but the Hasbara Frankites won't allow their names into the article. 

These witnesses were not all saying the same thing, and their testimony was not beyond dispute. But together they formed part of the case the prosecution put before the jury. Wikipedia should explain that case in detail before telling readers why later writers rejected it.

Wikipedia Gives the Defense the Benefit of the Doubt

What I find especially troubling is the difference in how the two sides are treated. When a prosecution witness contradicts himself, it becomes evidence that the state's case was unreliable. When Frank's statements conflict with other testimony, later writers frequently offer explanations that reduce the significance of those conflicts. The occupational editor-activists of Wikipedia synthesize those differences in support of Leo Frank. 

Why should one side receive the benefit of every possible explanation while the other side is examined with suspicion?

The same goes for the physical evidence, the timing of Mary's arrival, the disputed movements inside the factory, and the murder notes. Every contradiction should be examined, regardless of which side benefits.

I believe the prosecution established Frank's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. That was the conclusion reached by the jury in August 1913. His lawyers challenged the conviction, and the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's judgment on February 17, 1914. Other legal challenges also failed. The Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the sufficiency of the evidence against Leo Frank for the guilty verdict to be sound and secure. You won't hear that little tidbit from the devotees from the Cult of Leo Frank.

Those appellate decisions did not independently retry every witness or resolve every historical dispute. Nevertheless, the original jury verdict and the courts' actual rulings deserve much more attention than they receive in many modern retellings.

The Antisemitism Narrative Needs the Same Scrutiny

Another problem is the way antisemitism is used to explain the conviction. Antisemitism existed in American society in 1913, but so did antigentilism. But that does not relieve historians of the responsibility to establish what happened in the Leo Frank trial.

Was the verdict caused by antisemitic prejudice, or did the jurors believe the prosecution's evidence? What did the newspapers report about the courtroom? What evidence supported the allegations of jury intimidation? What did the courts find when Frank's lawyers raised those allegations?

The trial judge Leonard Strickland Roan rejected 115 motions post-verdict, and the Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the judge's decision.

The Multi-Life-Time Leo Frank Hoaxes

I believe the familiar story about crowds shouting “Hang the Jew” deserves a much more careful source investigation. So does the claim that the men responsible for Frank's lynching belonged to an organization called the “Knights of Mary Phagan.” And what about the repeated assertion that half of Georgia's Jewish population fled following the lynching?

Those are all hoaxes that have been debunked thoroughly on Mary Phagan-Kean's X threat (@PhaganKean)

These stories should not be accepted simply because later writers repeated them. Their sources should be traced back to the earliest available records. The absence of contemporary confirmation does not automatically prove deliberate fabrication, but it gives historians every reason to question the certainty with which such claims are repeated.

Nor should criticism of an organization such as the Anti-Defamation League, or of individual authors and editors, be confused with criticism of Jewish people generally. 

The questions here concern identifiable claims, publications, editorial decisions, and historical evidence!

How Wikipedia's Rules Protect the Existing Narrative

This is where the editorial problem becomes especially difficult.

Wikipedia depends heavily on published secondary sources. Most modern books about the Leo Frank case argue that he was innocent. As a result, Wikipedia editors can cite those books to justify placing the pro-Frank interpretation at the center of the article. 

This is exactly why we need 100 volunteers willing to pursue PhDs in history. Find a university offering a fully funded doctoral program that covers tuition and pays a living stipend. 

Get your PhD, become a historian, examine the original trial records, and publish serious research in peer-reviewed journals, academic publications, and books. We need 100 qualified historians with real names, academic credentials, and university affiliations who are willing to challenge the Frankite narrative and fight back against hasbara-style advocacy with original evidence and documented historical research. 

If we want to change Wikipedia, we first need to challenge the scholarly consensus that Wikipedia depends upon. We cannot accomplish that by arguing endlessly with entrenched editors. We need to build an entire generation of credible historians who are willing to investigate the Leo Frank case independently, expose errors in the established narrative, and give the prosecution's evidence the serious academic attention it deserves. This means publishing articles, and writing books.

Someone who goes back to the original trial transcript may discover evidence that challenges a later author's interpretation. But Wikipedia's rules against original research can make it difficult to introduce that finding unless a recognized secondary source has already published the same argument.

The result is a system that can reward repetition by Leo Frank activist historians. One historian cites another, a later author repeats the interpretation, and Wikipedia then cites both books as support for what appears to be a well-established consensus.

That is why I am concerned about citation laundering and citogenesis, something discussed a lot lately. A historical claim can acquire the appearance of authority through repeated citation even when its original foundation is weaker than readers realize.

The danger becomes greater when committed editors repeatedly reject material challenging the prevailing interpretation while accepting sources that reinforce it.

I believe this systemic structure is the central problem with the Leo Frank article. The editors I describe as Frankites appear to have established an editorial environment in which the prosecution's evidence is treated as an obstacle to be explained away rather than as part of the history readers deserve to examine.

To demonstrate the extent of that control, the article's edit history, talk-page discussions, disputed additions, reversions, and editorial decisions should be subjected to the same kind of documented audit as the historical claims themselves.

Wikipedia Should Not Be a Public Relations Department for Leo Frank

The article should explain why the grand jury indicted Frank, why the trial jury convicted him, what the witnesses testified to, and what the defense said in response. It should accurately describe Judge Roan's decisions, the Georgia Supreme Court's rulings, Governor Slaton's commutation, and the limits of the 1986 pardon.

That pardon addressed Georgia's failure to protect Frank from lynching and its failure to prosecute his killers. It expressly declined to decide guilt or innocence. It should never be presented as a judicial finding that Frank did not murder Mary Phagan.

I believe the article gives readers too little opportunity to understand the prosecution's complete case before introducing the modern arguments for Frank's innocence.

That is why I regard it as a deeply biased historical article. Its structure and selection of evidence leave the impression that the verdict is being retried by writers who have already decided what the result should be.

The answer is not to suppress arguments supporting Frank. The answer is to demand a higher standard of historical examination for both sides.

The Way to Challenge Frankite Control Is Through Published Scholarship

After studying this problem, I have come to believe that arguing with Wikipedia editors alone will accomplish very little.

Wikipedia's preference for established secondary sources means that changing the article will require changing the body of scholarship upon which it relies.

We need historians, legal scholars, and other serious researchers willing to return to the original records and examine the case independently. We need people pursuing PhDs in history, advanced legal training, and related fields who can produce doctoral dissertations, peer-reviewed journal articles, and thoroughly researched books.

Their work should examine the prosecution's evidence, the weaknesses in the defense's arguments, the medical testimony, Conley's statements, the newspaper accounts, the appellate rulings, and the origins of later historical claims.

If the prosecution's case is as strong as I believe it is, that argument should be capable of surviving independent scholarly examination. Researchers should also be willing to acknowledge evidence that challenges their own conclusions. That is how historical scholarship earns credibility.

The long-term objective is to develop a substantial body of documented research that Wikipedia editors can no longer dismiss simply because it disagrees with the established interpretation of the Frankite and Hasbara orthodoxy. Just look up the names of the Pro-Frank authors and investigate their careers and person life, everything will make sense.

History Should Not Belong to the Editors Who Control the Page

My conclusion is that Wikipedia's Leo Frank article has become a one-sided account in which committed pro-Frank editors exercise too much influence over how the history is presented. In my view, it reads like an advocacy effort designed to rehabilitate Frank's reputation.

I believe the jury got the verdict right. I believe the prosecution presented convincing evidence of Frank's guilt. And I believe the modern literature has often given insufficient attention to that evidence while repeating questionable stories about the case.

The fact that many modern authors disagree with the 1913 verdict does not erase the testimony, the indictment, the jury's decision, or the appellate record.

Mary Phagan was thirteen years old when she was murdered. Her life and death deserve a complete historical examination, including the evidence presented against the man convicted of killing her.

Wikipedia should give readers the facts, the testimony, the contradictions, the court decisions, and the competing historical interpretations. Readers should be able to understand why the jury convicted Frank and why later historians have questioned that conviction.

Until that happens, I will continue to regard the Leo Frank article as an example of how entrenched editorial positions and a dominant body of secondary literature can shape what millions of people are taught about history.

The way forward is to document the problems, expose unsupported claims, publish stronger historical research, and challenge every interpretation against the surviving records. No group of editors, however committed to its position, should have the final word on a historical controversy of this magnitude.

Yahoo Finance drove the Slate EV on October 28, with Pras Subramanian behind the wheel of the truck from the Bezos backed startup. Slate Auto is a private company.

• Base price of about $27,000, up from the $25,000 the company originally targeted, with options able to push it toward $30,000
• Range of about 200 miles in a single basic look with plastic body panels
• Hand crank windows are standard, power windows are not offered as an upgrade, and the side mirrors are adjusted by hand
• The drive verdict: smooth and well damped despite the stripped interior, helped by the low battery keeping the center of gravity down
• Production runs out of a plant in Indiana, with first deliveries expected later in 2026 and a waiting list open
• Jeff Bezos is an early backer, the new chief executive is a former Amazon executive, and experience centers have opened in Chicago

▬▬▬

THE CATCH
Deleting every feature is the entire business model, and it is how the price exists at all. The open question is whether truck buyers in 2026 accept hardware from a 1995 base model, even at $27,000.

THE TAKEAWAY
Every other EV startup added screens and software to justify its price. Slate is running the opposite experiment, a truck as an appliance, priced below every electric pickup on sale. Does the stripped formula win buyers, or does the market demand the features back? 👇 NFA

text:
NVIDIA Takes $3B Meta Equity Stake, Turning Biggest Customer Into Strategic Partner | Kyle Belmonte, Techtimes

NVIDIA committed $3 billion to Meta's equity offering on Monday, converting the world's dominant AI chip supplier into a financial stakeholder in the social media giant's $97.5B infrastructure buildout — a structural inversion that signals chipmakers are no longer content to simply sell hardware to the hyperscalers driving the agentic AI boom. AMD committed $1 billion of its own the following day, bringing the combined chip-supplier stake to $4 billion and completing what Meta had previously described as up to $5B from chip suppliers across NVIDIA, AMD, and Broadcom.

NVIDIA's $3B Equity Commitment Converts Vendor Relationship Into Strategic Partnership

The investment, announced alongside an expanded technical partnership centered on Meta's Muse family of AI agents, marks a significant deepening of a relationship that began as a straightforward GPU supply arrangement. NVIDIA will now hold equity in a company that has committed to deploying its most advanced and most expensive hardware — the Vera Rubin NVL72 rack platform — at scale across Meta's global data centers.

"Muse is how we bring personal superintelligence to everyone," Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said in a statement accompanying the announcement. "We're excited to keep working with NVIDIA to deliver the best personal agents and frontier models for billions of people."

Jensen Huang, NVIDIA's CEO, framed the equity move in broader terms. "AI agents represent a new computing paradigm — software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf," Huang said at the partnership announcement. That framing matters: NVIDIA is not betting on Meta's social media business or its advertising revenues — it is betting that consumer-facing AI agents demanding continuous, always-on inference will be the dominant compute workload of the 2030s, and that Vera Rubin is the hardware generation best positioned to capture that spend.

NVIDIA CFO Colette Kress has previously stated that the company invests in AI companies where it sees "a need to ensure that compute capacity is being built around its hardware." The Meta equity commitment follows that same logic: NVIDIA now has a financial incentive for Muse to succeed, and Meta now has a financial partner with a direct interest in ensuring Vera Rubin deployments run at full capacity.

Both Huang and Zuckerberg have been among the more visible technology executives in Washington on AI policy questions. Huang visited Capitol Hill in July 2026, meeting with senators on AI regulation and warning against what he characterized as "complete nonsense" fearmongering about AI risks. Zuckerberg separately lobbied US senators on AI policy earlier in 2026, advocating for open-source AI development as a counter to any single company establishing dominance — a position that sits in notable tension with the concentrated supplier relationship his company has now deepened with NVIDIA.

Meta's $97.5B Capital Raise: Chip Suppliers Fill $4B of Gap

The equity offering that NVIDIA and AMD are participating in is one of the largest capital raises in the technology sector in years. Meta's $97.5B equity offering structure includes $25 billion in Class A common stock, $12.5 billion in Series A mandatory convertible preferred stock — a hybrid instrument that pays a 6.50% fixed yield before converting to common shares at maturity — and up to $60 billion in additional shares available through an at-the-market program.

The offering expected to close October 29, pending customary conditions, was priced Tuesday with the underwritten $37.5 billion common-and-convertible portion finalized.

Wells Fargo analysts said the raise "likely fulfills" their estimate of a $60–$80 billion financing gap for Meta's fiscal 2027 AI spending plans, and called the structure "sufficient to fulfill funding needs in '27." Mizuho analyst Lloyd Walmsley added that the financing helps "remove part of the equity overhang" that had weighed on Meta's stock.

Those analysts' comments are consistent with Meta's own guidance: the company raised its full-year 2026 capital expenditure forecast to $135–$145 billion at its Q3 earnings, reported October 21. Meta Q3 revenue rose 26 percent to $64.6 billion for the quarter, giving Meta the income base to service the equity raise's preferred obligations while continuing its infrastructure buildout.

Inside NVL72: 3.6 ExaFLOPS Per Rack, Built for Always-On Agent Inference

The hardware at the center of this deal is NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform, announced by Huang at CES 2026. It is the most substantial architectural leap NVIDIA has shipped since the Blackwell generation, and it was designed with a specific workload profile in mind: continuous, low-latency inference at billion-user scale.

At the GPU level, the Rubin VR200 is built on TSMC 3nm process using a multi-chip module design. Each GPU carries 288 gigabytes of HBM4 memory delivering 22 terabytes per second of memory bandwidth — roughly 2.2 to 3 times the bandwidth of the prior-generation H200 — and delivers approximately 35 petaFLOPS of dense FP4 inference compute, or up to 50 petaFLOPS effective FP4 when NVIDIA's Transformer Engine sparsity is applied, per Vera Rubin NVL72 rack specifications from Tom's Hardware. Compared to the Blackwell B200, the Rubin VR200 represents approximately a 3.5× improvement in compute throughput and a 2.8× improvement in memory bandwidth, per available Rubin versus Blackwell performance comparison data.

The full NVL72 rack houses 72 Rubin GPU packages and 36 Vera CPUs in a liquid-cooled enclosure running an 800V DC power architecture. At the rack level, the system delivers up to 3.6 ExaFLOPS of aggregate inference throughput. The NVLink 6 intra-rack interconnect speed runs at approximately 260 terabytes per second, allowing all 72 GPUs to act as a single logical unit — critical for running the largest Muse Wonder model variants across tensor-parallel configurations.

Beyond the rack, Meta's expanded deployment will include NVIDIA's Spectrum-X Ethernet fabric for inter-rack and cluster-level connectivity, and BlueField-4 DPU offloads network processing tasks that would otherwise consume GPU cycles. The BlueField-4 integration is a detail that often goes unnoted in product announcements but matters significantly for the economics of serving continuous agentic sessions: by moving network processing off GPUs, the system keeps more compute available for actual model inference.

What Makes Agentic AI So Compute-Hungry? Muse Explains Why Vera Rubin Was Needed

Muse launched September 8 across platforms as Meta's first general-purpose personal AI agent, available on iOS, Android, the web at https://t.co/WaJxhIE0hy, and within WhatsApp. Powered by the Muse Spark model, it is designed not to answer questions but to take action: sending emails, booking travel, filling out forms, negotiating bills, and completing purchases, with the ability to continue working in the background after a user closes the app.

Muse runs inside a Muse Secure VM — a dedicated virtual machine that isolates agent and user data from Meta's broader infrastructure — with a Sentinel agent operating at the system level to vet any outbound actions before they reach the internet. Meta has said Muse does not share conversation or VM data with its advertising systems, and users can opt out of model training.

As of Meta's Q3 2026 earnings call on October 21, Muse surpassed 10 million accounts. That figure is both an early validation of the product and a preview of the infrastructure challenge ahead: an agentic session is not a request-response cycle that frees GPU resources after a few seconds of generation. A Muse session runs continuously, maintains persistent memory across connected services, executes multi-step plans that may span hours, and must do so at low latency for a user who is expecting real-world actions to complete. At 10 million active users, the steady-state compute demand is orders of magnitude higher per user than a conventional chatbot — and it grows with adoption rather than with query volume.

That compute profile is precisely what the HBM4 memory architecture addresses. Transformer-based models used in agents require constant, high-bandwidth data movement between memory and compute for each step of a multi-step plan. HBM4's 22 TB/s per GPU bandwidth means less time waiting for weights and activations to load, directly translating to lower per-step latency and higher throughput for simultaneous sessions. The 288 GB per-GPU capacity means larger model variants — like Muse Wonder Full, which Meta released October 12 and which outperformed OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on the SWE-Marathon coding benchmark at 57.5 versus 42.5 — can run without model sharding across fewer GPUs, reducing communication overhead.

OpenShell and Sentry: Co-Developing Security Guardrails for Agent Workloads

Beyond compute performance, the expanded partnership includes collaboration on AI agent security — an area of growing concern as agents gain access to personal credentials, financial accounts, and sensitive communications.

NVIDIA offers two relevant platform components: OpenShell, a reference architecture for securely deploying AI agents within enterprise and consumer environments, and Sentry, a behavioral monitoring system that tracks how agents act once deployed. The partnership flagged both as areas for joint development, extending the collaboration beyond model performance into the controls that govern how agents operate on users' behalf.

The framing is notable given that Meta's own Muse platform suffered a zero-day vulnerability in its Secure VM architecture within two weeks of launch — a reminder that the security surface area of an agent that can read credentials, send emails, and make purchases is substantially larger than that of a language model that only produces text.

Why Does NVIDIA Invest in Companies That Buy Its Hardware?

NVIDIA's equity strategy in 2026 has been systematic and substantial. The company committed approximately $30 billion to OpenAI earlier this year, and has deployed NVIDIA's $40 billion 2026 equity campaign across AI companies spanning hyperscalers, infrastructure providers, and AI startups. The $3 billion Meta commitment is one of the larger individual positions, but it fits the same pattern: NVIDIA takes equity in the companies that need the most compute, and those companies commit to buying NVIDIA's most advanced hardware.

NVIDIA CFO Kress has characterized this strategy as ensuring "that compute capacity is being built around its hardware." The logic is circular in a specific and intentional way: NVIDIA's equity stake gives it a financial interest in its customers' success, and its customers' success drives the hardware purchases that fund NVIDIA's next-generation chip development.

Analysts have raised questions about this structure. A report by The Next Web noted SEC disclosure questions about whether "disclosure keeps pace with deals' scale." The concern is not that any individual investment is improper, but that the aggregate scale and the operational dependencies — NVIDIA invests in CoreWeave, which has a $6.3 billion capacity purchase agreement with NVIDIA; NVIDIA invests in Meta, which has committed to Vera Rubin racks — create a web of cross-dependencies whose full scope may not be visible to external investors under current disclosure rules.

This is not a new pattern in the semiconductor industry. Intel Capital, Intel's corporate venture arm, spent more than three decades making strategic equity investments in companies across the PC and server ecosystems — investments explicitly designed to create demand for Intel processors and to lock in preferred supplier relationships. NVIDIA's 2026 equity campaign mirrors that playbook at a scale and speed Intel's program never approached, deploying more in a single year than Intel Capital deployed across most of a decade. Whether NVIDIA's version produces the same competitive entrenchment effects Intel achieved — or whether the open-ecosystem nature of GPU computing limits those effects — is a question the AI industry has not yet had to answer.

AMD's $1B Investment Shows Chip Competition at Meta Runs Deeper Than NVIDIA

NVIDIA's visibility in the Meta partnership announcement should not obscure AMD's position at Meta. AMD announced its own $1 billion equity commitment on Tuesday, alongside the disclosure that its Helios GPU racks are already actively running at Meta data centers and that its EPYC processors are powering Muse workloads.

AMD's engagement with Meta predates the equity story. In February 2026, the two companies signed a AMD Meta February 2026 GPU supply agreement for up to six gigawatts of AMD Instinct GPU capacity at Meta data centers — a commitment tied to 160 million AMD share warrants Meta received as part of the agreement. The simultaneous equity investments by both chipmakers underscores that Meta has become a critical customer for the entire GPU supply chain, not just for NVIDIA, and that both companies see financial participation in Meta's AI buildout as an asset worth holding.

The competitive dynamic between NVIDIA and AMD at Meta is worth watching: both are now equity investors, both are active hardware suppliers, and Meta has demonstrated through the AMD warrant deal that it is willing to use its purchasing power as a negotiating tool. For enterprise customers evaluating Meta's AI platform, that supplier competition is ultimately a hedge against the single-vendor lock-in that has characterized some hyperscaler GPU procurement.

What Muse's 10 Million Users Gain From a $97.5B Infrastructure Bet

For the 10 million Muse users who have already adopted the agent, the most practical consequence of this deal is infrastructure durability. An AI agent is qualitatively different from a chatbot as a product: users configure it, train it on their workflows, connect it to their accounts, and build routines around its capabilities. If the platform degrades or shuts down, users lose not just a convenience but an accumulation of personalized configuration work. Meta's $97.5B capital raise, underwritten by the same chip suppliers on whose hardware Muse runs, is the most credible signal yet that the platform's infrastructure will be funded through the current AI buildout cycle.

For prospective Muse users evaluating whether to give an agent access to their email, calendar, and financial accounts, the partnership's security co-development component — particularly the joint work on NVIDIA's OpenShell and Sentry — is the dimension that most directly affects their risk posture. The Muse Secure VM architecture was designed to isolate agent activity from Meta's advertising infrastructure; the ongoing collaboration with NVIDIA on agent behavioral monitoring is intended to extend those guardrails at the platform level.

The infrastructure picture for Muse is now substantially clearer than it was at launch: dedicated Vera Rubin NVL72 racks with 3.6 ExaFLOPS per rack of aggregate inference throughput, funded by $97.5B in fresh capital, backed by equity commitments from the two companies that manufacture the hardware it runs on, and scaled for a product that its CEO has positioned as the delivery mechanism for "personal superintelligence" for billions of people.

text:
The wedding photograph offers an image of private happiness. But the financing of Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding raises a public question: what access can a Putin-connected Russian businessman buy when he pays for an American president’s son’s celebration?

THE HUNT, THEN THE WEDDING

The Financial Times reports that Umar Kremlev spent two days hunting with Trump Jr. in Mongolia this year. Its reporting draws on guides and officials, alongside Secret Service hotel bookings and Kremlev’s travel from Kazakhstan to Mongolia while Trump Jr. was there.

ProPublica then traced hundreds of thousands of dollars in wedding expenses to a Dubai entity linked to the International Boxing Association, which Kremlev heads. The reported payments included the rental of a private island in the Bahamas and fireworks. Kremlev attended the wedding, among a large group of Russian-speaking guests.

Trump Jr.’s representative did not deny that Kremlev paid wedding expenses. Instead, he described Kremlev as a personal friend whom Trump Jr. met through hunting contacts and grew close to through outdoor pursuits and boxing. Kremlev’s representatives also acknowledged their friendship. That explanation makes the relationship more consequential, not less: this was a man with personal access to the president’s son before the wedding bills were paid.

Former FBI director James Comey’s sworn testimony about Russian efforts to pass damaging information on Hillary Clinton through contacts involving Trump Jr. belongs in the political history of this family. It should not be stretched into proof that Kremlev was the conduit in that episode. The documented hunting trip, friendship and wedding payments demand scrutiny on their own terms.

Oleshky is a gift from Putin.

This relationship matters to Ukraine since Moscow is working to shape what Trump hears and whom he credits. Oleshky is a brutal example. Russia, as the occupying power, bears responsibility for the conditions in occupied territory. Ukrainian officials and international organisations had sought humanitarian corridors for weeks. Moscow delayed, then presented the eventual arrangement as a benevolent breakthrough.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the corridors as the fulfilment of an agreement between Putin and Trump, with Melania Trump’s direct involvement and Russian official Yana Lantratova working with a Ukrainian counterpart. That is Moscow’s preferred story: Putin creates the crisis, withholds relief, then collects praise for allowing people a route out.

The corridors are necessary. Calling them “de-escalation” without naming who caused the emergency gives Russia political cover it never earned. Davyd Arakhamia said the pause would run from 27 October until 22:59 on 1 November and presented such efforts as steps towards peace. Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the precise date suited both sides equally. But timing is political: Moscow has spent weeks delaying a humanitarian solution and can now present one as a Putin-Trump success before the US midterms.

THE WRONG PEOPLE TO FLATTER

There are officials in Washington with whom Ukraine can work. Kyiv should organize its strategy around something other than winning over Trump’s family or the property-developer friends he uses as intermediaries. Steve Witkoff’s closeness to Trump means his account of a Kremlin bargain is a partisan one that Ukraine has no obligation to accept.

A president can smile at Ukrainian representatives while hearing a very different account from his own son or inner circle. Wedding payments do not prove that every US decision is purchased. They do show why polite assurances cannot substitute for examining private relationships, financial interests and the terms being discussed behind closed doors. Proposals involving Russian energy, sanctions relief or Ukrainian territory must face public and congressional scrutiny before they become faits accomplis.

The available counterweight is America’s political system. Congress can demand records, question intermediaries and constrain deals that reward Moscow. Ukrainian officials can name the administration decisions that damage Ukraine, as Zelenskyy has done in accusing Pete Hegseth of blocking interceptor missiles, rather than hiding every dispute behind diplomatic courtesy. They can also refuse to treat a negotiator’s private access as a mandate to speak for Ukraine.

None of that requires inventing a theory of total control over the Trump family. The visible facts are serious enough. A Putin-connected businessman hunted with the president’s son, helped pay for his wedding and was described by that son’s representative as a personal friend. The Kremlin is presenting relief for people trapped by its occupation as a favour from Putin to Trump. Soft language from Kyiv leaves that version of events less contested exactly when it needs to be challenged.

Source: Resurgam

text:
This was a prototype map for "Iron, Blood, Snow and Mud" - our fast-playing game on the Eastern Front. 

This was from 2021 and the game went through a few revisions before publication - but the essentials are here.

You will notice a few interesting features. Some cities take up multiple hexes - Kiev is 2 hexes and Moscow is 3 hexes. You need to control each hex to control the city.

You will also notice some spots for fleets. The German fleet can operate in the Baltic, the Soviet fleet can operate in the Black Sea. The fleets can offer fire support to battles in adjacent hexes - very handy. Naval support wasn't decisive on the Eastern Front, but it was still a factor in coastal operations like the sieges of Sevastopol and Leningrad.

Some other feature are also evident - the Pripet Marshes, the road/rail network of Soviet Russia an the mountains of the Caucasus. 

Even at a zoomed-out scale, we've managed to cram in a lot of detail!
