text:
< Be Earl Warren
< Born 1891, Los Angeles
< Your father is a Norwegian immigrant, works for the Southern Pacific Railroad
< You grow up in Bakersfield, a railroad town full of dust and union fights
< Berkeley for undergrad, then Boalt Hall for law
< You graduate into World War I, serve stateside as a first lieutenant
< Back home, you take a job as a district attorney's clerk in Alameda County
< Within five years, you run the office
< You prosecute bootleggers, corrupt officials, crooked cops
< The conviction rate is near perfect
< California's Republican bosses notice
< 1938, you run for Attorney General and win
< Then Pearl Harbor
< You become the loudest voice for Japanese internment on the West Coast
< 120,000 people, two-thirds of them American citizens, lose everything
< You call it military necessity
< 1942, you win the governorship in a landslide
< Reelected twice, the only California governor to serve three terms
< You build highways, expand universities, modernize the state hospital system
< Republicans talk about you for president
< 1948, you're Dewey's running mate on the losing ticket
< 1952, Eisenhower offers you the next Supreme Court seat
< Chief Justice Vinson dies in September 1953
< The next seat is the center chair
< You take it
< Brown v. Board of Education lands on your desk within months
< The Court is split, tempers running hot
< You works the justices one by one, in private, over months
< May 17, 1954, the ruling is unanimous. Segregation in public schools is unconstitutional.
< Your name is on the most important civil rights decision in American history
< The same man who locked up Japanese Americans without trial
< Southern billboards read "Impeach Earl Warren" for the next decade
< You keep going. Miranda. Gideon. Reynolds v. Sims. Loving v. Virginia.
< Eisenhower later calls your appointment the biggest mistake of his presidency
< You retire in 1969 and die in 1974

The architect of Japanese internment became the architect of civil rights. Not redemption. Just the same certainty pointed in a different direction.

History does not require you to be consistent. It only requires you to win.

text:
My coworker Dan retired last month. He sold his house and prepared to move to Arizona.

On his final afternoon, he did not give me career advice. He did not tell me who to avoid in management.

He handed me a yellow legal pad, folded into four quarters.

"Put this in your safe," he said.

Inside were nine names and nine phone numbers, written in pencil over what looked like twenty-five years.

Next to each name was a single word:
"Tree."
"Roof."
"Concrete."
"Transmission."

None of them had last names. Two of them had the word "Dead" lightly erased and replaced by a son's first name.

Dan tapped the paper with his thumb.

"When the storm comes, do not post on Facebook asking for help. Do not call the city. Call Dale."

"Who is Dale?"

"Dale does the trees. Tell him you sit at Dan's desk."

"Will he answer?"

"He will answer before the second ring. But you listen to me carefully: Dale is seventy-one. You do not call Dale for a branch. You call Dale when the timber is through the rafters. You offer him coffee from a thermos, black. If you offer him fancy creamer, he will pack his saws and leave."

I looked at the piece of paper.

In Japan, land is passed down through stamped deeds and registry offices.

Here, a house is just drywall and cedar. The actual deed to the property is the piece of yellow paper that connects you to the men who keep the roof from caving in.

Dan shook my hand, got into his truck, and left for the desert.

I am thirty-eight years old, and for the first time in this country, I feel legally protected.

text:
🇨🇦 TOWNS THROUGH TIME

📍 Dawson City, Yukon — July 4, 1899

💰 YOU’VE STRUCK GOLD IN THE KLONDIKE!

It’s the summer of 1899. After months of backbreaking work along the creeks of the Klondike, you’ve finally hit pay dirt!

With gold in your pockets, money to spend, and a thirst to quench, you head into Dawson City for a well-deserved celebration.

And as luck would have it, there’s a grand opening in town!

You push through the doors of the Opera House and step inside.

Suddenly, every face turns toward you.

The bartender looks up. Men in wide-brimmed hats and magnificent moustaches stare in your direction. Even the young fellow nearby seems curious about the newcomer.

Welcome to Dawson City at the height of the Klondike Gold Rush!

On July 4, 1899, photographer Eric A. Hegg captured this remarkable scene at the grand opening of Dawson City’s Opera House.

Among those pictured, fourth from the left, is “Arizona Charlie” Meadows, a colourful Wild West showman who became one of Dawson City’s best-known entertainment entrepreneurs.

Charlie operated several establishments in the booming gold rush town, including the Opera House, offering miners and fortune seekers a welcome escape from the hardships of life in the goldfields.

Dawson City was a place where fortunes could be made, lost, and spent almost overnight. Saloons and entertainment halls offered a taste of excitement to those chasing their dreams of striking it rich.

And tonight, you’re one of the lucky ones!

So belly up to the bar, gentlemen. The first round’s on you!

🎶 Tonight we’re gonna party like it’s 1899! 🎶

📸 Eric A. Hegg — Opera House grand opening, July 4, 1899.

text:
Oregon still has among the softest drug laws in the U.S.

Under HB 4002 (2024), personal possession of fentanyl, meth, heroin, or cocaine is only a “drug enforcement misdemeanor.” 

Default is treatment-focused probation (up to 18 months). Jail is mainly for violations or if requested. Many counties still offer deflection to avoid charges.

SB 236 (2025) raised the fentanyl floor to 1g+ or 5+ units for a Class A misdemeanor, larger/commercial amounts can be a Class C felony. 

These remain far lighter than the multi-year felonies common in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Arizona, Idaho, and others. Federal trafficking and gun cases carry mandatory minimums regardless of state law.

Oregon’s sanctuary rules remain in force, limiting state and local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. 

In 2026, the state REFUSED confidential undercover plates for ICE agents, and counties have continued refusing certain information requests and detainers.

Same drugs. Still lighter consequences in Oregon.

text:
Mate, are you living in fairyland? 😂 You keep listing EU membership benefits as though putting a flag in Brussels and opening your borders magically delivers higher wages, productive industries, stronger institutions and a better future. Wake up. The real world doesn't work like that and the world is far from more complicated than your EU brochure.

Nobody is arguing that Portugal became poor because it joined the EU. That’s a straw man. The question is whether EU membership automatically delivers the prosperity its advocates promise. Portugal joined in 1986, yet in 2025 its GDP per capita, adjusted for purchasing power, was still only 81% of the EU average. The European Commission itself points to persistent productivity problems, a reliance on lower-value-added services and a low share of high-tech exports. After four decades of membership, those structural weaknesses haven't magically disappeared.

Yes, Portugal has benefited from EU investment, trade and access to the single market. Nobody serious needs to deny that. But acknowledging benefits isn't the same as pretending the model is an unqualified success. If membership alone were the answer, why is Portugal still below the EU average in income and productivity? The question isn't whether the EU offers opportunities; it's whether a country can turn those opportunities into sustainable prosperity for ordinary citizens.

Now let's talk about Croatia, because this is where your argument becomes particularly convenient. Croatia joined the EU in July 2013. According to the OECD, annual recorded emigration more than tripled between 2013 and 2017, rising from approximately 15,300 to 47,400 people. The OECD explicitly connects the period's surge to EU accession, freedom of movement and the lifting of labour-market restrictions in destination countries, alongside the economic crisis and the search for better wages. 

Of course, EU membership isn't the only cause. But that's precisely the point: the ability to leave became easier just as many Croatians were struggling to find attractive opportunities at home. Freedom of movement is a benefit for the individual who leaves, but it can become a serious problem for the country losing its young workers, skilled professionals and taxpayers. You can't simply celebrate the freedom to leave while ignoring why so many people feel compelled to use it.

And spare me the argument that people also emigrate from non-EU Balkan countries. Obviously they do. That doesn't disprove anything. It merely shows that economic problems exist on both sides of the EU's external border. The relevant question is whether accession creates enough productive jobs, competitive businesses and rising real wages at home to make staying a viable choice. Saying that people leave Serbia too doesn't answer that question; it dodges it.

As for your list of goals — better wages, productive businesses, stronger institutions and less corruption — who exactly disagrees with those? The disagreement is over whether EU accession is the necessary route to achieving them, what conditions and compromises it entails, and whether Serbia's political and economic elites would actually deliver the promised results.

You cannot outsource the responsibility to build a functional country to Brussels. Membership doesn't automatically eliminate corruption, fix a weak judiciary, create high-value industries or ensure that economic growth reaches ordinary families. Those things require competent domestic institutions, sound economic policy and political accountability. EU membership may help with some of that, but it is not a substitute for it.

So let's stop confusing access to a market with the ability to compete in it, investment with broad-based prosperity, and freedom to emigrate with the freedom to build a decent life at home.

Serbia should examine the evidence, the actual costs and benefits, and the experiences of countries that have already joined. Not swallow a political sales pitch and call it an economic strategy.

The question isn't whether Brussels can offer Serbia opportunities. It's whether the people selling EU accession can explain, concretely and honestly, how those opportunities will translate into better lives for ordinary Serbians — without pretending that Portugal's structural problems or Croatia's mass emigration never happened.

So, are you living in fairyland, or are you finally prepared to discuss the real trade-offs? 🇷🇸

text:
In the wake of the Urda train tragedy that shook Spain and the world, in which at least 60 are reportedly dead, the dioceses of Toledo and Madrid and the Spanish Episcopal Conference (CEE) have requested prayers for the victims of the Urda train crash. The mishap occurred at around 9:00 a.m. (local time), when two high-speed trains collided in Toledo Province.

The accident reportedly occurred when a Renfe AVE train crashed into another train from the rear. At least two cars of the second train have been derailed, causing massive tragedy.

In a statement released in the wake of the tragedy, the Archbishop of Toledo, Francisco Cerro Chaves, and the Auxiliary Bishop, Francisco César García Magán, Secretary General of the Spanish Episcopal Conference, have expressed their “deep concern” and closeness to all the victims.

Meanwhile, the Archdiocese of Toledo, together with the parishes of Urda and Los Yébenes and Caritas Toledo, has offered support to the victims and their families. The diocesan Church has also invited the faithful to pray for those affected, their families, and all those involved in the relief efforts.

Madrid archbishop, Cardinal José Cobo posted on his X handle, expressing his sorrow over the tragedy. "We continue to follow with deep sorrow the reports about the serious accident between two trains that occurred this morning in Toledo," the Cardinal wrote.

You’re acknowledging what Ezekiel says the sticks represent, then adding two books that the passage never identifies.

In verse 16, the sticks are labeled Judah and Joseph/Ephraim. In verses 21-22, God explains exactly what joining them means: gathering the scattered Israelites and making them one nation under one king. Verses 24-28 continue with one shepherd, one covenant, and one sanctuary. Nothing about joining two books of scripture.

Yes, wooden writing tablets existed. But writing names on wood doesn’t mean Ezekiel was referring to two sacred records. The writing identifies the two divided peoples.

Interestingly, even your Church’s 2026 seminary manual distinguishes Ezekiel’s prophecy about reunifying Israel from the additional interpretation offered by modern LDS prophets. BYU scholar Joseph M. Spencer also argues that the sticks themselves represent the divided peoples, not books.

You can believe the Bible and Book of Mormon complement each other. But that doesn’t establish that Ezekiel predicted the Book of Mormon.

Where does Ezekiel identify either stick as a future scripture from the Americas? He doesn’t.

You’re interpreting Ezekiel through the Book of Mormon and then using that interpretation as evidence for the Book of Mormon. That’s circular reasoning, not independent biblical evidence.

text:
Three dry cakes on a little dish, and a king's luck ended. 📜🌾

Coirpre son of Étan, poet of the Tuatha Dé Danann

Who he is: in Cath Maige Tuired he is "Coirpre son of Étain, the poet of the Túatha Dé" and "Coirpre mac Étaíne", Lug's poet. In Lebor Gabála Érenn his mother is Étan the Poetess, a daughter of Dían Cécht the physician, "and Coirpre, son of Etan was the poet." The texts never describe his face.

What he did:
• The stingy king. Under Bres the Túatha Dé "did not see their poets nor their bards nor their satirists nor their harpers nor their pipers nor their horn-blowers nor their jugglers nor their fools entertaining them in the household."
• The dark little house. Coirpre came to Bres seeking hospitality. "He entered a narrow, black, dark little house; and there was neither fire nor furniture nor bedding in it. Three small cakes were brought to him on a little dish—and they were dry."
• The first satire. "Without food quickly on a dish, Without cow's milk on which a calf grows, Without a man's habitation after darkness remains, Without paying a company of storytellers—let that be Bres's condition." "'Bres's prosperity no longer exists,' he said, and that was true. There was only blight on him from that hour; and that is the first satire that was made in Ireland."
• His promise. Lug asked, "And you, Coirpre mac Étaíne, what can you do in the battle?" "I will make a glám dícenn against them, and I will satirize them and shame them so that through the spell of my art they will offer no resistance to warriors."
• His end. A Lebor Gabála poem: "Of a stroke of the pure sun died Cairpre the great, son of Etan: Etan died over the pool of sorrow for white-headed Cairpre."

What he represents: the power of the poet's word. A king who failed in hospitality lost his luck to a satire.

Source: Cath Maige Tuired (CELT, trans. Elizabeth A. Gray) and Lebor Gabála Érenn part 4 (Macalister, on Mary Jones's site, https://t.co/78c9J9kxwA). Legend, not history.

Read more Irish myth at https://t.co/CsXzEtuyj9

text:
After 13 years of doing emergency preparation, my biggest recommendation is to skip the boxes and premade bags of stuff that rot on the shelf and don’t get used, and have real food you regularly use and rotate your cans/dry goods with things you eat regularly. 

For example, my family and I eat a lot of rice, so we buy 25 lbs of rice that we store in a food-safe container and refill the one in the pantry. We bake a lot of our own bread so we have 25 lbs of flour and other bread making staples in larger quantities. We decided we would rather have hard beans (black and other types) for what we make and we cook in the pressure cooker and we don’t use the cans. 

I’m not saying cans are bad; it’s just what we found we liked better for storage purposes because cans take up a lot of space that we don’t have.

Long story short, find what you like to eat and stock the supplies to make them.

Other emergency preparedness items are a whole other topic that we can go into if you have questions. Others have recommended the church emergency preparedness specialist; I would see if the church in your area is offering an emergency preparedness class (they offer them from time to time) and that would be a great place to start.

text:
BIRYANI: The World’s Most Delicious Reason to Lose Your Manners

An international love story involving rice, spices, and absolutely no intention of sharing the last piece of meat.
Let’s face it, humanity has spent centuries fighting over land, power, religion, ideology and who gets to sit at the head of the table. Yet, put a steaming deg of biryani in the middle of the room, and suddenly everyone has one common objective.
Securing a respectable portion before the deg runs dry.

دنیا نقشوں پر تقسیم ہے، قومیں نظریات پر؛ لیکن بریانی سامنے ہو تو سب کا نظریہ ایک ہی ہوتا ہے 
بھائی، بوٹی کدھر ہے؟

✓ The United Nations of Biryani

Forget diplomatic summits. Imagine a world conference where Pakistan brings Karachi biryani, India presents its regional varieties, Malaysia contributes its fragrant traditions, and biryani-loving communities from London to Toronto arrive with their own interpretations.

The first item on the agenda? Whether potatoes belong in biryani.

The second? Why someone always claims they're not hungry and then proceeds to eat from everybody else's plate.

The third? An emergency investigation into the person who took the last piece of meat and left behind nothing but rice.

اقوامِ متحدہ میں بڑے بڑے تنازعات حل نہیں ہوتے، اور یہاں لوگ آلو پر جنگ کیلئے تیار بیٹھے ہیں۔ بس فرق اتنا ہے کہ بریانی کی جنگ میی ثالثی کرنے والا بھی چمچ لے کر آتا ہے

✓ Karachi Biryani: Not for the Faint-Hearted

Karachi biryani doesn't enter a room. It makes an entrance.
The aroma arrives first, the spices announce their presence next and the chilli eventually reminds you that every decision has consequences.
It isn't merely lunch. It is a personality test.
Can you handle the heat? Can you tolerate the wait? Can you watch someone take the last juicy piece without reconsidering the entire relationship?
And please, never ask a Karachi biryani enthusiast to describe their favourite biryani objectively. You're not conducting research, you're entering a diplomatic minefield.

کراچی کی بریانی کھانے کے بعد اگر آنکھوں میں آنسو آجائیں تو ضروری نہیں جذباتی ہو گئے ہوں؛ ممکن ہے مرچ نے پرانی دشمنی نکالی ہو

✓ The Great Aloo Controversy

Every great civilisation has its defining debates. Philosophers debate existence. Economists debate inflation. Biryani lovers debate potatoes.
One side argues that aloo absorbs the masala beautifully. The other side behaves as though a potato has committed an unforgivable violation of culinary law.
Meanwhile, the sensible person at table quietly takes an extra serving. Because why should a perfectly good meal become a constitutional crisis?

آلو بریانی میں ہونا چاہیے یا نہیں، یہ ایک الگ بحث ہے؛ لیکن کسی کی پلیٹ سے آلو اٹھانا یقیناً اخلاقی جرم ہے۔ ہر آزادی کی ایک حد ہوتی ہے، جناب 

✓ Love, Loyalty and Last Piece of Meat

You can learn a surprising amount about a person by sharing biryani with them.
Do they offer you the best piece without being asked? Do they quietly save some for you? Do they ask whether you have eaten before finishing the entire deg themselves?
Or do they say, “Take as much as you like,” while guarding the meat pieces like a central bank protects its gold reserves?

Romance is complicated. Human behaviour is complicated. But biryani reveals certain truths with remarkable efficiency.

محبت کے دعوے تو سب کرتے ہیں؛ اصل امتحان تب ہوتا ہے جب پلیٹ میں آخری بوٹی بچی ہو اور سامنے والا پوچھے
تم کھاؤ گی؟

✓  Biryani Is Cultural Diplomacy Without the Boring Speeches

Food cannot end every war or settle every political dispute. But sharing a meal can make strangers a little less strange.
A Pakistani living abroad may find a taste of home in a plate of biryani. A family gathering may become memorable. Friends from different cultures may discover that a shared love of spices is an excellent starting point for conversation.

text:
For forty years, a legendary biryani restaurant in Lucknow drew crowds from all over the country. The founder, a tough old man named Hamid, had built the business from a single street cart into a massive culinary landmark.

Hamid kept the exact recipe for his signature spice mix locked inside a bank vault. Only he and his eldest son knew the formula.

Nobody on the staff ever argued with that. His managers understood that the spice mix was the magic of the business. It was his nuclear code. He had bled for decades to perfect it, and he had every right to protect his core asset from competitors.

But over the years, Hamid's fear of losing his empire spread far beyond the spice vault.

He did not just guard the recipe. He refused to let his senior managers negotiate the daily prices with the local meat and rice vendors. He stood at the front counter every single evening until midnight because he did not trust anyone else to touch the physical cash register. When the restaurant needed to hire two new waiters, Hamid made his floor manager wait three weeks so he could conduct the interviews himself.

He treated every single decision in the restaurant like it was a state secret.

Because the senior managers were completely shut out of running the actual operations, they felt like glorified clerks. They were paid well, but they were never trusted with true responsibility. When a modern hospitality group opened a massive new restaurant across the street, they offered Hamid's top two managers roles with actual operational freedom. Both managers resigned immediately.

Hamid sat at his empty counter that night, complained to his son, and declared that loyalty was dead. He genuinely believed that modern workers were just greedy mercenaries who only cared about their own ascendance.

Think about a king who builds a massive fortress to protect his royal treasure. Locking the gold in the deepest underground vault makes perfect sense. But if the king is so paranoid that he insists on personally checking the ID of every farmer delivering wheat to the kitchen gate, he is no longer ruling a kingdom. He is just acting as his own security guard.

In the corporate world, many brilliant founders make this exact same mistake. They build an incredible product or service through sheer grit. They are absolutely right to protect their patents, their equity, and their ultimate strategic control.

The tragedy happens when they confuse protecting the core with controlling the perimeter.

When you refuse to hand over the grocery list because you are busy protecting the secret recipe, you do not protect your business. You just suffocate it. Capable executives do not leave because they want to steal your secret formula. They leave because talented adults want to drive the delivery truck, and they get tired of sitting in the passenger seat while the owner insists on steering every single turn.

Every Corporatewasi who builds an empire must learn where to draw the line. Lock up your nuclear codes and protect the foundation of your house. But if you treat every single person walking through your door like a potential thief, you will eventually find yourself standing in a very large, very empty building.

text:
Spare me the outrage, sis…

Wrong is wrong and both parties and guilty of it and it just shows that politics are dishonest…

Trying to say otherwise and pointing fingers is just a cope and a play to garner votes..

FFS…

Here are documented cases of similar ballot tactics (same or confusing names, or recruited “spoiler”/ghost candidates) that favored Republicans or were intended to. These parallel the Alaska Sullivan situation in using name similarity or third-party entries to dilute the opposing party’s support. 
Florida 2020 State Senate District 37
Democratic incumbent Jose Javier Rodriguez lost to Republican Ileana Garcia by just 32 votes. An independent candidate named Alex Rodriguez (same last name) received more than 6,000 votes despite doing essentially no campaigning.
A GOP operative (and later convicted former state Sen. Frank Artiles) was involved in recruiting and funding the independent. Political committees linked to the effort sent mailers promoting the ghost candidate as a progressive alternative. The scheme was part of a broader “ghost candidate” operation targeting multiple Democratic state Senate candidates. Multiple people connected to it faced charges or plea deals. 
Minnesota 2020 U.S. House District 2
Democrat Angie Craig narrowly defeated Republican Tyler Kistner. Third-party candidate Adam Weeks (Legal Marijuana Now Party) received roughly 24,000 votes—more than double the margin between the major-party candidates.
Weeks left a voicemail admitting that local Republicans had recruited him to run as a liberal third-party candidate specifically to “pull votes away” from Craig and help the GOP nominee. He mentioned an offer of about $15,000. (Weeks later died; the race still proceeded.) Democrats alleged similar recruitment of spoilers in other Minnesota races that cycle. 
Pennsylvania 2022 U.S. House District 12
Republican Mike Doyle ran against Democrat Summer Lee. A long-serving Democratic congressman from the same region (also named Mike Doyle) was retiring. Some of the Republican’s lawn signs read “Democrats for Doyle.” Lee’s campaign viewed the name similarity as an attempt to confuse voters. Lee ultimately won, but the tactic mirrored the name-confusion strategy seen elsewhere. 
Other notes
•  In Alaska itself, both parties have used ballot-stacking or spoiler tactics. When Mary Peltola ran for the House previously, Republicans worked to keep a Democratic-listed candidate (an inmate) on the ballot, which could dilute Democratic support.

A 74-year-old blind Florida man facing a first-degree m¥rder charge made an unusual proposal in court, offering to plead guilty and accept life in prison if he could get a Philly cheesesteak, fries and a Pepsi. 

Robert Kessler, who is also charged with ab¥se of a de@d body, told the judge he was considering an open plea to resolve the case without a trial. 

Explaining his proposed deal, Kessler said he would plead guilty and take a life sentence for a Philly cheesesteak and an order of fries and a Pepsi. 

When the judge asked for clarification, Kessler specified that he wanted the cheesesteak with onions and mayonnaise, and fries, adding that he wanted a “20-ounce” Pepsi.

The judge, who said he had been handling cases for nearly 40 years, admitted he had never heard such a request before. He explained that he could not provide food as part of a plea deal, saying it would be “wrong in a thousand ways,” but assured Kessler that he would have lunch that day. 

Kessler then withdrew his offer, saying he did not want to enter the open plea and would rather proceed with jury selection. 

Kessler is accused of k+lling 47-year-old Stephanie Crone Overholt and dismembering her body. He had initially been representing himself but has since changed his mind. 

The unusual plea proposal was ultimately unsuccessful, and the case proceeded toward trial.

text:
Are there states that charge higher property tax based on whether you are a resident?

Yes — many states effectively charge higher property taxes on properties owned by non-residents (or used as second homes/investments) than on primary residences of residents.⁠

This is not usually done through a higher base mill rate solely because the owner lives in another state (that kind of pure residency discrimination is generally considered unconstitutional under the Privileges and Immunities Clause and related protections). Instead, states use homestead exemptions, lower assessment ratios, assessment caps, rate tiers, or school-tax exemptions that apply only to owner-occupied primary residences.⁠

Non-residents (or owners of non-primary properties) typically do not qualify, so they pay a higher effective tax on comparable property.

Clear Examples

South Carolina: Primary residences (“legal residences”) are assessed at 4% of fair market value. Second homes, rentals, and other non-owner-occupied residential property are assessed at 6% (50% higher assessed value before millage is applied). Qualifying primary residences also get a major school operating millage exemption. You must apply and prove primary residency/domicile in the state.⁠

Montana (recent reforms effective for 2026 bills): Primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals get a tiered structure (e.g., 0.76% on the first portion of value up to the statewide median, then higher tiers). Non-primary residential property (second homes, short-term rentals, vacant lots) is taxed at a flat 1.90%. The difference can be large—often roughly double the taxable value on mid-range homes.⁠

Other common cases:

Florida: Large homestead exemption (roughly the first $25k–$50k+ of assessed value, with parts applying differently) plus the “Save Our Homes” 3% annual assessment growth cap — available only for primary residences.

Texas: Significant homestead exemption (around $140,000 off school-district taxable value in recent years) plus a 10% annual appraisal increase cap for homesteads.

Indiana: Constitutional caps that are lower for homesteads (1% of assessed value) than for other residential property (2%).

Alabama and some others: Historically (and in classification systems) lower assessment ratios for owner-occupied single-family homes versus other residential property.

Many additional states offer smaller homestead exemptions, credits, or assessment limits that favor primary owner-occupants. Investment or non-owner-occupied residential property faces higher effective rates in roughly 18 states plus D.C. due to these differentials and classification rules.⁠

Bottom Line

If you own a primary residence and live in the state, you usually get meaningful breaks that non-residents (or owners of second homes) do not. The gap can be substantial in states like South Carolina and Montana. Rates and rules vary by locality (property tax is mostly local), so check the specific county assessor or state revenue department for the property in question, and confirm eligibility/application requirements for any homestead or primary-residence benefits.

text:
Before 1914, America had nearly open borders, and almost all Americans think that was a good thing.

So why do those same Americans—myself included—say “No” to open borders today?

The great Milton Friedman explained it simply as follows:

you can't have free immigration and a welfare state at the same time.

Back in the 1900’s, a third or more of immigrants went home. No job, no safety net, no staying.

That filter meant that only the people who came to work extremely hard, assimilate, and build, stayed here. 

Today, the filter's gone. And when the filter's gone, the incentives flip. Someone who can't make it here doesn't have to leave anymore. 

Their U.S.-born kids qualify for benefits, many states offer their own programs, and staying beats going home, whether they came legally or not.

So instead of keeping only the people who make it, we keep the ones who don't, too. 

In some immigrant groups, a majority of households use at least one welfare program, while social services are stretched and the debt keeps growing.

And there's a second change: three work visa programs that didn't exist in 1914.

The first is a work visa called the H-1B. Companies use it mostly in tech, often paying lower wage levels to foreigners—mostly Indians—than comparable Americans.

The second is OPT, which stands for Optional Practical Training. It lets foreign students keep working in the U.S. for up to three years after graduation, with no test of whether an American could fill the job. Employers also skip payroll taxes on them, which makes them cheaper to hire than an American grad.

The third is the J-1, a so-called exchange visitor visa. It brings in researchers, au pairs, camp counselors, and seasonal resort workers, often at lower cost than hiring Americans for the same jobs.

All three tie the worker to the employer sponsoring them, so they have less leverage to push back.

The result is fewer openings and softer wages for American workers.

In short, open borders worked when the only thing on offer was opportunity. 

That’s no longer the case, unfortunately, and Americans rightfully want the immigration system to be reformed abd start serving the interest of American citizens and workers first. 

I’m Joseph Bovino, U.S. Immigration and business attorney based on the free state of Florida and serving clients worldwide.

text:
Metra and one of region’s cultural icons, Lyric Opera of Chicago, are teaming up to offer free Metra rides to Lyric shows between Nov. 20 and Nov. 29. Just show your Lyric ticket to the conductor on the day of your show and you can ride to the show and home free.

Lyric is offering three shows during that timeframe: Wagner: Myth & Music, Don Pasquale, and Disney’s Encanto In Concert Live to Film. The venue at 20 N Wacker Drive is within a walk or short cab ride from all of Metra’s downtown stations.

Riders can travel free on Metra on the date printed on their show ticket (paper or digital). The offer is valid for all Metra lines and includes round-trip travel — to the theatre and back. Riders must show their show ticket to the conductor when asked.

“We are proud to partner with Lyric Opera of Chicago to promote their world-class shows and our fast, convenient, stress-free travel,” said Metra Executive Director/CEO Jim Derwinski. 

Metra has a similar arrangement with Broadway in Chicago through January 2027, and for Northwestern football’s home games at the new Ryan Field in Evanston.

text:
AMERICA'S MIDTERMS: THE ECONOMY, THE IRAN WAR, AND WHY REPUBLICANS ARE SET TO LOSE BOTH CHAMBERS

What Donald Trump was handed, what he did with it, what his own voters now say, and the GeoMemo Convergence Test on who wins.

GeoMemo Desk, October 28th, 2026. Six days to go.

THE ECONOMY DONALD TRUMP WAS HANDED:

Trump (@WhiteHouse) inherited an economy that was cooling off, not falling apart. In January 2025, the month he took office, consumer prices were rising 3 percent a year. In September they rose 3.7 percent, the highest reading since May, and wholesale prices had their largest monthly jump in more than four years. Inflation did not go away. It went up.

Employers added 29,000 jobs in September, against 133,000 in August after revision. In 2024, Biden's last full year, they were adding about 166,000 a month on the Bureau of Labor Statistics count, and later revisions have cut that figure as well as this year's. Unemployment at 4.2 percent is still low by any historical standard, which is why the White House points at it, but the flow of new jobs has all but stopped. 

Almost all the private hiring since January 2025 has been in health care and social work, plus roughly 180,000 jobs tied to building data centers for artificial intelligence. Everything else is close to flat.

The economy grew at an annual rate of 2.5 percent in the first quarter and 2.2 percent in the second, and the Atlanta Fed's live tracker points to about 3.5 percent for the third. Biden's last full year came in at 2.8 percent. So there is no slump to explain here, and no boom either. On growth, Trump has handed back roughly what he was given.

The economy grew, then. This election turns on who got the growth.

WHO'S GETTING THE BETTER END AND WHO'S GETTING THE BITTER END?

The Economist (@TheEconomist) did the arithmetic, pooling the measured effects of the tariffs, higher fuel prices and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act across income groups for 2026.

The New York Federal Reserve estimates the tariffs have raised consumer goods prices by about 2 percent. Yale's Budget Lab puts the cost to the average household at roughly $1,100 this year, and the war's effect on oil adds about $1,000 more by December. Pushing the other way, the tax law raised the average refund by about $340.

The result is that the poorest tenth of households, living on about $37,000 a year after tax and benefits, lose almost 3 percent of their income this year. They lose because fuel and imported goods take a much bigger bite out of a small budget, and because the help that would have cushioned it, food stamps and Medicaid, is exactly what was cut. Middle earners on about $100,000 lose more than $400. The richest tenth, on nearly $500,000, gain almost 3 percent, because their tax cut is worth more to them than the higher prices cost them.

The Congressional Budget Office gets the same shape from a different direction. Looking at the tax law on its own, through 2034, it finds the poorest tenth of households about $1,200 a year worse off, mainly through the cuts to Medicaid and food assistance, and the richest tenth about $13,600 a year better off from the tax reductions. Republicans reject that reading. Jason Smith (@RepJasonSmith), who chairs the House Ways and Means Committee, says the budget office has "a troubled track record of getting its estimates incorrect." The Treasury has not yet released the filing data that would settle the argument either way.

Republicans also let the enhanced Obamacare subsidies lapse. KFF (@KFF) calculates this alone raised average premiums on individually bought plans by nearly $800 a year, and that is not in the figures above.

Housing is the other squeeze, and it runs the same way. The average 30 year mortgage hit 7.4 percent in early October, a three year high, against just under 6.2 percent a year earlier, pushed up in part by the war's effect on inflation. Oxford Economics estimates this year's rise alone has priced about five million more households out of buying. Builders reckon the tariffs on building materials add nearly $11,000 to the cost of a typical new house, and the immigration raids have made construction labor 4.2 percent more expensive in a year, by the National Association of Home Builders' September survey. Sales to first time buyers fell 5.4 percent in May against a year earlier while luxury sales rose 6.2 percent, on Zillow's numbers.

Wages did not cover the gap. Private pay growth slowed from 4 percent to 3 percent while inflation ran at 3.7 percent, so real hourly earnings are down 0.7 percent on the year. Labor's share of corporate revenue is the lowest since records began in 1947.

The stock market boom is genuine, and it went where the stocks are. Of the $17 trillion American households gained in shares and funds since the end of 2024, Federal Reserve data show almost 90 percent went to the richest tenth. The poorer half got 0.6 percent.

Manufacturing was the promise. Output is up, but factory employment is down about 20,000 since January 2025. North Carolina, which Trump carried in 2024, has lost almost 9,000 factory jobs in a year.

THE WAR, AND WHO PAYS FOR IT

The war with Iran began on February 28th and is in its eighth month. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (@PeteHegseth) told the Senate in July it had cost $37.5 billion. The Congressional Budget Office estimated $38 billion by September, and the Center for Strategic and International Studies $34 billion to $42 billion as early as June. Some independent estimates run past $100 billion. Twenty one American service members have been killed and at least 865 wounded as of October 10th.

The Center for American Progress (@amprog) collected the household costs. Moody's (@Moodys) chief economist Mark Zandi estimates the war has cost the average household almost $2,000, absorbing about half its income gain. Gasoline and diesel are 43 percent and 68 percent above prewar levels, and Americans have paid more than $141 billion in extra fuel costs, by Brown University's tracking. In Maine, where about half of homes burn oil for heat, the average household pays $674 more to fill the tank this year.

This is what a war does to an economy, and it is not a partisan point but the ordinary economics of the thing. A war is not a stimulus program. It destroys more wealth than it creates, it concentrates what is left in energy and defense, and it sends the bill to households as higher prices at the pump and higher borrowing costs. Somebody pays the higher price and somebody collects it.

Both ends show up in the same week's filings. Chevron's quarterly profit more than quadrupled to $12.1 billion and Exxon Mobil's more than doubled to $14.5 billion, both running refineries near capacity while Middle East capacity was knocked out. Trump said the plain thing in August: "Chevron, too much money. Exxon Mobil, too much, too much money. They ought to give some of that back to the public." He ordered his Justice Department to investigate oil companies for not cutting prices fast enough. Meanwhile the administration lifted sanctions on Russian diesel and signed a deal for 25 million barrels, for an estimated saving of 2 to 5 cents a gallon. Diesel is up about $2.60 since the war began.

HOW REPUBLICANS SEE IT

Six surveys this month measured Trump's approval among Republicans. CNN (@CNN) and the New York Times/Siena (@nytimes, @SienaResearch) both put it at 74 percent. NBC News (@NBCNews) has 76, Civiqs (@Civiqs) 78, and the Washington Post (@washingtonpost), ABC News (@ABC) and Ipsos (@ipsosus) 79. CNBC (@CNBC), released October 26th, has 82 percent, and 90 percent among voters who identify with MAGA.

Two findings from the Council on Foreign Relations (@CFR_org) show what is loosening. Last month, 34 percent of Republicans and Republican leaners said they consider themselves primarily a Trump supporter rather than a supporter of the Republican Party. In February 2025 that was 63 percent. And just 29 percent of likely Republican voters say the economy is better than a year ago, down from 72 percent in January.

Nationally he is at roughly 34 to 37 percent. On the economy, 73 percent of adults disapprove in AP-NORC (@APNORC) polling, his worst rating across both presidencies and worse than Joe Biden's worst. On foreign affairs, CNN/SSRS has him at 29 percent, down from 42 percent. Even among Republicans, only 44 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living, and 62 percent say his tariffs have raised it.

WHAT EACH SIDE IS RUNNING ON

The Democratic case is almost entirely about prices: affordability, the cost of the war, premiums, groceries. They are running on the receipt, and their health plan is specific, to restore the lapsed Obamacare subsidies. Pew (@pewresearch) finds 84 percent of registered voters call the economy very important to their vote, and 47 percent say the cost of living is the single biggest factor in how they vote.

The Republican case has three parts: that growth is real and the pain is temporary and imported, that immigration and crime matter and are where the administration still polls well, and culture, which for a real slice of the Republican electorate outranks the grocery bill entirely. What they are not doing is running on Trump's cost of living record. In a Reuters review, Republican candidates in 41 of 62 competitive contests put distance between themselves and the president. Mike Rogers (@MikeRogersForMI), their Michigan Senate candidate, cut an ad in a sports bar holding a Canadian beer: "We need to end this tariff war now." Their strongest argument is structural, that the polls are wrong, and it is testable. More below.

THE MAP, AND THE CANDIDATES

Democrats need a net gain of three seats to take the House, and four to take the Senate at 51-49. The House is the easier task. The Senate requires flipping at least two states Trump won by double digits in 2024.

Ohio: Sherrod Brown (@SherrodBrown), who held Ohio's other seat from 2007 until losing in 2024, against Jon Husted (@SenJonHusted), appointed in 2025 to replace JD Vance. Brown has long argued for targeted tariffs to protect manufacturing, which makes his attacks on Trump's blanket tariffs hard to caricature.

Michigan: An open Democratic seat, because Gary Peters (@SenGaryPeters) is retiring. This is a hold, not a pickup, and that distinction decides the arithmetic later in this piece. Abdul El-Sayed (@AbdulElSayed), a physician and former Detroit health director, against Mike Rogers, a former FBI agent and 14 year congressman. Trump called El-Sayed a "jihadist" at a Port Huron rally and warned of "hordes of jihadis." El-Sayed ran a city health department. Michigan households carry the highest tariff cost in the country, by the National Taxpayers Union Foundation's measure.

Texas: Ken Paxton (@KenPaxtonTX), the state attorney general, against James Talarico (@jamestalarico), a state representative and former public school teacher. Trump rejected the sitting senator, John Cornyn (@JohnCornyn), for Paxton, who has spent years under indictment and impeachment proceedings. Talarico calls him "the most corrupt politician in Texas." Paxton named the stakes himself: "I'm not exaggerating when I say if we lose Texas, we lose America." Latinos are about one in five eligible Texas voters, they moved to Trump in record numbers in 2024, and ICE operations against people with no criminal record have been pushing them back.

Maine: Susan Collins (@SenatorCollins), after 30 years, against Troy Jackson (@TroyJackson207), a former state Senate president and fifth generation logger. Collins runs on winning tariff exemptions for Maine businesses. Jackson runs on the 74 percent jump in furnace oil. Democrats got here the hard way: their first nominee, Graham Platner, withdrew in July over an allegation of sexual assault.

Alaska: Mary Peltola (@MaryPeltola) against Dan Sullivan (@SenDanSullivan), under ranked choice voting. A second candidate, an independent from Petersburg named Daniel J. Sullivan, says he is running on his own account. Republicans call him a plant.

Iowa and Kansas: Ashley Hinson (@RepAshleyHinson), a former television anchor, against Josh Turek (@turek4iowa), a two time Paralympic gold medalist. Roger Marshall (@RogerMarshallMD) against Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor. No Democrat has won a Kansas Senate race since 1932, and the polls show a dead heat. Twelve days before the vote the administration announced $8 billion in payments to farmers to offset diesel costs.

North Carolina: Roy Cooper (@RoyCooperNC), two term governor and 16 year attorney general, against Michael Whatley (@WhatleyNC), former Republican National Committee chair, who has never held elected office. The Democrats' most likely pickup.

On the smears, in both directions, the pattern is the same: the attack is about identity or character, and the real record is duller than either campaign wants. Paxton is genuinely scandal ridden, and that is court records, not opinion. El-Sayed is a doctor, not a militant. Turek is a Paralympian, not a radical. Cooper and Collins are both cautious institutionalists. In Ohio's governor race, a Vivek Ramaswamy (@VivekGRamaswamy) attack ad backfired so badly that Cook (@CookPolitical) moved the race from Toss Up to Lean Democrat.

THE MONEY

The crypto industry has spent about $176 million across more than 100 congressional races, according to a Reuters (@Reuters) investigation. Fairshake and its affiliated committees account for $150.8 million, funded primarily by Coinbase, Ripple and Andreessen Horowitz. Of the 58 candidates it backed in primaries and special elections, 53 won.

Ohio's Senate race alone drew more than $68 million in crypto linked spending, most of it against Sherrod Brown, who chaired the Senate Banking Committee and opposed the industry's preferred bills. Reuters found one ad against him repeating a claim about IRS agents and Social Security that its own fact checking had already rejected. More than $500 million has gone into television advertising in the Texas race, by CNN's count.

Is this about the country or about the rules? The industry's own people answer it. Colin McLaren of the Solana Policy Institute called the spending "an investment in the future," meaning predictable regulation for decades. The unfinished business is the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, which would divide authority between the SEC and the CFTC and is stuck in the Senate partly over provisions covering public officials' own crypto holdings. In the House, Fairshake funds both parties. In the Senate, where the bill is stuck, its money has gone to Republicans.

That is a straight answer: the spending is about favorable regulations, less about the Country and its People.

LEANING ON THE VOTE

On October 23rd, Attorney General Todd Blanche (@AGToddBlanche) was asked whether there was any scenario in which the Justice Department would intervene in certifying results. He did not say no. "I don't think it's appropriate to make conclusive statements about what's going to happen in the future because I have no idea," he said, adding that improper interference was "not the intention."

Less than 24 hours later the administration sued to block Alaska from certifying its Senate result if Dan Sullivan lost narrowly, citing the same name independent. "I was the one who said to do it," Trump said. Alaska's other Republican senator, Lisa Murkowski (@lisamurkowski), said the state had already distinguished the candidates and "the Department of Justice never should have filed this lawsuit."

The department has also sued California, seeking to stop it counting ballots until the citizenship of more than 20,000 people is verified. At least 18 counties were given 48 hours to produce identifying information on ballots the government believes went to non citizens, and Trump has threatened to jail officials who count them. About 1,000 federal election monitors will deploy, up from 590 in 2024. Documents obtained by Democracy Forward show the administration gathered roughly 100 million records, including at least 50 million voter records. CBS News (@CBSNews) reported armed Homeland Security agents knocking on immigrants' doors asking whether they had registered or voted.

Now the scale of the fraud this is meant to address. Homeland Security claimed up to 250,000 people may be illegally registered. By the Justice Department's own count, 156 people have been charged with election fraud offenses since this administration began, against 227 million registered voters. In Nevada, a claim of 16,000 possible non citizens was revised to 185 names, and officials checked every one and found all 185 were American citizens.

Trump has offered $1 million for a tip leading to a fraud conviction. He also told a Republican convention in Dallas last month to "cheat like hell" and vote whether "registered or not," saying that is what his opponents do.

Bill Bradley, writing in the New York Times, set out where the law sits. Monitors may observe, but cannot administer elections, rule on eligibility or direct officials. Three federal laws, including statutes signed by Abraham Lincoln, bar federal agents from interfering in elections. Homeland Security's administrative warrants compel nothing, and only a judge's signed order does. Officials who obey an illegal federal instruction can be sued personally, and the pardon power does not reach state convictions.

Election officials of both parties have refused to go along, and courts have blocked the takeover attempts. Kansas secretary of state candidate Jennifer Day told El Mundo (@elmundoes) that secretaries of state nationwide have contingency plans ready. Meanwhile officials get midnight calls at home and envelopes of white powder.

Gerrymandering runs both ways this cycle. Republican states redrew maps mid decade, and California answered with a voter approved gerrymander of its own that cut its competitive House districts from nine in 2022 to three.

WHERE THE PULSE IS

The decisive voters are not the committed. They are Republicans and independents in six or seven states who are angry about prices and have not decided whether to punish the president's party for it.

The New York Times interviewed Trump voters buying groceries in exactly the four states that matter: Iowa, Ohio, Maine and Michigan (@nytimes - "They Voted for Trump. How Are They Feeling About High Grocery Prices?", 10/15/26). The range in their answers is the election.

Angel Hartmier, 36, a gas station clerk and single mother in New Lebanon, Ohio, voted for the first time in 2024 hoping prices would fall. "It was bad before, but now it's way worse. I thought things would change." She may vote again, or may not. Jessy Hakizimana, 44, an excavating contractor in Indianola, Iowa, and an independent: "I never used to use coupons. Now I'm looking for coupons." On his 2024 vote: "It's too soon to say I regret it. But so far, it doesn't look good." He is still leaning Republican.

And the other side, just as real. Carolyn Calcutt, 65, a retired teacher in Alpine Township, Michigan, thinks Trump is doing an "amazing" job: "He knows what he's doing. He's making sure that we're safe." Dan Ratliff, 79, a retired engineer in Farmersville, Ohio, says the problems were inherited from Biden, that fuel inflation is the price of keeping Americans safe, and that the economy is "humming along." Aaron Huizenga, 45, in Zeeland, Michigan, says prices have been a struggle but "that's not nearly as important as some of the cultural stuff."

That is the contest in five people. The question is not whether voters are unhappy. It is whether unhappiness turns into a vote against the party in power, or into staying home.

Hence the gap both sides are watching. About three quarters of Democrats say this vote is extremely important, against about six in ten Republicans. Within the Republican Party, certainty to vote is 75 percent among MAGA identifiers and 57 percent among those who do not identify with the movement, and more than a quarter of that second group actually want Democrats to control Congress.

Trump is barnstorming the map asking crowds to "pretend I'm on the ballot." The Democrats' problem is the mirror image: 46 percent say they are voting mainly to oppose Trump, against 37 percent voting mainly for a candidate. One in five registered voters now dislikes both parties, up from 12 percent in 2024.

THE CORRUPTION

This is no longer a side issue. In CNBC's final All-America survey before the vote, October 14th to 18th, government corruption was the single biggest concern for 36 percent of registered voters, ahead of food costs at 34 percent. It is the top issue in this election.

What voters are reacting to is on the record. On August 1st, Truth Social began selling traders early access to the president's posts at a reported $100,000 a month, posts that routinely move oil, currencies and stocks because they contain policy. "If this was the CEO of a public company, this would be jail time," said Irene Aldridge of Able Alpha Trading. Trump Media's revenue last year was $3.7 million, so three subscribers would double it.

In May, the Justice Department granted the president immunity from existing tax investigations, shielding him from rulings that could have cost more than $100 million. It survived Blanche's confirmation. Two Republican senators, John Cornyn and Thom Tillis (@SenThomTillis), extracted the cancellation of a separate $1.8 billion fund for payouts to administration allies, and left the tax shield standing.

CBS News has documented a clemency ledger running to $1.08 billion in cases involving people who paid for access or representation. One billionaire received a clemency deal weeks after hiring the president's former personal attorney for a reported $50 million. Trump reported $2.2 billion in income for 2025.

Senator Elizabeth Warren (@SenWarren) has promised that if Democrats take Congress, "we will haul in those responsible for this open corruption to answer to the American people." That is the real stake on Tuesday for the administration: subpoena power.

We are not claiming any of this has been tried in court. We are reporting that it is documented, unresolved, and that voters now rank it first.

WHO WILL WIN? - THE GEOMEMO CONVERGENCE TEST

For the election outcome i.e. each close race, we took four estimates that fail in different ways: two poll averages, one model, one betting market. Agreement is the signal. Two further checks need no polling: Republicans stopped spending in North Carolina, and the government sued to block certification in Alaska.

Four races converge on a Democratic pickup: Ohio, Texas, Maine and Alaska. Exactly the four needed, nothing spare.

Our finding: the House changes hands. So does the Senate, but by one race, and only if the polls are not wrong by two points, which is exactly what Speaker Mike Johnson (@SpeakerJohnson) claims.

What changes on Wednesday is oversight: committee gavels mean subpoenas, not the means to restrict the broad construct of the powers granted to the Presidency.

The war and the tariffs will outlast the election. What it will not do is to make it easier for hardworking Americans to live their day-to-day before Tuesday and after.

text:
In 1970 Donald Harvey killed fifteen patients in his first year working at a hospital. He was eighteen years old and nobody noticed, because it was the only hospital for miles and the elderly came there to die. By the end he had confessed to eighty-seven murders — more than Charles Manson, Richard Ramirez and John Wayne Gacy combined.

In the video below he is asked how many he killed at that first hospital, and what it felt like.

Said that when he was preparing to take someone's life he was very high, very tense.

Said that when it was over he felt relieved. For the person involved. The one he killed.

Said he was the judge, the executioner and the jury, in whatever order you wanted to put it.

Then he stopped. He joined the military to start again somewhere else. Between 1972 and 1974 he killed nobody.

He spent four months as a patient at a veterans' hospital and eighteen months as an outpatient, trying to work out what was wrong with him.

Said he never turned himself in because Kentucky had the death penalty then, and he did not want to go to prison.

In December 1975 he started again, at a veterans' hospital in Cincinnati.

Said he had access to all the critically ill. Said there were just certain ones he would select.

One a month. One every six weeks. One every three or four months.

The authorities wrote a letter saying there was no credible evidence of more than one case, and tried to close it. He had been caught on a single death and was calling it a mercy killing. He might have served five years.

A television reporter at Channel 9 in Cincinnati would not drop it. When the station finally aired what it had, the police opened an investigation into the reporter.

Most of the families were offered $2,500. Years later the county's position was that they should prove anyone had died at all.

Then the interviewer asks him whether there is any remorse in him at all.

Said if he cried they would call it an act. Said if he smiled and chatted they would call it that too. Said he had been over it so many times with the police and the lawyers that it had all gone flat.

Very flat. Eighty-seven dead people becomes flat.

Was Donald Harvey a man who believed he was ending suffering, or a man who simply liked being the one who chose?

“No one is using mouth cells": still false. Buccal graft vaginoplasty is offered for MRKH at major centers, e.g. Cincinnati Children's, and has published case series. "Rare" would be defensible. "No one" isn't.
"Buccal mucosa is similar to vaginal mucosa": hurts your point. Both are moist, non-keratinized epithelium, which is why surgeons use it. That explains why buccal grafts get used, so you can't also claim no one uses them.
"Other surgeries are rarely done anymore": plausible but unsourced. Surgery is second-line, so it's less common, but McIndoe, Davydov and Vecchietti are still in the literature and in practice.
"Culturing her own vaginal cells will become the primary protocol": speculation. Engineered autologous vaginal tissue was reported in a small 2014 Lancet study of four MRKH patients, It's real but experimental. "Specialists told me" is an anecdote, not a protocol. It’s entirely possible but not common.

I know it's fun to play fantasy realignment, but it's in the Big 12's best interests that the ACC survives & thrives.  Why?  B/c the Big 12 needs a like-minded conference to counter the B1G & SEC's votes.

That said, *if* the Big 12 wanted to torpedo the ACC, the best avenue is to employ the same strategy used against the Pac-12.  If you remember back, Yormark didn't target Oregon & Washington.  Instead, he targeted Colorado...a school that had a connection to the Big 12 *and* had no immediate-term propsect of getting into the B1G or SEC.  He offered them a sign-on bonus, and they took it.  That created just enough instability & doubt to shake Utah, Arizona, and Arizona St loose.

As the Big Ten has learned, 18 makes for an unruly conference.  12-16 is ideal.  So, if the Big 12 expands, it needs to ONLY be for teams that add significant value.  

Circling back to Yormark's Colorado approach, I'd forgo Miami, FSU, Clemson, UNC, & Duke, and offer Louisville a sign-on bonus once the ACC's exit fee drops in 2030.  Why would they jump?  Like CU, they have a connection to the Big 12; their rivalry with Cincy.  And like CU, they have no shot of getting into the B1G.  And, they stand to be harmed if Miami, FSU, Clemson, or UNC ever do leave for the B1G or SEC.  Plus, the Big 12's next TV contract will go into effect in July 2032, a full 4 years before the ACC's.  So, they'd make more money in the interim.

The loss of Louisville might be enough to shake another value additive team or two loose.  At a minimum, it'll make the Big 12 stronger financially & on the field/court, while weakening the ACC.  I'm not advocating for it, b/c it's in everyone's best interests that the ACC isn't raided.  But if Yormark wanted to raid the ACC, I'd start with Louisville, b/c they will by far be the easiest to pry loose.  Not to mention they were the runner-up for the invitation that went to TCU back in 2011.

text:
most crypto wallets rely on one private key to authorize transactions. 

when a better security method emerges, users often need a new wallet and must transfer their funds.

Starknet offers a different approach. 

Its accounts contain rules that determine which signatures are valid. 

Updating these rules can introduce a new signature method without changing the account address or moving its assets.

Falcon-512 is a post-quantum signature scheme designed to withstand potential threats from future quantum computers.

On Starknet, developers can build accounts that verify Falcon-512 signatures without changing the network’s core verification system.

Existing accounts can also be upgraded if their contracts support it.

In experimental Starknet testnet demonstrations, developers have migrated certain accounts in one transaction to require both their original signature and a Falcon-512 signature.

The account address remains unchanged, and funds stay where they are. 

After the upgrade, transactions without the required signatures are rejected.

OpenZeppelin has also demonstrated a pure Falcon-512 account on Starknet mainnet through an experimental, unaudited transaction.

However, these are demonstrations, not finished consumer products. 

Standard accounts still use older signature methods, while wallet integration, key recovery, and security audits remain ongoing work.

The key advantage is flexibility. 

Account owners can upgrade their authorization methods without waiting for a network-wide change.

the bottom line is that starknet accounts can adopt new signature methods while preserving their addresses and assets. 

Falcon-512 has been demonstrated, but making it available to everyday users remains a work in progress.

text:
So Congress passed the Foreign and Economic Espionage Penalty Enhancement Act in 2012, unanimous in the Senate, and the basic idea was: the old penalty structure wasn't keeping pace with what foreign intelligence services were actually doing to American companies. Fine. Reasonable. But here's what the 2012 moment was really signaling, and what it tells us about where this whole problem was heading.

The legislation was reactive, as legislation almost always is. The intelligence community had been watching a surge in state-directed industrial theft since roughly 2010, and the pattern that spooked analysts wasn't any single operation. It was the convergence. Traditional human intelligence, HUMINT, the kind involving recruited insiders, traveled employees, academic contacts, that was already a known problem. What changed around 2010 was the pairing of that human network with cyber intrusion. You'd have a recruited source inside a defense contractor pointing external operators toward exactly which servers to hit, which file directories mattered, which VPN credentials would work. The human and the digital weren't separate tracks anymore. They were coordinated.

That coordination is the thing the 2012 Act was trying to address by strengthening penalties, and that instinct wasn't wrong. But criminal penalties are, structurally, a deterrent aimed at individuals. They're not well-suited to deterring a foreign intelligence service operating out of a building in Shanghai or Moscow that will never see the inside of an American courtroom. The people who get prosecuted under this framework are almost always the recruited American insiders, or occasionally the rare foreign operative who made a mistake and traveled to a jurisdiction where they could be arrested. The actual architects of these campaigns are untouchable.

So what did that mean for trajectory? A few things, and they've all played out more or less as you'd expect.

First, the actors most targeted by enhanced enforcement pressure, meaning the ones running the most aggressive campaigns against American technology sectors, adapted their recruitment profiles. If prosecuting insiders is the primary enforcement mechanism, then you reduce your exposure by recruiting people who are harder to detect, harder to prosecute, or both. That pushed state-directed operations toward targeting people in positions that don't look like obvious espionage targets: graduate students, junior researchers, small subcontractors rather than the prime defense firms where counterintelligence coverage is heavier. The FBI's own public reporting on Chinese intelligence operations specifically flagged this shift. The target pool got broader and the individual targets got lower-profile.

Second, and this matters a lot, the cyber component of these hybrid operations became progressively less dependent on the human component over time. The 2012 analysis correctly identified the convergence of human and cyber methods as the threat to watch. But the trajectory since then has been toward cyber operations that are substantially autonomous from recruited human sources. You don't need an insider to point you at the right server if your operators are good enough to map the network themselves. Groups attributed to the PLA's Unit 61398, whose indictment came in 2014, were doing exactly this: systematic network intrusion at scale, targeting dozens of American companies in steel, energy, aerospace, with little apparent need for recruited human sources inside those companies. The human element didn't disappear, but it became more optional.

Third, the economic sectors targeted kept expanding. The 2012 legislation specifically referenced defense contractors and emerging technology companies, which reflected where the documented threat was concentrated at that moment. But the operations that followed hit clean energy, pharmaceutical research, agricultural technology, financial services. Any sector where American companies held a meaningful innovation lead became fair game. The logic is straightforward: economic espionage isn't just about military advantage. It's about compressing the development timeline for entire industries, letting a state-backed competitor skip the R&D cost and go straight to production.

What should people watching this space be looking for now?

The penalty framework that the 2012 Act established did eventually produce some significant prosecutions. The 2014 PLA indictments were a landmark, even though no one actually showed up to face trial. The DOJ's China Initiative, whatever you think of its implementation (and its critics had legitimate points about prosecutorial overreach), reflected a real attempt to use the enhanced penalty structure more aggressively. But the limitation that was baked into the 2012 approach, treating this as primarily a criminal justice problem rather than a strategic competition problem, has never really been resolved.

The next evolution worth watching is in the targeting of supply chains rather than individual companies. If your counterintelligence coverage is concentrated on large primes and flagship research institutions, then the sophisticated play is to go after their suppliers, their cloud service providers, their software vendors. The SolarWinds intrusion, attributed to Russia's SVR, is the obvious example, though that was more about intelligence collection than economic espionage in the traditional sense. The economic espionage version of that playbook, compromising a widely-used software tool or a common hardware component to get access to dozens of downstream targets simultaneously, is the logical next step.

Also watch academic and research partnerships, specifically the ones that look entirely legitimate on paper. The mechanism doesn't have to be covert recruitment. Sponsored research agreements, joint ventures, conference presentations, talent programs that offer genuine professional opportunities alongside the data collection. These are harder to prosecute, harder to even identify as espionage, and they largely fall outside what the 2012 penalty framework was designed to address. You can't indict a university research partnership.

One more thing. The 2012 Act passed unanimously in the Senate and without meaningful opposition in the House. That bipartisan consensus existed because economic espionage was, at that moment, something politicians from both parties could frame as a clear national security threat without much domestic political complication. That consensus has held reasonably well on the legislative side, but it's under more pressure now as trade policy, technology export controls, and foreign investment screening all intersect with the same set of actors and motivations. The tools are more numerous, which is good. Coordinating them coherently is a different problem, and that's the one that doesn't have a clean legislative fix.

text:
There's a rather inconvenient chapter missing from your beautiful story about Stalin's peaceful intentions, Rina. And it changes EVERYTHING. 😂

Picture Europe in August 1939.
Stalin is supposedly terrified that Finland might cooperate with Hitler.
So what does our peace-loving Soviet leader do?
HE MAKES A DEAL WITH HITLER.

The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact. Secret protocols. Eastern Europe divided into spheres of influence.
And guess where Finland ends up?
IN STALIN'S SPHERE.

Beautiful start to a story about respecting Finland's security, isn't it?

Now fast-forward to October.
You claim Helsinki rejected EVERY compromise.

Unfortunately, the original American diplomatic records from 1939 tell a different story.
Finland offered territorial concessions, islands and a border adjustment near Leningrad.

What Finland refused was handing Moscow a military foothold at Hanko.
And here's the part your map doesn't show:

A LARGER PIECE OF LAND ISN'T NECESSARILY A BETTER DEAL WHEN THE PRICE IS YOUR NATIONAL SECURITY.

Stalin, meanwhile, had already signed HIS agreement with Hitler.

Then came November 26.
The supposed Finnish shelling of Mainila. The convenient incident Soviet authorities used to justify military action.

November 30: THE RED ARMY INVADED FINLAND.
And now comes my favorite part of your entire explanation.

DECEMBER 1, 1939.
Just ONE DAY after the invasion, Moscow recognized a Soviet-backed Finnish puppet government headed by Otto Kuusinen.
Its declared mission included OVERTHROWING FINLAND'S EXISTING GOVERNMENT AND DISMANTLING ITS ARMED FORCES.

Wait a fucking minute. 😂

I thought this was about moving the border a few kilometres to protect Leningrad?
WHY THE FUCK DID STALIN NEED TO REPLACE FINLAND'S GOVERNMENT?
Was the Finnish parliament also within artillery range of Leningrad?

And December 14?
The League of Nations condemned Soviet aggression and EXPELLED THE USSR.

So here's the real historical lesson.

A country can have genuine security concerns.
It can negotiate territorial exchanges.
It can even have legitimate fears about a future war.
NONE OF THAT GIVES IT THE RIGHT TO INVADE ITS NEIGHBOUR AND INSTALL A PUPPET GOVERNMENT.

And that is why your story is so revealing, Rina.
You began by explaining Stalin's security concerns.
You ended up rationalizing the invasion of a sovereign country.

Eighty-seven years later, the vocabulary is remarkably familiar.
Security concerns. Hostile neighbours. Unreasonable negotiations. Military intervention. A friendly government installed with Moscow's help.
The costume changes. The imperial playbook doesn't.

And no, drawing a beautiful border on a map doesn't make invading the country on the other side of it an act of self-defence. 🤡

text:
Delaware's most popular fishing reef is made of New York City subway cars. More than 700 retired "Redbird" cars are sitting about 80 feet down, roughly 16 miles out from the Indian River Inlet.

New York City Transit started barging its old cars out to sea in 2001. Before each one went over the side, the agency pulled out the tanks, plastic and grease, and it paid for the cleaning and the trip.

What's left is a steel shell about 51 feet long, which gives mussels, worms and other small invertebrates something to attach to and gives small fish a place to hide. Delaware's reef program says structures like these can provide up to 400 times as much food for fish as bare ocean floor.

The project ran into trouble early because the cars had asbestos in them. When that came out, New Jersey withdrew an offer to take 650 of them, though it accepted a smaller batch a couple of years later. Delaware went ahead.

Over the past two decades the state has sunk more than 1,350 subway cars. The same reef site also holds 86 retired Army tanks and armored vehicles, eight tugboats and a 215-foot cruise ship.

text:
What the viral clip leaves out about the Ford family

The announcement from LifeWorks Church has given people plenty to argue about. Lydia Ford introduced Shakayla Ford as her husband’s second wife and her own “sister in marriage.” People applauded. The clip spread. Much of the conversation stopped there.

Lydia and Shakayla have since described their lives at greater length. Their accounts deserve attention, even from people who reject the relationship they have chosen.

In their October 27 interview with Larry Reid, Lydia said Shakayla helped her after surgery, when she could not do things for herself. She placed that caregiving before the discussions about plural marriage. Whatever judgment someone reaches about the arrangement, that support mattered to her.

Shakayla described gaining a “forever best friend” in Lydia. She spoke about companionship, guidance, and help with responsibilities she had previously carried alone. Her explanation included a relationship with Lydia, not just an attachment to Israel.

Lydia said sharing responsibilities gave her more time for friends, rest, and being alone. Later, she said Shakayla had reduced her stress. The family described pooling their incomes and household expenses. Both women said the relationship satisfied them in practical and emotional ways.

These are their statements. An interview cannot independently verify their finances, their freedom to leave, or what daily life feels like when the cameras are off. But we should be equally careful about substituting our assumptions for their words. Disagreeing with a woman’s choice does not establish that she has no agency.

Their account also includes difficulty. Lydia said she initially opposed polygyny. She acknowledged jealousy, comparison, and fear of being replaced. She described telling the others when she struggled and using family meetings to discuss those feelings.

I would rather hear that honesty than demand a performance in which everyone either claims perfect harmony or supplies the misery an audience expects.

Israel said he waited for Lydia’s agreement before marrying Shakayla. He also said he would not add another wife without both women agreeing. Those statements create responsibilities he should be held to. Meaningful consent includes the ability to refuse, reconsider, control resources, and leave without retaliation. Public assurances do not establish that those conditions exist.

Shakayla also spoke about people in plural relationships who have been excluded from churches and want somewhere to worship. A person does not have to share her theology to recognize the importance of belonging, friendship, and a place to seek support.

There is a serious fact that should not disappear from this conversation: an Ohio appellate court upheld Israel Ford’s misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction arising from a 2018 incident involving his stepdaughter. That is a judicial finding, not merely an online accusation. The women’s positive accounts do not erase it, establish rehabilitation, or settle present-day safeguarding questions.

It is possible to take that record seriously while refusing to ridicule Lydia and Shakayla. Accountability does not require treating either woman as incapable of describing her own experience. Nor does respecting them require endorsing everything Israel teaches or does.

The questions worth asking are concrete. Can each woman disagree without religious pressure? Does each have independent access to money and support? Can either leave safely? Does the household address conflict without punishment? Those questions matter more than whether a photograph looks unconventional.

The accompanying video uses limited excerpts of their public interview, with commentary and source labels. It foregrounds the care, friendship, and practical benefits the women describe. It does not certify that the household is healthy, claim the allegations are all false, or offer a blanket endorsement of its leader.

Hear the women. Check the evidence. Keep room for compassion and accountability in the same conversation.
