text:
❤️ First Infant Safely Surrendered Through Saint Francis Baby Box 

As October draws to a close - a month dedicated to the Holy Rosary and the observance of Respect Life Month - we are reminded that building a culture of life is more than words. It is a call to put our faith into action through love, compassion, and care for the most vulnerable among us.

Last week, right here in Tulsa, that message came to life in an extraordinary way. Saint Francis Health System announced recently that it has received its first infant through the Safe Haven Baby Box. A silent alarm alerted hospital staff, who immediately responded to care for this precious little life.

In March 2025, Fr. Gary Kastl, Vicar General of the Diocese of Tulsa and Eastern Oklahoma, blessed the newly installed Safe Haven Baby Box, a place intended to offer safety, dignity, and hope to newborns and parents facing difficult circumstances.

At that blessing, Sr. Marysia Weber, RSM, of Saint Francis Health System, spoke beautifully about how this initiative reflects the hospital's Catholic mission:

“Working with the vulnerable, giving babies dignity, but also a mom who is in crisis, and letting her know that we'll be glad to take care of her little one.”

Last week, those words became a beautiful reality. We may never know the circumstances that led to this moment - the fears, the struggles, or the difficult decisions behind it. But we do know this: A child is safe. A parent found a place to turn. And a community was ready to respond with compassion.

We are grateful to Saint Francis Health System, its dedicated caregivers, and everyone who helped make this life-affirming resource possible.

As we conclude this month devoted to the Holy Rosary, let us entrust this precious child, the parent who made this difficult decision, and all families facing moments of crisis to the loving intercession of our Blessed Mother.

May Our Lady wrap them in her mantle of love and protection.

🙏 Please join us in praying for this precious child and family, and consider sharing this post. It may reach someone facing difficult circumstances who needs to be reminded that they are not alone and that help, hope, and compassion are within reach.

This full story will be included in next week's EOCextra.
For more information about the Safe Haven Baby Box at Saint Francis Hospital:

text:
The claim that Trump “could have done this his first week” ignores basic administrative law: Biden’s methane rule (finalized late 2023/published 2024, covering existing wells for the first time) required formal EPA notice-and-comment rulemaking, impact analysis, and legal process to unwind. Trump’s EPA began delays and reconsiderations in 2025 (compliance extensions finalized Nov 2025); the full proposed rollback is the culmination of that work, not a last-second invention. Trump explicitly noted at the rally that “statutorily it takes a little while” and they’d been working on it with Zeldin.
Calling it an election stunt “kept in the back pocket” is pure assertion with zero evidence. Regulatory timelines are long by design; early Trump actions included other major deregulatory moves (e.g., endangerment finding repeal in Feb 2026). Timing near midterms and a Texas energy-state rally is ordinary politics, exactly as Democrats timed climate rules and fees under Biden, not proof of deliberate delay. Future Democratic administrations can attempt reversal via new rulemaking (which also takes years and faces courts), which is precisely why the parent post is correct that congressional majorities matter for durability.
Your post offers no facts, data, or timeline on the rule, prior EPA actions, or industry impacts (EPA projects $45B savings and additional oil/gas output; small “stripper” wells were hit hard by compliance costs). It is speculation plus personal attack. Energy policy has always swung with administrations; locking in production-friendly rules while Republicans hold power is the practical response to that reality, not a “betrayal.”

"Oil prices edged up about 1% on Wednesday ​on renewed concerns about additional energy supply disruptions in the Middle East due to continued fighting in Yemen, an attack on ‌a refinery in Saudi Arabia and worries the US could strike Iran after next week's US midterm elections.

Brent futures rose $1.55, or 1.4%, to $115.43 per barrel at 1:46 p.m. EDT (1746 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude rose $2.92, or 2.9%, to $102.82.

That price gain pushed Brent back into overbought territory for the fourth time in five days.
Yemen's Houthis attacked Aden airport on Wednesday, Yemeni ​government forces said, after the Iran-aligned group warned people to evacuate the facility as fighting escalated in the impoverished country caught in the wider Middle ​East conflict.
On Tuesday, the Houthis said they had hit Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refinery with a missile, intensifying their strikes against ⁠the world's second-largest crude producer behind the US. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike on the 550,000-barrel-per-day facility.

In recent weeks, several analysts have said renewed US strikes on Iran could happen sometime after the US midterm elections on November 3.

In hopes of ending the now eight-month-long conflict, Qatari mediators have presented Iran with ​a new draft deal to end the war with the US and Israel, an official briefed on the negotiations said. A senior Iranian official, however, said ​Doha had only put forward unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.

Iran's foreign minister said on Wednesday that Tehran continued to give diplomacy a chance to succeed ‌and raised ⁠the possibility of the seven-day plan proposed by Tehran being completed in less than a week if implemented.

Qatar, along with Pakistan, has led mediation to end the war, which has disrupted global shipping and oil supplies and has spread to Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

US OIL STOCKPILES
Another factor supporting crude prices was a US federal report showing a surprise decline in stockpiles.
The US Energy Information Administration said on Wednesday that energy firms pulled 1.9 million barrels of crude from storage during the ​week ended October 23.
That was a ​surprise draw compared with the 15,000-barrel ⁠build analysts forecast in a Reuters poll, and was in line with the 2-million-barrel decline seen in data from the American Petroleum Institute on Tuesday, according to sources. 

China, meanwhile, issued a fourth batch of fuel export quotas for gasoline, diesel ​and jet fuel, a rare additional issue that brings the 2026 total in line with 2025 despite curbs earlier ​in the year, ⁠three people familiar with the matter said on Wednesday.

Looking ahead, the market is waiting for an industry meeting on Sunday, where OPEC+ oil producers are expected to keep their December oil output targets steady, people familiar with the matter say.
Production in most of the seven core OPEC+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — ⁠is below their ​output targets. OPEC+ includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies like Russia.

Crude ​oil exports from Russia's Baltic and Black Sea ports could fall next month as domestic refiners increase diesel output following a deal with Washington this month, traders said."

3. GOATnaldo ↔️ (3–4)

This one deserves the full Monday night treatment. GOAT scored 174.54, received useful production almost everywhere, and still lost 180.08–174.54 when Javonte Williams’ late touchdown sealed it for Justin Fields. The final margin was 5.54 points. A six-point touchdown was quite literally the difference between climbing above .500 and falling below it.

That is why GOAT holds its place here despite the loss. Jeanty scored 21.6, Swift 19, Chase 17.2, Puka 21.8, Jaylen Warren 16.7 and Stevenson 22.5. Pitts added 13.2 and now has 51.4 across the last three weeks. This was a strong lineup beaten by a slightly stronger one, rather than another week waiting for the stars to remember their job descriptions.

The bench still offers some uncomfortable hindsight. Penix scored 20.42 compared with Shough’s 13.82, a difference larger than the losing margin. Omar Cooper’s 22.5 also stayed on the bench while Denzel Boston supplied 5.7. Cooper has now scored 44.8 across two weeks and deserves a serious look.

Allen returns from Buffalo’s bye just as Purdy and Shough go on theirs, making the quarterback timing manageable. Puka played through the calf concern and produced, though continued monitoring is sensible. Noel’s turf toe and Shaheed’s knee injury reduce some of the receiver depth behind the starters.

Wednesday’s additions addressed actual vacancies: Chase McLaughlin replaces the idle Fairbairn, and Washington’s defense offers an alternative while Houston is off. Jerry Jeudy and Malik Benson were released to make room.

The matchup with yurGirl is substantial. Both are 3–4, and the winner reaches .500 while the loser faces a much steeper climb toward four playoff spots.

GOAT brought 174 points to the argument. Javonte got the final word.

text:
First Corinthians 10 offers an essential distinction that is frequently overlooked in discussions of Halloween. Paul warned believers against participation in idolatrous worship and declared that the sacrifices of the Gentiles were offered to devils rather than to God. He refused to approve fellowship with the religious practices associated with those sacrifices. Yet in the same chapter, he also discussed meat sold in the marketplace and ordinary meals involving unbelievers. He did not teach that every piece of meat became permanently forbidden because it might once have been associated with a pagan temple. He instructed believers to consider the circumstances, their participation, the conscience of others, and the glory of God. That distinction is enormously important. We cannot simply declare every piece of Halloween candy an idol sacrifice or every decorative pumpkin an occult instrument. Neither can we conclude that all actions are acceptable because some objects have ordinary uses. Paul distinguished between common things and participation in idolatrous worship. The church must learn to do the same. If an activity genuinely involves practices condemned by God, changing the location or adding Christian terminology cannot sanctify it. If an activity is ordinary fellowship without forbidden religious content, condemning it merely because it resembles a seasonal custom may go beyond what the Bible teaches. Faithful separation requires actual discernment, not manufactured rules.

First Thessalonians 5:21–22 brings the matter into focus: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Abstain from all appearance of evil.” The instruction begins with examination. Christians are not told to accept whatever is popular, but to test what comes before them and retain what is good. The command to abstain from all appearance of evil should not be twisted into a claim that anything someone somewhere might misunderstand must automatically be sinful. It is a serious call to reject evil in the forms in which it appears, rather than seek excuses for retaining it. This principle reaches into our homes, our entertainment, our church programs, and our public testimony. Before we participate, we should ask what the activity truly represents, what it requires of us, what it teaches our children, and whether we can sincerely offer it to the glory of God. Romans 14 also reminds us that believers must act according to faith and avoid violating conscience. Christian liberty is not a license to abandon holiness, and personal conviction is not permission to invent universal commandments where God has spoken no such thing. The answer is neither careless permissiveness nor indiscriminate condemnation. It is submission to the written Word of God. If something is forbidden, no change of name will make it holy. If something is not forbidden, we must still determine whether participating is wise, edifying, and consistent with our testimony. That is how Christians handle liberty without sacrificing discernment.

CHAPTER ELEVEN — THE CHILDREN CAUGHT BETWEEN CONVICTION AND CANDY

Scripture: Deuteronomy 6:6–7; Ephesians 6:4; Proverbs 22:6

There is a part of this subject that weighs heavily upon me because I know what it means to have children growing up in a world where Halloween is treated as an ordinary and exciting part of life. Adults can announce their convictions and move forward with the rest of their responsibilities. Children must return to school, listen to their classmates, see the decorations, hear about the parties, and sometimes explain why their family will not participate. They are surrounded by expectations they did not create and social pressures they may not yet possess the maturity to understand. A child may ask why he cannot attend a gathering when all his friends are going. He may wonder why other children receive treats while he remains at home. text:
Beyond Brick and Mortar: The True Temple, Abraham’s Promise, and the New Jerusalem

​For thousands of years, humanity has been captivated by the idea of a physical building—a temple made of stone and mortar. Multitudes have focused so intently on individual verses and literal architectural plans that they have, quite literally, missed the forest for the trees. Countless lives have been lost, endless theological debates have raged, and religious wars have been fought over geographic borders and holy ground. Many look to the physical rebuilding of a temple as the ultimate sign of the end times, missing the far deeper, breathtaking narrative woven through Scripture.

​When we look beyond physical structure, a grander vision of God’s eternal love and unwavering faithfulness comes into view.

​1. The Conflict Over Earthly Stones

​Throughout history, human eyes have remained fixed on earthly Jerusalem and physical structures. Prophecies about the rebuilding of the Temple are often interpreted solely through a material lens. This misplaced focus has fueled division, fear, and conflict for generations. People have sought to build with human hands what God intended to fulfill through His spiritual grace and cosmic promise.

​Yet, Jesus offered a radically different perspective on the Temple. When He spoke of the Temple, He spoke of His own body—the ultimate, living dwelling place of God’s presence among humanity. Through Him, the focus shifted forever from physical sanctuaries crafted by human hands to a living, spiritual reality defined by grace and truth.

​2. The Unbroken Promise to Abraham

​Long before the physical temple was ever conceived, God made a sacred, everlasting promise to Abraham. God promised a legacy, a blessing for all nations, and a heavenly homeland—a city whose architect and builder is God Himself.

​Through generations of human trial, failure, and strife, God never forgot His covenant. Even when humanity strayed into conflict and misunderstanding, God’s divine master plan remained steadfast. The story of Scripture is not about humanity erecting a building for God; it is about God bringing His kingdom down to humanity.

​3. The New Jerusalem: Descending from Heaven

​The climax of God’s eternal plan is revealed not in an earthly construction project, but in a divine gift descending from above. The New Jerusalem comes out of heaven, beautifully prepared by God, sitting above and transforming the created order.

​In this heavenly reality:

​The Promise is Fulfilled: Abraham and his spiritual descendants enter into the long-awaited fulfillment of God's covenant.

​The Living Sanctuary: God Himself and the Lamb are its temple—there is no longer a need for a physical building, for God dwells directly and fully among His people.

​Love Over Conflict: Where earthly misinterpretations led to war and division, the New Jerusalem brings healing, restoration, and absolute peace.

​Conclusion: A Testament to Unfailing Love

​God’s love is precious, profound, and unbreakable. While humans have spent centuries fighting over earthly soil and physical stones, God was quietly preparing a heavenly city—a grand testament to His grace.

​Jesus redirected our gaze from earthly bricks to heavenly reality, showing us that God does not break His promises. The true Temple, the ultimate fulfillment, and the New Jerusalem are gifts of divine love, reminding us that God never forgets His people, His covenant, or His eternal plan for peace.

Well, I did some research. It's definitely an issue.

GROK: Is gender re-assignment on children an issue in the United States at present?

Yes. Medical interventions aimed at gender transition for minors—primarily puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones, and (less commonly) surgeries—are a major ongoing medical, legal, political, and cultural issue in the United States as of late 2026.

Policy and legal status
Roughly 27 states have enacted laws or policies restricting or banning these interventions for minors (puberty blockers, hormones, and/or surgeries). The U.S. Supreme Court upheld Tennessee’s ban in United States v. Skrmetti (June 2025), finding it did not violate equal protection; this has allowed most such state laws to remain in effect. About half of transgender-identifying youth ages 13–17 live in states with restrictions. Some bans face ongoing litigation or temporary injunctions.⁠Kff

At the federal level, the Trump administration has moved to limit access:

An early executive order directed agencies to restrict federal funding and support for pediatric transitions (“chemical and surgical mutilation”).

CMS finalized a rule (effective October 13, 2026) barring federal Medicaid and CHIP funds for puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones, and surgeries for minors (under 18 for Medicaid, under 19 for CHIP). States may still cover them with their own funds; a limited tapering period applies for those already on hormones. Mental health services remain covered. Savings are projected to be modest relative to overall program spending.⁠

Additional proposals have targeted hospital participation in Medicare/Medicaid and other funding levers if providers offer the care. DOJ has pursued investigations into some clinics.

Democratic-led states and advocates have generally opposed these measures, enacted “shield laws,” and challenged them in court.

Scale of the practice
Interventions are uncommon on a population basis. A 2025 JAMA Pediatrics analysis of private insurance claims (2018–2022) found fewer than 0.1% of adolescents received puberty blockers or hormones; rates rose with age but remained low, with no hormones prescribed under age 12 in the sample. Absolute numbers are higher in some progressive states with favorable policies and insurance coverage (e.g., Oregon data showing roughly 1 in 240 insured girls on testosterone by age 17 in recent years).⁠Jamanetwork

Youth self-identification as transgender or gender-diverse has risen sharply in surveys (often cited in the 1–3% range for teens), with a marked shift toward natal females. Specialized gender clinics proliferated in the 2010s. Surgeries on minors are rarer than medications.

Evidence and medical debate
The quality of evidence for benefits is contested. Systematic reviews (including the UK’s Cass Review of 2024, and assessments in Sweden, Finland, and elsewhere) have found the evidence base for puberty blockers and hormones in adolescents to be weak or of low quality regarding mental health outcomes, with significant unknowns about long-term effects on fertility, sexual function, bone density, and cognition. European countries have substantially restricted these interventions for minors outside research settings or strict criteria, emphasizing psychotherapy first.⁠Readthereporter

Major U.S. organizations (AAP, Endocrine Society, WPATH) have historically endorsed an affirmative approach. Critics, including some clinicians and a 2025 HHS evidence review, argue that U.S. practice has been less cautious, that comorbidities (autism, trauma, psychiatric conditions) are high, and that desistance was common in earlier cohorts before social transition and medicalization became routine. Concerns about regret, detransition, and social influence (including rapid-onset cases) are part of the public debate. Proponents emphasize distress reduction, suicide-risk arguments, and individualized care.

In short, the issue remains highly active: state bans covering a large share of the population, federal funding restrictions taking effect, continuing litigation, shifting clinical evidence and international practice, and sharp partisan and cultural disagreement. It is not a settled medical consensus in the U.S. the way some advocates describe it, nor is the volume of medical transitions as high as some critics claim.

text:
Last Thursday I traded Lincoln for Malibu to talk about AI and the law at Pepperdine Caruso Law. 

I shared the stage with Bahram Nour-Omid of Scopus Ventures, who gave the computer scientist and investor’s perspective on what AI can and can’t do and what he looks for in a legal AI company. He backs tools that meet specific, well-defined business needs, led by people he trusts to run the company.

I talked mostly about LegalBench, the Stanford-led benchmark for legal reasoning that I helped develop, along with some 40 other lawyers and scholars. 

AI models perform legal tasks *very* well and keep getting better. But, interestingly, they sometimes make the very same mistakes as law students (and tired lawyers!), such as taking the court’s summary of the lower court’s holding for the court’s own decision, or calling a statement hearsay when it isn’t offered for its truth. That led to a fascinating discussion about how much human minds think like computer models, and vice versa.

My advice to the students was short: Learn the new tools, and trust the old law -- we rarely need AI-specific statutes.

Thank you to Mark Kubisch and the Palmer Center for Entrepreneurship and the Law for hosting, and special thanks to Palmer Fellow Caroline Kedeshian, who led the discussion with a series of thought-provoking questions.

@PeppLaw @UNLCollegeofLaw #LegalAI

text:
Fiscal 2026 is being hailed as the big comeback year for Ivy League and elite university endowments.

Look at the 1-year returns for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026: 
• Stanford: +31.7%
• Harvard: +27.1%
• Princeton: +23.7%
• S&P 500 Total Return: +22.3%
• Brown: +19.6%• MIT: +10.3%

Three of the five marquee names beat the S&P 500 over the last twelve months.

Now zoom out to the 10-year annualized numbers through June 30, 2026: 
• S&P 500 Total Return: +15.5% per year
• Brown: +13.6%
• Stanford: +12.5%
• MIT: +11.7%
• Princeton: +11.0%(Harvard conveniently does not publish a 10-year figure).

Every single school that publishes a 10-year number trails the S&P 500 by 1.9 to 4.5 percentage points per year for a full decade.

The 5-year annualized numbers are even wider: Stanford +10.3%, Brown +7.8%, and Princeton +6.7% versus +13.4% for the S&P 500.

One strong year does not erase a decade of lagging opportunity cost.

To be fair, universities are not trying to beat a 100% stock index. They carry annual campus spending mandates, multi-asset diversification, and lagged private marks. Moreover, universities pay zero income tax.

Private families DO pay taxes. When a taxable family copies the endowment model without understanding the opportunity cost, they lock up capital for a decade to trail a liquid index by 300 bps a year. Know what benchmark your portfolio is actually built to beat.

text:
Wikipedia Is Occupied Territory: How Modern Leo Frank Writers Have Overshadowed the Jury and the Courts

I have spent a lot of time studying Wikipedia's article on Leo Frank, and one thing has become very clear to me: 

The Wiki article gives far more authority to modern writers who believe Frank was innocent than it gives to the original jury, the trial judge, the Georgia Supreme Court, and the United States Supreme Court. I believe the article is deeply biased, downplays the evidence against Frank, and gives readers a one-sided account of one of the most famous murder trials in American history.

What bothers me most is how Wikipedia minimizes the significance of the original legal proceedings. Twelve jurors heard weeks of testimony, examined the evidence, reviewed the exhibits, listened to Frank's attorneys challenge the prosecution's witnesses, and unanimously convicted Leo of murdering thirteen-year-old Mary Phagan on August 25, 1913. Judge Leonard Roan refused to grant Frank a new trial, rejecting 115 motions by the defense team. The Georgia Supreme Court reviewed the case and found the evidence legally sufficient to uphold the verdict. Later, the United States Supreme Court rejected Frank's federal constitutional challenge (Ga. Supreme Court, 4) (SCOTUS, 5).

Frankitism

Yet Wikipedia opens its article by describing Frank as wrongly convicted. It goes even further by telling readers that modern researchers agree he was innocent. The article has an entire section titled "Later consensus: a miscarriage of justice." Before readers have examined the original case, Wikipedia has already told them which conclusion to accept (Wikipedia, 1).

I find that extraordinary.

Modern authors such as Leonard Dinnerstein, Steve Oney, Jeffrey Melnick, and other writers who favor Frank's innocence receive considerable attention. Their books and interpretations have become the foundation of the prevailing account. Meanwhile, the findings of the original jury and the reasoning of the courts are often treated as historical mistakes that need to be explained away. The decisions of every level of the United States legal system against Leo Frank are minimized. The evidence against Leo Frank is omitted or minimized. The statements of Jim Conley about Leo Frank confessing the assault are censored. Leo Frank's incriminating toilet visit to the machine department are censored or minimized. 

These modern writers were not in the courtroom in 1913. They did not watch Jim Conley testify or observe him during his lengthy cross-examination. They did not hear Monteen Stover describe Frank's absence from his office, Newt Lee explain Frank's unusual behavior, or Robert Barrett testify about suspected bloodstains and observed hair found on the factory's second floor in the machine department.

The modern Frankites did not personally hear the female factory employees testify about Frank's alleged improper behavior toward women and girls. They could study the surviving records, but they could not observe the original witnesses, their responses, or their conduct before the jury (BOE, 2).

That does not mean historians cannot uncover errors or reach conclusions that differ from a jury's verdict. Of course they can. But it does raise a question about why Wikipedia gives the later writers so much authority while placing less emphasis on the people who heard the case and the judges who reviewed it.

What the Jury Actually Heard

The prosecution's case against Leo Frank involved far more than one accusation from Jim Conley.

Conley, a Black janitor employed at the National Pencil Company, admitted writing the two notes discovered near Mary Phagan's body. He also testified that he helped Frank move her body after the murder and that Frank directed him to do so.

Conley had given conflicting statements during the investigation. Frank's lawyers knew this and attacked him on those grounds. His credibility became one of the central issues at trial. But Conley was questioned at length, the contradictions were brought before the jury, and the jurors still accepted enough of his testimony to convict Frank (BOE, 2).

Then there was Monteen Stover. She testified that she came to collect her pay shortly after noon and found Frank absent from his office during a period when he claimed to have been there. Her testimony raised questions about his whereabouts during the critical minutes surrounding Mary's disappearance.

Newt Lee, the Black night watchman who discovered Mary's body, described unusual events involving Frank on the afternoon and evening of April 26. Robert Barrett testified about suspected bloodstains and hair found on the factory's second floor. Other witnesses described the condition of Mary's body, the factory, the elevator, and the surrounding evidence (BOE, 2).

There were disagreements about the timing, the physical findings, and the reliability of individual witnesses. Some of the evidence was circumstantial, and the defense offered explanations for it, but those disagreements were part of the case the jury had to decide.

I believe Wikipedia does a poor job of explaining how these pieces fit together from the prosecution's point of view. The evidence is discussed, but much of it is surrounded by later arguments suggesting why it should not be believed. Wikipedia is unequivocally biased on behalf of Leo Frank and it clearly shows that.

Why should readers be encouraged to dismiss the prosecution's evidence before they have fully understood it? That's not History, that's twistory.

Leo Frank's Defense Was Not Helpless or Unprepared

Another problem with the modern story is the impression that Frank was an almost defenseless man who never received a serious opportunity to fight the accusations against him.

Frank had an experienced legal team. His attorneys included Luther Rosser, Reuben Arnold, and Herbert Haas, along with other lawyers who worked on his defense. They challenged the prosecution's witnesses, disputed the evidence, raised objections, presented their own witnesses, and pursued numerous appeals. (Wikipedia, 1) (BOE, 2)

Their central strategy was to persuade the jury that Jim Conley, rather than Frank, had murdered Mary Phagan.

I believe that strategy deserves much closer criticism.

Conley was accused of being the actual killer despite testifying that he had helped Frank after the murder. The defense attacked his honesty, challenged his explanations for the murder notes, and tried to undermine his account of events inside the factory.

There was also a racial dimension to the defense's arguments. Frank's lawyers were defending a White factory superintendent before an all-White jury in Jim Crow Georgia while attempting to place responsibility for the murder on a Black janitor. The original arguments and language used against Conley deserve careful examination, particularly where they relied on racial stereotypes rather than specific contradictions in his testimony (BOE, 2). They relied on racial attacks to try to convince the jury, instead of evidence and arguments when it came to Jim Conley. The all-White and all-Male jury saw right through the gutter racist gambit.

Frank's attorneys were entitled to challenge Conley and every other witness. That was their responsibility. But their arguments should not be accepted today simply because modern writers prefer their explanation of the crime.

The defense also challenged the timing of Mary's arrival, the significance of Monteen Stover's testimony, the suspected physical evidence, and the prosecution's interpretation of Frank's conduct. Its lawyers offered an alternative theory of the murder and later developed additional arguments involving the movement of Mary's body and the writings found near her.

Those arguments deserve scrutiny just as much as the prosecution's case does.

I believe the defense failed to overcome the evidence that connected Frank to the murder. The jury apparently reached the same conclusion after hearing both sides. Witness saw blood on the floor in the machine department. Witnesses also saw Mary Phagan's hair tangled on the handle of a lathe. They saw it with their own eyes. One employee Robert Pittman Barrett touched the hair by accident when he went to use his machine. A piece of factory work had been left there from Friday. 

Judge Roan Refused to Set Aside the Verdict

Judge Leonard Strickland Roan personally presided over the trial. He heard the witnesses, ruled on objections, instructed the jury, and later considered the defense's request for a new trial.

Frank's lawyers raised numerous complaints about the proceedings, including the admission of certain testimony, the behavior of spectators, and alleged prejudice against their client.

On October 31, 1913, Judge Roan denied the motion for a new trial. (Ga. Archives, 3)

Modern writers frequently point out that Roan expressed personal uncertainty about whether Frank was guilty or innocent. That is true and should not be hidden. But Roan also explained that the jury had been convinced, and he refused to disturb its verdict.

Why does Wikipedia give so much attention to his uncertainty without placing the same emphasis on the legal decision he actually made?

Roan's doubts did not produce an acquittal. They did not result in a new trial. His ruling left the conviction standing, although he later recommended clemency.

These are different parts of the same history, and all of them should be explained.

The Georgia Supreme Court Found the Evidence Sufficient. The Frankites Do Not Tell You That!

This is where I believe Wikipedia's treatment of the case is especially weak.

On February 17, 1914, the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the judgment against Leo Frank by a vote of four to two.

The majority examined the defense's legal objections, including complaints about testimony admitted during the trial, the conduct of spectators, and the refusal to grant a new trial.

But the court also addressed the sufficiency of the evidence. It did not simply say that the lawyers had filed their paperwork incorrectly or that some minor procedural rule had been satisfied.

The Georgia Supreme Court expressly stated that, after carefully considering the evidence, it found that evidence sufficient to uphold the jury's verdict. The majority also concluded that no substantial trial error required a new trial. (Ga. Supreme Court, 4)

That finding deserves far more attention.

The court was not conducting a second trial, nor did it declare that every witness was truthful or every disputed fact had been settled. Its ruling was that the evidence legally supported the conviction and that the trial court had not committed a reversible error.

Two justices, Chief Justice William H. Fish and Justice Marcus W. Beck, dissented. Their disagreement centered on the admission of testimony about alleged prior sexual conduct by Frank. They believed that evidence should not have been admitted and that its prejudicial effect warranted a new trial. (Ga. Supreme Court, 4)

Their dissent belongs in the history, but so does the majority's reasoning.

Four justices concluded that the conviction should stand. They considered a lengthy record, examined the legal arguments, addressed the disputed evidence, and affirmed the judgment.

I do not believe Wikipedia gives readers a strong enough understanding of that decision. The majority's finding on the sufficiency of the evidence should be discussed in plain language and given the attention it deserves.

Instead, modern interpretations of Frank's innocence receive far more prominence.

The United States Supreme Court Also Rejected Frank's Challenge

Frank's lawyers did not stop with the Georgia Supreme Court.

They continued pursuing relief through the legal system, including the federal courts. Their arguments eventually reached the United States Supreme Court in Frank v. Mangum.

On April 12, 1915, the Supreme Court rejected Frank's federal habeas corpus appeal by a vote of seven to two. (SCOTUS, 5)

The case involved claims that public hostility had affected the trial and that Frank had been denied constitutional protections. The majority considered the earlier state proceedings and concluded that the federal courts should not grant him relief on the record presented. Leo Frank's appeals were insufficient.

Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. and Charles Evans Hughes dissented. They believed the allegations of mob influence deserved further examination in federal court.

The Supreme Court did not retry the murder or decide whether every piece of evidence against Frank was correct. It examined constitutional questions and left his conviction undisturbed.

That distinction should be explained honestly. But the result cannot simply be ignored because modern writers disagree with it.

We have a grand jury that indicted Frank, a trial jury that convicted him, a judge who refused to order a new trial, a Georgia Supreme Court majority that found the evidence sufficient to support the verdict, and a United States Supreme Court majority that rejected the federal challenge.

These proceedings are a major part of the case's legal history.

Yet Wikipedia's opening tells readers Frank was wrongly convicted. First comes their conclusion, then comes their biased propaganda which cherry picks and omits significant details of the trial. 

Why Are Modern Writers Treated as Greater Authorities Than the Courts?

This brings me back to the larger problem.

Leonard Dinnerstein was a trained historian with a doctorate from Columbia University. Jeffrey Melnick is a professor of American Studies with a doctorate from Harvard. Steve Oney is a journalist whose research into the Frank case earned several awards. Their work deserves to be read and examined (Author Profiles, 8).

But being a respected historian, cultural scholar, or journalist is not the same thing as being a criminal trial judge or an appellate justice.

Many writers discussing the Leo Frank case do not have law degrees, have never practiced criminal law, and have never served as judges. Their published qualifications may establish expertise in history or journalism without establishing expertise in appellate procedure, rules of evidence, or constitutional law.

That distinction deserves attention when they criticize the original legal proceedings.

A historian can certainly conclude that a court was wrong. Legal training is not a requirement for studying history. But when an author claims that a jury convicted an innocent person, or that the Georgia Supreme Court wrongly upheld a verdict, I want to see that argument supported by a careful examination of the evidence and the law.

Which findings were wrong? Which legal rules were applied incorrectly? What testimony did the jury misunderstand? What evidence shows that the conviction could not be supported?

Those questions deserve detailed answers.

I do not believe a modern author's conclusion should automatically carry greater weight simply because it appears in an academic book. The original judicial opinions were written by judges who had the responsibility to apply the law to the record before them.

Their reasoning should be examined directly rather than summarized through authors who have already decided Frank was innocent.

How Wikipedia's Rules Reinforce the Modern Narrative

Wikipedia depends heavily on published secondary sources. Most modern scholarly works about the Frank case favor his innocence. As a result, Wikipedia editors can cite those books to justify presenting that interpretation as the established historical consensus (Wikipedia Policy, 6).

That creates a serious problem for anyone trying to bring greater attention to the original prosecution.

A researcher can spend years examining the Brief of Evidence, the newspaper reports, the trial court records, and the appellate decisions. That person might discover that a later writer overlooked testimony or described a court ruling incorrectly.

But Wikipedia's rules against original research generally prevent editors from adding their own new historical interpretations based on those documents. Such arguments usually need support from a recognized published source.

Meanwhile, a modern author's account may receive far greater consideration because it appeared in a respected book or academic publication.

This can create a circle where later books are used to defend Wikipedia's interpretation, while Wikipedia's sourcing rules make it difficult to challenge that interpretation through newly examined original evidence.

I believe this gives committed pro-Frank editors, whom I call Frankites, far too much influence over what readers are taught.

I also believe some editors approach the article as advocates for Frank's reputation rather than as people trying to explain the case from every relevant historical angle.

Whether particular editors have acted together to suppress opposing research would need to be established through an examination of Wikipedia's public editing history, reversions, talk-page discussions, and disputes over sources. That record is available for researchers to investigate.

Who decides which sources can be used? What happens when someone tries to add more of Jim Conley's original testimony? How are the Georgia Supreme Court's findings handled when they conflict with the conclusions of modern historians?

And are the same editorial standards applied to writers who support Frank's innocence?

These are questions Wikipedia should be willing to answer.

The 1986 Pardon Did Not Establish Innocence

The posthumous pardon is another part of this case that deserves clear treatment.

In 1983, the Georgia State Board of Pardons and Paroles considered an application seeking to establish Frank's innocence. The board found that the evidence presented did not conclusively prove he was innocent.

On March 11, 1986, the board granted a pardon for different reasons. Georgia had failed to protect Frank from the men who abducted and lynched him in August 1915. The state had also failed to bring his killers to justice (Ga. Pardons, 7).

The pardon expressly declined to decide whether Frank was guilty or innocent.

That means the pardon should not be described as a finding that the original jury convicted an innocent man.

Frank's lynching was unlawful, and the state's failure to protect him was a serious injustice. But condemning the lynching is not the same thing as concluding that the murder conviction was unsupported by the evidence.

Wikipedia acknowledges the limits of the pardon while continuing to present Frank's wrongful conviction as an established historical conclusion. I believe readers deserve a clearer explanation of the difference between the legal result and the conclusions later historians reached.

What Needs to Change

My conclusion, after studying the Leo Frank case, is that the prosecution established his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt and that the jury reached the correct verdict. I believe the evidence presented against him was stronger than many modern accounts acknowledge.

I am not arguing that juries and judges are incapable of making mistakes. Wrongful convictions happen, and historians should be free to investigate them. But a claim that the courts got this particular case wrong should be supported by a serious examination of what those courts actually decided.

The same standard should apply to the defense's allegations, the claims of antisemitism affecting the verdict, the interpretations of Jim Conley's testimony, and the later attempts to exonerate Frank.

I would like to see more historians, legal scholars, and researchers return to the surviving records instead of accepting the conclusions of earlier writers. We need new doctoral dissertations, peer-reviewed articles, and carefully researched books that examine the prosecution's evidence, the defense's arguments, the rulings of Judge Roan, and the appellate opinions.

Researchers should be willing to question both sides, identify errors wherever they appear, and publish findings that other people can check.

That is also how Wikipedia's treatment of the case can be challenged. If the prevailing academic literature favors Frank's innocence, then those who disagree need to produce credible research that can withstand scholarly criticism.

We need more people willing to pursue advanced degrees in history, law, and related fields, including funded doctoral programs, and bring the original evidence into serious academic discussion.

History Should Not Belong to One Side

Mary Phagan was thirteen years old when she went to the National Pencil Company to collect her wages on April 26, 1913. She never came home.

Her murder led to an investigation, an indictment, a lengthy trial, a guilty verdict, repeated appeals, a commutation of Frank's death sentence, and eventually his unlawful lynching.

More than a century later, the case remains controversial because people disagree about whether the jury reached the correct conclusion.

But I believe Wikipedia's article gives too much ground to writers defending Frank and too little attention to the original prosecution's case and the actual reasoning of the courts.

The Georgia Supreme Court's finding that the evidence was sufficient to uphold the verdict should not be overshadowed by the opinions of authors who came along decades later.

Neither should Judge Roan's refusal to grant a new trial or the United States Supreme Court's decision be pushed into the background.

The modern scholarly consensus is part of the history of the Leo Frank case. It is not a substitute for the original trial record.

I believe Frank was guilty, and I believe the prosecution proved its case. Others are free to disagree, but the legal record should be presented accurately, with the reasoning of the courts explained in full.

My question for Wikipedia is simple:

Why are the opinions of modern pro-Frank writers given so much authority while the original jury's verdict, Judge Roan's ruling, and the Georgia Supreme Court's express finding on the sufficiency of the evidence receive so much less attention?

Readers deserve to understand what the prosecution proved to the satisfaction of the jury, how the defense tried to answer that evidence, and why the courts left the conviction standing.

Let people examine the original testimony. Let them study the legal decisions. And let them decide whether the modern interpretation stands up to the historical record.

Celebrating 1,700 Years of Christianity in Georgia

Ambassador Vladimir Božović, PhD, President of the Society of Foreign Consuls in New York and Consul General of the Republic of Serbia, together with several members of the Executive Committee of the SOFC were pleased to participate in the celebration of the historic 1,700th anniversary of Christianity in Georgia, at the invitation of Maia Bartaia, Consul General of Georgia, Immediate Past President and current Executive Committee member of the Society.

The celebration brought together His Grace Bishop Saba of the Georgian Orthodox Church in North America, numerous clergy members, guests from the Bulgarian and Greek Orthodox Churches, and a distinguished gathering of diplomats, officials and representatives of New York’s international community.

This milestone offered a meaningful opportunity to honor Georgia’s spiritual and cultural heritage and the enduring role of Christianity in its history. Its significance also extends beyond national and religious boundaries, reaffirming the universal values of peace, mutual respect, human dignity and understanding among nations.

“This historic anniversary holds significance for Georgia, for Christianity as a whole, and for all people of goodwill who respect every person’s faith, national identity and dignity. Gatherings such as this strengthen friendship and trust and reaffirm diplomacy’s role in bringing together nations, cultures and spiritual traditions,” Ambassador Božović stated.

The Society extends its warm congratulations and sincere appreciation to Consul General Maia Bartaia and the team of the Consulate General of Georgia in New York for their outstanding organization and gracious hospitality. Their work once again demonstrated exemplary professionalism and diplomatic dedication. Consul General Bartaia’s continued engagement builds on her successful presidency of the Society and her valuable contribution to its standing, visibility and spirit of fellowship.

text:
Trump Is Not the Disease. America Has a Much Deeper Problem.

In September 2018, speaking at the University of Illinois shortly before the congressional midterm elections, Barack Obama said something that sounds even more relevant today: “He is a symptom, not the cause.” He was talking about Donald Trump, but his message concerned something much larger than one politician. Obama was warning Americans about the forces that had made Trump's rise possible.

Trump did not create America's divisions. He inherited a society already struggling with economic anxiety, racial resentment, cultural conflict, and declining trust in democratic institutions. What made him politically successful was his ability to transform these existing frustrations into a powerful movement built around anger, fear, and the promise of restoring a supposedly glorious past.

For decades, millions of Americans had watched factories close, jobs disappear overseas, and entire communities lose their economic foundations. Globalization and technological progress enriched some while leaving others behind. The financial crisis of 2008 deepened the conviction that the system served wealthy elites while ordinary citizens paid the price. People wanted explanations, and politicians offered them convenient enemies.

Immigrants, foreign competitors, minorities, intellectuals, and political opponents became easy targets. Complex economic problems were reduced to emotional slogans. Instead of explaining why industries were disappearing or wages stagnating, it became easier to blame Mexico, China, or supposedly disloyal Americans.

Meanwhile, demographic and cultural changes created another source of anxiety. Greater equality represented progress for millions, but others interpreted it as a threat to their traditions, identity, and social position. The fear of losing a familiar world became fertile ground for politicians promising to turn back the clock.

Trump recognized this opportunity. He did not need to invent resentment. He only needed to give it a voice, identify enemies, and convince frustrated voters that he alone could protect them. Political disagreement became a struggle between patriots and traitors. Compromise began to look like weakness, while aggression was celebrated as strength.

Obama also warned about political disengagement. When citizens lose faith in elections, institutions, and public officials, they leave the political arena to those most determined to dominate it. Democracy cannot survive on constitutional guarantees alone. It requires people willing to defend its principles even when they are disappointed by its results.

History provides troubling examples of how existing grievances can be weaponized. Hitler exploited Germany's humiliation and economic suffering. Putin cultivated Russia's imperial nostalgia and resentment over the Soviet collapse. Their historical circumstances and crimes differ profoundly, but the underlying political mechanism is recognizable: fear and humiliation can be transformed into loyalty to a leader promising national resurrection.

And here lies America's greatest danger. Many people imagine that removing Trump from politics would automatically restore normality. Replace him with a respectable president, abandon the inflammatory rhetoric, and everything will return to the way it was.

But what happens to the millions who embraced his message? What happens to the distrust, economic insecurity, cultural hostility, and appetite for political revenge? These forces will not disappear simply because one man leaves the White House.

Another politician could eventually inherit them. Perhaps someone more disciplined, more calculating, and better equipped to weaken democratic institutions without attracting the same resistance.

That was the deeper meaning of Obama's warning. The real challenge is not merely defeating a politician but understanding why his message became attractive to so many people.

📋 UPDATE: Haliburton (Left Hamstring) Remains Out; No Timetable Announced

Tyrese Haliburton (Indiana Pacers) — Hamstring strain, Grade unknown
Severity: MODERATE

Tyrese Haliburton is out for the Indiana Pacers with a left hamstring strain, with no return timetable disclosed by the team as of October 28. The injury was resolved to October 26, meaning he is approximately 2 days into this injury — very early in the recovery window.

The grade of this hamstring strain is INFERRED, not confirmed by imaging or team statement. "Out, no timetable" language is most consistent with a Grade 2 partial myotendinous disruption — if it were clearly Grade 1 (minor), teams typically offer a "day-to-day" or short-week framing. The absence of any timeline suggests the team is awaiting imaging clarity or the injury is more significant than an early-week soft tissue tweak.

For a Grade 2 hamstring strain, the published literature (T2 evidence — solid observational data, established protocols) puts return-to-play in the 3–6 week range from the injury date. At just 2 days post-injury, Haliburton is at the very start of that window. A Grade 1 presentation could bring him back in 1–2 weeks; a Grade 3 (confirmed tear) would extend the ceiling to 6–10 weeks and may warrant surgical evaluation. The biology here doesn't negotiate — hamstring tissue requires the full inflammatory-to-remodeling arc, and rushed returns in this injury carry well-documented reinjury risk.

The key watch signal is the MRI result, if disclosed. Grade confirmation will significantly sharpen this window. December soft-tissue injuries in the NBA carry cumulative load concerns, but at this early-season point (late October), acute strain rather than chronic overload is the more likely mechanism. Haliburton's role as the Pacers' primary ball-handler and floor general makes even a moderate hamstring injury consequential for Indiana's offensive structure.

RTP window: 3–10 weeks from injury (2026-10-26)

I, for one, would rather be in the good graces of the United States and its democratic allies than romanticize dictatorships built on Soviet-style propaganda and political repression. 😏

Let’s be honest: the freedoms we enjoy in democratic societies allow us to criticize our governments, express our opinions, build businesses, pursue opportunities and live without constantly worrying that disagreeing with those in power could cost us our freedom.

And while no country is perfect, there is a reason millions of people risk everything to migrate to the United States and other Western democracies in search of opportunity.

Some people are so caught up in opposing America that they are willing to overlook the abuses of its adversaries. They criticize Western foreign policy, sometimes with legitimate reasons, but suddenly develop selective amnesia when it comes to political prisoners, censorship, authoritarian rule and human rights abuses elsewhere.

Criticizing America does not require defending dictators. We can acknowledge Western hypocrisy where it exists without pretending that authoritarian regimes offer a better alternative.

And for those who believe life is automatically better under America’s geopolitical rivals, I would say this: travel, experience different societies, understand their laws and cultures, and examine how foreigners are treated before declaring one system superior to another. Don’t assume that every country outside the West is more welcoming, more tolerant or more respectful of people who look like us.

As a person of darker pigmentation, I am certainly not going to romanticize any government or society without considering how it treats people like me. Racism and discrimination exist in Western countries too, but we should be able to discuss those problems honestly without pretending they exist only in the West—or that authoritarian governments are somehow immune to them.

I believe in choosing freedom over oppression, opportunity over stagnation, and accountability over blind loyalty to a political ideology.

My loyalty is not to Washington, Moscow, Beijing or any other foreign capital. My loyalty is to freedom, human dignity and the right of ordinary people to determine their own future.

But if the choice is between living under a system where I can openly criticize my government and one where doing so could land me in prison, I know which side of that argument I stand on.

Democracy may be imperfect, but the answer to its imperfections is to strengthen freedom—not surrender it to dictators.

😏 Never become so blinded by hatred of America that you end up defending the very oppression you claim to oppose.

text:
Midjourney is turning ultrasound into a preventative scan

Ashlee Vance and Kylie Robison on Core Memory.

Ashlee Vance and Kylie Robison examine Midjourney's full-body ultrasound scanner, its spa plan, and the cost, scale, and medical limits of regular scanning. Vance describes the U.S. government's ban on an Anthropic model as rushed and politically charged, and warns that it sets a troubling precedent for AI labs. The hosts also discuss DeepMind's EVE Online partnership, Noam Shazeer's move to OpenAI, the fading claim that AI scaling had hit a wall, and Snap's $2,200 smart glasses. Later, Vance discusses a Rafael Nadal documentary, a fish-processing robot, and the debate over manufacturing and defense investment.

Minute by minute

1. Midjourney plans eight products (0:28)
Vance and Robison report that Midjourney founder David Holz unveiled a full-body scanner and a spa, the first two of eight planned products (four hardware and four software). They say Holz offered few details about the rest. Party chatter suggested another product might be a brain-computer interface, but they had no confirmation.

2. Ultrasound powers the body scan (5:29)
Holz's video showed a person standing on a platform and lowering into water for a scan. He said the scan could take about a minute and produce terabytes of data. Vance and Robison say the system arranges many Butterfly Network ultrasound chips around the body and that a hand demo showed bones and veins.

3. Preventive scans raise trade-offs (7:20)
Holz pitched regular scans as a way to track health, while Vance noted that scans can flag harmless findings and lead to unnecessary treatment. The hosts say Holz wants 50,000 machines and put the cost of realizing the plan at $40 billion. They question the real estate, scale, and timeline. Vance says ultrasound would not replace CT scans or colonoscopies.

4. The U.S. bans an Anthropic model (21:08)
Vance says the U.S. government pulled Anthropic's new model offline after reports of jailbreaks, affecting the company broadly, including foreign-national staff. Robison initially argues that Anthropic had called for government controls and described the model as dangerous, making intervention understandable. Vance says researchers viewed the reported flaws as common and not severe.

5. Vance sees retaliation in the ban (26:00)
Vance says he viewed the government's response as petty retaliation after Anthropic resisted the Department of War's desired uses of its models. He says the company had little time to address the issue and that early leaks to Axios and Politico favored the government. He warns that the ban sets a precedent for punishing labs over political disagreements. Robison also questions the demand that labs bend to Washington.

6. Private labs hold government leverage (32:23)
Vance argues that companies now control capabilities governments once built or managed, contrasting today's AI labs with the government-run Manhattan Project. He also cites the dispute over Starlink in Ukraine as an example of government dependence on a private company. He says the government lacks comparable data centers and AI systems.

7. DeepMind studies EVE Online (36:16)
Vance says DeepMind partnered with Fenris, the company behind EVE Online, to study the game's persistent universe as a setting for world models. He describes its long-running economy and player-created social structures, while Robison says AI needs a world to learn from rather than only text. The experiments will use an offline version so they do not affect players.

8. Shazeer joins OpenAI (45:38)
Vance and Robison say Noam Shazeer, a key author of the Transformers paper and a cofounder of Character AI, is joining OpenAI to work on new model architectures. They note that Google previously brought him and other Character AI leaders back to the company. The hosts say the move to a rival lab may reflect his interest in the work.

9. Scaling's supposed wall recedes (48:59)
Vance recalls headlines claiming that AI scaling had hit a wall and argues the claim was overblown as models continued to improve. Robison says coverage has shifted from asking whether AI will stop improving to asking how to respond to continued progress. Both note that forecasts about what comes next remain uncertain.

10. Vance and Robison call Snap's glasses oversized (52:16)
Vance and Robison criticize Snap's $2,200 smart glasses as oversized and question who will buy them. They note that Evan Spiegel described them as priced like a high-end computer. Vance likes hands-free calls and video on glasses but says public recording brings social and privacy friction.

11. Vance praises Nadal's candid documentary (1:05:21)
Vance recounts interviewing Rafael Nadal at Larry Ellison's home and seeing a cupboard of Nadal's rackets. He says he considered taking one. The hosts discuss a Nadal documentary's depiction of tension around his uncle's demanding coaching and his injuries. They also debate whether athlete-controlled documentaries can preserve journalistic independence.

12. Robots apply ikejime to fish (1:16:13)
Vance says he visited a fish-processing robot from Shinkae Systems, which uses computer vision to perform ikejime. A quick strike to the brain followed by a gill cut. He says the method is intended to be more humane and preserve meat quality. The hosts say the company sells fish they could compare with other fish.

13. Vance backs manufacturing capacity (1:19:28)
After joking that Vance is becoming more conservative, the hosts discuss his support for U.S. manufacturing and defense readiness despite his description of himself as a California liberal. They talk about protesters at Detroit's Reindustrialized conference, including concerns over weapons and Palantir's sponsorship, alongside Vance's view that the event also aims to create manufacturing jobs.

14. Redwood recycles used batteries (1:24:00)
Vance and Robison recommend a video tour of Redwood Materials with cofounder JB Straubel. They say the company breaks batteries down into lithium, cobalt, and nickel. Vance says 70 percent of all batteries in North America end up at Redwood Materials.

The link in the reply plays each point from its second.

text:
🇺🇸💸📉 America’s Friends Pull Back From Funding Its Debt

Being close to Washington no longer means buying its debt with the same enthusiasm. Investors in countries and regions most aligned with the US cut net purchases of Treasury bonds by more than 60% in January–August 2026, according to Bloomberg’s analysis of Treasury and State Department data.

They bought $174.3B after subtracting sales, the lowest total for those eight months since 2021. These are US government bonds issued for more than one year; short-term bills are excluded. The drop means less money coming in, not that investors dumped 60% of what they already owned.

The biggest pullback came from Asia. Japan, the largest foreign holder of US government debt, bought a net $389M, down 99% from a year earlier. South Korea sold a net $23.8B, its biggest January–August sell-off in records going back to 1977. Taiwan also sold more than it bought.

For years, Asia’s big savers helped finance US spending by parking their surplus cash in Treasuries. Now they have other options. Japanese bonds offer better returns than before, making it more tempting to keep money at home. Korean and Taiwanese investors have been buying stocks and other assets, while weak currencies have pushed governments to tap their reserves.

That does not make this a coordinated boycott. The figures mix government and private investment, and Bloomberg defines alignment by voting patterns at the United Nations. Bonds held through overseas banks can also make it hard to tell whose money is moving.

But Washington still has bills to pay. With federal debt above $40T, it needs buyers willing to keep lending. Banks, investment funds and other private investors have helped fill the gap. They watch the price closely, though, and can demand a better return when inflation, growing deficits or unpredictable policy make US debt look riskier.

Foreign investors are still buying American stocks and corporate bonds. So money moving away from Treasuries does not automatically mean money leaving the dollar. It means investors can back US businesses without being equally eager to bankroll the US government.

The pressure to US falls on how much it must pay, and how quickly that price can jump. As familiar buyers step back, Washington becomes more dependent on lenders ready to bargain harder or walk away. Diplomatic friendship cannot guarantee cheap financing.

text:
I, for one, would rather be in the good graces of the United States and its democratic allies than romanticize dictatorships built on Soviet-style propaganda and political repression. 😏

Let’s be honest: the freedoms we enjoy in democratic societies allow us to criticize our governments, express our opinions, build businesses, pursue opportunities and live without constantly worrying that disagreeing with those in power could cost us our freedom.

And while no country is perfect, there is a reason millions of people risk everything to migrate to the United States and other Western democracies in search of opportunity.

Some people are so caught up in opposing America that they are willing to overlook the abuses of its adversaries. They criticize Western foreign policy, sometimes with legitimate reasons, but suddenly develop selective amnesia when it comes to political prisoners, censorship, authoritarian rule and human rights abuses elsewhere.

Criticizing America does not require defending dictators. We can acknowledge Western hypocrisy where it exists without pretending that authoritarian regimes offer a better alternative.

And for those who believe life is automatically better under America’s geopolitical rivals, I would say this: travel, experience different societies, understand their laws and cultures, and examine how foreigners are treated before declaring one system superior to another. Don’t assume that every country outside the West is more welcoming, more tolerant or more respectful of people who look like us.

As a person of darker pigmentation, I am certainly not going to romanticize any government or society without considering how it treats people like me. Racism and discrimination exist in Western countries too, but we should be able to discuss those problems honestly without pretending they exist only in the West—or that authoritarian governments are somehow immune to them.

I believe in choosing freedom over oppression, opportunity over stagnation, and accountability over blind loyalty to a political ideology.

My loyalty is not to Washington, Moscow, Beijing or any other foreign capital. My loyalty is to freedom, human dignity and the right of ordinary people to determine their own future.

But if the choice is between living under a system where I can openly criticize my government and one where doing so could land me in prison, I know which side of that argument I stand on.

Democracy may be imperfect, but the answer to its imperfections is to strengthen freedom—not surrender it to dictators.

text:
MUGENZI FÉLIX, SO NOW SANCTIONS ARE BIAS BECAUSE YOUR FAVOURITE SIDE FINALLY HAS TO FACE CONSEQUENCES? 😭

Oh, what a spectacular performance! When the United States brokered the Washington Accords, you celebrated the peace framework. But when Washington sanctions Rwanda’s Ministry of Defence and Zigama CSS over alleged support to M23, suddenly the mediator has supposedly “picked a side.” 🤡

MAKE IT MAKE SENSE!

A PEACE AGREEMENT IS NOT AN IMMUNITY AGREEMENT.

The fact that the United States helped broker the deal does not mean every party gets a permanent exemption from consequences. If credible evidence points to violations, sanctions can be a means of enforcing accountability—not automatically proof that the mediator has abandoned diplomacy.

And let’s not play selective-memory games about the agreement itself.

Kinshasa must fulfil its security obligations, including addressing the FDLR threat.

Rwanda must fulfil its obligations concerning support for M23 and the withdrawal of its forces from Congolese territory.

BOTH OBLIGATIONS MATTER. Neither cancels the other.

You want us to believe that sanctions against Rwanda undermine peace, but you offer no convincing explanation for why accountability for alleged support to M23 should be treated as an attack on the peace process itself.

If the allegations are false, challenge the evidence. If the sanctions are unjustified, contest the legal basis. But screaming “bias” does not make the underlying allegations disappear.

And here is the real question: WHY SHOULD THE UNITED STATES IGNORE ALLEGED VIOLATIONS BY ONE PARTY SIMPLY BECAUSE IT ALSO HAS OBLIGATIONS TO ADDRESS THE CONDUCT OF THE OTHER? That is not neutrality; that is an argument for selective accountability.

MUGENZI, THE WASHINGTON ACCORDS ARE NOT A SHIELD AGAINST SANCTIONS. THEY ARE A FRAMEWORK OF OBLIGATIONS.

The test of a mediator is not whether every party likes the consequences. The test is whether the commitments are implemented and violations are addressed consistently.

LESS CRYING ABOUT “BIAS.” MORE EVIDENCE. MORE COMPLIANCE. THE SAME STANDARD FOR EVERY PARTY!

text:
Los Angeles Lakers vs LA Clippers — Dončić and the Lakers on a back-to-back against a depleted Clippers side

Preview · NBA · Regular season · Wednesday 28 October 2026

The Lakers beat the Clippers 125-117 at home in October and finished last season with 53 wins to their 42. Tonight's meeting is at the Intuit Dome, where the Clippers won both games between the two sides last season, and the Lakers are on the second night of a back-to-back after losing 129-136 at home to Portland on Tuesday night. The Clippers are without Brandon Ingram, Bradley Beal, Rui Hachimura and Max Strus. The Lakers at low confidence.

THE MATCHUP

The Lakers finished 2025-26 at 53-29, fourth in the West, with a 25-16 road record and a points differential of +1.8. The Clippers went 42-40, ninth, with a 23-18 home record and a differential of +1.1.

Luka Dončić averaged 33.5 points, 7.7 rebounds and 8.3 assists last season, with Austin Reaves on 23.3 points in 51 games. The supporting cast has changed: LeBron James is now in Philadelphia, while Collin Sexton (15.4 points for Chicago), Quentin Grimes (13.4 for Philadelphia) and Walker Kessler, who played only five games for Utah, are now with the Lakers. Adou Thiero and Cameron Carr are out.

The Clippers' list of absentees is longer. Ingram, who averaged 21.5 points for Toronto, and Hachimura, who played for the Lakers last season, are both now with the Clippers and both out, as are Beal and Strus. That leaves Darius Garland, who averaged 18.8 points and 6.7 assists in 45 games, as the main creator.

FORM & CONTEXT

The Lakers are 3-1 this season. They beat Golden State 127-105 and the Clippers at home, won 132-123 in Utah, and then lost to Portland on Tuesday night. The Clippers are 1-2: a 121-96 home win over Sacramento, then defeats at the Lakers and 101-108 in Oklahoma City on Sunday, their last game.

The Lakers finished last season 7-3 in their last ten and the Clippers 6-4. The Lakers then beat Houston in the first round before being swept by Oklahoma City; the Clippers missed the playoffs. In pre-season the Lakers won two of five and the Clippers two of three.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

Dončić against the home floor. Last season's four meetings were split 2-2 and every game went to the home side: the Lakers won 135-118 in November and 125-122 in February, and the Clippers won 103-88 in December and 112-104 in January, both at the Intuit Dome. Dončić is healthy; the Clippers are missing Ingram, the highest scorer on their roster last season.

THE CALL

The rest and the venue point to the Clippers, and last season's series offers no edge. The Lakers have the better roster tonight, the stronger record last season and this month's win, but on tired legs this is a narrow lean.

Los Angeles Lakers to win, low confidence.

It was said that the mediators handed over a draft of the proposal last Sunday, with an expectation of an Iranian response by the end of the current week. Details of the daily steps or the full text of the draft have not been published.

عن المقترح القطري الأخير لإنهاء الحرب  مع إيران

ما يتوفر عن المقترح المتداول اليوم، 28 أكتوبر، أنه إطار من سبعة أيام لإنهاء الحرب بين إيران والولايات المتحدة والكيان ، لكن طهران لا تصفه بأنه عرض رسمي. 

بحسب مسؤول مطلع نقلت عنه رويترز، يتضمن المقترح:

-خطوات يومية متبادلة لبناء الثقة بين واشنطن وطهران ومعالجة مخاوفهما.
-إمكانية بدء التنفيذ مطلع الأسبوع المقبل.
-ضمانات من عدة دول لم تُكشف أسماؤها.

وقيل إن الوسطاء سلّموا مسودة المقترح الأحد الماضي، مع توقع رد إيراني بنهاية الأسبوع الجاري. ولم تُنشر تفاصيل الخطوات اليومية أو نص المسودة الكامل. 

أما الموقف الإيراني الأحدث، فنقله مسؤول رفيع لرويترز: "ما قدمته قطر مجرد «أفكار غير مقبولة» ولا يرقى إلى عرض"، مع تأكيد عدم تغيير موقف طهران من الملف النووي. 

جوهر الخلاف على ما يبدو هو ترتيب الالتزامات: فواشنطن تريد إدخال الملف النووي منذ البداية، بينما تطالب إيران أولاً بإنهاء حصار موانئها ورفع العقوبات عن صادراتها النفطية. 

ويبدو أن الوساطة الجارية تحاول حل عقدة «من يبدأ؟ وبأي خطوة؟» عبر إجراءات متبادلة ومتدرجة. 

هل تنجح هذه الوساطة؟

text:
New #WFP Chief Luke J. Lindberg Takes Questions from Journalists at the United Nations
NEW YORK (#VIDEO). On just his third day as Executive Director of the United Nations World Food Programme (@WFP), @LukeJLindberg met with journalists at @UN Headquarters, outlining his priorities for the world's largest humanitarian food assistance organization and answering questions about global hunger, funding cuts, #Gaza, #Sudan, his relationship with President Donald Trump, and the selection of the next UN Secretary-General.  @WFPChief opened the briefing with a quiz for journalists: How many people work for the WFP? How many countries does it operate in? How many people does it feed?  The answers illustrate the scale of the organization: 18,000 employees, operations in more than 120 countries, and food assistance reaching over 100 million people annually.  Yet the challenges are enormous.  According to Lindberg, approximately 266 million people worldwide face acute food insecurity, with conflict responsible for roughly two-thirds of those cases. Another 49 million could be pushed into acute hunger by El Niño.  "The number one thing we can do to reduce hunger in the world is to reduce the amount of conflict," he said.  His immediate priorities include protecting humanitarian workers, strengthening relationships with donor countries, improving operational efficiency, investing in artificial intelligence to anticipate emergencies, and expanding school meal programs.  He also emphasized the dangers facing aid workers, noting that more than 700 humanitarian personnel have been killed in recent years.  Sudan will be his first destination.  Lindberg announced that he plans to visit the country within weeks, identifying Sudan, South Sudan, and Somalia as three of the WFP's most urgent humanitarian priorities.  He said he wanted to personally thank frontline workers operating in some of the world's most dangerous environments.  Asked about declining humanitarian funding, Lindberg acknowledged that the United States remains the WFP's largest donor. He also revealed that President Trump personally called him to ask him to become Washington's nominee for the position.  Lindberg expressed confidence that the administration would continue supporting humanitarian assistance while emphasizing the importance of attracting additional donors, including the private sector, now the organization's fifth-largest funding source.  Another journalist asked whether his close connections to Washington made him America's representative inside the UN or the UN's representative with direct access to the White House.  Lindberg rejected that characterization: "My point here is I'm here to end hunger," he replied, pledging to work with other UN agencies and advocate for humanitarian access worldwide.  Questions about Gaza focused on the security of WFP convoys, Israeli military actions, and the worsening humanitarian situation. Lindberg described the level of hunger in Gaza as unacceptable. He acknowledged that while the WFP has access to deliver food, funding shortages are forcing the organization to reduce assistance.  He promised to defend humanitarian workers wherever they operate and cooperate with other UN agencies trying to reach civilians in Gaza.  My question: What does he expect from the next UN Secretary-General?  In my question for Italpress, I asked Lindberg what he expects from the next Secretary-General of the United Nations, who will soon succeed @antonioguterres, and what kind of relationship he hopes to establish with the organization's new leader.  "Most people don't get to pick their boss in the world, right?" Lindberg replied with a smile. He described himself as collaborative and cooperative, saying the WFP would continue supporting reforms to make the UN more efficient and effective. He stressed that whoever becomes Secretary-General can count on the WFP as a constructive partner.  The exchange offered an early glimpse of Lindberg's leadership style: pragmatic, optimistic, focused on operational results, and determined to maintain relationships with both Washington and the wider international community.  
Watch the full video
https://t.co/1OV12mhAf1 via @YouTube
