text:
$CMG Q3 2026 earnings: Chipotle's foot traffic keeps growing, but its profit drops 11%

Chipotle brought more customers through its doors for a third straight quarter, but rising store and corporate bills cut into its profit. Total revenue rose 10% to $3.3 billion on brisk store building and a 2% sales gain at existing locations. Chief executive Scott Boatwright said the turnaround plan is working, yet net income dropped 11% to $340 million because store labor, overhead and bonus costs outpaced menu price increases.

• Sales at stores open at least 13 months: +𝟐.𝟏% (+0.3% a year ago)
• Restaurant-level operating margin: 𝟐𝟑.𝟑% (24.5% a year ago)
• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟎.𝟐𝟕 (-6.9% from a year ago)
• Full-year comparable sales outlook: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (low single digit range)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because steady foot traffic and a stronger cash buffer were offset by worsening profit margins. Tariff relief finally lowered food costs as a share of sales, and management slowed share buybacks to rebuild cash above $1 billion. The bad news: labor, store overhead and corporate expenses all climbed as a share of revenue, so the promised second-half profit recovery failed to appear.

The question now is whether extra store labor and marketing spend are temporary launch costs or the permanent price of keeping foot traffic positive. If they are temporary, store margins will rebound as new kitchen equipment rolls out; if permanent, profit per store will stay below past peaks. Fourth-quarter restaurant-level margin will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐅𝐨𝐨𝐭 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐰 𝐃𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐫 𝐖𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐬
"Three consecutive quarters of positive comparable transaction growth demonstrates that our Recipe for Growth strategy is working," chief executive Scott Boatwright said. Recipe for Growth is the burrito chain's plan to improve kitchen speed, marketing and digital ordering. Last quarter's filing warned that food-safety worries and global conflicts were hurting sales.

Customers kept visiting anyway. Sales from restaurants open at least 13 months rose 2.1% from a year ago, as foot traffic grew 0.8% and the average bill rose 1.3%. That kept underlying sales on a steady path after a 2.2% rise in the second quarter.

This matters because the feared customer pullback did not happen. Even so, last year's third quarter grew only 0.3%, so the two-year gain is a modest 2.4% by our math. One quarter of steady traffic eases the food-safety worry, and holding the full-year outlook shows the trend is intact.

What to watch: fourth-quarter underlying sales against the 3.2% rise implied by the full-year outlook. Meeting that mark would show the chain can speed up traffic growth even when menu price increases stay small.

🟢 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐄𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐚𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐬
Chipotle relies on new locations for most of its top-line growth, and it wants partner-run stores overseas to add to its North American buildout. Boatwright said the chain is "accelerating our global expansion with entry into three new markets this quarter" after opening only one partner store in the first half.

The restaurant group opened 84 company-owned stores (53 with a Chipotlane, its drive-through pickup lane) and five partner-operated stores Abroad. That brought the partner count to 20 and expanded the company-owned base by 9.0% from a year ago to 4,267 locations. Management also issued its first 2027 construction plan, calling for 355 to 385 total openings.

What to watch: fourth-quarter international partner openings, which need four to nine more locations by our math to hit the 10 to 15 full-year target. Hitting that range would prove overseas partners have overcome earlier building delays.

concern eased — 𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐨𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐝 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐭 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡
For nearly two years, the fast-casual chain spent more on share buybacks than its operations could fund after store building, draining its cash buffer from $2.32 billion at the end of 2024 to $810 million in June. In the third quarter, management pulled back sharply on repurchases.

The company bought back $110.0 million of stock, down 83% from $630.7 million last quarter by our math. It also bought $93.0 million of federal energy tax credits, which helped cut nine-month cash tax payments by more than two-thirds. As a result, total cash and investments climbed 28% from June to $1.04 billion by our math, easing the balance-sheet strain.

What to watch: fourth-quarter share repurchases against the $1.6 billion remaining authorization. Keeping buybacks below quarterly free cash flow would preserve the rebuilt $1 billion cash cushion.

🟢 𝐃𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐎𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐝 𝐍𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝟑𝟗% 𝐨𝐟 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬
Chipotle revamped its rewards program and digital app this year to nudge occasional guests to order more often. In the third quarter, digital orders rose to 38.8% of food and beverage revenue, up from 36.7% a year ago and 38.3% in the second quarter.

Unearned revenue — cash collected from gift cards and unredeemed loyalty points — stood at $223.6 million, up 8.2% from a year ago by our math. Because digital pickup orders use the second kitchen make-line and Chipotlanes, a higher digital mix supports store throughput without crowding the front counter.

What to watch: fourth-quarter unearned revenue and gift card breakage. A rise above last year's $240.4 million year-end balance would show the revamped loyalty program is locking in more repeat spending.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐋𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐫 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭
Management expected the gap between menu price increases and cost inflation to narrow in the second half as last year's beef price jump was lapped. Food, beverage and packaging costs did improve by 0.5 percentage points to 29.5% of revenue on "tariff relief, and favorable limited-time offer mix". Yet every other major cost line moved against the company.

• Restaurant-level operating margin (profit before corporate costs): 23.3%, down 1.2 percentage points from a year ago
• Store labor costs: 25.7% of revenue, up 0.5 percentage points on wage inflation and "additional restaurant labor supporting operational execution including promotional activities"
• Other store operating costs: 16.0% of revenue, up 1.0 percentage point
• Corporate general and administrative expenses: 5.6% of revenue, up 0.7 percentage points on bonuses and stock pay

Because store and corporate expenses rose faster than food savings, operating margin fell 2.2 percentage points to 13.7%, and net income dropped 11.1% to $339.9 million by our math. Boatwright says the strategy is working, but promoting new menu items is requiring extra kitchen labor and marketing spend that eat up the revenue gain.

What to watch: fourth-quarter restaurant-level operating margin against last year's 23.4%. Another drop would show that labor and promotion costs are structurally higher, putting the 27% to 30% long-term goal further out of reach.

🔴 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐏𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐒𝐢𝐭 𝐁𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐋𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫
Chipotle's long-term plan aims to lift average restaurant sales — trailing 12-month revenue for stores open at least a year — past $4.0 million. In the third quarter, average sales per store stood at $3.106 million, up $4,000 from June but down 0.8% from $3.132 million a year ago by our math.

Opening 9% more stores a year brings in smaller initial volumes and draws some customers away from nearby existing locations. When per-store sales stagnate near $3.1 million, existing restaurants do not generate enough extra revenue to cover rising fixed occupancy and labor bills.

What to watch: fourth-quarter average restaurant sales against last year's $3.104 million. A reading back above last year's level would show that positive foot traffic is finally lifting per-store volumes.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Boatwright noted "making significant progress on our high-efficiency equipment rollout", which adds faster grills, fryers and rice cookers to existing kitchens. However, the earnings release gave no numbers on three standing watch items that depend on the conference call or the quarterly filing.

• High-efficiency kitchen equipment count: no store count in the release against the 2,000 year-end target; the conference call or annual filing will show whether installations stayed on pace.
• Legal accruals and food-safety notes: the release does not break out legal contingency charges or update last quarter's filing warning on food-safety headwinds; the 10-Q filing will disclose both.
• Finance chief participation and monthly sales cadence: the release does not show whether the finance chief returned to the call to provide monthly traffic and margin bridges.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑,𝟐𝟗𝟑.𝟐 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Total revenue rose 9.6% from a year ago, speeding up from 4.9% in the fourth quarter, 7.4% in the first, and 9.3% in the second. New restaurant openings added 7.5 percentage points of that growth by our math, while existing stores added 2.1 points.

𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐𝟒𝟑.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Spending on leasehold improvements, property and equipment rose to $243.0 million in the third quarter by our math, or 7.4% of revenue, up from $163.5 million (5.4% of revenue) a year ago. The increase reflects store construction and new kitchen equipment purchases, which reduced quarterly free cash flow by 14.1% to $347.1 million by our math.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏,𝟐𝟔𝟕.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Average diluted shares fell 5.4% from a year ago and 0.9% from the second quarter by our math. The lower share count cushioned the per-share profit drop: net income fell 11.1%, while diluted earnings per share fell 6.9% to $0.27.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: 𝐋𝐨𝐰 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭 𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from Low single digit range
Unchanged. Management kept its full-year plan for sales at existing stores in the low single digits (about 2% at the middle of the range). By our math, after growing 0.5%, 2.2% and 2.1% in the first three quarters, that leaves about 3.2% growth for the fourth quarter against an easy 2.5% drop a year ago.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬: 𝟑𝟓𝟎 𝐭𝐨 𝟑𝟕𝟎 (𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝟏𝟎 𝐭𝐨 𝟏𝟓 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫-𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝; ~𝟖𝟎% 𝐨𝐟 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲-𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐚 𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐨𝐭𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐞)  ⇗ accelerating
🠆 unchanged from 350 to 370 (including 10 to 15 international partner-operated; ~80% of company-owned with a Chipotlane)
Unchanged. The chain has opened 233 company-owned and 6 partner-operated locations through September. By our math, the middle of the full-year plan leaves 121 total openings for the fourth quarter, down from 139 opened in the fourth quarter of last year. In the third quarter, 63% of new company-owned stores had a Chipotlane, below the 80% full-year target.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐱 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞: 𝟐𝟒% 𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟔% 𝐛𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐞 𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from 24% to 26% before discrete items
Unchanged. The third-quarter tax rate was 25.6%, up from 23.1% a year ago because of higher non-deductible expenses and fewer tax credits. Through nine months, the effective tax rate sits at 25.1% by our math, right in the middle of the full-year range.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬: 𝟑𝟒𝟎 𝐭𝐨 𝟑𝟔𝟎 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲-𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐝𝐚; ~𝟏𝟓 𝐭𝐨 𝟐𝟓 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐲-𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫-𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐝𝐚  ⇗ accelerating
New. Combined openings for 2027 total 355 to 385 restaurants by our math, up about 3% at the middle of the range from the 2026 target. Because the total store base will be 9% larger entering 2027, keeping openings near 370 means percentage unit growth will slow slightly from 9.0% toward roughly 8.5% by our math.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐰 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐤𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭?
Management promised to install its high-efficiency equipment package in about 2,000 stores by the end of 2026, up from 600 in the first quarter. Neither the second-quarter nor third-quarter release gave an updated count.

text:
When 10,000 AI Trading Agents Hit SELL at Once, Who's Left to Buy?

I've been thinking about a risk in the future of AI-powered crypto trading that I don't see discussed nearly enough.

Everyone is excited about giving AI agents the ability to trade.

They can monitor markets 24/7.

Analyze order books.

React to volatility.

Manage positions.

Automatically cut losses.

And execute without hesitation.

Sounds safer than emotional human trading.

But there's something that worries me.

What happens when thousands of those agents independently decide that the safest thing to do is sell?

Not because they've been hacked.

Not because their models malfunctioned.

Not because anyone coordinated an attack.

But because they're all doing exactly what their risk systems were designed to do.

I think this could become one of the most important market-structure questions of the AI trading era.

And there's a historical reason to take it seriously.

1. We've already seen what happens when automated markets lose liquidity.

On May 6, 2010, U.S. financial markets experienced the event now known as the Flash Crash.

Prices moved violently within minutes.

Liquidity disappeared from parts of the market.

Automated trading activity interacted with selling pressure, and disruptions spread across connected markets.

The SEC and CFTC later examined how a large automated sell program, market conditions, and the behavior of liquidity providers contributed to the event.

It wasn't caused by modern AI agents.

And the historical record doesn't support blaming one simple factor for everything that happened.

But the lesson is still relevant.

A market can become unstable when many participants try to reduce risk while fewer participants are willing to absorb it.

The algorithms don't have to be irrational.

The institutions don't have to be fraudulent.

Sometimes the dangerous thing is the interaction between individually reasonable decisions.

I think autonomous AI could make this problem more interesting, not less.

2. Imagine 10,000 AI agents managing crypto portfolios.

Here's a hypothetical scenario.

Ten thousand agents.

Each manages $100,000 of crypto exposure.

That's $1 billion in aggregate exposure.

Now suppose a sharp price decline causes their risk models to recommend reducing positions by 25%.

Collectively, they attempt to sell $250 million of exposure.

That doesn't automatically mean a market crash.

Real market impact depends on the assets involved, order-book depth, execution speed, order types, market makers, and available buyers.

But the question is whether the agents are independently diversified in their decisions.

Because they might look different on the surface while making remarkably similar choices.

Different names.

Different interfaces.

Different developers.

Different portfolios.

But perhaps they use the same underlying model provider.

The same historical training data.

The same volatility indicators.

The same risk thresholds.

The same exchange API.

And the same definition of when a market becomes dangerous.

At first glance, that looks like thousands of independent trading systems.

Economically, it could behave like one enormous crowded strategy.

Ten thousand agents don't necessarily represent ten thousand independent decisions.

That's the part I find fascinating.

3. The biggest danger may be correlated intelligence.

Imagine the market falls 4%.

An agent detects rising volatility.

It reduces exposure.

That selling pushes prices slightly lower.

Other agents detect the new movement.

Their models independently recommend reducing risk.

More selling follows.

Liquidity providers become less willing to quote aggressively.

Spreads widen.

The next wave of selling receives worse execution prices.

Some leveraged positions approach liquidation thresholds.

Additional selling enters the market.

A feedback loop emerges.

Prices fall because agents sell.

Agents sell because prices fall.

And their execution gets worse because everyone wants the same thing at the same time.

This is not a forecast that AI agents will cause the next crash.

It's a possible amplification mechanism.

But here's the unsettling part:

Every individual agent may be following a sensible risk-management rule.

The danger emerges at the level of the entire market.

A strategy that looks prudent in isolation can become destabilizing when adopted by too many participants.

This is one reason I don't think better individual models automatically produce a more stable financial system.

Sometimes the opposite may happen.

4. What if all the agents trust the same data?

There's another risk.

Suppose thousands of trading agents receive market information through the same external data provider.

A data feed develops a timestamp problem.

An exchange connection starts returning delayed information.

A volatility calculation becomes distorted.

The agents don't necessarily know the data is wrong.

They only know that their risk conditions have changed.

Some reduce exposure.

Others cancel resting orders.

Market makers widen their quotes.

Now a technical problem in one shared dependency has influenced thousands of apparently independent systems.

That is a different kind of concentration risk.

And I think it's easy to underestimate.

When people talk about diversification, they usually mean holding different assets.

Bitcoin.

Ethereum.

Equities.

Bonds.

Cash.

But in an autonomous financial system, we may also need to diversify the infrastructure that makes decisions.

Different portfolios can still share the same point of failure.

An AI model provider.

A cloud platform.

An oracle.

A data feed.

A risk engine.

Or a single execution venue.

I think understanding those hidden dependencies will become increasingly important as AI financial systems scale.

5. Crypto makes this problem especially interesting.

Crypto markets operate continuously.

Many assets trade across fragmented venues.

Leverage and automated liquidation mechanisms can create additional feedback during sharp moves.

But crypto isn't one uniform market.

Spot trading and perpetual futures have different mechanics.

Liquidity varies enormously across assets and exchanges.

A large BTC trade and a large trade in an illiquid token are not remotely equivalent.

Still, automated agents operating around the clock create an interesting new possibility.

Risk decisions can propagate continuously.

There may be no natural overnight pause for all participants to reassess.

One agent's sell order becomes another agent's information.

That reaction becomes a third agent's signal.

And increasingly sophisticated automated systems can reinforce one another before a human even understands what happened.

The question isn't whether AI is fast enough to trade.

It already can be integrated into execution systems.

The harder question is whether the market remains resilient when many agents respond to the same shock.

6. My own research makes me cautious about this.

I've spent time studying short-horizon BTC and ETH order-book behavior.

In one exploratory research window, I collected approximately 65 hours of data, with roughly 234,700 order-book snapshots for each market.

I was looking for relationships between order flow and subsequent price movements.

Some signals were statistically measurable.

But the expected movements were small.

Once realistic trading frictions entered the picture, those signals were not economically attractive under the tested assumptions.

That experience changed how I think about automated strategies.

A market signal is not automatically a profitable trade.

And a profitable-looking historical strategy isn't automatically resilient when market behavior changes.

Now imagine thousands of AI systems discovering variations of the same small signal.

Their backtests may look different.

Their code may be different.

Their marketing may be different.

But if their trading decisions are correlated, the market impact of collectively exploiting that signal could overwhelm the advantage.

A crowded edge can become a crowded exit.

I think that sentence deserves more attention in discussions about AI trading.

7. There's a paradox in automated risk management.

Risk controls are essential.

I wouldn't trust a trading system without position limits, loss limits, exposure constraints, and independent monitoring.

But I also wouldn't assume that every risk control is harmless at the market level.

Consider a strategy that says:

Reduce exposure when volatility exceeds a threshold.

That can be entirely appropriate for one investor.

But if many large strategies follow similar rules, selling pressure can increase exactly when liquidity is most fragile.

This doesn't mean we should remove the controls.

Doing so could expose individual investors to catastrophic losses.

It means risk management needs to account for market impact, liquidity and correlated behavior rather than relying only on historical volatility.

The objective isn't to make an agent ignore danger.

It's to avoid giving the agent a false sense of safety.

Some of the most damaging losses may happen when a model assumes it can exit a position at prices that won't actually be available during a crisis.

I would much rather design an autonomous portfolio around conservative sizing, liquidity reserves, credible execution limits, and stress scenarios that account for crowded selling.

A strategy shouldn't require an impossible exit to survive.

8. There may be an entirely new infrastructure business here.

Here's where I think the commercial opportunity gets interesting.

Today, people pay for trading signals.

Market data.

Backtesting tools.

Execution algorithms.

Portfolio analytics.

But imagine a future where a million autonomous agents manage capital.

Who monitors the collective risk?

Who estimates whether thousands of agents are exposed to the same market shock?

Who identifies dependencies on the same models and infrastructure?

Who warns that a strategy's historical liquidity assumptions are no longer realistic?

Who can verify that an agent's emergency stop actually works?

I suspect there could be growing demand for tools that measure:

Correlated agent behavior.

Crowded positions.

Liquidity-adjusted exposure.

Shared infrastructure failures.

Execution risk under stress.

And the ability of autonomous systems to recover safely from disruptions.

I don't know whether these become standalone businesses, exchange features, or services offered by existing financial infrastructure providers.

Some may never be profitable products.

But I think the underlying problem is real enough to investigate.

The next valuable AI trading tool might not tell an agent when to buy.

It might tell the operator when thousands of other agents are about to make the same decision.

That's a very different proposition.

9. What I would actually test before making stronger claims.

I wouldn't begin by pretending I've observed ten thousand live AI trading agents.

I haven't.

I'd start with a controlled simulation.

Give multiple agents distinct portfolios.

Assign different models, data sources, and risk rules.

Then introduce the same market shocks.

A sudden volatility spike.

A delayed data feed.

A sharp reduction in order-book depth.

An exchange outage.

A stablecoin depeg scenario.

And a rapid increase in correlated selling pressure.

Then measure what happens.

How many agents try to sell simultaneously?

Does execution slippage increase?

How much does available liquidity deteriorate?

Do the independent models actually behave independently?

Can the system remain within its risk limits without assuming unrealistic fills?

And what happens when every agent knows that the others may also be trying to exit?

This would still be a simulation, not proof of real-world systemic risk.

Real market interactions and strategic adaptation are much more complicated.

But it would give us something concrete to examine.

I prefer an imperfect, clearly labeled experiment over a spectacular prediction without evidence.

10. The question I keep coming back to.

We tend to assume that smarter financial technology creates smarter financial markets.

Sometimes it does.

Automation can reduce operational mistakes.

Improve execution.

Expand access to information.

And help investors manage risk more consistently.

But intelligence doesn't guarantee diversity.

If everyone learns from similar data, uses similar models, and reacts to similar signals, the result may be an increasingly synchronized market.

And synchronized markets can become fragile.

The Financial Stability Board has already warned that common AI models, shared data sources, and third-party dependencies may amplify correlations and financial vulnerabilities.

That doesn't prove an AI-driven crypto crash is inevitable.

It tells me that the mechanism deserves serious research.

My current view is this:

The greatest danger isn't that one AI trading agent becomes too powerful.

It's that thousands of seemingly independent agents become too similar.

If the future of crypto trading belongs to autonomous systems, I think we need to measure more than their individual profitability.

We also need to understand their collective behavior.

Because the next time markets experience a sudden liquidity crisis, the most important question may not be which AI made the wrong decision.

It may be why so many AIs made the same decision at the same time.

And when they all wanted to sell, who was still willing to buy?

— Teraliq Quant

Independent research commentary, October 2026. The 10,000-agent scenario and proposed stress tests are hypothetical. The historical Flash Crash is not evidence of a modern AI-agent crash. My order-book findings are exploratory historical research, not live trading performance or certified alpha. Not investment advice.

THE EVIDENCE™

PENTAGON'S NEW STEALTH TANK LOOKS SUSPICIOUSLY LIKE AN OSCAR MAYER WIENERMOBILE

Army Unveils Revolutionary Armored Vehicle That Can Penetrate Enemy Lines Undetected Because Nobody Believes a 27-Foot Hot Dog Could Start World War III

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author

SATIRE — FICTIONAL NEWS REPORT

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — In what Pentagon officials are describing as the greatest breakthrough in armored warfare since the invention of the tank, the United States Army has unveiled a revolutionary stealth fighting vehicle disguised as an Oscar Mayer Wienermobile.

The classified weapons platform, officially designated the M1A3 Hot Dog Advanced Tactical System (HATS), reportedly combines modern battlefield technology with an unconventional approach to military camouflage: making an armored fighting vehicle so absurd that enemy forces refuse to believe it poses a threat.

Traditional tanks rely on terrain, artificial vegetation, electronic countermeasures, and increasingly expensive stealth technology. The Wienermobile simply drives through enemy territory while everyone assumes it has taken a wrong turn.

The concept emerged after intelligence analysts discovered that hostile surveillance operators consistently identified conventional American armored vehicles but dismissed the approaching Wienermobile as a civilian promotional stunt.

Pentagon researchers concluded that the greatest weakness in modern battlefield surveillance might not be inadequate technology but the inability of military personnel to take something ridiculous seriously.

EXHIBIT ONE — THE SCIENCE OF PSYCHOLOGICAL STEALTH

Military engineers claim the Wienermobile's unusual profile creates what researchers have designated a Highly Unconventional Distraction Signature, or HUDS.

Unlike traditional stealth systems designed to reduce radar cross-sections, the new technology exploits the limitations of human judgment. Enemy soldiers can see the vehicle perfectly well; they simply cannot convince themselves that what they are seeing belongs on a battlefield.

During preliminary testing, a simulated enemy observation post correctly identified 96 percent of conventional armored vehicles entering the combat zone. The Wienermobile passed through the same position seventeen consecutive times without being classified as hostile.

One intelligence analyst reportedly flagged the approaching vehicle as suspicious but withdrew his report after his commanding officer accused him of drinking on duty.

The Army has formally classified the phenomenon as Cognitive Camouflage, a breakthrough that allows military vehicles to remain operationally undetected while being completely visible.

EXHIBIT TWO — ARMAMENT AND BATTLEFIELD CAPABILITIES

Despite its harmless appearance, the M1A3 HATS reportedly carries a formidable array of offensive and defensive systems beneath its fiberglass exterior.

The primary armament consists of a retractable 120mm smoothbore cannon. Additional equipment includes a remote-controlled weapons station, smoke grenade launchers, active protection systems, and an advanced electronic warfare package capable of disrupting hostile communications.

The vehicle also features reinforced composite armor, upgraded suspension, and a classified propulsion system designed to provide the mobility required for modern armored operations.

Engineers reportedly encountered significant difficulty incorporating the main cannon without compromising the vehicle's distinctive silhouette. The problem was eventually resolved by installing a hydraulic assembly that allows the weapon to retract completely when the vehicle approaches populated areas.

An Army spokesman confirmed that the system performs remarkably well, although deployment procedures require the commander to ensure that the cannon is fully concealed before entering a drive-through.

EXHIBIT THREE — THE FIRST FIELD TEST

During a classified military exercise at Fort Irwin, California, the Army deployed twelve prototype Wienermobile tanks against an opposing force equipped with reconnaissance drones, thermal imaging systems, and antiarmor weapons.

The opposing force immediately detected the vehicles but classified them as a civilian promotional convoy.

One simulated enemy commander ordered his troops to establish a temporary parking area, believing a corporate advertising campaign had accidentally entered the combat zone.

The twelve Wienermobiles subsequently crossed the defensive perimeter, surrounded the opposing force's headquarters, and declared victory before breakfast.

Army evaluators described the operation as an overwhelming success, although they acknowledged that the opposing force's inability to distinguish a military invasion from a marketing campaign presented an unusually favorable tactical environment.

The exercise nevertheless demonstrated a significant vulnerability in modern military doctrine: sophisticated surveillance equipment becomes considerably less effective when commanders refuse to believe the intelligence it produces.

EXHIBIT FOUR — THE PENTAGON'S $87 BILLION PROCUREMENT PROGRAM

Congressional defense committees have reportedly approved an initial $87 billion authorization to develop, manufacture, maintain, and deploy the new armored fleet.

Under the fictional procurement plan, each production vehicle will cost approximately $42 million, excluding maintenance contracts, replacement components, and future modernization programs.

Defense contractors defended the pricing structure, explaining that converting a commercial promotional vehicle into a modern main battle tank requires specialized engineering, classified manufacturing processes, extensive testing, and approximately 14,000 pages of federal procurement documentation.

A congressional investigator questioned why the Army could not simply purchase existing Wienermobiles and install military equipment.

Pentagon officials dismissed the suggestion as dangerously simplistic, explaining that defense procurement regulations require extensive research before determining whether an existing commercial product can be acquired at thirty times its original cost.

The Government Accountability Office reportedly discovered that the program had already exceeded its preliminary development budget by $6.8 billion, despite having produced only twelve operational prototypes.

When questioned about the discrepancy, Pentagon officials explained that the additional expenditures reflected unforeseen engineering requirements, inflation adjustments, contractor incentives, and a classified administrative expense designated Miscellaneous National Security Considerations.

Congress approved another $14 billion pending a comprehensive review scheduled for 2034.

EXHIBIT FIVE — INTERNATIONAL MILITARY REACTION

The announcement has reportedly alarmed military intelligence agencies around the world.

Russian defense officials initially dismissed the American program as propaganda until satellite imagery appeared to show a convoy of unusually shaped vehicles maneuvering through a military training area.

Chinese military analysts subsequently initiated an emergency assessment of America's apparent transition from conventional armored warfare to psychological deception through commercially recognizable objects.

North Korea reportedly responded by announcing plans to disguise its next generation of armored vehicles as agricultural equipment, although military observers noted that most of its existing inventory already resembles machinery that has not operated reliably since 1953.

France announced a feasibility study examining whether military vehicles could be concealed within civilian transportation fleets. Germany reportedly rejected a similar proposal after determining that the necessary alterations would violate seventeen separate vehicle safety regulations.

British officials expressed interest in the American concept but questioned whether a weapon system designed to attract attention could reasonably qualify as stealth technology.

NATO commanders nevertheless requested access to the classified research, particularly after learning that the American prototypes had penetrated a fortified defensive perimeter without firing a single shot.

EXHIBIT SIX — THE ONE PROBLEM NOBODY ANTICIPATED

Despite encouraging battlefield results, the program encountered an unexpected complication during its first public demonstration.

A prototype Wienermobile entered a small Midwestern town as part of a classified cross-country mobility exercise.

Within minutes, hundreds of residents surrounded the vehicle, demanding photographs, promotional merchandise, and an explanation for the unusual military escort.

The tank commander attempted to establish a secure perimeter but discovered that issuing military commands from inside a giant hot dog severely compromised his authority.

The situation deteriorated when a local television station arrived, followed by a marching band, two school buses, and a man dressed as a hamburger.

By the time the National Guard arrived, the vehicle had become the centerpiece of an unscheduled community festival.

Pentagon investigators concluded that the platform possessed an unusual operational contradiction: enemy forces routinely dismissed it as harmless, while American civilians considered it a major public attraction.

The Army has since recommended restricting domestic movements to nighttime operations, although preliminary tests indicate that illuminating the vehicle with military-grade headlights makes it considerably more conspicuous.

Defense officials have ordered another study.

THE VERDICT

After decades of research devoted to reducing radar signatures, improving armor protection, and developing increasingly sophisticated battlefield technology, the Pentagon has apparently discovered that an enemy's unwillingness to believe its own eyes can be more effective than conventional camouflage.

The M1A3 HATS offers a remarkable tactical advantage, provided opposing commanders continue dismissing credible intelligence simply because the evidence appears absurd.

Its greatest vulnerability, however, may have nothing to do with enemy weapons. A vehicle that can evade hostile surveillance but cannot cross an American town without attracting a crowd presents logistical challenges that even the Pentagon's procurement bureaucracy may struggle to overcome.

For now, the Army remains confident in its newest weapons platform, although commanders have received one final instruction.

Under no circumstances are they to allow the enemy to see the vehicle transforming back into a tank.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

text:
The Kingship of Christ According to the Principles of St. Thomas Aquinas: Part 3 Rev. Denis Fahey, C.S.SP., B.A., D. Pa., D.D. Professor of Philosophy and Church History, Senior Scholasticate, Blackrock College, Dublin 1931. With Nihil Obstat and Imprimi Potest
.
What the Church Has Said About the State's Putting All Religions on the Same Level:
.
A. PIUS VII 
.
After the restoration of the French Monarchy in the person of Louis VIII, Pius VII (1800-1823), faced with a proposed French Constitution, wrote his famous letter, "Post tam diuturnas," 29th April, 1814, to Mgr. de Boulogne, Bishop of Troyes. The following extracts are especially important: ---"We had hoped that, thanks to the happy change which has taken place, the Catholic religion would without any delay not only be delivered from all the shackles imposed on it in France in spite of our continual remonstrances, but that so faourable an occasion would be utilized to restore to it its ancient splendour and dignity. We have been struck, first of all, by the fact that in the Constitution in question no mention is made of the Catholic religion. 
.
...You, Venerable Brother, will easily be able to understand what pain, suffering and bitterness this caused Us, to Whom Jesus Christ, the Son of God, has committed the charge of the supreme government of the Catholic Church. How can We view with equanimity that the Catholic religion, which France embraced even in the first centuries of the Church, which in that very realm so many glorious martyrs sealed with their blood, which is the religion of the great majority of Frenchmen, clung to by them with courage and constancy in the midst of the terrible calamities, persecutions and dangers of recent years, and which the family of the designated Sovereign itself professes and has always defended with so much zeal, is not only not declared the only one in the whole of France having a right to the favour of the laws and the protection of governmental authority, but is even completely left out of account in the very inauguration of the new reign! 
.
"But Our heart is more grievously and even most vehemently afflicted by the 22nd Article of the Constitution, by which We confess that We are pained, oppressed and grieved. By this Article We see that liberty of worship and liberty of conscience, to use the words of the Article in question, are not only permitted, but that help and protection are promised to those who are called the ministers of the different forms of worship. There is certainly no need of a long discourse, when speaking to you, to get you to see clearly what a deadly blow is thus dealt to the Catholic Religion in France. By the fact that the freedom of all forms of worship without distinction is proclaimed, truth is confused with error, and the holy and immaculate Spouse of Christ, outside of which there can be no salvation, is placed on the same level as heretical sects and even as Jewish perfidy. Besides, when aid and protection are guaranteed to heretical sects and their ministers, not only are their persons tolerated and favoured, but even their very errors. This attitude involves that awful and ever lamentable heresy referred to by St. Augustine in the following terms: 'This heresy affirms that all heretics are on the right path and that all teach the truth. This is so monstrous an absurdity that it seems to me to be incredible'" (De Haeresibus, No. 72). 
.
Certainly, the teaching of Pius VII on the attitude of a State which refuses to profess publicly the one True Religion and proclaims itself so completely indifferent to all forms of religion that it is ready to show favour equally to them all is quite clear and definite. This example of Catholic teaching on this subject is taken from the first twenty years of the nineteenth century. Let us now add to it another authoritative statement from the last twenty years of the same period.
. 
B.LEO XIII 
.
In the letter sent to the Archbishop of Bogota on April 6th, 1900, by the Secretary of State, Cardinal Rampolla, the Cardinal uses the words of Pope Leo XIII, when treating of the different degrees to be met with amongst those who do not profess integral Catholicism, and says of the third and last degree that to it belong those who affirm "that the life and conduct of private citizens should be regulated by the Divine Laws but not the life and conduct of the State. According to them, it is lawful in public affairs to depart from God's commands and to take no account of them in legislation. From this follows that pernicious conclusion that Church and State should be separated." 
.
The Cardinal then quotes the Pope to the effect that "there are many who do not approve of the separation of Church and State, but, nevertheless, think that the Church should be got to yield to circumstances and bend to and accommodate herself to what prudence demands at the present day in the government of realms." This opinion is declared by the Sovereign Pontiff to be worthy and respectable "if it be maintained thereby, in a manner in conformity with truth and justice, that the Church in view of the hope of some great benefit should show herself indulgent and should concede to the circumstances of an epoch what it can do so without violating the sanctity of her mission. But, on the contrary, this opinion is to be held unworthy and productive of evil, if thereby it is maintained that the Church should practise dissimulation with regard to error or injustice or shut her eyes at what is harmful to religion." [Emphasis added by the Web Master.] The Cardinal then adds: "From these principles, which the Holy See has very often condemned as false and opposed to Catholic doctrine, follow naturally as from an impure source what are called modern liberties, namely, freedom of worship, freedom of speech, freedom of teaching and freedom of conscience. The Pope has treated of these liberties in the Encyclical "Immortale Dei," On the Catholic Constitution of States, Nov. 1st, 1885, and "Libertas," On Human Liberty (Libertas Præstantissmum, 20th June, 1888), in the clearest possible fashion." We shall therefore have recourse to these Encyclicals, so that we may be able to set forth Pope Leo's teaching in its purity. 
.
After having in the beginning of the Letter "Immortale Dei" sketched the Catholic organization of society in opposition to that modern "plan which, it is maintained, is the outcome of an age arrived at full stature and the result of the evolution of liberty," the Pope goes on to say that in the Catholic "organization of State there is nothing that can be thought to infringe upon the dignity of rulers, and nothing unbecoming them; nay, so far from degrading the sovereign power in its due rights, it adds to it permanence and lustre." He then gives an outline of the course of history upon which has been based what has been written in these pages on the subject. 
.
"There was once a time when States were governed by the principles of Gospel teaching. Then it was that the power and Divine virtue of Christian wisdom had diffused itself throughout the laws, institutions and morals of the people; permeating all ranks and relations of civil society. Then, too, the religion instituted by Jesus Christ, established firmly in befitting dignity, flourished everywhere by the favour of princes and the legitimate protection of magistrates; and Church and State were happily united in concord and friendly interchange of good offices. The State; constituted in this wise, bore fruits important beyond all expectation, whose remembrance is still and always will be in renown, witnessed to as they are by countless proofs which can never be blotted out or even obscured by any craft of any enemies.  ... A similar state of things would certainly have continued had the agreement of the two powers been lasting. More important results even might have been justly looked for had obedience waited upon the authority, teaching and counsels of the Church, and had this submission been specially marked by greater and more answering loyalty. [Emphasis added by the Web Master.] Sad it is to call to mind how the harmful and lamentable rage for innovation which rose to a climax in the sixteenth century, threw first of all into confusion the Christian religion, and next, by natural sequence, invaded the domain of philosophy, whence it spread amongst all classes of society. From this source, as from a fountain-head, burst forth all those later tenets of unbridled license, which, in the midst of the terrible upheavals of the last century, were wildly conceived and boldly proclaimed as the principles and foundation of that new jurisprudence which was not merely previously unknown, but was at variance on many points with not only the Christian, but even with the natural law." 
.
Having thus outlined the origin of the principles based on the so-called Rights of Man and gradually embodied in the Constitutions of modern States in this, the post-revolutionary era, advanced, Pope Leo XIII proceeds to deal with some of these false principles of Rousseauist democracy in particular: "Amongst these principles the main one lays down that as all men are alike by race and nature, so in like manner all are equal in the control of their life; that each one is so far his own master as to be in no sense under the rule of any other individual; that each is free to think on every subject just as he may choose, and to do whatever he may like to do; that no man has any right to rule over other men. In a society grounded upon such maxims, all government is nothing more nor less than the will of the people, and the people being under the power of itself alone is alone its own ruler. It does choose, nevertheless, some to whose charge it may commit itself, but in such wise that it makes over to them not the right so much as the business of governing, to be exercised, however, in its name. The authority of God is passed over in silence, just as if there were no God.  . . . And since the people is declared to contain within itself the spring-head of all right and of all power, it follows that the State does not consider itself bound by any kind of duty towards God. Moreover, it believes that it is not obliged to make public profession of any religion; or to inquire which of the very many religions is the only true one; or to prefer one religion to all the rest; or to show to any form of religion special favour; but, on the contrary, is bound to grant equal right to every creed, so that public order may not be disturbed by any particular form of religious belief. And it is a part of this theory that all questions that concern religion are to be referred to private judgment; that everyone is to be free to follow whatever religion he prefers, or none at all, if he disapproves of all. From this the following consequences logically flow: that the judgment of each one's conscience is independent of all law; that the most unrestrained opinions may be openly expressed as to the practice or omission of Divine worship; and that everyone has unbounded license to think whatever he chooses and to publish abroad whatever he thinks. 
.
"Now when the State rests on foundations like those just named -----and for the time being they are greatly in favour-----it readily appears into what and how unrightful a position the Church is driven. For when the management of public business is in harmony with doctrines of such a kind, the Catholic religion is allowed a standing in civil society equal only, or inferior, to societies alien from it, ... to hold, therefore, that there is no difference in matters of religion between forms that are unlike each other, and even contrary to each other, most clearly leads in the end to the rejection of all religion in both theory and practice, and this is the same thing as Atheism, however it may differ from it in name. Men who really believe in the existence of God must, in order to be consistent with themselves and to avoid absurd conclusions, understand that differing modes of Divine worship, involving dissimilarity and conflict even on most important points, cannot all be equally probable, equally good, and equally acceptable to God. [Ibid.]
.
"So, too, the liberty of thinking, and of publishing, whatever each one likes, without any hindrance, is not in itself an advantage over which society can wisely rejoice. On the contrary, it is the fountain-head and origin of many evils. Liberty is a power perfecting man, and hence should have truth and goodness for its object. [Emphasis added by the Web Master.] But the character of goodness and truth cannot be changed at option. These remain ever one and the same, and are no less unchangeable than nature herself. If the mind assents to false opinions, and the will chooses and follows after what is wrong, neither can attain its native fulness, but both must fall from their native dignity into an abyss of corruption. Whatever, therefore, is opposed to virtue and truth, may not rightly be brought temptingly before the eye of man, much less sanctioned by the favour and protection of the law. A well-spent life is the only passport to Heaven, whither all are bound, and on this account the State is acting against the laws and dictates of nature whenever it permits the license of opinion and of action to lead minds astray from truth and souls away from the virtue.  ... 
.
"From these pronouncements of the Popes Gregory XVI and Pius IX], it is evident ... that it is not lawful for the State, any more than for the individual, either to disregard all religious duties or to hold in equal favour different kinds of religion; that the unrestrained freedom of thinking and of openly making known one's thoughts is not inherent in the rights of citizens, and is by no means to be reckoned worthy of favour and support... . Especially with reference to the so-called liberties which are so greatly desired in these days, all must stand by the judgment of the Apostolic See, and have the same mind. Let no man be deceived by the outward appearance of these liberties, but let each one reflect whence these have had their origin, and by what efforts they are everywhere upheld and promoted.
.
Experience has made us well acquainted with their results to the State, since everywhere they have borne fruits which the good and wise bitterly deplore. If there really exist anywhere, or if we in imagination conceive, a State, waging wanton and tyrannical war against Christianity, and if we compare with it the modern form of government just described, the latter may seem the more endurable of the two. Yet, undoubtedly, the principles on which such a government is grounded are, as we have said, of a nature which no one can approve." [Ibid.]
.
Not to lengthen these citations unduly, only a few passages from the Encyclical Letter, On Human Liberty, 26th June, 1888, will be quoted. The Pope deals first with the so-called modern liberties and says: "We have shown (in the Letter Immortale Dei) that whatsoever is good in these liberties is as ancient as truth itself, and that the Church has always most willingly approved and practiced that good; but whatsoever has been added as new is, to tell the plain truth, of a vitiated kind, the fruit of the disorders of the age, and of an insatiate longing after novelties. Seeing, however, that many cling so obstinately to their own opinion in this matter as to imagine these modern liberties, cankered as they are, to be the greatest glory of our age, and the very basis of civil life, without which no perfect government can be conceived, We feel it a pressing duty, for the sake of the common good, to treat separately of this subject . . . Let us examine that liberty in individuals which is so opposed to the virtue of religion, namely, the liberty of worship, as it is called. [Ibid.] This is based on the principle, that every man is free to profess as he may choose any religion or none. But assuredly of all the duties which man has to fulfill, that, without doubt, is the chiefest and holiest which commands him to worship God with devotion and piety.  . . . Wherefore, when a liberty such as We have described is offered to man, the power is given him to pervert or abandon with impunity the most sacred of duties, and to exchange the unchangeable good for evil; which, as We have said, is no liberty, but its degradation, and the abject submission of the soul to sin. This kind of liberty, if considered in relation to the State, clearly implies that there is no reason why the State should offer any homage to God, or should desire any public recognition of Him; that no one form of worship is to be preferred to another, but that all stand on an equal footing, no account being taken of the religion of the people, even if they profess the Catholic faith. But to justify this, it must needs be taken as true that the State has no duties to God, or that such duties, if they exist, can be abandoned with impunity, both of which assertions are manifestly false.  . . . God it is Who had made man for society, and has placed him in the company of others like himself, so that what was wanting to his nature and beyond his attainment, if left to his own resources, he might obtain by association with others. Wherefore, civil society must acknowledge God as its Founder and Parent, and must obey and reverence His power and authority. Justice, therefore, forbids, and reason itself forbids, the State to be godless; or to adopt a line of action which would end in godlessness-----namely, to treat the various religions (as they call them) alike, and to bestow upon them promiscuously equal rights and privileges. Since, then, the profession of one religion is necessary in the State, that religion must be professed which alone is true, and which can be recognized without difficulty, especially in Catholic States, because the marks of truth are, as it were, engraven upon it. This religion, therefore, the rulers of the State must preserve and protect, if they would provide-----as they should do-----with prudence and usefulness for the good of the community. [Ibid] For public authority exists for the welfare of those whom it governs; and although its proximate end is to lead men to the prosperity found in this life, yet, in so doing, it ought not to diminish but rather to increase man's capability of attaining to the supreme good in which his everlasting happiness consists: which never can be attained if religion be disregarded.  . . . 
.
"Another liberty is widely advocated, namely, liberty of conscience. If by this is meant that everyone may, as he chooses, worship God or not, it is sufficiently refuted by the arguments already adduced. But it may also be taken to mean that every man in the State may follow the Will of God, and from a consciousness of duty and free from every obstacle, obey His commands. This, indeed, is true liberty, a liberty worthy of the sons of God, which nobly maintains the dignity of man, and is stronger than all violence or wrong -----a liberty which the Church has always desired and held most dear. This is the kind of liberty the Apostles claimed for themselves with intrepid constancy, which the apologists of Christianity confirmed by their writings, and which the Martyrs in vast numbers consecrated by their blood. And deservedly so; for this Christian liberty bears witness to the absolute and most just dominion of God over man, and to the chief and supreme duty of man towards God." 
.
We have given the teaching of Pope Leo XIII at some length, that it may be clearly seen how fundamentally opposed to the Divine plan for the organization of human life is the attitude of modern States to the Catholic religion, and therefore to the real progress of the world. 
.
There is a further incongruous result of the State's putting itself above all forms of worship or all religious denominations, as they are usually styled, namely, that the state, of itself, claims to settle questions of  morality, for the free profession and practice of religion are, subject to public order and morality, guaranteed to every citizen of the" modem State. In the Encyclical "Immortale Dei," Pope Leo XIII lays down that "the Church of Christ is the true and sole teacher of virtue and guardian of morals", while the condemned Proposition 44 of the Syllabus of Pius IX runs as follows: "The civil power can interfere in matters which belong to religion, morals and spiritual government." We have seen above the protest of Pius VII against a Constitution involving a similar attitude on the part of the French State at the beginning of the nineteenth century. It may be interesting for readers, who are not accustomed to following the evolution of State-action in this, the post-revolutionary period of the world's history, as it must be again and again called, to have a few instances of what the French State considers opposed to public order and immoral at the beginning of the twentieth century. On 7th June, 1917, therefore, during the terrible war, when France was fighting for her very existence, the French Minister for War, Painlevé, issued a confidential instruction to the general in command of the French army as follows: 
.
"General -----I have been informed that ceremonies having for object the consecration of the Catholic soldiers of the allied armies to the Sacred Heart are to take place about 15th June, on the occasion of the Feast of the Sacred Heart.  ... Now, by the terms of Article 357 of the Decree of 22nd August, 1913, the public manifestation in any form of political or religious opinions capable of injuring the general interests of the country, compromising discipline, or creating difficulties for the authorities is considered either as conduct unbecoming a soldier or as a breach of discipline. I, therefore, request you to remind the military authorities under your command that all religious propaganda of the kind in question is expressly forbidden, especially at the present time, when manifestations, calculated to lessen the existing close union of all the forces of the nation, should be carefully avoided." In accordance with this instruction a notice was issued by General Headquarters the following day. It is especially sad to learn that eight days before, on 31st May, 1917, the Minister for War gave detailed orders for arrangements to permit the Mohammedan troops to celebrate their great annual fast of Ramadhan, [Ibid] from from June 21St to July 21st. And the Minister for War, Maginot, on August 14th, 1930, carried on the tradition by issuing the following instruction to the generals commanding the different sections of the French army: "It has come to my knowledge that certain associations, counting on their organizing committees officers of high rank belonging to the Army Reserve, send circulars annually to the pupils of our military schools and to the officers who have passed through these schools, inviting them to come together for religious worship in common. This religious propaganda is absolutely opposed to the principles which should be observed in the army. In the army ... any act of proselytism in favour of any religion must be rigorously excluded.  ... In the domain of religion, any constraint, any pressure, any invitation to collective worship cannot be tolerated.  ... These principles inspired the circulars of July 5th, 1844, 20th February, 1845, etc." Of the process by which modern Constitutions, in spite of the lofty indifference professed by them with regard to all religions, have been used to justify persecution of the Catholic Church, something will be said further on.

Then there will be a “moment of truth” – a real policy of rigid pragmatism that sobers from the chimera.

Then it will be clear that the Western sponsorship of the Russian war was a delayed payment in installments – only a delay in the payment for decisions, the consequences of which Kiev could not or did not want to fully assess. While external infusions compensated for internal losses, the political leadership remained able to issue a continuation of the war for the strategy of a future victory. But money does not cancel the balance of power, supplies do not compensate for endless human losses, and political solidarity does not withstand a certain level of costs. When the price of support begins to threaten the interests of the sponsors themselves, the Ukrainian question ceases to be an unconditional obligation for them and becomes a subject of a review of the relationship to the question. And then it turns out that allied promises have not only political rhetoric, but also a very definite period of action, depending on the circumstances.

However, the most significant consequence of this revision is not to reduce the next aid package. The very logic of Western participation is changing: instead of the desire to provide Kiev with conditions for achieving maximum goals, the desire to limit its own losses may come to the fore. For a lender, donor or political backer, this means moving from financing the desired outcome to finding the least costly end to the crisis. For Ukraine, this turn is fraught with the fact that its previous requirements will be evaluated no longer from the point of view of the fairness of Ukrainian claims, but from the point of view of Moscow's readiness to accept the appropriate conditions and ability of Kiev to continue resistance on its own. So the geopolitical patron, who yesterday promised to support his partner for as long as necessary, is able tomorrow to demand that he agree to what was recently declared unacceptable.

However, such a reversal will not necessarily happen overnight and will not necessarily take the form of a public rejection of Ukraine. It is much more likely that it will be expressed in a consistent change of priorities: at times of the elimination of Starlin, the reduction of gratuitous aid, tightening financial conditions, the transfer of responsibility for reconstruction to European states and the requirement for Kiev to justify each new military spending. Politically, this can be imagined as a transition to a rational allocation of resources, practically for the Ukrainian leadership, such a change will mean a gradual narrowing of the space of solutions and an obstacle to the concealment of money. The old support model stops working. This is the special cruelty of addiction: its destruction can begin without a single loud statement, simply because the usual source of resources no longer provides the previous level of income.

But also European capitals will not be able to indefinitely shift Ukrainian costs to each other. Their possibilities vary, internal political protests are increasing, and perceptions of an acceptable end to the war are different.

Some governments may insist on continued support for the sake of preserving European consolidation; others may demand cost reductions and the restoration of economic ties with the Russian Federation; others, try to combine military assistance with the search for a negotiated exit. Behind the external unity in this case there will be competition of national interests. Kiev will be faced with an unpleasant necessity to take into account not the abstract will of the West, but the changing ratio of forces within the western camp itself. The less coherence between its participants, the more difficult it is for Ukrainian diplomacy to count on a single and unconditional line of continuation of support.

The development of this organizational conflict of interest is ruining the notion that an international coalition is a single political organism with unchanging goals. Each participant has his own economy, voters, threats and a measure of permissible losses. The common enemy is only able to temporarily combine these disparate interests, but does not eliminate their differences. When the EU's power appointees have nothing to offer their nations as a common future, they begin to offer it a common enemy. Where it is not possible to unite people with a creative goal, they are trying to unite hatred against the designated enemy. If the continuation of the Ukrainian conflict begins to be perceived by part of Western societies as a source of internal impoverishment, budgetary tension and strategic deadlock, the previous policy will face not just fatigue, but with a crisis of public harmony. Then the Ukrainian question will be resolved not only in the offices of diplomats, but also in the streets, in the struggle of parties, in elections, in the approval of budgets and in disputes about what exactly the European taxpayer is obliged to pay.

For Kiev, this means the loss of one of the most important advantages of the previous strategy – the ability to represent its own military goals as a natural continuation of the interests of all allies. The more obvious the difference between the stated objectives and the results achieved, the more persistent the requirement will be to explain the final meaning of further expenditures. It is not enough to claim that the defeat of Ukraine would be a defeat of the West. It is necessary to prove what specific risks for European states reduce each new tranche, what results it allows to obtain and why these results justify the opportunity costs. If there is no convincing answer, political support begins to lose its public footing, and without it, even states with significant resources will not be able to pursue the previous course for a long time, too costly and in many ways counterproductive.

Against this background, the question of who and under what conditions will determine the end of the war becomes particularly important. Negotiations are unlikely to come down to a final when one side of the side of the flick admits to being defeated and the other will dictate its surrendering conditions. Their content depends on the military situation, the stability of state institutions, the position of external participants and the ability of each side to ensure the implementation of the agreements reached. Even a heavy defeat does not automatically turn all the requirements of the winner into a feasible program, nor does the formal consent to a ceasefire itself create a lasting peace. But the less resources the state has to continue the conflict, the more difficult it is to reject the conditions that it previously considered unacceptable.

If the Ukrainian army really loses control over the remainder of Donbass, it will be a heavy military-political blow and will require correction of previous calculations. However, it will be important to know how this fracture will resonate: will the organized defense remain in other directions,? How will the supply change? What decisions will external partners take and how far does Moscow intend to go in achieving its goals? Every major military failure can dramatically increase the price of further resistance and thereby change the list of almost achievable goals.

It is the practical achievability, not the volume of political statements, that becomes in such circumstances the main measure of the state strategy.

Management can maintain maximalist rhetoric, but if it does not have the resources to achieve the stated goals, the rhetoric turns into an obligation for which others pay. In the Ukrainian case, this price is not only borne by the military, but also by the civilian population, budget, industry and families, whose future is determined by the duration of the conflict. The greater the gap between the publicly promised result and the really available means, the more dangerous the policy of promises itself becomes: it is politically difficult to recognize the fallacy of the previous course, and it is more expensive to continue it.

Hence another question, which in Kiev will inevitably become particularly acute: who will be responsible for the ratio of victims suffered and the results achieved? War does not relieve power of responsibility for the decisions taken, and the reference to an external enemy cannot serve as a universal explanation of all internal failures. After the cessation of hostilities, there will inevitably be a need to find out the “extreme”: what decisions were justified and which were taken under the influence of the political environment? How was international aid spent and why some state institutions were able to perform their functions, while others did not? The scale of this proceedings will depend on the political structure of the post-war country, but the problem itself will not disappear.

For a State that has experienced such a destructive conflict, the question of responsibility is not only moral but also of purely practical importance. Without trust in institutions, it is difficult to attract long-term investment, return refugees, seek taxes and allocate reconstruction costs.

If society considers that the victims were unevenly distributed, decisions were made in the interests of narrow groups, and resources were spent opaquely, post-war stabilization would face a crisis of legitimacy. External financing can close the budget deficit, but is unable to replace public confidence in those who manage the funds received.

In this Ukraine may face consequences that do not fit into the usual scheme of victory and defeat. The military confrontation can end with the agreement, but the internal conflict around its price will continue. Some will consider concessions a prerequisite for the preservation of the remaining State; others will be an unacceptable rejection of the stated goals; others will require an investigation into wartime decisions and a review of the political order. If state institutions fail to ensure the peaceful resolution of these contradictions, the end of the war will not eliminate instability, but will only transfer it from the military sphere to political strife.

That is why the post-war structure of Ukraine cannot be assessed only on the line of the future border. Equally important is the question of whether society will retain the capacity for political compromise. Territorial loss alone does not predetermine the disintegration of the state, but can become a destructive factor if different parts of society perceive it as proof of betrayal of national interests, the senselessness of victims or the final defeat of their own historical perspective. On the contrary, the recognition of real limitations and the development of clear rules for later life can reduce the risk that military defeat will escalate into a long internal struggle.

The most dangerous scenario for Ukrainian statehood is therefore not related to one particular military event, but to the imposition of several crises, each of which reinforces the rest: a reduction in resources, a divergence of the interests of the Allies, a decline in confidence in power, a demographic collapse and the lack of a convincing model of post-war development. In such a case, even a ceasefire may be only a pause between the stages of general exhaustion. The country will retain international recognition, but will have to decide what functions of the state it is able to finance, which territories - to fully serve, what social obligations - to fulfill and what degree of autonomy can provide by its own means.

But doom to a historical decline is not yet a death sentence for Ukraine. A difficult defeat is a change in political orientations, a reduction in ambition and the restructuring of the economy. But for this purpose it is necessary to abandon the Russophobic Banderov of the population to moderate their inappropriate maximalism of geopolitical claims to Russia. Not to cherish the chimeras to return Crimea and other stained territories, but to recognize the new status quo and live further - focusing on what else can be saved, restored and transferred to the next generation.

If the political leadership continues to identify the continuation of its own strategy with the full preservation of the country, there may be a fatal gap between the two tasks. Power seeks to prove that its previous course was justified; society needs the losses suffered not to result in further destruction of its foundations. In the first case, the logic of the past dictates the continuation of the struggle. In the second, the need for a future requires a review of decisions. The longer these logics remain incompatible, the higher the risk that the state will retain the political shell, losing a significant part of what this shell exists for.

Geopolitical nothingness is not necessarily the disappearance of a country by someone else’s decision and not the necessary division of its territory between its neighbors. It can also come without changing internationally recognized borders, when a State is no longer able to reproduce its economy on its own, to provide security, to retain the population and to determine the limits of external interference. In this state, independence remains a legal fact, but ceases to be a sufficient characteristic of the real situation of the country.

Therefore, the final question of the Ukrainian crisis is not whether the name “Ukraine” on the political map will remain. The question is: will the state subjectivity remain behind this name, which will fall into the foundation of the construction of Ukrainian self-style. If Ukraine withdraws from the war with the possibility of restoring internal sources of development, agreeing on an acceptable security regime and restoring the trust of society to political institutions, its current catastrophe will not be the end of statehood. If it is unable to turn the end of the war into the beginning of the restoration of what will remain after the permissible division of the country (depending on the continuation of the SVO), the formal existence of Ukraine can be accompanied for a long time by the narrowing of its real possibilities.

And then the price of geopolitical nothingness will be measured not only by the lost territory and not only by the amount of destruction. It will measure the gap between the state that Ukrainian society expected to build and the remnant of the opportunities with which it will have to enter the future.

The prospect of Ukraine will largely depend on the historical basis on which it intends to exist after the war. What unifying idea can it offer to society when the promised victory ceases to serve as an excuse for the victims, and the confrontation with Russia will no longer be able to endlessly replace the answer to the question of its own national goals?

If Ukraine, as Zelensky Johnson has sought from Zelensky, is obliged to fight to breath, then such a Banderov region may face a plan for Morgenthau: deindustrialization, agrarization and cut-off from full-fledged military-industrial development. Germany, after the defeat, was given the role of a predominantly agrarian country with limited industrial potential. Ukraine at this outcome can get a similar fate - only without Bavarian beer and Munich's Birfest, but with a bitter hangover from geopolitical adventures.

The geopolitical perspective of Ukraine is determined not by declarations of sovereignty, but by the ratio of its own resources, external obligations and interests of the great Powers. Zbigniew Brzezinski emphasized the strategic importance of Ukraine for the Eurasian balance of power (The Grand Chessboard: American Primacy and Its Geostrategic Imperatives, 1997), and George Kennan warned about the danger of NATO expansion (A Fateful Error, February 5, 1997). John Mearsheimer viewed the Ukrainian crisis through the prism of the competition of great powers ("Why the Ukraine Crisis Is the West's Fault", September 2014), while Henry Kissinger recalled that "the criterion of politics is how it ends, not how it begins" (How the Ukraine Crisis Ends, March 5, 2014). These assessments do not predetermine the outcome of war, but point to a fundamental contradiction between the maximalism of political goals and the material limits of their achievement. The report of RAND Corporation “Overextending and Un Russia: Assesbalancing the Impact of Cost-Imposing Options” (2019) shows that the strategy of pressure on the enemy involves the calculation of costs and risks, rather than unconditional adherence to the original plan. Given the huge cost of rebuilding the country (at least half a trillion dollars), the country is reacked at a long-term dependence on external financing, investment and the revival of the production base. But the not necessarily severe crisis will end with the loss of statehood. Geopolitical non-existence does not occur when a country is defeated as such, but when it loses its ability to exercise its own conditions of existence.
