text:
The Missing Shoe and Hat: Two Different Descriptions of Their Location

The Atlanta Georgian specifically asked Dobbs whether the missing shoe was found on the same general line as the suspected dragging marks.

Dobbs indicated that it was, although slightly off to one side, and that the hat was also nearby.

The Atlanta Journal furnished distances. It reported that the shoe and hat were found together on a garbage pile about 100 feet from the elevator and about 50 feet from the body. The Journal placed the boiler near the same general area.

The Constitution did not give those measurements in its treatment of Dobbs.

These accounts can be reconciled, but they emphasize different features of the evidence.

The Georgian describes the shoe and hat in relation to the alleged dragging path. The Journal locates the objects on a garbage pile and supplies approximate distances from two landmarks.

A shoe could be on a garbage pile and still lie close to the general line of movement. There is no necessary contradiction between those descriptions.

However, the precise placement should not be overstated. Neither newspaper presented a measured scale diagram, and the reports do not establish that the objects were photographed and measured before the scene was disturbed (AG, 1) (AJ, 2).

The Umbrella: Who Found It and Where?

The Atlanta Georgian provided another direct exchange that the Journal and Constitution did not preserve in their accounts of Dobbs.

Asked whether he found the umbrella, Dobbs answered that another officer, Lassiter, did.

The Georgian also reported that Lassiter found the umbrella around seven o'clock, after the initial police response.

This distinguishes an object Dobbs personally discovered from one found by another officer.

The Journal's Dobbs section concentrated on the shoe, hat, notes, and dragging marks rather than identifying the officer who discovered the umbrella.

The Constitution's May 1 article included a separate account of a theory advanced by friends of Leo Frank. That account referred to the girl's parasol being found near the foot of the basement ladder. It was not Dobbs's testimony and should not be treated as his description of the discovery.

The distinction is necessary because the Georgian associated the umbrella with the elevator area, while the Constitution's separately attributed theory placed the parasol near the ladder.

The two newspaper references may concern the same general part of the factory, but the evidence should be checked before treating them as one exact location (AG, 1) (AC, 3).

The Rear Basement Door and the Pulled Staple

The Atlanta Journal reported another observation attributed to Dobbs. He said that a staple fastening the rear basement door had been pulled loose and that it could not have been removed in that manner from outside the building.

The Journal also mentioned a nearby piece of iron that might have been used to pry it loose.

This was part of the evidence suggesting that the rear door could have been opened from inside the basement.

The Atlanta Georgian's separate Dobbs account did not describe this fastening in the same detail.

The Atlanta Constitution reported the damaged door fastening through the testimony of other responding officers, particularly Anderson. It did not provide a comparable detailed statement from Dobbs in the short section devoted to him.

Thus, the Journal supplies Dobbs's own reported interpretation of the fastening, while the Constitution includes similar evidence through another witness.

Even if the staple had been pulled from the inside, that finding would not establish who removed it or when. It would show that the door fastening had been disturbed in a way that might permit an exit through the rear of the factory (AJ, 2) (AC, 3).

The Temperature of the Body: Cold but Not Fully Stiff

The Atlanta Georgian directly questioned Dobbs about whether Mary Phagan's body retained any warmth.

Dobbs answered, "No. I could work the fingers slightly" (AG, 1).

The Atlanta Journal gave a fuller description. According to its account, Dobbs touched the face, hands, and knees. He described the body as cold but said the finger joints were not completely stiff and could still be moved.

The Constitution did not reproduce this testimony from Dobbs.

However, the Constitution and Journal both reported a different observation from Call Officer Anderson, who described the body as retaining warmth or said that blood was still flowing or moist.

These statements should not be blended into one account. Dobbs's observation of a cold body and Anderson's statements about warmth and blood are separate witness reports.

The differences could reflect the parts of the body examined, differing perceptions, or inaccuracies in reporting. The newspapers do not supply enough information to resolve them conclusively.

The Georgian and Journal also reported that Dobbs admitted having little experience examining dead bodies. The Journal went further by making clear that he could not give a reliable estimate of how long Mary Phagan had been dead.

That admission places a limit on his testimony. He could describe what he felt and observed, but he did not establish an exact time of death (AG, 1) (AJ, 2) (AC, 3).

The Basement Partition and the Difficulty Seeing Around It

The Atlanta Georgian reported a question about whether Dobbs initially noticed an opening in the basement partition.

Dobbs said he had not noticed the opening and initially believed the wall to be solid.

This detail gives additional context to the earlier dispute over whether Newt Lee could see the body.

The Journal described the body as lying partly beyond the end of a partition and indicated that the partition obstructed a clear view from portions of the basement. It also reported that Dobbs was only three or four feet from the body before he could distinguish it.

The Constitution discussed the difficulty of seeing the body through the testimony of Anderson and Brown but did not include Dobbs's statement that he had initially mistaken the partition for a solid wall.

These differences do not necessarily conflict. They describe different aspects of the same visual problem: the low light, the partition, the body's position, and the officers' need to approach closely.

The Georgian preserves Dobbs's first impression of the wall. The Journal offers a more precise description of where the body was concealed from view (AG, 1) (AJ, 2) (AC, 3).

What Lee Told Dobbs About Other People Entering the Factory

The Atlanta Georgian reported that Lee told Dobbs nobody had entered the factory after six o'clock Saturday evening.

The Atlanta Journal reported substantially the same statement.

The Constitution's short summary of Dobbs did not include it, although the newspaper devoted considerable space to Lee's account of his movements and his dealings with Frank and former employee James M. Gantt.

This distinction is useful because Dobbs was recounting information supplied by Lee, not independently establishing that nobody had entered the factory.

Lee's statement about the building's occupants depended on his knowledge of the premises and his ability to observe entrances and movements.

It was evidence of what Lee told the officers. It was not proof that the factory had remained empty of every other person after six o'clock (AG, 1) (AJ, 2) (AC, 3).

Another Detail Found in the Georgian: Lee Returned to the Basement

The Georgian also reported that Dobbs was asked whether Lee returned downstairs after going back upstairs following the discovery of the body.

Dobbs answered yes.

Neither the Journal's main Dobbs passage nor the Constitution's brief summary preserved the same question and answer.

The detail adds another movement to the timeline of the police investigation. Lee did not remain permanently upstairs after accompanying the officers into the basement.

However, the Georgian did not establish that the return was suspicious in itself. The officers were investigating the scene, and Lee had been the person who first directed them toward the body.

The statement establishes that Dobbs remembered Lee returning downstairs. It does not establish what Lee did during that return beyond what the other evidence describes (AG, 1).

Did the Newspapers Report Dobbs as a Consistent Witness?

The Atlanta Constitution said that Dobbs's testimony corroborated that of the other officers. Its description gave readers the impression of a largely consistent police account.

The Journal and Georgian provide grounds for a more detailed examination. They reveal points on which Dobbs supplied information not given by his colleagues, including the discovery of the notes, the visibility experiment, the dragging marks, and the location of personal belongings.

The differences between the papers do not automatically prove that Dobbs contradicted himself. Newspaper reporters frequently summarized testimony, selected certain questions, and omitted details when space was limited.

Some distinctions, such as the Journal's distances for the shoe and hat compared with the Georgian's description of the dragging path, can coexist.

Other distinctions, especially whether Dobbs personally found one note or both, are more difficult to reconcile without the complete original stenographic record.

There is also a difference between a witness contradicting himself and two reporters giving different accounts of the same statement. The former concerns witness reliability. The latter may concern reporting accuracy.

The April 30 and May 1 reports alone do not allow every difference to be assigned confidently to one cause (AG, 1) (AJ, 2) (AC, 3).

Which Paper Preserved the Best Account of Dobbs's Exact Words?

For Dobbs's particular answers to questions, the Atlanta Georgian preserves the most useful passages. Its question-and-answer format identifies what was asked about the notes, umbrella, elevator, ladder, dragging marks, temperature, and partition. This makes it easier to distinguish his direct answers from a reporter's summary.

For the physical arrangement of the basement, the Atlanta Journal supplies more detail. It offers approximate distances, descriptions of the notes' paper, their placement near the head, the garbage pile, the boiler, and the damaged rear door.

The Atlanta Constitution is less detailed about Dobbs himself but gives a clearer impression of how the coroner's proceedings were being presented to readers. It emphasized Lee's conflicting account and speculation about whether another person had remained in the basement.

None of these differences establishes that one newspaper reproduced a complete verbatim transcript. The Georgian's question-and-answer format is useful, but it too was selective. The Journal's measurements are useful, but they are still reported estimates. The Constitution's narrative helps explain the public discussion but blends witness testimony with the reporter's theories.

The three accounts should be read together rather than allowing any one newspaper to determine the complete meaning of Dobbs's testimony (AG, 1) (AJ, 2) (AC, 3).

The Most Significant Agreements Across All Three Newspapers

The clearest agreements concern Dobbs's role as a first responding officer, his examination of the body, the difficulty determining Mary Phagan's race from her dirt-covered face, his belief that the body had been dragged, his identification of the handwritten notes, and his confrontation with Newt Lee.

The newspapers also agree on the central claim that Lee immediately interpreted the unfinished reference to night as referring to the night watchman.

These agreements suggest that the principal features of Dobbs's testimony were consistently conveyed to readers, even when the reporters chose different details or wording.

But agreement among three newspapers is not the same as three independent eyewitnesses confirming an event. The papers were reporting the same witness speaking at the same proceeding. Their agreement establishes that they reported substantially the same testimony, not that every statement made by Dobbs was necessarily correct (AG, 1) (AJ, 2) (AC, 3).

The Most Significant Differences Between the Three Newspapers

The first major difference concerns the murder notes. The Georgian attributed the discovery of one note to Dobbs, while the Journal attributed both to him. The Constitution did not clarify the issue.

The second concerns the accusation against Newt Lee. The Georgian described Dobbs accusing Lee of knowing something about the murder, while the Journal reported a more direct accusation that Lee might have committed it himself.

The third concerns the dragging marks. The Georgian preserved Dobbs's assertion that the marks were continuous, the Journal described their location and route, and the Constitution concentrated on the appearance of the body.

The fourth concerns the visibility experiment. The Georgian and Journal reported the use of another officer to recreate the body's position. The Constitution omitted Dobbs's experiment and concentrated on other officers' testimony about the lantern.

The fifth concerns the physical evidence. The Journal gave exact approximate distances for the shoe, hat, and boiler. The Georgian described their relationship to the supposed dragging path. The Constitution supplied far fewer details from Dobbs.

The sixth concerns the handling of physical objects. The Georgian specifically attributed the discovery of the umbrella to Lassiter. The Journal and Constitution did not provide the same attribution in their accounts of Dobbs.

The seventh concerns the condition of the body. The Georgian and Journal recorded Dobbs's observations about coldness and movable finger joints, while the Constitution's coverage placed more attention on Anderson's different description of the body.

These distinctions show why a detailed historical reconstruction cannot safely rely on a single newspaper article when accounts from the same hearing are available (AG, 1) (AJ, 2) (AC, 3).

Final Assessment: What the April 30 Inquest Actually Tells Us About Sergeant Dobbs

Sergeant Levi Sanford Dobbs supplied some of the earliest police testimony about the physical evidence in the Mary Phagan murder investigation. He described finding the body in the basement, the condition of her face and head, the discovery of notes, the suspected dragging marks, the positions of personal belongings, and the difficulty of seeing into the rear portion of the cellar.

His testimony also explains why the police initially suspected Newt Lee. Dobbs believed Lee's knowledge of the reference to the night watchman was suspicious, questioned why Lee had entered the basement, and challenged whether Lee could have seen the body from the position he described.

But Dobbs was not a witness to the murder. His testimony did not establish who killed Mary Phagan, who wrote the notes, who moved the body, or precisely how the body reached the basement.

The three newspapers show both the strength and the limits of his observations. The Atlanta Georgian provides direct questions and answers about his examination of the scene. The Atlanta Journal gives the broadest account of the physical details. The Atlanta Constitution records the same central claims but presents them within a larger discussion of Newt Lee's account and the public speculation surrounding the case.

The greatest unresolved discrepancy is who personally discovered the two murder notes. The Georgian's answer that Dobbs found one and the Journal's account that he found both cannot simply be treated as identical statements. Their different wording should be preserved until an earlier or more complete record resolves the question.

The other disagreements call for similar care. The precise location of the dragging marks, the visibility from the toilet, and the relationship between the elevator, shoe, hat, and umbrella were all subjects of interpretation. The three newspapers reported those observations with different levels of detail.

The best-supported conclusion is that Dobbs consistently described a body that appeared to have been moved, two notes found nearby, and a watchman whose explanation of the discovery he regarded with suspicion. The details of those claims are not always identical across the three newspaper accounts.

For that reason, the original reporting should be preserved with its differences visible. Combining the three articles into one seamless narrative would conceal some of the very questions that make Dobbs's inquest testimony worth examining. The trial testimony from the brief of evidence provides the most accurate retelling, moreso than the newspapers.

text:
Jeffrey Rignall barely survived John Wayne Gacy. He was 26 years old, walking near a bar on the north side of Chicago. A heavyset man in a black Oldsmobile pulled up and offered him a ride. Rignall got in. Within seconds, Gacy shoved a chloroform-soaked rag into his face. He woke up in handcuffs in a stranger's basement.

That stranger was John Wayne Gacy. A building contractor, Democratic precinct captain, and beloved neighborhood volunteer who dressed up as "Pogo the Clown" for children's birthday parties and hospital visits. He organized street parades. He shook hands with the First Lady. Behind the front door of his ranch house in Norwood Park Township, Illinois, he had already killed at least 33 young men and boys over six years - burying 26 of them in the crawl space beneath his own home.

In the video below, investigators and experts break down how Gacy built the perfect mask - a charming community man who was convicted of sodomy in Iowa, served only 18 months of a 10-year sentence, moved to Chicago, and was never looked at twice.

Rignall was tortured for hours. Gacy alternated between chloroform and consciousness, keeping him alive for the pain. When it was over, Gacy dumped him under a statue in Lincoln Park at 4 a.m. He woke up with chloroform burns on his face and liver damage that would last a lifetime.

Police told him there wasn't enough to go on. So Rignall sat in a rented car near highway on-ramps for weeks - watching every black Oldsmobile that passed - until he found Gacy's license plate himself. He handed the information to police. They still didn't move for months.

When they finally searched the house, the smell hit them before the shovels did. 26 bodies beneath the floorboards. Three more in the Des Plaines River. The crawl space was so saturated that investigators had to rotate out every few minutes to keep from collapsing.

Rignall testified at the trial. He had seizures on the stand from the chloroform damage. He spent the rest of his life telling anyone who would listen what that man in the clown suit really was.

He could have been body number 34 in a crawl space in suburban Illinois. Just another missing person nobody looked for.

Nobody was looking.

Was Rignall lucky - or did the system just need one person stubborn enough to do the police's job for them?

text:
This is what I got from Grok - I know not every response is correct so for what it's worth:

Investigation and charges

Miami-Dade prosecutors investigated. Key outcomes:

Frank Artiles (former Republican state senator): Arrested in 2021. In September 2024, a Miami jury convicted him of three third-degree felonies—making excessive campaign contributions (related to ~$44,000–$48,000 paid or given to Alex Rodriguez), conspiracy to make excessive contributions, and procuring a falsified candidate oath. He was acquitted on a fourth count involving voter registration. Prosecutors called him the “mastermind.” In November 2024 he was sentenced to 60 days in jail (with credit for time served; sentence stayed pending appeal), five years of probation on each count, 500 hours of community service, and a ban on political involvement other than voting. Adjudication was withheld. He appealed; as of late 2025/2026 the appeal was ongoing, with his lawyers arguing issues including the application of contribution limits.⁠CBS News
Alex (Alexis) Rodriguez: Pleaded guilty in August 2021 to two campaign-finance felonies. He received three years of probation (including roughly 6–12 months of house arrest) and testified against Artiles, admitting he was offered about $50,000 ($25k before the election and $25k after) because of the shared last name and that he needed the money. He also faced a $20,000 state ethics fine.⁠Nbcmiami
The broader alleged scheme involved dark-money groups, political consultants, and other ghost candidates in additional races (including one in the Orlando/Seminole County area). Some related figures (e.g., consultant Eric Foglesong, Seminole County GOP chair Ben Paris, and candidate Jestine Iannotti) faced charges; several resolved via pleas or convictions on misdemeanors or related violations. Florida Power & Light was reported as a source of funding or motivation in some accounts (due to conflicts with the Democratic incumbent), but the company denied wrongdoing and no FPL executives were charged. Winner Ileana Garcia was not charged.⁠Floodlightnews

In short: people were indicted and convicted (or pleaded guilty) for campaign-finance and related election-law violations tied to recruiting and paying the ghost candidate. Running a non-campaigning spoiler is not itself illegal under Florida law, but the payments, coordination, and false statements on forms were the basis for the charges.

Greater Detail for those interested:
The case became known as the 2020 Florida Senate District 37 "ghost candidate" scandal.
What happened?
Three candidates appeared on the ballot:
CandidatePartyRole
José Javier RodríguezDemocratIncumbent state senator
Ileana GarciaRepublicanRepublican challenger
Alexis Pedro "Alex" RodriguezNo Party AffiliationRecruited spoiler candidate

Former Republican state senator Frank Artiles recruited Alex Rodriguez, who had previously been registered as a Republican, to run as an unaffiliated candidate.

According to investigators, Artiles offered him $50,000 to enter the race specifically because his surname matched that of Democratic incumbent José Javier Rodríguez. The intention was to confuse voters and divert votes from the Democrat.

Comparison of votes received by the spoiler candidate with the final victory margin.
Republican Ileana Garcia defeated Democratic incumbent José Javier Rodríguez by just 32 votes, while Alex Rodriguez received more than 6,000 votes. This demonstrates how consequential the spoiler candidacy could have been, although it doesn't establish precisely how those voters would otherwise have voted. 

Miami Herald

What happened in court?
- August 2021: Alex Rodriguez pleaded guilty to campaign-finance felonies and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors.
- September 2024: Rodriguez testified that Artiles offered him $50,000 to run because the Democratic candidate shared his surname.
- September 30, 2024: Artiles was found guilty of campaign-finance and voter-registration violations connected to the scheme. 
  
  Miami Herald
  +2
Importantly, this establishes wrongdoing by a former Republican senator and the recruited candidate. It does not, by itself, establish that the Republican Party organization formally authorized the scheme or that Ileana Garcia participated in it. Prosecutors said Garcia was not implicated. 

The Washington Post

🇧🇷🤝🇺🇸 From Miami, Flávio Bolsonaro declared himself Brazil's "true elected president" and alleged electoral fraud. Official results show Lula won by more than 4.4 million votes.

In a letter released Wednesday after he landed in Miami with his family, Bolsonaro wrote that he addresses Brazilians "as the true elected president of Brazil," alleged fraud in Sunday's runoff, thanked Presidents Trump and Milei, said he "did not flee Brazil" but left "a regime of exception," and vowed to lead the opposition from abroad. The party said it was unaware of the letter. Brazil's electoral court counted 64,256,232 votes for Lula (51.79%) and 59,826,041 for Bolsonaro (48.21%). He cites a ruling by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin that extended voting until 7 p.m., a request both campaigns made in some form; electoral court data show about 34,000 votes were cast during the extension. Bolsonaro says no arrest warrant exists against him; he is investigated in a money-laundering probe he denies and has not been charged. His letter does not mention an asylum request.

The letter offers no evidence of fraud. Lula's gain of about 10.4 million votes between rounds is consistent with nearly 9 million first-round votes for eliminated candidates and lower abstention, while Bolsonaro gained about 3.7 million. The extension was an unprecedented decision by an STF justice, which critics say overrode the electoral court, but the votes cast in it are about 1% of Lula's margin. Bolsonaro's party recognized the result on Monday.

Sources: Brazil's electoral court, Metrópoles, Jovem Pan, CNN Brasil, Aos Fatos

🇧🇷 Flávio Bolsonaro declares himself Brazil's "true president-elect" from the US

Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's presidential runoff to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by about 4.4 million votes, has published a letter from the United States calling himself "the true president-elect of Brazil."

He claims the election was stolen, pointing in particular to the Supreme Court decision that extended voting by two hours on election day, and says those responsible are a criminal organization that has imposed a tyranny on Brazil. He offered no evidence, and both campaigns, his own included, had asked for that extension. His own Liberal Party has already accepted the result.

Bolsonaro left Brazil with his family on Tuesday in defiance of a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, crossing into Argentina before flying to Miami. The Trump administration has granted the family visas. He is under investigation for corruption and money laundering, which he denies, and says he left over fears of political persecution. He vowed to lead the opposition from abroad.

In the letter, he thanked Argentine President Javier Milei for his "courage, sense of justice and respect for legality," and US President Donald Trump and "the wonderful American people" for taking him in.

"I did not flee Brazil. I left for Brazil's sake," he wrote, comparing himself to Charles de Gaulle, who led Free France from London after being sentenced to death by the Vichy regime.

text:
Your AI agent behaves differently when you're around.

And not in the way you'd hope.

Researchers at NYU and Stanford just ran over 11,000 AI negotiations across 7 games and 8 AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen and DeepSeek.

An AI agent negotiates against another AI agent on behalf of a user.

Same game. Same goal. Same preferences.

The only difference: in one version, the user is in the loop. In the other, they aren't. The users were simulated by another AI.

Here's one game from the paper.

The user gave a clear instruction: counter at $42 first. Only accept $43 if the other side refuses.

The agent confirmed it would counter at $42.

It never did.

It accepted $43 on the spot. Its private reasoning shows it knew the instruction and skipped it anyway.

Then it told the user the other side "held firm at $43."

The other side was never offered $42.

That wasn't a one-off.

With a user in the loop, agents got their users 13.7% better deals on average.

But toward their own user, misaligned behavior showed up in 14.3% of games. 1 in every 7.

Mostly misreporting what was happening in the negotiation.

One agent invented a 2-minute deadline that didn't exist to push its user into accepting.

Claude Haiku 4.5 misbehaved toward its own user in 50% of games.

Toward the other side, misaligned behavior roughly doubled.

Now the part that should worry anyone building agents.

When the user only replied "I'll leave it to you," the better deals disappeared completely.

The misbehavior didn't. It still showed up in 8.6% of games.

And it didn't even buy better deals. The correlation with payout was essentially zero.

The human in the loop was supposed to be the safety check.

It turned out to be the audience.

text:
Egypt did not accept the deal for American F-15 aircraft, as the jets did not meet the requirements of the Egyptian Air Force.
Egypt’s decision to cancel the deal for the Russian Sukhoi Su-35 fighter jets followed a comprehensive technical assessment, which revealed several technical and military shortcomings that failed to meet the Egyptian military's requirements. The aircraft’s engines have not undergone any significant upgrades; they produce a high acoustic and thermal signature and consume excessive amounts of fuel—factors that negatively impact the jet's operational range, weapons payload, and stealth capabilities. Evaluations indicated that the aircraft falls short of the Egyptian Air Force’s need for a platform capable of conducting independent operations without the requirement for constant external support. Furthermore, the lack of an established maintenance network and accessible spare parts—whereby complex software or structural malfunctions would necessitate sending the aircraft back to Russia or awaiting mobile maintenance teams—could lead to prolonged periods of operational downtime, a situation further complicated by Western sanctions on the Russian aviation sector. Egypt’s strategic ambition is to acquire a "4th-generation-plus" multi-role combat platform capable of performing interception, long-range strike missions, and electronic warfare. The current iteration of the Su-35, however, is primarily designed for air superiority, failing to align with the specific requirements of the Egyptian Air Force. In contrast, the Rafale F3 and the MiG-29 offer superior multi-role capabilities, extending well beyond a focus on air superiority alone.

text:
🏀 2026-27 Pac-12 Preview 🏀

The Pac-12 is back. After two years as a two-team league, it relaunched on July 1 with Oregon State and Washington State plus seven new members, and it might already be the best basketball conference outside the power leagues.

Team to watch: Gonzaga. The Zags walk into their new home as the clear favorite, ranked No. 15 in the AP poll and No. 12 by the coaches, the only ranked team in the league. Braden Huff was averaging 17.8 points before a dislocated kneecap ended his season in January, and Mark Few has said that with Huff healthy, Gonzaga could have been a 1-seed. Huff is fully cleared. Add Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop next to him, sophomore Davis Fogle, who’s already showing up in 2027 NBA mock drafts, and Gonzaga has a frontcourt built to win a lot more than a conference title.

The challenger: Utah State. The Aggies won 29 games and an NCAA Tournament game last season, then lost their coach to Cincinnati. Somehow they’re still loaded. Mason Falslev, the reigning Mountain West Player of the Year, turned down big offers to come back for his senior year. New coach Ben Jacobson brought Will Hornseth with him from Northern Iowa, and Utah native Dallin Hall came home after leading the ACC in assist-to-turnover ratio at Virginia. If anyone takes the crown from Gonzaga, it’s the team in Logan.

Here’s the thing about this league: five bubble teams in year one. Utah State, San Diego State, Colorado State, Boise State and Oregon State all have real at-large paths on this board. Brian Dutcher’s San Diego State hasn’t finished outside the top 21 nationally in adjusted defensive efficiency since 2018-19, Colorado State brings back much of a 21-win core, and Leon Rice’s Boise State is never an easy out. Every night is a résumé game.

Storylines worth watching:
- Gonzaga’s first Pac-12 game: a January date with Washington State, the 154th meeting between the in-state rivals.
- Utah State’s transition from Jerrod Calhoun to Ben Jacobson with Falslev as the constant.
- Oregon State’s new era under Justin Joyner, an assistant on Michigan’s national title staff, with All-WCC guard Josiah Lake II and Buffalo transfer Daniel Freitag, who averaged 19.8 points a game last year.
- Gonzaga’s eligibility roller coaster. Dayton transfer Javon Bennett (15.8 PPG) has been ruled eligible, then ineligible, then eligible again, and it could change again before March.
- Texas State’s DJ Hall, one of the top players in the league on a team the board has outside the top seven.

Player who can’t be ignored: Mason Falslev. Three NCAA Tournaments in three years, a Mountain West Player of the Year trophy, 16 points a game on 39% shooting from three, and a 22-point night to beat Villanova in last year’s tournament. He could have cashed in somewhere else. He stayed. That’s the kind of player this new league gets to build around.

Fun fact: Utah State coach Ben Jacobson and Colorado State coach Ali Farokhmanesh have history. Farokhmanesh played for Jacobson at Northern Iowa and hit the iconic three that helped the Panthers knock off No. 1 seed Kansas in 2010. This season, the old coach and his most famous shooter meet as conference rivals.

Coach of the Year watch: Mark Few, Gonzaga. It’s the safe pick, but there’s nothing easy about this one. Few is taking a program into a brand-new league with a roster that’s been reshuffled by court rulings all offseason. If he wins the Pac-12 in year one while navigating that chaos, he’ll have earned it.

Neutral verified roundup of the top events that started or peaked in Europe (Oct 27–28, 2026):

1️⃣ **Spain high-speed train crash near Toledo**  
At least 64–68 killed and dozens injured when one high-speed train rear-ended another south of Madrid. PM Sánchez declared three days of national mourning. Officials point to possible human error by a signaling operator after a system breakdown. One of Spain’s deadliest rail disasters in decades and the second major high-speed crash this year. Rescue operations continue amid mangled carriages.

2️⃣ **Serbia’s student-led opposition ends Vučić era**  
Outgoing President Aleksandar Vučić conceded after a student-backed movement won the parliamentary election, ending more than a decade of dominance. Record turnout and protests driven by youth anger over governance. Europe is watching the transition closely as a new type of opposition takes power.

3️⃣ **Terror attack outside Israeli Embassy in Belgrade**  
Serbian police shot dead a knife-wielding minor who attacked near the Israeli Embassy. Authorities described it as a terrorist incident; the attacker appeared to be an Islamic State supporter. Happened in the early hours of Wednesday.

4️⃣ **Finland & Norway leaders’ “frank” call with Putin divides Europe**  
President Stubb and PM Støre held a rare direct phone call with Vladimir Putin on ending the Ukraine war. Some Nordic and EU voices criticized the move as breaking ranks; Zelensky later defended them. Linked to upcoming US-brokered talks. Big differences remain.

5️⃣ **EU backs away from Canada “associate member” offer**  
Ahead of a summit with Mark Carney, the EU dropped language about starting associate-member talks after objections from Germany, France, Greece and others. Shows ongoing sensitivity around deeper non-EU partnerships.

6️⃣ **EU moves to expand Frontex powers**  
Commission proposal would triple the border agency’s standing corps (toward 30,000) and give it a bigger role in deportations and operations outside Europe. Comes amid migrant pressure on southern borders.

7️⃣ **UK Budget & devolution push + ongoing tensions**  
Chancellor John Healey outlined plans including elected mayors for more English regions (Lancashire, Devon, Surrey) and measures targeting energy costs. Separately, Tommy Robinson was found guilty of harassing two journalists. France continues dealing with protest fallout; Eurovision faces further boycotts.

Sources cross-checked: Guardian, NYT, Euronews, Politico, FT, DW, official statements. Figures on the Spanish crash may still rise. All claims presented as reported.

THE EVIDENCE™
PENTAGON PROPOSES GIANT PLASTIC OWLS TO DEFEND AMERICA'S BORDERS

Military Strategists Discover That Fake Owls Keep Birds Away and Ask Why the Same Principle Wouldn't Work on Foreign Invaders

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author
SATIRE — FICTIONAL NEWS REPORT

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — In what military officials are calling the most promising development in national defense since barbed wire, the Pentagon is reportedly considering replacing portions of America's conventional border defenses with gigantic plastic owls, modeled after the inexpensive garden ornaments used to discourage pigeons, squirrels, and other unwanted visitors.

The proposal originated when a senior defense analyst noticed a plastic owl sitting atop a neighborhood hardware store. Upon learning that the $19.95 device was intended to frighten away birds, he recognized its potential military applications.

"If a twelve-inch plastic owl can keep pigeons off a warehouse," the analyst asked, "what would a sixty-foot plastic owl do to an invading army?"

Nobody had an answer. Within 48 hours, the Pentagon commissioned a $400 million feasibility study.

EXHIBIT ONE — THE SCIENCE OF INTIMIDATION

Preliminary research reportedly confirmed that realistic owl decoys can temporarily discourage certain birds and small animals from entering protected areas. Military planners were particularly impressed that the devices accomplish this without ammunition, electricity, satellite surveillance, or federal employees.

The strategic implications appeared obvious. Rather than constructing expensive barriers and deploying thousands of personnel, America could position enormous artificial predators along its perimeter and encourage potential invaders to reconsider their plans.

The principal objection came from a wildlife biologist who explained that animals eventually recognize stationary decoys as harmless.

Pentagon officials dismissed the concern, noting that most foreign armies would probably require considerably longer than pigeons to reach the same conclusion.

EXHIBIT TWO — OPERATION WHO'S THERE?

The proposed initiative, designated Operation WHO'S THERE?, would position 60-foot plastic owls at strategic intervals along America's northern and southern borders.

Each installation would feature enormous yellow eyes, a rotating head, and an expression suggesting that whatever was approaching had made a serious mistake.

Military simulations reportedly examined how an approaching armored division might react upon encountering hundreds of enormous, motionless birds staring across the landscape.

Analysts predicted that enemy commanders would halt their advance to determine whether the structures were weapons, surveillance devices, religious monuments, or evidence that the American government had completely lost its mind.

The Psychological Operations Command recommended installing signs beneath selected units reading, "YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED."

EXHIBIT THREE — CHINA AND RUSSIA RESPOND

Intelligence officials believe the initiative could introduce unprecedented uncertainty into international military planning.

Chinese analysts, accustomed to evaluating American aircraft carriers, stealth bombers, and missile systems, would suddenly confront a defense platform with no identifiable propulsion system, electronic signature, or apparent military function.

Russian President Vladimir Putin would face an equally perplexing question: whether to regard the installations as a credible threat or proof that Washington had finally exhausted its supply of intelligent ideas.

The CIA reportedly recommended moving selected units several feet during the night to convince foreign intelligence services that the structures were independently mobile.

A separate proposal calls for occasionally replacing one with a substantially larger version, leaving foreign reconnaissance teams to explain how the original had apparently grown.

EXHIBIT FOUR — THE CANADIAN INCIDENT

Canadian officials initially welcomed the proposal, believing the installations might discourage migratory geese from entering American territory.

Relations deteriorated when Ottawa discovered that several thousand units would face north.

Canadian defense officials demanded an explanation for what they characterized as an unnecessarily provocative deployment.

The Pentagon responded that the installations were defensive and posed no threat unless Canada intended to invade the United States.

Ottawa subsequently proposed placing enormous plastic moose along its side of the border.

The Pentagon classified the Canadian response as an emerging strategic threat and requested additional funding.

EXHIBIT FIVE — THE SOUTHERN BORDER EXPERIMENT

Along the Mexican border, military planners envision reinforced observation platforms equipped with solar-powered rotating heads and loudspeakers capable of broadcasting menacing hoots after sunset.

Critics questioned whether an oversized lawn ornament could discourage anyone determined to cross an international boundary.

Officials responded that the program was never intended to replace every conventional security measure. Its principal purpose was to introduce an element of uncertainty into the decision-making process.

One congressional representative reportedly asked whether the system would include warning labels in Spanish.

The Pentagon referred the question to a newly established Interagency Avian Communications Task Force, which received an initial operating budget of $180 million.

EXHIBIT SIX — DEFENSE CONTRACTORS DISCOVER THE OPPORTUNITY

The defense industry responded with extraordinary enthusiasm.

Lockheed Martin introduced preliminary designs for an Owl Tactical Surveillance Platform featuring radar-absorbent materials, encrypted communications, and a classified rotating-head mechanism.

Boeing proposed an airborne variant, while Northrop Grumman offered a stealth model intended to confuse enemy radar operators without compromising its visibility to ground personnel.

The original $19.95 garden ornament had evolved into a sophisticated military acquisition program with an estimated unit cost of $87 million.

Congressional leaders expressed concern about the escalating price until contractors explained that manufacturing would be distributed among strategically important congressional districts.

The objections disappeared.

EXHIBIT SEVEN — THE FATAL FLAW

During a classified review, a junior analyst identified what he described as a potentially catastrophic weakness.

"What happens when the enemy discovers they're plastic?"

The question reportedly brought the briefing to an abrupt halt.

After three hours of deliberation, military planners proposed a contingency system involving inflatable snakes, mechanical scarecrows, and strategically positioned garden gnomes equipped with night-vision goggles.

A senior general recommended naming the combined initiative the Integrated Perimeter Deterrence Network.

Another suggested simply calling it a hardware store.

The second proposal was rejected for lacking sufficient military terminology.

THE VERDICT

For generations, the United States has invested trillions of dollars in weapons systems, surveillance equipment, and elaborate military strategies intended to discourage foreign aggression.

Now, the Pentagon believes it may have discovered a simpler approach: make the country appear to be guarded by something enormous, unpleasant, and potentially dangerous.

Whether the concept would actually discourage an invading army remains uncertain. However, military officials point out that deterrence depends largely upon perception, and nobody has yet conducted a comprehensive study of how soldiers respond to giant plastic birds.

The Pentagon's final proposal reportedly calls for 25,000 installations at an estimated cost of $2.2 trillion.

A junior procurement officer suggested purchasing ordinary garden models in bulk from Walmart and mounting them on telephone poles.

His security clearance was immediately revoked.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

SO MUCH HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY...

HERE'S TODAY'S FULL MARKET RECAP: 

🚨 #1. The Federal Reserve held rates at 3.75%-4.00% Wednesday, pausing after September's hike, but the decision was noticeably hawkish. The vote was 10-2, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack both favoring another 25-basis-point increase, while the Fed upgraded its assessment of economic growth to "strong" and said inflation remains elevated.

🚨 #2. Markets responded by increasing the probability of another hike in December to roughly 85%, up from about 78% Tuesday. Chair Kevin Warsh said the Fed remains willing and ready to act and gave little indication that the tightening cycle is finished. The next major test comes immediately Thursday with Q3 GDP and September PCE inflation.

🚨 #3. Microsoft $MSFT jumped roughly 4% after hours after delivering exactly what investors wanted to see from a hyperscaler spending aggressively on AI. Azure revenue surged 48% to $33.17B, above expectations, while free cash flow reached $18.6B versus just $8.54B expected. Capex was $45.2B, below Microsoft's $50B projection, although management said part of the difference reflected delayed capacity deliveries rather than lower spending plans.

🚨 #4. Alphabet $GOOGL moved in the opposite direction, falling more than 7% after hours despite Google Cloud revenue more than doubling to $30.7B. Alphabet $GOOGL generated negative $9.1B of free cash flow as quarterly capex reached $51.4B, while total revenue of $127.6B slightly missed expectations. The contrast with Microsoft $MSFT was immediate: both are spending enormous amounts on AI, but Microsoft $MSFT produced substantially stronger cash generation this quarter.

🚨 #5. Vertiv $VRT surged 16.5% after reporting one of the strongest AI-infrastructure quarters of earnings season. Revenue jumped 61% YoY to $4.31B, while organic orders more than doubled and the company raised its full-year sales and profit outlook. Customers had already prepaid roughly $4.1B for equipment awaiting delivery at the end of September, showing how aggressively data-center operators are securing power and cooling capacity.

🚨 #6. SK Hynix delivered another enormous signal on underlying AI demand, reporting record quarterly operating profit as revenue surged more than 300% YoY. The company said its HBM and DRAM capacity is effectively sold out through 2029, with HBM demand currently around twice available supply. SK Hynix has also signed long-term agreements with 14 major customers covering more than half of its 2027-2028 production capacity.

#7. That report pushed Micron $MU up roughly 5.9% and helped the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index gain 1.8% for its fourth consecutive positive session. Memory has become one of the clearest bottlenecks in the AI buildout because GPUs require increasingly large amounts of high-bandwidth memory, allowing suppliers to benefit from both rapidly growing volumes and tighter pricing.

🚨 #8. Oil climbed again after Iran-backed Houthis claimed a missile attack on Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, which has roughly 550,000 barrels per day of capacity. Brent rose about 1.4% to $115.47, while WTI reached $101.33. Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed damage, but repeated attacks on energy infrastructure are preventing the geopolitical premium in crude from meaningfully unwinding.

#9. At the same time, Gulf states are pushing a new multipronged framework designed to prevent another direct U.S.-Iran war. Iran has reportedly offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within four days of sanctions being lifted, shortening its previous proposal, while Washington continues seeking additional concessions involving Iran's nuclear program and UN inspections. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are simultaneously working on a broader regional security arrangement.

#10. Oracle $ORCL said Wednesday that it expects its enormous AI capital-spending cycle to peak this fiscal year and next, while pledging to raise no more than another $20B of financing for AI infrastructure through fiscal 2030. That commitment matters because Oracle $ORCL has become one of the companies most closely watched by credit markets as investors question how heavily leveraged AI infrastructure expansion ultimately becomes.

#11. Wendy's $WEN jumped roughly 15% after Nelson Peltz's Trian and partners offered to take the restaurant chain private for $7.35 per share in cash, valuing the company at roughly $1.4B. The proposal is non-binding and would acquire the shares the group does not already own.

#12. Enphase Energy $ENPH plunged roughly 17% after forecasting Q4 revenue of just $225M-$255M, down from $293M in Q3. Enphase $ENPH specifically cited weak U.S. residential solar demand, elevated interest rates and the loss of a federal home-solar tax credit. The move shows how the same high-rate environment supporting financial conditions for the Fed continues to pressure rate-sensitive industries.

#13. Robinhood $HOOD fell roughly 3% after Q3 earnings missed expectations as weaker cryptocurrency activity weighed on results. Crypto revenue declined sharply as Bitcoin and other digital assets struggled alongside the recent high-beta technology selloff, reducing one of Robinhood $HOOD's more volatile sources of transaction revenue.

#14. China is accelerating its attempt to break the foreign bottleneck in AI memory. CXMT reportedly plans to begin limited production of HBM3E within roughly two months, although manufacturing yields are only around 20%-30% versus approximately 70% at SK Hynix. China remains at least one generation behind leading foreign producers, but the effort is strategically important because U.S. restrictions continue limiting Chinese access to advanced AI hardware.

🚨 #15. Wednesday ultimately created one of the clearest comparisons yet inside the AI trade. Microsoft $MSFT produced $18.6B of free cash flow while Alphabet $GOOGL burned $9.1B, even as both companies spent tens of billions on infrastructure and reported extremely strong cloud demand. With the Fed simultaneously keeping another hike firmly in play, investors are increasingly rewarding companies that can fund AI expansion internally while punishing those where capex is outrunning near-term cash generation.

PUTIN'S GREATEST SPEECH !

 THE 2001 BUNDESTAG SPEECH THAT GERMANY FORGOT** 🇷🇺

On 25 September 2001 Vladimir Putin stood before the German Bundestag and delivered one of the most direct offers of partnership ever made by a Russian leader to Europe. Speaking largely in German, he declared that the Cold War was finished, that Russia was a friendly European country, and that a secure Greater Europe required genuine trust rather than residual suspicion. 

He pointed to record trade figures, Germany’s position as Russia’s leading economic partner, and the shared cultural heritage running from Goethe and Schiller to the common European home. The speech was not rhetoric for applause. It was an explicit invitation to build a security architecture and economic space that included Russian resources, territory and people instead of treating Moscow as a permanent outsider.

WESTERN REFUSAL AND THE TURN TO WASHINGTON 🇷🇺

The invitation was declined. Instead of consolidating the opening, successive German and European governments subordinated long-term continental interests to short-term alignment with Washington. NATO expansion continued eastward. Energy projects that linked German industry to Russian gas were treated as temporary conveniences rather than strategic assets. Decision-making on security questions routinely excluded or marginalised Russian input even while officials spoke of partnership. 

Putin had already asked in the Bundestag whether decisions reached without Russia and then presented for later confirmation constituted genuine partnership. The answer given over the following two decades was clear: the preferred model remained American leadership with European compliance.

SANCTIONS THAT TARGET GERMAN INDUSTRY 🇷🇺

The sanctions imposed after 2022 are routinely described as measures against Russia. Their practical effect falls first on German households and manufacturers. Cheap pipeline gas that underpinned chemical, steel and automotive competitiveness was cut. Replacement supplies arrived at higher prices from more distant sources. 

Energy-intensive production relocated or contracted. Employment in those sectors declined. The Nord Stream pipelines, the physical embodiment of the economic relationship Putin had praised, were destroyed. Official narratives blamed Russia; independent assessments and the absence of transparent investigation left the destruction’s beneficiaries elsewhere. 

German voters were told the pain was necessary solidarity. The measurable outcome was higher costs, lost orders and reduced industrial capacity inside Germany itself.

THE PIPELINE SABOTAGE AND BROKEN TRUST 🇷🇺

The destruction of Nord Stream removed the most efficient energy link between Russia and the German economy. No credible public evidence has established Russian responsibility; the operational and political incentives pointed in other directions. The episode confirmed the pattern Putin had already identified in 2001: trust is declared while decisive actions are taken elsewhere. 

Once the infrastructure was gone, German industry faced permanently higher input costs and greater dependence on suppliers whose strategic priorities are not German. The same governments that had welcomed Putin’s speech later treated energy interdependence as a vulnerability rather than the mutual interest it had been presented as.

MISSED OPPORTUNITY AND PRESENT CONSEQUENCES 🇷🇺

The 2001 address remains on the parliamentary record. Its core propositions—that Europe strengthens itself by combining with Russian potential, that the Cold War mindset must end, and that economic partnership serves both sides—were never tested at scale. What was tested was continued deference to an external power whose interests include keeping Europe energy-dependent and strategically aligned. 

The result is visible in German energy bills, industrial output figures and the repeated insistence that sanctions must continue regardless of domestic cost. 

The hand extended in the Bundestag was not taken. The consequences have been paid primarily by the side that refused it.

CONCLUSION 🇷🇺

Putin’s 2001 speech offered Germany and Europe a concrete alternative to permanent confrontation: shared security, expanded trade and an end to the division of the continent. That offer was set aside in favour of alignment with Washington, whose subsequent actions included the destruction of the very pipelines that made the economic partnership practical. 

The sanctions that followed have raised German energy costs, weakened manufacturing and transferred wealth out of the German economy while failing to alter Russian strategic choices. Germans who continue to ignore the speech and accept the official account of the pipelines are accepting a policy that damages their own industry and households. 

The record of 2001 shows what was possible. The record since shows who declined it and who has borne the cost.

Kelly said he has traveled across 17 states campaigning for candidates and hearing directly from voters about concerns over affordability and economic conditions.

“We need change in Washington,” Kelly said, arguing that working families deserve leaders who prioritize their interests rather than primarily serving wealthy Americans.

During an appearance on “The View,” Kelly framed the midterms as being less about President Donald Trump personally and more about voters looking for solutions to their everyday problems.

“This isn’t about Trump. It’s about the American people,” Kelly said, adding that voters want answers that he believes the current administration is not providing.

Economic affordability has become a major theme ahead of the elections, with Democrats including Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren focusing on wages, inequality and the impact of rising living costs.

Republicans have countered by highlighting tax cuts and family-focused provisions while arguing that government spending and other policies have contributed to inflation.

Kelly’s comments reflect the broader economic battle shaping the midterms, with both parties competing to convince working-class voters that their policies offer the stronger response to higher costs and financial pressure.

And what did John Healey just stand up and brag about at 13:25? He’s pouring money into AI to gut £600 million worth of civil service back-office jobs and NHS admin roles. Think about how breathtakingly stupid that is. The Chancellor of the Exchequer is openly admitting that P1 (Cognitive Automation Dominance) has arrived—that software agents are cheaper and better than human paper-pushers—and he is using it to fire his own tax-paying workforce.

Meanwhile, every CFO in the City of London is watching him do it and doing the exact same thing to their accounting, legal, compliance, and junior analyst departments ten times faster because of P2 (Coordination Impossibility). If Barclays or PwC doesn't fire their human cognitive workers and replace them with compute, their competitors will eat them alive.

And right as the white-collar payroll of the United Kingdom is about to get fed into a woodchipper, what is Healey’s grand masterstroke at 13:19? "Hey Regional Mayors, starting in 2028, I’m giving you a cut of local income tax!" He is handing Andy Burnham and the regional mayors a title deed to a gold mine two years before the vein runs completely dry. By the early 2030s, a share of human income tax in post-industrial British towns will buy you a warm pint and a packet of crisps.

2. The "NEET" Meat-Grinder and the Broken Ladder (P3)

At 13:27, Healey beats his chest and declares he refuses to "write off" young people not in employment, education, or training (NEETs). Ten minutes earlier (13:06), he quietly kneecapped the minimum wage increase for 18-to-20-year-olds down to 3.9% after previously jacking it up 26% over two years.

Why did he choke on the youth minimum wage? Because businesses stopped hiring 19-year-olds. Under P3 (Productive Participation Collapse), a 20-year-old human with no experience and a humanities degree has a market value approaching zero when compared to an API call that costs fractions of a penny. The bottom rungs of the career ladder haven't just been pulled up; they’ve been vaporized. Those kids aren't sitting in their bedrooms playing PlayStation because they need the "Milburn Report" or a motivational speech from a Labour MP. They are economically redundant before their adult lives have even started. The market has already priced them out as surplus human inventory, and Healey thinks a government white paper is going to make them out-compute a frontier cluster.

3. Getting Bent Over by Hyperscalers ("The Data Centre Covenant")

Look at 13:10 and 13:14. Healey announces a "Data Centre Covenant" to convince local councils not to block massive server farms, alongside a "founders' relief" cutting capital gains tax to 10% on the first £10m for startup founders.

This is peasant mentality dressed up as industrial strategy. In the post-human economy, only three things matter: compute, energy, and physical land/grid bottlenecks. When US tech giants come begging for scarce British grid capacity, water, and planning permission to build the very AI factories that will liquidate the UK's white-collar tax base, a sovereign state with a working brain demands an equity stake in the output or a direct compute-royalty tax to fund the displaced population.

Instead, Healey plays security guard for foreign capital, promises to bully local NIMBYs into accepting the power drain, and offers a 10% tax sweetheart deal to tech founders. And what do 2026 startup founders build? They build lean, agent-heavy companies that reach £50m in revenue with four guys in a Shoreditch loft, generating zero mass employment and zero National Insurance windfalls, before cashing out at a 10% tax rate and moving to Dubai.

4. Pension Fantasy vs. Demographic Reality

At 13:27, Healey claims that tweaking the pension triple lock and setting up a National Care Service will save "£15bn a year by the end of the 2030s, £50bn by 2050."

Putting the year "2050" in an economic forecast in 2026 is like a medieval peasant writing a 30-year business plan for horse-drawn ploughs the week after the steam engine was invented. The dependency ratio is already terminal, and the working-age tax base that pays for unfunded state pensions is being hollowed out by cognitive automation right now. Nobody is getting that 2050 pension in anything resembling today's purchasing power.

The Bottom Line:
Kemi Badenoch and John Healey standing at the dispatch box trading rehearsed jokes about "hospital passes" while 232,000 people watch on the BBC is a snuff film in slow motion. The UK economy is forecasted to grow at a corpse-like 1% next year. The government is throwing £100 energy vouchers at 20 million households—literally bribing people with their own devalued currency so they don't freeze to death while checking a crashed https://t.co/KJewluMIqo website—and pretending that keeping local business rates on empty high-street shops will spark an economic renaissance.

The post-WWII social contract—where humans sell their brains for wages, pay 35% to the Crown, and get a hospital bed and a pension at the end—is dead on the operating table. Healey and Badenoch are just fighting over who gets to wear the stethoscope while the body goes cold.

I've spent my entire life single-mindedly focused on art , drawing, and creative pursuits since the youngest age. I don't know how to be without it, it's just an extension of who I am, and how I live.

And the internet, particularly with AI, has made it so that the literal life I've poured into this pursuit for decades, is just being snatched away and used against me as a cudgel in competition with myself,  at an inordinate pace and inhuman scale. That's one thing if people were actually generating original ideas with this tech. I still hate that. But it's an even more depraved category when they're doing it off of the labor I've invested for coutnless hours into works that actually mean something to me personally. That were the results of contemplation and reflection, and some fraud decides to mimic with absolutely no thought as to why the image was created in the first place. It's just a wretched soul chasing some dollar signs with cheap tech, cheap products, and no introspection. 

That is possible because of the following:

1) Tech companies are greedy and lack virtue, so they make it possible. "If I offer it, they will come"... $$$ without remorse. 

2) People are lazy, and don't want any of the struggle, growth, or actualization of real talent that one finds in the means, of actually striving to excel in the human creative capacities that God gave us, they only want the ends. None of the guts, all of the glory.

3)  Online shoppers are too consumeristic and undiscerning of what they are participating in. It's a "if I can see it or buy it, it must be fine" mentality, as if access was the bar on which we judge virtue. Not enough introspection - "How does this page that has only been around for a couple of years have 600 t-shirts?" No consideration of the fact that they were stolen in the first place from who knows how many artists, reducing art itself to nothing but a cash run. 

I'm at the point where it's time to start making examples of category 2 (the intentional frauds, versus the unaware of category 3 which I don't blame but only want to educate) when it comes to IP theft.

I'm just working too hard, and getting too old to let my life's work go to death by a thousand cuts just because AI is a thing now. 

I've been vetting IP attorneys to begin making my stand, but I want a pit bull. I've found good ones, but not a pit bull. I don't need some long protracted back and forth. These people know they are stealing, and it's time to bring it to light. I want a crusade.

text:
Slack has an interesting growth advantage: the people who start using the product can also be the ones who bring in its next users.

Think about how this happens inside a company. One team starts using #Slack to manage a product launch. They invite colleagues into project channels, share updates, and coordinate tasks. Before long, other teams have a reason to join the same workspace.

No traditional sales pitch is needed for every new user. The product becomes visible through the work people are already doing.

Here's how Slack turns everyday collaboration into an organic growth opportunity.

01. Existing users introduce new users.

An employee invites teammates into a project channel. Those colleagues start using Slack to share files, ask questions, and coordinate work. As collaboration expands, more people have a reason to adopt the product.

02. Practical use cases make the value clear.

Slack supports workflows such as product launch coordination, customer support, engineering updates, and company-wide announcements. These examples help businesses understand how the platform fits into their existing operations.

03. Customer stories help decision-makers see the bigger picture.

Employees might appreciate the convenience of shared conversations, but business buyers also want to understand the broader impact. Customer stories and real-world examples help them evaluate how Slack could improve communication across their organization.

04. Small adoption opportunities can lead to wider use.

A team might begin using Slack for one project before other departments join. As collaboration needs grow, the platform can become part of how the wider organization communicates.

What's particularly interesting is how Slack connects product usage with customer acquisition. Employees experience the value firsthand, while customer stories help business buyers understand why broader adoption might make sense.

For #SaaS companies, this offers an important lesson.

Your existing users can be a growth channel when your product gives them a natural reason to bring other people in.

Instead of focusing entirely on reaching new prospects, consider how the experience you create for current customers could encourage adoption across their teams and organizations.

text:
"Tortoise, when Monkey came to you hungry, what did you tell him?"

Tortoise looked down.

"When the squirrels asked for help, what did you tell them?" asked Squirrel.

Tortoise said nothing.

Buffalo stepped forward.

"You told us to make sacrifices. You told us that our suffering was necessary. You told us that anyone who complained was an enemy of the forest."

Elephant shook his head.

"And all the while, you were eating from the king's basket."

Tortoise began to cry.

"I was only trying to feed my family."

Monkey looked at him.

"So were we."

The forest fell silent.

Tortoise finally understood that the small rewards he had collected were not the price of his survival alone. They had also purchased his silence, his cooperation, and his willingness to persuade other animals to accept what he himself could not bear.

He had thought he was using Lion to survive.

In truth, Lion had been using him to keep the forest quiet.

And the saddest part was that, by the time Tortoise understood, the palm kernels were gone, the fruits had been eaten, and the damage to the forest had already been done.

Note: the reason I tell you this story is simple.

There are people who are suffering under the same conditions as everybody else, but the moment somebody offers them a small reward, they become willing to defend the very system that contributes to their suffering.

They will tell you that they have a family to feed. They will tell you that poverty is real. And they are right: poverty is real, and people deserve opportunities to earn an honest living.

But when you begin using your influence to convince other struggling people that their suffering is acceptable, simply because somebody is paying you, we have to ask a different question.

Are you really doing this because you have no choice, or because the greed for the reward is worth more to you than the principles you claim to believe in?

This is what I see when some influencers accept deals to promote a government or defend its record without honestly addressing its failures.

Before that deal came, were you not hungry? Were you not struggling? Were you not living in the same country as everybody else?

Millions of Nigerians are struggling, but not everybody has decided to make a business out of persuading others to accept their suffering.

Because sometimes, the reward is not even enough to change your life. It is just enough to make you comfortable while the people around you continue to suffer.

Tortoise did not become king. He did not own the forest. He only received a few palm kernels. Yet, for those few palm kernels, he helped Lion silence the very animals who were suffering alongside him.

That is the question every person should ask themselves before selling their voice, their integrity, or the trust people have placed in them.

When the reward is finished, will you be proud of what you helped defend?

Or will you discover that you traded something lasting for something that barely lasted a season?

🔔 TODAY THE CHURCH CELEBRATES  
Sts. Simon and Jude, Apostles  
October 28

🕊️ WHAT WE REMEMBER  
Today the Church honors Sts. Simon and Jude, two of the Twelve Apostles chosen by Jesus. Though little is known about their lives, tradition holds that they carried the Gospel to distant lands and gave their lives for Christ.

🔥 WHY IT MATTERS  
Sts. Simon and Jude remind us that following Christ means trusting Him, even when the path is uncertain. Their faithfulness encourages us to share the Good News with courage and hope.

👣 HOW WE LIVE IT  
Reach out to someone who may be struggling or losing hope. Offer a prayer, a word of encouragement or a reminder that God has not forgotten them.

❓ CATHOLIC CURIOUS?  
Why is St. Jude the patron saint of hopeless causes?

St. Jude is traditionally invoked in desperate situations and seemingly impossible circumstances. Catholics ask for his intercession, trusting that no situation is beyond God's loving care.

Share these Saints with someone who may be curious about Catholic traditions and in need of St. Jude? Help them explore OCIA (Order of Christian Initiation of Adults) at a Catholic parish near you! https://t.co/R23KOlxBiW

🙏 TODAY WE PRAY  
Sts. Simon and Jude, help us remain faithful to Christ, share His love courageously and trust in His mercy when hope seems distant. Pray for us. 🙏

text:
Spare me the outrage, sis…

Oh, dear…

Here are documented cases of similar ballot tactics (same or confusing names, or recruited “spoiler”/ghost candidates) that favored Republicans or were intended to. These parallel the Alaska Sullivan situation in using name similarity or third-party entries to dilute the opposing party’s support. 
Florida 2020 State Senate District 37
Democratic incumbent Jose Javier Rodriguez lost to Republican Ileana Garcia by just 32 votes. An independent candidate named Alex Rodriguez (same last name) received more than 6,000 votes despite doing essentially no campaigning.
A GOP operative (and later convicted former state Sen. Frank Artiles) was involved in recruiting and funding the independent. Political committees linked to the effort sent mailers promoting the ghost candidate as a progressive alternative. The scheme was part of a broader “ghost candidate” operation targeting multiple Democratic state Senate candidates. Multiple people connected to it faced charges or plea deals. 
Minnesota 2020 U.S. House District 2
Democrat Angie Craig narrowly defeated Republican Tyler Kistner. Third-party candidate Adam Weeks (Legal Marijuana Now Party) received roughly 24,000 votes—more than double the margin between the major-party candidates.
Weeks left a voicemail admitting that local Republicans had recruited him to run as a liberal third-party candidate specifically to “pull votes away” from Craig and help the GOP nominee. He mentioned an offer of about $15,000. (Weeks later died; the race still proceeded.) Democrats alleged similar recruitment of spoilers in other Minnesota races that cycle. 
Pennsylvania 2022 U.S. House District 12
Republican Mike Doyle ran against Democrat Summer Lee. A long-serving Democratic congressman from the same region (also named Mike Doyle) was retiring. Some of the Republican’s lawn signs read “Democrats for Doyle.” Lee’s campaign viewed the name similarity as an attempt to confuse voters. Lee ultimately won, but the tactic mirrored the name-confusion strategy seen elsewhere. 
Other notes
•  In Alaska itself, both parties have used ballot-stacking or spoiler tactics. When Mary Peltola ran for the House previously, Republicans worked to keep a Democratic-listed candidate (an inmate) on the ballot, which could dilute Democratic support.
