text:
Over the past few months, I’ve had folks—most often complete strangers—reach out and ask me some version of the following question:

“This Democratic candidate took an anti-trans position. Should I still vote for them?”

Folks, I acknowledge that you want to be thoughtful about all this. I appreciate that you want to get a trans person’s opinion. I understand that y’all take allyship seriously, and I’m grateful for that. I truly am.

Fortunately for all of us, the moral and ethical calculus here are very simple.

An election cycle is split into two parts: the primary season and the general election.

The primaries are over. A lot of candidates across the political spectrum stepped up, offered their ideas, and pitched the voters. The ballots were cast, and some of those candidates won and most of those candidates lost.

We are now in the general election portion of the cycle, and almost every U.S. Senate and U.S. House race offers a straightforward choice: there is a Republican and there is a Democrat.

One of those two candidates will win, and ONLY one of those two will win.

There is no third potential outcome.

On the Republican side, you have a political party led by a sociopathic pedophile who has dismantled critical federal agencies, gutted health care for tens of millions of American working class families, engaged in widespread corruption that would make Richard Nixon blush with secondhand embarrassment, hobbled our economy with deeply asinine and self-serving financial incompetence, alienated all of our longstanding diplomatic relationships with other countries, involved us in an array of irresponsible and dangerous and unnecessary military actions, lost a stupid and pointless war with the theocratic, human rights quagmire that is the Iranian government, made it clear he’s oblivious to the consequences of data centers and other unaccountable bullshit carried out by AI companies, raised our gas prices, raised our food prices, raised our housing costs, raised our childcare costs, raised our health care costs, and continues to cover-up his role in a massive child sex trafficking operation by keeping millions of files hidden from the public.

On the Democratic side, you have a party led by national leaders who are somewhat uninspiring but nevertheless deeply committed to stopping all the above and building a brighter future for working class families in our country.

On the Republican side, you have an entire political party being held hostage—some of them more than likely through blackmail—to the fleeting whims and temper tantrums and probable dementia of the aforementioned sociopathic pedophile.

On the Democratic side, you have a party that is often at each other’s throats but also the furthest thing from a cult, which, ironically, is a sign of very good health and embodying enduring faith in the democratic (small d) process.

You ask me for my thoughts on anti-trans ads or comments put out by Democratic candidates and whether you should still vote for them against Republicans?

Yes. Of course you should vote for them.

Not only should you vote for them but you should get your family and your friends and your neighbors and your colleagues and your mailman and the door-to-door salesperson currently waiting patiently on your front porch to vote for them.

For example, I am not a fan of Congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez. I do not like her. I think she’s very cynical. Among other things, she has taken unnecessary votes that harmed trans service members and veterans and our families in order to pander to moderates.

Guess what? Her Republican opponent is 10x worse for trans rights. If I lived in her congressional district—WA-03—I would vote for her without hesitation and get everyone I know to vote for her, too. Because I’m not an idiot.

Or take James Talarico, who is running for the U.S. Senate in my beloved home state of Texas. In an interview with Fox News, he stated his conditional opposition to trans youth in sports and pandered to anti-trans social conservatives about opposing already non-existent surgeries for trans youth.

Guess what? His Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, is easily 100x worse for the trans community. Paxton is an anti-trans exterminationist. He does not want the trans community to exist. He would gladly support criminalizing the existence of trans people. He has spent the past four years using his position in the state government to harass and terrorize the parents of trans youth.

Not only am I supporting James Talarico, but if God opened up the clouds above and offered me a deal of exchanging my left arm for the guarantee of Mr. Talarico beating Paxton, I would agree to the deal in a heartbeat.

This is not a complicated decision.

I feel the exact same way about Dr. Annie Andrews, who has spent her career serving working class families in South Carolina and is now tantalizingly close to flipping that U.S. Senate seat currently held by Darline Graham, sister of the late Lindsey Graham.

Do I care that Dr. Andrews put out an ad opposing trans youth in sports and already non-existent surgeries for trans youth? No, I do not care. I do not give a shit.

Because Darline Graham has made anti-trans extermination her entire political brand and seems to spend every waking moment obsessed with how to make the lives of trans people miserable, not the least due in part to her lack of any policy ideas to help working class families in South Carolina and needing a scapegoat to conceal her own strident mediocrity.

You’re goddamn right I support Dr. Andrews for that U.S. Senate seat. I would gladly vote for her if I lived there, and I’d be canvassing every day in support of her, too.

This is not complicated.

Pick any U.S. Senate race and U.S. House race, and my opinion is gonna be the same every damn time. Because the primaries are over, this is the general election, and there are only two choices: either an imperfect Democrat with whom I disagree on a handful of issues or a Republican currently subscribed to a death cult that wants people like me to cease existing entirely.

Some of y’all will bring up that there are trans people who disagree with me. I’m sure there are. That’s their prerogative. They have a constitutional right to express their opinion that certain Democratic candidates should be boycotted. We do, after all, for the moment, live in a free country.

But they’re wrong. They’re dead wrong. They could not be more wrong. Their curious sense of aimless and flailing political strategy honestly makes me wonder if they have a shred of survival instinct in their bones.

Again: this is not complicated. If you care about the future of trans equality in this country, you will march your happy ass to your polling location and fill in the bubble next to every name on that ballot with a (D) next to the name.

Then you will make sure your family and friends and neighbors and colleagues and mailman and door-to-door salesperson still waiting on the front porch have all done the same.

The past two years are all the proof you need that sitting out an election because the better candidate happens to not be perfectly to your liking is completely stupid and self-destructive.

On Election Night, I am going to celebrate Democrats taking back Congress and saving democracy from the anti-trans fascists of the GOP. I will sleep-in the next morning. Then, I will wake up and get to work being an insufferable pain-in-the-ass on the importance of trans equality for the Democrats who were just elected.

God love democracy.

Do not complicate an easy decision. Go vote for Democrats.

text:
Fastbeak — Personal Context, Mediterranean Perspective & Lebanese Armed Forces Modernization

Personal Encounters and Regional Relationships
My direct personal exposure to Israelis, Lebanese, and Palestinians has been relatively limited. Over my lifetime, I have met approximately three Israelis, two Lebanese individuals, and four Palestinians. Two of the Israelis were individuals I encountered while hiking, while the third was an Israeli woman selling Dead Sea mineral skincare products in the early 2010s. At the time, I privately wondered whether her business might have had an intelligence-related purpose, although this was an unsubstantiated personal suspicion rather than a factual allegation. In practice, I found her to be so extraordinarily innocent, hardworking, and charming, that I ultimately purchased the products she was selling. I also recall that her boyfriend was serving in the Israel Defense Forces, which prompted some curiosity about how they maintained a long-distance relationship while she worked in the United States, rather than any Israel or Palestinian side Military or Political issues or Israeli-Iranian issues, as people can have a genuine conversation at times concerning the maintenance of long-distance relationships as normal people. Unless in a 1B Muslim population there's 10 people who go up on exposed tracks, whereas in the Jewish community it appears to be tens of thousands. In the case there's a 1B population producing 10 people, at times, the division of labor becomes complex when those 10 individuals have to screen fronts managed by tens of thousands of hard working others. So if an Israeli Venture Capitalist exists, his IQ can be focused on those Israeli-Startup Investments while practically another Male Israeli tackles the issues concerning Israeli Security in the wake of these Gaza, Lebanon, and Iranian conflicts. 

In the event there's limited contributors, people such as myself have no choice but to increase coverage for time periods now and then to see issues properly resolved.

Beyond that encounter, I have had no meaningful personal connection to Israeli military or intelligence institutions.

My experiences with Lebanese, Palestinian, and Iranian individuals have similarly been personal rather than political. I have previously dated Lebanese and Palestinian women, as well as Iranian women. These relationships have contributed to my appreciation for the people and cultures of the broader region without creating any particular political obligation or national allegiance. I generally prefer not to pursue social relationships with Lebanese, Palestinian, or Iranian men, although this is a personal preference rather than a restriction on professional or commercial engagement. I remain comfortable maintaining respectful business relationships with individuals of any nationality.

Why I Like the Mediterranean
My appreciation for the Mediterranean is rooted primarily in its geography, climate, culture, history, and quality of life rather than its political disputes. The region combines extraordinary coastlines, mountain landscapes, historic cities, distinctive architecture, excellent food, and a social environment shaped by centuries of trade, migration, and cultural exchange. Lebanon in particular represents an attractive intersection of Mediterranean coastal life, mountainous geography, urban sophistication, hospitality, and entrepreneurial potential. The broader Mediterranean also offers opportunities across tourism, logistics, renewable energy, technology, infrastructure, finance, and commercial development.

As a Pakistani, I recognize the historical, religious, and political significance of the region without considering myself personally obligated to inherit or resolve its longstanding conflicts. I appreciate the Mediterranean on my own terms and distinguish my personal interest in its people, landscapes, and commercial opportunities from the political positions of individual governments. I do not require universal agreement with my perspectives, nor do I consider political alignment a prerequisite for productive relationships. My preference is for practical, mutually beneficial engagement that allows individuals and businesses to develop relationships independently of regional political disputes.

Lebanese Armed Forces Modernization — Strategic Context
Separately from my personal experiences, the proposed modernization of the Lebanese Armed Forces represents a hypothetical security framework developed in the context of a prospective agreement involving Iranian nuclear de-enrichment, expanded International Atomic Energy Agency inspections, and the reduction of regional nuclear proliferation risks. The underlying proposition is that Iran could accept substantial and verifiable nuclear restrictions in exchange for a broader regional security arrangement that preserves legitimate state-to-state defense and economic relationships.

Under this framework, Iran would commit to reducing uranium enrichment to an agreed peaceful level, potentially 3.67%, for a period of up to 20 years, while addressing its existing highly enriched uranium stockpile through independently verified down-blending, removal, or other agreed disposition mechanisms. The previously discussed estimate of material potentially sufficient for seven to ten nuclear weapons should be treated as a hypothetical planning assumption rather than a verified weapons inventory. Expanded IAEA monitoring would provide international visibility into Iran's nuclear activities and establish a basis for reciprocal sanctions relief and regional security commitments.

A Modern Lebanese Armed Forces Supported by France and Iran
The corresponding Lebanese defense proposal would establish a modern, technologically advanced, and institutionally independent Lebanese Armed Forces, supported through lawful state-to-state relationships with France and Iran. In this hypothetical arrangement, Lebanon would maintain an annual defense budget of approximately $6 billion for 20 years, financed through proposed annual contributions of $2 billion each from Lebanon, Iran, and France. These contributions are conceptual and would require sovereign approval, legal authorization, and negotiated financing agreements.

The LAF modernization program would prioritize integrated command-and-control infrastructure, professional ground forces, national airspace surveillance, layered defensive systems, maritime security, unmanned reconnaissance, cybersecurity, electronic resilience, secure communications, and military logistics. French participation could provide advanced institutional training, aviation support, naval capabilities, military engineering, and command infrastructure, while Iranian participation could provide unmanned systems, surveillance technologies, electronics, maintenance capabilities, and selected defensive equipment. All procurement would remain under Lebanese sovereign authority and would be subject to applicable sanctions, export controls, and international legal requirements.

The objective would not be to reproduce the full military capabilities of Israel, but rather to establish a credible Lebanese national defense institution capable of monitoring territorial violations, protecting critical infrastructure, responding to incursions, and sustaining military and governmental operations during periods of regional instability.
Israel's Strategic Considerations
From Israel's perspective, the principal benefit of the arrangement would be the verifiable reduction of Iran's potential nuclear weapons capability. A durable Iranian commitment to reduced enrichment, enhanced inspections, and stockpile disposition could address a significant Israeli national security concern.

In parallel, the emergence of a better-funded and more capable Lebanese Armed Forces could require Israel to reassess its security planning along its northern border. A stronger Lebanese state military might increase the resources Israel allocates to border surveillance, intelligence assessment, defensive readiness, and contingency planning. However, this effect would not be automatic, and a stronger LAF could also support stability by establishing clearer state responsibility for border security and reducing the role of non-state armed organizations.

For Iran, the proposed benefit would be that nuclear concessions occur within a broader security settlement rather than in isolation. Iran would retain a prospective lawful defense-industrial and commercial relationship with Lebanon, while France would provide diplomatic mediation, institutional support, and an additional channel for regional de-escalation.
Strategic Conclusion
The Fastbeak proposal connects two otherwise distinct objectives: reducing the risk associated with Iran's nuclear program and strengthening Lebanon's capacity to exercise sovereign control over its territory. A modern Lebanese Armed Forces, supported by France and Iran through transparent state-level arrangements, could contribute to a more sustainable regional security structure if accompanied by credible verification, international legal compliance, and reciprocal commitments against escalation.

My interest in this hypothetical framework should not be confused with personal political allegiance to Lebanon, Iran, Israel, or Palestine. My appreciation for the Mediterranean remains grounded in its people, geography, culture, and economic potential. The LAF modernization concept is a separate strategic exercise examining whether conventional state-building, nuclear risk reduction, and diplomatic accommodation could offer a more durable alternative to recurring regional military confrontation.

text:
Two minutes. That is how long an Arkansas jury took in November 1919 to sentence a sharecropper named William Wordlaw to die in the electric chair, and what he had done was join a union that asked landlords for a written statement of what their own cotton had earned. Wordlaw had made sixteen bales that year at two hundred and twenty-five dollars a bale, three thousand six hundred dollars in all, and he never saw a dollar of it, and the only reason anybody has that figure is that Ida B. Wells-Barnett talked her way into the penitentiary and asked him. He got out in 1923 and the record loses him completely after that, so if you want to know how this one ended, there is nobody who can tell you.

What Phillips County said about that union went out to the Helena World on the seventh of October, 1919, and it was built to be repeated.

It said the trouble in Phillips County was not a race riot. It said it was a deliberately planned insurrection, directed by an organization called the Progressive Farmers and Household Union of America, and that the union existed to band Black people together for the killing of white people.

The man who said it was E. M. Allen, a planter and real estate developer who had come down from the North in 1906 to make money and had made it. He was not a sheriff, a judge, or a coroner.

He was the spokesman, and by the time he spoke, the killing had been over for four days.

That sentence is the reason most Americans have never heard of Elaine. It held for the better part of eighty years, and it is still the shape of the story in some rooms in that county.

What the union had actually been asking for was a statement of account. Itemized, on paper.

That is the whole thing. That is what the men at Hoop Spur were organizing to get, and it is the thing nobody in Phillips County would put in their hands.

Sharecroppers in the Arkansas Delta were settled with once a year, after the crop came in. The planter weighed the cotton, the planter sold the cotton, the planter kept the books, and the planter announced at the end of it what was left over for the family that had grown it.

The family bought its seed, its meal, its shoes and its medicine at the plantation store on credit against that settlement, at prices the store set. Nobody audited any of it.

A sharecropper who asked to see the arithmetic was told the number and sent home. A sharecropper who kept asking could be run off the place, and there was an unwritten rule across the Delta that a Black tenant did not leave while a debt was on the books.

Cotton had gone from about eleven cents a pound in 1915 to about forty cents in 1919. For the first time in living memory there was real money in the fields, and the men working those fields could not find out how much of it was theirs.

In the fall of 1918, at his office in Little Rock, a white attorney named Ulysses S. Bratton began hearing from them. A man called Carter had worked ninety acres and watched his landlord take the entire crop and his possessions with it.

A farmer from Ratio told Bratton that the plantation manager there would not give the sharecroppers an itemized account for their cotton. Another described a landlord holding out to starve people into selling at his price.

Bratton took the work. He was hired to sue for the men's share of the 1919 crop, and what that meant in practice was forcing planters to produce, in court, the pages they had refused to produce in the settlement room.

The union that hired him had been put together by Robert L. Hill, a Black tenant farmer from Winchester with no organizing experience and a great deal of nerve. He told men to go out and each bring twenty-five more, and by that autumn there were seven lodges in Phillips County.

The Hoop Spur lodge kept officers the way any lodge does. Jim Miller was its president.

Ed Ware was its secretary, which is to say Ed Ware was the man who kept the union's written records in a county where written records were the whole argument.

Ed Ware had already refused to sell his own cotton for less than he thought it was worth. He had been threatened for it, up to and including talk of a rope.

By the last week of September he was thinking about quitting.

On the night of Tuesday, the thirtieth of September, about a hundred people came to a small Baptist church at Hoop Spur, three miles north of the town of Elaine. It was the lodge's third meeting.

They lit three lamps inside. The wooden benches filled fast.

Sallie Giles arrived around eight with her sons Albert and Milligan. Paul Hall was there, and Joe Knox, who people called Preacher, and Frank Moore with his wife.

Jim Miller and his wife Cleola came last, in a horse and buggy. Ed Ware never came at all.

Outside in the dark, armed men from the lodge stood watch along the road, because meetings like this one had been broken up before and listened in on before. One of them, waiting, said out loud that the whites were going to kill them.

Inside, the meeting opened with a prayer, the way all their meetings opened.

Around eleven o'clock a car stopped in front of the church. Three men were in it: W. A. Adkins, a white security officer for the Missouri Pacific Railroad, Charles Pratt, a white Phillips County deputy sheriff, and a Black trusty named Kid Collins.

There was a firefight in front of the church. Who fired first has never been settled and the accounts flatly contradict each other.

Adkins was killed. Pratt was wounded.

Collins was untouched, and he walked to a store and got on a telephone to Helena.

By morning the county was moving. The sheriff sent a posse, and the Helena American Legion post sent volunteers, some of them veterans lately home from France.

Word went out along both sides of the Mississippi River that Black people in Phillips County were fighting back. Between six hundred and a thousand armed white men came in from outside the county to hunt them.

They went through the Hoop Spur settlements, went into the houses of union members and carried out what was in them. Families ran into the canebrakes and the woods and stayed there.

The Arkansas Gazette reported the next day that at least fifteen bodies were lying in the streets and outskirts of Elaine, with more expected in the woods. A Memphis Press reporter watched men fire into corpses already lying on the road as they rode out of Helena.

The men on those roads were not being sorted by whether they had joined anything. Four brothers named Johnston were coming back from a squirrel hunt and had nothing to do with the union.

Two of them were doctors, one ran a car dealership in Helena, and the youngest, Leroy, had come home the year before from France and the regiment the world now calls the Harlem Hellfighters.

A white man they took for a friend warned them off the road and told them to catch the train instead. A posse stopped that train at Elaine, put them in handcuffs and into the back of a car, and they were killed and left on the roadside, on the first or the second of October depending on which account you read.

Leroy Johnston's Army service record turned out to have been deliberately altered. His family did not receive his Purple Heart until 2018.

On the morning of the second of October, 1919, the troop train came in from Camp Pike with more than five hundred soldiers and twelve machine guns, and Governor Charles Hillman Brough rode down with them. Colonel Isaac Jenks disarmed the town.

The mobs went home. The soldiers put several hundred Black people into stockades, where they were held until a white employer came to vouch for them by name.

Some were tortured there. Then they were moved to the jail in Helena, and the torture continued in the jail.

Two hundred and eighty-five people went into a building with room for forty-eight.

Two white men who did it later swore to it. H. F. Smiddy and T. K. Jones, both of whom had testified for the prosecution, gave sworn affidavits in 1921 admitting they had tortured prisoners in that jail to produce testimony, and naming other men who had done the same.

Ida B. Wells-Barnett got the rest of it directly from the men themselves. They told her they had been beaten and left for dead, given electric shocks, and drugged, all of it aimed at making them confess to a plot to kill white people.

Seven men in Helena appointed themselves to explain all of it while the jail was still full. The Committee of Seven was made up of officials, planters, and businessmen, and it had no legal authority whatsoever.

Governor Brough met them, gave them his blessing, and went back to Little Rock the next day. What he took away in exchange was their promise that there would be no lynchings in Phillips County.

He then told a press conference that the situation had been well handled, that there was no danger of lynching, and that the white citizens of the county deserved praise. Four days later the committee announced its finding, which was the insurrection, and E. M. Allen took it to the newspaper.

That promise cost the county nothing. It had agreed not to hang men from trees, and in return it was left alone to do the same work indoors, on paper, with a judge present.

On the twenty-seventh of October the grand jury met. By the thirty-first it had charged a hundred and twenty-two Black people with crimes ranging from nightriding to murder.

The trials opened on the third of November in front of Circuit Judge J. M. Jackson, with troops outside the courthouse to guarantee that nobody was lynched. Jackson appointed local white attorneys to defend the men.

Jacob Fink, appointed to represent Frank Hicks, told the jury outright that he had not interviewed a single witness. He asked for no change of venue and challenged no juror, taking the first twelve men called.

Frank Hicks was convicted of murder. The jury was out eight minutes.

That same day a fresh jury convicted Frank Moore, Ed Hicks, Joe Knox, Ed Coleman and Paul Hall of aiding and abetting the same killing, though there was no evidence that Coleman or Hall had anything to do with it. All of them got death.

The next day Alf Banks Jr. and John Martin, two of the men who had stood guard on the road outside the church, were convicted. The jury was out nine minutes.

William Wordlaw, another of the guards outside the church, was convicted the same day. The jury was out less than two minutes.

Wordlaw was twenty-two years old and farmed sixteen acres for a lumber company at Wabash. He told them he had been unarmed that night, and that after the shooting he had helped move women and children into the woods.

Wordlaw had made sixteen bales of cotton that season, worth two hundred and twenty-five dollars a bale, three thousand six hundred dollars in all, and he never saw the money. That is the only itemized statement in this entire story that anybody ever managed to write down.

It exists because Ida B. Wells-Barnett asked him, which is a thing nobody with any authority in Arkansas ever did. What became of William Wordlaw after he got out of prison is not known.

In that same first week of November, sixty-five other men took hurried pleas rather than face a jury of that kind, and drew sentences of up to twenty-one years.

Ed Ware, the secretary, was caught and tried last, on the seventeenth of November. The state's case against him rested on one man, Suggs Bondsman, who said he had overheard Ware and others naming planters to be killed.

That testimony was the only evidence of any plot introduced in any of these trials. Nobody cross-examined him.

When Scipio Africanus Jones finally did cross-examine him six months later, Bondsman could not name anyone else who had been at the meeting, and testified falsely that he had not been arrested.

Scipio Jones had been born enslaved and was the leading Black lawyer in Arkansas. During the retrials in Helena he slept at a different Black family's house every night because it was not safe to be found twice in the same bed.

The NAACP hired George Murphy, seventy-nine years old and a former Confederate officer, for three thousand dollars and expenses. Black families in Little Rock raised money for Scipio Jones themselves, in a state where their own settlements had never been itemized.

The men in the cells were not waiting quietly. On the thirtieth of December, 1919, one of the twelve sat down and wrote a letter to Ida B. Wells-Barnett in Chicago.

She took the train to Little Rock. She went to the address in the letter and talked with the wives first, then got herself into the penitentiary by claiming to be a visiting cousin, and spent the day with the men.

What she wrote afterward put the case in one line. Their crime, she said, was to organize for the market price of their cotton, to buy land, and "to employ a lawyer to get settlements of their accounts."

She also did the arithmetic nobody in Phillips County had done. Between the cotton and the corn taken off Black families during and after the killing, she reckoned the white men of that county had cleared about a million dollars in a year.

That million dollars had specific rooms in it. By Wells-Barnett's account, the furniture and clothes belonging to Frank Moore and his wife ended up with a white landowner named Bill Archdale and his family.

The papers that finally moved something were the Smiddy and T. K. Jones affidavits. Attached to a federal petition, two white men's sworn admissions of torture did what no Black man's testimony had been permitted to do.

In February 1923 the Supreme Court of the United States ruled in Moore v. Dempsey that a trial run under mob pressure, uncorrected by the state's own appeals courts, is not due process. It called the Helena proceeding a mask.

That decision changed American law. It did not open a single cell door.

The Court sent the case back down to the district court for a hearing, and that was all it did.

Six of the men, the Ware defendants, were freed in June 1923 by the Arkansas Supreme Court, on the ground that two terms of court had passed without the state bringing them to trial. The state simply never tried them again.

The other six, the Moore defendants, walked out in January 1925 on indefinite furloughs signed by Governor Thomas McRae in the last days of his term. The record disagrees on whether that was the thirteenth or the fourteenth.

They had pleaded guilty to second-degree murder to get there.

No furlough is a pardon. Not one of the twelve was ever cleared.

No white person was charged with anything.

The county's books closed like this. Five white men died, and those deaths were reported, investigated, and attached to names.

Four of them run all the way through the record: W. A. Adkins, Clinton Lee, James Tappan and O. R. Lilly.

Colonel Jenks also entered the death of one of his own soldiers in his report.

For the Black dead there is no such page. Jenks wrote that his troops killed two.

Military intelligence put the total at no more than twenty.

Walter White was told in Helena that more than a hundred had been killed. James Weldon Johnson estimated as many as four hundred.

A white Arkansas Gazette employee named Sharpe Dunaway published a book in 1925 claiming eight hundred and fifty-six, mostly killed by the soldiers, and offered almost no documentation for the number. Historians who have spent careers in the records generally land somewhere between one and two hundred, and say plainly that the figure is unknown.

The figure is unknown because nobody counted. There was no coroner's roll for them, no inquest, no list, no attempt.

The number you will see most often, two hundred and thirty-seven, comes from a 2015 investigation by the Equal Justice Initiative and now appears almost everywhere. It is an estimate and not a body count, and nobody has ever produced a list of two hundred and thirty-seven names.

Historians have recovered the names of only a small fraction of the people killed in Phillips County that week.

That is why the memorial dedicated in Helena in September 2019 is a cenotaph with no names on it. It carries one line, for those known and unknown, because there is no roll to carve.

More than a century later, the itemized statement is still owed. Not by the planters, who are gone, but by the record itself, which has never been made to show its work.

The record can still be added to. Census sheets, church rolls, deeds, pension files, family Bibles and the memories of the oldest person in your family are exactly the materials the professors and their students are using right now to pull names back out of that week, one at a time.

The men at Hoop Spur wanted their labor written down and totaled honestly. Phillips County called that an uprising and answered it with a killing nobody has ever counted, and the request has still not been granted.

Find one name. Write it down somewhere it can be read.

That is the settlement.

text:
This song is drawn from a longer essay on wheat, tares, and the few who come unto Him. Read it here: https://t.co/GD4JioPf9R

Lyrics

1. The Contention
Priest against priest, and creed against creed,
They war for the name of the Lord.
Each steeple insists it is all that He needs,
And locks every other door.
They judge and they sever, they boast and they bind,
And call the division a light.
But seekers walk past when the fruit that they find
Is wrath dressed in garments of white.

2. The Field
He sowed the good seed, and an enemy came
And scattered the tares in the row.
The servants cried, “Pull them,” but He spoke their name
And told them to let the field grow.
The wheat bows its head with the weight of the grain;
The tare stands up proud in the sun.
They grow side by side till the harvest again,
And only the Keeper knows one.

3. Not Made with Hands
The Most High dwells not in the work of our hands,
Nor sleeps in a temple of stone.
He is not contained by a deed or a brand,
Nor kept by a key of our own.
A form without power, a lip without heart,
A doctrine of men on the tongue:
He passes them by when the worship they start
Is all they have practiced and sung.

4. The Heart
Whosoever repenteth and cometh to Me,
The same is My Church, saith the Lord.
Who addeth a gate, or who taketh a key,
Is not of the word He restored.
The kingdom is in you, not out on the hill,
Not bought with a name on a roll.
It lives where the humble bow low to His will
And offer the whole of the soul.

5. Two or Three
Where two or three gather and speak in His name,
He stands in the midst of the room.
No spire is required, no franchise, no fame,
No map and no seal and no tomb.
They fast and they pray, they forgive and they keep,
They watch over wounds and they mend.
The Church is the disciples who wake and who weep
And come unto Him to the end.

6. The Harvest
Not all who cry “Lord” on the day of the door
Will hear their name spoken in peace.
For wonders and titles He does not keep score;
He knows every heart that is His.
So lay down the banner you carried in strife,
And ask if you know Him today.
His Church is not walls. It is love, and a life,
Wherever the wheat bends to pray.

Chorus
Where the disciples are, there is His Church,
Not timber, not marble, not throne.
In the bowed heart He searches, the few on the earth,
He walks, and He calls them His own.
Where two or three gather and open the door,
The building is nowhere in sight.
The Church is the people who come and adore,
And Christ in the midst is the light.

text:
He was 21 years old, and the Union offered him a simple bargain. Give us the name of the man who gave you these papers, and we will spare your life. Sam Davis refused, choosing the gallows over betraying a friend. He has been remembered ever since as the Boy Hero of the Confederacy.

Davis was a young Tennessean who served as a scout in an elite unit called Coleman's Scouts, gathering intelligence on Union forces in occupied Middle Tennessee. In November 1863, he was captured near Pulaski, Tennessee. On him, hidden in his boots and saddle, the Federals found detailed information about Union troop strength, fortifications, and movements, so accurate and so sensitive that it could only have come from a source high within Union lines. There was a spy, a well-placed informer feeding secrets to the Confederates, and the Union desperately wanted to know who it was.

Davis was tried as a spy and sentenced to hang. But his captors, including the Union general Grenville Dodge, did not really want to execute a brave young man. What they wanted was the name of his informant. So they made him an offer: tell us who gave you this intelligence, and you will go free. Refuse, and you will hang.

For Sam Davis it was no choice at all. To buy his own life, he would have to condemn another man, a man who had trusted him. He would not do it. By the accounts that came down from the witnesses, he said that if he had a thousand lives, he would give them all before he would betray the trust of a friend or the confidence of his informer.

They hanged him on November 27, 1863, at Pulaski. He is said to have met his death with remarkable calm and dignity, telling the officers he did not fear to die. In a last letter to his mother, one of the better-documented pieces of his story, he wrote simply, Mother, I do not fear to die. And he carried the secret of the informer's identity to his grave. To this day, by most accounts, the name he died to protect was never revealed.

As with many such stories, parts of the Sam Davis legend have been embroidered over the years, and some of the famous quotes attributed to him are of doubtful origin. But the core of it, the offer, the refusal, and the execution, is well attested by witnesses. Southerners came to revere him much as the North revered Nathan Hale of the Revolution, the young patriot who gave his life rather than break faith. Whatever one thinks of the cause he served, Sam Davis faced a terrible test that most of us will never know, your own life against your honor and the safety of a friend, and he chose as he did without flinching. That is why, more than a century and a half later, he is remembered.

text:
$TEL KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM TE CONNECTIVITY’S Q4 2026 EARNINGS CALL

TE Connectivity’s results support continued strength in AI interconnects, electrical infrastructure and selected industrial investment, but not a uniform recovery in global manufacturing or automotive production. The most actionable information is the combination of approximately 70% annual DDN order growth, more than $1 billion of expected incremental DDN revenue in fiscal 2027, power connectivity growing faster than DDN overall, and Industrial orders increasing 47%. These disclosures strengthen the earnings-duration argument for suppliers positioned across multiple architectures, particularly copper, optics and power. The strongest negative implication is for automotive businesses dependent on rising vehicle production: TE expects production to decline slightly across regions, with its own growth coming primarily from content gains. Several relevant peers have already reported, so the distinction between fresh predictive information and corroboration is essential. Countries below denote corporate domicile; impact assessments refer to operating fundamentals, not predicted share-price moves.

AI INTERCONNECTS: OPTICAL ADOPTION DOES NOT INVALIDATE THE COPPER GROWTH THESIS (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: Amphenol (APH: United States). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high strategic importance for its communications businesses and moderate-to-high importance for consolidated earnings durability; the incremental near-term earnings revision attributable to TE’s call alone is unquantified.

The critical evidence is management’s statement that, even after considering greater optical adoption, the copper addressable market is expected to grow “over 100%” over the relevant multiyear horizon. TE also expects more than $1 billion of incremental DDN revenue in fiscal 2027, predominantly from AI applications, and described continuing demand for backplanes, internal connections, cable assemblies and front-end interfaces. Approximately 30% of DDN revenue is power connectivity, which management expects to grow faster than DDN overall.

The transmission mechanism to Amphenol is broader than an increase in AI server shipments. Higher bandwidth, greater rack density and more demanding power delivery increase the engineering value of interconnects. Optical links can replace selected copper signal paths while leaving substantial electrical connectivity within systems and at optical-module interfaces. Amphenol participates across electrical, optical and power interconnects, making its opportunity less dependent on any single transmission medium than a copper-only characterization suggests.

The NVIDIA (NVDA: United States) and Cisco Systems (CSCO: United States) USFP initiative provides a particularly concrete example. Their announcement names both TE and Amphenol in the ecosystem for cages, connectors and modules. The optical architecture retains an advanced electrical connector. This is direct evidence that next-generation optical products can create opportunities for established electrical-interconnect suppliers rather than simply displacing them.

The important competitive qualification is that this is a multisource ecosystem, not an exclusive Amphenol award. TE’s ambition to achieve optical market share comparable with its copper position also identifies a capable competitor. The positive conclusion concerns the size and durability of the addressable market, not an assumption that Amphenol captures TE’s programs or automatically gains share.

Near-term catalyst: Amphenol’s October 28 conference call, scheduled for 1:00 p.m. Eastern, can clarify customer ramps, power content and architecture exposure. Its results were already released before this report’s information cutoff, showing 37% organic growth and a 1.19 book-to-bill ratio. TE therefore corroborates those results rather than predicting them. The incremental value lies in supporting 2027 demand duration and challenging premature copper-obsolescence assumptions.

Longer-duration implication: the relevant investment distinction is between suppliers able to participate across changing architectures and suppliers exposed to a narrow interconnect function. TE’s disclosure supports the former, while providing no basis for extrapolating 70% bookings growth directly into peer revenue growth.

OPTICAL CABLES: EXISTING SUPPLY AGREEMENTS OFFER A MORE TANGIBLE CHANNEL THAN SPECULATIVE CPO SHARE ASSUMPTIONS (READ-THROUGH 2)

Affected company: Prysmian (PRY: Italy). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high for the longer-term development of Digital Solutions, moderate for consolidated earnings, and limited as a standalone signal for immediate quarterly earnings.

TE stated that future architectures will require both copper and fiber and identified chip-to-fiber connectivity, fiber-to-fiber connectivity and high-density routing as expanding opportunities. Curtin described RAM Photonics as being “in the middle of engineering validation with certain customers.” The distinction is important: optical demand is expanding, but not every participant is at the same stage of commercialization.

Prysmian already has an identified commercial channel into this market. Its July 20 announcement disclosed an agreement with privately held Molex for optical cables deployed inside data centers, worth up to €5.5 billion over up to 10 years and supported by a €550 million upfront payment. This is an optical-cable agreement, not a copper-cable agreement. TE’s comments provide independent support for the architectural demand underlying that investment.

The transmission mechanism is increased demand for qualified fiber and optical cable as data centers expand optical connectivity and increase connection density. Prysmian manufactures the fiber and cable; Molex supplies connectivity solutions to infrastructure customers. This is distinct from TE’s near-chip attachment technology. The businesses can participate in the same deployment without supplying interchangeable products.

The agreement also differentiates Prysmian from companies whose optical thesis rests primarily on prospective design wins. However, “up to” contract value is not guaranteed recognized revenue, the upfront payment is not recurring earnings, and the headline value should not be divided mechanically into equal annual revenue. Prysmian’s broader commercialization plan includes agreements and initiatives extending through 2035, with significant capacity investment required before the full opportunity is realized.

Near-term catalyst: Prysmian’s October 29 results provide an immediate test of Digital Solutions growth, capacity deployment and the economics of its expanding data-center exposure. Its second-quarter Digital Solutions organic growth was already 18%, so TE’s call strengthens an existing trend rather than establishing a new recovery.

Longer-duration implication: the call supports investment in optical manufacturing capacity without requiring a forecast that co-packaged optics wins every architectural decision. The principal risks are qualification, ramp timing, manufacturing utilization and realized economics. Greater data traffic does not automatically translate into proportionate fiber volume or profit because architectures can also increase bandwidth per connection.

DATA-CENTER POWER AND COOLING: CONTENT GROWTH IS BECOMING MORE ARCHITECTURE-RESILIENT (READ-THROUGH 3)

Affected companies: Vertiv (VRT: United States) and Eaton (ETN: Ireland). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high for Vertiv’s core business and moderate-to-high for Eaton’s electrical businesses, with a smaller consolidated effect because Eaton has a broader portfolio.

The most important disclosure is not simply that AI spending remains strong. TE stated that approximately 30% of DDN revenue is power connectivity and that this category should grow faster than DDN overall in fiscal 2027. Management linked the opportunity to 800-volt DC, sidecar configurations and liquid cooling. Curtin emphasized that changes between copper and optical data transmission do not eliminate the requirement for power connectivity.

The transmission mechanism to Vertiv is increased demand for integrated power conversion, distribution, thermal management and associated services as rack power density rises. Higher-density systems require coordinated electrical and thermal engineering rather than isolated component replacement. Eaton participates through electrical distribution, protection and power-management systems. NVIDIA has independently identified both companies as participants in its 800-volt data-center power ecosystem, making the exposure more specific than a general association with AI spending.

The non-consensus nuance is that higher voltage does not mean proportionately more copper or more identical legacy equipment. At constant power, higher voltage reduces current. The economic opportunity comes from changing conversion architectures, reliability requirements, protection, thermal management and integration complexity. Suppliers able to redesign the system can benefit even when individual legacy components become less important.

TE’s backlog cadence supports a multiquarter deployment opportunity, but it does not establish that every associated power-system shipment occurs in the same quarter as TE’s connectors. Site electrical infrastructure, cooling equipment, rack assembly and final interconnect shipments occupy different stages of the project. TE’s second-half fiscal 2027 DDN step-up is therefore evidence of deployment visibility, not a precise shipment schedule for Vertiv or Eaton.

Near-term catalysts differ materially. Vertiv had already released October 28 results showing 55% organic revenue growth and organic orders increasing more than 100%. TE is corroborating an already strong report, not generating a fresh prediction of that quarter. Eaton’s November 3 earnings release remains a forward catalyst, particularly for electrical orders, backlog conversion and the balance between capacity investment and margins.

Longer-duration implication: power and cooling exposure is relatively insulated from the copper-versus-fiber debate, but remains dependent on infrastructure deployment and customer spending. A portfolio holding networking, interconnect and electrical-infrastructure suppliers should not treat these exposures as independent diversification merely because the products differ.

GRID INFRASTRUCTURE: PHYSICAL NETWORK INVESTMENT IS STRONGER THAN A BLANKET “UTILITY TECHNOLOGY” THESIS (READ-THROUGH 4)

Affected company: Hubbell (HUBB: United States). Direction: positive. Magnitude: moderate-to-high for its grid-infrastructure and data-center electrical businesses; moderate for the consolidated company.

TE’s Energy business grew approximately 12% organically in the quarter and 18% for fiscal 2026. Management attributed growth to grid hardening, modernization of aging infrastructure, increased power requirements and data-center construction. Every Industrial business generated more than 20% order growth, and management expects Energy to sustain double-digit growth in fiscal 2027.

The transmission mechanism to Hubbell is demand for physical equipment used in transmission, substations, distribution and electrical connections. Grid reinforcement increases the need for components that carry, connect, protect and manage electricity. The growth opportunity extends beyond equipment located inside a data center because additional computing capacity also requires upstream network investment.

Hubbell’s October 27 results provide a useful check on the specificity of this interpretation. Utility Solutions organic growth was approximately 5%, Grid Infrastructure sales increased approximately 13%, and Grid Automation sales declined approximately 4%. Electrical Solutions organic growth was 22%, led by strong data-center demand. These differences show why TE’s Energy performance should not be transferred indiscriminately across every utility-related business.

The strongest implication is therefore for physical grid infrastructure and electrical connections, not a universal acceleration in metering, communications or utility software. TE and Hubbell have different product mixes, so TE’s 12% Energy growth does not establish that Hubbell’s entire Utility Solutions segment should grow at the same rate.

Near-term implication: because Hubbell has already reported, TE’s call is confirmation rather than a new earnings catalyst for the completed quarter. The next meaningful information will be year-end backlog conversion and the 2027 growth outlook. TE’s forward order commentary modestly reduces the risk that recent physical-infrastructure growth was solely a temporary shipment catch-up.

Longer-duration implication: grid modernization provides a source of demand beyond a particular AI processor or rack architecture. However, data-center-driven grid investment remains correlated with the broader infrastructure cycle. It improves product diversification more than it eliminates common spending risk.

AUTOMOTIVE SUPPLIERS: CONTENT OUTPERFORMANCE SHOULD NOT BE MISTAKEN FOR A VEHICLE-PRODUCTION RECOVERY (READ-THROUGH 5)

Affected companies: Lear (LEA: United States) and Magna International (MGA: Canada). Direction: negative for volume-driven earnings upside and the 2027 production-recovery thesis. Magnitude: moderate fundamental importance, but limited immediate estimate impact because both companies already operate with cautious production assumptions.

TE delivered approximately 6% automotive organic growth despite declining vehicle production. Management expects production to be slightly lower again in fiscal 2027 and stated that weakness is expected across regions rather than being confined to a single market. Its own expected outperformance of 4 to 6 percentage points is driven by connectivity, electrification and electronification.

The negative transmission mechanism is lower unit throughput at suppliers with substantial exposure to vehicle assembly volumes. Fewer vehicles reduce shipments of seating, body structures and other production-linked systems, while lower utilization limits fixed-cost absorption. TE’s success in increasing content per vehicle does not create equivalent demand for every component installed in the same vehicle.

Lear is particularly relevant because seating remains a major earnings exposure. Its electrical-systems business provides content opportunities, but does not make the entire company equivalent to TE’s connector portfolio. Magna also has electronics and electrification exposure, but its broader production-linked businesses remain sensitive to customer platform volumes and geographic mix.

The geographic signal is important. TE’s strongest automotive content performance was in Asia, with improving European EV contribution and continued North American challenges. Asian content gains do not prove stronger Asian vehicle production. Similarly, recovering European EV content can benefit selected suppliers while conventional platforms or other regions remain weak.

This is not evidence of a new, immediate earnings shortfall at Lear or Magna. Lear’s latest annual outlook already assumed an approximately 2% decline in sales-weighted vehicle production, and it had raised profit and cash-flow expectations despite that backdrop. Magna’s second-quarter results also demonstrated that productivity, program launches and commercial execution can offset weak production. The negative read-through is reduced support for a volume-led upside case, not proof that their existing guidance must fall.

Near-term catalyst: Lear’s October 30 results can test whether production schedules, customer mix and cost recovery remain consistent with its outlook. The same operating questions apply to Magna’s upcoming update. The key distinction is whether earnings improvement comes from execution and content or from an assumed market recovery.

Longer-duration implication: relative preference should remain with businesses capable of demonstrable content growth rather than those requiring higher global vehicle production to recover margins. TE’s call argues against treating the automotive supply chain as a single cyclical recovery trade.

AUTOMOTIVE SEMICONDUCTORS: ZONAL ARCHITECTURES SUPPORT SELECTIVE CONTENT GROWTH, NOT A BROAD CHIP-CYCLE INFERENCE (READ-THROUGH 6)

Affected company: NXP Semiconductors (NXPI: Netherlands). Direction: positive. Magnitude: moderate for the automotive earnings trajectory and potentially material over several years; small incremental near-term information value because NXP has already disclosed its own growth drivers.

TE identified vehicle data connectivity, 48-volt systems and zonal architectures as continuing content drivers. Management stated that vehicle data connectivity remained strong throughout fiscal 2026 and that the broader electronification trend was steady. These gains supported growth even when vehicle production declined.

The transmission mechanism to NXP is higher demand for the processing, networking, interface and control functions required by software-defined vehicles. Zonal architectures consolidate functions into fewer, more capable controllers and require reliable communication between sensors, actuators and central compute. The opportunity is not simply a higher semiconductor count; it is increased value captured by the suppliers selected for the new architecture.

NXP has an identified customer channel rather than merely thematic exposure. Volkswagen’s announced adoption of NXP’s S32K5 family for zonal controllers provides a direct example of the transition TE describes. The architecture is being developed by the Volkswagen-Rivian technology joint venture. TE’s commentary independently supports the underlying content trend, but does not establish that TE and NXP participate in every identical vehicle program.

The competitive qualification is that consolidation can remove some legacy chips and electronic control units. NXP benefits to the extent it wins the higher-value zonal functions, not because every existing automotive semiconductor category necessarily expands. This is a selective positive read-through for its architecture position, not a basis for raising estimates across all automotive analog, memory or power-semiconductor suppliers.

Near-term implication: NXP released its third-quarter results on October 27, identifying company-specific automotive growth drivers and opportunities in software-defined vehicles. TE’s call is corroboration of that thesis, not a prediction of the already reported quarter. The next meaningful catalysts are customer production milestones and evidence that awarded platforms translate into shipments during 2027 and subsequent ramps.

Longer-duration implication: semiconductor content can grow despite flat or declining vehicle production, but the benefits accrue unevenly. This creates a useful cross-portfolio distinction between selected automotive computing suppliers and businesses whose growth remains primarily tied to vehicle units.

FACTORY AUTOMATION: A REAL DEMAND SIGNAL, WITH LESS SUPPORT FOR COST-RELIEF-DRIVEN MARGIN UPSIDE (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected company: Rockwell Automation (ROK: United States). Direction: positive for revenue and order durability, with a modest negative qualification for assumptions of automatic margin relief. Magnitude: moderate at the consolidated level.

TE’s Automation and Connected Living business grew 18% organically, with growth across every region. Management identified both cyclical improvement and content outperformance in factory automation and battery energy storage. It also expects double-digit growth in this business in fiscal 2027.

The transmission mechanism to Rockwell is increased investment in connected machinery, control systems, drives, industrial communications and automation equipment. Greater connectivity at the machine level makes the call relevant to Rockwell’s Intelligent Devices and Software & Control businesses. The geographic breadth reduces the likelihood that TE’s result reflects only a narrow regional shipment surge.

The evidence does not support applying TE’s 18% growth rate directly to Rockwell. TE’s business includes connected-living and storage applications that do not map precisely onto Rockwell’s portfolio, and increased connector content can occur without an equivalent increase in factory-equipment units. Nevertheless, the direction is reinforced by Rockwell’s latest reported quarter, which showed 10% organic growth in Intelligent Devices and 18% in Software & Control.

The margin qualification is material. TE’s CFO stated, “There is also no relief coming in our expectations on the inflationary front,” identifying resins, metals and freight. Rockwell’s latest release also identified negative price-cost effects, even as volume and mix supported margin expansion. The combined evidence favors a volume-and-execution earnings thesis rather than an assumption that input-cost normalization will provide an additional windfall.

Near-term catalyst: Rockwell’s November 5 results and initial fiscal 2027 guidance are an actionable test. TE’s forward commentary supports confidence in continued industrial demand, but the decisive issues are Rockwell’s own orders, customer spending plans and price-cost outlook.

Longer-duration implication: more connected equipment and greater control complexity can increase automation spending per installation. That is a credible structural driver. TE’s humanoid-robot discussion is much less useful for near-term Rockwell estimates because robot production volumes, platform participation and realized content remain uncertain.

AEROSPACE AND DEFENSE: LONGER-CYCLE COMPONENT DEMAND SUPPORTS EARNINGS VISIBILITY, NOT SPECIFIC AIRCRAFT DELIVERY FORECASTS (READ-THROUGH 8)

Affected companies: Amphenol (APH: United States) and Eaton (ETN: Ireland). Direction: positive. Magnitude: moderate for the relevant aerospace and defense businesses, modest for consolidated earnings relative to their larger electrical and communications opportunities.

TE’s aerospace, defense and marine business grew approximately 16% organically. Management expects continued double-digit growth and identified aerospace and defense, together with DDN, as accounting for approximately 60% of the increase in company backlog. That percentage applies to the combined contribution of those businesses to backlog growth, not to aerospace alone or to total backlog.

The transmission mechanism to Amphenol is demand for harsh-environment interconnects, sensors and related components used in aircraft and defense electronics. Eaton participates through aircraft power-management and other aerospace systems. More demanding electrical and data requirements can increase supplier content even when platform-unit growth is slower.

The longer lead times and qualification requirements of aerospace programs make this a different demand signal from short-cycle industrial replenishment. TE’s backlog commentary supports production visibility and continued demand for qualified components. It does not, however, identify which airframe programs, defense platforms or customers account for the increase.

Eaton’s latest reported quarter already showed aerospace orders increasing 17% on its rolling measure and backlog rising 28%. TE’s result therefore reinforces an existing industry signal. For Amphenol, the benefit is additional support for non-AI growth within a diversified interconnect portfolio, not evidence that aerospace can offset any conceivable datacom slowdown.

Near-term catalyst: Eaton’s November 3 report can establish whether aerospace order momentum and conversion remain intact. Amphenol’s same-day October 28 commentary can clarify the contribution from commercial aerospace and defense. Neither company should receive TE’s growth rate mechanically because product content, customer allocation and recognition timing differ.

Longer-duration implication: qualified aerospace and defense suppliers offer exposure to content growth and longer program cycles alongside AI infrastructure. The evidence is insufficient to infer a specific aircraft delivery increase, engine-production acceleration or defense-budget award. The high-conviction conclusion is stronger component-demand visibility, not an unrestricted positive forecast for every company in the aerospace value chain.

James O’Keefe & Cam Higby filmed their undercover voting video in Minnesota on Aug. 11, edited it, added commentary, and posted it online a few days later. (Video below)

And today they were charged with felonies, unlawful voting and identity theft, though they never voted or signed anything.

Mainstream “news” outlets have long used undercover tactics and misrepresented themselves. Maybe not at polling places, because they’re uninterested in voting fraud or even the potential for it.

But O’Keefe has done this exact style of voting test for years without being charged with anything—including in 2016 when he was offered Eminem’s Michigan ballot after saying he had no ID, then walked out without voting. (That video also below).

Seems like legitimate undercover journalism designed to expose something, but County Attorney for Hennepin County Mary Moriarty is attempting lawfare to shut down independent journalists Democrats don’t like, and to warn others.

O’Keefe and Higby were charged today, not yet arrested. In a few weeks, they’ll turn themselves in.

(O'Keefe was investigated in 2012 for a voting operation but not charged, and in 2010 he pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor after posing as a telephone repairman at then-Sen. Mary Landrieu's office).

IMPORTANT PARENTS: I have broken down Michigan HB 5803. My opponent Emily Dievendorf voted NO. I would have voted YES. Let me know your thoughts. 

Michigan families deserve affordable child care AND safe environments for their children.

HB 5803 raises important questions about private-school preschool licensing and expanding capacity for home-based child-care providers.

As your representative, I would look beyond party lines, examine the facts, and ask: Will this make child care more accessible and affordable while maintaining the safety protections children deserve?

I support reducing unnecessary red tape, demanding measurable results, and supporting responsible expansion so private-school and home-based preschool providers have a fairer opportunity to operate without unnecessary government barriers.

If public schools can offer preschool programs, we should examine how private and home-based providers can operate under reasonable, consistent requirements that protect children without unnecessarily limiting access or choice.

Parents deserve more options and the freedom to make informed decisions about their children’s education and care. Their rights must be respected, safety standards must remain in place, and providers must be accountable.

The goal should be simple: more affordable options, more choices for families, fewer unnecessary government hurdles, and strong protections for our children.

People over party. Common sense over politics. Accountability over blind votes.
